. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Numerical Discourses

Dukanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Book of Twos (Dukanipāta-aṭṭhakathā)

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Kammakāraṇavaggo

1. The Chapter on Punishments

1. Vajjasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Vajja Sutta

1. Dukanipātassa [V 2.0001][M 2.0001][P 2.0088] paṭhame vajjānīti dosā aparādhā. Diṭṭhadhammikanti diṭṭheva dhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve uppannaphalaṃ. Samparāyikanti samparāye anāgate attabhāve uppannaphalaṃ. Āgucārinti pāpakāriṃ aparādhakārakaṃ. Rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārenteti coraṃ gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā rājapurisā karonti, rājāno pana tā kārenti nāma. Taṃ coraṃ evaṃ [V 2.0002] kammakāraṇā kāriyamānaṃ esa passati. Tena vuttaṃ – “passati coraṃ āgucāriṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārente”ti. Addhadaṇḍakehīti muggarehi, pahārasādhanatthaṃ vā catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ dvedhā chetvā gahitadaṇḍakehi. Bilaṅgathālikanti kañjiyaukkhalikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā sīsakaṭāhaṃ uppāṭetvā tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ saṇḍāsena gahetvā tattha pakkhipanti, tena matthaluṅgaṃ pakkuthitvā [M 2.0002] uttarati. Saṅkhamuṇḍikanti saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā uttaroṭṭhaubhatokaṇṇacūḷikagalavāṭakaparicchedena [P 2.0089] cammaṃ chinditvā sabbakese ekato gaṇṭhiṃ katvā daṇḍakena veṭhetvā uppāṭenti, saha kesehi cammaṃ uṭṭhahati. Tato sīsakaṭāhaṃ thūlasakkharāhi ghaṃsitvā dhovantā saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ karonti. Rāhumukhanti rāhumukhakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā saṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antomukhe dīpaṃ jālenti, kaṇṇacūḷikāhi vā paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ nikhādanena khananti, lohitaṃ paggharitvā mukhaṃ pūreti.

1. In the first sutta of the Dukanipāta, vajjāni means faults, offenses. Diṭṭhadhammikaṃ means fruit produced in this very existence, in this present state of being. Samparāyikaṃ means fruit produced in a future existence, in a life to come. Āgucāriṃ means one who commits evil, an offender. 'Kings, having captured him, order various punishments': royal men inflict various punishments on a thief, but it is said that the kings cause them to be done. He sees that thief being punished in such ways. Therefore it is said: 'He sees a thief, an offender, whom the kings have seized and subjected to various punishments.' Addhadaṇḍakehi means with mallets, or with rods obtained by splitting a four-cubit staff in two for the purpose of striking. Bilaṅgathālikaṃ is the punishment of the gruel pot. Those carrying it out, having removed the skullcap, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs and place it therein, causing the brain to boil up and overflow. Saṅkhamuṇḍikaṃ is the punishment of the conch-shell head. Those executing it cut the skin along the boundary of the upper lip, both ear-tips, and the throat, gather all the hair into a single knot, bind it with a rod, and tear it off—the skin comes away with the hair. Then, scrubbing the skullcap with coarse gravel and washing it, they make it the color of a conch shell. Rāhumukhaṃ is the punishment of Rāhu's mouth. Those performing it pry open the mouth with a spike and light a lamp inside; or, starting from the ear-tips, they carve out the mouth with a chisel, and blood flows out and fills the mouth.

Jotimālikanti sakalasarīraṃ telapilotikāya veṭhetvā ālimpenti. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthe telapilotikāya veṭhetvā dīpaṃ viya pajjālenti. Erakavattikanti erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā heṭṭhāgīvato paṭṭhāya cammavaṭṭe kantitvā gopphake ṭhapenti, atha naṃ yottehi bandhitvā kaḍḍhanti. So attano cammavaṭṭe akkamitvā akkamitvā patati. Cīrakavāsikanti cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā tatheva cammavaṭṭe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti, kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapenti, uparimehi heṭṭhimasarīraṃ cīrakanivāsananivatthaṃ viya hoti. Eṇeyyakanti eṇeyyakakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā ubhosu kapparesu ca ubhosu jāṇukesu ca ayavalayāni datvā ayasūlāni koṭṭenti. So catūhi ayasūlehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahati. Atha naṃ parivāretvā aggiṃ karonti. “Eṇeyyako jotipariggaho yathā”ti āgataṭṭhānepi idameva vuttaṃ. Taṃ kālena kālaṃ sūlāni apanetvā catūhi aṭṭhikoṭīhiyeva ṭhapenti. Evarūpā kammakāraṇā nāma natthi.

Jotimālikā is when they wrap the entire body with an oil-soaked rag and set it on fire. Hatthapajjotikā is when they wrap the hands with an oil-soaked rag and make them blaze like a lamp. Erakavattikā is the punishment with strips like eraka-grass. In performing it, they cut strips of skin starting from below the neck down to the ankles. Then, they bind him with thongs and pull him. He falls, repeatedly treading upon his own strips of skin. Cīrakavāsika is the punishment of the bark-cloth garment. In performing it, they likewise cut strips of skin down to the waist; then, starting from the waist, they cut strips down to the ankles. With the upper strips, the lower body becomes as if dressed in a bark-cloth garment. Eṇeyyaka is the punishment like an antelope. In performing it, they attach iron rings to both elbows and both knees and drive in iron stakes. He is fixed to the ground by the four iron stakes. Then, surrounding him, they make a fire. In the passage where it is stated, 'like an antelope surrounded by flames,' it is this very thing that is meant. From time to time, they remove the stakes and make him stand only on the four bone-ends. Such punishments by name do not exist.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti [P 2.0090] ubhatomukhehi baḷisehi paharitvā cammamaṃsanhārūni uppāṭenti. Kahāpaṇikanti sakalasarīraṃ tiṇhāhi vāsīhi koṭito paṭṭhāya kahāpaṇamattaṃ, kahāpaṇamattaṃ pātentā koṭṭenti. Khārāpatacchikanti sarīraṃ tattha tattha āvudhehi paharitvā kocchehi khāraṃ ghaṃsanti, cammamaṃsanhārūni paggharitvā aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāva tiṭṭhati. Palighaparivattikanti ekena passena nipajjāpetvā kaṇṇacchiddena ayasūlaṃ koṭṭetvā pathaviyā ekābaddhaṃ karonti. Atha naṃ pāde [V 2.0003] gahetvā āviñchanti. Palālapīṭhakanti cheko [M 2.0003] kāraṇiko chavicammaṃ acchinditvā nisadapotehi aṭṭhīni bhinditvā kesesu gahetvā ukkhipati, maṃsarāsiyeva hoti. Atha naṃ keseheva pariyonandhitvā gaṇhanti, palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvā puna veṭhenti. Sunakhehipīti katipayāni divasāni āhāraṃ adatvā chātakasunakhehi khādāpenti. Te muhuttena aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikameva karonti. Sūle uttāsenteti sūle āropente.

Baḷisamaṃsika is hooking with fishhooks having points at both ends and tearing out the skin, flesh, and sinews. Kahāpaṇika is chopping the entire body with sharp adzes, starting from the edge, a coin's breadth at a time, causing pieces to fall. Khārāpatacchika is striking the body with weapons here and there, then rubbing it with caustic alkali using bristle brushes, causing the skin, flesh, and sinews to dissolve until only a framework of bones remains. Palighaparivattika is making a person lie on one side, driving an iron stake through the ear-hole, and fixing it to the ground. Then, grasping the feet, they spin him around. Palālapīṭhaka is when a skilled torturer, without cutting the outer and inner skin, shatters the bones with small stones, grabs the person by the hair, and lifts him up, so that he becomes just a heap of flesh. Then, having wrapped him up entirely with his own hair, they take him, making him like a bundle of straw, and wrap him again. Sunakhehipi is not giving food for several days and then having the person eaten by hungry dogs. In a moment, they reduce him to a mere skeleton. Sūle uttāsente means impaling on a stake.

Na paresaṃ pābhataṃ vilumpanto caratīti paresaṃ santakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ parammukhaṃ ābhataṃ antamaso antaravīthiyaṃ patitaṃ sahassabhaṇḍikampi disvā “iminā jīvissāmī”ti vilumpanto na vicarati, ko iminā atthoti piṭṭhipādena vā pavaṭṭetvā gacchati.

‘He does not go about plundering what is brought by others’ means: Upon seeing goods belonging to others—brought in one's absence, or at the very least, a bundle of goods worth a thousand fallen in the middle of the road—he does not go about plundering them with the thought, ‘With this I will live.’ Rather, thinking, ‘What use is this?’ he rolls it away with the back of his foot and goes on his way.

Pāpakoti [P 2.0091] lāmako. Dukkhoti aniṭṭho. Kiñca tanti kiṃ nāma taṃ kāraṇaṃ bhaveyya. Yāhanti yena ahaṃ. Kāyaduccaritanti pāṇātipātādi tividhaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Kāyasucaritanti tassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tividhaṃ kusalakammaṃ. Vacīduccaritanti musāvādādi catubbidhaṃ akusalaṃ vacīkammaṃ. Vacīsucaritanti tassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ catubbidhaṃ kusalakammaṃ. Manoduccaritanti abhijjhādi tividhaṃ akusalakammaṃ. Manosucaritanti tassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tividhaṃ kusalakammaṃ. Suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatīti ettha duvidhā suddhi – pariyāyato ca nippariyāyato ca. Saraṇagamanena hi pariyāyena suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharati nāma. Tathā pañcahi sīlehi, dasahi sīlehi – catupārisuddhisīlena, paṭhamajjhānena…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanena, sotāpattimaggena, sotāpattiphalena…pe… arahattamaggena pariyāyena suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharati nāma. Arahattaphale patiṭṭhito pana khīṇāsavo chinnamūlake pañcakkhandhe nhāpentopi khādāpentopi bhuñjāpentopi nisīdāpentopi nipajjāpentopi nippariyāyeneva suddhaṃ nimmalaṃ attānaṃ pariharati paṭijaggatīti veditabbo.

Pāpako means base (lāmako). Dukkho means undesirable (aniṭṭho). 'Kiñca taṃ' means: 'What indeed might that action be?' 'Yāhaṃ' means: 'by which reason, I.' Kāyaduccaritaṃ (bodily misconduct) means the threefold unwholesome bodily action, such as killing living beings. Kāyasucaritaṃ (bodily good conduct) means its opposite, the threefold wholesome bodily action. Vacīduccaritaṃ (verbal misconduct) means the fourfold unwholesome verbal action, such as false speech. Vacīsucaritaṃ (verbal good conduct) means its opposite, the fourfold wholesome verbal action. Manoduccaritaṃ (mental misconduct) means the threefold unwholesome mental action, such as covetousness. Manosucaritaṃ (mental good conduct) means its opposite, the threefold wholesome mental action. Regarding 'suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharati' (one maintains oneself pure), here purity is twofold: figurative and non-figurative. For by taking refuge, one is said to maintain oneself pure figuratively. Likewise, by the five precepts, the ten precepts, the fourfold purity of virtue, the first jhāna... up to... the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry... up to... the path of arahantship, one is said to maintain oneself pure figuratively. But one established in the fruit of arahantship, an Arahant whose cankers are destroyed, even while attending to the five aggregates whose roots have been cut off—bathing them, causing them to eat hard food, causing them to eat soft food, seating them, or laying them down—maintains and cares for oneself purely and immaculately in a non-figurative sense. Thus it should be understood.

Tasmāti yasmā imāni dve vajjāneva, no na vajjāni, tasmā. Vajjabhīrunoti vajjabhīrukā. Vajjabhayadassāvinoti vajjāni bhayato dassanasīlā. Etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhanti etaṃ icchitabbaṃ, etaṃ avassaṃbhāvīti attho. Yanti nipātamattaṃ, kāraṇavacanaṃ vā yena kāraṇena parimuccissati sabbavajjehi[M 2.0004]. Kena pana kāraṇena parimuccissatīti? Catutthamaggena ceva catutthaphalena ca. Maggena [P 2.0092] hi parimuccati nāma, phalaṃ patto parimutto nāma hotīti. Kiṃ pana [V 2.0004] khīṇāsavassa akusalaṃ na vipaccatīti? Vipaccati, taṃ pana khīṇāsavabhāvato pubbe kataṃ. Tañca kho imasmiṃyeva attabhāve, samparāye panassa kammaphalaṃ nāma natthīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

The word 'therefore' (tasmā) is used because these two are indeed faults, not non-faults; therefore. 'Fearful of faults' (vajjabhīruno) means those who are afraid of faults. 'Seeing danger in faults' (vajjabhayadassāvino) means those whose nature is to see faults as a danger. 'This is to be expected' (etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ) means this [freedom from faults] is to be desired, this will surely come to be—such is the meaning. The word 'yaṃ' is merely a particle, or it is a word indicating a reason, meaning: by which reason one will be freed from all faults. But by what reason will one be freed? By the fourth path and the fourth fruit. For by the path, one is said to be in the process of being freed; having attained the fruit, one is said to be freed. But does unwholesome kamma not ripen for one whose taints are destroyed? It does ripen, but that was done before the state of being one whose taints are destroyed. And that, indeed, is in this very existence; but in a future existence, there is for them no such thing as a karmic result. The First [Sutta].

2. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta

2. Dutiye padhānānīti vīriyāni. Vīriyañhi padahitabbato padhānabhāvakaraṇato vā padhānanti vuccati. Durabhisambhavānīti dussahāni duppūriyāni, dukkarānīti attho. Agāraṃ ajjhāvasatanti agāre vasantānaṃ. Cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānuppadānatthaṃ padhānanti etesaṃ cīvarādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ anuppadānatthāya padhānaṃ nāma durabhisambhavanti dasseti. Caturatanikampi hi pilotikaṃ, pasatataṇḍulamattaṃ vā bhattaṃ, caturatanikaṃ vā paṇṇasālaṃ, telasappinavanītādīsu vā appamattakampi bhesajjaṃ paresaṃ dethāti vattumpi nīharitvā dātumpi dukkaraṃ ubhatobyūḷhasaṅgāmappavesanasadisaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

2. In the second sutta, 'strivings' (padhānāni) means efforts (vīriyāni). Indeed, effort (vīriyaṃ) is called 'striving' (padhānaṃ) because it is to be exerted, or because it is the cause of the state of striving. 'Hard to accomplish' (durabhisambhavāni) means difficult to endure, difficult to fulfill, difficult to do—such is the meaning. 'Living in a household' (agāraṃ ajjhāvasataṃ) means for those living in a house. By the passage beginning 'striving for the sake of providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites,' it shows that the striving for the sake of providing these four requisites, beginning with robes, is hard to accomplish. Indeed, even to say to others, 'Give a worn cloth of four cubits, or food amounting to a handful of rice, or a leaf-hut of four cubits, or even a small amount of medicine from among oil, ghee, butter, and so on,' and to bring it out and give it, is difficult, like entering a battle arrayed on both sides. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Dānañca yuddhañca samānamāhu,

Appāpi santā bahuke jinanti;

Appampi ce saddahāno dadāti,

Teneva so hoti sukhī paratthā”ti. (jā. 1.8.72; saṃ. ni. 1.33);

“Giving and battle, the wise say, are the same; those who give even a little conquer many unwholesome states. If, having faith, one gives even a little, by that alone one is happy in the next world.”

Agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitānanti gehato nikkhamitvā agārassa gharāvāsassa hitāvahehi kasigorakkhādīhi virahitaṃ anagāriyaṃ pabbajjaṃ upagatānaṃ. Sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggatthāya padhānanti sabbesaṃ khandhūpadhikilesūpadhiabhisaṅkhārūpadhisaṅkhātānaṃ upadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa atthāya vipassanāya ceva maggena ca sahajātavīriyaṃ. Tasmāti [P 2.0093] yasmā imāni dve padhānāni durabhisambhavāni, tasmā. Dutiyaṃ.

‘For those who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness’ means for those persons who, having departed from home, have undertaken the homeless life, which is devoid of such activities as farming and cattle-tending that bring about the welfare of a householder. ‘Striving for the sake of relinquishing all substrates of existence’ means the effort that arises together with insight and with the path, for the sake of Nibbāna, which is called the relinquishment of all the substrates, namely, those designated as the substrate of aggregates, the substrate of defilements, the substrate of formations, and the substrate of sensual pleasures. ‘Therefore’ means: because these two strivings are difficult to accomplish, therefore. The Second [Sutta].

3. Tapanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Tapanīya Sutta

3. Tatiye [M 2.0005] tapanīyāti idha ceva samparāye ca tapantīti tapanīyā. Tappatīti cittasantāpena [V 2.0005] tappati anusocati kāyaduccaritaṃ katvā nandayakkho viya nandamāṇavo viya nandagoghātako viya devadatto viya dvebhātikā viya ca. Te kira gāvaṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ dve koṭṭhāse akaṃsu. Tato kaniṭṭho jeṭṭhakaṃ āha – “mayhaṃ dārakā bahū, imāni me antāni dehī”ti. Atha naṃ so “sabbaṃ maṃsaṃ dvedhā vibhattaṃ, puna kiṃ maggasī”ti paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Nivattitvā ca naṃ olokento mataṃ disvā “bhāriyaṃ me kammaṃ kata”nti cittaṃ uppādesi. Athassa balavasoko uppajji. So ṭhitaṭṭhānepi nisinnaṭṭhānepi tadeva kammaṃ āvajjeti, cittassādaṃ na labhati. Asitapītakhāyitasāyitampissa sarīre ojaṃ na pharati, aṭṭhicammamattameva ahosi. Atha naṃ eko thero disvā – “upāsaka, tvaṃ pahūtaannapāno, aṭṭhicammamattameva te avasiṭṭhaṃ, atthi nu kho te kiñci tapanīyakamma”nti? So “āma, bhante”ti sabbaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ thero “bhāriyaṃ te upāsaka kammaṃ kataṃ, anaparādhaṭṭhāne aparaddha”nti āha. So teneva kammena kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatto. Vacīduccaritena suppabuddhasakkakokālikaciñcamāṇavikādayo viya tappati. Sesamettha catutthe ca uttānatthameva. Tatiyaṃ.

3. In the third sutta, `tapanīyā` (tormenting things) are so called because they cause torment (`tapanti`) both here in this present life and in the life to come. `Tappati` means one is tormented by mental anguish, one grieves. This is like the yakkha Nanda, the young man Nanda, the cattle-killer Nanda, Devadatta, and the two brothers, after having committed bodily misconduct. It is said that those two brothers killed a cow and divided the meat into two portions. Then the younger brother said to the elder, 'I have many children; give me these entrails.' But the elder, saying, 'All the meat has been divided in two; why do you ask for more?' struck him and brought about his death. Turning back and seeing him dead, he thought, 'I have done a grave deed.' Then intense sorrow arose in him. Whether standing or sitting, he kept reflecting on that very deed and found no peace of mind. The food and drink he consumed did not nourish his body; he became mere skin and bones. Then a certain elder, seeing him, said, 'Lay follower, you have much food and drink, yet only skin and bones remain of you. Have you, I wonder, done some tormenting deed?' He replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' and related the whole matter. Then the elder said to him, 'Lay follower, you have done a grave deed; you have transgressed against one who was without offense.' Because of that very deed, he died and was reborn in hell. One is tormented by verbal misconduct like Suppabuddha the Sakyan, Kokālika, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others. The rest here and in the fourth sutta is clear in meaning. The Third [Sutta].

5. Upaññātasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Upaññāta Sutta

5. Pañcame dvinnāhanti dvinnaṃ ahaṃ. Upaññāsinti upagantvā guṇaṃ aññāsiṃ, jāniṃ paṭivijjhinti attho. Idāni te dhamme dassento yā ca asantuṭṭhitātiādimāha. Imañhi [P 2.0094] dhammadvayaṃ nissāya satthā sabbaññutaṃ patto, tasmā tassānubhāvaṃ dassento evamāha. Tattha asantuṭṭhitā kusalesu dhammesūti iminā imaṃ dīpeti – “ahaṃ jhānamattakena vā obhāsanimittamattakena vā asantuṭṭho hutvā arahattamaggameva uppādesiṃ. Yāva so na uppajji, na tāvāhaṃ santuṭṭho ahosiṃ. Padhānasmiṃ ca anukkaṇṭhito hutvā anosakkanāya ṭhatvāyeva padhānakiriyaṃ akāsi”nti imamatthaṃ dassento yā ca appaṭivānitātiādimāha. Tattha appaṭivānitāti appaṭikkamanā anosakkanā. Appaṭivānī sudāhaṃ[M 2.0006], bhikkhave, padahāmīti ettha sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, anosakkanāyaṃ ṭhito bodhisattakāle sabbaññutaṃ patthento padhānamakāsinti ayamettha attho.

5. In the fifth, `dvinnāhaṃ` is `dvinnaṃ ahaṃ`. The phrase `upaññāsiṃ` means: 'Having approached, I knew the quality; I knew; I penetrated'; this is the meaning. Now, to show those qualities, he says, 'And the lack of contentment,' etc. Indeed, by relying on this pair of qualities, the Teacher attained omniscience; therefore, to show their power, he speaks thus. Herein, by 'discontent with wholesome qualities,' he explains this: 'I, not being content merely with jhāna or with the sign of light, caused only the path to Arahantship to arise. Until that arose, I was not content. And in striving, not being wearied, having stood firm in non-slackening, I performed the act of striving.' To show this meaning, he says, 'And the unremitting,' etc. Herein, `appaṭivānitā` means not retreating, not slackening. In 'I, bhikkhus, strive unremittingly,' the word `sudaṃ` is merely a particle. The meaning here is: 'I, bhikkhus, stood without slackening, aspiring for omniscience during the time of the bodhisatta, and made the exertion.'

Idāni yathā tena taṃ padhānaṃ kataṃ, taṃ dassento kāmaṃ taco cātiādimāha. Tattha pattabbanti [V 2.0006] iminā pattabbaṃ guṇajātaṃ dasseti. Purisathāmenātiādinā purisassa ñāṇathāmo ñāṇavīriyaṃ ñāṇaparakkamo ca kathito. Saṇṭhānanti ṭhapanā appavattanā osakkanā, paṭippassaddhīti attho. Ettāvatā tena caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyādhiṭṭhānaṃ nāma kathitaṃ. Ettha hi kāmaṃ taco cāti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, nhāru cāti ekaṃ, aṭṭhi cāti ekaṃ, maṃsalohitanti ekaṃ, imāni cattāri aṅgāni. Purisathāmenātiādīni adhimattavīriyādhivacanāni. Iti purimehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatena hutvā evaṃ adhiṭṭhitaṃ vīriyaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyādhiṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā [P 2.0095] tena bodhipallaṅke attano āgamanīyapaṭipadā kathitā.

Now, wishing to show in what manner that striving was undertaken by Him, He spoke the passage beginning with, 'Let the skin...' Therein, by 'to be attained,' He shows the collection of qualities to be attained. By the passage beginning with 'by a man's strength,' the strength associated with knowledge, the energy associated with knowledge, and the exertion associated with knowledge of a man are spoken of. 'Saṇṭhānaṃ' means setting down, non-proceeding, retreating, and pacification; this is the meaning. By this much, what is called the resolution of energy endowed with four factors has been spoken of by Him. Herein, 'Let the skin...' is one factor; 'and sinews' is one; 'and bones' is one; 'and flesh and blood' is one. These are the four factors. The words beginning with 'by a man's strength' are terms for excessive energy. Thus, it should be understood that energy thus resolved, being endowed with the former four factors, is called 'the resolution of energy endowed with four factors.' By this much, His own preliminary practice at the seat of Awakening, which is the cause for attaining the distinction of jhāna, path, and fruition, has been spoken of by Him.

Idāni tāya paṭipadāya paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ kathetuṃ tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha appamādādhigatāti satiavippavāsasaṅkhātena appamādena adhigatā, na suttappamattena laddhā. Sambodhīti catumaggañāṇañceva sabbaññutaññāṇañca. Na hi sakkā etaṃ suttappamattena adhigantunti. Tenāha – “appamādādhigatā sambodhī”ti. Anuttaro yogakkhemoti na kevalaṃ bodhiyeva, arahattaphalanibbānasaṅkhāto anuttaro yogakkhemopi appamādādhigatova.

Now, in order to speak of the quality attained through that preliminary practice, He spoke the words beginning with, 'For me, O bhikkhus...' Therein, 'attained through diligence' means attained by diligence, which is defined as the non-absence of mindfulness; it is not gained by one who is drowsy and heedless. 'Sambodhi' means the knowledge of the four paths and the knowledge of omniscience. Indeed, it is not possible for this to be attained by one who is drowsy and heedless. Therefore, He said, 'Sambodhi is attained through diligence.' Regarding 'the unexcelled security from yokes': not only Bodhi, but also the unexcelled security from yokes—defined as the fruition of Arahantship and Nibbāna—is indeed attained through diligence.

Idāni attanā paṭiladdhaguṇesu bhikkhusaṅghaṃ samādapento tumhe cepi bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha yassatthāyāti yassa atthāya, yaṃ upasampajja viharitukāmā hutvāti attho. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānabhūtaṃ ariyaphalaṃ. Abhiññā sacchikatvāti abhiññāya uttamapaññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upasampajja viharissathāti paṭilabhitvā pāpuṇitvā viharissatha. Tasmāti yasmā appaṭivānapadhānaṃ nāmetaṃ bahūpakāraṃ uttamatthasādhakaṃ, tasmā. Pañcamaṃ.

Now, wishing to establish the community of monks in the qualities he himself had attained, he spoke the words beginning, 'And you too, monks.' Herein, 'for whose sake' means for the sake of which, having attained which, you desire to dwell—this is the meaning. 'That unsurpassed' means that unsurpassed. 'The culmination of the holy life' means the noble fruit which is the culmination of the holy life of the path. 'Having directly known and realized' means having made it directly present by means of special knowledge, by supreme wisdom. 'You will dwell having attained' means having obtained, having reached, you will dwell. 'Therefore' means because this, called unremitting striving, is of great benefit and accomplishes the highest goal, therefore. Fifth.

6. Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Fetters

6. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0007] saṃyojaniyesu dhammesūti dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ paccayabhūtesu tebhūmakadhammesu. Assādānupassitāti assādato passitā passanabhāvoti attho. Nibbidānupassitāti nibbidāvasena ukkaṇṭhanavasena passanabhāvo. Jātiyāti khandhanibbattito. Jarāyāti khandhaparipākato. Maraṇenāti khandhabhedato. Sokehīti antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇehi sokehi. Paridevehīti [V 2.0007][P 2.0096] tannissitalālappitalakkhaṇehi paridevehi. Dukkhehīti kāyapaṭipīḷanadukkhehi. Domanassehīti manovighātadomanassehi. Upāyāsehīti adhimattāyāsalakkhaṇaupāyāsehi. Dukkhasmāti sakalavaṭṭadukkhato. Pajahatīti maggena pajahati. Pahāyāti ettha pana phalakkhaṇo kathito. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

6. In the sixth, 'in things that are conducive to fetters' means in the phenomena of the three planes that are the condition for the ten fetters. 'Observing gratification' means the state of seeing, seeing in terms of gratification—this is the meaning. 'Observing disenchantment' means the state of seeing by way of disenchantment, by way of revulsion. 'By birth' means from the arising of the aggregates. 'By aging' means from the maturing of the aggregates. 'By death' means from the breaking up of the aggregates. 'By sorrows' means by sorrows that have the characteristic of inner burning. 'By lamentations' means by lamentations that have the characteristic of wailing dependent on that sorrow. 'By pains' means by bodily pains that oppress the body. 'By displeasures' means by displeasures that are mental vexation. 'By despairs' means by despairs that have the characteristic of excessive anguish. 'From suffering' means from all the suffering of the round of existence. 'Abandons' means one abandons by means of the path. As for 'having abandoned,' here the moment of fruition is spoken of. In this discourse, the round and that which is free from the round are spoken of. The sixth.

7. Kaṇhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Dark

7. Sattame kaṇhāti na kāḷavaṇṇatāya kaṇhā, kaṇhatāya pana upanentīti nipphattikāḷatāya kaṇhā. Sarasenāpi vā sabbākusaladhammā kaṇhā eva. Na hi tesaṃ uppattiyā cittaṃ pabhassaraṃ hoti. Ahirikanti ahirikabhāvo. Anottappanti anottāpibhāvo. Sattamaṃ.

7. In the seventh, 'dark' does not mean they are called dark because of having a black color; rather, because they lead to a dark state, they are called dark due to having a completed dark result. Alternatively, by their own nature, all unwholesome states are indeed dark. For by the arising of those states, the mind is not radiant. 'Shamelessness' means the state of being without shame. 'Lack of dread' means the state of being without dread. The seventh.

8. Sukkasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Bright

8. Aṭṭhame sukkāti na vaṇṇasukkatāya sukkā, sukkatāya pana upanentīti nipphattisukkatāya sukkā. Sarasenāpi vā sabbakusaladhammā sukkā eva. Tesaṃ hi uppattiyā cittaṃ pabhassaraṃ hoti. Hirī ca ottappañcāti ettha pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī, bhāyanalakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vitthārato vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

8. In the eighth, the term 'bright' does not mean they are bright due to their color; rather, because they lead to a bright destiny, they are called 'bright' due to their accomplished bright result. Or, by their very nature, all wholesome qualities are indeed bright. For by their arising, the mind becomes radiant. Herein, in the phrase 'moral shame and moral dread,' moral shame has the characteristic of disgust for evil; moral dread has the characteristic of fear of evil. Whatever should be said here in detail has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. The eighth.

9. Cariyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Cariya Sutta

9. Navame lokaṃ pālentīti lokaṃ sandhārenti ṭhapenti rakkhanti. Nayidha paññāyetha mātāti imasmiṃ loke janikā mātā “ayaṃ me mātā”ti [M 2.0008] garucittīkāravasena na paññāyetha. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Sambhedanti saṅkaraṃ mariyādabhedaṃ vā. Yathā ajeḷakātiādīsu ete hi sattā “ayaṃ me mātā”ti vā “mātucchā”ti vā garucittīkāravasena na jānanti. Yaṃ vatthuṃ [P 2.0097] nissāya uppannā, tattheva vippaṭipajjanti. Tasmā upamaṃ āharanto “yathā ajeḷakā”tiādimāha. Navamaṃ.

9. In the ninth, 'protecting the world' means they maintain, establish, and guard the world. 'Here, a mother would not be discerned' means that in this world, the birth-giver as mother is not discerned with the thought, “This is my mother,” in terms of respect and reverence. The same method applies to the remaining cases. 'Mingling' refers to mixture or the breaking of conventions. Just as among goats, sheep, etc., for these beings do not recognize with thoughts of respect and reverence, “This is my mother” or “maternal aunt.” They misconduct themselves right there with regard to the very person from whom they arose. Therefore, adducing the simile, He said, “Just as among goats, sheep,” etc. The ninth.

10. Vassūpanāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Sutta

10. Dasamaṃ [V 2.0008] aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kataraaṭṭhuppattiyaṃ? Manussānaṃ ujjhāyane. Bhagavatā hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsati vassāni vassūpanāyikā appaññattā ahosi. Bhikkhū anibaddhavāsā vassepi utuvassepi yathāsukhaṃ vicariṃsu. Te disvā manussā “kathañhi nāma samaṇā sakyaputtiyā hemantampi gimhampi vassampi cārikaṃ carissanti haritāni tiṇāni sammaddantā ekindriyaṃ jīvaṃ viheṭhentā bahū khuddake pāṇe saṅghātaṃ āpādentā. Ime hi nāma aññatitthiyā durakkhātadhammā vassāvāsaṃ allīyissanti saṃkasāyissanti, ime nāma sakuṇā rukkhaggesu kulāvakāni katvā vassāvāsaṃ allīyissanti saṃkasāyissantī”tiādīni vatvā ujjhāyiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā imaṃ suttaṃ desento paṭhamaṃ tāva “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassaṃ upagantu”nti (mahāva. 184) ettakamevāha. Atha bhikkhūnaṃ “kadā nu kho vassaṃ upagantabba”nti uppannaṃ vitakkaṃ sutvā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vassāne vassaṃ upagantu”nti āha. Atha kho bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “kati nu kho vassūpanāyikā”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā sakalampi idaṃ suttaṃ desento dvemā, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha vassūpanāyikāti vassūpagamanāni. Purimikāti aparajjugatāya āsāḷhiyā upagantabbā purimakattikapuṇṇamipariyosānā paṭhamā temāsī. Pacchimikāti māsagatāya āsāḷhiyā upagantabbā pacchimakattikapariyosānā pacchimā temāsīti. Dasamaṃ.

10. The tenth sutta was spoken due to an occasion arising. What occasion? The criticism of people. Indeed, for twenty years from his first enlightenment, the rains-residence had not been laid down by the Blessed One. The monks, having no fixed residence, wandered as they pleased during the rainy season as well as the other seasons. Seeing them, people criticized, saying: 'How is it that the ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, go on tour during winter, summer, and the rainy season, trampling green grass, harming life with one faculty, and causing the destruction of many small living beings? Indeed, these other sectarians, whose doctrine is badly proclaimed, adhere to the rains-residence and remain settled. Even these birds, having made nests in the treetops, adhere to the rains-residence and remain settled.' Having said these and other things, they criticized. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking this as the occasion for teaching this sutta, first said only this much: 'I allow, monks, to enter upon the rains-residence.' Then, having heard the thought that had arisen in the monks—'When, indeed, should the rains-residence be entered upon?'—he said: 'I allow, monks, to enter upon the rains-residence during the rainy season.' Then this thought occurred to the monks: 'How many rains-entry periods are there?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. Having heard this, he taught this entire sutta, beginning with: 'There are two, O monks...' Therein, 'rains-entry periods' means the undertakings of the rains-residence. The earlier period is the first three-month period to be entered upon on the day after the Āsāḷhā full moon, ending on the first Kattika full moon. The later period is the later three-month period to be entered upon when a month of Āsāḷhā has passed, ending on the later Kattika full moon. The tenth.

Kammakāraṇavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on the Cause of Action.

2. Adhikaraṇavaggavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Chapter on Legal Questions.

11. Dutiyassa [V 2.0009][M 2.0009][P 2.0098] paṭhame balānīti kenaṭṭhena balāni. Akampiyaṭṭhena balāni nāma, tathā durabhibhavanaṭṭhena anajjhomaddanaṭṭhena ca. Paṭisaṅkhānabalanti paccavekkhaṇabalaṃ. Bhāvanābalanti brūhanabalaṃ vaḍḍhanabalaṃ. Suddhaṃ attānanti idaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tatrāti tesu dvīsu balesu. Yamidanti yaṃ idaṃ. Sekhānametaṃ balanti sattannaṃ sekhānaṃ ñāṇabalametaṃ. Sekhañhi so, bhikkhave, balaṃ āgammāti sattannaṃ sekhānaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ ārabbha sandhāya paṭicca. Pajahatīti maggena pajahati. Pahāyāti iminā pana phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Yaṃ pāpanti yaṃ pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ. Yasmā panetāni dvepi vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā ettha etadaggaṃ nāgatanti veditabbaṃ.

11. In the first sutta of the second chapter, regarding 'strengths' (balāni)—by what meaning are they strengths? They are called strengths by the meaning of being unshakable, and also by the meaning of being difficult to overcome and unassailable. 'The strength of reflection' (paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ) is the strength of reviewing. 'The strength of development' (bhāvanābalaṃ) is the strength of increasing and augmenting. 'A pure self' (suddhaṃ attānaṃ)—this should be understood according to the method explained previously. 'There' (tatrāti)—among those two strengths. The word `yamidaṃ` is to be parsed as `yaṃ idaṃ`. 'This is the strength of the trainees' (sekhānametaṃ balanti)—this is the knowledge-strength of the seven trainees. The passage 'For, relying on the trainee's strength, O monks...' (sekhañhi so, bhikkhave, balaṃ āgammāti) is said concerning, with reference to, and dependent on the knowledge-strength of the seven trainees. 'He abandons' (pajahatīti)—he abandons by means of the path. By this word 'having abandoned' (pahāya), however, the fruit is spoken of. 'Whatever is bad' (yaṃ pāpaṃ)—whatever is evil and base. And because one attains Arahantship by developing both of these, therefore, it should be understood that the declaration of the foremost is not given here.

12. Dutiye satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetītiādīsu ayaṃ heṭṭhā anāgatānaṃ padānaṃ vasena atthavaṇṇanā – vivekanissitanti vivekaṃ nissitaṃ. Vivekoti vivittatā. Svāyaṃ tadaṅgaviveko vikkhambhana-samuccheda-paṭippassaddhi-nissaraṇavivekoti pañcavidho. Tasmiṃ pañcavidhe viveke. Vivekanissitanti tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, nissaraṇavivekanissitañca satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetīti ayamattho veditabbo. Tathā hi satisambojjhaṅgabhāvanānuyutto yogī vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ, maggakāle pana kiccato samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti. Pañcavidhavivekanissitampīti eke. Te hi na kevalaṃ balavavipassanāmaggaphalakkhaṇesuyeva [P 2.0099] bojjhaṅge uddharanti, vipassanāpādakakasiṇajjhānaānāpānāsubhabrahmavihārajjhānesupi uddharanti, na ca paṭisiddhā aṭṭhakathācariyehi. Tasmā tesaṃ matena etesaṃ jhānānaṃ pavattikkhaṇe kiccato eva vikkhambhanavivekanissitaṃ. Yathā ca “vipassanākkhaṇe ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissita”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ “paṭippassaddhivivekanissitampi bhāvetī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo virāganissitantiādīsu. Vivekatthā eva hi virāgādayo.

12. In the second sutta, in the phrases beginning 'develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness,' etc., this is the explanation of the meaning of terms not previously occurring: 'based on seclusion' (vivekanissitaṃ) means based on seclusion (vivekaṃ nissitaṃ). 'Seclusion' (viveka) means solitude (vivittatā). And this seclusion is of five kinds: seclusion by substitution (tadaṅgaviveka), seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhanaviveka), seclusion by cutting off (samucchedaviveka), seclusion by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhiviveka), and seclusion by escape (nissaraṇaviveka). Among these five kinds of seclusion, the meaning of 'based on seclusion' is that one develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness based on seclusion by substitution, based on seclusion by cutting off, and based on seclusion by escape. This is how it should be understood. For thus, a yogī devoted to developing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, at the moment of insight, develops it based on seclusion by substitution in terms of function and based on seclusion by escape in terms of inclination; and at the time of the path, however, based on seclusion by cutting off in terms of function and based on seclusion by escape in terms of object. Some say it is also based on the fivefold seclusion. For they extract the enlightenment factors not only at the moments of strong insight, path, and fruition, but also in the jhānas that are the basis for insight, such as the kasiṇa jhānas, mindfulness of breathing, meditations on the unlovely, and the divine abidings. And they are not prohibited by the commentary masters. Therefore, according to their opinion, at the moment of the occurrence of these jhānas, it is developed as based on seclusion by suppression in terms of function alone. And just as it is said, 'at the moment of insight, it is based on seclusion by escape in terms of inclination,' so too it is proper to say, 'it is also developed as based on seclusion by tranquillization.' This same method applies to phrases such as 'based on dispassion,' etc. For dispassion and the others indeed have precisely the meaning of seclusion.

Kevalaṃ [M 2.0010] hettha vossaggo duvidho pariccāgavossaggo ca pakkhandanavossaggo cāti. Tattha pariccāgavossaggoti [V 2.0010] vipassanākkhaṇe ca tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe ca samucchedavasena kilesappahānaṃ. Pakkhandanavossaggoti vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe pana ārammaṇakaraṇena nibbānapakkhandanaṃ. Tadubhayampi imasmiṃ lokiyalokuttaramissake atthavaṇṇanānaye vaṭṭati. Tathā hi ayaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo yathāvuttena pakārena kilese pariccajati, nibbānañca pakkhandati. Vossaggapariṇāminti iminā pana sakalena vacanena vossaggatthaṃ pariṇamantaṃ pariṇatañca, paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcāti idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi bojjhaṅgabhāvanānuyutto bhikkhu yathā satisambojjhaṅgo kilesapariccāgavossaggatthaṃ nibbānapakkhandanavossaggatthañca paripaccati, yathā ca paripakko hoti, tathā naṃ bhāvetīti. Esa nayo sesabojjhaṅgesu.

Here, relinquishment (vossaggo) is simply twofold: relinquishment by abandonment (pariccāgavossaggo) and relinquishment by leaping forward (pakkhandanavossaggo). Of these, relinquishment by abandonment is the abandoning of defilements by way of substitution at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the path. Relinquishment by leaping forward is the leaping forward to Nibbāna by way of its inclination at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the path. Both of these are applicable in this method of explanation, which is a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. Indeed, this mindfulness enlightenment factor abandons defilements in the manner described and leaps forward to Nibbāna. By this entire phrase, 'culminating in relinquishment' (vossaggapariṇāmiṃ), this is stated: that which is inclining and has inclined, that which is maturing and has matured, for the purpose of relinquishment. For this monk, devoted to the development of the enlightenment factors, develops it in such a way that the mindfulness enlightenment factor matures for the purpose of relinquishment by abandoning defilements and for the purpose of relinquishment by leaping forward to Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes fully mature. This is the method for the remaining enlightenment factors.

Idha pana nibbānaṃyeva sabbasaṅkhatehi vivittattā viveko, sabbesaṃ virāgabhāvato virāgo, nirodhabhāvato nirodhoti vuttaṃ. Maggo eva [P 2.0100] ca vossaggapariṇāmī, tasmā satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattiyā vivekanissitaṃ, tathā virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ. Tañca kho ariyamaggakkhaṇuppattiyā kilesānaṃ samucchedato pariccāgabhāvena ca nibbānapakkhandanabhāvena ca pariṇataṃ paripakkanti ayameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo sesabojjhaṅgesu. Iti ime satta bojjhaṅgā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā. Imesupi dvīsu balesu etadaggabhāvo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Here, however, Nibbāna alone is called seclusion (viveka) because of its being secluded from all conditioned things; dispassion (virāga) because it is the fading away of all conditioned things; and cessation (nirodha) because it is the state of cessation. The path itself culminates in relinquishment. Therefore, one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, which is based on seclusion because it proceeds having made seclusion its object, and is similarly based on dispassion and based on cessation. And that factor, at the moment of the arising of the Noble Path, has inclined and matured by way of abandonment due to the eradication of defilements, and by way of leaping forward to Nibbāna—this very meaning should be understood. This is the method for the remaining enlightenment factors. Thus, these seven enlightenment factors are spoken of as mixed—mundane and supramundane. In these two powers as well, their pre-eminence should be understood in the very way that has been stated.

13. Tatiye vivicceva kāmehītiādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ pāḷiattho ca bhāvanānayo ca sabbo sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.69-70) vitthāritoyeva. Imāni pana cattāri jhānāni eko bhikkhu cittekaggatthāya bhāveti, eko vipassanāpādakatthāya, eko abhiññāpādakatthāya, eko nirodhapādakatthāya, eko bhavavisesatthāya. Idha pana tānipi vipassanāpādakāni adhippetāni. Ayaṃ hi bhikkhu imāni jhānāni samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā hetupaccayapariggahaṃ katvā sappaccayaṃ [M 2.0011] nāmarūpañca vavatthapetvā indriyabalabojjhaṅgāni samodhānetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Evametāni jhānāni lokiyalokuttaramissakāneva kathitāni. Imasmimpi baladvaye etadaggabhāvo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

13. In the third Sutta, the Pāḷi meaning and the method of cultivation for all four jhānas, beginning with 'vivicceva kāmehi' and so forth, have been explained in detail in every respect in the Visuddhimagga. These four jhānas, however, are cultivated by one bhikkhu for the sake of one-pointedness of mind, by another as a basis for insight, by another as a basis for higher knowledge, by another as a basis for the attainment of cessation, and by another for the sake of a special state of existence. Here, however, those that are a basis for insight are intended. For this bhikkhu, having attained these jhānas and emerged from the attainment, contemplates the formations, comprehends causes and conditions, determines name-and-form along with its conditions, unifies the faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors, and attains arahantship. Thus, these jhānas are spoken of as mixed—mundane and supramundane. In this pair of powers as well, their pre-eminence should be understood in the very way that has been stated.

14. Catutthe [V 2.0011] saṃkhittena ca vitthārena cāti saṃkhittadhammadesanā vitthāradhammadesanā cāti dveyeva dhammadesanāti dasseti. Tattha mātikaṃ uddisitvā kathitā desanā saṃkhittadesanā nāma. Tameva mātikaṃ vitthārato vibhajitvā kathitā vitthāradesanā nāma. Mātikaṃ vā ṭhapetvāpi aṭṭhapetvāpi vitthārato vibhajitvā kathitā vitthāradesanā nāma[P 2.0101]. Tāsu saṃkhittadesanā nāma mahāpaññassa puggalassa vasena kathitā, vitthāradesanā nāma mandapaññassa. Mahāpaññassa hi vitthāradesanā atipapañco viya hoti. Mandapaññassa saṅkhepadesanā sasakassa uppatanaṃ viya hoti, neva antaṃ na koṭiṃ pāpuṇituṃ sakkoti. Saṅkhepadesanā ca ugghaṭitaññussa vasena kathitā, vitthāradesanā itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vasena. Sakalampi hi tepiṭakaṃ saṅkhepadesanā vitthāradesanāti ettheva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

14. In the fourth Sutta, by 'in brief and in detail' it is shown that there are only two kinds of Dhamma teaching: concise teaching and elaborate teaching. Herein, a teaching given after stating the outline is called a concise teaching. That same outline, analyzed and taught in detail, is called an elaborate teaching. Alternatively, whether establishing an outline or not, a teaching analyzed and taught in detail is called an elaborate teaching. Among these, a concise teaching is said to be spoken according to the capacity of a person of great wisdom, while an elaborate teaching is for one of dull wisdom. For a person of great wisdom, an elaborate teaching is like excessive proliferation. For one of dull wisdom, a concise teaching is like the leap of a rabbit; they are not able to reach the end or the limit. A concise teaching is spoken according to the capacity of one of quick understanding, while an elaborate teaching is for the other three types of individuals. Indeed, the entire Tipiṭaka falls into the classification of either concise or elaborate teachings.

15. Pañcame yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, adhikaraṇeti vivādādhikaraṇaṃ, anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ, kiccādhikaraṇanti imesaṃ catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ yasmiṃ adhikaraṇe. Āpanno ca bhikkhūti āpattiṃ āpanno bhikkhu ca. Tasmetanti tasmiṃ etaṃ. Dīghattāyāti dīghaṃ addhānaṃ tiṭṭhanatthāya. Kharattāyāti dāsa-koṇḍa-caṇḍāla-venāti evaṃ kharavācāpavattanatthāya. Vāḷattāyāti pāṇi leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paharaṇavasena kakkhaḷabhāvatthāya. Bhikkhū ca na phāsuṃ viharissantīti aññamaññaṃ vivādāpanne bhikkhusaṅghe yepi uddesaṃ vā paripucchaṃ vā gahetukāmā padhānaṃ vā anuyuñjitukāmā, te phāsuṃ na viharissanti. Bhikkhusaṅghasmiṃ hi uposathapavāraṇāya ṭhitāya uddesādīhi atthikā uddesādīni gahetuṃ na sakkonti, vipassakānaṃ cittuppādo na ekaggo hoti, tato visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkonti. Evaṃ bhikkhū ca na phāsuṃ viharissanti. Na dīghattāyātiādīsu vuttapaṭipakkhanayena attho veditabbo.

15. In the fifth Sutta. Herein, 'in which legal issue, O monks': among these four legal issues—the legal issue of dispute, the legal issue of accusation, the legal issue of an offense, and the legal issue of duties—in whichever legal issue. 'And a monk who has committed an offense' means a monk who has incurred an offense. 'Tasmetaṃ' means: in that legal issue, this legal issue of dispute. 'For lengthiness' means for the purpose of lasting a long time. 'For harshness' means for the purpose of the arising of harsh speech like that of a slave, a person without virtue, an outcaste, or a bamboo-worker. 'For ferocity' means for the purpose of a harsh state by way of striking with stones, clods of earth, sticks, and so on. 'And the monks will not dwell at ease' means that in a Saṅgha of monks that has fallen into mutual dispute, even those who wish to undertake the recitation of the texts or the inquiry into them, or who wish to strive in meditation, will not dwell at ease. For when the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are suspended in the Saṅgha of monks, those who need to undertake recitation and so on are not able to do so; the mind-moment of insight meditators does not become one-pointed; therefore, they are not able to generate special attainments. Thus, the monks will not dwell at ease. In 'not for lengthiness' and so on, the meaning should be understood in the manner opposite to what has been said.

Idhāti [M 2.0012][P 2.0102] imasmiṃ sāsane. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti evaṃ paccavekkhati. Akusalaṃ āpannoti ettha akusalanti āpatti adhippetā, āpattiṃ āpannoti attho. Kañcideva desanti na sabbameva āpattiṃ, āpattiyā pana kañcideva desaṃ aññataraṃ āpattinti attho. Kāyenāti karajakāyena. Anattamanoti atuṭṭhacitto. Anattamanavācanti atuṭṭhavācaṃ. Mamevāti maṃyeva. Tatthāti tasmiṃ adhikaraṇe. Accayo accagamāti aparādho atikkamitvā madditvā gato, ahamevettha aparādhiko. Suṅkadāyakaṃva bhaṇḍasminti yathā suṅkaṭṭhānaṃ pariharitvā nīte bhaṇḍasmiṃ [V 2.0012] suṅkadāyakaṃ aparādho abhibhavati, so ca tattha aparādhiko hoti, na rājāno na rājapurisāti attho.

“Here” means in this Dispensation. “Reflecting thus” means reviewing thus. In “committed an unwholesome deed,” herein ‘unwholesome’ is intended to mean an offense; the meaning is, “has incurred an offense.” “Some part” means not the entire offense, but some part of an offense; the meaning is any particular offense. “With the body” means with the physical body. “Displeased” means with a dissatisfied mind. “Displeased in speech” means dissatisfied speech. “Me alone” means me alone. “In that” means in that legal issue. “A transgression has overcome” means a fault has overstepped, crushed, and occurred; I alone am at fault here. “Like one who should pay tax in regard to goods” means: just as when goods are carried while avoiding the customs post, the fault overcomes the one who should pay the tax, and he alone is at fault in that matter—not the kings, not the royal officials—that is the meaning.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo hi raññā ṭhapitaṃ suṅkaṭṭhānaṃ pariharitvā bhaṇḍaṃ harati, taṃ saha bhaṇḍasakaṭena ānetvā rañño dassenti. Tattha neva suṅkaṭṭhānassa doso atthi, na rañño na rājapurisānaṃ, pariharitvā gatasseva pana doso, evamevaṃ yaṃ so bhikkhu āpattiṃ āpanno, tattha neva āpattiyā doso, na codakassa. Tīhi pana kāraṇehi tasseva bhikkhuno doso. Tassa hi āpattiṃ āpannabhāvenapi doso, codake anattamanatāyapi doso, anattamanassa sato paresaṃ ārocanenapi doso. Codakassa pana yaṃ so taṃ āpattiṃ āpajjantaṃ addasa, tattha doso natthi. Anattamanatāya codanāya pana doso. Tampi amanasikaritvā ayaṃ bhikkhu attanova dosaṃ paccavekkhanto “iti mameva tattha accayo accagamā suṅkadāyakaṃva [P 2.0103] bhaṇḍasmi”nti evaṃ paṭisañcikkhatīti attho. Dutiyavāre codakassa anattamanatā ca anattamanatāya coditabhāvo cāti dve dosā, tesaṃ vasena “accayo accagamā”ti ettha yojanā kātabbā. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

This is the meaning: Whoever, having avoided the toll station established by the king, transports goods, is brought along with the cart of goods and presented to the king. In that case, there is no fault with the toll station, nor with the king, nor with the king's men; the fault is solely with the one who avoided it and went. In this very same way, whatever offense that monk has committed, there is no fault with the offense itself, nor with the accuser. However, the fault is with that monk alone for three reasons: there is a fault in his having committed an offense, a fault in his displeasure towards the accuser, and a fault in that, being displeased, he informs others. But as for the accuser, there is no fault in his having seen that monk committing the offense. There is a fault, however, in an accusation made with displeasure. Not paying attention to that, this monk reflects on his own fault, thinking, 'Thus, in this matter, the transgression has overcome me alone, just as a transgression overcomes one liable for the toll with respect to the goods.' This is the meaning. In the second instance, for the accuser there are two faults: displeasure, and having accused out of displeasure. By means of these, the phrase 'the transgression has overcome' should be applied here. The rest here is self-evident.

16. Chaṭṭhe aññataroti eko apākaṭanāmo brāhmaṇo. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti yenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Tasmā yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo[M 2.0013]? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gato tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti.

16. In the sixth sutta, 'a certain one' means a Brahmin whose name was not well-known. Regarding 'he approached the Blessed One,' the word 'yena' is an instrumental word used in a locative sense. Therefore, the meaning here is to be understood thus: he approached where the Blessed One was. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: for whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, for that reason he approached. And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? With the intention of attaining various kinds of superior qualities; just as a great tree constantly bearing fruit is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying delicious fruit. 'He approached' means 'he went'; thus it is said. 'Having approached' indicates the completion of approaching. Alternatively, it is also said that having gone thus, from that place he went to a place even closer, which is designated as the Blessed One’s vicinity.

Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodīti yathā ca khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tena, evaṃ sopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi, sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamāsi. Yāya ca “kacci, bho gotama, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto gotamassa ca sāvakānañca appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya [V 2.0013] sammodi, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātassa sammodassa jananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato vā sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato sāraṇīyaṃ, tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya [P 2.0104] sāraṇīyanti evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ kathaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhapetvā yenatthena āgato, taṃ pucchitukāmo ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

Regarding the phrase, 'He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One': Just as the Blessed One, inquiring about his well-being and other such matters, had a mutually agreeable exchange of pleasantries with him, so too did he have a mutually agreeable exchange of pleasantries with the Blessed One, just as cool water, having mingled with hot water, reaches a state of oneness. And by whatever conversation he exchanged greetings, such as, 'Venerable Gotama, I trust you are well? I trust you are managing? I trust that the venerable Gotama and his disciples are free from illness, free from affliction, agile, strong, and dwelling at ease?', that conversation is amiable because it generates the pleasantness known as joy and delight, and because it is suitable for exchanging pleasantries; and it is memorable because, due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it is worthy of being recalled and continuously carried on for a very long time, and because it is fit to be remembered. Alternatively, it is amiable because of the pleasure experienced while hearing it, and memorable because of the pleasure experienced while recalling it. Likewise, it is amiable because of the purity of its phrasing, and memorable because of the purity of its meaning. Thus, in many ways, having concluded and finished this amiable and memorable conversation, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come, he sat down to one side.

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti, tathā nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nisīdīti upāvisi. Paṇḍitā hi purisā garuṭṭhānīyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti. Ayañca nesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

The word 'ekamantaṃ' is a designation of the neuter in an abstract sense, as in such phrases as, 'The sun and moon revolve unevenly.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: he sat in such a way as to be seated to one side. Alternatively, this is a word in the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. 'Nisīdi' means he sat near. For wise men, having approached a venerable person, sit to one side due to their skill in seating. And this brahmin was one of them; therefore, he sat to one side.

Kathaṃ nisinno pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti? Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ – atidūraṃ, accāsannaṃ, uparivātaṃ, unnatappadesaṃ, atisammukhaṃ atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti[M 2.0014]. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

Now, how is one who is seated said to be seated to one side? By avoiding the six faults in sitting. What are these? Being too far, too close, upwind, in a high place, directly in front, or directly behind. For one who sits too far, if wishing to speak, must speak with a loud voice. One who sits too close causes physical contact. One who sits upwind afflicts with body odor. One who sits in a high place displays disrespect. One who sits directly in front, if wishing to look, must look eye to eye. One who sits directly behind, if wishing to look, must stretch out the neck to look. Therefore, this brahmin too, having avoided these six faults in sitting, sat down. For that reason, it was said, 'he sat to one side.'

Etadavocāti duvidhā hi pucchā – agārikapucchā, anagārikapucchā ca. Tattha “kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusala”nti (ma. ni. 3.296) iminā nayena agārikapucchā āgatā. “Ime nu kho, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā”ti (ma. ni. 3.86) iminā nayena anagārikapucchā. Ayaṃ pana attano anurūpaṃ agārikapucchaṃ pucchanto etaṃ “ko nu kho, bho gotama, hetu ko paccayo”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha hetu paccayoti ubhayampetaṃ kāraṇavevacanameva. Adhammacariyāvisamacariyāhetūti adhammacariyāsaṅkhātāya visamacariyāya hetu, taṃkāraṇā tappaccayāti attho[P 2.0105]. Tatrāyaṃ padattho – adhammassa cariyā adhammacariyā, adhammakāraṇanti [V 2.0014] attho. Visamaṃ cariyā, visamassa vā kammassa cariyāti visamacariyā. Adhammacariyā ca sā visamacariyā cāti adhammacariyāvisamacariyā. Etenupāyena sukkapakkhepi attho veditabbo. Atthato panettha adhammacariyāvisamacariyā nāma dasa akusalakammapathā, dhammacariyāsamacariyā nāma dasa kusalakammapathāti veditabbā.

Regarding `Etadavoca`: Indeed, there are two kinds of questions: questions by householders and questions by renunciates. Among these, a question by a householder is presented in this way: 'What, venerable sir, is skillful, what is unskillful?' A question by a renunciate is presented in this way: 'Are these, venerable sir, the five aggregates subject to clinging?' This brahmin, however, wishing to ask a question suitable for himself, a householder's question, spoke this utterance beginning with 'What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition?' Therein, both `hetu` and `paccayo` are synonyms for 'cause'. `Adhammacariyāvisamacariyāhetu` means 'the cause for the uneven conduct designated as unrighteous conduct'; the meaning is 'because of that cause, because of that condition.' Herein, this is the meaning of the terms: conduct of unrighteousness is `adhammacariyā`; the meaning is the doing of unrighteousness. Uneven conduct, or the conduct of uneven action, is `visamacariyā`. That which is unrighteous conduct and is uneven conduct is `adhammacariyāvisamacariyā`. By this method, the meaning should also be understood in the case of the bright side. In terms of meaning, herein, `adhammacariyāvisamacariyā` should be understood as the ten unskillful courses of action, and `dhammacariyāsamacariyā` as the ten skillful courses of action.

Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamāti ettha ayaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. “Abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu (udā. 45; cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

Regarding 'Excellent, Master Gotama': Here, this word `abhikkanta` is seen in the meanings of cessation, goodness, excellent form, and approval. For, in passages such as 'The night, venerable sir, has passed; the first watch is over; the Sangha of monks has been seated for a long time,' it is seen in the sense of cessation. In passages such as 'This person is more excellent and more sublime among these four persons,' it is seen in the sense of goodness.

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. –

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with psychic power and glory, with surpassing beauty illuminating all directions?”

Ādīsu [M 2.0015] (vi. va. 857) abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bhante”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.250; pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā sādhu sādhu, bho gotamāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In passages such as these, it is in the sense of 'excellent form'. In passages such as, 'Excellent, venerable sir!', it is in the sense of appreciation. Here, too, it is in the sense of appreciation. And because it is in the sense of appreciation, it therefore means, 'Well said, well said, Master Gotama!' Thus it should be understood.

“Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho”ti. –

“In fear, in anger, in praise, in haste, in commotion and wonder, in mirth, in sorrow, and in serene confidence, a wise person should use repetition.”

Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Atha vā abhikkantanti abhikkantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti.

And by this characteristic, it should be understood that here it is spoken twice by way of serene confidence and praise. Or alternatively, `abhikkantaṃ` means most desired, most pleasing, and most beautiful—thus it is said.

Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – abhikkantaṃ, bho [P 2.0106] gotama, yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi – bhoto gotamassa vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato[V 2.0015], tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato, aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, with one 'abhikkanta' word, he praises the teaching; with the other, his own serene confidence. This is the intended meaning here: 'Excellent, Master Gotama, is this teaching of Master Gotama; excellent is this serene confidence that has arisen in me on account of Master Gotama's teaching.' Alternatively, he praises the Blessed One's speech by referring to pairs of meanings: the speech of Master Gotama is excellent for destroying faults and excellent for attaining virtues; likewise, for generating faith and for generating wisdom; for being complete with meaning and for being complete with phrasing; for having clear words and for having profound meaning; for being pleasant to the ear and for entering the heart; for not exalting oneself and for not disparaging others; for being cool with compassion and for being purified by wisdom; for being delightful at first hearing and for withstanding scrutiny; for being pleasant while being heard and for being beneficial when investigated. It should be connected with these and other such qualities.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti uparimukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādichāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasīaḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame. Ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching with four similes. Herein, 'overturned' means placed face-down, or having a downward-facing opening. 'One might set upright' means one would make it face upwards. 'Covered' means covered by grass, leaves, and so on. 'One might uncover' means one would open it. 'To one who is lost' means to one bewildered as to direction. 'One might show the path' means taking one by the hand, one would say, 'This is the path.' 'In darkness' means in the four-factored darkness of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest thicket, and a layer of clouds. This, to begin with, is the meaning of the unclear terms.

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ [M 2.0016] sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhāraṇena [P 2.0107] mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

This, however, is the interpretation of the intended meaning: Just as someone might set upright what is overturned, so too, by causing me, who had turned away from the True Dhamma and had fallen into non-Dhamma, to arise from that non-Dhamma; just as one might uncover what is covered, so too, by revealing the Dispensation, which had been covered by the thicket of wrong views ever since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; just as one might show the path to one who had gone astray, so too, by making manifest the path to heaven and liberation to me, who had entered upon the contemptible path, the wrong path; just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so too, for me, who was sunk in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the nature of the jewels such as the Buddha, by holding up the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which obscures them—because it was revealed to me by the Venerable Gotama through these various means, the Dhamma was revealed in many ways.

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhavaṃ me gotamo saraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ aghassa tātā hitassa ca vidhātāti iminā adhippāyena bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi sevāmi payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gati attho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tasmā gacchāmīti imassa jānāmi bujjhāmīti ayamattho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca catūsu apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo. So atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca[V 2.0016], apica kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttañhetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne –

Thus having praised the discourse, with a mind confident in the Triple Gem through this discourse, and making a gesture of confidence, he spoke the words beginning with, “Esāhaṃ.” Therein, “esāhaṃ” is parsed as “eso ahaṃ” (this I). “I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge” means: with the intention, “The venerable Gotama is my refuge, my final resort, the protector from suffering and the ordainer of welfare,” I go to, associate with, serve, and attend upon the venerable Gotama; or, thus I know, I understand. Indeed, verbal roots meaning ‘to go’ also mean ‘to know.’ Therefore, for “gacchāmi,” the meaning “I know, I understand” is stated. Furthermore, herein [in “and the Dhamma and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha”]: because it sustains those who have attained the path, realized cessation, and practice as instructed, by not letting them fall into the four states of deprivation, it is called Dhamma. In meaning, it is both the Noble Path and Nibbāna. And this was stated: “Bhikkhus, inasmuch as there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them.” The detailed explanation should be understood thus. And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the scriptural Dhamma along with the Noble Fruits. This was stated in the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

“The fading of passion, unagitated, sorrowless, the unconditioned Dhamma, agreeable; this sweet, proficient, well-analyzed Dhamma—approach for the sake of refuge.”

Ettha rāgavirogoti maggo kathito. Anojamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ [P 2.0108] paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā sabbadhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena saṃhatoti saṅgho. So atthato aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiyeva vimāne –

Herein, by “the fading of passion,” the Path is taught. By “unagitated, sorrowless,” the Fruit is taught. By “the unconditioned Dhamma,” Nibbāna is taught. By “agreeable, this sweet, proficient, well-analyzed,” all the aggregates of the Dhamma, as divided into the three Piṭakas, are taught. Because they are united by a commonality of view and virtue, they are called the Saṅgha. In meaning, it is the community of the eight noble individuals. Indeed, in that very same Vimāna it was stated:

“Yattha ca dinnamahapphalamāhu, catūsu sucīsu purisayugesu;

Aṭṭha ca puggaladhammadasā te, saṅghamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 888);

“Wherein, in the four pure pairs of persons, a gift given is said to be of great fruit; and those persons who have seen the Dhamma are eight—approach this Saṅgha for the sake of refuge.”

Bhikkhūnaṃ [M 2.0017] saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā brāhmaṇo tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi.

The community of bhikkhus is the Bhikkhusaṅgha. By this much, the brahmin professed the three goings for refuge.

Idāni tesu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo, saraṇagamanaphalaṃ, saṃkileso, bhedoti ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo.

Now, in regard to those goings for refuge, for the sake of skillfulness, this method should be known: the refuge, the going for refuge, he who goes for refuge, the distinction of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, the defilement, and the breaking.

Seyyathidaṃ – padatthato tāva hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ, saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiparikilesaṃ hanati vināsetīti attho, ratanattayassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Atha vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti buddho, bhavakantārā uttāraṇena lokassa assāsadānena ca dhammo, appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho. Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihatakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgīsatto saraṇaṃ gacchati, vuttappakārena cittuppādena “etāni me tīṇi ratanāni saraṇaṃ, etāni parāyaṇa”nti evaṃ upetīti attho. Evaṃ tāva saraṇaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati idaṃ tayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

That is to say: first, regarding the meaning of the word, it is 'refuge' (saraṇa) because it destroys (hiṃsati). The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge, by that very going for refuge, it destroys and eliminates fear, terror, suffering, and the affliction of a woeful state. This is a designation for the Three Jewels. Alternatively, the Buddha destroys the fear of beings by promoting their welfare and turning them away from what is not their welfare; the Dhamma, by rescuing from the wilderness of existence and by giving solace to the world; and the Saṅgha, by causing the acquisition of abundant fruit even for small deeds. Therefore, by this reason also, the Three Jewels are a 'refuge'. The arising of a thought, with defilements destroyed by confidence in and reverence for them, proceeding in the manner of having them as the ultimate resort, is the 'going for refuge'. A being endowed with that goes for refuge. The meaning is that with the arising of a thought of the kind described, one approaches thus: 'These three jewels are my refuge, these are my ultimate reliance.' Thus, first, this triad should be known: the refuge, the going for refuge, and he who goes for refuge.

Saraṇagamanappabhede [V 2.0017][P 2.0109] pana duvidhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ lokuttaraṃ lokiyañcāti. Tattha lokuttaraṃ diṭṭhasaccānaṃ maggakkhaṇe saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhati. Lokiyaṃ puthujjanānaṃ saraṇagamanupakkilesavikkhambhanena ārammaṇato buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā ijjhati. Taṃ atthato buddhādīsu vatthūsu saddhāpaṭilābho, saddhāmūlikā ca sammādiṭṭhi dasasu puññakiriyāvatthūsu diṭṭhijukammanti vuccati.

Furthermore, in the distinction of going for refuge, the going for refuge is twofold: supramundane and mundane. Therein, the supramundane is accomplished for those who have seen the truths at the moment of the path by the eradication of the defilements of going for refuge; by way of object, having Nibbāna as its object, and by way of function, in the entire Three Jewels. The mundane is accomplished for worldlings by the suppression of the defilements of going for refuge; by way of object, having the qualities of the Buddha and so on as its object. In meaning, that is called the acquisition of faith in the objects such as the Buddha, and right view rooted in faith, which is the straightening of views among the ten grounds for meritorious action.

Tayidaṃ catudhā pavattati attasanniyyātanena tapparāyaṇatāya sissabhāvūpagamanena paṇipātenāti. Tattha attasanniyyātanaṃ nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa, saṅghassā”ti evaṃ buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo, dhammaparāyaṇo, saṅghaparāyaṇo iti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ tapparāyaṇabhāvo. Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhassa [M 2.0018] antevāsiko, dhammassa, saṅghassa iti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ sissabhāvūpagamo. Paṇipāto nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādana-paccuṭṭhāna-añjalikamma-sāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ karomi iti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ buddhādīsu paramanipaccakāro. Imesañhi catunnampi ākārānaṃ aññatarampi karontena gahitaṃyeva hoti saraṇagamanaṃ.

This mundane going for refuge occurs in four ways: by self-dedication, by making them one's final resort, by undertaking discipleship, and by profound veneration. Therein, self-dedication means: 'From today onward, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha'—thus it is the abandoning of oneself to the Buddha and so forth. Making them one's final resort means: 'From today onward, I have the Buddha as my final resort, the Dhamma as my final resort, the Saṅgha as my final resort—may you remember me thus'—this is the state of having them as one's final resort. Undertaking discipleship means: 'From today onward, I am a resident pupil of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, and of the Saṅgha—may you remember me thus'—this is the undertaking of discipleship. Profound veneration means: 'From today onward, I perform acts of reverence, rising up, making the añjali gesture, and proper duties only towards the three objects, the Buddha and so forth—may you remember me thus'—thus it is the supreme act of reverence towards the Buddha and so forth. For by a person doing even any one of these four modes, the going for refuge is indeed taken.

Apica “bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi, dhammassa, saṅghassa attānaṃ pariccajāmi, jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, pariccattoyeva me attā, pariccattaṃyeva me jīvitaṃ, jīvitapariyantikaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, buddho me saraṇaṃ leṇaṃ tāṇa”nti evampi attasanniyyātanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Satthārañca [P 2.0110] vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) evampi mahākassapassa saraṇagamane viya sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, self-dedication should be understood thus: 'I abandon myself to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, to the Saṅgha. I abandon my life. My self is indeed abandoned, my life is indeed abandoned. For as long as life lasts, I go to the Buddha for refuge. The Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, and my protection.' Likewise, undertaking discipleship should be seen, as in the going for refuge of Mahākassapa: 'Oh, that I might see the Teacher, indeed the Blessed One; oh, that I might see the Sugata, indeed the Blessed One; oh, that I might see the Perfectly Enlightened One, indeed the Blessed One!'

“So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammata”nti. (su. ni. 194; saṃ. ni. 1.246);

I shall wander from village to village, from town to town, venerating the Perfectly Enlightened One and the excellence of the Dhamma.

Evampi āḷavakādīnaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ viya tapparāyaṇatā veditabbā. “Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo [V 2.0018] uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena ca paricumbati, pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati, nāmañca sāveti – ‘brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo; brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo’”ti (ma. ni. 2.394) evampi paṇipāto veditabbo.

Thus also, the state of having that as the ultimate resort should be understood, like the going for refuge of Āḷavaka and others. In this way also, prostration should be understood: 'Then the brahmin Brahmāyu, having risen from his seat and arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, fell with his head at the feet of the Blessed One. He both kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth and massaged them with his hands, and announced his name, saying: “I am Brahmāyu, venerable Gotama, a brahmin; I am Brahmāyu, venerable Gotama, a brahmin.”'

So panesa ñātibhayācariyadakkhiṇeyyavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, na itarehi. Seṭṭhavaseneva hi saraṇaṃ gaṇhāti, seṭṭhavasena ca bhijjati. Tasmā yo sākiyo vā koliyo vā “buddho amhākaṃ ñātako”ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā “samaṇo gotamo rājapūjito mahānubhāvo avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyā”ti bhayena vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā bodhisattakāle bhagavato santike kiñci uggahitaṃ saramāno buddhakāle vā –

Furthermore, this prostration is fourfold: by way of relatives, fear, teachers, and those worthy of supreme offerings. Among these, the going for refuge occurs through prostration to one as worthy of supreme offerings; it does not occur through the others. Indeed, one takes refuge only by way of what is supreme, and it is broken only by way of what is supreme. Therefore, if a Sakyan or a Koliyan pays homage, thinking, 'The Buddha is our relative,' the refuge is indeed not taken. Or if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and is of great power; if not paid homage, he might bring about harm,' the refuge is indeed not taken. Or if one, remembering something learned in the presence of the Blessed One during the time he was a Bodhisatta, or during the time he was a Buddha—

“Ekena [M 2.0019] bhoge bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye;
