Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissatī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.265) –

‘With one portion, one should enjoy wealth; with two, one should engage in work; and the fourth, one should set aside, for it will be needed in times of adversity.’

Evarūpaṃ [P 2.0111] anusāsaniṃ uggahetvā “ācariyo me”ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo pana “ayaṃ loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo”ti vandati, teneva gahitaṃ hoti saraṇaṃ.

Having learned such an instruction and paying homage, thinking, 'He is my teacher,' the refuge is indeed not taken. But whoever pays homage, thinking, 'This one is the foremost in the world worthy of supreme offerings,' by that very person is the refuge taken.

Evaṃ gahitasaraṇassa ca upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā aññatitthiyesu pabbajitampi ñātiṃ “ñātako me aya”nti vandato saraṇagamanaṃ na bhijjati, pageva apabbajitaṃ. Tathā rājānaṃ bhayavasena vandato. So hi raṭṭhapūjitattā avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyāti. Tathā yaṃ kiñci sippaṃ sikkhāpakaṃ titthiyaṃ “ācariyo me aya”nti vandatopi na bhijjatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanappabhedo veditabbo.

Thus, for a male or female lay disciple who has taken refuge, their taking of refuge is not broken even when paying homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sectarians, thinking, 'This is my relative'—how much more so for one who has not gone forth. Similarly, for one who pays homage to a king out of fear, the taking of refuge is not broken. For that king, being honored by the country, might cause harm if not paid homage to. Furthermore, even for one who pays homage to a sectarian who is a teacher of some craft, thinking, 'This is my teacher,' it is not broken. In this way, the breaking of the taking of refuge should be understood.

Ettha ca lokuttarassa saraṇagamanassa cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphalaṃ, sabbadukkhakkhayo ānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, for the supramundane taking of refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the resultant fruit, and the exhaustion of all suffering is the consequential fruit. For this was said:

“Yo [V 2.0019] ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati. (dha. pa. 190);

Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:

“Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ;

Ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ. (dha. pa. 191);

Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the stilling of suffering.

“Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 192);

This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge. Having come to this refuge, one is freed from all suffering.

Apica niccato anupagamanādivasenapetassa ānisaṃsaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, the consequential fruit of this taking of refuge should also be understood by way of not approaching formations as permanent, and so on. For this was said:

“Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya, sukhato upagaccheyya, kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, pitaraṃ, arahantaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, paduṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.128-130; a. ni. 1.272-277).

Monks, it is an impossibility, there is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view would approach any formation as permanent, would approach it as pleasant, would approach any phenomenon as self; that they would deprive their mother of life, their father, or an Arahant; that with a corrupted mind they would cause the blood of a Tathāgata to flow; that they would split the Saṅgha; or that they would point to another teacher. That situation does not exist.

Lokiyassa [M 2.0020][P 2.0112] pana saraṇagamanassa bhavasampadāpi bhogasampadāpi phalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Now, for the worldly taking of refuge, both excellence in existence and excellence in wealth are indeed the fruit. For this was said:

“Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse,

Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ,

Devakāyaṃ paripūressantī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge will not go to the plane of misery. Having abandoned the human body, they will fill the company of devas.”

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

And furthermore, it was said:

“Atha kho sakko devānamindo asītiyā devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno [V 2.0020] etadavoca – ‘sādhu kho, devānaminda, buddhasaraṇagamanaṃ hoti. Buddhasaraṇagamanahetu kho devānaminda evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti. Te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhanti dibbena āyunā dibbena vaṇṇena sukhena yasena ādhipateyyena dibbehi rūpehi saddehi gandhehi rasehi phoṭṭhabbehī’”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341).

“Then Sakka, lord of the devas, with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna… Standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to Sakka, lord of the devas: ‘It is indeed good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha. Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. They surpass other devas in ten respects: with divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, divine sovereignty, and with divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects.’”

Eseva nayo dhamme saṅghe ca. Apica velāmasuttādivasenāpi (a. ni. 9.20 ādayo) saraṇagamanassa phalaviseso veditabbo. Evaṃ saraṇagamanaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This same method applies in the case of the Dhamma and the Sangha. Furthermore, the special fruit of going for refuge is to be understood by way of the Velāmasutta and others. Thus, the fruit of going for refuge is to be understood.

Tattha lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ tīsu vatthūsu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇādīhi saṃkilissati, na mahājutikaṃ hoti na mahāvipphāraṃ. Lokuttarassa natthi saṃkileso. Lokiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa duvidho bhedo sāvajjo anavajjo ca. Tattha sāvajjo aññasatthārādīsu attasanniyyātanādīhi hoti, so aniṭṭhaphalo. Anavajjo kālakiriyāya, so avipākattā aphalo. Lokuttarassa pana nevatthi bhedo. Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako aññaṃ satthāraṃ na uddisatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanassa saṃkileso ca bhedo ca veditabbo.

Among these, the mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so on, regarding the three objects; it is not of great radiance nor of great pervasiveness. For the supramundane, there is no defilement. And the breaking of the mundane going for refuge is of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. Among these, the blameworthy breaking occurs through dedicating oneself to other teachers and so on; that has an undesirable fruit. The blameless breaking occurs through death; that, being without result, is fruitless. But for the supramundane, there is no breaking at all. For indeed, even in another existence, a noble disciple does not designate another as teacher. Thus, the defilement and the breaking of going for refuge are to be understood.

Upāsakaṃ [M 2.0021][P 2.0113] maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretūti maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo “upāsako aya”nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho. Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ panettha ko upāsako, kasmā upāsakoti vuccati, kimassa sīlaṃ, ko ājīvo, kā vipatti, kā sampattīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“May the venerable Gotama hold me as a lay follower.” This means: “May the venerable Gotama hold me thus, ‘This is a lay follower’; may he know me.” For the sake of skill in the way of a lay follower, this miscellaneous matter should be known: Who is a lay follower? Why is one called a lay follower? What is their virtue? What is their livelihood? What is their downfall? What is their attainment?

Tattha ko upāsakoti yo koci saraṇagato gahaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Therein, who is a lay follower? Any householder who has gone for refuge. For this has been said:

“Yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti. Ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

“Mahānāma, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower.”

Kasmā [V 2.0021] upāsakoti. Ratanattayassa upāsanato. So hi buddhaṃ upāsatīti upāsako. Dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ upāsatīti upāsakoti.

Why is one called a lay follower? Because of attending upon the Triple Gem. For one attends upon the Buddha, thus one is a lay follower. One attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, thus one is a lay follower.

Kimassa sīlanti. Pañca veramaṇiyo. Yathāha –

What is their virtue? The five abstinences. As it is said:

“Yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā, kāmesumicchācārā, musāvādā, surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti. Ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako sīlavā hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

“Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from misconduct in sensual pleasures, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.”

Ko ājīvoti. Pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya dhammena samena jīvikakappanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

What is their livelihood? It is the arranging of a livelihood righteously and equitably, having abandoned the five wrong trades. For this has been said:

“Pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā. Katamā pañca. Satthavaṇijjā, sattavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, majjavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā”ti (a. ni. 5.177).

“Bhikkhus, these five trades are not to be practiced by a lay follower. Which five? Trading in weapons, trading in living beings, trading in meat, trading in intoxicants, and trading in poison. These, bhikkhus, are the five trades not to be practiced by a lay follower.”

Kā vipattīti. Yā tasseva sīlassa ca ājīvassa ca vipatti, ayamassa vipatti. Apica yāya esa caṇḍālo ceva hoti malañca patikuṭṭho ca, sāpi tassa vipattīti veditabbā. Te ca atthato assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā honti. Yathāha –

What is their downfall? Whatever is the downfall of that same virtue and livelihood, this is their downfall. Furthermore, that by which one becomes an outcast, a stain, and despised, that too should be known as their downfall. And these, in meaning, are the five qualities beginning with faithlessness. As it is said:

“Pañcahi[M 2.0022], bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti upāsakamalañca upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho hoti, dussīlo hoti, kotūhalamaṅgaliko [P 2.0114] hoti, maṅgalaṃ pacceti no kammaṃ, ito ca bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati, tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

“Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is an outcast among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and a despised lay follower. With what five? One is faithless, immoral, given to omens and auspicious signs, believes in auspicious signs and not in kamma, seeks a recipient worthy of offerings outside of this Dispensation, and performs one's first good deed there.”

Kā sampattīti. Yā cassa sīlasampadā ca ājīvasampadā ca, sā sampatti. Ye cassa ratanabhāvādikarā saddhādayo pañca dhammā. Yathāha –

What is accomplishment? Whatever is his perfection of virtue and perfection of livelihood, that is accomplishment. And also the five qualities, beginning with faith, that make him become like a jewel, and so on. As it is said:

“Pañcahi[V 2.0022], bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakaratanañca hoti upāsakapadumañca upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, kammaṃ pacceti no maṅgalaṃ, na ito bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati, idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

“Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a jewel among lay followers, a red lotus among lay followers, and a white lotus among lay followers. With what five? One is faithful, virtuous, not given to omens and auspicious signs, believes in kamma and not in auspicious signs, does not seek a recipient worthy of offerings outside of this Dispensation, and performs one's first good deed here.”

Ajjataggeti ettha ayaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. “Ajjatagge samma, dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi dissati. “Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya (kathā. 441). Ucchaggaṃ veḷagga”ntiādīsu koṭiyaṃ. “Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā (saṃ. ni. 5.374), anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 318) koṭṭhāse. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvāti evamettha attho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvaṃ. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, dakāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti attho.

In `ajjatagge` [from this day forward], this word `agga` is seen in the senses of beginning, tip, portion, and excellence. For in passages such as, ‘From this day forward, friend doorkeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs,’ it is seen in the sense of beginning. In passages such as, ‘With that very fingertip, one might touch that fingertip,’ and ‘the tip of a sugarcane, the tip of a bamboo,’ it is seen in the sense of tip. In passages such as, ‘Whether a sour portion, a sweet portion, or a bitter portion,’ and ‘I allow, bhikkhus, to divide by monastery portion or by precinct portion,’ it is seen in the sense of portion. In passages such as, ‘As far as beings, bhikkhus, whether footless or… the Tathāgata is declared foremost among them,’ it is seen in the sense of excellence. Here, however, this word should be understood in the sense of beginning. Therefore, in `ajjatagge`, the meaning should be understood thus: ‘making today the beginning.’ `Ajjataṃ` means ‘the state of being today.’ Alternatively, the reading is `ajjadagge`; the letter ‘d’ is for euphonic conjunction, and the meaning is ‘making today the beginning.’”

Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva [P 2.0115] upetaṃ, anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ “na buddho”ti vā dhammaṃ “na [M 2.0023] dhammo”ti vā saṅghaṃ “na saṅgho”ti vā vadeyyanti evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ gantvā catūhi ca paccayehi pavāretvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti.

Pāṇupetaṃ means endowed with life; that is, endowed for as long as my life continues. May the Venerable Gotama remember and know me as a lay follower and one who does what is proper, who has gone for refuge with the three refuges, and who has no other teacher. For even if my head were to be severed by a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' or of the Dhamma, 'It is not the Dhamma,' or of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha.' Having thus gone for refuge by entrusting himself, and having invited the Buddha with the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him thrice, and departed.

17. Sattame jāṇussoṇīti jāṇussoṇiṭhānantaraṃ kira nāmekaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ, taṃ yena kulena laddhaṃ, taṃ jāṇussoṇikulanti vuccati. Ayaṃ tasmiṃ kule jātattā rañño santike ca laddhajāṇussoṇisakkārattā jāṇussoṇīti vuccati. Tenupasaṅkamīti “samaṇo kira gotamo paṇḍito byatto bahussuto”ti sutvā “sace so liṅgavibhattikārakādibhedaṃ jānissati, amhehi ñātameva jānissati, aññātaṃ kiṃ jānissati. Ñātameva kathessati, aññātaṃ kiṃ kathessatī”ti cintetvā mānaddhajaṃ paggayha siṅgaṃ ukkhipitvā mahāparivārehi parivuto yena bhagavā [V 2.0023] tenupasaṅkami. Katattā ca, brāhmaṇa, akatattā cāti satthā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo idha āgacchanto na jānitukāmo atthagavesī hutvā āgato, mānaṃ pana paggayha siṅgaṃ ukkhipitvā āgato. Kiṃ nu khvassa yathā pañhassa atthaṃ jānāti, evaṃ kathite vaḍḍhi bhavissati, udāhu yathā na jānātī”ti cintetvā “yathā na jānāti, evaṃ kathite vaḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “katattā ca, brāhmaṇa, akatattā cā”ti āha.

17. In the seventh sutta, 'Jāṇussoṇi' is explained thus: Jāṇussoṇi, it is said, was the name of a certain official rank. The family that obtained that rank was called the Jāṇussoṇi family. Because he was born in that family and had gained the honor of Jāṇussoṇi from the king, he was called Jāṇussoṇi. 'He approached'—having heard, 'The ascetic Gotama is wise, articulate, and learned,' he thought, 'If he knows the distinctions of gender, inflection, case, and so on, he will only know what we already know. What unknown thing could he know? He will only speak of what is known. What unknown thing could he speak of?' Thus, raising the banner of pride and lifting his horn, surrounded by a large retinue, he approached the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase 'By what is done, brahmin, and by what is not done,' the Teacher, hearing his words, thought, 'This brahmin, in coming here, has not come as one wishing to know or seeking the meaning; rather, he has come raising his pride and lifting his horn. Will there be growth for him if the meaning of the question is explained in a way he understands, or in a way he does not understand?' Having reflected, 'Growth will come if it is explained in a way he does not understand,' and knowing this, he said, 'By what is done, brahmin, and by what is not done.'

Brāhmaṇo taṃ sutvā “samaṇo gotamo katattāpi akatattāpi niraye nibbattiṃ vadati, idaṃ ubhayakāraṇenāpi ekaṭṭhāne nibbattiyā kathitattā dujjānaṃ mahandhakāraṃ, natthi [P 2.0116] mayhaṃ ettha patiṭṭhā. Sace panāhaṃ ettakeneva tuṇhī bhaveyyaṃ, brāhmaṇānaṃ majjhe kathanakālepi maṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘tvaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ mānaṃ paggayha siṅgaṃ ukkhipitvā gatosi, ekavacaneneva tuṇhī hutvā kiñci vattuṃ nāsakkhi, imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā kathesī’ti. Tasmā parājitopi aparājitasadiso hutvā puna saggagamanapañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā ko nu kho, bho gotamāti imaṃ dutiyapañhaṃ ārabhi.

Having heard that, the brahmin thought: 'The ascetic Gotama teaches of arising in hell on account of what has been done and also on account of what has not been done. Since this is taught as arising in one place from both causes, it is difficult to understand, a great darkness. I have no footing here. Moreover, if I were to become silent with only this much, in the midst of the brahmins, even during discussion, they would say this to me: “You went to the presence of the ascetic Gotama, having held up your pride and raised your horn, yet having become silent with just one word, you were unable to say anything. Why do you speak in this matter?” Therefore, even though defeated, becoming like one who is not defeated, I will again ask the question concerning the way to heaven.' Having thought thus, he began this second question: 'Now then, good Gotama...'

Evampi [M 2.0024] tassa ahosi – “uparipañhena heṭṭhāpañhaṃ jānissāmi, heṭṭhāpañhena uparipañha”nti. Tasmāpi imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Satthā purimanayeneva cintetvā yathā na jānāti, evameva kathento punapi “katattā ca, brāhmaṇa, akatattā cā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo tasmimpi patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto “alaṃ, bho, na īdisassa purisassa santikaṃ āgatena ajānitvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati, sakavādaṃ pahāya samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ anuvattitvā mayhaṃ atthaṃ gavesissāmi, paralokamaggaṃ sodhessāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā satthāraṃ āyācanto na kho ahantiādimāha. Athassa nihatamānataṃ ñatvā satthā upari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento tena hi, brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha tena hīti kāraṇaniddeso. Yasmā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa atthaṃ ajānanto vitthāradesanaṃ yācasi, tasmāti attho. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

This thought also occurred to him: 'By means of the upper question, I will understand the lower question; by means of the lower question, I will understand the upper question.' For that reason also, he asked this question. The Teacher, having reflected in the same way as before, speaking in such a manner that he would not understand, again said, 'On account of what is done, brahmin, and on account of what is not done.' The brahmin, unable to find a footing in that either, made this resolution: 'Enough, sirs! It is not proper for one who has come into the presence of such a man to depart without understanding. Having abandoned my own doctrine, I will follow the ascetic Gotama, seek my own welfare, and clear the path to the next world.' Having made this resolution, and requesting the Teacher, he spoke the words beginning with 'Indeed, I do not...' Then, the Teacher, having known that his pride was destroyed, extending the teaching further, spoke the words beginning with 'In that case, brahmin...' Therein, 'in that case' is an indication of a reason. The meaning is: 'Because, not understanding the meaning of what was spoken concisely, you request a detailed teaching, therefore...' The remainder here has an obvious meaning.

18. Aṭṭhame āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ. Ānandoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Ekaṃsenāti ekantena. Anuviccāti anupavisitvā. Viññūti paṇḍitā. Garahantīti nindanti, avaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Sesamettha navame ca sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

18. In the eighth, 'Venerable' is an affectionate term. 'Ānanda' is the name of that elder. 'Ekaṃsena' means absolutely. 'Anuvicca' means having penetrated. 'Viññū' means the wise. 'Garahanti' means they blame, they speak dispraise. The rest here and in the ninth are all of obvious meaning.

20. Dasame [V 2.0024][P 2.0117] dunnikkhittañca padabyañjananti uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitapāḷipadameva hi atthassa byañjanattā byañjananti vuccati. Ubhayametaṃ pāḷiyāva nāmaṃ. Attho ca dunnītoti parivattetvā uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitā aṭṭhakathā. Dunnikkhittassa, bhikkhave, padabyañjanassa atthopi dunnayo hotīti parivattetvā uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitāya pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathā nāma dunnayā dunnīhārā dukkathā nāma hoti. Ekādasame vuttapaṭipakkhanayena attho veditabboti.

20. In the tenth, 'poorly placed words and expressions' means the Pāḷi taken out of order. Indeed, it is the word itself that is called 'expression' because it expresses the meaning. Both of these are names for the Pāḷi itself. 'And the meaning is badly inferred' means the commentary that is taken out of order, having been inverted. 'For poorly placed words and expressions, monks, the meaning is also badly inferred' means that the commentary on Pāḷi that is taken out of order, having been inverted, is called badly inferred, badly extracted, and badly spoken. In the eleventh, the meaning should be known by the method that is the opposite of what has been said.

Adhikaraṇavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Legal Questions, the Second.

3. Bālavaggavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Chapter on Fools

22. Tatiyassa [V 2.0025] paṭhame accayaṃ accayato na passatīti “aparajjhitvā aparaddhaṃ mayā”ti attano aparādhaṃ na passati, aparaddhaṃ mayāti vatvā daṇḍakammaṃ [M 2.0025] āharitvā na khamāpetīti attho. Accayaṃ desentassāti evaṃ vatvā daṇḍakammaṃ āharitvā khamāpentassa. Yathādhammaṃ nappaṭiggaṇhātīti “puna evaṃ na karissāmi, khamatha me”ti vuccamāno accayaṃ imaṃ yathādhammaṃ yathāsabhāvaṃ na paṭiggaṇhāti. “Ito paṭṭhāya puna evarūpaṃ mā akāsi, khamāmi tuyha”nti na vadati. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhanayeneva veditabbo.

22. In the first of the third, 'he does not see a transgression as a transgression' means that after transgressing, he does not see his own offense as 'I have done wrong'. The meaning is: having said 'I have done wrong' and brought about a penalty, he does not ask for forgiveness. 'Of one who is confessing a transgression' means of one who, having spoken thus and brought about a penalty, is asking for forgiveness. 'He does not accept it rightfully' means that when told, 'I will not do this again, forgive me,' he does not accept this transgression according to the Dhamma, according to its nature. He does not say, 'From now on, do not do such a thing again; I forgive you.' The bright side should be known by the method that is the opposite of what has been said.

23. Dutiye abbhācikkhantīti abhibhavitvā ācikkhanti, abhūtena vadanti. Dosantaroti antare patitadoso. Evarūpo hi “natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammo”tiādīni vadanto sunakkhatto viya tathāgataṃ abbhācikkhati. Saddho [P 2.0118] vā duggahitenāti yo hi ñāṇavirahitāya saddhāya atisaddho hoti muddhappasanno, sopi “buddho nāma sabbalokuttaro, sabbe tassa kesādayo bāttiṃsa koṭṭhāsā lokuttarāyevā”tiādinā nayena duggahitaṃ gaṇhitvā tathāgataṃ abbhācikkhati. Tatiyaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

23. In the second, 'they accuse falsely' means they oppress and accuse; they speak what is untrue. 'With underlying faults' means a fault has fallen within. Indeed, one like Sunakkhatta, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states,' and so on, falsely accuses the Tathāgata. 'Or a faithful one with a wrong grasp' means: for one who, with faith devoid of wisdom, is excessively faithful and blindly devoted, he too, having taken up a wrong view by way of such reasoning as, 'The one called Buddha is entirely supramundane; all his thirty-two parts, beginning with the hair, are themselves supramundane,' falsely accuses the Tathāgata. The third is of obvious meaning.

25. Catutthe neyyatthaṃ suttantanti yassa attho netabbo, taṃ netabbatthaṃ suttantaṃ. Nītattho suttantoti dīpetīti kathitattho ayaṃ suttantoti vadati. Tattha “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, dveme, bhikkhave, puggalā, tayome, bhikkhave, puggalā, cattārome, bhikkhave, puggalā”ti evarūpo suttanto neyyattho nāma. Ettha hi kiñcāpi sammāsambuddhena “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave”tiādi vuttaṃ, paramatthato pana puggalo nāma natthīti evamassa attho netabbova hoti. Ayaṃ pana attano bālatāya nītattho ayaṃ suttantoti dīpeti. Paramatthato hi puggale asati na tathāgato “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave”tiādīni vadeyya. Yasmā pana tena vuttaṃ, tasmā paramatthato atthi puggaloti gaṇhanto taṃ neyyatthaṃ suttantaṃ nītattho suttantoti dīpeti. Nītatthanti aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti evaṃ kathitatthaṃ. Ettha hi aniccameva dukkhameva anattāyevāti attho. Ayaṃ pana attano bālatāya “neyyattho ayaṃ suttanto, atthamassa āharissāmī”ti [V 2.0026] “niccaṃ nāma atthi, sukhaṃ nāma atthi, attā nāma atthī”ti gaṇhanto nītatthaṃ suttantaṃ neyyattho suttantoti dīpeti nāma. Pañcamaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

25. In the fourth sutta, 'a sutta with meaning to be inferred' is a sutta whose meaning is to be inferred. 'He declares it to be a sutta with explicit meaning' means he says, 'This sutta has a stated meaning.' Herein, a sutta such as, 'Bhikkhus, one person; bhikkhus, these two persons; bhikkhus, these three persons; bhikkhus, these four persons'—this type of sutta is called one with meaning to be inferred. For here, although the Perfectly Enlightened One has said, 'Bhikkhus, one person,' and so on, ultimately, however, there is no such thing as a person—thus its meaning is to be inferred. But this person, due to his own foolishness, declares, 'This sutta is one with explicit meaning.' For ultimately, if a person did not exist, the Tathāgata would not say, 'Bhikkhus, one person,' and so on. But because he has spoken thus, this person, taking it to mean that ultimately a person exists, declares that sutta with meaning to be inferred to be a sutta with explicit meaning. 'With explicit meaning' means having a stated meaning, such as: impermanent, suffering, not-self. Herein, indeed, the meaning is simply impermanence, simply suffering, and simply not-self. But this person, due to his own foolishness, saying, 'This sutta has meaning to be inferred, I will bring out its meaning,' and taking it to mean, 'Permanence indeed exists, happiness indeed exists, self indeed exists,' declares a sutta with explicit meaning to be a sutta with meaning to be inferred. The fifth sutta is simply one with obvious meaning.

27. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0026] paṭicchannakammantassāti pāpakammassa. Pāpaṃ [P 2.0119] hi paṭicchādetvā karonti. No cepi paṭicchādetvā karonti, pāpakammaṃ paṭicchannamevāti vuccati. Nirayoti sahokāsakā khandhā. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ khandhāva labbhanti. Sattamaṭṭhamāni uttānatthāneva.

27. In the sixth sutta, 'of one whose deeds are concealed' refers to one of evil deeds. For they do evil by concealing it. Even if they do not do it by concealing it, an evil deed is still called 'concealed.' 'Hell' means the aggregates together with their location. In the animal realm, only the aggregates are obtained. The seventh and eighth suttas are simply of obvious meaning.

30. Navame paṭiggāhāti paṭiggāhakā, dussīlaṃ puggalaṃ dve ṭhānāni paṭiggaṇhantīti attho.

30. In the ninth sutta, 'recipients' means those that receive. The meaning is that two states receive an immoral person.

31. Dasame atthavaseti kāraṇāni. Araññavanapatthānīti araññāni ca vanapatthāni ca. Tattha kiñcāpi abhidhamme nippariyāyena “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā, sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) vuttaṃ, tathāpi yaṃ taṃ “pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) āraññakaṅganipphādakaṃ senāsanaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva adhippetanti veditabbaṃ. Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasīyati na vapīyati. Pantānīti pariyantāni atidūrāni, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti lokiyalokuttaraṃ phāsuvihāraṃ. Pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamānoti pacchime mama sāvake anukampanto.

31. In the tenth sutta, 'reasons' means causes. 'Forests and remote tracts' means both forests and wilderness areas. Therein, although in the Abhidhamma it is stated unequivocally, 'having gone beyond the boundary pillar, all that is wilderness,' what is meant here, it should be understood, is that dwelling place that enables the forest-dweller's practice, described as being 'at a minimum, five hundred bow-lengths away.' 'Wilderness areas' are places beyond the vicinity of a village, where people do not frequent, and where no plowing or sowing is done. 'Secluded' means on the periphery, very far. 'Dwelling happily in this very life' refers to a pleasant abiding, both worldly and supramundane. 'Having compassion for future generations' means having compassion for my future disciples.

32. Ekādasame vijjābhāgiyāti vijjākoṭṭhāsikā. Samathoti cittekaggatā. Vipassanāti saṅkhārapariggāhakañāṇaṃ. Kamatthamanubhotīti katamaṃ atthaṃ ārādheti sampādeti paripūreti. Cittaṃ bhāvīyatīti maggacittaṃ bhāvīyati brūhīyati vaḍḍhīyati. Yo rāgo, so pahīyatīti yo rajjanakavasena rāgo, so pahīyati. Rāgo hi maggacittassa paccanīko, maggacittaṃ rāgassa ca. Rāgakkhaṇe [P 2.0120] maggacittaṃ natthi, maggacittakkhaṇe rāgo natthi. Yadā pana rāgo uppajjati, tadā maggacittassa uppattiṃ nivāreti, padaṃ pacchindati. Yadā pana maggacittaṃ uppajjati, tadā rāgaṃ samūlakaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā samugghātentameva uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ – “rāgo pahīyatī”ti.

32. In the eleventh sutta, 'pertaining to knowledge' means belonging to the portion of knowledge. 'Tranquility' is one-pointedness of mind. 'Insight' is the knowledge that comprehends formations. 'For what purpose does one experience it?' means what benefit does one accomplish, achieve, and fulfill? 'The mind is developed' means the path-mind is developed, augmented, and increased. 'Whatever lust, that is abandoned' means whatever lust there is by way of attachment, that is abandoned. For lust is an adversary to the path-mind, and the path-mind is an adversary to lust. At the moment of lust, the path-mind is not present; at the moment of the path-mind, lust is not present. But when lust arises, it prevents the arising of the path-mind; it cuts off its basis. But when the path-mind arises, it arises only by having pulled out lust together with its root and utterly eradicating it. Therefore, it is said: 'Lust is abandoned.'

Vipassanā, bhikkhave, bhāvitāti vipassanāñāṇaṃ brūhitaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Paññā bhāvīyatīti maggapaññā [V 2.0027] bhāvīyati brūhīyati vaḍḍhīyati. Yā avijjā, sā pahīyatīti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vaṭṭamūlikā mahāavijjā pahīyati. Avijjā hi maggapaññāya paccanīkā, maggapaññā avijjāya. Avijjākkhaṇe maggapaññā natthi[M 2.0027], maggapaññākkhaṇe avijjā natthi. Yadā pana avijjā uppajjati, tadā maggapaññāya uppattiṃ nivāreti, padaṃ pacchindati. Yadā maggapaññā uppajjati, tadā avijjaṃ samūlikaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā samugghātayamānāva uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ – “avijjā pahīyatī”ti. Iti maggacittaṃ maggapaññāti dvepi sahajātadhammāva kathitā.

'Insight, bhikkhus, when developed,' means insight-knowledge is augmented and increased. 'Wisdom is developed' means path-wisdom is developed, augmented, and increased. 'Whatever ignorance, that is abandoned' means the great ignorance which is the root of the cycle of existence is abandoned in eight instances. For ignorance is the adversary to path-wisdom, and path-wisdom is the adversary to ignorance. At the moment of ignorance, path-wisdom is not present; at the moment of path-wisdom, ignorance is not present. But when ignorance arises, it prevents the arising of path-wisdom; it cuts off its basis. When path-wisdom arises, it does so only while uprooting ignorance together with its root and completely eradicating it. Therefore, it is said: 'Ignorance is abandoned.' Thus, both path-mind and path-wisdom are spoken of as co-arisen phenomena.

Rāgupakkiliṭṭhaṃ vā, bhikkhave, cittaṃ na vimuccatīti rāgena upakkiliṭṭhattā maggacittaṃ na vimuccatīti dasseti. Avijjupakkiliṭṭhā vā paññā na bhāvīyatīti avijjāya upakkiliṭṭhattā maggapaññā na bhāvīyatīti dasseti. Iti kho, bhikkhaveti evaṃ kho, bhikkhave. Rāgavirāgā cetovimuttīti rāgassa khayavirāgena cetovimutti nāma hoti. Phalasamādhissetaṃ nāmaṃ. Avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttīti avijjāya khayavirāgena paññāvimutti nāma hoti. Imasmiṃ sutte nānākkhaṇikā samādhivipassanā kathitāti.

'A mind defiled by lust, bhikkhus, is not liberated'—this shows that the path-mind is not liberated because of being defiled by lust. 'Or wisdom defiled by ignorance is not developed'—this shows that path-wisdom is not developed because of being defiled by ignorance. 'Thus indeed, bhikkhus' means 'in this way indeed, bhikkhus.' 'Through the fading away of lust, there is liberation of mind'—this is called liberation of mind through the destruction and fading away of lust. This is a name for the concentration of fruition. 'Through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom'—this is called liberation by wisdom through the destruction and fading away of ignorance. In this sutta, concentration and insight occurring at different moments are taught.

Bālavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the Foolish.

4. Samacittavaggavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Composed Mind

33. Catutthassa [V 2.0028][P 2.0121] paṭhame asappurisabhūmīti asappurisānaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ. Sappurisabhūmiyampi eseva nayo. Akataññūti kataṃ na jānāti. Akatavedīti kataṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā na jānāti. Upaññātanti vaṇṇitaṃ thomitaṃ pasatthaṃ. Yadidanti yā ayaṃ. Akataññutā akataveditāti parena katassa upakārassa ajānanañceva pākaṭaṃ katvā ajānanañca. Kevalāti sakalā. Sukkapakkhepi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

33. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, 'the ground of an ignoble person' means the foundation of ignoble persons. For 'the ground of a noble person' as well, this is the method. 'Ungrateful' means one who does not acknowledge a favor that has been done. 'Unthankful' means one who does not make known the favor that was done. 'Upaññāta' means lauded, celebrated, praised. 'Yadidaṃ' means 'that which.' 'Ungratitude and unthankfulness' means not acknowledging the help done by another, and not making that help known. 'Kevalā' means entire. In the bright counterpart as well, the meaning should be understood in the same way that has been stated.

34. Dutiye mātu ca pitu cāti janakamātu ca janakapitu ca. Ekena, bhikkhave, aṃsena mātaraṃ parihareyyāti ekasmiṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā mātaraṃ paṭijaggeyya. Ekena aṃsena pitaraṃ parihareyyāti ekasmiṃ aṃsakūṭe ṭhapetvā pitaraṃ paṭijaggeyya. Vassasatāyuko vassasatajīvīti vassasatāyukakāle jāto sakalaṃ vassasataṃ jīvanto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace putto nāma “mātāpitūnaṃ paṭikarissāmī”ti uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya dakkhiṇe aṃsakūṭe mātaraṃ, vāme pitaraṃ [M 2.0028] ṭhapetvā vassasatāyuko sakalampi vassasataṃ jīvamāno parihareyya. So ca nesaṃ ucchādanaparimaddananhāpanasambāhanenāti so ca putto nesaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ aṃsakūṭesu ṭhitānaṃyeva duggandhapaṭivinodanatthaṃ sugandhakaraṇena ucchādanena, parissamavinodanatthaṃ hatthaparimaddanena, sītuṇhakāle ca uṇhodakasītodakanhāpanena, hatthapādādīnaṃ ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanasaṅkhātena sambāhanena upaṭṭhānaṃ kareyya. Te ca tatthevāti te ca mātāpitaro tattheva tassa aṃsakūṭesu nisinnāva muttakarīsaṃ cajeyyuṃ. Natveva [P 2.0122], bhikkhaveti, bhikkhave, evampi natveva mātāpitūnaṃ kataṃ vā hoti paṭikataṃ vā.

34. In the second discourse, 'of mother and of father' means one's birth mother and birth father. 'Bhikkhus, with one shoulder one should carry the mother' means, having placed the mother on one shoulder-tip, one should attend to her. 'With one shoulder one should carry the father' means, having placed the father on one shoulder-tip, one should attend to him. 'Having a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years' means being born at a time when the lifespan is a hundred years and living for the entire hundred years. This is what is meant: If a son, thinking, 'I will repay my parents,' were to rise up and place his mother on his right shoulder and his father on his left, and having a lifespan of a hundred years, were to carry them for the entire hundred years while living; and if he were to attend to them, while they are on his shoulders, with anointing by fragrant applications to dispel foul odors, with massaging by hand to dispel fatigue, with bathing in hot and cold water during cold and hot seasons, and with rubbing, which is the stretching and contracting of their hands and feet; and if those parents, while seated right there on his shoulders, were to discharge urine and feces—still, Bhikkhus, even by this, what should be done for his parents has not been done, nor has it been repaid.

Issarādhipacce rajjeti cakkavattirajjaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Āpādakāti vaḍḍhakā anupālakā. Puttā hi mātāpitūhi vaḍḍhitā ceva anupālitā ca. Posakāti hatthapāde vaḍḍhetvā hadayalohitaṃ pāyetvā posakā. Puttā hi mātāpitūhi puṭṭhā bhatā annapānādīhi paṭijaggitā. Imassa lokassa dassetāroti sace hi mātāpitaro jātadivaseyeva puttaṃ pāde gahetvā araññe vā nadiyaṃ vā papāte vā khipeyyuṃ, imasmiṃ loke iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ na passeyya. Evaṃ akatvā āpāditattā [V 2.0029] positattā esa imasmiṃ loke iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ mātāpitaro nissāya passatīti tyāssa imassa lokassa dassetāro nāma honti. Samādapetīti gaṇhāpeti. Imasmiṃ sutte saddhāsīlacāgapaññā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā. Dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherasadisova bhikkhu tesu patiṭṭhāpeti nāmāti veditabbo.

He said the words, 'reigns with sovereignty and supremacy,' only with reference to the state of a wheel-turning monarch. As for 'bringers-forth' (āpādakā): they are those who cause to grow and those who constantly protect. Indeed, children are both caused to grow and constantly protected by their parents. As for 'nourishers' (posakā): they are those who nourish by causing the hands and feet to grow and by giving them the heart's blood to drink. Indeed, children are nourished, supported, and tended to with food, drink, and so on by their parents. 'Showers of this world' (imassa lokassa dassetāro): For if parents, on the very day of birth, were to take their child by the feet and throw him into a forest, or a river, or off a cliff, he would not see desirable and undesirable objects in this world. Because they do not do so, and because he has been brought forth and nourished, this child sees desirable and undesirable objects in this world by depending on his parents. Therefore, they are called 'showers of this world' to him. 'He causes to undertake' (samādapeti) means 'he causes to grasp' (gaṇhāpeti). In this sutta, faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom are taught. It should be understood thus: a bhikkhu who is just like the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, is one who establishes (others) in these qualities.

35. Tatiye tenupasaṅkamīti so hi brāhmaṇo “samaṇo kira gotamo kathitaṃ vissajjeti, pucchāyassa virajjhanaṃ nāma natthi. Ahamassa virajjhanapañhaṃ abhisaṅkharissāmī”ti paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā gabbhadvāraṃ pidahitvā nisinno cintetuṃ ārabhi. Athassa etadahosi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne uccāsaddamahāsaddo vattati, cittaṃ na ekaggaṃ hoti, bhūmigharaṃ kāressāmī”ti bhūmigharaṃ kāretvā tattha pavisitvā – “evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ kathessati, evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ kathessatī”ti ekaṃ gaṇhitvā ekaṃ [M 2.0029] vissajjento sakaladivasaṃ kiñci passituṃ nāsakkhi. Tassa imināva nīhārena cattāro māsā vītivattā. So catunnaṃ māsānaṃ accayena ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ nāma [P 2.0123] addasa. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ahaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘kiṃvādī bhava’nti pucchissāmi. Sace ‘kiriyavādimhī’ti vakkhati, ‘sabbākusalānaṃ nāma tumhe kiriyaṃ vadethā’ti naṃ niggaṇhissāmi. Sace ‘akiriyavādimhī’ti vakkhati, ‘kusaladhammānaṃ nāma tumhe akiriyaṃ vadethā’ti naṃ niggaṇhissāmi. Idañhi ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho neva uggilituṃ sakkhissati na niggilituṃ. Evaṃ mama jayo bhavissati, samaṇassa gotamassa parājayo”ti uṭṭhāya apphoṭetvā bhūmigharā nikkhamma “evarūpaṃ pañhaṃ pucchantena na ekakena gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti nagare ghosanaṃ kāretvā sakalanāgarehi parivuto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Kiṃvādīti kiṃladdhiko. Kimakkhāyīti kiṃ nāma sāvakānaṃ paṭipadaṃ akkhāyīti pucchi. Athassa bhagavā catūhi māsehi pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā “diṭṭho me samaṇassa gotamassa parājayapañho”ti mānaṃ paggayha āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā ekapadeneva taṃ pañhaṃ bhindanto kiriyavādī cāhaṃ, brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Atha brāhmaṇo attano mānaṃ apanetvā bhagavantaṃ āyācanto yathākathaṃ panātiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

35. In the third discourse, 'he approached' means that brahmin thought, “The ascetic Gotama, it is said, can answer what is asked; there is no such thing as his being defeated in questioning. I shall devise a question that will cause his failure.” After eating choice food, he sealed the door of his private chamber and sat down to ponder. Then it occurred to him: “A great clamor prevails here; my mind is not concentrated. I shall construct an underground chamber.” Having constructed an underground chamber, he entered it and thought, “If asked thus, he will answer thus; if asked thus, he will answer thus.” Thus, grasping one answer and dismissing another, he was unable to make any headway throughout the day. In this way, four months passed for him. At the end of the four months, he found a double-edged question. It occurred to him thus: “I shall approach the ascetic Gotama and ask, ‘What is your doctrine?’ If he says, ‘I profess action,’ I shall refute him by saying, ‘Do you then profess the action of all unwholesome things?’ If he says, ‘I profess non-action,’ I shall refute him by saying, ‘Do you then profess the non-action of wholesome things?’ Asked this double-edged question, he will be unable either to swallow it or to spit it out. Thus, I shall win, and the ascetic Gotama will be defeated.” Rising up and clapping his hands, he emerged from the underground chamber. Thinking, ‘One should not go alone to ask such a question,’ he had a proclamation made in the city. Then, surrounded by the entire populace, he approached the Blessed One. “What do you profess?” means “What view do you hold?” “What do you declare?” means “What practice do you declare for your disciples?” he asked. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the brahmin had come with his question prepared for four months, swollen with pride and thinking, ‘I have found the question for the defeat of the ascetic Gotama,’ shattered his question with a single word, saying, ‘I profess action, brahmin,’ and so on. Then the brahmin, setting aside his pride, entreated the Blessed One, saying, ‘How is that?’ and so on. The rest here is clear in meaning.

36. Catutthe dakkhiṇeyyāti dakkhiṇā vuccati dānaṃ, tassa paṭiggahaṇayuttā kati puggalāti pucchati. Sekhoti iminā satta sekkhe dasseti. Ettha ca sīlavantaputhujjanopi sotāpanneneva [V 2.0030] saṅgahito. Āhuneyyā yajamānānaṃ hontīti dānaṃ dadantānaṃ āhunassa arahā dānapaṭiggāhakā nāma hontīti attho. Khettanti vatthu patiṭṭhā, puññassa viruhanaṭṭhānanti attho.

36. In the fourth sutta, regarding 'worthy of offerings': a gift is called a 'dakkhiṇā'. He asks, 'How many persons are suitable for receiving it?' By 'a learner,' he indicates the seven learners. And here, even a virtuous ordinary person is included with the stream-enterer. As for 'they are worthy of offerings for those who give,' the meaning is: for those who give gifts, they are worthy recipients of the offering, that is, they are called recipients of the gift. As for 'a field,' the meaning is: it is a basis, a foundation, a place for the sprouting of the seed of merit.

37. Pañcame [P 2.0124] pubbārāmeti sāvatthito puratthimadisābhāge ārāme. Migāramātupāsādeti visākhāya upāsikāya pāsāde. Sā hi migāraseṭṭhinā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapitattāpi, sabbajeṭṭhakassa puttassa ayyakaseṭṭhinova samānanāmakattāpi migāramātāti vuccati. Tāya kārito sahassagabbho pāsādo migāramātupāsādo nāma. Thero [M 2.0030] tasmiṃ viharati. Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputtoti tasmiṃ pāsāde viharanto dhammasenāpatisāriputtatthero.

37. In the fifth sutta, as for 'in the Pubbārāma': in the park in the eastern quarter from Sāvatthī. As for 'in the Migāramātupāsāda': in the mansion of the female lay disciple Visākhā. Indeed, she is called 'Migāramātā' both because she was placed in the position of a mother by the merchant Migāra, and also because her eldest son had the same name as his grandfather, the merchant. The mansion with a thousand chambers, caused to be built by her, is named the Migāramātupāsāda. The Elder dwells therein. As for 'There, the Venerable Sāriputta': it refers to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, dwelling in that mansion.

Bhikkhū āmantesīti kasmiṃ kāle āmantesi? Kānici hi suttāni purebhatte bhāsitāni atthi, kānici pacchābhatte, kānici purimayāme, kānici majjhimayāme, kānici pacchimayāme. Idaṃ pana samacittapaṭipadāsuttaṃ pacchābhatte bhāsitaṃ. Tasmā sāyanhasamaye āmantesi.

As for 'He addressed the bhikkhus': at what time did he address them? Indeed, some suttas are spoken before the meal, some after the meal, some in the first watch, some in the middle watch, and some in the last watch. This Samacittapaṭipadā Sutta, however, was spoken after the meal. Therefore, he addressed them in the evening.

Na kevalaṃ cetaṃ thereneva bhāsitaṃ, tathāgatenāpi bhāsitaṃ. Kattha nisīditvāti? Visākhāya ratanapāsāde nisīditvā. Tathāgato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsati vassāni anibaddhavāso hutvā yattha yattha phāsukaṃ hoti, tattha tattheva gantvā vasi. Paṭhamaṃ antovassañhi isipatane dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā aṭṭhārasa mahābrahmakoṭiyo amatapānaṃ pāyetvā bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya isipatane vasi. Dutiyaṃ antovassaṃ rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane, tatiyacatutthānipi tattheva, pañcamaṃ antovassaṃ vesāliṃ upanissāya mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ antovassaṃ makulapabbate, sattamaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavane, aṭṭhamaṃ bhagge susumāragiraṃ nissāya bhesakaḷāvane, navamaṃ kosambiyaṃ, dasamaṃ pālileyyake vanasaṇḍe, ekādasamaṃ nālāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāme, dvādasamaṃ verañjāyaṃ, terasamaṃ cāliyapabbate, cuddasamaṃ jetavane, pañcadasamaṃ kapilavatthusmiṃ, soḷasamaṃ āḷavakaṃ dametvā caturāsītipāṇasahassāni amatapānaṃ pāyetvā āḷaviyaṃ, sattarasamaṃ rājagaheyeva, aṭṭhārasamaṃ cāliyapabbateyeva, tathā ekūnavīsatimaṃ, vīsatimaṃ pana antovassaṃ rājagahaṃyeva [P 2.0125] upanissāya vasi. Evaṃ vīsati vassāni anibaddhavāso hutvā yattha yattha phāsukaṃ hoti, tattha tattheva vasi.

And not only was this spoken by the Elder, but it was also spoken by the Tathāgata. Where did he sit? He sat in Visākhā's jeweled mansion. For the Tathāgata, for the first twenty years after his enlightenment, lived without a fixed abode, going wherever it was comfortable and staying there. During the first rains-retreat, after setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at Isipatana, he caused eighteen koṭis of great Brahmās to drink the deathless nectar and stayed near Bārāṇasī, at Isipatana. During the second rains-retreat, he stayed near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. The third and fourth also there. During the fifth rains-retreat, he stayed near Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Peaked-Roof Hall. During the sixth rains-retreat, on Mount Makula. The seventh, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The eighth, near Susumāragira in the Bhaggas country, in the Bhesakaḷā forest. The ninth, in Kosambī. The tenth, in the Pālileyyaka forest thicket. The eleventh, in the brahmin village of Nālā. The twelfth, in Verañjā. The thirteenth, on Mount Cāliya. The fourteenth, in Jetavana. The fifteenth, in Kapilavatthu. During the sixteenth, after taming Āḷavaka and causing eighty-four thousand beings to drink the deathless nectar, he stayed in Āḷavī. The seventeenth, again in Rājagaha. The eighteenth, again on Mount Cāliya. Likewise the nineteenth. But during the twentieth rains-retreat, he stayed right near Rājagaha. Thus, for twenty years, he lived without a fixed abode, staying wherever it was comfortable.

Tato [V 2.0031] paṭṭhāya pana dve senāsanāni dhuvaparibhogāni akāsi. Katarāni dve? Jetavanañca pubbārāmañca. Kasmā? Dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ guṇamahantatāya. Anāthapiṇḍikassa hi visākhāya ca guṇaṃ sandhāya guṇaṃ paṭicca satthā tāni senāsanāni dhuvaparibhogena paribhuñji. Utuvassaṃ cārikaṃ caritvāpi hi antovasse dvīsuyeva senāsanesu vasati. Evaṃ vasanto [M 2.0031] pana jetavane rattiṃ vasitvā punadivase bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto dakkhiṇadvārena sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā pubbārāme divāvihāraṃ karoti. Pubbārāme rattiṃ vasitvā punadivase pācīnadvārena sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā jetavane divāvihāraṃ karoti. Tasmiṃ pana divase sammāsambuddho jetavaneyeva vasi. Yattha katthaci vasantassa cassa pañcavidhakiccaṃ avijahitameva hoti. Taṃ heṭṭhā vitthāritameva. Tesu kiccesu pacchimayāmakiccakāle bhagavā lokaṃ olokento sāvatthivāsīnañca samantā ca sāvatthiyā gāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanaparame ṭhāne aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhisamayabhāvaṃ addasa.

From that time onwards, however, He made two monasteries His places of permanent use. Which two? The Jetavana and the Pubbārāma. Why? Because of the greatness of the virtue of two families. Indeed, with reference to and on account of the virtue of Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, the Teacher made use of those monasteries as His permanent residences. Indeed, even after travelling on tour during the winter and summer seasons, He would reside in only these two monasteries during the rains-retreat. Now, while residing thus, having stayed the night at Jetavana, on the next day, surrounded by the community of monks, He would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the southern gate, and departing through the eastern gate, He would make His day-sojourn at the Pubbārāma. Having stayed the night at the Pubbārāma, on the next day He would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the eastern gate, and departing through the southern gate, He would make His day-sojourn at the Jetavana. On that particular day, however, the Perfectly Enlightened One resided in the Jetavana itself. And for Him, residing in any place whatsoever, the fivefold duty is indeed not abandoned. That has indeed been elaborated upon below. Among those duties, at the time for the duty of the last watch of the night, the Blessed One, while surveying the world, saw the potential for realization of the residents of Sāvatthī and of innumerable beings in places within the range of a gāvuta, half a yojana, and a yojana all around Sāvatthī.

Tato “kasmiṃ nu kho kāle abhisamayo bhavissatī”ti olokento “sāyanhasamaye”ti disvā “mayi nu kho kathente abhisamayo bhavissati, sāvake kathente bhavissatī”ti “sāriputtatthere kathente bhavissatī”ti addasa. Tato “kattha nisīditvā kathente bhavissatī”ti olokento “visākhāya ratanapāsāde nisīditvā”ti disvā “buddhānaṃ nāma tayo sāvakasannipātā honti, aggasāvakānaṃ eko. Tesu ajja dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa sāvakasannipāto bhavissatī”ti addasa. Disvā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā nivatthanivāsano [P 2.0126] sugatacīvaraṃ pārupitvā selamayapattaṃ ādāya bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā piṇḍāya caranto bhikkhusaṅghassa sulabhapiṇḍapātaṃ katvā vātappahatā viya nāvā paṭinivattitvā dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā bahidvāre aṭṭhāsi. Tato asīti mahāsāvakā bhikkhuniparisā upāsakaparisā upāsikāparisāti catasso parisā satthāraṃ parivārayiṃsu.

Then, while looking, 'At what time, I wonder, will the realization occur?' he saw, 'In the evening time.' Having seen this, he considered, 'I wonder, will the realization occur while I am teaching, or while a disciple is teaching?' and saw, 'It will occur while the Elder Sāriputta is teaching.' Then, while looking, 'Where, having sat down, will it occur while he is teaching?' he saw, 'Having sat down in Visākhā's jeweled mansion.' Having seen this, he saw, 'For Buddhas, there are three assemblies of disciples; for the chief disciples, there is one. Among these, today the assembly of disciples of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, will occur.' Having seen this, early in the morning, having attended to his body, having put on his under-robe and draped the Sugata's outer robe, and having taken the stone bowl, surrounded by the community of monks, he entered the city by the southern gate. While wandering for alms-food, having made alms-food easy to obtain for the community of monks, he turned back like a boat struck by the wind. Having exited by the southern gate, he stood outside the gate. Then, the eighty great disciples, the assembly of bhikkhunīs, the assembly of male lay disciples, and the assembly of female lay disciples—these four assemblies—surrounded the Teacher.

Satthā sāriputtattheraṃ āmantesi – “sāriputta, tayā pubbārāmaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati, tava ca parisaṃ gahetvā gacchāhī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero attano parivārehi pañcahi bhikkhusatehi parivuto pubbārāmaṃ agamāsi. Eteneva niyāmena asīti mahāsāvake pubbārāmameva pesetvā sayaṃ ekena ānandatthereneva saddhiṃ jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Ānandattheropi vihāre satthu vattaṃ [V 2.0032] katvā vanditvā “pubbārāmaṃ gacchāmi, bhante”ti āha. Evaṃ [M 2.0032] karohi ānandāti. Satthāraṃ vanditvā tattheva agamāsi. Satthā ekakova jetavane ohīno.

The Teacher addressed the Elder Sāriputta, 'Sāriputta, it is suitable for you to go to the Eastern Monastery. Take your assembly and go.' 'Very well, Venerable Sir,' the Elder replied, and surrounded by his own retinue of five hundred monks, he went to the Eastern Monastery. In this very manner, having sent the eighty great disciples to the Eastern Monastery, he himself went to Jetavana accompanied only by the Elder Ānanda. The Elder Ānanda, too, having performed his duties for the Teacher in the monastery and paid homage, said, 'Venerable Sir, I am going to the Eastern Monastery.' 'Ānanda, do so.' Having paid homage to the Teacher, he went to that very place. The Teacher remained all alone in Jetavana.

Taṃ divasañhi catasso parisā therasseva dhammakathaṃ sotukāmā ahesuṃ. Kosalamahārājāpi balakāyena parivuto pubbārāmameva gato. Tathā pañcasataupāsakaparivāro anāthapiṇḍiko. Visākhā pana mahāupāsikā dvīhi jaṅghasahassehi parivuto agamāsi. Sattapaṇṇāsāya kulasatasahassānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne sāvatthinagare gehapālakadārake ṭhapetvā sesajano gandhacuṇṇamālādīni gahetvā pubbārāmameva agamāsi. Catūsu dvāragāmesu gāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanaparamaṭṭhāne sabbeyeva manussā gandhacuṇṇamālādihatthā pubbārāmameva agamaṃsu. Sakalavihāro missakapupphehi abhikiṇṇo viya ahosi.

Indeed, on that day, the four assemblies were desirous of hearing only the Elder's Dhamma talk. The great King of Kosala, too, surrounded by his army, went only to the Pubbārāma. Likewise, Anāthapiṇḍika, with a retinue of five hundred lay disciples, also went. But Visākhā, the great female lay disciple, surrounded by two thousand attendants, went as well. In the city of Sāvatthī, the dwelling place of fifty-seven hundred thousand families, having left behind the young boys guarding the houses, the remaining people took fragrant powders, garlands, and so forth, and went only to the Pubbārāma. From the four gate-villages, from places at a distance of a gāvuta, half a yojana, and a yojana, all the people, with fragrant powders, garlands, and so forth in hand, went only to the Pubbārāma. The entire monastery was as if strewn with a mix of flowers.

Dhammasenāpatisāriputtattheropi kho vihāraṃ gantvā vihārapariveṇe aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Bhikkhū therassa āsanaṃ paññāpayiṃsu. Thero tattha nisīditvā upaṭṭhākattherena vatte kate bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādaṃ katvā gandhakuṭiṃ [P 2.0127] pavisitvā samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdi. So paricchinnakālavasena samāpattito vuṭṭhāya aciravatiṃ gantvā rajojallaṃ pavāhetvā paṭippassaddhadaratho otiṇṇatittheneva uttaritvā nivatthanivāsano saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā aṭṭhāsi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi sammukhasammukhaṭṭhānena otaritvā sarīre rajojallaṃ pavāhetvā paccuttaritvā theraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Antovihārepi therassa dhammāsanaṃ paññāpayiṃsu. Catassopi parisā attano attano okāsaṃ ñatvā maggaṃ ṭhapetvā nisīdiṃsu. Sāriputtattheropi pañcabhikkhusataparivāro dhammasabhaṃ āgantvā sīhamatthakappatiṭṭhite samussitasetacchatte ratanapallaṅke cittabījaniṃ gahetvā puratthābhimukho nisīdi. Nisīditvā parisaṃ oloketvā – “mahatī vatāyaṃ parisā, imissā na appamattikā parittakadhammadesanā anucchavikā, kataradhammadesanā nu kho anucchavikā bhavissatī”ti tīṇi piṭakāni āvajjamāno imaṃ saṃyojanapariyāya dhammadesanaṃ addasa.

The Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, also, having gone to the Pubbārāma monastery, stood in an open space within the monastery compound. The monks prepared a seat for the Elder. The Elder, having sat down in that place, after the duties had been performed by the attendant Elder, gave an exhortation to the Saṅgha of monks, entered the perfumed chamber, and having entered into meditative attainment, sat down. That Elder, having emerged from meditative attainment at the determined time, went to the Aciravatī river, and having washed away the adventitious dust and bodily impurities, with his distress calmed, he ascended by the very ford where he had descended. Having put on his lower robe and draped his outer robe, he stood. The Saṅgha of monks also, having descended from a place directly opposite, washed away the adventitious dust and bodily impurities from their bodies, ascended again, and surrounded the Elder. Inside the monastery also, they prepared a Dhamma-seat for the Elder. The four assemblies also, knowing their own respective places, left the path open and sat down. The Elder Sāriputta also, surrounded by five hundred monks, having come to the Dhamma hall, took a decorated fan and sat facing east on the jeweled couch, which was established on a lion's head and had a well-raised white umbrella. Having sat down and looked upon the assembly, he reflected: 'Indeed, this assembly is great. For this assembly, a Dhamma discourse of small measure, a brief one, is not suitable. What Dhamma discourse, I wonder, would be suitable?' Thus, while reflecting upon the three Piṭakas, he saw this Dhamma discourse, the Exposition of the Fetters.

Evaṃ [M 2.0033] desanaṃ sallakkhetvā taṃ desetukāmo bhikkhū āmantesi āvuso, bhikkhaveti. Āvusoti hi avatvā, bhikkhaveti vacanaṃ buddhālāpo nāma hoti, ayaṃ panāyasmā “dasabalena samānaṃ ālapanaṃ na karissāmī”ti satthu gāravavasena sāvakālāpaṃ karonto, “āvuso [V 2.0033] bhikkhave”ti āha. Etadavocāti etaṃ “ajjhattasaṃyojanañca, āvuso, puggalaṃ desessāmi bahiddhāsaṃyojanañcā”ti dhammadesanāpadaṃ avoca.

Thus, having noted the discourse and wishing to teach it, he addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' Indeed, the address 'monks,' without saying 'friends,' is called the address of a Buddha. But this venerable one, out of respect for the Teacher, thinking, 'I will not make an address similar to that of the Ten-Powered One,' made the address of a disciple, saying, 'Friends, monks.' As for etadavoca ('he said this'), he spoke this phrase of the Dhamma discourse: 'Friends, I will teach of the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters.'

Tasmiṃ pana ratanapāsāde adhivattho eko sotāpanno devaputto atthi, so buddhehi vā sāvakehi vā desanāya āraddhamattāyayeva jānāti – “ayaṃ desanā uttānikā bhavissati, ayaṃ gambhīrā. Ayaṃ jhānanissitā bhavissati, ayaṃ vipassanānissitā. Ayaṃ magganissitā ayaṃ phalanissitā, ayaṃ nibbānanissitā”ti. So tasmimpi divase therena desanāya [P 2.0128] āraddhamattāya evaṃ aññāsi – “yena nīhārena mayhaṃ ayyena dhammasenāpatinā sāriputtattherena desanā āraddhā, ayaṃ desanā vipassanāgāḷhā bhavissati, chahi mukhehi vipassanaṃ kathessati. Desanāpariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissanti, sotāpannādīnaṃ pana devamanussānaṃ paricchedo na bhavissati. Desanāya anucchavikaṃ katvā mayhaṃ ayyassa sādhukāraṃ dassāmī”ti devānubhāvena mahantaṃ saddaṃ katvā – “sādhu sādhu ayyā”ti āha.

In that jeweled pavilion, there dwells a stream-enterer deva who, when a discourse by the Buddhas or their disciples is just begun, immediately knows: 'This discourse will be superficial; this one, profound. This one will be based on jhāna; this one, on insight. This one will be based on the path, this on the fruit, and this on Nibbāna.' On that very day, when the Elder had just begun his discourse, the deva understood: 'From the way my noble one, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, has begun this discourse, it will be deeply imbued with insight. He will teach insight through six aspects. At the conclusion of the discourse, one hundred thousand koṭis of devas will attain Arahantship, and there will be no limit to the number of stream-enterers and others among devas and humans. Having done what is fitting for the discourse, I shall give acclamation to my noble one.' With his divine power, he made a great sound, saying, 'Excellent, excellent, noble one!'

Devarājena sādhukāre dinne parivārakapāsādasahasse adhivatthā devatā sabbāva sādhukāraṃ adaṃsu. Tāsaṃ sādhukārasaddena sabbā pubbārāme vasanadevatā, tāsaṃ saddena gāvutamatte devatā, tato aḍḍhayojane yojaneti etenupāyena ekacakkavāḷe, dvīsu cakkavāḷesu, tīsu cakkavāḷesūti dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā sādhukāramadaṃsu. Tāsaṃ sādhukārasaddena pathaviṭṭhakanāgā ca ākāsaṭṭhakadevatā ca. Tato abbhavalāhakā, uṇhavalāhakā, sītavalāhakā, vassavalāhakā, cātumahārājikā cattāro mahārājāno, tāvatiṃsā devatā, sakko devarājā, yāmā devatā, suyāmo devarājā[M 2.0034], tusitā devatā, santusito devarājā, nimmānaratī devatā, sunimmito devarājā, vasavattī devatā, vasavattī devarājā, brahmapārisajjā, brahmapurohitā, mahābrahmāno, parittābhā, appamāṇābhā, ābhassarā, parittasubhā, appamāṇasubhā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalā, avihā, atappā, sudassā, sudassī, akaniṭṭhā devatāti asaññe ca arūpāvacarasatte ca ṭhapetvā sotāyatanapavattiṭṭhāne sabbā devatā sādhukāramadaṃsu.

When the king of devas gave his approval, all the devas dwelling in the thousand surrounding pavilions also gave their approval. At the sound of their approval, all the devas residing in the Eastern Park gave their approval; at their sound, the devas within a gāvuta, then half a yojana, a full yojana, and so on—by this method, throughout one world-system, two world-systems, three world-systems, up to ten thousand world-systems, the devas gave their approval. At the sound of their approval, the nāgas beneath the earth and the devas established in the sky also gave their approval. Then, the devas of the ordinary clouds, the devas of the hot clouds, the devas of the cold clouds, and the devas of the rain clouds; the devas of the Cātumahārājika realm and the Four Great Kings; the devas of the Thirty-Three, Sakka the king of devas; the Yāma devas, Suyāma the king of devas; the Tusita devas, Santusita the king of devas; the Nimmānarati devas, Sunimmita the king of devas; the Vasavattī devas, Vasavattī the king of devas; the devas of Brahmā’s retinue, the devas of Brahmā’s ministers, the Great Brahmās; the devas of limited radiance, immeasurable radiance, and streaming radiance; the devas of limited glory, immeasurable glory, and replete glory; the Vehapphala devas, the Aviha devas, the Atappa devas, the Sudassa devas, the Sudassī devas, and the Akaniṭṭha devas—thus, setting aside the non-percipient beings and the beings of the formless realms, all devas throughout the sphere where the ear-base occurs gave their approval.

Tato khīṇāsavamahābrahmāno – “mahā vatāyaṃ sādhukārasaddo, pathavitalato paṭṭhāya yāva akaniṭṭhalokaṃ āgato, kimatthaṃ nu kho eso”ti āvajjento “dhammasenāpatisāriputtatthero pubbārāme [V 2.0034][P 2.0129] visākhāya ratanapāsāde nisīditvā saṃyojanapariyāyadhammadesanamārabhi, amhehipi tattha kāyasakkhīhi bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā tattha agamaṃsu. Pubbārāmo devatāhi paripuṇṇo, samantā pubbārāmassa gāvutaṃ aḍḍhayojanaṃ, yojananti sakalacakkavāḷaṃ heṭṭhā pathavitalena tiriyaṃ cakkavāḷapariyantena paricchinnaṃ dasahi cakkavāḷasahassehi sannipatitāhi devatāhi nirantaramahosi, āragganitudanamatte ṭhāne uparimakoṭiyā saṭṭhi devatā sukhumattabhāve māpetvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Then the Great Brahmās who were Arahants reflected, “This sound of approval is indeed great, having come from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha realm. For what reason has it arisen?” Discerning, “The General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, seated in Visākhā’s jeweled mansion in the Eastern Park, has begun the Dhamma Discourse on the Exposition of the Fetters. It is fitting for us too to be personal witnesses there,” and having thought thus, they went there. The Eastern Park was filled with devas. All around the Eastern Park for a gāvuta, half a yojana, and a yojana, and indeed the entire world-system—bounded below by the surface of the earth and horizontally by the world-system’s boundary—was packed without interval by devas assembled from ten thousand world-systems. In a space the size of an awl's point, at the upper extremity, sixty devas stood, having created subtle forms for themselves.

Athāyasmā sāriputto “mahantaṃ vatidaṃ halāhalaṃ, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti āvajjento dasasahassacakkavāḷe ṭhitānaṃ devatānaṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitabhāvaṃ addasa. Atha yasmā buddhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi, parisaparimāṇeneva passanti ceva saddañca sāventi. Sāvakānaṃ pana adhiṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā thero samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya mahaggatacittena adhiṭṭhāsi – “cakkavāḷapariyantā parisā sabbāpi maṃ passatu, dhammañca me desentassa saddaṃ suṇātū”ti. Adhiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya dakkhiṇajāṇupasse ca cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyañca nisīditvā “dhammasenāpatisāriputtatthero nāma kīdiso dīgho rasso sāmo odāto”ti vattabbakāraṇaṃ nāhosi, sabbesampi sabbadisāsu nisinnānaṃ abhimukheyeva paññāyittha, nabhamajjhe ṭhitacando viya ahosi. Dhammaṃ desentassāpissa [M 2.0035] dakkhiṇajāṇupasse ca cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyañca nisinnā sabbe ekakaṃseneva saddaṃ suṇiṃsu.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, reflecting, “This is indeed a great commotion! What, I wonder, is this?” saw that the devas from the ten-thousand world-systems had assembled in one world-system. Now, for Buddhas there is no need for an act of determination; they see and make their voice heard only according to the measure of the assembly. For disciples, however, an act of determination is suitable. Therefore, the Elder, having entered into meditative attainment and having emerged from it, made a determination with a mind of great scope: “May the entire assembly, up to the limit of the world-system, see me, and may they hear the sound of me teaching the Dhamma.” From the time of his determination onwards, there was no occasion to ask, “What is the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, like? Is he tall, short, dark, golden, or fair?” To all those seated in every direction, he appeared directly before them; he was like the moon in the middle of the sky. As he was teaching the Dhamma, all those seated—both at his right knee and at the rim of the world-system—heard his voice without exception.

Evaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā thero ajjhattasaṃyojanañca, āvusoti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha [P 2.0130] ajjhattanti kāmabhavo. Bahiddhāti rūpārūpabhavo. Kiñcāpi hi sattā kāmabhave appaṃ kālaṃ vasanti kappassa catutthameva koṭṭhāsaṃ, itaresu tīsu koṭṭhāsesu kāmabhavo suñño hoti tuccho, rūpabhave bahuṃ kālaṃ vasanti, tathāpi tesaṃ yasmā kāmabhave cutipaṭisandhiyo bahukā honti, appakā rūpārūpabhavesu. Yattha ca cutipaṭisandhiyo bahukā, tattha ālayopi patthanāpi abhilāsopi bahu hoti. Yattha appā, tattha appo. Tasmā kāmabhavo ajjhattaṃ nāma jātaṃ, rūpārūpabhavā bahiddhā nāma. Iti ajjhattasaṅkhāte kāmabhave chandarāgo ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ nāma, bahiddhāsaṅkhātesu rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo bahiddhāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Orambhāgiyāni vā pañca saṃyojanāni ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ nāma, uddhambhāgiyāni pañca bahiddhāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu, tattha upapattinipphādanato taṃ oraṃ bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni[V 2.0035]. Uddhaṃ vuccati rūpārūpadhātu, tattha upapattinipphādanato taṃ uddhaṃ bhajantīti uddhambhāgiyāni.

Having thus resolved, the elder began this Dhamma teaching with the words, 'Friends, internal fetters...' Herein, 'internal' is the realm of sensual existence. 'External' is the realm of form and the formless realm. Indeed, although beings dwell in the sensual realm for a short time—only the fourth part of an eon, for in the other three parts the sensual realm is empty and void—and they dwell in the form realm for a long time, nevertheless, since for them deaths and rebirth-linkings are numerous in the sensual realm but few in the form and formless realms. And where deaths and rebirth-linkings are numerous, there clinging, longing, and desire are also great. Where they are few, these are little. Therefore, the realm of sensual existence has come to be called 'internal,' and the form and formless realms 'external.' Thus, desire and lust in the sensual realm, designated as 'internal,' is called the internal fetter. Desire and lust in the form and formless realms, designated as 'external,' is called the external fetter. Alternatively, the five lower fetters are called the internal fetter, and the five higher fetters are called the external fetter. Herein, this is the verbal explanation: 'Lower' is said of the sensual realm. Since they pertain to that lower part by bringing about rebirth there, they are called 'pertaining to the lower part.' 'Higher' is said of the form and formless realms. Since they pertain to that higher part by bringing about rebirth there, they are called 'pertaining to the upper part.'

Evaṃ vuttappabhedena ajjhattasaṃyojanena saṃyutto puggalo ajjhattasaṃyojano, bahiddhāsaṃyojanena saṃyutto puggalo bahiddhāsaṃyojano. Ubhayampi cetaṃ na lokiyassa vaṭṭanissitamahājanassa nāmaṃ. Yesaṃ pana bhavo dvedhā paricchinno, tesaṃ sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmīnaṃ ariyasāvakānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Yathā hi mahāaraññe khadiravanasālavanādīni thambho tulāsaṅghāṭoti nāmaṃ na labhanti, khadiravanaṃ sālavananti nāmameva labhanti. Yadā pana tato rukkhā tiṇhāya kuṭhāriyā chinditvā thambhādisaṇṭhānena tacchitā honti, tadā thambho tulāsaṅghāṭoti nāmaṃ labhanti. Evamevaṃ aparicchinnabhavo bahalakileso puthujjano [P 2.0131] etaṃ nāmaṃ na labhati, bhavaṃ paricchinditvā kilese tanuke katvā ṭhitā sotāpannādayova labhanti.

Thus, with the distinction already stated, a person bound by the internal fetter is called 'one with an internal fetter,' and a person bound by the external fetter is called 'one with an external fetter.' And this twofold designation is not for the worldly multitude dependent on the cycle of existence. Rather, this is the designation for those noble disciples—stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners—for whom existence is delimited in two ways. For just as in a great forest, acacia groves, sal groves, and so on do not obtain the designation 'post,' 'beam,' or 'rafter,' but obtain only the name 'acacia grove' or 'sal grove.' But when trees from there are cut with a sharp axe and fashioned into the shape of posts, beams, and rafters, they then obtain the designation 'post,' 'beam,' or 'rafter.' In the very same way, a worldling with undelimited existence and thick defilements does not obtain this designation; only the stream-enterers and others, who stand having delimited their existence and made their defilements thin, obtain it.

Imassa ca panatthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ idaṃ vacchakasālopamaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vacchakasālaṃ hi katvā anto khāṇuke koṭṭetvā vacchake yottehi bandhitvā [M 2.0036] tesu upanibandhanti, yottesu appahontesu kaṇṇesupi gahetvā tattha vacchake pavesenti, antosālāya okāse appahonte bahi khāṇuke koṭṭetvāpi evameva karonti. Tattha koci antobaddho vacchako bahinipanno hoti, koci bahibaddho antonipanno, koci antobaddho antova nipanno, koci bahibaddho bahiyeva nipanno. Koci antopi abaddhova carati, bahipi abaddhova. Tattha antobaddhassa bahinipannassa bandhanaṃ dīghaṃ hoti. So hi uṇhādipīḷito nikkhamitvā bahi vacchakānaṃ abbhantare nipajjati. Bahibaddhe antonipannepi eseva nayo. Yo pana antobaddho antonipanno, tassa bandhanaṃ rassaṃ hoti. Bahibaddhe bahinipannepi eseva nayo. Ubhopi hi te divasampi khāṇukaṃ anuparigantvā tattheva sayanti. Yo pana anto abaddho tattheva vacchakānaṃ antare vicarati. Ayaṃ sīlavā vacchako kaṇṇe gahetvā vacchakānaṃ antare vissaṭṭho divasampi aññattha agantvā tattheva carati. Bahi abaddhe tattheva vicarantepi eseva nayo.

To clarify this meaning, this simile of the calf-pen should be understood. For, having made a calf-pen, they drive stakes inside, and having tied the calves with ropes, they tether them to those stakes. If the ropes are not sufficient, they also grab them by the ears and lead the calves inside. If the space inside the pen is insufficient, they also drive stakes outside and do just the same. Therein, some calf tied inside lies down outside; some tied outside lies down inside; some tied inside lies down right inside; some tied outside lies down right outside. Some wander untied inside, and some also wander untied outside. For a calf tied inside that lies down outside, the tether is long. Indeed, oppressed by heat and the like, it goes out and lies down among the other calves outside. The same applies to one tied outside that lies down inside. But for a calf tied inside that lies down inside, the tether is short. The same applies to one tied outside that lies down outside. Indeed, both of these spend the whole day circling the stake and lie down right there. As for the one that is untied inside, it wanders right there among the other calves. This well-behaved calf, having been grabbed by the ear and released among the calves, wanders right there for the whole day without going elsewhere. The same applies to the one that is untied outside and wanders right there.

Tattha vacchakasālā viya tayo bhavā veditabbā. Vacchakasālāyaṃ khāṇukā viya avijjākhāṇuko. Vacchakabandhanayottaṃ viya dasa saṃyojanāni. Vacchakā viya tīsu bhavesu nibbattasattā[V 2.0036]. Antobaddho bahisayitavacchako viya [P 2.0132] rūpārūpabhavesu sotāpannasakadāgāmino. Te hi kiñcāpi tattheva vasanti, saṃyojanaṃ pana tesaṃ kāmāvacarūpanibaddhameva. Kenaṭṭhena? Appahīnaṭṭhena. Rūpārūpabhavesu puthujjanopi eteheva saṅgahito. Sopi hi kiñcāpi tattha vasati, saṃyojanaṃ panassa kāmāvacarūpanibaddhameva. Bahibaddho antosayitavacchako viya kāmāvacare anāgāmī. So hi kiñcāpi kāmāvacare vasati, saṃyojanaṃ panassa rūpārūpabhavūpanibaddhameva. Antobaddho antonipanno viya kāmāvacare sotāpannasakadāgāmino. Te hi sayampi kāmāvacare vasanti, saṃyojanampi tesaṃ kāmāvacarūpanibaddhameva. Bahibaddho bahinipanno viya rūpārūpabhavesu anāgāmī. So hi sayampi tattha vasati, saṃyojanampissa rūpārūpabhavūpanibaddhameva. Antoabaddho antovicaraṇavacchako viya kāmāvacare khīṇāsavo. Bahiabaddho bahivicaraṇavacchako [M 2.0037] viya rūpārūpabhave khīṇāsavo. Saṃyojanesu pana sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāsoti imāni tīṇi gacchantaṃ nivārenti, gataṃ paṭiānenti. Kāmacchando byāpādoti imāni pana dve saṃyojanāni samāpattiyā vā avikkhambhetvā maggena vā asamucchinditvā rūpārūpabhave nibbattituṃ na sakkoti.

Herein, the three existences should be understood as being like a calf-pen. The post of ignorance should be understood as being like a post in the calf-pen. The ten fetters are like the rope for tying calves. Beings reborn in the three existences are like the calves. A stream-enterer or once-returner in the form and formless realms is like a calf tied inside but lying outside. Indeed, although they dwell right there, their fetter is one connected only with the sense-sphere realm. For what reason? By reason of its not having been abandoned. In the form and formless realms, a worldling is also included together with these. Indeed, although they too dwell there, their fetter is one connected only with the sense-sphere realm. A non-returner in the sense-sphere realm is like a calf tied outside but lying inside. Indeed, although they dwell in the sense-sphere realm, their fetter is one connected only with the form and formless existences. A stream-enterer or once-returner in the sense-sphere realm is like a calf tied inside and lying inside. Indeed, they themselves dwell in the sense-sphere realm, and their fetter is also one connected only with the sense-sphere realm. A non-returner in the form and formless realms is like a calf tied outside and lying outside. Indeed, they themselves dwell there, and their fetter is also one connected only with the form and formless existences. An Arahant in the sense-sphere realm is like a calf untied inside and wandering inside. An Arahant in the form and formless realms is like a calf untied outside and wandering outside. Now, among the fetters, these three—identity view, doubt, and clinging to rites and rituals—prevent one who is going and bring back one who has gone. However, regarding these two fetters—sensual desire and ill will—without having suppressed them by attainment or cut them off by the path, one is not able to be reborn in the form and formless existences.

Katamo cāvusoti idaṃ thero yathā nāma puriso dve ratanapeḷā passe ṭhapetvā sampattaparisāya dve hatthe pūretvā sattavidhaṃ ratanaṃ bhājetvā dadeyya, evaṃ paṭhamaṃ ratanapeḷaṃ datvā dutiyampi tatheva dadeyya. Evamevaṃ “ajjhattasaṃyojanañca, āvuso, puggalaṃ desessāmi bahiddhāsaṃyojanañcā”ti imāni dve padāni mātikāvasena ṭhapetvā idāni aṭṭhavidhāya parisāya bhājetvā dassetuṃ vitthārakathaṃ ārabhi.

In reference to the question, 'Which, friends?', the Elder began the detailed discourse. Just as a man, having placed two jewel caskets at his side, might fill both hands and distribute the seven kinds of jewels to the assembled company, giving from the first jewel casket and then giving from the second in the same way; in this very way, having established these two phrases—'I will teach, friend, the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters'—by way of a mātikā, he now began to distribute and explain to the eightfold assembly.

Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Sīlavā [P 2.0133] hotīti catupārisuddhisīlehi sīlasampanno hoti. Iti thero ettāvatā ca kira catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti iminā tattha jeṭṭhakasīlaṃ vitthāretvā dassesīti dīpavihāravāsī summatthero āha. Antevāsiko panassa tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero āha – “ubhayatthāpi pātimokkhasaṃvarova vutto. Pātimokkhasaṃvaroyeva hi sīlaṃ, itarāni pana tīṇi sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī”ti ananujānanto uttari āha – indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhāmattakameva, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammena samena paccayuppattimattakaṃ, paccayasannissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye “idamattha”nti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ, nippariyāyena pana pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ[V 2.0037]. Yassa so bhinno, ayaṃ chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo. Yassa pana so arogo, ayaṃ acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā sīlavāti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ uddisitvā taṃ vitthārento “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”tiādimāhāti.
