Herein, 'in this' means in this Dispensation. 'He is virtuous' means he is endowed with virtue through the fourfold purification of virtue. Thus, the Elder Summa, a resident of Dīpavihāra, said: 'The Elder, having thus far indicated the fourfold purification of virtue, explained by elaborating on the principal virtue among them with the words "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint".' However, his pupil, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: 'In both places, only the Pātimokkha restraint is spoken of. For the Pātimokkha restraint alone is virtue.' And not admitting that 'there is indeed a place where the other three are called virtue,' he said further: 'Restraint of the sense-faculties is merely the guarding of the six doors; purification of livelihood is merely the production of requisites righteously and impartially; virtue dependent on requisites is merely consuming the obtained requisites after reflecting, "It is for this purpose." But in an absolute sense, the Pātimokkha restraint alone is virtue. For whom that [restraint] is broken, this person is like a man with his head cut off: it cannot be said that he will protect his hands, feet, and the remaining virtues. But for whom that [restraint] is unimpaired, this person is like a man whose head is not cut off: he is able to protect his life and the remaining virtues, having restored them to their natural state. Therefore, by this word 'virtuous,' having indicated the Pātimokkha restraint, and elaborating on it, he said, "restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint," and so on.'

Tattha [M 2.0038] pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgato. Ācāragocarasampannoti ācārena ca gocarena ca sampanno. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassī. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā. Sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhati. Apica samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu sikkhitabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā, taṃ sabbaṃ sammā ādāya sikkhati. Ayamettha [P 2.0134] saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana sabbānetāni pātimokkhasaṃvarādīni padāni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.14 ādayo) vuttāni, catupārisuddhisīlañca sabbākārena vibhajitvā dassitaṃ. Aññataraṃ devanikāyanti chasu kāmāvacaradevaghaṭāsu aññataraṃ devaghaṭaṃ. Āgāmī hotīti heṭṭhā āgāmī hoti. Āgantā itthattanti itthattaṃ mānusakapañcakkhandhabhāvameva āgantā hoti. Tatrūpapattiko vā uparūpapattiko vā na hoti, puna heṭṭhāgāmīyeva hotīti dasseti. Iminā aṅgena sukkhavipassakassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikabhikkhuno heṭṭhimaṃ maggadvayañceva phaladvayañca kathitaṃ.

Here, "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Perfect in conduct and range" means accomplished in both conduct and range. `Aṇumattesu` means in what is slight; `vajjesu` means in unwholesome states. "Seeing danger" means perceiving danger. "Undertakes" means properly taking up. "He trains in the training rules" means he trains, undertaking each training rule. Furthermore, "he trains by undertaking the training rules" means he properly takes up and trains in whatever should be trained—whether bodily or verbal—in all the training rules, the sections on training. This is the summary here. In detail, however, all these terms—beginning with "restraint of the Pātimokkha"—are explained in the Visuddhimagga, and the fourfold purification of virtue is analyzed and shown in every aspect. "One of the divine hosts" refers to one of the six groups of sense-sphere deities. "He is a returner" means he becomes a returner to what is below. "He returns to this state" means he only returns to this human state of the five aggregates. He is not reborn there or in a higher realm; rather, he remains only a returner to what is below—this is shown. By this factor, the lower two paths and two fruits are described for a monk practicing dry insight whose meditation subject is the elements.

Aññataraṃ santaṃ cetovimuttinti aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu aññataraṃ catutthajjhānasamāpattiṃ. Sā hi paccanīkakilesānaṃ santattā santā, teheva ca kilesehi cetaso vimuttattā cetovimuttīti vuccati. Aññataraṃ devanikāyanti pañcasu suddhāvāsadevanikāyesu aññataraṃ. Anāgantā itthattanti puna imaṃ pañcakkhandhabhāvaṃ anāgantā, heṭṭhūpapattiko na hoti, uparūpapattiko vā hoti tattheva vā parinibbāyīti dasseti. Iminā aṅgena samādhikammikassa bhikkhuno tayo maggā tīṇi ca phalāni kathitāni.

One attainment of peaceful liberation of mind refers to the fourth jhāna attainment, one of the eight attainments. Indeed, it is called `santā` (peaceful) because of the calming of opposing defilements, and it is called `cetovimutti` (liberation of mind) because the mind is liberated from those very defilements. One of the divine hosts refers to one of the five Pure Abodes divine hosts. Not returning to this state means not returning again to this five-aggregate existence; one is not destined for rebirth below, but is destined for rebirth above or attains final Nibbāna there itself—this is shown. Through this factor, three paths and three fruits are described for a monk engaged in the work of concentration.

Kāmānaṃyeva nibbidāyāti duvidhānampi kāmānaṃ nibbindanatthāya ukkaṇṭhanatthāya. Virāgāyāti virajjanatthāya. Nirodhāyāti appavattikaraṇatthāya. Paṭipanno hotīti paṭipattiṃ paṭipanno hoti. Ettāvatā sotāpannassa ca sakadāgāmino ca pañcakāmaguṇikarāgakkhayatthāya anāgāmimaggavipassanā [V 2.0038] kathitā hoti. Bhavānaṃyevāti tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ. Iminā anāgāmino bhavarāgakkhayatthāya arahattamaggavipassanā kathitā hoti. Taṇhākkhayāya paṭipanno hotīti imināpi [M 2.0039] sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃyeva [P 2.0135] pañcakāmaguṇikataṇhākkhayakaraṇatthaṃ anāgāmimaggavipassanā kathitā. So lobhakkhayāyāti imināpi anāgāmino bhavalobhakkhayatthāya arahattamaggavipassanāva kathitā. Aññataraṃ devanikāyanti suddhāvāsesveva aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ. Anāgantā itthattanti imaṃ khandhapañcakabhāvaṃ anāgantā, heṭṭhūpapattiko na hoti, uparūpapattiko vā hoti, tattheva vā parinibbāyati.

For disenchantment with sensual pleasures indeed: for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with both kinds of sensual pleasures, for the purpose of aversion. For dispassion: for the purpose of becoming dispassionate. For cessation: for the purpose of causing non-recurrence. One practices accordingly: one is practicing the path. Thus far, the insight for the path of the non-returner has been taught for the purpose of destroying the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure in the stream-enterer and the once-returner. Of existences indeed: of the three existences. By this, the insight for the path of Arahantship has been taught for the purpose of destroying the lust for existence in the non-returner. Also by this phrase, 'One practices for the destruction of craving,' the insight for the path of the non-returner is taught for the purpose of causing the destruction of craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure in the stream-enterer and once-returner only. Also by this phrase, 'For the destruction of greed,' the insight for the path of Arahantship indeed is taught for the purpose of destroying the greed for existence in the non-returner. A certain divine realm: a certain divine realm among the Pure Abodes indeed. Not returning to this state: not returning to this state of being of the five aggregates; one is not reborn below, but is reborn above, or attains final Nibbāna right there.

Iti paṭhamena aṅgena sukkhavipassakassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikabhikkhuno heṭṭhimāni dve maggaphalāni kathitāni, dutiyena samādhikammikassa tīṇi maggaphalāni, “so kāmāna”nti iminā sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ pañcakāmaguṇikarāgakkhayāya upari anāgāmimaggavipassanā, “so bhavānaṃyevā”ti iminā anāgāmissa upari arahattamaggavipassanā, “so taṇhākkhayāyā”ti iminā sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ pañcakāmaguṇikataṇhākkhayāya upari anāgāmimaggavipassanā, “so lobhakkhayāyā”ti iminā anāgāmino bhavalobhakkhayāya upari arahattamaggavipassanā kathitāti evaṃ chahi mukhehi vipassanaṃ kathetvā desanaṃ yathānusandhiṃ pāpesi. Desanāpariyosāne koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sotāpannādīnaṃ paricchedova nāhosi. Yathā ca imasmiṃ samāgame, evaṃ mahāsamayasutte maṅgalasutte ca cūḷarāhulovādasutte ca koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sotāpannādīnaṃ devamanussānaṃ paricchedo nāhosi.

Thus, by the first factor, the two lower paths and fruits were explained for the monk practicing dry insight whose meditation subject is the elements. By the second factor, the three paths and fruits were for the one engaged in the practice of concentration. With the phrase 'so kāmānaṃ,' insight for the non-returner's path was explained for the destruction of desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure in stream-enterers and once-returners. With the phrase 'so bhavānaṃyeva,' insight for the Arahant's path was explained for the non-returner. With the phrase 'so taṇhākkhayāya,' insight for the non-returner's path was explained for the destruction of craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure in stream-enterers and once-returners. With the phrase 'so lobhakkhayāyā,' insight for the Arahant's path was explained for the destruction of greed for existence in the non-returner. Thus, having explained insight through six aspects, He brought the teaching to its proper conclusion. At the end of the discourse, a hundred thousand crores of devas attained Arahantship, and there was no measure of those who became stream-enterers and so forth. And just as in this assembly, so too in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, and the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, a hundred thousand crores of devas attained Arahantship, and there was no measure of the devas and humans who became stream-enterers and so forth.

Samacittā devatāti cittassa sukhumabhāvasamatāya samacittā. Sabbāpi hi tā attano attabhāve sukhume cittasarikkhake katvā māpesuṃ. Tena samacittā nāma jātā. Aparenapi kāraṇena samacittā – “therena samāpatti tāva kathitā, samāpattithāmo [P 2.0136] pana na kathito. Mayaṃ dasabalaṃ pakkositvā samāpattiyā thāmaṃ kathāpessāmā”ti sabbāpi ekacittā ahesuntipi samacittā. Aparampi kāraṇaṃ – “therena ekena pariyāyena samāpattipi samāpattithāmopi kathito, ko nu kho imaṃ samāgamaṃ sampatto, ko na sampatto”ti olokayamānā tathāgatassa asampattabhāvaṃ disvā “mayaṃ tathāgataṃ pakkositvā [M 2.0040] parisaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ karissāmā”ti sabbāpi ekacittā ahesuntipi samacittā. Aparampi kāraṇaṃ – anāgate kocideva bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī [V 2.0039] vā devo vā manusso vā “ayaṃ desanā sāvakabhāsitā”ti agāravaṃ kareyya, sammāsambuddhaṃ pakkositvā imaṃ desanaṃ sabbaññubhāsitaṃ karissāma. Evaṃ anāgate garubhāvanīyā bhavissatīti sabbāva ekacittā ahesuntipi samacittā. Aparampi kāraṇaṃ – sabbāpi hi tā ekasamāpattilābhiniyo vā ahesuṃ ekārammaṇalābhiniyo vāti evampi samacittā.

The devas of even-mindedness are so called because of the sameness in the state of subtlety of their minds. Indeed, all of them fashioned their own subtle existences to resemble their minds. For that reason, they came to be called 'even-minded'. They are even-minded for another reason as well: 'The Elder has taught only the attainment, but the power of the attainment has not been taught. We shall invite the One with Ten Powers and have the power of the attainment taught.' As all were of one mind in this, they are also called 'even-minded'. And for another reason: 'The Elder has, in one way, taught both the attainment and the power of the attainment. Who, indeed, has arrived at this assembly, and who has not?' Looking about and seeing that the Tathāgata had not arrived, they thought: 'We shall invite the Tathāgata and make the assembly complete.' As all were of one mind in this, they are also called 'even-minded'. And for another reason: 'In the future, some monk, nun, deva, or human might show disrespect, thinking, "This teaching was spoken by a disciple." We shall invite the Perfectly Enlightened One and make this teaching one spoken by the Omniscient One. Thus, in the future, it will be worthy of reverence.' As all were of one mind in this, they are also called 'even-minded'. And for another reason: Indeed, all of them were either attainers of the same attainment or attainers of the same object. In this way also, they are even-minded.

Haṭṭhāti tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā āmoditā pamoditā. Sādhūti āyācanatthe nipāto. Anukampaṃ upādāyāti na therassa anukampaṃ kāruññaṃ anuddayaṃ paṭicca, na ca imasmiṃ ṭhāne therassa anukampitabbakiccaṃ atthi. Yasmiṃ hi divase thero sūkarakhataleṇadvāre bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanākammaṭṭhāne (ma. ni. 2.206) kathiyamāne tālavaṇṭaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ bījamāno ṭhito parassa vaḍḍhitabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā khudaṃ vinodento viya parassa sajjitapasādhanaṃ sīse paṭimuñcanto viya ca sāvakapāramiñāṇassa nippadesato matthakaṃ patto, tasmiṃyeva divase bhagavatā anukampito nāma. Avasesānaṃ pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampattānaṃ devamanussānaṃ anukampaṃ upādāya gacchatu bhagavāti bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu.

“Delighted” means pleased, exceedingly joyful, rejoiced, and exceedingly rejoiced. “Sādhu” is a particle in the sense of entreaty. “Out of compassion” does not mean on account of compassion, kindness, or sympathy for the Elder, nor is there in this situation any duty to show compassion to the Elder. For on the day the Elder, while standing and fanning the Teacher with a palm-leaf fan at the entrance of the Sūkarakhata cave as the meditation subject on feelings was being taught to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, he reached the very pinnacle of the perfection of a disciple's knowledge without remainder—like one who dispels hunger by eating food served for another, and like one who places on his head an ornament prepared for another. On that very day, he was indeed shown compassion by the Blessed One. However, out of compassion for the remaining devas and humans who had arrived at that place, they entreated the Blessed One, saying, “May the Blessed One go.”

Balavā purisoti dubbalo hi khippaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ [P 2.0137] kātuṃ na sakkoti, balavāva sakkoti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sammukhe pāturahosīti sammukhaṭṭhāne puratoyeva pākaṭo ahosi. Bhagavā etadavocāti etaṃ “idha sāriputtā”tiādinā nayena attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ avoca. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “sace koci bālo akataññū bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā evaṃ cinteyya – ‘sāriputtatthero mahantaṃ parisaṃ alattha, sammāsambuddho ettakaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto usūyāya parisaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ āgato’ti. So imaṃ mayi manopadosaṃ katvā apāye nibbatteyyā”ti. Athattano āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathento etaṃ “idha sāriputtā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Regarding “a strong man”: a weak man is unable to quickly bend and stretch; only a strong man is able. For that reason, this was said. “He appeared in front” means he became manifest right in front, in a face-to-face position. “The Blessed One spoke thus” means he stated the reason for his arrival by the method beginning with, “Here, Sāriputta…” It seems this thought occurred to him: “If some foolish, ungrateful monk, nun, male lay follower, or female lay follower were to think: ‘The Elder Sāriputta has gained a large assembly; the Perfectly Enlightened One, unable to endure such a thing, has come out of envy to make the assembly rise,’ then that person, having generated this mental corruption towards me, would be reborn in a state of loss.” Then, explaining the reason for his arrival, he spoke this utterance beginning with, “Here, Sāriputta…”

Evaṃ [M 2.0041] attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathetvā idāni samāpattiyā thāmaṃ kathetuṃ tā kho pana, sāriputta, devatā dasapi hutvātiādimāha. Tattha yasavasena vā atthaṃ āharituṃ vaṭṭati samāpattivasena vā. Yasavasena tāva mahesakkhā devatā dasa dasa ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu, tāhi appesakkhatarā vīsati vīsati ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu, tāhi appesakkhatarā…pe… saṭṭhi saṭṭhi ekaṭṭhāne [V 2.0040] aṭṭhaṃsu. Samāpattivasena pana yāhi paṇītā samāpatti bhāvitā, tā saṭṭhi saṭṭhi ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu. Yāhi tato hīnatarā, tā paññāsa paññāsa…pe… yāhi tato hīnatarā samāpatti bhāvitā…pe… tā dasa dasa ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu. Yāhi vā hīnā bhāvitā, tā dasa dasa ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu. Yāhi tato paṇītatarā bhāvitā, tā vīsati vīsati. Yāhi tato paṇītatarā…pe… tā saṭṭhi saṭṭhi ekaṭṭhāne aṭṭhaṃsu.

Having thus explained the reason for his own coming, now, in order to explain the power of meditative attainment, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Then, Sāriputta, those devas, being ten...' Therein, it is proper to derive the meaning either by way of glory or by way of meditative attainment. Firstly, by way of glory: the devas of great power, ten by ten, stood in one place; those of lesser power than them, twenty by twenty, stood in one place; those of even lesser power... sixty by sixty, stood in one place. However, by way of meditative attainment: those by whom a sublime meditative attainment was developed, they, sixty by sixty, stood in one place. Those by whom a more inferior attainment than that was developed, they, fifty by fifty... those by whom a meditative attainment more inferior than that was developed... they, ten by ten, stood in one place. Or, those by whom an inferior attainment was developed, they, ten by ten, stood in one place. Those by whom a more sublime attainment than that was developed, they, twenty by twenty. Those by whom a more sublime attainment than that... they, sixty by sixty, stood in one place.

Āraggakoṭinitudanamatteti āraggakoṭiyā patanamatte okāse. Na [P 2.0138] ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhentīti evaṃ sambādhe ṭhāne tiṭṭhantiyopi aññamaññaṃ na byābādhenti na ghaṭṭenti, asampīḷā asambādhāva ahesuṃ. “Tava hattho maṃ bādhati, tava pādo maṃ bādhati, tvaṃ maṃ maddantī ṭhitā”ti vattabbakāraṇaṃ nāhosi. Tattha nūnāti tasmiṃ bhave nūna. Tathācittaṃ bhāvitanti tenākārena cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ. Yena tā devatāti yena tathābhāvitena cittena tā devatā dasapi hutvā…pe… tiṭṭhanti, na ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhentīti. Idheva khoti sāsane vā manussaloke vā bhummaṃ, imasmiṃyeva sāsane imasmiṃyeva manussaloketi attho. Tāsañhi devatānaṃ imasmiṃyeva manussaloke imasmiṃyeva ca sāsane taṃ cittaṃ bhāvitaṃ, yena tā sante rūpabhave nibbattā, tato ca pana āgantvā evaṃ sukhume attabhāve māpetvā ṭhitā. Tattha kiñcāpi kassapadasabalassa sāsane tīṇi maggaphalāni nibbattetvā brahmaloke nibbattadevatāpi atthi, sabbabuddhānaṃ pana ekāva anusāsanī ekaṃ sāsananti katvā “idheva kho, sāriputtā”ti aññabuddhānaṃ sāsanampi imameva sāsanaṃ karonto āha. Ettāvatā tathāgatena samāpattiyā thāmo kathito.

Āraggakoṭinitudanamatte means in a space the measure of an awl-point's fall. Na ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti means that even when standing in such a confined place, they did not hinder or bump into one another; they were uncompressed and uncrowded. There was no cause to say, “Your hand presses upon me, your foot presses upon me, you are standing crushing me.” Tattha nūna means surely in that existence. Tathācittaṃ bhāvitaṃ means the mind was developed in that manner. Yena tā devatā means by which mind, so developed, those deities, even ten of them... stand, and do not obstruct one another. Idheva kho refers to the Dispensation or the human world, and it is a locative term; the meaning is “in this very Dispensation” or “in this very human world.” For it was in this very human world and in this very Dispensation that those deities developed that mind, by which they were reborn in the peaceful fine-material realm. And then, having come from there, they stood, having manifested such subtle individual existences. Here, although in the Dispensation of Kassapa of the Ten Powers there were deities who were reborn in the Brahma world after having produced the three paths and fruits, yet, on the basis that for all Buddhas the instruction is one and the teaching is one, He said, “Idheva kho, Sāriputta,” thereby treating the Dispensation of other Buddhas as this very Dispensation. To this extent, the power of the attainment has been described by the Tathāgata.

Idāni [M 2.0042] sāriputtattheraṃ ārabbha tantivasena anusāsaniṃ kathento tasmātiha, sāriputtāti āha. Tattha tasmāti yasmā tā devatā idheva santaṃ samāpattiṃ nibbattetvā sante bhave nibbattā, tasmā. Santindriyāti pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ santatāya nibbutatāya paṇītatāya santindriyā. Santamānasāti mānasassa santatāya nibbutatāya paṇītatāya santamānasā. Santaṃyeva upahāraṃ upaharissāmāti kāyacittūpahāraṃ santaṃ nibbutaṃ paṇītaṃyeva upaharissāma. Sabrahmacārīsūti [P 2.0139] samānaṃ ekuddesatādiṃ brahmaṃ carantesu sahadhammikesu. Evañhi vo, sāriputta, sikkhitabbanti iminā ettakena vārena bhagavā desanaṃ sabbaññubhāsitaṃ akāsi. Anassunti naṭṭhā [V 2.0041] vinaṭṭhā. Ye imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ nāssosunti ye attano pāpikaṃ tucchaṃ niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ nissāya imaṃ evarūpaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sotuṃ na labhiṃsūti yathānusandhinā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Now, wishing to deliver an instruction concerning the Elder Sāriputta by way of the textual lineage, He said, 'Therefore, Sāriputta.' Herein, as for 'therefore': because those deities, having produced a peaceful attainment right here, were reborn in a peaceful becoming, therefore. As for 'peaceful faculties': due to the tranquility, the quenched state, and the sublimity of the five faculties, they have peaceful faculties. As for 'peaceful mind': due to the tranquility, the quenched state, and the sublimity of the mind, they have a peaceful mind. As for 'We will offer only a peaceful offering': we will offer the offering of body and mind that is indeed peaceful, quenched, and sublime. As for 'among fellow practitioners of the holy life': among companions in the Dhamma who share the noble practice, beginning with the same recitation of the Pātimokkha. With this much of a passage, 'Thus indeed, Sāriputta, should you train,' the Blessed One rendered the teaching as one spoken by the Omniscient One. As for anassu: they are destroyed, they are ruined. As for 'those who did not hear this discourse on the Dhamma': those who, relying on their own evil, empty, and worthless wrong view, did not get to hear this Dhamma teaching of such a nature—thus, He concluded the teaching in accordance with the connection.

38. Chaṭṭhe varaṇāyaṃ viharatīti varaṇā nāma ekaṃ nagaraṃ, taṃ upanissāya viharati. Kāmarāgābhinivesavinibandhapaligedhapariyuṭṭhānajjhosānahetūti kāmarāgābhinivesahetu, kāmarāgavinibandhahetu, kāmarāgapaligedhahetu, kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhānahetu, kāmarāgaajjhosānahetūti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yvāyaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe nissāya uppajjati kāmarāgo, tassābhinivesādihetu. Kāmarāgena abhiniviṭṭhattā vinibaddhattā tasmiṃyeva ca kāmarāge mahāpaṅke viya paligedhattā anupaviṭṭhattā teneva ca kāmarāgena pariyuṭṭhitattā gahitattā kāmarāgeneva ca ajjhositattā gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahitattāti. Diṭṭhirāgādipadesupi eseva nayo. Diṭṭhirāgoti panettha dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo nissāya uppajjanakarāgo veditabbo. Puratthimesu janapadesūti therassa vasanaṭṭhānato sāvatthijanapado puratthimadisābhāge hoti, thero ca nisīdantopi tatomukhova nisinno, tasmā evamāha. Udānaṃ udānesīti udāhāraṃ udāhari. Yathā hi yaṃ telaṃ mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ avasesakoti [P 2.0140] vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati[M 2.0043], taṃ oghoti vuccati, evamevaṃ yaṃ pītivacanaṃ hadayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, adhikaṃ hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahi nikkhamati, taṃ udānanti vuccati, evarūpaṃ pītimayavacanaṃ nicchāresīti attho.

38. In the sixth sutta. “He dwelt at Varaṇā” means Varaṇā is the name of a city; he dwelt in dependence on it. “The cause of adherence, bondage, being mired in, being overwhelmed, and being consumed by sensual lust” means: the cause of adherence to sensual lust, the cause of bondage by sensual lust, the cause of being mired in sensual lust, the cause of being overwhelmed by sensual lust, and the cause of being consumed by sensual lust. This is the meaning. This is what is said: whatever sensual lust arises in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure, that is a cause of adherence and so forth. Because one is adhered to by sensual lust, bound by it, mired in it as in a great swamp, has deeply entered into it, is overwhelmed by it, seized by it, and is consumed by it—thus, one is seized, having been swallowed and brought to an end. The same method applies to passages on lust for views and so on. Herein, “lust for views” should be understood as the lust that arises in dependence on the sixty-two views. “In the eastern districts” means: from the elder’s dwelling place, the district of Sāvatthī is in the eastern direction. And the elder, even when sitting, was seated facing that way; therefore, he said thus. “He uttered an inspired utterance” means he uttered an exclamation. For just as oil that a measure cannot hold flows out and is lost, it is called 'leftover.' And just as water that a reservoir cannot hold overflows, it is called a 'flood.' In the very same way, a joyful utterance that the heart cannot hold, becoming excessive and not remaining inside, goes outside—that is called an 'inspired utterance.' He uttered such a speech filled with joy—this is the meaning.

39. Sattame gundāvaneti evaṃ nāmake vane. Upasaṅkamīti “mahākaccānatthero kira nāma attano pitumattampi ayyakamattampi disvā neva abhivādeti na paccuṭṭheti na āsanena nimantetī”ti sutvā “na sakkā ettakena niṭṭhaṃ gantuṃ, upasaṅkamitvā naṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti bhuttapātarāso yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami. Jiṇṇeti jarājiṇṇe. Vuddheti vayovuddhe. Mahallaketi jātimahallake. Addhagateti dīghakāladdhānaṃ atikkante. Vayoanuppatteti pacchimavayaṃ anuppatte. Tayidaṃ, bho kaccāna, tathevāti, bho kaccāna, yaṃ taṃ amhehi kevalaṃ sutameva, taṃ iminā diṭṭhena sameti. Tasmā taṃ tatheva, na aññathā. Na hi bhavaṃ kaccāno brāhmaṇeti idaṃ attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – amhe evaṃ mahallake disvā bhoto kaccānassa abhivādanamattampi paccuṭṭhānamattampi [V 2.0042] āsanena nimantanamattampi natthīti. Na sampannamevāti na yuttameva na anucchavikameva.

39. In the seventh sutta. Gundāvane means: in the forest so named. Upasaṅkami means: Having heard, “The elder named Mahākaccāna, it is said, upon seeing someone of his father’s age or his grandfather’s age, neither pays homage, nor rises up, nor invites them with a seat,” and having intended, “It is not possible to reach a conclusion with only this much; having approached him, I will investigate,” he, having eaten his morning meal, approached the place where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was. Jiṇṇe means: aged by old age. Vuddhe means: old in years. Mahallake means: old in lineage. Addhagate means: having passed a long period of time. Vayoanuppatte means: having reached the final age. Tayidaṃ, bho kaccāna, tatheva means: O Kaccāna, that which we had merely heard matches this which is now seen. Therefore, that is just so, not otherwise. This phrase, Na hi bhavaṃ kaccāno brāhmaṇe, he says with reference to himself. This, it seems, is his intention: “Having seen us who are so old, there is not even the mere act of paying homage, the mere act of rising up, or the mere act of inviting with a seat on the part of the venerable Kaccāna.” Na sampannameva means: it is not right indeed, not suitable indeed.

Thero brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo neva vuddhe jānāti na dahare, ācikkhissāmissa vuddhe ca dahare cā”ti desanaṃ vaḍḍhento atthi brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha jānatāti sabbaṃ neyyaṃ jānantena. Passatāti tadeva hatthe ṭhapitaṃ āmalakaṃ viya passantena. Vuddhabhūmīti yena kāraṇena vuddho nāma hoti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Daharabhūmīti [P 2.0141] yena kāraṇena daharo nāma hoti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Āsītikoti asītivassavayo. Nāvutikoti navutivassavayo. Kāme paribhuñjatīti vatthukāme kilesakāmeti duvidhepi kāme kamanavasena paribhuñjati. Kāmamajjhāvasatīti duvidhepi kāme ghare gharassāmiko viya vasati adhivasati. Kāmapariyesanāya ussukoti duvidhānampi kāmānaṃ pariyesanatthaṃ ussukkamāpanno. Bālo na therotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti so na thero bālo mandotveva gaṇanaṃ gacchati. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

Hearing the brahmin’s words, the elder thought, "This brahmin knows neither the old nor the young; I will explain to him both the old and the young." Expanding the teaching, he said, "There is, brahmin..." Herein, 'one who knows' means one who knows all that is to be known. 'One who sees' means one who sees that very thing as clearly as a myrobalan fruit placed in the hand. 'The state of being old' means the reason why one is called old. 'The state of being young' means the reason why one is called young. 'Eighty' means eighty years of age. 'Ninety' means ninety years of age. 'Indulges in sensual pleasures' means one indulges in both kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual objects and sensual defilements—by way of desire. 'Lives amidst sensual pleasures' means one dwells and resides amidst both kinds of sensual pleasures like a master of the house in his home. 'Strives for sensual pleasures' means one has undertaken the effort to seek both kinds of sensual pleasures. 'A fool is not reckoned as an elder' means he is not reckoned as an elder, but is reckoned only as a fool, a dull person. For this was said:

“Na [M 2.0044] tena thero so hoti, yenassa palitaṃ siro;

Paripakko vayo tassa, moghajiṇṇoti vuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 260);

“Not by reason of a grey head is one an elder; one is ripe in age, but is called ‘old-in-vain’.”

Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanena samannāgato. Susukāḷakesoti suṭṭhu kāḷakeso. Bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatoti yena yobbanena samannāgato yuvā, taṃ yobbanaṃ bhadraṃ laddhakanti dasseti. Paṭhamena vayasāti paṭhamavayo nāma tettiṃsa vassāni, tena samannāgatoti attho. Paṇḍito therotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti so evarūpo puggalo paṇḍitoti ca theroti ca gaṇanaṃ gacchati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Young' means youthful. 'Youthful' means endowed with youth. 'With very black hair' means having very black hair. 'Endowed with fortunate youth' shows that the youth with which one is endowed is good and worthy. 'In the first stage of life': the first stage of life is thirty-three years; endowed with that is the meaning. 'A wise one is reckoned as an elder' means such a person is reckoned as wise and as an elder. And this was also said:

“Yamhi saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Sa ve vantamalo dhīro, thero iti pavuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 261);

“He in whom there is truth and Dhamma, non-violence, restraint, and control—he, the wise one who has discarded impurities, is indeed called an elder.”

40. Aṭṭhame [P 2.0142] corā balavanto hontīti pakkhasampannā, parivārasampannā, dhanasampannā, nivāsaṭṭhānasampannā, vāhanasampannā ca honti. Rājāno tasmiṃ samaye dubbalā hontīti tasmiṃ samaye rājāno tāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ abhāvena dubbalā honti. Atiyātunti bahiddhā janapadacārikaṃ [V 2.0043] caritvā icchiticchitakkhaṇe antonagaraṃ pavisituṃ. Niyyātunti “corā janapadaṃ vilumpanti maddanti, te nisedhessāmā”ti paṭhamayāme vā majjhimayāme vā pacchimayāme vā nikkhamituṃ phāsukaṃ na hoti. Tato uṭṭhāya corā manusse pothetvā acchinditvā gacchanti. Paccantime vā janapade anusaññātunti gāmaṃ vāsakaraṇatthāya setuṃ attharaṇatthāya pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpanatthāya sālādīnaṃ karaṇatthāya paccantime janapade anusaññātumpi na sukhaṃ hoti. Brāhmaṇagahapatikānanti antonagaravāsīnaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ. Bāhirāni vā kammantānīti bahigāme ārāme khettakammantāni. Pāpabhikkhū balavanto hontīti pakkhuttarā yasuttarā puññavanto bahukehi upaṭṭhākehi ca upaṭṭhākīhi ca samannāgatā rājarājamahāmattasannissitā. Pesalā bhikkhū tasmiṃ samaye dubbalā hontīti tasmiṃ samaye piyasīlā bhikkhū tāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ abhāvena dubbalā honti. Tuṇhībhūtā tuṇhībhūtāva saṅghamajjhe saṅkasāyantīti [M 2.0045] nissaddā hutvā saṅghamajjhe nisinnā kiñci ekavacanampi mukhaṃ ukkhipitvā kathetuṃ asakkontā pajjhāyantā viya nisīdanti. Tayidanti [P 2.0143] tadetaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo.

40. In the eighth, ‘thieves become powerful’ means they are endowed with factions, followers, wealth, places to stay, and vehicles. ‘Kings become weak at that time’ means that at that time, kings are weak due to the lack of those endowments. ‘Atiyātunti’ means to enter the city at any desired moment after roaming outside the country. ‘Niyyātunti’ means it is not easy to go out in the first, middle, or last watch of the night, thinking, ‘We will stop the thieves who plunder and oppress the country.’ Then, rising up, the thieves beat people, rob them, and go away. ‘Paccantime vā janapade anusañcaritunti’ means it is not pleasant to travel about in the border country for the purpose of establishing a village, building a bridge, having a pond dug, or making halls and so on. ‘Brāhmaṇagahapatikānanti’ refers to the brahmins and householders living inside the city. ‘Bāhirāni vā kammantānīti’ means work in parks and fields outside the village. ‘Wicked monks become powerful’ means they are superior in faction, superior in fame, meritorious, endowed with many male and female supporters, and dependent on kings and royal ministers. ‘Virtuous monks become weak at that time’ means at that time, monks of amiable virtue are weak due to the lack of those endowments. ‘Tuṇhībhūtā tuṇhībhūtāva saṅghamajjhe saṅkasāyantīti’ means, having become silent, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, unable to raise their mouths to say even a single word, they sit as if brooding. ‘Tayidanti’ means this is the cause. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been said.

41. Navame micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetūti micchāpaṭipattiyā kāraṇahetu paṭipajjanahetūti attho. Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalanti sahavipassanakaṃ maggaṃ. Evarūpo hi sahavipassanakaṃ maggaṃ ārādhetuṃ sampādetuṃ pūretuṃ na sakkoti. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo. Imasmiṃ sutte saha vipassanāya maggo kathito.

41. In the ninth, ‘because of the reason of wrong practice’ means: the reason for performing and the reason for practicing wrong practice. ‘The right Dhamma, skillful’ means the noble path together with insight. Indeed, such a person is not able to complete, accomplish, or fulfill the noble path together with insight. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been stated. In this discourse, the noble path together with insight is taught.

42. Dasame duggahitehīti uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitehi. Byañjanappatirūpakehīti byañjanaso patirūpakehi akkharacitratāya laddhakehi. Atthañca dhammañca paṭibāhantīti suggahitasuttantānaṃ atthañca pāḷiñca paṭibāhanti, attano duggahitasuttantānaṃyeva atthañca pāḷiñca uttaritaraṃ katvā dassenti. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo. Imasmiṃ sutte sāsanassa vuddhi ca parihāni ca kathitāti.

42. In the tenth, ‘wrongly grasped’ means grasped out of sequence. ‘With counterfeit expressions’ means with those that are imitations in terms of wording, obtained through elaborate lettering. ‘They obstruct the meaning and the Dhamma’ means they obstruct the meaning and the Pāḷi of well-grasped suttantas, and present the meaning and the Pāḷi of their own wrongly-grasped suttantas as superior. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been stated. In this discourse, the growth and decline of the Dispensation are taught.

Samacittavaggo catuttho.

The Chapter on the Even Mind is the fourth.

5. Parisavaggavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Chapter on the Assembly

43. Pañcamassa [V 2.0044] paṭhame uttānāti pākaṭā appaṭicchannā. Gambhīrāti guḷhā paṭicchannā. Uddhatāti uddhaccena samannāgatā. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā, uṭṭhitatucchamānāti vuttaṃ hoti. Capalāti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādinā cāpallena yuttā. Mukharāti mukhakharā kharavacanā. Vikiṇṇavācāti asaṃyatavacanā divasampi niratthakavacanapalāpino. Muṭṭhassatīti [P 2.0144] vissaṭṭhasatino. Asampajānāti nippaññā. Asamāhitāti cittekaggatāmattassāpi alābhino. Pākatindriyāti pakatiyā ṭhitehi vivaṭehi arakkhitehi indriyehi samannāgatā. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo.

43. In the first of the fifth, ‘shallow’ means manifest, unconcealed. ‘Deep’ means secret, concealed. ‘Agitated’ means endowed with agitation. ‘Arrogant’ means with pride like a raised reed; that is to say, with arisen, empty conceit. ‘Fickle’ means endowed with fickleness, such as by adorning the bowl and robes. ‘Harsh-spoken’ means with a harsh mouth, with harsh speech. ‘Of scattered speech’ means with unrestrained speech, speaking meaningless chatter even for the whole day. ‘Of lapsed mindfulness’ means with mindfulness lost. ‘Without clear comprehension’ means without wisdom. ‘Unconcentrated’ means not obtaining even a measure of one-pointedness of mind. ‘With faculties in their natural state’ means endowed with faculties, such as the eye, that stand in their natural state, are open, and are unguarded. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been stated.

44. Dutiye [M 2.0046] bhaṇḍanajātāti bhaṇḍanaṃ vuccati kalahassa pubbabhāgo, taṃ tesaṃ jātanti bhaṇḍanajātā. Tathā “mayaṃ tumhe daṇḍāpessāma bandhāpessāmā”tiādivacanappavattiyā sañjātakalahā. Ayaṃ tāva gihīsu nayo. Pabbajitā pana āpattivītikkamavācaṃ vadantā kalahajātā nāma. Vivādāpannāti viruddhavādaṃ āpannā. Mukhasattīhi vitudantāti guṇānaṃ chindanaṭṭhena dubbhāsitā vācā mukhasattiyoti vuccanti, tāhi vitudantā vijjhantā. Samaggāti ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatāti etesaṃ karaṇena samaggatāya sahitā. Piyacakkhūhīti mettācakkhūhi.

44. In the second sutta, regarding `bhaṇḍanajātā` (those for whom contention has arisen): `bhaṇḍana` (contention) is said to be the preliminary stage of a conflict. That has arisen for them, hence they are `bhaṇḍanajātā`. Similarly, through the utterance of words such as, ‘We will have you punished; we will have you bound,’ they become those for whom conflict has arisen. This, in the first place, is the principle regarding householders. Monastics, however, who speak words that constitute a transgression of a rule, are called `kalahajātā` (those for whom conflict has arisen). `Vivādāpannā` (engaged in disputes) means they have adopted a contrary view. `Mukhasattīhi vitudantā` (piercing with mouth-spears) means: ill-spoken words are called ‘mouth-spears’ in the sense that they cut off virtues; with these they pierce and wound. `Samaggā` (united) means endowed with unity through the performance of a single formal act, a single recitation, and having the same training. `Piyacakkhūhīti` (with loving eyes) means with eyes of loving-kindness.

45. Tatiye aggavatīti uttamapuggalavatī, aggāya vā uttamāya paṭipattiyā samannāgatā. Tato viparītā anaggavatī. Bāhulikāti cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā. Sāsanaṃ sithilaṃ gaṇhantīti sāthalikā. Okkamane pubbaṅgamāti ettha okkamanaṃ vuccati avagamanaṭṭhena pañca nīvaraṇāni, tena pañcanīvaraṇapūraṇe pubbaṅgamāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paviveketi upadhiviveke nibbāne. Nikkhittadhurāti tividhepi viveke oropitadhurā. Na vīriyaṃ ārabhantīti duvidhampi vīriyaṃ na karonti. Appattassa pattiyāti pubbe appattassa jhānavipassanāmaggaphalavisesassa pattiatthāya. Itaraṃ [P 2.0145] padadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pacchimā janatāti saddhivihārikaantevāsikajano[V 2.0045]. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatīti ācariyupajjhāyehi kataṃ anukaronto diṭṭhassa tesaṃ ācārassa anugatiṃ āpajjati nāma. Sesaṃ vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbaṃ.

45. In the third sutta, `aggavatī` means possessing excellent persons, or, alternatively, endowed with the highest, excellent practice. The opposite of this is `anaggavatī`. `Bāhulikā` means those who are practicing for an abundance of robes and so forth. `Sāthalikā` means they take the teaching loosely. Regarding `okkamane pubbaṅgamā` (leaders in descending): here, `okkamana` (descending) is said of the five hindrances in the sense of going down; thus it is said they are leaders in fulfilling the five hindrances. Regarding `paviveka` (seclusion): in Nibbāna, the seclusion from the substrates. `Nikkhittadhurā` (those who have laid down the burden) means those who have laid down the burden in regard to the three kinds of seclusion. `Na vīriyaṃ ārabhanti` (they do not arouse energy) means they do not undertake both kinds of energy. `Appattassa pattiyā` (for the attainment of the unattained) means for the sake of attaining a previously unattained distinction in jhāna, insight, path, and fruit. The other two phrases are synonyms of this very one. `Pacchimā janatā` (the later generation) refers to the community of co-resident pupils and apprentices. `Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjati` (falls into following what is seen) means that by imitating what is done by their teachers and preceptors, one is said to fall into following their seen conduct. The remainder should be understood by the method that is the opposite of what has been said.

46. Catutthe ariyāti ariyasāvakaparisā. Anariyāti puthujjanaparisā. “Idaṃ dukkha”nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānantīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ nāma, ettakameva dukkhaṃ, ito uddhaṃ dukkhaṃ natthīti yathāsabhāvato nappajānanti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Sesapadesu pana tassa dukkhassa samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayo nāma, tassāyeva taṇhāya, dvinnampi vā tesaṃ saccānaṃ accantakkhayo asamuppatti dukkhanirodho nāma, aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā nāmāti [M 2.0047] evaṃ imasmiṃ sutte catūhi saccehi cattāro maggā ca cattāri ca phalāni kathitāni.

46. In the fourth sutta, ‘noble’ means the assembly of noble disciples. ‘Ignoble’ means the assembly of worldlings. ‘They do not understand “This is suffering” as it really is’: setting aside craving, the five aggregates belonging to the three planes are called the truth of suffering; the truth of suffering is only this much, and beyond this there is no truth of suffering—thus, they do not understand according to its true nature. This is the method throughout. However, in the remaining phrases, the craving in a previous existence that gives rise to that suffering is called the origin; the utter destruction and non-arising of that very craving, or of both those truths, is called the cessation of suffering; the Noble Eightfold Path is called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus, in this sutta, the four paths and the four fruits are taught by means of the four truths.

47. Pañcame parisākasaṭoti kasaṭaparisā kacavaraparisā palāpaparisāti attho. Parisāmaṇḍoti pasannaparisā sāraparisāti attho. Chandāgatiṃ gacchantīti chandena agatiṃ gacchanti, akattabbaṃ karontīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Imāni pana cattāri agatigamanāni bhaṇḍabhājanīye ca vinicchayaṭṭhāne ca labbhanti. Tattha bhaṇḍabhājanīye tāva attano bhārabhūtānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ amanāpe bhaṇḍake patte taṃ parivattetvā manāpaṃ dento chandāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Attano pana abhārabhūtānaṃ manāpe bhaṇḍake patte taṃ parivattetvā amanāpaṃ dento dosāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Bhaṇḍakabhājanīyavatthuñca ṭhitikañca ajānanto mohāgatiṃ [P 2.0146] gacchati nāma. Mukharānaṃ vā rājādinissitānaṃ vā “ime me amanāpe bhaṇḍake dinne anatthampi kareyyu”nti bhayena parivattetvā manāpaṃ dento bhayāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo pana evaṃ na gacchati, sabbesaṃ tulābhūto pamāṇabhūto majjhatto hutvā yaṃ yassa pāpuṇāti, taññeva tassa deti, ayaṃ catubbidhampi agatigamanaṃ na gacchati nāma. Vinicchayaṭṭhāne pana attano bhārabhūtassa garukāpattiṃ lahukāpattīti katvā kathento chandāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Itarassa lahukāpattiṃ garukāpattīti katvā kathento dosāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ pana samuccayakkhandhakañca ajānanto mohāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Mukharassa vā rājapūjitassa vā “ayaṃ me garukaṃ katvā āpattiṃ kathentassa anatthampi kareyyā”ti garukameva lahukāti katvā kathento bhayāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo pana sabbesaṃ yathābhūtameva katheti, ayaṃ catubbidhampi agatigamanaṃ na gacchati nāma.

47. In the fifth sutta, ‘parisākasaṭa’ means an assembly of dregs, an assembly of rubbish, an assembly of chaff. ‘Parisāmaṇḍa’ means an assembly of the devout, an assembly of the excellent. ‘Chandāgatiṃ gacchanti’ means they go to partiality through desire, doing what should not be done. The same method applies to the remaining terms. These four ways of going to partiality, however, are found both in the distribution of requisites and in the place of judgment. There, in the distribution of requisites: if one, having exchanged an undesirable requisite that has come to monks dependent on oneself, gives a desirable one, this is called going to partiality through desire. But if, having exchanged a desirable requisite that has come to monks not dependent on oneself, one gives an undesirable one, this is called going to partiality through aversion. And if one does not know the basis for distributing requisites and the established procedure, this is called going to partiality through delusion. Or if, through fear that ‘if an undesirable requisite is given to these talkative monks or those dependent on kings, they might do me harm,’ one exchanges and gives a desirable one, this is called going to partiality through fear. But whoever does not go thus, being an impartial one, a standard, a measure for all, gives each what is due to them—this one is said not to go to any of the four kinds of partiality. In the place of judgment, however, if one, having made a serious offense of one dependent on oneself into a light offense, speaks thus, this is called going to partiality through desire. If one, having made a light offense of another into a serious offense, speaks thus, this is called going to partiality through aversion. But if one does not know the rehabilitation from an offense and the Samuccayakkhandhaka, this is called going to partiality through delusion. Or if, through fear that ‘if I declare this offense as serious for this talkative one or one honored by kings, he might do harm to me,’ one makes a serious offense into a light one and speaks thus, this is called going to partiality through fear. But whoever declares everything truthfully as it is to all, this one is said not to go to any of the four kinds of partiality.

48. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0046] okkācitavinītāti dubbinītā. No paṭipucchāvinītāti na pucchitvā vinītā. Gambhīrāti pāḷivasena gambhīrā sallasuttasadisā. Gambhīratthāti atthavasena gambhīrā mahāvedallasuttasadisā. Lokuttarāti lokuttaraatthadīpakā[M 2.0048]. Suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti sattasuññaṃ dhammamattameva pakāsakā asaṅkhatasaṃyuttasadisā. Na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapentīti vijānanatthāya cittaṃ na upaṭṭhapenti, niddāyanti vā aññavihitā vā honti. Uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbanti uggahetabbe ca pariyāpuṇitabbe ca. Kavitāti [P 2.0147] kavīhi katā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Cittakkharāti vicitraakkharā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Bāhirakāti sāsanato bahibhūtā. Sāvakabhāsitāti tesaṃ tesaṃ sāvakehi bhāsitā. Sussūsantīti akkharacittatāya ceva sarasampattiyā ca attamanā hutvā suṇanti. Na ceva aññamaññaṃ paṭipucchantīti aññamaññaṃ atthaṃ vā anusandhiṃ vā pubbāparaṃ vā na pucchanti. Na ca paṭivicarantīti pucchanatthāya cārikaṃ na vicaranti. Idaṃ kathanti idaṃ byañjanaṃ kathaṃ ropetabbaṃ kinti ropetabbaṃ? Imassa ko atthoti imassa bhāsitassa ko attho, kā anusandhi, kiṃ pubbāparaṃ? Avivaṭanti paṭicchannaṃ. Na vivarantīti na ugghāṭenti. Anuttānīkatanti apākaṭaṃ kataṃ. Na uttāniṃ karontīti pākaṭaṃ na karonti. Kaṅkhāṭhāniyesūti kaṅkhāya kāraṇabhūtesu. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo.

48. In the sixth, 'okkācitavinīta' means ill-trained. 'No paṭipucchāvinīta' means not trained by questioning. 'Gambhīra' means profound in terms of the Pāli text, like the Sallasutta. 'Gambhīrattha' means profound in meaning, like the Mahāvedallasutta. 'Lokuttara' means revealing supramundane meanings. 'Suññatāpaṭisaṃyutta' means revealing only phenomena, which are empty of a self, like the Asaṅkhatasaṃyutta. 'They do not apply their minds for the purpose of knowing' means they do not apply their minds for the purpose of knowing; they either fall asleep or are otherwise minded. 'To be learned and mastered' means both what is to be learned and what is to be mastered. 'Kavikata' means composed by poets. The other is a synonym for that same word. 'Cittakkhara' means having ornate letters. The other is a synonym for that same word. 'Bāhiraka' means outside the Dispensation. 'Sāvakabhāsita' means spoken by their disciples. 'They listen eagerly' means they listen with delight, pleased by the ornateness of the letters and the excellence of the sound. 'They do not question one another' means they do not ask each other about the meaning, the connection, or the sequence. 'Nor do they inquire' means they do not wander about to inquire. 'How is this?' means: how should this expression be construed, in what way should it be construed? 'What is the meaning of this?' means: what is the meaning of this utterance, what is its connection, what is its sequence? 'Unrevealed' means concealed. 'They do not reveal' means they do not uncover. 'Not made plain' means not made manifest. 'They do not make it plain' means they do not make it manifest. 'In grounds for doubt' means in things that are a cause for doubt. The bright side should be known by way of the reverse of what has been said.

49. Sattame āmisagarūti catupaccayagarukā lokuttaradhammaṃ lāmakato gahetvā ṭhitaparisā. Saddhammagarūti nava lokuttaradhamme garuke katvā cattāro paccaye lāmakato gahetvā ṭhitaparisā. Ubhatobhāgavimuttoti dvīhi bhāgehi vimutto. Paññāvimuttoti paññāya vimutto sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavo. Kāyasakkhīti kāyena jhānaphassaṃ phusitvā pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikatvā ṭhito. Diṭṭhippattoti [P 2.0148] diṭṭhantaṃ patto. Ime dvepi chasu ṭhānesu labbhanti. Saddhāvimuttoti saddahanto vimutto. Ayampi chasu ṭhānesu labbhati. Dhammaṃ anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Saddhaṃ anussaratīti saddhānusārī. Ime dvepi paṭhamamaggasamaṅgino. Kalyāṇadhammoti sundaradhammo. Dussīlo pāpadhammoti nissīlo lāmakadhammo. Imaṃ kasmā gaṇhanti? Sabbesu hi ekasadisesu jātesu [M 2.0049] sīlavantesu balavagāravaṃ na hoti, ekaccesu pana dussīlesu sati sīlavantānaṃ upari balavagāravaṃ hotīti maññantā gaṇhanti. Te tena lābhaṃ labhantīti te bhikkhū ekaccānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ ekaccānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kathetvā cattāro paccaye labhanti. Gathitāti taṇhāya ganthitā. Mucchitāti taṇhāvaseneva mucchitā. Ajjhopannāti ajjhosāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā [V 2.0047] ṭhitā. Anādīnavadassāvinoti apaccavekkhitaparibhoge ādīnavaṃ apassantā. Anissaraṇapaññāti catūsu paccayesu chandarāgaapakaḍḍhanāya nissaraṇapaññāya virahitā idamatthaṃ etanti ajānantā. Paribhuñjantīti sacchandarāgā hutvā paribhuñjanti.

49. In the seventh, 'āmisagaru' refers to an assembly that esteems material things, taking the four requisites as important and regarding the supramundane Dhamma as inferior. 'Saddhammagaru' refers to an assembly that esteems the nine supramundane Dhammas as important and regards the four requisites as inferior. 'Ubhatobhāgavimutta' means liberated in both ways. 'Paññāvimutta' means liberated by wisdom, a dry-insight meditator whose taints are destroyed. 'Kāyasakkhī' is one who, having touched the jhāna-contact with the body, afterwards realizes cessation, Nibbāna, and is established therein. 'Diṭṭhippatta' means one who has attained to the end of view. These two are found in six instances. 'Saddhāvimutta' means one liberated by faith. This one also is found in six instances. Because one follows after the Dhamma, one is a 'Dhamma-follower'. Because one follows after faith, one is a 'faith-follower'. These two are endowed with the first path. 'Kalyāṇadhammo' means one of beautiful qualities. 'Dussīlo pāpadhammo' means one without virtue, of base qualities. Why do they accept such a person? Because when all are equally virtuous, strong reverence does not arise; but when some are immoral, strong reverence arises towards the virtuous—thinking thus, they accept them. 'By that, they obtain gain' means: those monks, by speaking praise of some and dispraise of others, obtain the four requisites. 'Gathitā' means bound by craving. 'Mucchitā' means infatuated by the power of craving. 'Ajjhopannā' means they are established, having been swallowed and brought to completion by overwhelming attachment. 'Anādīnavadassāvino' means not seeing the danger in unreflective consumption. 'Anissaraṇapaññā' means lacking the wisdom of escape for withdrawing desire and lust from the four requisites, not knowing, 'This is for this purpose.' 'Paribhuñjanti' means they consume with desire and lust.

Sukkapakkhe ubhatobhāgavimuttotiādīsu ayaṃ sattannampi ariyapuggalānaṃ saṅkhepapakāsanā – eko bhikkhu paññādhurena abhiniviṭṭho aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti. So tasmiṃ khaṇe dhammānusārī nāma hoti, sotāpattiphalādīsu chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhi nāma, arahattaphalakkhaṇe ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma. Samāpattīhi vikkhambhanavimuttiyā maggena samucchedavimuttiyāti dvikkhattuṃ vā dvīhi vā bhāgehi vimuttoti attho. Aparo paññādhurena abhiniviṭṭho samāpattiyo nibbattetuṃ [P 2.0149] asakkonto sukkhavipassakova hutvā sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti. So tasmiṃ khaṇe dhammānusārī nāma hoti, sotāpattiphalādīsu chasu ṭhānesu diṭṭhippatto nāma, arahattaphalakkhaṇe paññāvimutto nāma. Aparo saddhādhurena abhiniviṭṭho aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti. So tasmiṃ khaṇe saddhānusārī nāma hoti, sotāpattiphalādīsu chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhi nāma, arahattaphalakkhaṇe ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma. Aparo saddhādhurena abhiniviṭṭho samāpattiyo nibbattetuṃ asakkonto sukkhavipassakova hutvā sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti. So tasmiṃ khaṇe saddhānusārī nāma hoti, sotāpattiphalādīsu chasu ṭhānesu saddhāvimutto nāma, arahattaphalakkhaṇe paññāvimutto nāma.

In the bright side, concerning 'ubhatobhāgavimutta' and so forth, this is a concise explanation of the seven noble individuals: One bhikkhu, committed to the vehicle of wisdom, having developed the eight attainments, attains the stream-entry path. At that moment, he is called a Dhamma-follower. In the six instances from the stream-entry fruition onward, he is called a body-witness. At the moment of Arahant fruition, he is called one liberated in both ways. The meaning is: liberated by the attainments through liberation by suppression and by the path through liberation by eradication; or, liberated twice; or, liberated from two parts (the form-body and the mind-body). Another, committed to the vehicle of wisdom but unable to develop the attainments, being a dry-insight meditator, attains the stream-entry path. At that moment, he is called a Dhamma-follower. In the six instances from the stream-entry fruition onward, he is called one attained to view. At the moment of Arahant fruition, he is called one liberated by wisdom. Another, committed to the vehicle of faith, having developed the eight attainments, attains the stream-entry path. At that moment, he is called a faith-follower. In the six instances from the stream-entry fruition onward, he is called a body-witness. At the moment of Arahant fruition, he is called one liberated in both ways. Another, committed to the vehicle of faith but unable to develop the attainments, being a dry-insight meditator, attains the stream-entry path. At that moment, he is called a faith-follower. In the six instances from the stream-entry fruition onward, he is called one liberated by faith. At the moment of Arahant fruition, he is called one liberated by wisdom.

50. Aṭṭhame visamāti sapakkhalanaṭṭhena visamā. Samāti nipakkhalanaṭṭhena samā. Adhammakammānīti uddhammāni kammāni. Avinayakammānīti ubbinayāni kammāni.

50. In the eighth, 'uneven' means uneven in the sense of stumbling. 'Even' means even in the sense of not stumbling. 'Unrighteous deeds' are deeds apart from the Dhamma. 'Deeds contrary to the Vinaya' are deeds apart from the Vinaya.

51. Navame [M 2.0050] adhammikāti niddhammā. Dhammikāti dhammayuttā.

51. In the ninth, 'unrighteous' means devoid of Dhamma. 'Righteous' means endowed with Dhamma.

52. Dasame adhikaraṇanti vivādādhikaraṇādicatubbidhaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ. Ādiyantīti gaṇhanti. Saññāpentīti jānāpenti. Na ca saññattiṃ upagacchantīti saññāpanatthaṃ na sannipatanti. Na ca nijjhāpentīti na pekkhāpenti. Na ca nijjhattiṃ upagacchantīti aññamaññaṃ nijjhāpanatthāya na sannipatanti. Asaññattibalāti asaññattiyeva balaṃ etesanti asaññattibalā[V 2.0048]. Appaṭinissaggamantinoti yesaṃ hi evaṃ hoti – “sace amhehi gahitaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ dhammikaṃ bhavissati, gaṇhissāma. Sace adhammikaṃ, vissajjessāmā”ti, te paṭinissaggamantino nāma [P 2.0150] honti. Ime pana na tathā mantentīti appaṭinissaggamantino. Thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissāti diṭṭhithāmena ca diṭṭhiparāmāsena ca abhinivisitvā. Idameva saccanti idaṃ amhākaṃ vacanameva saccaṃ. Moghamaññanti avasesānaṃ vacanaṃ moghaṃ tucchaṃ. Sukkapakkho uttānatthoyevāti.

52. In the tenth sutta, adhikaraṇaṃ (legal question) refers to the fourfold legal question, beginning with the legal question of dispute. Ādiyanti (they take up) means they grasp. Saññāpenti (they make known) means they cause to know. Na ca saññattiṃ upagacchanti (they do not come to an agreement) means they do not assemble for the purpose of making it known. Na ca nijjhāpenti (they do not cause to consider) means they do not cause one to reflect. Na ca nijjhattiṃ upagacchanti (they do not come to a consensus) means they do not assemble for the purpose of causing one another to consider. Asaññattibalā (those whose power is non-declaration) means: for these persons, their power is simply non-declaration; therefore, they are called asaññattibalā. Regarding appaṭinissaggamantino (those who do not deliberate on relinquishment): those for whom there is the thought, 'If the legal question we have taken up is in accordance with the Dhamma, we will accept it. If it is not in accordance with the Dhamma, we will relinquish it,' are called paṭinissaggamantino (those who deliberate on relinquishment). But these persons do not deliberate thus; therefore, they are appaṭinissaggamantino. Thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa (having adhered with strength and misapprehension) means having adhered through the strength of a view and through the misapprehension of a view. Idameva saccaṃ (this alone is true) means this statement of ours alone is true. Moghamaññaṃ (the other is vain) means the statement of the others is vain and empty. The sukkapakkho (white faction) is of obvious meaning.

Parisavaggo pañcamo.

The fifth is the Chapter on Assemblies.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is concluded.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Puggalavaggavaṇṇanā

(6) 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Individuals

53. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakassa [V 2.0049][M 2.0051] paṭhame cakkavattinā saddhiṃ gahitattā “lokānukampāyā”ti na vuttaṃ. Ettha ca cakkavattino uppattiyā dve sampattiyo labhanti, buddhānaṃ uppattiyā tissopi.

53. In the first sutta of the Second Fifty, because it is taken together with the wheel-turning monarch, 'out of compassion for the world' is not stated. And here, through the arising of a wheel-turning monarch, two accomplishments are obtained; through the arising of Buddhas, all three are also obtained.

54. Dutiye acchariyamanussāti āciṇṇamanussā abbhutamanussā.

54. In the second sutta, acchariyamanussā (wondrous humans) means unprecedented humans, marvelous humans.

55. Tatiye bahuno janassa anutappā hotīti mahājanassa anutāpakārī hoti. Tattha cakkavattino kālakiriyā ekacakkavāḷe devamanussānaṃ anutāpaṃ karoti, tathāgatassa kālakiriyā dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu.

55. In the third sutta, bahuno janassa anutappā hoti (he causes distress to many people) means he is a cause of distress for the great multitude. Therein, the death of a wheel-turning monarch causes distress to devas and humans in one world-system; the death of a Tathāgata, in ten thousand world-systems.

56. Catutthe thūpārahāti thūpassa yuttā anucchavikā. Cakkavattino hi cetiyaṃ paṭijaggitvā dve sampattiyo labhanti, buddhānaṃ cetiyaṃ paṭijaggitvā tissopi.

56. In the fourth sutta, thūpārahā (worthy of a stupa) means suitable and appropriate for a stupa. Indeed, by tending to the shrine of a wheel-turning monarch, they obtain two accomplishments; by tending to the shrine of the Buddhas, they also obtain all three.

57. Pañcame buddhāti attano ānubhāvena cattāri saccāni buddhā.

57. In the fifth sutta, as for 'buddhā': they are persons who have understood the four truths by their own power.

58. Chaṭṭhe phalantiyāti saddaṃ karontiyā. Na santasantīti na bhāyanti. Tattha khīṇāsavo attano sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pahīnattā na bhāyati, hatthājānīyo sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā balavattāti. Sattamaṭṭhamesupi [P 2.0151] eseva nayo.

58. In the sixth sutta, as for 'phalantiyā': it means making a sound. As for 'na santasanti': it means they do not fear. Among them, the one whose taints are destroyed does not fear because his identity-view has been abandoned; the thoroughbred elephant does not fear because of the strength of its identity-view. In the seventh and eighth suttas also, this is the same method.

61. Navame kiṃpurisāti kinnarā. Mānusiṃ vācaṃ na bhāsantīti manussakathaṃ na kathenti. Dhammāsokassa kira ekaṃ kinnaraṃ ānetvā dassesuṃ. So “kathāpetha na”nti āha. Kinnaro kathetuṃ [V 2.0050] na icchati. Eko puriso “ahametaṃ kathāpessāmī”ti heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ otāretvā dve khāṇuke koṭṭetvā ukkhaliṃ āropesi. Sā ubhatopassehi patati. Taṃ disvā kinnaro “kiṃ aññaṃ ekaṃ khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetuṃ [M 2.0052] na vaṭṭatī”ti ettakameva āha. Puna aparabhāge dve kinnare ānetvā dassesuṃ. Rājā “kathāpetha ne”ti āha. Te kathetuṃ na icchiṃsu. Eko puriso “ahamete kathāpessāmī”ti te gahetvā antarāpaṇaṃ agamāsi. Tattheko ambapakkañca macche ca addasa, eko kabiṭṭhaphalañca ambilikāphalañca. Tattha purimo “mahāvisaṃ manussā khādanti, kathaṃ te kilāsino na hontī”ti āha. Itaro “kathaṃ ime etaṃ nissāya kuṭṭhino na hontī”ti āha. Evaṃ mānusiṃ vācaṃ kathetuṃ sakkontāpi dve atthe sampassamānā na kathentīti.

61. In the ninth sutta, as for 'kiṃpurisā': they are kinnaras. As for 'they do not speak human speech': they do not utter human talk. It is said that they brought a kinnara and showed him to King Dhammāsoka. He said, 'Make it speak.' The kinnara did not wish to speak. A certain man, saying, 'I will make it speak,' took it down below the palace, drove in two stakes, and placed a pot on them. It falls from both sides. Seeing that, the kinnara said only this much: 'Is it not proper to drive in another stake?' Then, on a later occasion, they brought two kinnaras and showed them to the king. The king said, 'Make them speak.' They did not wish to speak. A certain man, saying, 'I will make them speak,' took them and went to the inner market. There, one saw a ripe mango and fish, and the other saw a wood-apple fruit and a tamarind fruit. Among them, the first said, 'Humans eat great poison; how is it that they are not afflicted with skin disease?' The other said, 'Relying on this, how is it that these humans do not become leprous?' In this way, although they are able to speak human language, they do not speak, seeing two reasons for this.

62. Dasame appaṭivānoti anukaṇṭhito apaccosakkito.

62. In the tenth sutta, as for 'appaṭivāno': it means not being weary, not shrinking back.

63. Ekādasame asantasannivāsanti asappurisānaṃ sannivāsaṃ. Na vadeyyāti ovādena vā anusāsaniyā vā na vadeyya, mā vadatūti attho. Therampāhaṃ na vadeyyanti ahampi theraṃ bhikkhuṃ ovādānusāsanivasena na vadeyyaṃ. Ahitānukampīti ahitaṃ icchamāno. No hitānukampīti hitaṃ anicchamāno. Noti naṃ vadeyyanti “ahaṃ tava vacanaṃ na karissa”nti naṃ vadeyyaṃ. Viheṭheyyanti vacanassa akaraṇena viheṭheyyaṃ. Passampissa [P 2.0152] nappaṭikareyyanti passantopi jānantopi ahaṃ tassa vacanaṃ na kareyyaṃ. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Sukkapakkhe pana sādhūti naṃ vadeyyanti “sādhu bhaddakaṃ sukathitaṃ tayā”ti tassa kathaṃ abhinandanto naṃ vadeyyanti attho.

63. In the eleventh sutta, 'asantasannivāsa' means association with unvirtuous people. 'Na vadeyya' means one should not speak with advice or with instruction; the meaning is 'let one not speak.' 'Therampāhaṃ na vadeyyaṃ' means I too would not speak to an elder monk by way of advice and instruction. 'Ahitānukampī' means wishing for what is not beneficial. 'No hitānukampī' means not wishing for what is beneficial. 'No'ti naṃ vadeyyaṃ' means one should say to him, 'I will not follow your word.' 'Viheṭheyyaṃ' means one would vex him by not following his word. 'Passampissa nappaṭikareyyaṃ' means even seeing, even knowing, I would not follow his word. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances. However, in the positive case, 'sādhū'ti naṃ vadeyyaṃ' means that, while rejoicing in his speech, one should say to him, 'Good, excellent, well-spoken by you'; this is the meaning.

64. Dvādasame ubhato vacīsaṃsāroti dvīsupi pakkhesu aññamaññaṃ akkosanapaccakkosanavasena saṃsaramānā vācā vacīsaṃsāro. Diṭṭhipaḷāsoti diṭṭhiṃ nissāya uppajjanako yugaggāhalakkhaṇo paḷāso diṭṭhipaḷāso nāma. Cetaso āghātoti kopo. So hi cittaṃ āghātento uppajjati. Appaccayoti atuṭṭhākāro, domanassanti attho. Anabhiraddhīti kopoyeva. So hi anabhirādhanavasena anabhiraddhīti vuccati. Ajjhattaṃ avūpasantaṃ hotīti sabbampetaṃ niyakajjhattasaṅkhāte [M 2.0053] attano citte ca saddhivihārikaantevāsikasaṅkhātāya [V 2.0051] attano parisāya ca avūpasantaṃ hoti. Tasmetanti tasmiṃ etaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

64. In the twelfth sutta, 'ubhato vacīsaṃsāro' means speech that goes back and forth between both sides by way of mutual abuse and counter-abuse is 'vacīsaṃsāro'. 'Diṭṭhipaḷāso' means the worthless contention, characterized by partisan grasping, that arises based on a view; this is called 'diṭṭhipaḷāso'. 'Cetaso āghāto' means anger. For it arises while afflicting the mind. 'Appaccayo' means a state of displeasure, mental distress; this is the meaning. 'Anabhiraddhī' means anger itself. For it is called 'anabhiraddhī' by way of its failure to accomplish welfare. 'Ajjhattaṃ avūpasantaṃ hoti' means all of this is unpacified in one's own mind, reckoned as internal, and in the minds of one's own assembly, reckoned as co-residents and pupils. 'Tasmetaṃ' is to be parsed as 'tasmiṃ etaṃ'. The rest should be understood in the way already explained.

Puggalavaggo paṭhamo.

The first is the Chapter on Individuals.

(7) 2. Sukhavaggavaṇṇanā

(7) 2. Commentary on the Happiness Chapter

65. Dutiyassa [V 2.0052] paṭhame gihisukhanti gihīnaṃ sabbakāmanipphattimūlakaṃ sukhaṃ. Pabbajitasukhanti pabbajitānaṃ pabbajjāmūlakaṃ sukhaṃ.

65. In the first discourse of the second chapter, 'happiness of householders' (gihisukha) means the happiness of householders rooted in the accomplishment of all desires. 'Happiness of renunciants' (pabbajitasukha) means the happiness of renunciants rooted in renunciation.

66. Dutiye kāmasukhanti kāme ārabbha uppajjanakasukhaṃ. Nekkhammasukhanti nekkhammaṃ vuccati pabbajjā, taṃ ārabbha uppajjanakasukhaṃ.

66. In the second discourse, 'sensual happiness' (kāmasukha) is the happiness that arises in dependence on sensual pleasures. As for 'the happiness of renunciation' (nekkhammasukha): 'going forth' is called 'renunciation'; it is the happiness that arises in dependence on that.

67. Tatiye [P 2.0153] upadhisukhanti tebhūmakasukhaṃ. Nirupadhisukhanti lokuttarasukhaṃ.

67. In the third discourse, 'happiness with substrates' (upadhisukha) is the happiness of the three planes. 'Happiness without substrates' (nirupadhisukha) is supramundane happiness.

68. Catutthe sāsavasukhanti āsavānaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ vaṭṭasukhaṃ. Anāsavasukhanti tesaṃ apaccayabhūtaṃ vivaṭṭasukhaṃ.

68. In the fourth discourse, 'happiness with taints' (sāsavasukha) is the happiness of the cycle that is a condition for the taints. 'Happiness without taints' (anāsavasukha) is the happiness of that which is not the cycle, which is not a condition for them.

69. Pañcame sāmisanti saṃkilesaṃ vaṭṭagāmisukhaṃ. Nirāmisanti nikkilesaṃ vivaṭṭagāmisukhaṃ.

69. In the fifth discourse, 'worldly happiness' (sāmisa) is defiled happiness that leads to the cycle. 'Spiritual happiness' (nirāmisa) is undefiled happiness that leads to that which is not the cycle.

70. Chaṭṭhe ariyasukhanti aputhujjanasukhaṃ. Anariyasukhanti puthujjanasukhaṃ.

70. In the sixth discourse, 'noble happiness' (ariyasukha) is the happiness of non-worldlings. 'Ignoble happiness' (anariyasukha) is the happiness of worldlings.

71. Sattame kāyikanti kāyaviññāṇasahajātaṃ. Cetasikanti manodvārikasukhaṃ. Taṃ lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ kathitaṃ.

71. In the seventh discourse, 'bodily' (kāyika) is that which is co-arisen with body-consciousness. 'Mental' (cetasika) is happiness at the mind-door. That is said to be mixed, worldly and supramundane.

72. Aṭṭhame sappītikanti paṭhamadutiyajjhānasukhaṃ. Nippītikanti tatiyacatutthajjhānasukhaṃ. Tattha lokiyasappītikato lokiyanippītikaṃ, lokuttarasappītikato ca lokuttaranippītikaṃ agganti evaṃ bhummantaraṃ abhinditvā aggabhāvo veditabbo.

72. In the eighth discourse, 'that with rapture' (sappītika) is the happiness of the first and second jhānas. 'That without rapture' (nippītika) is the happiness of the third and fourth jhānas. Therein, worldly happiness without rapture is superior to worldly happiness with rapture, and supramundane happiness without rapture is superior to supramundane happiness with rapture. Thus, the state of superiority should be understood without breaking the distinction of planes.

73. Navame [M 2.0054] sātasukhanti tīsu jhānesu sukhaṃ. Upekkhāsukhanti catutthajjhānasukhaṃ.

73. In the ninth discourse, 'pleasant happiness' (sātasukha) is the happiness in the three jhānas. 'Equanimity-happiness' (upekkhāsukha) is the happiness of the fourth jhāna.

74. Dasame [V 2.0053] samādhisukhanti appanaṃ vā upacāraṃ vā pattasukhaṃ. Asamādhisukhanti tadubhayaṃ appattasukhaṃ.

74. In the tenth discourse, 'happiness of concentration' (samādhisukha) is the happiness that has attained either absorption or access concentration. 'Happiness without concentration' (asamādhisukha) is the happiness that has not attained either of those two.

75. Ekādasame sappītikārammaṇanti sappītikaṃ jhānadvayaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasukhaṃ. Nippītikārammaṇepi eseva nayo. Dvādasamepi imināva upāyena attho veditabbo.

75. In the eleventh discourse, 'that which has an object with rapture' (sappītikārammaṇa) is the happiness that arises for one reviewing the pair of jhānas with rapture. This same method applies also in the case of an object without rapture. In the twelfth discourse also, the meaning should be understood by this same method.

77. Terasame rūpārammaṇanti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānārammaṇaṃ, yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ ārabbha uppajjanakaṃ vā. Arūpārammaṇanti arūpāvacarajjhānārammaṇaṃ, yaṃkiñci arūpaṃ ārabbha uppajjanakaṃ vāti.

77. In the thirteenth discourse, 'that which has a form-object' (rūpārammaṇa) is happiness that has the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna as its object, or it is that which arises in dependence on any form whatsoever. 'That which has a formless-object' (arūpārammaṇa) is happiness that has an immaterial-sphere jhāna as its object, or it is that which arises in dependence on any formless phenomenon whatsoever.

Sukhavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Happiness, the Second.

(8) 3. Sanimittavaggavaṇṇanā

(8) 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Signs

78-79. Tatiyassa [V 2.0054][P 2.0154] paṭhame sanimittāti sakāraṇā. Dutiyādīsupi eseva nayo. Nidānaṃ hetu saṅkhāro paccayo rūpanti sabbānipi hi etāni kāraṇavevacanāneva.

78-79. In the first discourse of the third chapter, 'with signs' (sanimittā) means 'with a cause.' In the second discourse and so on, this is the same method. Indeed, 'source' (nidāna), 'cause' (hetu), 'formation' (saṅkhāra), 'condition' (paccaya), and 'form' (rūpa)—all these are indeed just synonyms for the word 'cause'.

84. Sattame savedanāti paccayabhūtāya sampayuttavedanāya satiyeva uppajjanti, nāsatīti attho. Aṭṭhamanavamesupi eseva nayo.

84. In the seventh discourse, 'with feeling' (savedanā) means: they arise only when there is associated feeling that has become a condition; they do not arise when it is not present. This is the meaning. In the eighth and ninth discourses also, this is the same method.

87. Dasame saṅkhatārammaṇāti paccayanibbattaṃ saṅkhatadhammaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvāva uppajjanti. No asaṅkhatārammaṇāti asaṅkhataṃ pana nibbānaṃ ārabbha na uppajjanti. Na hontīti maggakkhaṇe na honti nāma, phale patte nāhesunti. Evametesu dasasupi ṭhānesu yāva arahattā desanā desitāti.

87. In the tenth discourse, 'having a conditioned object' (saṅkhatārammaṇā) means: they arise only after having taken as object a conditioned phenomenon produced by a cause. 'Not having an unconditioned object' (no asaṅkhatārammaṇā) means: they do not arise taking the unconditioned, that is, Nibbāna, as object. 'They are not' (na honti) means: at the moment of the path, they are not, so to speak; when the fruit is attained, they were not. Thus, in these ten instances, the teaching was taught up to Arahantship.

Sanimittavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Signs, the Third.

(9) 4. Dhammavaggavaṇṇanā

(9) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Dhamma

88. Catutthassa [V 2.0055][M 2.0055] paṭhame cetovimuttīti phalasamādhi. Paññāvimuttīti phalapaññā.

88. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti) is the concentration of fruition. 'Liberation by wisdom' (paññāvimutti) is the wisdom of fruition.

89. Dutiye paggāhoti vīriyaṃ. Avikkhepoti cittekaggatā.

89. In the second discourse, 'exertion' (paggāha) is energy. 'Non-distraction' (avikkhepa) is one-pointedness of mind.

90. Tatiye nāmanti cattāro arūpakkhandhā. Rūpanti rūpakkhandho. Iti imasmiṃ sutte dhammakoṭṭhāsaparicchedañāṇaṃ nāma kathitaṃ.

90. In the third discourse, 'name' (nāma) is the four immaterial aggregates. 'Form' (rūpa) is the material aggregate. Thus, in this discourse, what is called 'the knowledge that discerns the divisions of phenomena' has been taught.

91. Catutthe vijjāti phalañāṇaṃ. Vimuttīti taṃsampayuttā sesadhammā.

91. In the fourth discourse, 'knowledge' (vijjā) is the knowledge of fruition. 'Liberation' (vimutti) is the remaining states associated with it.

92. Pañcame bhavadiṭṭhīti sassatadiṭṭhi. Vibhavadiṭṭhīti ucchedadiṭṭhi. Chaṭṭhasattamāni uttānatthāneva.

92. In the fifth discourse, 'the view of being' (bhavadiṭṭhi) is the eternalist view. 'The view of non-being' (vibhavadiṭṭhi) is the annihilationist view. The sixth and seventh discourses have a plain meaning.

95. Aṭṭhame dovacassatāti dubbacabhāvo. Pāpamittatāti pāpamittasevanabhāvo. Navamaṃ [P 2.0155] vuttavipariyāyena veditabbaṃ.

95. In the eighth discourse, 'difficulty in being admonished' (dovacassatā) is the state of being difficult to admonish. 'Having bad friends' (pāpamittatā) is the state of associating with bad friends. The ninth discourse should be understood in the opposite way of what was stated.

97. Dasame dhātukusalatāti aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo dhātūti jānanaṃ. Manasikārakusalatāti tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ aniccādivasena lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā jānanaṃ.

97. In the tenth discourse, 'skill in the elements' (dhātukusalatā) is knowing the eighteen elements as 'elements.' 'Skill in attention' (manasikārakusalatā) is knowing by applying the three characteristics, by way of impermanence and so on, to those same elements.

98. Ekādasame āpattikusalatāti pañcannañca sattannañca āpattikkhandhānaṃ jānanaṃ. Āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatāti desanāya vā kammavācāya vā āpattīhi vuṭṭhānajānananti.

98. In the eleventh discourse, 'skill in offenses' (āpattikusalatā) is knowing the five and the seven groups of offenses. 'Skill in rising from an offense' (āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā) is knowing the rising up from offenses either by confession or by a formal act.

Dhammavaggo catuttho.

The Chapter on the Dhamma, the Fourth.

(10) 5. Bālavaggavaṇṇanā

(10) 5. Commentary on the Chapter on the Fool

99. Pañcamassa [V 2.0056] paṭhame anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahatīti “sammajjanī padīpo ca, udakaṃ āsanena ca, chandapārisuddhiutukkhānaṃ, bhikkhugaṇanā ca ovādo, pātimokkhaṃ therabhāroti vuccatī”ti imaṃ dasavidhaṃ therabhāraṃ navako hutvā [M 2.0056] therena anajjhiṭṭho karonto anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahati nāma. Āgataṃ bhāraṃ na vahatīti thero samāno tameva dasavidhaṃ bhāraṃ attanā vā akaronto paraṃ vā asamādapento āgataṃ bhāraṃ na vahati nāma. Dutiyasuttepi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

99. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, 'one carries a burden that has not come' (anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahati) means: a junior monk who, without being requested by an elder, undertakes this tenfold elder's burden—which is said to be: “Sweeping and a lamp; water along with a seat; conveying consent, conveying purity, and announcing the season; counting the monks; the exhortation; and reciting the Pātimokkha—this is called the elder's burden”—is called one who carries a burden that has not come to him. 'One does not carry a burden that has come' (āgataṃ bhāraṃ na vahati) means: an elder who, being one, either does not undertake that same tenfold burden himself or does not encourage another to do so, is called one who does not carry a burden that has come to him. In the second discourse as well, the meaning should be understood in this very way.

101. Tatiye akappiye kappiyasaññīti akappiye sīhamaṃsādimhi “kappiyaṃ ida”nti evaṃsaññī. Kappiye akappiyasaññīti kumbhīlamaṃsabiḷāramaṃsādimhi kappiye “akappiyaṃ ida”nti evaṃsaññī. Catutthaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

101. In the third discourse, 'perceiving the unallowable as allowable' (akappiye kappiyasaññī) means: in regard to what is unallowable, such as lion's meat, one has the perception, “This is allowable.” 'Perceiving the allowable as unallowable' (kappiye akappiyasaññī) means: in regard to what is allowable, such as crocodile's meat or cat's meat, one has the perception, “This is unallowable.” The fourth discourse should be understood in the way already stated.

103. Pañcame anāpattiyā āpattisaññīti āpucchitvā bhaṇḍakaṃ dhovantassa, pattaṃ pacantassa, kese chindantassa, gāmaṃ pavisantassātiādīsu anāpatti, tattha “āpatti aya”nti evaṃsaññī. Āpattiyā anāpattisaññīti tesaññeva vatthūnaṃ anāpucchākaraṇe āpatti, tattha “anāpattī”ti evaṃsaññī. Chaṭṭhepi [P 2.0156] vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Sattamādīni uttānatthāneva.

103. In the fifth discourse, 'perceiving a non-offense as an offense' (anāpattiyā āpattisaññī) means: for a monk who, having asked permission, washes requisites, fires a bowl, cuts hair, or enters a village, and in other such cases, there is no offense; therein, regarding that non-offense, one has the perception, “This is an offense.” 'Perceiving an offense as a non-offense' (āpattiyā anāpattisaññī) means: in doing those very things without asking permission, there is an offense; therein, regarding that offense, one has the perception, “There is no offense.” In the sixth discourse as well, the meaning should be understood in the way already stated. The seventh discourse and so on have a plain meaning.

109. Ekādasame āsavāti kilesā. Na kukkuccāyitabbanti saṅghabhogassa apaṭṭhapanaṃ avicāraṇaṃ na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ nāma, taṃ kukkuccāyati. Kukkuccāyitabbanti tasseva paṭṭhapanaṃ vicāraṇaṃ, taṃ na kukkuccāyati. Dvādasamādīni heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbānīti.

109. In the eleventh sutta, āsavā means defilements. Na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ (what should not be worried about) is the non-arranging and non-investigating of the property of the Saṅgha; this is called 'what should not be worried about,' yet one worries about it. Kukkuccāyitabbaṃ (what should be worried about) is the arranging and investigating of that same property, yet one does not worry about it. The twelfth sutta and so on should be understood in the way stated previously.

Bālavaggo pañcamo.

The Fifth, the Chapter on the Fool.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is completed.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty

(11) 1. Āsāduppajahavaggavaṇṇanā

(11) 1. The Commentary on the Chapter on Aspirations Difficult to Abandon

119. Tatiyassa [V 2.0057][M 2.0057] paṇṇāsakassa paṭhame āsāti taṇhā. Duppajahāti duccajā dunnīharā. Lābhāsāya duppajahabhāvena sattā dasapi vassāni vīsatipi saṭṭhipi vassāni “ajja labhissāma, sve labhissāmā”ti rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahanti, kasikammādīni karonti, ubhatobyūḷhaṃ saṅgāmaṃ pakkhandanti, ajapathasaṅkupathādayo paṭipajjanti, nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pavisanti. Jīvitāsāya duppajahattā sampatte maraṇakālepi vassasatajīviṃ attānaṃ maññanti. So kammakammanimittādīni passantopi “dānaṃ dehi pūjaṃ, karohī”ti anukampakehi vuccamāno “nāhaṃ marissāmi, jīvissāmi”cceva āsāya kassaci vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti.

119. In the first sutta of the third fifty, “aspiration” (āsā) means craving. “Hard to abandon” (duppajahā) means difficult to abandon, difficult to extract.
