Due to the difficulty of abandoning the aspiration for gain, beings attend upon kings for ten, twenty, or even sixty years, thinking, “Today we will gain, tomorrow we will gain.” They engage in farming and other work, plunge into battles arrayed on both sides, traverse goat tracks, spike paths, and the like, and enter the great ocean by ship. Due to the difficulty of abandoning the aspiration for life, even when the time of death has arrived, they think they will live for a hundred years. That person, even while seeing signs of kamma, kamma-nimittas, and the like, and being told by compassionate ones, “Give a gift, make an offering,” does not accept anyone's words due to his aspiration, thinking only, “I will not die, I will live.”

120. Dutiye pubbakārīti paṭhamaṃ upakārassa kārako. Kataññūkatavedīti tena kataṃ ñatvā pacchā kārako. Tesu pubbakārī “iṇaṃ demī”ti saññaṃ karoti, pacchā kārako “iṇaṃ jīrāpemī”ti saññaṃ karoti.

120. In the second sutta, “one who has done a prior service” (pubbakārī) is one who performs a service first. “Grateful and thankful” (kataññūkatavedī) is one who, having known what was done by that person, does something in return afterward. Among them, the one who has done a prior service makes the perception, “I am giving a loan,” while the one who does something afterward makes the perception, “I am clearing a debt.”

121. Tatiye titto ca tappetā cāti paccekabuddho ca tathāgatasāvako ca khīṇāsavo titto nāma, tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho titto ca tappetā ca.

121. In the third sutta, regarding “satisfied” (titto) and “satiating” (tappetā): a Paccekabuddha and a disciple of the Tathāgata whose taints are destroyed are called “satisfied.” The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is both “satisfied” and “satiating.”

122. Catutthe duttappayāti dāyakena duttappayā tappetuṃ na sukarā. Nikkhipatīti [P 2.0157] nidahati na paribhuñjati. Vissajjetīti paresaṃ deti.

122. In the fourth sutta, “hard to satisfy” (duttappayā) means they are hard to be satisfied by a donor, not easy to satisfy. “He lays aside” (nikkhipati) means he stores it away and does not use it. “He gives away” (vissajjeti) means he gives to others.

123. Pañcame na vissajjetīti sabbaṃyeva paresaṃ na deti, attano pana yāpanamattaṃ gahetvā avasesaṃ deti.

123. In the fifth sutta, “does not give away” (na vissajjeti) means he does not give everything to others; rather, taking just enough for his own sustenance, he gives away the remainder.

124. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0058] subhanimittanti iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ.

124. In the sixth sutta, “the beautiful sign” (subhanimittaṃ) means a desirable object.

125. Sattame [M 2.0058] paṭighanimittanti aniṭṭhanimittaṃ.

125. In the seventh sutta, “the sign of aversion” (paṭighanimittaṃ) means a disagreeable sign.

126. Aṭṭhame parato ca ghosoti parassa santikā assaddhammasavanaṃ.

126. In the eighth sutta, “a sound from another” (parato ca ghoso) means hearing the false Dhamma from another.

127. Navame parato ca ghosoti parassa santikā saddhammasavanaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

127. In the ninth sutta, “a sound from another” (parato ca ghoso) means hearing the true Dhamma from another. The rest has a clear meaning throughout.

Āsāduppajahavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: On Aspirations Hard to Abandon.

(12) 2. Āyācanavaggavaṇṇanā

(12) 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Aspiration

131. Dutiyassa [V 2.0059] paṭhame evaṃ sammā āyācamāno āyāceyyāti saddho bhikkhu uṭṭhahitvā “yādiso sāriputtatthero paññāya, ahampi tādiso homi. Yādiso mahāmoggallānatthero iddhiyā, ahampi tādiso homī”ti evaṃ āyācanto pihento patthento yaṃ atthi, tasseva patthitattā sammā pattheyya nāma. Ito uttari patthento micchā pattheyya. Evarūpā hi patthanā yaṃ natthi, tassa patthitattā micchāpatthanā nāma hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Esā, bhikkhave, tulā etaṃ pamāṇanti yathā hi suvaṇṇaṃ vā hiraññaṃ vā tulentassa tulā icchitabbā, dhaññaṃ minantassa mānanti tulane tulā, minane ca mānaṃ pamāṇaṃ hoti, evameva mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ esā tulā etaṃ pamāṇaṃ yadidaṃ sāriputtamoggallānā. Te gahetvā “ahampi ñāṇena vā iddhiyā vā etampamāṇo homī”ti attānaṃ tuletuṃ vā pamāṇetuṃ vā sakkā, na ito aññathā.

131. In the first sutta of the second chapter, regarding 'one who is rightly aspiring should aspire thus': A faithful monk, having risen, should think, “As the Elder Sāriputta is in wisdom, so may I be. As the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is in psychic power, so may I be.” Aspiring thus, because of aspiring for that very thing which exists, it is called rightly aspiring. Aspiring for anything beyond this would be wrongly aspiring. For such an aspiration, because of aspiring for that which does not exist, is called a wrong aspiration. What is the reason? “Monks, this is the balance, this is the measure.” Indeed, just as for one weighing gold or silver, a balance should be desired, and for one measuring grain, a measure should be desired—in weighing, the balance, and in measuring, the measure is the standard—even so, among my disciples who are monks, this is the balance, this is the measure: namely, Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Taking them as the standard, one can weigh or measure oneself, thinking, “May I too be of such a measure in knowledge or psychic power.” It is not possible to do so in any other way.

132. Dutiyādīsupi eseva nayo. Idaṃ [P 2.0158] panettha visesamattaṃ – khemā ca bhikkhunī uppalavaṇṇā cāti etāsu hi khemā paññāya aggā, uppalavaṇṇā iddhiyā. Tasmā “paññāya vā [M 2.0059] iddhiyā vā etādisī homī”ti sammā āyācamānā āyāceyya. Tathā citto gahapati paññāya aggo, hatthako rājakumāro mahiddhikatāya. Tasmā “paññāya vā iddhiyā vā ediso homī”ti sammā āyācamāno āyāceyya. Khujjuttarāpi mahāpaññatāya aggā, nandamātā mahiddhikatāya. Tasmā “paññāya vā iddhiyā vā etādisī homī”ti sammā āyācamānā āyāceyya.

132. In the second and following suttas, this is the same method. This, however, is the only point of difference here: among the bhikkhunī Khemā and the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, Khemā is foremost in wisdom, and Uppalavaṇṇā is foremost in psychic power. Therefore, a female disciple aspiring should rightly aspire, “May I be of such a kind in wisdom or in psychic power.” Similarly, the householder Citta is foremost in wisdom, and the prince Hatthaka is foremost in great psychic power. Therefore, a male disciple aspiring should rightly aspire, “May I be of such a kind in wisdom or in psychic power.” Khujjuttarā is also foremost in great wisdom, and Nandamātā is foremost in great psychic power. Therefore, a female disciple aspiring should rightly aspire, “May I be of such a kind in wisdom or in psychic power.”

135. Pañcame khatanti guṇānaṃ khatattā khataṃ. Upahatanti guṇānaṃ upahatattā upahataṃ, chinnaguṇaṃ naṭṭhaguṇanti attho. Attānaṃ pariharatīti nigguṇaṃ attānaṃ jaggati gopāyati. Sāvajjoti sadoso. Sānuvajjoti saupavādo. Pasavatīti paṭilabhati. Ananuviccāti ajānitvā avinicchinitvā. Apariyogāhetvāti ananupavisitvā. Avaṇṇārahassāti avaṇṇayuttassa micchāpaṭipannassa titthiyassa vā titthiyasāvakassa vā. Vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti “suppaṭipanno [V 2.0060] esa sammāpaṭipanno”ti guṇaṃ katheti. Vaṇṇārahassāti buddhādīsu aññatarassa sammāpaṭipannassa. Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti “duppaṭipanno esa micchāpaṭipanno”ti aguṇaṃ katheti. Avaṇṇārahassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti idhekacco puggalo duppaṭipannānaṃ micchāpaṭipannānaṃ titthiyānaṃ titthiyasāvakānaṃ “itipi duppaṭipannā itipi micchāpaṭipannā”ti avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Vaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti suppaṭipannānaṃ sammāpaṭipannānaṃ buddhānaṃ buddhasāvakānaṃ “itipi suppaṭipannā itipi sammāpaṭipannā”ti vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

135. In the fifth sutta, “ruined” (khataṃ) means ruined due to the ruining of virtues. “Corrupted” (upahataṃ) means corrupted due to the corruption of virtues—that is, one whose virtues are cut off, whose virtues are lost. “He guards himself” (attānaṃ pariharati) means he protects and watches over his self, which is devoid of virtues. “Blameworthy” (sāvajjo) means with fault. “Reproachable” (sānuvajjo) means with reproach. “Begets” (pasavati) means acquires. “Without investigating” (ananuvicca) means without knowing, without determining. “Without scrutinizing” (apariyogāhetvā) means without penetrating. “Of one worthy of dispraise” (avaṇṇārahassa) refers to one fit for dispraise, one of wrong practice, such as a sectarian or a disciple of a sectarian. “Speaks praise” (vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati) means one speaks of virtues, saying, “This one is of good practice, of right practice.” “Of one worthy of praise” (vaṇṇārahassa) refers to one of right practice, such as any of the Buddhas and so forth. “Speaks dispraise” (avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati) means one speaks of faults, saying, “This one is of bad practice, of wrong practice.” “Speaks dispraise of one worthy of dispraise” (avaṇṇārahassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati) means a certain person here speaks dispraise of those of bad practice, those of wrong practice, sectarians, and their disciples, saying, “For this reason they are of bad practice, for this reason they are of wrong practice.” “Speaks praise of one worthy of praise” (vaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati) means one speaks praise of those of good practice, those of right practice, the Buddhas, and the Buddha's disciples, saying, “For this reason they are of good practice, for this reason they are of right practice.”

136. Chaṭṭhe appasādanīye ṭhāneti appasādakāraṇe. Pasādaṃ [P 2.0159] upadaṃsetīti duppaṭipadāya micchāpaṭipadāya “ayaṃ suppaṭipadā sammāpaṭipadā”ti pasādaṃ janeti. Pasādanīye ṭhāne appasādanti suppaṭipadāya sammāpaṭipadāya “ayaṃ duppaṭipadā micchāpaṭipadā”ti appasādaṃ janetīti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

136. In the sixth discourse, “in a situation unfit for inspiring confidence” (appasādanīye ṭhāne) means in a cause of lack of confidence. “He inspires confidence” (pasādaṃ upadaṃseti) means with regard to bad practice and wrong practice, one generates confidence, saying, “This is good practice, this is right practice.” “Lack of confidence in a situation fit for inspiring confidence” (pasādanīye ṭhāne appasādaṃ) means with regard to good practice and right practice, one generates lack of confidence, saying, “This is bad practice, this is wrong practice.” The rest here is self-explanatory.

137. Sattame dvīsūti dvīsu okāsesu dvīsu kāraṇesu. Micchāpaṭipajjamānoti micchāpaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjamāno. Mātari ca pitari cāti mittavindako viya mātari, ajātasattu viya pitari. Sukkapakkho vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

137. In the seventh discourse, “in two” (dvīsu) means in two instances, in two reasons. “Practicing wrongly” (micchāpaṭipajjamāno) means one who is practicing wrong conduct. “Towards mother and father” (mātari ca pitari ca) refers to one like Mittavindaka towards his mother, and like King Ajātasattu towards his father. The bright side should be understood in the same way as stated.

138. Aṭṭhame tathāgate ca tathāgatasāvake cāti devadatto viya tathāgate, kokāliko viya ca tathāgatasāvake. Sukkapakkhe [M 2.0060] ānandatthero viya tathāgate, nandagopālakaseṭṭhiputto viya ca tathāgatasāvake.

138. In the eighth discourse, “in the Tathāgata and in the Tathāgata's disciples” (tathāgate ca tathāgatasāvake ca) means like Devadatta towards the Tathāgata, and like Kokālika towards the Tathāgata's disciples. In the bright faction, it means like the Elder Ānanda towards the Tathāgata, and like Nandagopālaka, the son of the wealthy man, towards the Tathāgata's disciples.

139. Navame sacittavodānanti sakacittassa vodānaṃ, aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Na ca kiñci loke upādiyatīti loke ca rūpādīsu dhammesu kiñci ekaṃ dhammampi na gaṇhāti na parāmasati. Evamettha anupādānaṃ nāma dutiyo dhammo hoti. Dasamekādasamāni uttānatthānevāti.

139. In the ninth discourse, “the cleansing of one's own mind” (sacittavodānaṃ) means the cleansing of one's own mind—this is a name for the eight attainments. “And he does not cling to anything in the world” (na ca kiñci loke upādiyati) means in the world, among phenomena such as form and so on, he does not grasp or misapprehend any single phenomenon. Thus, herein, non-clinging is the second phenomenon. The tenth and eleventh discourses are of clear meaning.

Āyācanavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Entreaty is the second.

(13) 3. Dānavaggavaṇṇanā

(13) 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Giving

142. Tatiyassa [V 2.0061] paṭhame dānānīti diyyanakavasena dānāni, deyyadhammassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Savatthukā vā cetanā dānaṃ, sampattipariccāgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Āmisadānanti cattāro paccayā diyyanakavasena āmisadānaṃ nāma. Dhammadānanti idhekacco amatapattipaṭipadaṃ kathetvā deti, idaṃ dhammadānaṃ nāma.

In the first discourse of the third chapter, “gifts” (dānāni) are so called in the sense of being given; this is a name for an object to be given. Or, “giving” (dāna) is volition together with its object; this is a name for the relinquishing of one's possessions. “Material giving” (āmisadāna): the four requisites, in the sense of being given, are called ‘material giving’. “Giving of the Dhamma” (dhammadāna): herein, a certain person teaches and gives the practice leading to the attainment of the Deathless; this is called ‘giving of the Dhamma’.

143. Dutiye [P 2.0160] cattāro paccayā yajanakavasena yāgo nāma dhammopi yajanakavasena yāgoti veditabbo.

142. In the second discourse, the four requisites, in the sense of being offered, are called “sacrifice” (yāga). The Dhamma, too, in the sense of being offered, should be understood as “sacrifice” (yāga).

144. Tatiye āmisassa cajanaṃ āmisacāgo, dhammassa cajanaṃ dhammacāgo. Catutthe upasaggamattaṃ viseso.

143. In the third discourse, the relinquishing of material things is “material relinquishing” (āmisacāga); the relinquishing of the Dhamma is “Dhamma relinquishing” (dhammacāgo). In the fourth discourse, the difference is merely a prefix.

146. Pañcame catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ bhuñjanaṃ āmisabhogo, dhammassa bhuñjanaṃ dhammabhogo. Chaṭṭhe upasaggamattaṃ viseso.

144. In the fifth discourse, the enjoyment of the four requisites is “material enjoyment” (āmisabhoga); the enjoyment of the Dhamma is “Dhamma enjoyment” (dhammabhoga). In the sixth discourse, the difference is merely a prefix.

148. Sattame catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ saṃvibhajanaṃ āmisasaṃvibhāgo, dhammassa saṃvibhajanaṃ dhammasaṃvibhāgo.

146. In the seventh discourse, the sharing of the four requisites is “material sharing” (āmisasaṃvibhāga); the sharing of the Dhamma is “Dhamma sharing” (dhammasaṃvibhāgo).

149. Aṭṭhame catūhi paccayehi saṅgaho āmisasaṅgaho, dhammena saṅgaho dhammasaṅgaho.

148. In the eighth discourse, support by means of the four requisites is “material support” (āmisasaṅgaho); support by means of the Dhamma is “Dhamma support” (dhammasaṅgaho).

150. Navame [M 2.0061] catūhi paccayehi anuggaṇhanaṃ āmisānuggaho, dhammena anuggaṇhanaṃ dhammānuggaho.

149. In the ninth discourse, assistance by means of the four requisites is “material assistance” (āmisānuggaho); assistance by means of the Dhamma is “Dhamma assistance” (dhammānuggaho).

151. Dasame catūhi paccayehi anukampanaṃ āmisānukampā, dhammena anukampanaṃ dhammānukampāti.

150. In the tenth discourse, compassion by means of the four requisites is “material compassion” (āmisānukampā); compassion by means of the Dhamma is “Dhamma compassion” (dhammānukampā).

Dānavaggo tatiyo.

151. The Chapter on Giving is the third.

(14) 4. Santhāravaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 4. Commentary on the Chapter on Spreading

152. Catutthassa [V 2.0062] paṭhame catūhi paccayehi attano ca parassa ca antarapaṭicchādanavasena santharaṇaṃ āmisasanthāro, dhammena santharaṇaṃ dhammasanthāro. Dutiye upasaggamattaṃ viseso.

In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, conciliation by means of the four requisites for oneself and for others, by way of covering the interval, is 'material conciliation' (āmisasanthāra); conciliation by means of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma conciliation' (dhammasanthāra). In the second discourse, the difference is merely a prefix.

154. Tatiye vuttappakārassa āmisassa esanā āmisesanā, dhammassa esanā dhammesanā. Catutthe upasaggamattameva viseso.

In the third discourse, the seeking of material things of the kind described is 'material seeking' (āmisesanā); the seeking of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma seeking' (dhammesanā). In the fourth discourse, the only difference is the prefix.

156. Pañcame matthakappattā āmisapariyesanā āmisapariyeṭṭhi, matthakappattāva dhammapariyesanā dhammapariyeṭṭhīti vuttā.

152. In the fifth discourse, the search for material things that has reached its culmination is 'material search' (āmisapariyeṭṭhi); and the search for the Dhamma that has reached its culmination is called 'Dhamma search' (dhammapariyeṭṭhi).

157. Chaṭṭhe āmisena pūjanaṃ āmisapūjā, dhammena pūjanaṃ dhammapūjā.

154. In the sixth discourse, honoring by means of material things is 'material homage' (āmisapūjā); honoring by means of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma homage' (dhammapūjā).

158. Sattame [P 2.0161] ātitheyyānīti āgantukadānāni. Atitheyyānītipi pāṭho.

156. In the seventh discourse, 'hospitalities' (ātitheyyāni) means gifts for guests. There is also the reading 'atitheyyāni'.

159. Aṭṭhame āmisaṃ ijjhanakasamijjhanakavasena āmisiddhi, dhammopi ijjhanakasamijjhanakavasena dhammiddhi.

157. In the eighth discourse, material things, by way of accomplishment and thorough accomplishment, are 'material success' (āmisiddhi); the Dhamma, too, by way of accomplishment and thorough accomplishment, is 'Dhamma success' (dhammiddhi).

160. Navame āmisena vaḍḍhanaṃ āmisavuddhi, dhammena vaḍḍhanaṃ dhammavuddhi.

158. In the ninth discourse, increase by means of material things is 'material increase' (āmisavuddhi); increase by means of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma increase' (dhammavuddhi).

161. Dasame ratikaraṇaṭṭhena āmisaṃ āmisaratanaṃ, dhammo dhammaratanaṃ.

159. In the tenth discourse, because of the meaning of causing delight, material things are 'material treasure' (āmisaratanaṃ); the Dhamma is 'Dhamma treasure' (dhammaratanaṃ).

162. Ekādasame [V 2.0063][M 2.0062] āmisassa cinanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ āmisasannicayo, dhammassa cinanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ dhammasannicayo.

160. In the eleventh discourse, the acquiring and increasing of material things is 'material accumulation' (āmisasannicayo); the acquiring and increasing of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma accumulation' (dhammasannicayo).

163. Dvādasame āmisassa vipulabhāvo āmisavepullaṃ, dhammassa vipulabhāvo dhammavepullanti.

161. In the twelfth discourse, the state of being extensive of material things is 'material extensiveness' (āmisavepullaṃ); the state of being extensive of the Dhamma is 'Dhamma extensiveness' (dhammavepullaṃ).

Santhāravaggo catuttho.

162. The Chapter on Conciliation is the fourth.

(15) 5. Samāpattivaggavaṇṇanā

(15) 5. Commentary on the Chapter on Attainments

164. Pañcamassa [V 2.0064] paṭhame samāpattikusalatāti āhārasappāyaṃ utusappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā samāpattisamāpajjane chekatā. Samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatāti yathāparicchedena gate kāle viyatto hutvā uṭṭhahanto vuṭṭhānakusalo nāma hoti, evaṃ kusalatā.

163. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, 'skill in attainment' is adeptness in entering attainment, having investigated the suitability of food and climate. 'Skill in emerging from attainment' is that a person who, being capable, emerges when the determined time has come, is called one skilled in emerging. Such is the skillfulness.

165. Dutiye ajjavanti ujubhāvo. Maddavanti mudubhāvo.

In the second discourse, 'uprightness' (ajjavaṃ) is the state of being straightforward. 'Gentleness' (maddavaṃ) is the state of being soft.

166. Tatiye khantīti adhivāsanakhanti. Soraccanti susīlyabhāvena suratabhāvo.

In the third discourse, 'patience' (khanti) is the patience of endurance. 'Meekness' (soraccaṃ) is the state of being agreeable through good virtue.

167. Catutthe sākhalyanti saṇhavācāvasena sammodamānabhāvo. Paṭisanthāroti āmisena vā dhammena vā paṭisantharaṇaṃ.

164. In the fourth discourse, 'affability' (sākhalyam) is the state of being friendly by way of gentle speech. 'Friendly welcome' (paṭisanthāro) is conciliation with material things or with the Dhamma.

168. Pañcame avihiṃsāti karuṇāpubbabhāgo. Soceyyanti sīlavasena sucibhāvo. Chaṭṭhasattamāni uttānatthāneva.

165. In the fifth discourse, 'non-harming' (avihiṃsā) is the compassion that is the preliminary part of the compassion jhāna. 'Purity' (soceyyaṃ) is the state of being pure by way of morality. The sixth and seventh discourses are simply of clear meaning.

171. Aṭṭhame paṭisaṅkhānabalanti paccavekkhaṇabalaṃ.

166. In the eighth discourse, 'the power of reflection' (paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ) is the power of reviewing.

172. Navame [P 2.0162] muṭṭhassacce akampanena satiyeva satibalaṃ. Uddhacce akampanena samādhiyeva samādhibalaṃ.

167. In the ninth discourse, because of not wavering due to the state of lapsed mindfulness, mindfulness itself is the power of mindfulness. Because of not wavering due to the state of agitation, concentration itself is the power of concentration.

173. Dasame samathoti cittekaggatā. Vipassanāti saṅkhārapariggāhakaññāṇaṃ.

168. In the tenth discourse, 'serenity' (samatho) is one-pointedness of mind. 'Insight' (vipassanā) is the knowledge that comprehends formations.

174. Ekādasame [M 2.0063] sīlavipattīti dussīlyaṃ. Diṭṭhivipattīti micchādiṭṭhi.

171. In the eleventh discourse, 'failure in moral conduct' (sīlavipatti) is the state of having bad morality. 'Failure in view' (diṭṭhivipatti) is wrong view.

175. Dvādasame sīlasampadāti paripuṇṇasīlatā. Diṭṭhisampadāti sammādiṭṭhikabhāvo. Tena [V 2.0065] kammassakatasammādiṭṭhi, jhānasammādiṭṭhi, vipassanāsammādiṭṭhi, maggasammādiṭṭhi, phalasammādiṭṭhīti sabbāpi pañcavidhā sammādiṭṭhi saṅgahitā hoti.

175. In the twelfth discourse, 'accomplishment in moral conduct' is the state of having perfect morality. 'Accomplishment in view' is the state of having right view. By that, all five kinds of right view are included: the right view that kamma is one's own property, the right view associated with jhāna, the right view associated with insight, the right view associated with the path, and the right view associated with the fruit.

176. Terasame sīlavisuddhīti visuddhisampāpakaṃ sīlaṃ. Diṭṭhivisuddhīti visuddhisampāpikā catumaggasammādiṭṭhi, pañcavidhāpi vā sammādiṭṭhi.

176. In the thirteenth discourse, 'purification of moral conduct' is the moral conduct that leads to purification. 'Purification of view' is the right view associated with the four paths that leads to purification, or alternatively, the five kinds of right view.

177. Cuddasame diṭṭhivisuddhīti visuddhisampāpikā sammādiṭṭhiyeva. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti heṭṭhimamaggasampayuttaṃ vīriyaṃ. Tañhi tassā diṭṭhiyā anurūpattā “yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhāna”nti vuttaṃ.

177. In the fourteenth discourse, 'purification of view' is simply the right view that leads to purification. And 'striving in accordance with one’s view' is the energy associated with a lower path. Indeed, it is called 'striving in accordance with one’s view' because that energy is in accordance with that view.

178. Pannarasame asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesūti aññatra arahattamaggā kusalesu dhammesu asantuṭṭhibhāvo.

178. In the fifteenth discourse, 'and dissatisfaction with wholesome qualities' is the state of being unsatisfied with wholesome qualities, apart from the path of arahantship.

179. Soḷasame muṭṭhassaccanti muṭṭhassatibhāvo. Asampajaññanti aññāṇabhāvo.

179. In the sixteenth discourse, 'lapsed mindfulness' is the state of having lapsed mindfulness. 'Lack of clear comprehension' is the state of not knowing.

180. Sattarasame apilāpanalakkhaṇā sati. Sammā pajānanalakkhaṇaṃ sampajaññanti.

180. In the seventeenth discourse, mindfulness has the characteristic of not floating away. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of correctly and distinctly knowing.

Samāpattivaggo pañcamo. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The fifth is the Chapter on Attainments. The Third Fifty is concluded.

1. Kodhapeyyālaṃ

1. The Repetition Series on Anger

181. Ito [M 2.0064][V 2.0066] paresu kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho. Upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho. Sukatakaraṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇo palāso. Usūyanalakkhaṇā issā. Pañcamaccherabhāvo [P 2.0163] macchariyaṃ. Taṃ sabbampi maccharāyanalakkhaṇaṃ. Katapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā. Kerāṭikalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. Alajjanākāro ahirikaṃ. Upavādato abhāyanākāro anottappaṃ. Akkodhādayo tesaṃ paṭipakkhavasena veditabbā.

181. Herein and henceforth: Anger has the characteristic of getting angry. Enmity has the characteristic of bearing a grudge. Contempt has the characteristic of disparaging a good deed done by another. Rivalry has the characteristic of seizing the yoke. Envy has the characteristic of being jealous of another's prosperity. Stinginess is the state of the five kinds of stinginess, and all of it also has the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity. Deceit has the characteristic of concealing a fault one has committed. Fraud has the characteristic of being crafty and crooked. Shamelessness is the manner of not being ashamed. Fearlessness of blame is the manner of not being afraid of the accusations of others. Non-anger and the rest should be known by way of their opposites.

185. Sekkhassa bhikkhunoti sattavidhassāpi sekkhassa upariupariguṇehi parihānāya saṃvattanti, puthujjanassa pana paṭhamataraṃyeva parihānāya saṃvattantīti veditabbā. Aparihānāyāti upariupariguṇehi aparihānatthāya.

185. As for 'for a trainee monk': for the trainee, even one of the seven kinds, they lead to decline from higher and higher virtues; but for an ordinary person, it should be understood that they lead to decline from the very beginning. As for 'for non-decline': it means for the purpose of non-decline from higher and higher virtues.

187. Yathābhataṃ nikkhittoti yathā ānetvā nikkhitto, evaṃ niraye patiṭṭhito vāti veditabbo.

187. As for 'as brought and placed down': it means that just as one is brought and placed down, so too is one established in hell; thus it should be known.

190. Ekaccoti yassete kodhādayo atthi, so ekacco nāma.

190. As for 'a certain one': a person for whom these things such as anger exist is called 'a certain one'.

Kodhapeyyālaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Repetition Series on Anger is concluded.

2. Akusalapeyyālaṃ

2. The Repetition Series on the Unwholesome

191-200. Sāvajjāti [V 2.0067] sadosā. Anavajjāti niddosā. Dukkhudrayāti dukkhavaḍḍhikā. Sukhudriyāti sukhavaḍḍhikā. Sabyābajjhāti sadukkhā. Abyābajjhāti niddukkhā. Ettāvatā vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

'Blameworthy' means with fault. 'Blameless' means without fault. 'Resulting in suffering' means increasing suffering. 'Resulting in happiness' means increasing happiness. 'With affliction' means with suffering. 'Without affliction' means without suffering. By this much, only the round of existence and the escape from the round have been taught.

Akusalapeyyālaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Repetition Series on the Unwholesome is concluded.

3. Vinayapeyyālaṃ

3. The Repetition Series on the Discipline

201. Dveme[V 2.0068][M 2.0065], bhikkhave, atthavase paṭiccāti, bhikkhave, dve atthe nissāya dve kāraṇāni sandhāya. Sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti sikkhākoṭṭhāso ṭhapito. Saṅghasuṭṭhutāyāti saṅghassa suṭṭhubhāvāya, “suṭṭhu, bhante”ti vatvā sampaṭicchanatthāyāti attho. Saṅghaphāsutāyāti saṅghassa phāsuvihāratthāya. Dummaṅkūnanti dussīlānaṃ. Pesalānanti pīyasīlānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānanti diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vītikkamapaccayā paṭiladdhabbānaṃ vadhabandhanādidukkhadhammasaṅkhātānaṃ āsavānaṃ. Saṃvarāyāti pidahanatthāya. Samparāyikānanti [P 2.0164] tathārūpānaṃyeva apāyadukkhasaṅkhātānaṃ samparāye uppajjanakaāsavānaṃ. Paṭighātāyāti paṭisedhanatthāya. Verānanti akusalaverānampi puggalaverānampi. Vajjānanti dosānaṃ. Te eva vā dukkhadhammā vajjanīyattā idha vajjāti adhippetā. Bhayānanti cittutrāsabhayānampi bhayahetūnaṃ tesaṃyeva dukkhadhammānampi. Akusalānanti akkhamaṭṭhena akusalasaṅkhātānaṃ dukkhadhammānaṃ. Gihīnaṃ anukampāyāti gihīsu ujjhāyantesu paññattasikkhāpadaṃ gihīnaṃ anukampāya paññattaṃ nāma. Pāpicchānaṃ pakkhupacchedāyāti pāpicchā pakkhaṃ nissāya saṅghaṃ bhindeyyunti tesaṃ pakkhupacchedanatthāya. Appasannānaṃ pasādāyāti pubbe appasannānampi paṇḍitamanussānaṃ sikkhāpadapaññattisampadaṃ disvā pasāduppattiatthāya. Pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāyāti pasannānaṃ uparūparipasādabhāvāya. Saddhammaṭṭhitiyāti saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ. Vinayānuggahāyāti pañcavidhassāpi vinayassa anuggaṇhanatthāya.

201. As for 'Monks, for two reasons': it means, monks, relying on two purposes and referring to two causes. As for 'The training rule is laid down': it means the portion of training is established. As for 'For the well-being of the Sangha': it means for the Sangha's welfare, with the intention of accepting it by saying, "Well done, venerable sir." As for 'For the comfort of the Sangha': it means for the Sangha's ease of living. As for 'The unruly': it refers to the unprincipled. As for 'The virtuous': it refers to those of amiable conduct. As for 'The taints pertaining to this life': it means those taints, to be obtained due to the cause of transgression in this very existence, which are designated as states of suffering such as execution, imprisonment, and so on. As for 'For restraint': it means for the purpose of preventing. As for 'The taints pertaining to future lives': it means those taints that are to arise in a future life, which are designated as the suffering of the plane of misery. As for 'For warding off': it means for the purpose of repelling. As for 'Hostilities': it refers to both unwholesome hostilities and personal hostilities. As for 'Faults': it refers to flaws. Or, those same states of suffering are intended here as 'faults' because they should be avoided. As for 'Dangers': it refers to both fears that are terrors of the mind and to those same states of suffering which are the causes of fear. As for 'Unwholesome': it refers to states of suffering designated as 'unwholesome' in the sense of being unendurable. As for 'Out of compassion for householders': it means that when householders criticize, the training rule is laid down out of compassion for them. As for 'To cut off the faction of the wicked': it is for the purpose of cutting off the faction of those with evil desires, lest they split the Sangha by depending on a faction. As for 'To inspire confidence in the faithless': it is for the purpose of the arising of confidence in wise people who were previously faithless, upon seeing the excellence of the laying down of the training rules. As for 'To increase the faith of the faithful': it means for the faith of those who are already faithful to become ever greater. As for 'For the longevity of the true Dhamma': it is for the purpose of the long-standing of the true Dhamma. As for 'For the support of the discipline': it is for the purpose of upholding the five kinds of discipline.

202-230. Pātimokkhaṃ paññattanti bhikkhupātimokkhaṃ bhikkhunipātimokkhanti duvidhaṃ pātimokkhaṃ paññattaṃ. Pātimokkhuddesoti bhikkhūnaṃ pañca, bhikkhunīnaṃ cattāroti nava pātimokkhuddesā paññattā. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapananti uposathaṭṭhapanaṃ. Pavāraṇā paññattāti cātuddasikā pannarasikāti dve pavāraṇā paññattā. Pavāraṇaṭṭhapanaṃ paññattanti sāpattikassa bhikkhuno pavāraṇā uttiyā vattamānāya pavāraṇaṭṭhapanaṃ paññattaṃ. Tajjanīyakammādīsu [M 2.0066] bhikkhū vācāsattīhi vitudantānaṃ paṇḍukalohitakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tajjanīyakammaṃ (cūḷava. 1 ādayo) paññattaṃ. Bālassa [P 2.0165] abyattassa seyyasakassa [V 2.0069] bhikkhuno niyassakammaṃ paññattaṃ. Kuladūsake assajipunabbasuke bhikkhū ārabbha pabbājanīyakammaṃ (cūḷava. 21 ādayo) paññattaṃ. Gihīnaṃ akkosakassa sudhammattherassa paṭisāraṇīyakammaṃ (cūḷava. 33 ādayo) paññattaṃ. Āpattiyā adassanādīsu ukkhepanīyakammaṃ paññattaṃ. Garukāpattiṃ āpannassa paṭicchannāya āpattiyā parivāsadānaṃ paññattaṃ. Parivāse antarāpattiṃ āpannassa mūlāya paṭikassanaṃ paññattaṃ. Paṭicchannāyapi appaṭicchannāyapi āpattiyā mānattadānaṃ paññattaṃ. Ciṇṇamānattassa abbhānaṃ paññattaṃ. Sammā vattantassa osāraṇīyaṃ paññattaṃ. Asammāvattanādīsu nissāraṇīyaṃ paññattaṃ.

202-230. The Pātimokkha has been laid down in two forms: the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. The recitation of the Pātimokkha has been laid down in nine ways: five for bhikkhus and four for bhikkhunīs. The suspension of the Pātimokkha is the suspension of the Uposatha. The Pavāraṇā has been laid down in two forms: the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā and the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. The suspension of the Pavāraṇā has been laid down for a bhikkhu who has an offense while the formal motion for Pavāraṇā is proceeding. In the case of the Tajjanīya Kamma and others, the Tajjanīya Kamma has been laid down for the bhikkhus named Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, who were piercing other bhikkhus with verbal spears. The Nissaya Kamma has been laid down for the foolish and incompetent bhikkhu named Seyyasaka. The Pabbājanīya Kamma has been laid down concerning the bhikkhus named Assaji and Punabbasu, who were corrupters of families. The Paṭisāraṇīya Kamma has been laid down for the Elder Sudhamma, who abused laypeople. The Ukkhepanīya Kamma has been laid down for not seeing an offense and so forth. The granting of probation has been laid down for one who has committed a grave offense that has been concealed. The sending back to the beginning has been laid down for one who commits an interim offense during probation. The granting of penance has been laid down for an offense that is both concealed and unconcealed. Rehabilitation has been laid down for one who has completed the penance. Reinstatement has been laid down for one who conducts himself properly. Expulsion has been laid down for misconduct and so forth.

Ehibhikkhūpasampadā saraṇagamanūpasampadā ovādūpasampadā pañhābyākaraṇūpasampadā ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā garudhammūpasampadā ubhatosaṅghe upasampadā dūtena upasampadāti aṭṭhavidhā upasampadā paññattā. Ñattikammaṃ nava ṭhānāni gacchatīti evaṃ navaṭṭhānikaṃ ñattikammaṃ paññattaṃ. Ñattidutiyakammaṃ satta ṭhānāni gacchatīti evaṃ sattaṭṭhānikameva ñattidutiyakammaṃ paññattaṃ. Ñatticatutthakammaṃ satta ṭhānāni gacchatīti evaṃ sattaṭṭhānikameva ñatticatutthakammaṃ paññattaṃ. Paṭhamapārājikādīnaṃ paṭhamapaññatti apaññatte paññattaṃ. Tesaṃyeva anupaññatti paññatte anupaññattaṃ. Dhammasammukhatā vinayasammukhatā saṅghasammukhatā puggalasammukhatāti imassa catubbidhassa sammukhībhāvassa vasena sammukhāvinayo paññatto. Sativepullappattassa khīṇāsavassa acodanatthāya sativinayo paññatto. Ummattakassa [P 2.0166] bhikkhuno amūḷhavinayo paññatto. Appaṭiññāya cuditakassa āpattiyā ataraṇatthaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ paññattaṃ. Bahutarānaṃ dhammavādīnaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā adhikaraṇavūpasamanatthaṃ. Yebhuyyasikā paññattā. Pāpussannassa puggalassa niggaṇhanatthaṃ tassapāpiyasikā paññattā. Bhaṇḍanādivasena bahuṃ assāmaṇakaṃ katvā āpattiṃ āpannānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhapetvā thullavajjaṃ ṭhapetvā gihipaṭisaṃyuttañca avasesāpattīnaṃ vūpasamanatthāya tiṇavatthārako paññatto.

The 'Come, Bhikkhu' ordination, the ordination by going for refuge, the ordination by accepting exhortation, the ordination by answering a question, the ordination by an act with a motion as the fourth, the ordination by accepting the eight weighty rules, the ordination in the dual Sangha, and the ordination by a messenger—thus, eight kinds of ordination have been laid down. The act consisting of a motion extends to nine instances; thus, the nine-instance act consisting of a motion has been laid down. The act with a motion as the second extends to seven instances; thus, the seven-instance act with a motion as the second has been laid down. The act with a motion as the fourth extends to seven instances; thus, the seven-instance act with a motion as the fourth has been laid down. Of the first Pārājika offense and others, the initial prescription was laid down when a training rule had not yet been laid down. For those same offenses, a supplementary prescription was laid down when a training rule had already been laid down. Presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, presence of the Sangha, and presence of the individual—by means of this fourfold presence, the procedure for a verdict in the presence of has been laid down. For an Arahant who has attained abundant mindfulness, the procedure for a verdict of mindfulness has been laid down for the purpose of not being accused. For a bhikkhu who is insane, the procedure for a verdict of past insanity has been laid down. For one who is accused and does not confess, the procedure of obtaining an acknowledgement has been laid down for the purpose of dealing with the offense. For the purpose of settling a dispute by accepting the view of the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma, the procedure of taking a majority vote has been laid down. For the purpose of restraining a person who is full of evil, the procedure for one who is corrupt has been laid down. For bhikkhus who, by means of quarreling and so forth, have committed much that is unbecoming and have fallen into offenses—setting aside grave offenses and those connected with householders—the procedure of covering over with grass has been laid down for the purpose of settling the remaining offenses.

Vinayapeyyālaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Vinaya Repetition Series is concluded.

4. Rāgapeyyālaṃ

4. The Repetition Series on Lust

231. Rāgassa[V 2.0070][M 2.0067], bhikkhave, abhiññāyāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa abhijānanatthaṃ paccakkhakaraṇatthaṃ. Pariññāyāti parijānanatthaṃ. Parikkhayāyāti parikkhayagamanatthaṃ. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthaṃ. Khayāya vayāyāti khayavayagamanatthaṃ. Virāgāyāti virajjanatthaṃ. Nirodhāyāti nirujjhanatthaṃ. Cāgāyāti cajanatthaṃ. Paṭinissaggāyāti paṭinissajjanatthaṃ.

231. The phrase 'Rāgassa, bhikkhave, abhiññāya' means: for the purpose of knowing with higher knowledge, for the purpose of directly realizing the lust that has the five cords of sensual pleasure as its object. The phrase 'Pariññāya' means: for the purpose of comprehensively knowing. The phrase 'Parikkhayāya' means: for the purpose of reaching exhaustion. The phrase 'Pahānāya' means: for the purpose of abandoning. The phrase 'Khayāya vayāya' means: for the purpose of reaching destruction and passing away. The phrase 'Virāgāya' means: for the purpose of becoming dispassionate. The phrase 'Nirodhāya' means: for the purpose of ceasing. The phrase 'Cāgāya' means: for the purpose of relinquishing. The phrase 'Paṭinissaggāya' means: for the purpose of relinquishing back.

232-246. Thambhassāti kodhamānavasena thaddhabhāvassa. Sārabbhassāti kāraṇuttariyalakkhaṇassa sārabbhassa. Mānassāti navavidhamānassa. Atimānassāti atikkamitvā maññanamānassa. Madassāti majjanākāramadassa. Pamādassāti sativippavāsassa, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggassa. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

232-246. The phrase 'Thambhassa' means: of the state of being hard and stiff by the power of anger and conceit. The phrase 'Sārambhassa' means: of the impetuosity which has the characteristic of acting excessively. The phrase 'Mānassa' means: of the nine-fold conceit. The phrase 'Atimānassa' means: of the conceit of thinking in a surpassing way. The phrase 'Madassa' means: of the intoxication that has the manner of being intoxicated. The phrase 'Pamādassa' means: of the absence of mindfulness, of the releasing of the mind into the five cords of sensual pleasure. The remainder has an obvious meaning everywhere.

Rāgapeyyālaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Repetition Series on Lust is concluded.

Manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Dukanipātassa saṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Book of the Twos is concluded.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Tikanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Book of the Threes

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Bālavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Fool

1. Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Bhaya Sutta

1. Tikanipātassa [V 2.0071][M 2.0069][P 2.0167] paṭhame bhayānītiādīsu bhayanti cittutrāso. Upaddavoti anekaggatākāro. Upasaggoti upasaṭṭhākāro tattha tattha lagganākāro.

1. In the first sutta of the Tikanipāta, among terms beginning with 'bhayāni', the word 'bhayaṃ' means terror of the mind. The word 'upaddavo' means the state of not having a single object. The word 'upasaggo' means the state of being afflicted, the state of clinging to this and that.

Tesaṃ evaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ – pabbatavisamanissitā corā janapadavāsīnaṃ pesenti – “mayaṃ asukadivase nāma tumhākaṃ gāmaṃ paharissāmā”ti. Te taṃ pavattiṃ sutakālato paṭṭhāya bhayaṃ [V 2.0072] santāsaṃ āpajjanti. Ayaṃ cittutrāso nāma. “Yathā no te corā kupitā anatthampi āvaheyyu”nti hatthasāraṃ gahetvā dvipadacatuppadehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha tattha bhūmiyaṃ nipajjanti ḍaṃsamakasādīhi khajjamānā, gumbantarāni pavisantā khāṇukaṇṭake maddanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ vicarantānaṃ vikkhittabhāvo anekaggatākāro nāma. Tato coresu yathāvutte divase anāgacchantesu “tucchakasāsanaṃ bhavissati, gāmaṃ pavisissāmā”ti saparikkhārā gāmaṃ pavisanti. Atha tesaṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā gāmaṃ parivāretvā dvāre aggiṃ datvā manusse ghātetvā corā sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ vilumpitvā gacchanti. Tesu ghātitāvasesā aggiṃ nibbāpetvā koṭṭhakacchāyābhitticchāyādīsu tattha tattha laggitvā nisīdanti naṭṭhaṃ anusocamānā. Ayaṃ upasaṭṭhākāro lagganākāro nāma.

Their distinction should be understood thus: Bandits dwelling in rugged mountains send word to the villagers: 'On such and such a day, we will raid your village.' From the time they hear this news, they fall into fear and terror. This is called mental trepidation. Thinking, 'Lest those angry bandits bring us harm,' they take their valuable possessions and, along with their bipeds and quadrupeds, enter the forest. There, they lie down on the ground in various places, being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; entering thickets, they tread on stumps and thorns. For them wandering thus, their scattered state is called the state of manifold distraction. Then, when the bandits do not arrive on the appointed day, thinking, 'It must have been a false report; we will enter the village,' they enter the village with their belongings. Then, knowing they have entered, the bandits surround the village, set fire to the gates, kill the people, plunder all their wealth, and depart. Among them, those who remain after the slaughter extinguish the fires and sit clinging here and there in the shade of granaries, walls, and so on, grieving for what is lost. This is called the state of being beset, the state of clinging.

Naḷāgārāti [P 2.0168] naḷehi channapaṭicchannaagārā. Sesasambhārā panettha rukkhamayā honti. Tiṇāgārepi eseva nayo. Kūṭāgārānīti kūṭasaṅgahitāni agārāni. Ullittāvalittānīti anto ca bahi ca littāni. Nivātānīti nivāritavātappavesāni. Phusitaggaḷānīti chekehi vaḍḍhakīhi katattā [M 2.0070] piṭṭhasaṅghāṭamhi suṭṭhu phusitakavāṭāni. Pihitavātapānānīti yuttavātapānāni. Iminā padadvayena kavāṭavātapānānaṃ niccapihitataṃ akathetvā sampattiyeva kathitā. Icchiticchitakkhaṇe pana tāni pidhīyanti ca vivarīyanti ca.

'Reed houses' means houses thatched and covered with reeds. Herein, the other building materials are made of wood. This same principle applies to a grass-thatched house. 'Peaked houses' means houses counted by their peaks. 'Plastered and daubed' means plastered both inside and outside. 'Without wind' means having the entrance of wind prevented. 'With fitted bolts' means having door-panels that are well-fitted in the door-frame, because they are made by skilled carpenters. 'With closed windows' means having fitted windows. By these two terms, it is not the state of the doors and windows being permanently closed that is stated, but only their excellence. However, at any desired moment, they can be both closed and opened.

Bālato uppajjantīti bālameva nissāya uppajjanti. Bālo hi apaṇḍitapuriso rajjaṃ vā oparajjaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ patthento katipaye attanā sadise vidhavaputte mahādhutte gahetvā “etha ahaṃ tumhe issare karissāmī”ti pabbatagahanādīni nissāya antamante gāme paharanto dāmarikabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā anupubbena nigamepi janapadepi paharati. Manussā gehāni chaḍḍetvā khemaṭṭhānaṃ patthayamānā pakkamanti. Te nissāya vasantā bhikkhūpi bhikkhuniyopi attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni pahāya pakkamanti. Gatagataṭṭhāne bhikkhāpi senāsanampi dullabhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ catunnampi parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hoti. Pabbajjitesupi dve bālā bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ paṭṭhapetvā codanaṃ ārabhanti. Iti kosambivāsikānaṃ viya mahākalaho uppajjati. Catunnaṃ parisānaṃ bhayaṃ āgatameva hotīti evaṃ yāni kānici bhayāni [P 2.0169] uppajjanti, sabbāni tāni bālato uppajjantīti yathānusandhinā desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

'They arise from a fool' means they arise in dependence on a fool. For a foolish, unwise man, aspiring to kingship, viceroyalty, or some other great position, takes a few sons of widows, great scoundrels, who are similar to himself, and saying, 'Come, I will make you lords,' relies on mountains, forest thickets, and so on. Striking even villages at the very least, he makes known his state as a bandit and sequentially strikes towns and also districts. People abandon their homes and depart, desiring a place of safety. The bhikkhus and bhikkhunis who were living in dependence on them also abandon their respective dwelling places and depart. In whatever place they go, both alms-food and lodging become difficult to obtain. Thus, danger has indeed come to the four assemblies. Also among the ordained, two foolish bhikkhus, having initiated a dispute with one another, begin an accusation. Thus, a great quarrel arises, like that of the residents of Kosambī. Danger has indeed come to the four assemblies. In this way, whatever dangers arise, all of them arise from a fool. Thus, he concluded the discourse in accordance with the connection.

2. Lakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta

2. Dutiye [V 2.0073] kāyadvārādipavattaṃ kammaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sañjānanakāraṇaṃ assāti kammalakkhaṇo. Apadānasobhanī paññāti yā paññā nāma apadānena sobhati, bālā ca paṇḍitā ca attano attano cariteneva pākaṭā hontīti attho. Bālena hi gatamaggo rukkhagacchagāmanigamādīni jhāpetvā gacchantassa indaggino gatamaggo viya hoti, jhāmaṭṭhānamattameva aṅgāramasichārikāsamākulaṃ paññāyati. Paṇḍitena gatamaggo kusobbhādayo pūretvā vividhasassasampadaṃ āvahamānena catudīpikameghena gatamaggo viya hoti. Yathā tena gatamagge udakapūrāni ceva vividhasassaphalāphalāni ca tāni tāni ṭhānāni paññāyanti, evaṃ paṇḍitena gatamagge sampattiyova paññāyanti no vipattiyoti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

2. In the second sutta, 'one whose characteristic is action' (kammalakkhaṇo) is so called because for that person, action occurring through the body-door and so on is the characteristic and the cause for recognition. 'Wisdom that is adorned by conduct' (apadānasobhanī paññā) means that wisdom is adorned by conduct; the meaning is that fools and the wise become manifest only by their own respective conduct. Indeed, the path taken by a fool is like the path of a fire with fuel that goes along burning trees, bushes, villages, and towns; only the burnt place, filled with charcoal, soot, and ashes, is apparent. The path taken by a wise person is like the path of a great rain cloud over the four continents, which fills pools and so on, and brings an abundance of various crops. Just as on the path taken by that cloud, those various places become apparent, filled with water and with various grains and fruits, so on the path taken by the wise person, only accomplishments are apparent, not destructions. The remainder here has an obvious meaning.

3. Cintīsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Cintī Sutta

3. Tatiye [M 2.0071] bālalakkhaṇānīti “bālo aya”nti etehi lakkhīyati ñāyatīti bālalakkhaṇāni. Tānevassa sañjānanakāraṇānīti bālanimittāni. Bālāpadānānīti bālassa apadānāni. Duccintitacintīti cintayanto abhijjhābyāpādamicchādassanavasena duccintitameva cinteti. Dubbhāsitabhāsīti bhāsamānopi musāvādādibhedaṃ dubbhāsitameva bhāsati. Dukkaṭakammakārīti karontopi pāṇātipātādivasena dukkaṭakammameva karoti. Paṇḍitalakkhaṇānītiādi vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Sucintitacintītiādīni cettha manosucaritādīnaṃ vasena yojetabbāni.

3. In the third sutta, 'characteristics of a fool' (bālalakkhaṇāni) are so called because by these one is marked and known as 'this is a fool.' These very things are the causes for recognizing him, hence they are 'signs of a fool' (bālanimittāni). 'Conduct of a fool' (bālāpadānāni) means the distinguishing conduct of a fool. 'One who thinks ill-thought thoughts' (duccintitacintī) means that when thinking, by way of covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, one thinks only ill-thought thoughts. 'One who speaks ill-spoken speech' (dubbhāsitabhāsī) means that even when speaking, one speaks only ill-spoken speech, which has divisions such as false speech and so on. 'One who does ill-done deeds' (dukkaṭakammakārī) means that even when acting, by way of destroying life and so on, one does only ill-done deeds. The passage beginning with 'characteristics of a wise person' should be understood by following the method already stated. And here, the texts beginning with 'one who thinks well-thought thoughts' should be connected by way of good mental conduct and so on.

4. Accayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Accaya Sutta

4. Catutthe [P 2.0170] accayaṃ accayato na passatīti attano aparādhaṃ aparādhato na passati. Accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ nappaṭikarotīti “aparaddhaṃ mayā”ti ñatvāpi yo dhammo, taṃ na karoti, daṇḍakammaṃ āharitvā accayaṃ na deseti nakkhamāpeti. Accayaṃ desentassa yathādhammaṃ nappaṭiggaṇhātīti parassa “viraddhaṃ mayā”ti ñatvā daṇḍakammaṃ āharitvā khamāpentassa nakkhamati. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhato veditabbo.

4. In the fourth sutta, 'not seeing a transgression as a transgression' means not seeing one's own offense as an offense. 'Having seen a transgression, one does not make amends according to the Dhamma' means that even knowing, 'I have offended,' one does not perform the act required by the Dhamma; one does not undertake the penalty, confess the offense, and ask for forgiveness. 'Not accepting the proper redress when another confesses a transgression' means that when another, knowing, 'I have erred,' brings a penalty and asks for forgiveness, one does not forgive. The bright side should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

5. Ayonisosuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ayoniso Sutta

5. Pañcame [V 2.0074] ayoniso pañhaṃ kattā hotīti “kati nu kho, udāyi, anussatiṭṭhānānī”ti vutte “pubbenivāso anussatiṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā lāḷudāyitthero viya anupāyacintāya apañhameva pañhanti kattā hoti. Ayoniso pañhaṃ vissajjetā hotīti evaṃ cintitaṃ pana pañhaṃ vissajjentopi “idha, bhante, bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jāti”ntiādinā nayena soyeva thero viya ayoniso vissajjetā hoti, apañhameva pañhanti katheti. Parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehīti ettha padameva atthassa byañjanato padabyañjanaṃ. Taṃ akkharapāripūriṃ katvā dasavidhaṃ byañjanabuddhiṃ aparihāpetvā [M 2.0072] vuttaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ nāma hoti, evarūpehi padabyañjanehīti attho. Siliṭṭhehīti padasiliṭṭhatāya siliṭṭhehi. Upagatehīti atthañca kāraṇañca upagatehi. Nābbhanumoditāti evaṃ yoniso sabbaṃ kāraṇasampannaṃ katvāpi vissajjitaṃ parassa pañhaṃ nābhinumodati nābhinandati sāriputtattherassa pañhaṃ lāḷudāyitthero viya. Yathāha –

5. In the fifth sutta, 'one asks a question improperly' means that when asked, for example, “How many, Udāyi, are the bases of recollection?” one thinks, “The recollection of past lives will be a basis of recollection,” and like the Elder Lāḷudāyi, due to improper reflection, one poses as a question what is not the true question. 'One answers a question improperly' means that even when answering a question thus reflected upon, one might answer in the manner of, “Here, venerable sir, a monk recollects his manifold past lives. That is to say, one birth,” and so on. Like that very elder, one answers improperly, speaking of what is not the answer as if it were the answer. 'With well-rounded words and phrases'—here, a word itself, because it expresses the meaning, is called a 'word-phrase.' When it is spoken having made the syllables complete and without neglecting the tenfold understanding of expression, it is called 'well-rounded.' This is the meaning: with such words and phrases. 'Polished' means polished due to the smoothness of the words. 'Appropriate' means fitting both the meaning and the reason. 'Not approving' means that one does not approve or delight in another's answer, even when it has been given properly and is complete with all reasons, just as the Elder Lāḷudāyi did not approve of the Elder Sāriputta's answer. As it is said—

“Aṭṭhānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, anavakāso, yaṃ so atikkammeva kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ aññataraṃ [P 2.0171] manomayaṃ kāyaṃ upapanno saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjeyyāpi vuṭṭhaheyyāpi, natthetaṃ ṭhāna”nti (a. ni. 5.166).

“Friend Sāriputta, it is impossible, it is not a possibility, that a person—who, having transcended the companionship of devas who subsist on edible food, has arisen in some mind-made body—might enter into and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling. That possibility does not exist.”

Yoniso pañhaṃ kattātiādīsu ānandatthero viya yonisova pañhaṃ cintetvā yoniso vissajjitā hoti. Thero hi “kati nu kho, ānanda, anussatiṭṭhānānī”ti pucchito “ayaṃ pañho bhavissatī”ti yoniso cintetvā yoniso vissajjento āha – “idha, bhante, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi…pe… catutthajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ, bhante, anussatiṭṭhānaṃ evaṃbhāvitaṃ evaṃbahulīkataṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattatī”ti. Abbhanumoditā hotīti tathāgato viya yoniso abbhanumoditā hoti. Tathāgato hi ānandattherena pañhe vissajjite “sādhu sādhu, ānanda, tena hi tvaṃ, ānanda, imampi chaṭṭhaṃ anussatiṭṭhānaṃ dhārehi. Idhānanda, bhikkhu satova abhikkamati satova paṭikkamatī”tiādimāha. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāneva.

In the texts beginning with 'one who asks a question properly,' etc., like the Elder Ānanda, having considered the desired meaning properly, one is skilled in answering properly. For the Elder, when asked, 'How many, Ānanda, are the bases for recollection?' having considered properly, 'This will be the desired meaning,' and wishing to answer properly, said: 'Here, venerable sir, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This, venerable sir, is a basis for recollection that, when so developed and so cultivated, conduces to a pleasant abiding in this very life.' 'One who rejoices' means that, like the Tathāgata, one rejoices properly. For when the Elder Ānanda had answered the question, the Tathāgata said: 'Good, good, Ānanda! In that case, Ānanda, you should also bear in mind this sixth basis for recollection. Here, Ānanda, a monk goes forward mindfully and returns mindfully,' and so on. The sixth sutta and so on have an obvious meaning.

9. Khatasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Khata Sutta

9. Navame [V 2.0075] sukkapakkho pubbabhāge dasahipi kusalakammapathehi paricchinno, upari yāva arahattamaggā labbhati. Bahuñca puññaṃ pasavatīti ettha lokiyalokuttaramissakapuññaṃ kathitaṃ.

9. In the ninth sutta, the wholesome aspect, in its initial part, is defined by the ten courses of wholesome action; further on, it is obtained up to the path of Arahantship. Here, in the text 'and it generates much merit,' merit that is a mixture of the mundane and supramundane is taught.

10. Malasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Mala Sutta

10. Dasame dussīlabhāvo dussīlyaṃ, dussīlyameva malaṃ dussīlyamalaṃ. Kenaṭṭhena malanti? Anudahanaṭṭhena duggandhaṭṭhena kiliṭṭhakaraṇaṭṭhena ca. Tañhi nirayādīsu apāyesu anudahatīti anudahanaṭṭhenapi malaṃ. Tena samannāgato [M 2.0073] puggalo mātāpitūnampi santike bhikkhusaṅghassāpi antare bodhicetiyaṭṭhānesupi jigucchanīyo hoti, sabbadisāsu cassa “evarūpaṃ kira tena pāpakammaṃ kata”nti avaṇṇagandho vāyatīti duggandhaṭṭhenapi malaṃ. Tena ca samannāgato puggalo gatagataṭṭhāne upatāpañceva labhati, kāyakammādīni cassa asucīni honti apabhassarānīti [P 2.0172] kiliṭṭhakaraṇaṭṭhenapi malaṃ. Apica taṃ devamanussasampattiyo ceva nibbānasampattiñca milāpetīti milāpanaṭṭhenapi malanti veditabbaṃ. Issāmalamaccheramalesupi eseva nayo.

10. In the tenth sutta, the state of being without virtue is immorality; immorality itself is a stain, the stain of immorality. In what sense is it a stain? In the sense of burning, in the sense of a foul odor, and in the sense of causing defilement. For it burns in the woeful states, beginning with hell; thus, it is a stain also in the sense of burning. A person endowed with it becomes repulsive even in the presence of his parents, in the midst of the community of monks, and at the sites of Bodhi trees and cetiyas. And in all directions, the odor of his dispraise spreads—'It is said that such an evil deed was done by him'—thus, it is a stain also in the sense of a foul odor. And a person endowed with it encounters torment wherever he goes, and his bodily actions and so forth become impure and lead to another destination; thus, it is a stain also in the sense of causing defilement. Furthermore, it should be understood as a stain also in the sense of causing to wither, for it causes both the attainments of devas and humans and the attainment of Nibbāna to wither. For the stains of envy and stinginess as well, this is the same method.

Bālavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on the Fool.

2. Rathakāravaggo

2. The Chapter on the Chariot-Maker

1. Ñātasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Ñāta Sutta

11. Dutiyassa [V 2.0076] paṭhame ñātoti paññāto pākaṭo. Ananulomiketi sāsanassa na anulometīti ananulomikaṃ, tasmiṃ ananulomike. Kāyakammeti pāṇātipātādimhi kāyaduccarite. Oḷārikaṃ vā etaṃ, na evarūpe samādapetuṃ sakkoti. Disā namassituṃ vaṭṭati, bhūtabaliṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti evarūpe samādapeti gaṇhāpeti. Vacīkammepi musāvādādīni oḷārikāni, attano santakaṃ parassa adātukāmena “natthī”ti ayaṃ vañcanamusāvādo nāma vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti evarūpe samādapeti. Manokammepi abhijjhādayo oḷārikā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ visaṃvādetvā kathento pana ananulomikesu dhammesu samādapeti nāma dakkhiṇavihāravāsitthero viya. Taṃ kira theraṃ eko upaṭṭhāko amaccaputto upasaṅkamitvā “mettāyantena paṭhamaṃ kīdise puggale mettāyitabba”nti pucchi. Thero sabhāgavisabhāgaṃ anācikkhitvā “piyapuggale”ti āha. Tassa ca bhariyā piyā hoti manāpā, so taṃ ārabbha mettāyanto ummādaṃ pāpuṇi. Kathaṃ panesa bahujanaahitāya paṭipanno hotīti? Evarūpassa hi saddhivihārikādayo ceva upaṭṭhākādayo ca tesaṃ ārakkhadevatā ādiṃ katvā tāsaṃ tāsaṃ mittabhūtā yāva brahmalokā [M 2.0074] sesadevatā ca “ayaṃ bhikkhu na ajānitvā karissatī”ti [P 2.0173] tena katameva karonti, evamesa bahujanaahitāya paṭipanno hoti.

11. In the first discourse of the second chapter, 'known' means recognized or evident. 'Inappropriate' means not in accordance with the Teaching; thus, it is inappropriate, in that which is inappropriate. 'Bodily action' refers to bodily misconduct, such as the destruction of life. Or, this is gross, and one is not able to persuade others to undertake such a thing. He encourages and makes one undertake such things as saying, 'It is proper to worship the directions; it is proper to make an offering to spirits.' In verbal action also, things beginning with false speech are gross. He causes others to undertake such things by saying, 'Because of not wishing to give one's own property to another, it is proper to say, "It does not exist"—this is called deceitful false speech.' In mental action also, things beginning with covetousness are gross. However, one who speaks after distorting a meditation subject is called one who causes others to undertake things not in accordance with the Teaching, like the elder who dwelt in the Dakkhiṇavihāra. It is said that a minister’s son who was an attendant approached that elder and asked, "By one developing loving-kindness, toward what kind of person should loving-kindness first be developed?" Without explaining the similar and dissimilar, the elder said, "Toward a beloved person." Now, for that man, his wife was dear and pleasing. Taking her as the object while developing loving-kindness, he went mad. But how is this one practicing for the harm of many? For of such a one, his co-resident pupils and attendants, as well as the remaining deities up to the Brahmā world—beginning with the guardian deities of those people, and including the friends of those deities—think, 'This monk would not act without knowing,' and so they do only what has been done by him. In this way, he is practicing for the harm of many.

Sukkapakkhe pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādīnaṃyeva vasena kāyakammavacīkammāni veditabbāni. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ pana avisaṃvādetvā kathento anulomikesu dhammesu samādapeti nāma koḷitavihāravāsī catunikāyikatissatthero viya. Tassa kira jeṭṭhabhātā nandābhayatthero nāma potaliyavihāre vasanto ekasmiṃ roge samuṭṭhite kaniṭṭhaṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “āvuso, mayhaṃ sallahukaṃ katvā ekaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathehī”ti. Kiṃ, bhante, aññena kammaṭṭhānena, kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ pariggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti? Kimatthiko esa, āvusoti? Bhante, kabaḷīkārāhāro upādārūpaṃ, ekasmiñca upādārūpe diṭṭhe tevīsati upādārūpāni pākaṭāni hontīti[V 2.0077]. So “vaṭṭissati, āvuso, ettaka”nti taṃ uyyojetvā kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ pariggaṇhitvā upādārūpaṃ sallakkhetvā vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ theraṃ bahivihārā anikkhantameva pakkositvā, “āvuso, mahāavassayosi mayhaṃ jāto”ti kaniṭṭhattherassa attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocesi. Bahujanahitāyāti etassapi hi saddhivihārikādayo “ayaṃ na ajānitvā karissatī”ti tena katameva karontīti bahujanahitāya paṭipanno nāma hotīti.

In the wholesome aspect, bodily and verbal actions should be understood by way of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth. Furthermore, one who, without deceiving, instructs and establishes others in dhammas that are in conformity with the Dispensation, is so called, like the Elder Tissa, a resident of the Koḷita Monastery, who was versed in the four Nikāyas. It is said that his elder brother, the Elder named Nandābhaya, while living at the Potaliya Monastery, when lust arose, summoned his younger brother and said: 'Friend, having made it light for me, teach me a meditation subject.' 'Venerable sir, what is the use of another meditation subject? It is proper to comprehend edible food.' 'What is the purpose of this, friend?' 'Venerable sir, edible food is derived matter, and when one derived matter is seen, the twenty-three derived matters become manifest.' He said, 'This much will suffice, friend,' and sent him away. Then, having comprehended edible food, having contemplated the derived matter and developed insight, he attained Arahantship. Then, summoning the elder who had not even gone outside the monastery, he said, 'Friend, you have become a great support for me,' and announced to the younger elder the quality he himself had attained. Regarding 'For the welfare of the many': Indeed, of this person also, his co-resident pupils and others, thinking, 'This monk will not act without knowing,' do only what has been done by him. Therefore, he is called one who has practiced for the welfare of the many.

2. Sāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta

12. Dutiye khattiyassāti jātiyā khattiyassa. Muddhāvasittassāti rājābhisekena muddhani abhisittassa. Sāraṇīyāni bhavantīti saritabbāni asammussanīyāni honti. Jātoti [P 2.0174] nibbatto. Yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyanti daharakāle jānitumpi na sakkā, aparabhāge pana mātāpituādīhi ñātakehi vā dāsādīhi vā “tvaṃ asukajanapade asukanagare asukadivase asukanakkhatte jāto”ti ācikkhite sutvā tato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ sarati na sammussati. Tena vuttaṃ – “yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ hotī”ti.

12. In the second, 'of a khattiya' means a khattiya by birth. 'Anointed on the head' means one who has been anointed on the head with the royal consecration. 'Are to be remembered' means they are to be remembered, not to be forgotten. 'Born' means born. 'Memorable for life': In youth, it is not possible even to know, but later, when told by parents and others, or by relatives, or by servants and others, 'You were born in such-and-such a district, in such-and-such a city, on such-and-such a day, under such-and-such a constellation,' having heard this, from that time onwards one remembers for as long as life lasts and does not forget. Therefore it is said: 'It is memorable for life.'

Idaṃ[M 2.0075], bhikkhave, dutiyanti abhisekaṭṭhānaṃ nāma rañño balavatuṭṭhikaraṃ hoti, tenassa taṃ yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ. Saṅgāmavijayaṭṭhānepi eseva nayo. Ettha pana saṅgāmanti yuddhaṃ. Abhivijinitvāti jinitvā sattumaddanaṃ katvā. Tameva saṅgāmasīsanti tameva saṅgāmaṭṭhānaṃ. Ajjhāvasatīti abhibhavitvā āvasati.

This, O monks, 'the second' refers to the place of anointment, which causes great delight for a king; therefore, it is to be remembered by him for as long as he lives. This same method applies also to the place of victory in battle. Here, furthermore, 'battle' means war. 'Having completely conquered' means having conquered and crushed the enemy. 'That very head of the battle' means that very place of battle. 'He dwells' means he dwells having overpowered it.

Idāni yasmā sammāsambuddhassa rañño jātiṭṭhānādīhi kattabbakiccaṃ natthi, imasmiṃ pana sāsane tappaṭibhāge tayo puggale dassetuṃ idaṃ kāraṇaṃ ābhataṃ, tasmā te dassento evameva kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hotīti ettha catupārisuddhisīlampi pabbajjānissitamevāti veditabbaṃ. Sāraṇīyaṃ hotīti “ahaṃ asukaraṭṭhe asukajanapade asukavihāre asukamāḷake asukadivāṭṭhāne asukacaṅkame asukarukkhamūle pabbajito”ti evaṃ yāvajīvaṃ saritabbameva hoti na sammussitabbaṃ.

Now, since for the Perfectly Enlightened One there is no duty to be performed with regard to a birthplace and so on, as there is for a king, but in this Dispensation this reason has been brought forth to show three persons comparable to that king, therefore, showing them, he spoke the text beginning with, 'Even so, O monks.' Therein, in the passage 'he has gone forth into homelessness,' it should be known that the fourfold purity of virtue is also indeed dependent on the going forth. It is to be remembered for as long as one lives, and not to be forgotten, thus: 'I went forth in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a district, in such-and-such a monastery, in such-and-such a hall, in such-and-such a day-dwelling, on such-and-such a walking path, at the root of such-and-such a tree.'

Idaṃ [V 2.0078] dukkhanti ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito uddhaṃ dukkhaṃ atthi. Ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti ettako dukkhasamudayo, na ito uddhaṃ dukkhasamudayo atthīti. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Evamettha catūhi saccehi sotāpattimaggo kathito. Kasiṇaparikammavipassanāñāṇāni pana maggasannissitāneva honti. Sāraṇīyaṃ [P 2.0175] hotīti “ahaṃ asukaraṭṭhe…pe… asukarukkhamūle sotāpanno jāto”ti yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ hoti asammussanīyaṃ.

'This is suffering' means suffering is only this much; there is no suffering beyond this. 'This is the origin of suffering' means the origin of suffering is only this much; there is no origin of suffering beyond this. This same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. Thus, herein the path of stream-entry is taught by means of the four truths. Furthermore, the preliminary kasina practice and the insight knowledges are indeed dependent on the path. 'It is to be remembered' means that 'I became a stream-enterer in such-and-such a country... at the root of such-and-such a tree' is to be remembered for as long as one lives and is not to be forgotten.

Āsavānaṃ khayāti āsavānaṃ khayena. Cetovimuttinti phalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti phalapaññaṃ. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāva abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upasampajja viharatīti paṭilabhitvā viharati. Sāraṇīyanti “mayā asukaraṭṭhe…pe… asukarukkhamūle arahattaṃ patta”nti attano arahattapattiṭṭhānaṃ nāma yāvajīvaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ hoti asammussanīyanti yathānusandhināva desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi.

'Through the destruction of the taints' means by the destruction of the taints. 'Liberation of mind' means the concentration associated with fruition. 'Liberation by wisdom' means the wisdom associated with fruition. 'Having realized by himself through direct knowledge' means having personally made it manifest with superior wisdom. 'He enters and dwells in it' means having attained it, he dwells. 'Memorable' means that the place of one's attainment of arahantship, namely, 'I attained arahantship in such-and-such a country... at the root of such-and-such a tree,' is to be remembered for as long as one lives and not to be forgotten. Thus, he concluded the discourse in accordance with the connection.

3. Āsaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Āsaṃsa Sutta

13. Tatiye santoti atthi upalabbhanti. Saṃvijjamānāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Lokasminti sattaloke. Nirāsoti anāso apatthano. Āsaṃsoti [M 2.0076] āsaṃsamāno patthayamāno. Vigatāsoti apagatāso. Caṇḍālakuleti caṇḍālānaṃ kule. Venakuleti vilīvakārakule. Nesādakuleti migaluddakānaṃ kule. Rathakārakuleti cammakārakule. Pukkusakuleti pupphacchaḍḍakakule.

13. In the third (sutta), 'santo' means 'they exist, they are found.' 'Saṃvijjamāna' is a synonym for that very word. 'Lokasmiṃ' means 'in the world of beings.' 'Nirāso' means one without desire, one without longing. 'Āsaṃso' means one who hopes, one who desires. 'Vigatāso' means one whose longing has departed. 'Caṇḍālakule' means 'in a family of caṇḍālas.' 'Venakule' means 'in a family of bamboo-workers.' 'Nesādakule' means 'in a family of hunters.' 'Rathakārakule' means 'in a family of leather-workers.' 'Pukkusakule' means 'in a family of flower-sweepers.'

Ettāvatā kulavipattiṃ dassetvā idāni yasmā nīcakule jātopi ekacco aḍḍho hoti mahaddhano, ayaṃ pana na tādiso, tasmāssa bhogavipattiṃ dassetuṃ daliddetiādimāha. Tattha daliddeti dāliddiyena samannāgate. Appannapānabhojaneti parittakaannapānabhojane. Kasiravuttiketi [P 2.0176] dukkhajīvike, yattha vāyāmena payogena jīvitavuttiṃ sādhenti, tathārūpeti attho. Yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhatīti yasmiṃ kule dukkhena yāgubhattaghāso ca kopīnamattaṃ acchādanañca labbhati.

Having thus shown the corruption of family, now, because even someone born in a low family may be rich and wealthy, but this person is not so, therefore, to show his corruption of wealth, He said 'poor', and so on. Therein, 'dalidde' means endowed with poverty. 'Appannapānabhojane' means having little food, drink, and meals. 'Kasiravuttike' means having a difficult livelihood, that is, one with a miserable living, in which they sustain their livelihood through effort and exertion; this is the meaning. 'Where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty' means in which family food, that is, gruel and rice, and clothing sufficient for a mere loincloth, are obtained with difficulty.

Idāni yasmā ekacco nīcakule jātopi upadhisampanno hoti attabhāvasamiddhiyaṃ ṭhito[V 2.0079], ayañca na tādiso, tasmāssa sarīravipattimpi dassetuṃ so ca hoti dubbaṇṇotiādimāha. Tattha dubbaṇṇoti paṃsupisācako viya jhāmakhāṇuvaṇṇo. Duddasikoti vijātamātuyāpi amanāpadassano. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako. Kāṇoti ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā. Kuṇīti ekahatthakuṇī vā ubhayahatthakuṇī vā. Khañjoti ekapādakhañjo vā ubhayapādakhañjo vā. Pakkhahatoti hatapakkho pīṭhasappī. Padīpeyyassāti vaṭṭitelakapallakādino padīpaupakaraṇassa. Tassa na evaṃ hotīti. Kasmā na hoti? Nīcakule jātattā.

Now, since even someone born in a low family may be endowed with physical endowments and established in bodily prosperity, but this one is not such, therefore, to show his bodily misfortune, it is said: 'he is ugly' and so on. Therein, 'ugly' means 'like a dust-demon, with the color of a scorched stump.' 'Unpleasant to see' means 'unpleasant to see even for his own mother.' 'Dwarfish' means 'like a water pot.' 'Blind' means 'blind in one eye or blind in both eyes.' 'Crippled' means 'crippled in one hand or crippled in both hands.' 'Lame' means 'lame in one foot or lame in both feet.' 'Paralyzed' means 'with a paralyzed lower body, one who moves about on a wheeled board.' 'Of what is to be lit' means 'of the equipment for a lamp, such as a wick, oil-dish, and so on.' 'For him, it is not so.' Why is it not so? Because he was born in a low family.

Jeṭṭhoti aññasmiṃ jeṭṭhe sati kaniṭṭho āsaṃ na karoti, tasmā jeṭṭhoti āha. Ābhisekoti jeṭṭhopi na abhisekāraho āsaṃ na karoti, tasmā ābhisekoti āha. Anabhisittoti abhisekārahopi kāṇakuṇiādidosarahito sakiṃ abhisitto puna abhiseke āsaṃ na karoti, tasmā anabhisittoti āha[M 2.0077]. Acalappattoti jeṭṭhopi ābhiseko anabhisitto mando uttānaseyyako, sopi abhiseke āsaṃ na karoti. Soḷasavassuddesiko pana paññāyamānamassubhedo acalappatto nāma [P 2.0177] hoti, mahantampi rajjaṃ vicāretuṃ samattho, tasmā “acalappatto”ti āha. Tassa evaṃ hotīti kasmā hoti? Mahājātitāya.

'Eldest' means that when there is another who is elder, the younger one does not have a desire for consecration; therefore, it is said 'eldest.' 'Worthy of consecration' means that even if one is the eldest, if he is not worthy of consecration, he does not have a desire for it; therefore, it is said 'worthy of consecration.' 'Not yet consecrated' means that even one who is worthy of consecration and free from defects such as being blind or crippled, if consecrated once, does not have a desire for consecration again; therefore, it is said 'not yet consecrated.' 'One who has reached the unshaken state' means: Even if one is the eldest, worthy of consecration, or not yet consecrated, if he is a dull infant who just lies on his back, he too does not have a desire for consecration. A prince of sixteen years, however, on whom the beard becomes distinct, is called 'one who has reached the unshaken state,' as he is capable of administering even a great kingdom; therefore, it is said 'one who has reached the unshaken state.' 'For him, it is so.' Why is it so? Because of his high birth.

Dussīloti nissīlo. Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo. Asucīti asucīhi kāyakammādīhi samannāgato. Saṅkassarasamācāroti saṅkāhi saritabbasamācāro, kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ iminā kataṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyasamācāro, attanāyeva vā saṅkāhi saritabbasamācāro, sāsaṅkasamācāroti attho. Tassa hi divāṭṭhānādīsu sannipatitvā kiñcideva mantayante bhikkhū disvā “ime ekato hutvā mantenti, kacci nu kho mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti evaṃ sāsaṅkasamācāro hoti. Paṭicchannakammantoti paṭicchādetabbayuttakena pāpakammena samannāgato. Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiññoti assamaṇo hutvāva samaṇapatirūpakatāya “samaṇo aha”nti evaṃ paṭiñño. Abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiññoti aññe brahmacārino sunivatthe supārute sumbhakapattadhare gāmanigamarājadhānīsu piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappente disvā sayampi tādisena ākārena tathā paṭipajjanato “ahaṃ brahmacārī”ti paṭiññaṃ dento viya hoti. “Ahaṃ bhikkhū”ti vatvā uposathaggādīni pavisanto pana brahmacāripaṭiñño hotiyeva, tathā saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ gaṇhanto. Antopūtīti pūtinā kammena anto [V 2.0080] anupaviṭṭho. Avassutoti rāgādīhi tinto. Kasambujātoti sañjātarāgādikacavaro. Tassa na evaṃ hotīti. Kasmā na hoti? Lokuttaradhammaupanissayassa natthitāya. Tassa [P 2.0178] evaṃ hotīti. Kasmā hoti? Mahāsīlasmiṃ paripūrakāritāya.

‘Immoral’ means without virtue. ‘Of evil nature’ means of base qualities. ‘Impure’ means endowed with impure bodily actions and the like. ‘Of suspicious conduct’ means conduct that should be recalled with suspicion; conduct that is liable to be suspected by others, who, upon seeing some impropriety, think, “This must have been done by him”; or, conduct that should be recalled with suspicion by oneself. The meaning is conduct accompanied by suspicion. For, upon seeing monks gathered in a day-time resting place and discussing something, his conduct becomes suspicious as he thinks, “These monks have gathered to discuss something. Could it be that they are discussing a deed I have done, having come to know of it?” ‘Of concealed deeds’ means endowed with evil action that ought to be concealed. ‘Not an ascetic, but professing to be one’ means one who, though not an ascetic, professes, “I am an ascetic,” on account of his resemblance to an ascetic. ‘Not a celibate one, but professing to be one’ means one who, seeing other celibate ones—well-robed, well-covered, carrying their earthen bowls, and making their living by going for alms in villages, towns, and royal capitals—is like one making the claim, “I am a celibate one,” because he himself also behaves in the same way with a similar appearance. Furthermore, one who enters the Uposatha hall and so forth, saying, “I am a monk,” is indeed one who professes to be celibate; likewise is one who accepts gains belonging to the Sangha. ‘Putrid within’ means one into whom putrid action has entered. ‘Lecherous’ means steeped in lust and the like. ‘Full of rubbish’ means one in whom the rubbish of lust and the like has arisen. “For him, it is not so.” Why is it not so? Because of the absence of a supporting condition for the supramundane states. “For him, it is so.” Why is it so? Because of his practice of fulfilling the great virtue.

4. Cakkavattisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta

14. Catutthe catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ rañjetīti rājā. Cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavattī. Vattitaṃ vā anena cakkanti cakkavattī. Dhammo assa [M 2.0078] atthīti dhammiko. Dhammeneva dasavidhena cakkavattivattena rājā jātoti dhammarājā. Sopi na arājakanti sopi aññaṃ nissayarājānaṃ alabhitvā cakkaṃ nāma vattetuṃ na sakkotīti attho. Iti satthā desanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā yathānusandhiṃ apāpetvāva tuṇhī ahosi. Kasmā? Anusandhikusalā uṭṭhahitvā anusandhiṃ pucchissanti, bahū hi imasmiṃ ṭhāne tathārūpā bhikkhū, athāhaṃ tehi puṭṭho desanaṃ vaḍḍhessāmīti. Atheko anusandhikusalo bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ pucchanto ko pana, bhantetiādimāha. Bhagavāpissa byākaronto dhammo bhikkhūtiādimāha.

14. In the fourth sutta: He is called a 'king' (rājā) because he pleases (rañjeti) the people with the four bases of sympathy. He is called a 'wheel-turner' (cakkavattī) because he causes the wheel-treasure to turn (cakkaṃ vatteti). Or, he is called a 'wheel-turner' because the wheel-treasure has been caused to turn by him. He is called 'righteous' (dhammiko) because he possesses righteousness (dhamma). He is called a 'righteous king' (dhammarājā) because he is a king born only through the Dhamma, that is, the tenfold practice of a wheel-turning monarch. Thus, the Teacher, having set forth the teaching, became silent without bringing it to its conclusion according to the connection. Why? (He thought:) 'Monks skilled in making connections will rise and ask about the connection, for in this place there are many such monks. Then, having been asked by them, I will expand the teaching.' Then a certain monk skilled in making connections, wishing to ask the Blessed One, said the words beginning with, 'But who, venerable sir...'. The Blessed One also, wishing to answer him, spoke the words beginning with, 'The Dhamma, O monk...'.

Tattha dhammoti dasakusalakammapathadhammo. Dhammanti tameva vuttappakāraṃ dhammaṃ. Nissāyāti tadadhiṭṭhānena cetasā tameva nissayaṃ katvā. Dhammaṃ sakkarontoti yathā kato so dhammo suṭṭhu kato hoti, evametaṃ karonto. Dhammaṃ garuṃ karontoti tasmiṃ gāravuppattiyā taṃ garukaronto. Dhammaṃ apacāyamānoti tasseva dhammassa añjalikaraṇādīhi nīcavuttitaṃ karonto. Dhammaddhajo dhammaketūti taṃ dhammaṃ dhajamiva purakkhatvā ketumiva ukkhipitvā pavattiyā dhammaddhajo dhammaketu ca hutvāti attho. Dhammādhipateyyoti dhammādhipatibhūtāgatabhāvena dhammavaseneva ca sabbakiriyānaṃ karaṇena dhammādhipateyyo hutvā. Dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidahatīti dhammo assā [P 2.0179] atthīti dhammikā, rakkhā ca āvaraṇañca gutti ca rakkhāvaraṇagutti. Tattha “paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhatī”ti vacanato khantiādayo rakkhā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “kathañca, bhikkhave, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati.
