Khantiyā avihiṃsāya mettacittatāya anuddayāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.385). Nivāsanapārupanagehādīni āvaraṇaṃ. Corādiupaddavanivāraṇatthaṃ gopāyanā gutti. Taṃ sabbampi suṭṭhu vidahati pavatteti ṭhapetīti attho.

Herein, 'Dhamma' is the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Dhammaṃ' means that very Dhamma of the aforementioned kind. 'Nissāya' (relying on) means: with a mind having that as its foundation, having made that very Dhamma a reliance. 'Dhammaṃ sakkaronto' (honoring the Dhamma) means acting in such a way that when that Dhamma is practiced, it is well-practiced. 'Dhammaṃ garuṃ karonto' (revering the Dhamma) means revering it through the arising of reverence for it. 'Dhammaṃ apacāyamāno' (paying homage to the Dhamma) means conducting oneself humbly toward that very Dhamma through gestures such as making the añjali gesture. 'Dhammaddhajo dhammaketu' (having the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard) means that by placing that Dhamma foremost like a banner and raising it up like a standard in one's conduct, one becomes he who has the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his standard; this is the meaning. 'Dhammādhipateyyo' (governed by the Dhamma) means having become one for whom the Dhamma is sovereign, because one's state comes from the Dhamma which has become sovereign, and because one performs all actions solely by the power of the Dhamma. As for 'Dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidahati' (He provides righteous protection, shelter, and guard): 'dhammikā' (righteous) is so called because the Dhamma pertains to it. 'Rakkhā' (protection), 'āvaraṇa' (shelter), and 'gutti' (guard) together are 'rakkhāvaraṇagutti' (protection, shelter, and guard). Therein, according to the saying, 'Protecting another, one protects oneself,' patience and so forth are 'rakkhā' (protection). For this was said by the Blessed One: 'And how, monks, does one who protects another protect oneself? Through patience, non-harming, a mind of loving-kindness, and compassion.' Lower garments, upper garments, houses, and so forth are 'āvaraṇa' (shelter). 'Gutti' (guard) is the watching over for the purpose of warding off dangers from thieves and so forth. All of that he arranges, maintains, and establishes well—this is the meaning.

Idāni [V 2.0081] yattha sā saṃvidahitabbā, taṃ dassento antojanasmintiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – antojanasaṅkhātaṃ puttadāraṃ sīlasaṃvare patiṭṭhāpento vatthagandhamālādīni cassa dadamāno sabbopaddave cassa nivārayamāno dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidahati nāma. Khattiyādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – abhisittakhattiyā bhadraassājānīyādiratanasampadānenapi [M 2.0079] upagaṇhitabbā, anuyantā khattiyā tesaṃ anurūpayānavāhanasampadānenapi paritosetabbā, balakāyo kālaṃ anatikkametvā bhattavetanasampadānenapi anuggahetabbo, brāhmaṇā annapānavatthādinā deyyadhammena, gahapatikā bhattabījanaṅgalabalibaddādisampadānena, tathā nigamavāsino negamā janapadavāsino ca jānapadā. Samitapāpabāhitapāpā pana samaṇabrāhmaṇā samaṇaparikkhārasampadānena sakkātabbā, migapakkhino abhayadānena samassāsetabbā.

Now, to show for whom that provision should be made, he begins with 'regarding one's own people,' and so on. Herein is the brief meaning: By establishing one's wives and children, known as one's own people, in moral restraint; by giving them clothing, perfumes, garlands, and so forth; and by warding off all dangers from them, one is said to provide righteous protection, shelter, and guard. The same principle applies to the noble warrior class and others. This, however, is the distinction: Anointed noble warriors should be supported with the gift of treasures such as excellent thoroughbred horses; attendant noble warriors should be gratified with the provision of suitable conveyances and mounts; the army should be supported with timely provisions and wages; brahmins should be supported with offerings of food, drink, clothing, and so forth; householders should be supported with the provision of food, seeds, plows, and oxen. Likewise, town-dwellers are called 'negamā,' and country-dwellers are called 'jānapadā.' But ascetics and brahmins, who have pacified and banished evil, should be honored with the provision of the requisites of an ascetic. Wild animals and birds should be reassured by the granting of safety.

Dhammeneva cakkaṃ vattetīti dasakusalakammapathadhammeneva cakkaṃ pavatteti. Taṃ hoti cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyanti taṃ tena evaṃ pavattitaṃ āṇācakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ hoti. Kenaci [P 2.0180] manussabhūtenāti devatā nāma attanā icchiticchitameva karonti, tasmā tā aggaṇhitvā “manussabhūtenā”ti vuttaṃ. Paccatthikenāti paṭiatthikena, paṭisattunāti attho. Dhammikoti cakkavattī dasakusalakammapathavasena dhammiko, tathāgato pana navalokuttaradhammavasena. Dhammarājāti navahi lokuttaradhammehi mahājanaṃ rañjetīti dhammarājā. Dhammaṃyevāti navalokuttaradhammameva nissāya tameva sakkaronto taṃ garukaronto taṃ apacāyamāno. Sovassa dhammo abbhuggataṭṭhena dhajoti dhammaddhajo. Sovassa ketūti dhammaketu. Tameva adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā viharatīti dhammādhipateyyo. Dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttinti lokiyalokuttaradhammadāyikarakkhañca āvaraṇañca guttiñca. Saṃvidahatīti ṭhapeti paññapeti. Evarūpanti tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ na sevitabbaṃ, sucaritaṃ sevitabbanti evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Saṃvidahitvāti ṭhapetvā kathetvā. Dhammeneva anuttaraṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattetīti navalokuttaradhammeneva asadisaṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavatteti. Taṃ hoti cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyanti taṃ evaṃ pavattitaṃ dhammacakkaṃ etesu samaṇādīsu ekenapi paṭivattetuṃ paṭibāhituṃ na sakkā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Dhammeneva cakkaṃ vatteti' (He turns the wheel by Dhamma alone) means he sets the wheel in motion by the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Taṃ hoti cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ' (That wheel becomes irreversible) means that the wheel of authority thus set in motion by him becomes irreversible. 'Kenaci manussabhūtena' (by any human being): deities act solely according to their own wishes; therefore, disregarding them, it is said 'by any human being.' 'Paccatthikena' (by an enemy) means by an adversary, by a hostile foe; this is the meaning. 'Dhammiko' (righteous): the wheel-turning monarch is righteous by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, while the Tathāgata is so by way of the nine transcendent Dhammas. 'Dhammarājā' (King of Dhamma): he is the King of Dhamma because he delights the great multitude with the nine transcendent Dhammas. 'Dhammaṃyeva' (Dhamma alone): relying solely on the nine transcendent Dhammas, honoring them, revering them, and paying homage to them. 'Dhammaddhajo' (Dhamma-banner): that Dhamma of his is a banner in the sense of being exalted. 'Dhammaketu' (Dhamma-standard): that Dhamma of his is also a standard. 'Dhammādhipateyyo' (governed by Dhamma): he abides having made that very Dhamma his sovereign, his chief. 'Dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ' (righteous protection, restraint, and guarding) means protection that bestows worldly and transcendent Dhamma, as well as restraint and guarding. 'Saṃvidahati' (he provides) means he establishes, he prescribes. 'Evarūpaṃ' (such): threefold bodily misconduct is not to be practiced, while good conduct is to be practiced—thus should the meaning be understood everywhere. 'Saṃvidahitvā' (having provided) means having established, having declared. 'Dhammeneva anuttaraṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavatteti' (By Dhamma alone he sets in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma) means he turns the incomparable wheel of Dhamma by the nine transcendent Dhammas alone. 'Taṃ hoti cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ' (That wheel becomes irreversible) means that the wheel of Dhamma, thus set in motion, cannot be turned back or obstructed by even one among these ascetics and others. The rest is clear everywhere.

5. Sacetanasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Sacetana Sutta

15. Pañcame isipataneti buddhapaccekabuddhasaṅkhātānaṃ isīnaṃ dhammacakkappavattanatthāya ceva uposathakaraṇatthāya [V 2.0082] ca āgantvā patane, sannipātaṭṭhāneti attho. Padanetipi pāṭho, ayameva attho. Migadāyeti [M 2.0080] migānaṃ abhayatthāya dinne. Chahi māsehi chārattūnehīti so kira raññā āṇattadivaseyeva [P 2.0181] sabbūpakaraṇāni sajjetvā antevāsikehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā gāmadvāragāmamajjhadevakulasusānādīsu ṭhitarukkhe ceva jhāmapatitasukkharukkhe ca vivajjetvā sampannapadese ṭhite sabbadosavivajjite nābhiaranemīnaṃ anurūpe rukkhe gahetvā taṃ cakkaṃ akāsi. Tassa rukkhe vicinitvā gaṇhantassa ceva karontassa ca ettako kālo vītivatto. Tena vuttaṃ – “chahi māsehi chārattūnehī”ti. Nānākaraṇanti nānattaṃ. Nesanti na esaṃ. Atthesanti atthi esaṃ. Abhisaṅkhārassa gatīti payogassa gamanaṃ. Ciṅgulāyitvāti paribbhamitvā. Akkhāhataṃ maññeti akkhe pavesetvā ṭhapitamiva.

15. In the fifth, 'Isipatana' means the place of descent, the place of assembly, where sages called Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas descend, having come for the purpose of turning the Wheel of Dhamma and for performing the Uposatha. There is also the reading 'Padane'; the meaning is the same. 'Migadāya' means in the park given as a sanctuary for deer. As for 'in six months less six nights': it is said that the wheelwright, on the very day he was commanded by the king, prepared all the equipment and entered the forest with his apprentices. Having avoided trees standing at village gates, in the middle of villages, at shrines, and in cemeteries, as well as burnt, fallen, and dry trees, he took trees that were standing in a perfect location, free from all faults, and suitable for the nave, spokes, and rim, and fashioned that wheel. For him, this much time passed while searching for and taking the trees, and while making the wheel. Therefore it was said, 'in six months less six nights.' 'Nānākaraṇaṃ' means difference. 'Nesaṃ' is 'na esaṃ' (not of these). 'Atthesaṃ' is 'atthi esaṃ' (there is of these). 'The course of formation' means the movement of effort. 'Ciṅgulāyitvā' means having spun around. 'Akkhāhataṃ maññe' means as if inserted and placed in the axle.

Sadosāti sagaṇḍā uṇṇatoṇataṭṭhānayuttā. Sakasāvāti pūtisārena ceva pheggunā ca yuttā. Kāyavaṅkātiādīni kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ nāmāni. Evaṃ papatitāti evaṃ guṇapatanena patitā. Evaṃ patiṭṭhitāti evaṃ guṇehi patiṭṭhitā. Tattha lokiyamahājanā papatitā nāma, sotāpannādayo patiṭṭhitā nāma. Tesupi purimā tayo kilesānaṃ samudācārakkhaṇe papatitā nāma, khīṇāsavā pana ekanteneva patiṭṭhitā nāma. Tasmāti yasmā appahīnakāyavaṅkādayo papatanti, pahīnakāyavaṅkādayo patiṭṭhahanti, tasmā. Kāyavaṅkādīnaṃ pana evaṃ pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ – pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ micchācāro musāvādo pisuṇāvācā micchādiṭṭhīti ime tāva cha sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti, pharusāvācā byāpādoti dve anāgāmimaggena, abhijjhā samphappalāpoti dve arahattamaggenāti.

Sadosā means with blemishes, endowed with knots and uneven places. Sakasāvā means associated with impurities, endowed with rotten heartwood and sapwood. 'Crookedness of body' and so on are names for bodily misconduct and the like. Thus fallen means thus fallen by the decline of virtues. Thus established means thus established by virtues. Among them, ordinary worldly people are called 'fallen,' while stream-enterers and the like are called 'established.' Even among these, the first three are called 'fallen' at the moment of the occurrence of defilements, but the destroyers of cankers are called 'established without exception.' Therefore—because those whose crookedness of body and the like are not abandoned fall, while those whose crookedness of body and the like are abandoned are established, therefore. Now, the abandonment of crookedness of body and the like should be understood thus: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, and wrong view—these six, for a start, are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; harsh speech and ill will—these two by the path of non-returning; covetousness and idle chatter—these two by the path of arahantship.

6. Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe apaṇṇakapaṭipadanti aviraddhapaṭipadaṃ ekaṃsapaṭipadaṃ niyyānikapaṭipadaṃ kāraṇapaṭipadaṃ sārapaṭipadaṃ maṇḍapaṭipadaṃ apaccanīkapaṭipadaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ [P 2.0182] dhammānudhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti, na takkaggāhena vā nayaggāhena vā. Evaṃ gahetvā paṭipanno hi bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā manussadevanibbānasampattīhi hāyati parihāyati, apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ [M 2.0081] paṭipanno pana tāhi sampattīhi na parihāyati. Atīte kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipannesu dvīsu satthavāhesu yakkhassa vacanaṃ gahetvā bālasatthavāho saddhiṃ satthena [V 2.0083] anayabyasanaṃ patto, yakkhassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā “udakadiṭṭhaṭṭhāne udakaṃ chaḍḍessāmā”ti satthake saññāpetvā maggaṃ paṭipanno paṇḍitasatthavāho viya. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

16. In the sixth, 'the unerring path' (apaṇṇakapaṭipadā) means one practices the unfailing path, the certain path, the path leading to liberation, the causal path, the essential path, the cream of the path, the unopposed path, and the conforming path, not by grasping at logic or inference. Indeed, a monk, nun, layman, or laywoman who practices having grasped thus declines and falls away from human, divine, and Nibbānic attainments. But one who practices the unerring path does not fall away from those attainments. In the past, when two caravan leaders were traveling along a dangerous road, the foolish caravan leader, accepting the yakkha’s words, met with ruin along with his caravan. But the wise caravan leader, not accepting the yakkha's words, having convinced his caravan that 'we will discard water only where water is seen,' set out on the path. This is what was meant when it was said—

“Apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānameke, dutiyaṃ āhu takkikā;

Etadaññāya medhāvī, taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇaka”nti. (jā. 1.1.1);

Some have taken the infallible course; the speculators, it is said, took the second. A wise person, having understood this, should adopt that which is infallible.

Yoni cassa āraddhā hotīti ettha yonīti khandhakoṭṭhāsassapi kāraṇassapi passāvamaggassapi nāmaṃ. “Catasso kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.152) hi khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāma. “Yoni hesā bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.226) kāraṇaṃ. “Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava”nti (ma. ni. 2.457; dha. pa. 396) ca “tamenaṃ kammajavātā nivattitvā uddhaṃpādaṃ adhosiraṃ samparivattetvā mātu yonimukhe sampaṭipādentī”ti ca ādīsu passāvamaggo. Idha pana kāraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Āraddhāti paggahitā paripuṇṇā.

Here, in the phrase 'And for him the yoni is undertaken,' the word yoni is a name for a portion of the aggregates, for a cause, and for the urinary passage. For, in passages such as, 'There are, Sāriputta, these four yonis,' yoni is the name for a portion of the aggregates. In passages such as, 'This, Bhūmija, is the yoni for the attainment of the fruit,' it means cause. In passages such as, 'Nor do I call a brahmin one who is born from the passage, of paternal origin,' and 'Then, the karma-born winds, turning him around, head down and feet up, establish him at the entrance of the mother’s urinary passage,' it means the urinary passage. Here, however, 'cause' is the intended meaning. Āraddhā means undertaken, perfected.

Āsavānaṃ khayāyāti ettha āsavantīti āsavā, cakkhutopi…pe… manatopi sandanti pavattantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammato yāva gotrabhu, okāsato yāva bhavaggā savantīti [P 2.0183] vā āsavā, ete dhamme etañca okāsaṃ antokaritvā pavattantīti attho. Antokaraṇattho hi ayaṃ ākāro. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādayo āsavā, āsavā viyātipi āsavā. Lokasmimpi hi cirapārivāsikā madirādayo āsavāti vuccanti, yadi ca cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena āsavā, eteyeva bhavitumarahanti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, ito pubbe avijjā nāhosī”tiādi (a. ni. 10.61). Āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantītipi āsavā. Purimāni cettha nibbacanāni yattha kilesā āsavāti āgacchanti, tattha yujjanti, pacchimaṃ kammepi. Na kevalañca kammakilesāyeva āsavā, apica kho nānappakārā upaddavāpi. Suttesu hi “nāhaṃ, cunda, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ [M 2.0082] desemī”ti (dī. ni. 3.182) ettha vivādamūlabhūtā kilesā āsavāti āgatā.

Regarding 'for the destruction of the taints': Herein, they are called taints (āsavā) because they flow; it is said that they flow and occur from the eye... and so on... up to the mind. Or, they are called taints because they flow up to the change-of-lineage consciousness in terms of phenomena, and up to the peak of existence in terms of realm; the meaning is that they occur encompassing these phenomena and this realm. For this prefix 'ā' has the meaning of encompassing. Due to the meaning of being long-matured, liquors and so forth are taints. Also, because they are like those liquors, they are called taints. Indeed, in the world, long-matured liquors and so forth are called taints. And if they are taints due to the meaning of being long-matured, then only these very things—namely greed, wrong view, and delusion—are fit to be so. For this has been said: 'Bhikkhus, the prior point of ignorance is not discerned, thinking: "Before this, there was no ignorance,"' and so on. Or, they are also called taints because they cause the long suffering of saṃsāra to flow and to be produced. Among these, the former etymologies are suitable where the defilements are given as taints, while the latter is also suitable for kamma. And not only kamma and defilements are taints, but also various kinds of calamities. For in the Suttas, in the passage, 'Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints in the present life,' the defilements that are the root of disputes are given as taints.

“Yena [V 2.0084] devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36) –

By which I might attain rebirth as a god, or as a gandhabba traveling through the sky; by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, and attain the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, demolished, and made like a palm stump.

Ettha tebhūmakaṃ ca kammaṃ avasesā ca akusalā dhammā. “Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39; a. ni. 2.202-230) ettha parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhādayo ceva apāyadukkhabhūtā ca nānappakārā upaddavā.

Herein, kamma pertaining to the three planes and the remaining unwholesome states are included. In the passage, “For the restraint of the taints in the present life and for the warding off of the taints in future lives,” calamities such as blame from others, remorse, killing, and bondage, as well as various calamities that constitute the suffering of the plane of misery, are included.

Te panete āsavā yattha yathā āgatā, tattha tathā veditabbā. Ete hi vinaye tāva “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39; a. ni. 2.202-230) dvedhā āgatā. Saḷāyatane “tayo me, āvuso, āsavā kāmāsavo bhavāsavo avijjāsavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.321) tidhā āgatā. Aññesu ca suttantesu (cūḷani. jatukaṇṇimāṇavapucchāniddeso 69; paṭi. ma. 1.107) abhidhamme (dha. sa. 1102-1106; vibha. 937) ca teyeva diṭṭhāsavena saha catudhā āgatā. Nibbedhikapariyāyena “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā nirayagāminiyā[P 2.0184], atthi āsavā tiracchānayonigāminiyā, atthi āsavā pettivisayagāminiyā, atthi āsavā manussalokagāminiyā, atthi āsavā devalokagāminiyā”ti (a. ni. 6.63) pañcadhā āgatā. Kammameva cettha āsavāti vuttaṃ. Chakkanipāte “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarāpahātabbā”tiādinā (a. ni. 6.58) nayena chadhā āgatā. Sabbāsavapariyāye (ma. ni. 1.14 ādayo) teyeva dassanena pahātabbehi saddhiṃ sattadhā āgatā. Idha pana abhidhammanayena cattāro āsavā adhippetāti veditabbā.

Furthermore, these taints should be understood in that way in that place, wherever and in whatever way they have come. For in the Vinaya, they have come in two ways: “for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives.” In the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta, they have come in three ways: “Friend, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of becoming, and the taint of ignorance.” And in other Suttantas and in the Abhidhamma, those same taints have come in four ways together with the taint of views. By way of the Nibbedhika discourse, they have come in five ways: “Monks, there are taints leading to hell, there are taints leading to the animal realm, there are taints leading to the realm of ghosts, there are taints leading to the human world, and there are taints leading to the celestial world.” And here, kamma itself is called a taint. In the Book of the Sixes, they have come in six ways by the method beginning “Monks, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint…” In the Sabbāsava discourse, those same taints have come in seven ways together with those to be abandoned by seeing. Here, however, it should be understood that according to the Abhidhamma method, four taints are intended.

Khayāyāti ettha pana āsavānaṃ sarasabhedopi khīṇākāropi maggaphalanibbānānipi “āsavakkhayo”ti vuccati. “Yo āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo paribhedo aniccatā antaradhāna”nti ettha hi āsavānaṃ sarasabhedo “āsavakkhayo”ti vutto. “Jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato [M 2.0083] āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.15; saṃ. ni. 2.23; itivu. 102) ettha [V 2.0085] āsavappahānaṃ āsavānaṃ accantakkhayo asamuppādo khīṇākāro natthibhāvo “āsavakkhayo”ti vutto.

Here, however, in the phrase “for the destruction” (khayāya), the destruction of the taints by their own nature, the state of their being exhausted, and also the path, fruition, and Nibbāna are called “the destruction of the taints.” For in the passage, “That which is the destruction, the waning, the breaking, the complete breaking, the impermanence, and the disappearance of the taints,” the destruction of the taints by their own nature is called “the destruction of the taints.” In the passage, “Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees,” the abandoning of the taints, the absolute destruction of the taints, their non-arising, the state of their being exhausted, and their state of non-existence are called “the destruction of the taints.”

“Sekhassa sikkhamānassa, ujumaggānusārino;

Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tato aññā anantarā”ti. (itivu. 62) –

For the learner who is training, following the straight path, first there is knowledge in the path of destruction; then, immediately following, is final knowledge.

Ettha maggo “āsavakkhayo”ti vutto. “Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.438) ettha phalaṃ.

Here, the path is called “the destruction of the taints.” In “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,” the fruition is meant.

“Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṃ ujjhānasaññino;

Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti. (dha. pa. 253) –

For one who looks for others’ faults, who is ever critical, his taints increase. He is far from the destruction of taints.

Ettha nibbānaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte phalaṃ sandhāya “āsavānaṃ khayāyā”ti āha, arahattaphalatthāyāti attho.

Here, Nibbāna is meant. In this sutta, however, it is said “for the destruction of the taints” with reference to the fruition, meaning for the purpose of the fruition of Arahantship.

Indriyesu guttadvāroti manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu pihitadvāro. Bhojane mattaññūti bhojanasmiṃ pamāṇaññū, paṭiggahaṇaparibhogapaccavekkhaṇamattaṃ jānāti pajānātīti attho. Jāgariyaṃ [P 2.0185] anuyuttoti rattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā pañcasu koṭṭhāsesu jāgaraṇabhāvaṃ anuyutto, jāgaraṇeyeva yuttappayuttoti attho.

“Guarded in the sense faculties” means having the doors closed in the six sense faculties which have the mind as the sixth. “Knowing moderation in food” means knowing the measure in food; the meaning is that one knows and understands the measure for receiving, consuming, and reflecting. “Devoted to wakefulness” means having divided day and night into six parts, one is devoted to the state of wakefulness in five parts; the meaning is that one is exceedingly devoted to wakefulness itself.

Evaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā idāni tameva ṭhapitapaṭipāṭiyā vibhajanto kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvātiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.15) vitthārito, tathā paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti neva davāyātiādīnaṃ (visuddhi. 1.18). Āvaraṇīyehi dhammehīti pañcahi nīvaraṇehi dhammehi. Nīvaraṇāni hi cittaṃ āvaritvā tiṭṭhanti, tasmā āvaraṇīyā dhammāti vuccanti. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappetīti sīho viya seyyaṃ kappeti. Pāde pādaṃ accādhāyāti vāmapādaṃ dakkhiṇapāde atiādhāya. Samaṃ ṭhapite hi pāde jāṇukena jāṇukaṃ gopphakena ca gopphakaṃ ghaṭīyati, tato vedanā uṭṭhahanti. Tasmā [V 2.0086] tassa dosassa parivajjanatthaṃ thokaṃ atikkamitvā esa pādaṃ ṭhapeti. Tena vuttaṃ – “pāde pādaṃ accādhāyā”ti.

Having thus set forth the outline, now, elaborating on that very outline according to the established sequence, he says, “And how, monks, does a monk…?” and so on. Here, the meaning of “having seen a form with the eye” and so on is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, as is that of “he consumes food reflectively and wisely, not for amusement…” and so on. “By obstructive states” means by the five states that are hindrances. For the hindrances obstruct the wholesome mind and remain; therefore they are called “obstructive states.” “He adopts the lion’s posture” means he makes his lying down like a lion. “Placing one foot over the other” means placing the left foot beyond the right foot. For if the feet are placed evenly, knee strikes against knee and ankle against ankle, and then painful feelings arise. Therefore, to avoid that fault, he places the foot slightly beyond. Hence it is said: “placing one foot over the other.”

Sato [M 2.0084] sampajānoti satiyā ceva sampajaññena ca samannāgato. Kathaṃ panesa niddāyanto sato sampajāno nāma hotīti? Purimappavattivasena. Ayaṃ hi caṅkame caṅkamanto niddāya okkamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā pavattamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapetvā mañce vā phalake vā nipanno niddaṃ upagantvā puna pabujjhamāno kammaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhāne gaṇhantoyeva pabujjhati. Tasmā niddāyantopi sato sampajāno nāma hoti. Ayaṃ tāva mūlakammaṭṭhāne nayova. Pariggahakammaṭṭhānavasenāpi panesa sato sampajāno nāma hoti. Kathaṃ? Ayaṃ hi caṅkamanto niddāya okkamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā pāsāṇaphalake vā mañce vā dakkhiṇena passena nipajjitvā paccavekkhati – “acetano kāyo acetane [P 2.0186] mañce patiṭṭhito, acetano mañco acetanāya pathaviyā, acetanā pathavī acetane udake, acetanaṃ udakaṃ acetane vāte, acetano vāto acetane ākāse patiṭṭhito. Tattha ākāsampi ‘ahaṃ vātaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhita’nti na jānāti, vātopi ‘ahaṃ ākāse patiṭṭhito’ti na jānāti. Tathā vāto na jānāti. ‘Ahaṃ udakaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhito’ti…pe… mañco na jānāti, ‘ahaṃ kāyaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhito’ti, kāyo na jānāti ‘ahaṃ mañce patiṭṭhito’ti. Na hi tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ ābhogo vā samannāhāro vā manasikāro vā cetanā vā patthanā vā atthī”ti. Tassa evaṃ paccavekkhato taṃ paccavekkhaṇacittaṃ bhavaṅge otarati. Evaṃ niddāyantopi sato sampajāno nāma hotīti.

'Mindful and clearly comprehending' means endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. But how is this yogi, while sleeping, called mindful and clearly comprehending? By virtue of the previously established meditation subject. Indeed, this yogi, while walking on the walking path, knowing the onset of sleep, sets aside the meditation subject in progress, lies down on a bed or a plank, falls asleep, and upon waking again, wakes up resuming the meditation subject from the place where it was established. Therefore, even while sleeping, one is called mindful and clearly comprehending. This, firstly, is the method concerning the fundamental meditation subject. Moreover, by virtue of the meditation subject taken up at the moment of sleeping, this yogi is also called mindful and clearly comprehending. How is this so? Indeed, this monk, while walking, knowing the onset of sleep, lies down on his right side on a stone slab or a bed and reflects: 'The inanimate body is established on the inanimate bed; the inanimate bed on the inanimate earth; the inanimate earth on the inanimate water; the inanimate water on the inanimate air; the inanimate air is established on the inanimate space. Therein, space does not know, "I stand supporting the air," and the air also does not know, "I am established on space." Likewise, the air does not know, "I stand supporting the water"... the bed does not know, "I stand supporting the body," and the body does not know, "I am established on the bed." For among them there is no mutual advertence, sustained attention, application of mind, volition, or aspiration.' For him reflecting thus, that reflective consciousness sinks into the life-continuum. Thus, even while sleeping, one is called mindful and clearly comprehending.

Uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasikaritvāti “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ gate cande vā tārakāya vā uṭṭhahissāmī”ti uṭṭhānakālaparicchedikaṃ saññaṃ manasikaritvā, citte ṭhapetvāti attho. Evaṃ karitvā sayito hi yathāparicchinneyeva kāle uṭṭhahati.

'Having attended to the perception of rising' means having attended to a perception that determines the time for rising, such as 'When the moon or a star has reached such a position, I will rise,' and having established it in the mind—this is the meaning. Indeed, one who has lain down having done so rises at the very time that was determined.

7. Attabyābādhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Attabyābādha Sutta

17. Sattame attabyābādhāyāti attadukkhāya. Parabyābādhāyāti paradukkhāya. Kāyasucaritantiādīni pubbabhāge dasakusalakammapathavasena āgatāni, upari pana yāva arahattā avāritāneva.

17. In the seventh sutta, 'for one's own harm' means for one's own suffering. 'For others' harm' means for the suffering of others. The terms such as 'good bodily conduct', in the earlier part, are presented by way of the ten wholesome courses of action; but subsequently, up to the fruit of Arahantship, they are indeed presented as unimpeded.

8. Devalokasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Devaloka Sutta

18. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0087][M 2.0085] aṭṭīyeyyāthāti aṭṭā pīḷitā bhaveyyātha. Harāyeyyāthāti lajjeyyātha. Jiguccheyyāthāti gūthe viya tasmiṃ vacane sañjātajigucchā bhaveyyātha. Iti kirāti ettha itīti padasandhibyañjanasiliṭṭhatā, kirāti anussavatthe nipāto. Dibbena kira āyunā aṭṭīyathāti evamassa sambandho veditabbo. Pageva kho panāti paṭhamataraṃyeva.

18. In the eighth sutta, 'aṭṭīyeyyātha' means you should be afflicted and oppressed. 'Harāyeyyātha' means you should feel ashamed. 'Jiguccheyyātha' means you should have disgust arise towards that speech, just as towards excrement. In the text 'iti kira', the word 'iti' is a particle for the connection of words and the smoothness of sentences; 'kira' is a particle in the sense of hearsay. 'Be wearied, it is said, by the divine lifespan'—thus its connection should be understood. 'Pageva kho pana' means even earlier.

9. Paṭhamapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Pāpaṇika Sutta

19. Navame pāpaṇikoti āpaṇiko, āpaṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā bhaṇḍavikkāyakassa vāṇijassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Abhabboti abhājanabhūto. Na [P 2.0187] sakkaccaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhātīti yathā adhiṭṭhitaṃ suadhiṭṭhitaṃ hoti, evaṃ sayaṃ attapaccakkhaṃ karonto nādhiṭṭhāti. Tattha paccūsakāle padasaddena uṭṭhāya dīpaṃ jāletvā bhaṇḍaṃ pasāretvā anisīdanto pubbaṇhasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. Ayaṃ hi yaṃ corā rattiṃ bhaṇḍaṃ haritvā “idaṃ amhākaṃ hatthato vissajjessāmā”ti āpaṇaṃ gantvā appena agghena denti, yampi bahuverino manussā rattiṃ nagare vasitvā pātova āpaṇaṃ gantvā bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhanti, yaṃ vā pana janapadaṃ gantukāmā manussā pātova āpaṇaṃ gantvā bhaṇḍaṃ kiṇanti, tappaccayassa lābhassa assāmiko hoti.

19. In the ninth sutta, 'pāpaṇiko' means a shopkeeper; this is a designation for a merchant who sells goods, having opened a shop. 'Abhabbo' means he is not a suitable vessel. 'He does not diligently attend to his work' means he does not attend to it himself, making it directly perceived by himself, in such a way that what is attended to becomes well-attended to. Therein, one who does not rise at dawn at the sound of footsteps, light a lamp, spread out his goods, and remain seated, is said not to diligently attend to his work in the morning. For he is not the owner of the profit that has this as its cause: the goods which thieves, having stolen them at night, go to the shop and give for a low price, thinking, 'We will let this go from our hands'; and the goods which many hostile people, having stayed in the city at night, go to the shop early in the morning and take; or the goods which people wishing to go to another district go to the shop early in the morning and buy.

Aññesaṃ bhojanavelāya pana bhuñjituṃ āgantvā pātova bhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā gharaṃ gantvā bhuñjitvā niddāyitvā sāyaṃ puna āpaṇaṃ āgacchanto majjhanhikasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. So hi yaṃ corā pātova vissajjetuṃ na sampāpuṇiṃsu, divākāle pana paresaṃ asañcārakkhaṇe āpaṇaṃ gantvā appagghena denti, yañca bhojanavelāya puññavanto issarā “āpaṇato idañcidañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pahiṇitvā āharāpenti, tappaccayassa lābhassa assāmiko hoti.

Furthermore, one who, at the mealtime of others, goes to eat—having packed up his goods early in the morning, gone home, eaten, slept, and then returned to the shop in the evening—is said not to diligently attend to his work at midday. For he is not the master of the profit that has this as its cause: that which thieves, unable to dispose of early in the morning, go to the shop during the day at a time of others' negligence and sell for a small price; and that which virtuous and powerful people, thinking, 'It is proper to obtain this and that from the shop,' send for and have brought at mealtime.

Yāva yāmabherinikkhamanā pana antoāpaṇe dīpaṃ jālāpetvā anisīdanto sāyanhasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ kammantaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. So hi yaṃ [M 2.0086] corā pātopi divāpi vissajjetuṃ na sampāpuṇiṃsu[V 2.0088], sāyaṃ pana āpaṇaṃ gantvā appagghena denti, tappaccayassa lābhassa assāmiko hoti.

Furthermore, one who does not remain seated inside the shop with a lamp lit until the sounding of the watch-drum is said not to diligently attend to his work in the evening. For he is not the master of the profit that has this as its cause: the goods which thieves, unable to dispose of either in the morning or during the day, go to the shop in the evening and sell for a small price.

Na sakkaccaṃ samādhinimittaṃ adhiṭṭhātīti sakkaccakiriyāya samādhiṃ na samāpajjati. Ettha ca pātova cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇesu vattaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā, tāva samāpattiṃ appetvā anisīdanto pubbaṇhasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ samādhinimittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. Pacchābhattaṃ pana piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaṃ [P 2.0188] pavisitvā yāva sāyanhasamayā samāpattiṃ appetvā anisīdanto majjhanhikasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ samādhinimittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. Sāyaṃ pana cetiyaṃ vanditvā therūpaṭṭhānaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā paṭhamayāmaṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā anisīdanto sāyanhasamayaṃ na sakkaccaṃ samādhinimittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti nāma. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhanayeneva veditabbo. Apicettha “samāpattiṃ appetvā”ti vuttaṭṭhāne samāpattiyā asati vipassanāpi vaṭṭati, samādhinimittanti ca samādhiārammaṇampi vaṭṭatiyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “samādhipi samādhinimittaṃ, samādhārammaṇampi samādhinimitta”nti.

‘He does not respectfully establish the sign of concentration’ means he does not enter into concentration with respectful action. Here, a lazy monk who in the early morning, after performing duties at the shrine courtyard or the Bodhi-tree courtyard, enters his dwelling, and does not remain in meditative attainment until the time for the alms-round, is called one who ‘in the morning, does not respectfully establish the sign of concentration.’ Furthermore, a lazy monk who, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, enters his day or night resting place, and does not remain in meditative attainment until evening, is called one who ‘at midday, does not respectfully establish the sign of concentration.’ Furthermore, a lazy monk who in the evening, after paying homage at the shrine and attending on the elders, enters his dwelling, and does not remain in meditative attainment during the first watch of the night, is called one who ‘in the evening, does not respectfully establish the sign of concentration.’ The bright side should be understood by the method that is the opposite of what has been said. Furthermore, here, where it is said, ‘having entered into meditative attainment,’ if there is no meditative attainment, insight is also suitable. And regarding ‘the sign of concentration,’ the object of concentration is also indeed suitable. And this has been said: ‘Concentration itself is the sign of concentration, and the object of concentration is also the sign of concentration.’

10. Dutiyapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse about the Shopkeeper

20. Dasame cakkhumāti paññācakkhunā cakkhumā hoti. Vidhuroti visiṭṭhadhuro uttamadhuro ñāṇasampayuttena vīriyena samannāgato. Nissayasampannoti avassayasampanno patiṭṭhānasampanno. Paṇiyanti vikkāyikabhaṇḍaṃ. Ettakaṃ mūlaṃ bhavissati ettako udayoti tasmiṃ “evaṃ kītaṃ evaṃ vikkāyamāna”nti vuttapaṇiye yena kayena taṃ kītaṃ, taṃ kayasaṅkhātaṃ mūlaṃ ettakaṃ bhavissati. Yo ca tasmiṃ vikkayamāne vikkayo, tasmiṃ vikkaye ettako udayo bhavissati, ettikā vaḍḍhīti attho.

20. In the tenth discourse, 'possessed of vision' means one is possessed of vision by the eye of wisdom. 'Vidhuro' means one is distinguished in bearing responsibility, supreme in bearing responsibility, endowed with energy associated with knowledge. 'Nissayasampanno' means well-supported, well-established. 'Paṇiyaṃ' means goods for sale. 'This much will be the principal, this much the profit' means that concerning the merchandise about which it is said, 'it was bought thus, it is being sold thus,' the principal, reckoned as the purchase price by which it was bought, will be this much. And whatever is the sale when it is being sold, in that sale, this much will be the profit, this much the increase; this is the meaning.

Kusalo hoti paṇiyaṃ ketuñca vikketuñcāti sulabhaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā kiṇanto dullabhaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vikkiṇanto ca ettha kusalo nāma hoti, dasaguṇampi vīsatiguṇampi lābhaṃ labhati.

'Skilled in buying and selling merchandise' means that one is called skilled in this matter by going to a place where goods are easily available and buying, and by going to a place where they are scarce and selling; one obtains a tenfold or even a twentyfold profit.

Aḍḍhāti [M 2.0087] issarā bahunā nikkhittadhanena samannāgatā. Mahaddhanāti vaḷañjanakavasena mahaddhanā[V 2.0089]. Mahābhogāti [P 2.0189] upabhogaparibhogabhaṇḍena mahābhogā. Paṭibaloti kāyabalena ceva ñāṇabalena ca samannāgatattā samattho. Amhākañca kālena kālaṃ anuppadātunti amhākañca gahitadhanamūlikaṃ vaḍḍhiṃ kālena kālaṃ anuppadātuṃ. Nipatantīti nimantenti. Nipātentītipi pāṭho, ayameva attho.

'Aḍḍha' means they are lords, endowed with much deposited wealth. 'Mahaddhana' means they have great wealth by way of wealth for daily use. 'Mahābhoga' means they have great possessions by way of goods for use and enjoyment. 'Paṭibala' means one is capable on account of being endowed with both bodily strength and the strength of wisdom. 'And to provide for us from time to time' means to give to us from time to time the borrowed principal along with its increase. 'Nipatanti' means they invite. 'Nipātenti' is also a reading; this very meaning should be understood.

Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāyāti kusaladhammānaṃ sampādanatthāya paṭilābhatthāya. Thāmavāti ñāṇathāmena samannāgato. Daḷhaparakkamoti thirena ñāṇaparakkamena samannāgato. Anikkhittadhuroti “aggamaggaṃ apāpuṇitvā imaṃ vīriyadhuraṃ na ṭhapessāmī”ti evaṃ aṭṭhapitadhuro.

'For the attainment of wholesome qualities' means for the purpose of accomplishing and acquiring wholesome qualities. 'Thāmavā' means one is endowed with the strength of wisdom. 'Daḷhaparakkamo' means one is endowed with steadfast effort accompanied by wisdom. 'Anikkhittadhuro' means one who has not laid down the burden, resolving, 'I will not lay down this burden of effort without having reached the highest path.'

Bahussutāti ekanikāyādivasena bahu buddhavacanaṃ sutaṃ etesanti bahussutā. Āgatāgamāti eko nikāyo eko āgamo nāma, dve nikāyā dve āgamā nāma, pañca nikāyā pañca āgamā nāma, etesu āgamesu yesaṃ ekopi āgamo āgato paguṇo pavattito, te āgatāgamā nāma. Dhammadharāti suttantapiṭakadharā. Vinayadharāti vinayapiṭakadharā. Mātikādharāti dvemātikādharā. Paripucchatīti atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ pucchati. Paripañhatīti “imaṃ nāma pucchissāmī”ti aññāti tuleti pariggaṇhāti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

'Bahussuta' means those by whom much of the Buddha’s word has been heard, such as one collection or more; they are called 'bahussuta'. 'Āgatāgama' means one collection is called one tradition, two collections two traditions, five collections five traditions; those by whom even one tradition among these traditions has been mastered, made fluent, and maintained, they are called 'āgatāgama'. 'Dhammadhara' means those who uphold the Sutta Piṭaka. 'Vinayadhara' means those who uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka. 'Mātikādhara' means those who uphold the two Mātikās. 'Paripucchati' means asking about what is beneficial and not beneficial, what is a cause and not a cause. 'Paripañhati' means one knows, weighs, and investigates, thinking, 'I will ask this particular question.' The rest here has an obvious meaning.

Imasmiṃ [P 2.0190] pana sutte paṭhamaṃ paññā āgatā, pacchā vīriyañca kalyāṇamittasevanā ca. Tattha paṭhamaṃ arahattaṃ patvā pacchā vīriyaṃ katvā kalyāṇamittā sevitabbāti na evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo, desanāya nāma heṭṭhimena vā paricchedo hoti uparimena vā dvīhipi vā koṭīhi. Idha pana uparimena paricchedo veditabbo. Tasmā kathentena paṭhamaṃ kalyāṇamittaupanissayaṃ dassetvā majjhe vīriyaṃ dassetvā pacchā arahattaṃ kathetabbanti.

However, in this sutta, wisdom came first; afterwards, energy and associating with good friends came. Among these, the meaning should not be understood thus: 'Having first reached Arahantship, and afterwards having exerted energy, good friends should be associated with.' For a teaching, indeed, the demarcation is by way of the lower, or by way of the higher, or by both ends. But here, the demarcation should be understood as by way of the higher. Therefore, one who is speaking should first show the support of good friends, show energy in the middle, and afterwards speak of Arahantship.

Rathakāravaggo dutiyo.

The Rathakāra Vagga, the Second.

3. Puggalavaggo

3. The Puggala Vagga

1. Samiddhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Samiddha Sutta

21. Tatiyassa [V 2.0090][M 2.0088] paṭhame jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati, pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhi. Diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti diṭṭhippatto. Saddahanto vimuttoti saddhāvimutto. Khamatīti ruccati. Abhikkantataroti atisundarataro. Paṇītataroti atipaṇītataro. Saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hotīti samiddhattherassa kira arahattamaggakkhaṇe saddhindriyaṃ dhuraṃ ahosi, sesāni cattāri sahajātindriyāni tasseva parivārāni ahesuṃ. Iti thero attanā paṭividdhamaggaṃ kathento evamāha. Mahākoṭṭhikattherassa pana arahattamaggakkhaṇe samādhindriyaṃ dhuraṃ ahosi, sesāni cattāri indriyāni tasseva parivārāni ahesuṃ. Tasmā sopi samādhindriyaṃ adhimattanti kathento attanā paṭividdhamaggameva kathesi. Sāriputtattherassa pana arahattamaggakkhaṇe paññindriyaṃ dhuraṃ ahosi. Sesāni cattāri indriyāni tasseva parivārāni ahesuṃ. Tasmā sopi paññindriyaṃ adhimattanti kathento attanā paṭividdhamaggameva kathesi.

21. In the first sutta of the third vagga: One is called a 'bodily witness' (kāyasakkhi) because one first reaches the contact that is jhāna, and afterwards realizes Nibbāna, the cessation of the round of existence. One is called 'one attained to view' (diṭṭhippatto) because one has reached the end of the path of stream-entry which is able to see Nibbāna. One is called 'faith-liberated' (saddhāvimutto) because, believing, one is liberated from defilements. Khamati means it is agreeable (ruccati). Abhikkantatara means exceedingly beautiful (atisundaratara). Paṇītatara means exceedingly sublime (atipaṇītatara). As for the phrase 'the faculty of faith is predominant': it is said that for the Elder Samiddha, at the moment of the path of Arahantship, the faculty of faith was the chief factor, and the remaining four conascent faculties were its retinue. Thus the Elder, while speaking of the path penetrated by himself, spoke in this way. But for the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, at the moment of the path of Arahantship, the faculty of concentration was the chief factor, and the remaining four faculties were its retinue. Therefore he too, speaking of 'the faculty of concentration being predominant,' spoke only of the path penetrated by himself. But for the Elder Sāriputta, at the moment of the path of Arahantship, the faculty of wisdom was the chief factor, and the remaining four faculties were its retinue. Therefore he too, speaking of 'the faculty of wisdom being predominant,' spoke only of the path penetrated by himself.

Na [P 2.0191] khvetthāti na kho ettha. Ekaṃsena byākātunti ekantena byākarituṃ. Arahattāya paṭipannoti arahattamaggasamaṅgiṃ dasseti. Evametasmiṃ sutte tīhipi therehi attanā paṭividdhamaggova kathito, sammāsambuddho pana bhummantareneva kathesi.

'Na khvettha' should be parsed as 'na kho ettha' (not indeed here). 'Ekaṃsena byākātuṃ' (to declare decisively) means to declare absolutely. 'Arahattāya paṭipanno' (practicing for Arahantship) indicates one endowed with the path to Arahantship. Thus, in this discourse, the path penetrated by themselves was spoken of by the three elders, but the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke by way of a difference of plane.

2. Gilānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Sick Person

22. Dutiye sappāyānīti hitāni vuddhikarāni. Patirūpanti anucchavikaṃ. Neva vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhāti iminā atekicchena vātāpamārādinā rogena samannāgato niṭṭhāpattagilāno kathito. Vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhāti iminā khipitakakacchutiṇapupphakajarādibhedo appamattaābādho kathito. Labhanto sappāyāni bhojanāni no alabhantoti iminā pana yesaṃ paṭijagganena phāsukaṃ hoti, sabbepi te ābādhā kathitā. Ettha ca patirūpo upaṭṭhāko nāma [V 2.0091] gilānupaṭṭhākaaṅgehi samannāgato paṇḍito dakkho analaso veditabbo. Gilānupaṭṭhāko anuññātoti bhikkhusaṅghena dātabboti anuññāto. Tasmiñhi gilāne attano dhammatāya yāpetuṃ asakkonte bhikkhusaṅghena [M 2.0089] tassa bhikkhuno eko bhikkhu ca sāmaṇero ca “imaṃ paṭijaggathā”ti apaloketvā dātabbā. Yāva pana te taṃ paṭijagganti, tāva gilānassa ca tesañca dvinnaṃ yenattho, sabbaṃ bhikkhusaṅghasseva bhāro.

22. In the second discourse, 'sappāyāni' (suitable things) means beneficial and growth-promoting. 'Patirūpaṃ' (appropriate) means fitting. By 'neva vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhā' (he does not recover from that illness), a terminally ill person afflicted with an incurable disease such as a wind disorder, epilepsy, and so forth, is meant. By 'vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhā' (he recovers from that illness), a minor ailment such as sneezing, scabies, grass-flower disease, or old age is meant. By 'labhanto sappāyāni bhojanāni no alabhanto' (obtaining suitable food, not obtaining it), however, are meant all those illnesses for which comfort comes through care. And here, a 'patirūpo upaṭṭhāko' (suitable attendant) should be understood as one who is endowed with the qualities of a sick-attendant: wise, skillful, and not lazy. 'Gilānupaṭṭhāko anuññāto' (a sick-attendant is permitted) means permitted in the sense of being assigned by the community of monks. For indeed, if a sick monk is unable to sustain himself naturally, the community of monks should, after announcing, "You should attend to this one," assign one monk and one novice to him. Furthermore, for as long as they attend to him, all the needs of the sick monk and of those two are the responsibility of the community of monks.

Aññepi gilānā upaṭṭhātabbāti itarepi dve gilānā upaṭṭhāpetabbā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yopi hi niṭṭhapattagilāno, so anupaṭṭhiyamāno “sace maṃ paṭijaggeyyuṃ, phāsukaṃ me bhaveyya. Na kho pana maṃ paṭijaggantī”ti manopadosaṃ katvā apāye nibbatteyya. Paṭijaggiyamānassa panassa evaṃ hoti “bhikkhusaṅghena yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ kataṃ. Mayhaṃ pana kammavipāko īdiso”ti. So bhikkhusaṅghe mettaṃ [P 2.0192] paccupaṭṭhāpetvā sagge nibbattissati. Yo pana appamattakena byādhinā samannāgato labhantopi alabhantopi vuṭṭhātiyeva, tassa vināpi bhesajjena vūpasamanabyādhi bhesajje kate khippataraṃ vūpasammati. So tato buddhavacanaṃ vā uggaṇhituṃ sakkhissati, samaṇadhammaṃ vā kātuṃ sakkhissati. Iminā kāraṇena “aññepi gilānā upaṭṭhātabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Other sick ones should be attended to' means: the other two sick monks should be attended to. For what reason? For, a person who is terminally ill, if not attended to, might generate malevolence of mind, thinking, 'If they were to attend to me, it would be comfortable for me. But they do not attend to me,' and be reborn in a plane of misery. But for one who is being attended to, this thought arises: 'The community of monks has done what should be done. This, however, is the result of my kamma.' He, having established loving-kindness toward the community of monks, will be reborn in a heavenly realm. Furthermore, for one who is endowed with a minor illness and recovers whether he obtains suitable requisites or not, an illness that would subside even without medicine subsides more quickly when medicine is administered. As a result, he will be able to learn the word of the Buddha or to practice the duty of a recluse. For this reason, it was said, 'Other sick ones should be attended to.'

Neva okkamatīti neva pavisati. Niyāmaṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu magganiyāmasaṅkhātaṃ sammattaṃ. Iminā padaparamo puggalo kathito. Dutiyavārena ugghaṭitaññū gahito sāsane nālakattherasadiso buddhantare ekavāraṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ santike ovādaṃ labhitvā paṭividdhapaccekabodhiñāṇo ca. Tatiyavārena vipañcitaññū puggalo kathito, neyyo pana tannissitova hoti.

'He does not enter' means he does not enter. 'The certainty in wholesome qualities' means the rightness, known as the certainty of the path, in wholesome qualities. By this, the padaparama person is spoken of. By the second instance, the ugghaṭitaññū is included: one in the Dispensation similar to the Elder Nālaka, and one who, in an interval between Buddhas, having received instruction once in the presence of Paccekabuddhas, has penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. By the third instance, the vipañcitaññū person is spoken of; but the neyya is dependent on that very person.

Dhammadesanā anuññātāti māsassa aṭṭha vāre dhammakathā anuññātā. Aññesampi dhammo desetabboti itaresampi dhammo kathetabbo. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Padaparamassa hi imasmiṃ attabhāve dhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ asakkontassāpi anāgate paccayo bhavissati. Yo pana tathāgatassa rūpadassanaṃ labhantopi alabhantopi dhammavinayañca savanāya labhantopi alabhantopi dhammaṃ abhisameti, so alabhanto tāva abhisameti. Labhanto pana khippameva abhisamessatīti iminā kāraṇena [M 2.0090] tesaṃ dhammo desetabbo. Tatiyassa pana punappunaṃ desetabbova.

‘The teaching of the Dhamma is permitted’—a Dhamma talk is permitted eight times a month. ‘The Dhamma should also be taught to others’—the Dhamma should be spoken to others. For what reason? Because for a person who is word-ultimate, even if they are unable to penetrate the Dhamma in this present existence, it will become a condition in the future. As for one who comprehends the Dhamma, whether obtaining a sight of the Tathāgata’s form or not, and whether obtaining an opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya or not, they comprehend even when not obtaining these. But when obtaining them, they will comprehend very quickly. For this reason, the Dhamma should be taught to them. As for the third person, however, it should be taught again and again.

3. Saṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Saṅkhāra Sutta

23. Tatiye [V 2.0092] sabyābajjhanti sadukkhaṃ. Kāyasaṅkhāranti kāyadvāre cetanārāsiṃ. Abhisaṅkharotīti āyūhati rāsiṃ karoti piṇḍaṃ karoti. Vacīmanodvāresupi eseva nayo. Sabyābajjhaṃ lokanti sadukkhaṃ lokaṃ. Sabyābajjhā phassā phusantīti sadukkhā vipākaphassā phusanti. Sabyābajjhaṃ [P 2.0193] vedanaṃ vediyatīti sadukkhaṃ vipākavedanaṃ vediyati, sābādhaṃ nirassādanti attho. Seyyathāpi sattā nerayikāti yathā niraye nibbattasattā ekantadukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyanti, evaṃ vediyatīti attho. Kiṃ pana tattha upekkhāvedanā natthīti? Atthi, dukkhavedanāya pana balavabhāvena sā abbohārikaṭṭhāne ṭhitā. Iti nirayova nirayassa upamaṃ katvā āhaṭo. Tatra paṭibhāgaupamā nāma kira esā.

23. In the third discourse, ‘with affliction’ means ‘with suffering’. ‘Bodily formation’ means the accumulation of volitions at the body-door. ‘He generates’ means he strives, he makes a heap, he makes a lump. The same method applies to the speech-door and the mind-door. ‘The world with affliction’ means the world with suffering. ‘Afflictive contacts touch’ means painful resultant contacts touch. ‘He feels an afflictive feeling’ means he feels a painful resultant feeling; the meaning is ‘distressing and without enjoyment’. ‘Just as beings in hell’ means that just as beings born in hell feel a feeling that is exclusively suffering, so it is felt; this is the meaning. But is there no equanimous feeling there? There is, but because of the great strength of painful feeling, it remains in a state not worth mentioning. Thus, hell itself has been brought as an example for hell. Therein, this is indeed called an analogy of correspondence.

Seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhāti idhāpi devalokova devalokassa upamaṃ katvā āhaṭo. Yasmā pana heṭṭhimesu brahmalokesu sappītikajjhānavipāko vattati, subhakiṇhesu nippītiko ekantasukhova, tasmā te aggahetvā subhakiṇhāva kathitā. Iti ayampi tatra paṭibhāgaupamā nāmāti veditabbā.

‘Just as the Subhakiṇha gods’: here too, the deva-world itself is brought forth as an example for the deva-world. But because in the lower Brahma-worlds the result of jhāna with rapture prevails, while among the Subhakiṇha gods it is without rapture and exclusively blissful, therefore, without taking those into account, only the Subhakiṇha are mentioned. Thus, this too should be understood as an analogy of correspondence there.

Vokiṇṇasukhadukkhanti vomissakasukhadukkhaṃ. Seyyathāpi manussāti manussānaṃ hi kālena sukhaṃ hoti, kālena dukkhaṃ. Ekacce ca devāti kāmāvacaradevā. Tesampi kālena sukhaṃ hoti, kālena dukkhaṃ. Tesaṃ hi hīnatarānaṃ mahesakkhatarā devatā disvā āsanā vuṭṭhātabbaṃ hoti, maggā ukkamitabbaṃ, pārutavatthaṃ apanetabbaṃ, añjalikammaṃ kātabbanti taṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ nāma hoti. Ekacce ca vinipātikāti vemānikapetā. Te hi kālena sampattiṃ anubhavanti kālena kammanti vokiṇṇasukhadukkhāva honti. Iti imasmiṃ sutte tīṇi sucaritāni lokiyalokuttaramissakāni kathitānīti veditabbāni.

‘Mixed with pleasure and pain’ means mingled pleasure and pain. As for ‘Just as among humans’: for humans, at times there is pleasure, at times there is pain. ‘And some devas’ means the sense-sphere devas. For them too, at times there is pleasure, at times there is pain. For indeed, the inferior among them, having seen more powerful deities, must rise from their seats, step aside from the path, remove their worn robe, and perform the gesture of reverence; all of that is called suffering. ‘And some who have fallen into a woeful state’ means the petas with mansions. Indeed, they at times experience prosperity and at times [the result of their] unwholesome kamma; thus, they are indeed ones with mixed pleasure and pain. Thus, it should be understood that in this sutta, three kinds of good conduct, which are a mixture of worldly and supramundane, have been explained.

4. Bahukārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bahukāra Sutta

24. Catutthe [M 2.0091] tayome, bhikkhave, puggalāti tayo ācariyapuggalā. Puggalassa [P 2.0194] bahukārāti antevāsikapuggalassa bahūpakārā. Buddhanti sabbaññubuddhaṃ. Saraṇaṃ gato hotīti avassayaṃ [V 2.0093] gato hoti. Dhammanti satantikaṃ navalokuttaradhammaṃ. Saṅghanti aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūhaṃ. Idañca pana saraṇagamanaṃ aggahitasaraṇapubbassa akatābhinivesassa vasena vuttaṃ. Iti imasmiṃ sutte saraṇadāyako sotāpattimaggasampāpako arahattamaggasampāpakoti tayo ācariyā bahukārāti āgatā, pabbajjādāyako buddhavacanadāyako kammavācācariyo sakadāgāmimaggasampāpako anāgāmimaggasampāpakoti ime ācariyā na āgatā, kiṃ ete na bahukārāti? No, na bahukārā. Ayaṃ pana desanā duvidhena paricchinnā. Tasmā sabbepete bahukārā. Tesu saraṇagamanasmiṃyeva akatābhiniveso vaṭṭati, catupārisuddhisīlakasiṇaparikammavipassanāñāṇāni pana paṭhamamaggasannissitāni honti, upari dve maggā ca phalāni ca arahattamaggasannissitānīti veditabbāni.

24. In the fourth [discourse], ‘these three persons, bhikkhus’ means three types of teachers. ‘They greatly benefit a person’ means they are of great benefit to a resident disciple. ‘The Buddha’ refers to the Omniscient Buddha. ‘He has gone for refuge’ means he has gone for reliance. ‘The Dhamma’ refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with the textual tradition. ‘The Saṅgha’ refers to the assembly of the eight noble individuals. This going for refuge, however, is spoken of in terms of one who has not previously taken refuge and has not made a firm commitment. Thus, in this sutta, it is stated that three teachers are of great benefit: the one who gives the refuges, the one who leads to the path of stream-entry, and the one who leads to the path of arahantship. The teacher who gives the going forth, the teacher who gives the Buddha's word, the teacher of the formal act, the one who leads to the path of the once-returner, and the one who leads to the path of the non-returner—these teachers are not mentioned. Are they not of great benefit? It is not that they are not of great benefit. This teaching, however, is delimited in two ways. Therefore, all of them are of great benefit. Among these, it is only in the case of going for refuge that it applies to one who has not made a firm commitment. The fourfold purity of virtue, the preparatory work of the kasiṇa, and insight knowledge, however, are dependent on the first path. The two higher paths and fruits should be understood as dependent on the path of arahantship.

Iminā puggalenāti iminā antevāsikapuggalena. Na suppatikāraṃ vadāmīti patikāraṃ kātuṃ na sukaranti vadāmi. Abhivādanādīsu anekasatavāraṃ anekasahassavārampi hi pañcapatiṭṭhitena nipatitvā vandanto āsanā vuṭṭhāya paccuggacchanto diṭṭhadiṭṭhakkhaṇe añjaliṃ paggaṇhanto anucchavikaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ karonto divase divase cīvarasataṃ cīvarasahassaṃ piṇḍapātasataṃ piṇḍapātasahassaṃ dadamāno cakkavāḷapariyantena sabbaratanamayaṃ āvāsaṃ karonto sappinavanītādinānappakāraṃ bhesajjaṃ anuppadajjamāno neva sakkoti ācariyena katassa patikāraṃ nāma kātunti evamattho veditabbo.

‘By this person’ means by this resident disciple. ‘I do not say it is easy to repay’ means: I say it is not easy to make repayment. Indeed, a person is not able to make what is called a repayment for what has been done by the teacher, even if they were to pay homage by prostrating with the five-point prostration hundreds and thousands of times in acts such as paying homage; rise from their seat to go and meet them; raise their joined palms at every moment they see them; perform suitable acts of reverence; give day after day a hundred robes and a thousand robes, a hundred alms-bowls and a thousand alms-bowls; build a monastery made of all jewels with the Cakkavāḷa as its boundary; and provide various kinds of medicines such as ghee and fresh butter. This is the meaning that should be understood.

5. Vajirūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Vajirūpama Sutta

25. Pañcame arukūpamacittoti purāṇavaṇasadisacitto. Vijjūpamacittoti ittarakālobhāsanena vijjusadisacitto. Vajirūpamacittoti [P 2.0195] kilesānaṃ [M 2.0092] mūlaghātakaraṇasamatthatāya vajirena sadisacitto. Abhisajjatīti laggati. Kuppatīti kopavasena kuppati. Byāpajjatīti pakatibhāvaṃ pajahati, pūtiko hoti. Patitthīyatīti thinabhāvaṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ āpajjati. Kopanti dubbalakodhaṃ. Dosanti dussanavasena tato balavataraṃ. Appaccayanti atuṭṭhākāraṃ domanassaṃ. Duṭṭhārukoti purāṇavaṇo. Kaṭṭhenāti daṇḍakakoṭiyā. Kaṭhalenāti kapālena. Āsavaṃ detīti aparāparaṃ savati. Purāṇavaṇo hi attano dhammatāyeva pubbaṃ lohitaṃ yūsanti imāni tīṇi savati, ghaṭṭito pana tāni adhikataraṃ savati.

25. In the fifth: ‘a mind like a sore’ means a mind similar to an old wound. ‘A mind like lightning’ means a mind similar to lightning due to momentary shining. ‘A mind like a diamond’ means a mind similar to a diamond because of its ability to destroy the roots of defilements. ‘Abhisajjati’ means it clings through anger. ‘Kuppati’ means it is corrupted by the power of anger. ‘Byāpajjati’ means it abandons its natural state and becomes putrid. ‘Patitthīyati’ means it attains a state of firmness and rigidity. ‘Kopa’ means weak anger. ‘Dosa’ means stronger anger due to resentment. ‘Appaccaya’ means displeasure and discontent. ‘Duṭṭhāruka’ means an old wound. ‘Kaṭṭhena’ means with the tip of a stick. ‘Kaṭhalena’ means with a potsherd. ‘Āsavaṃ deti’ means it oozes again and again. Indeed, an old wound by its very nature oozes these three things—pus, blood, and serum; but when struck, it oozes them even more.

Evameva [V 2.0094] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – duṭṭhāruko viya hi kodhanapuggalo, tassa attano dhammatāya savanaṃ viya kodhanassapi attano dhammatāya uddhumātassa viya caṇḍikatassa caraṇaṃ, kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā ghaṭṭanaṃ viya appamattaṃ vacanaṃ, bhiyyosomattāya savanaṃ viya “mādisaṃ nāma esa evaṃ vadatī”ti bhiyyosomattāya uddhumāyanabhāvo daṭṭhabbo.

Even so, here is the connection of the simile: The angry person is like a festering sore. Just as its natural oozing, so too is the angry person's natural swelling and violent behavior. Just as the striking with a stick or potsherd, so too is a trifling word. And just as the increased oozing, so too should the increased swelling be understood, due to the thought, ‘This person speaks to one such as me in this way!’

Rattandhakāratimisāyanti rattiṃ cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇena andhabhāvakaraṇe bahalatame. Vijjantarikāyāti vijjuppattikkhaṇe. Idhāpi idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – cakkhumā puriso viya hi yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo, andhakāraṃ viya sotāpattimaggavajjhā kilesā, vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya sotāpattimaggañāṇassa uppattikālo, vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa samantā rūpadassanaṃ viya [P 2.0196] sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ, puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggavajjhā kilesā, puna vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggañāṇassa uppādo, vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa samantā rūpadassanaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ, puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya anāgāmimaggavajjhā kilesā, puna vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya anāgāmimaggañāṇassa uppādo, vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa samantā rūpadassanaṃ viya anāgāmimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

“In the thick, gloomy darkness of night” means in the thickest darkness at night, which prevents the arising of eye-consciousness, thus causing a state of darkness. “In the interval of lightning” means at the moment of a lightning flash. Here too, this is the connection of the simile: a meditator should be regarded as being like a person with eyesight. The defilements to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry should be regarded as being like the darkness. The time of the arising of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry should be regarded as being like the flashing of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the path of stream-entry should be regarded as being like the seeing of forms all around by a person with eyesight in the interval of lightning. Again, the defilements to be abandoned by the path of once-returning should be regarded as being like the covering of darkness. Again, the arising of the knowledge of the path of once-returning should be regarded as being like the flashing of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the path of once-returning should be known as being like the seeing of forms all around by a person with eyesight in the interval of lightning. Again, the defilements to be abandoned by the path of non-returning should be regarded as being like the covering of darkness. Again, the arising of the knowledge of the path of non-returning should be known as being like the flashing of lightning. The seeing of Nibbāna at the moment of the path of non-returning should be known as being like the seeing of forms all around by a person with eyesight in the interval of lightning.

Vajirūpamacittatāyapi [M 2.0093] idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – vajiraṃ viya hi arahattamaggañāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, maṇigaṇṭhipāsāṇagaṇṭhi viya arahattamaggavajjhā kilesā, vajirassa maṇigaṇṭhimpi vā pāsāṇagaṇṭhimpi vā vinivijjhitvā agamanabhāvassa natthitā viya arahattamaggañāṇena acchejjānaṃ kilesānaṃ natthibhāvo, vajirena nibbiddhavedhassa puna apatipūraṇaṃ viya arahattamaggena chinnānaṃ kilesānaṃ puna anuppādo daṭṭhabboti.

Regarding the person with a diamond-like mind also, this is the connection of the simile: The knowledge of the path of arahantship should be seen as like a diamond. The defilements to be destroyed by the path of arahantship should be seen as like a lump of gems or a lump of stone. Just as there is no such thing as a diamond not passing through after piercing a lump of gems or a lump of stone, so it should be understood that there are no defilements that are not destroyed by the knowledge of the path of arahantship. Just as a hole pierced by a diamond is not filled again, so the non-arising again of the defilements cut off by the path of arahantship should be understood.

6. Sevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sevitabba Sutta

26. Chaṭṭhe sevitabboti upasaṅkamitabbo. Bhajitabboti allīyitabbo. Payirupāsitabboti santike nisīdanavasena punappunaṃ upāsitabbo. Sakkatvā garuṃ katvāti sakkārañceva garukārañca katvā. Hīno hoti sīlenātiādīsu upādāyupādāya hīnatā veditabbā. Tattha yo hi pañca sīlāni rakkhati, so dasa sīlāni rakkhantena na sevitabbo[V 2.0095]. Yo dasa sīlāni rakkhati, so catupārisuddhisīlaṃ rakkhantena na sevitabbo. Aññatra anuddayā aññatra anukampāti ṭhapetvā anuddayañca anukampañca. Attano atthāyeva hi evarūpo puggalo na sevitabbo, anuddayānukampāvasena pana taṃ upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati.

26. In the sixth sutta, 'to be associated with' (sevitabbo) means 'to be approached' (upasaṅkamitabbo). 'To be frequented' (bhajitabboti) means 'to be intimate with' (allīyitabbo). 'To be attended upon' (payirupāsitabboti) means 'to be repeatedly served by sitting nearby'. 'Having respected and revered' (sakkatvā garuṃ katvā) means 'having shown both respect and reverence'. In phrases such as 'he is inferior in virtue,' inferiority is to be known by considering each case. Herein, one who keeps the five precepts should not be associated with by one who keeps the ten precepts; one who keeps the ten precepts should not be associated with by one who keeps the virtue of fourfold purity. 'Except for sympathy, except for compassion' means 'setting aside sympathy and compassion'. Indeed, for one's own benefit, such a person should not be associated with, but by way of sympathy and compassion, it is proper to approach them.

Sīlasāmaññagatānaṃ satanti sīlena samānabhāvaṃ gatānaṃ santānaṃ. Sīlakathā [P 2.0197] ca no bhavissatīti evaṃ samānasīlānaṃ amhākaṃ sīlameva ārabbha kathā bhavissati. Sā ca no pavattinī bhavissatīti sā ca amhākaṃ kathā divasampi kathentānaṃ pavattissati na paṭihaññissati. Sā ca no phāsu bhavissatīti sā ca divasampi pavattamānā sīlakathā amhākaṃ phāsuvihāro sukhavihāro bhavissati. Samādhipaññākathāsupi eseva nayo.

‘Of good people who have attained sameness in virtue’ means of good people who have reached a state of sameness with respect to virtue. ‘And there will be talk of virtue for us’ means that for us who are of similar virtue, a talk concerning virtue itself will arise. ‘And it will be continuous for us’ means that our talk will proceed and not be obstructed, even if we speak all day. ‘And it will be comfortable for us’ means that this talk on virtue, proceeding even for a whole day, will be for us a comfortable abiding, a pleasant abiding. This same method applies to talks on concentration and wisdom.

Sīlakkhandhanti sīlarāsiṃ. Tattha tattha paññāya anuggahessāmīti ettha sīlassa asappāye anupakāradhamme vajjetvā sappāye upakāradhamme sevanto tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlakkhandhaṃ paññāya anuggaṇhāti nāma. Samādhipaññākkhandhesupi eseva nayo. Nihīyatīti attano hīnataraṃ puggalaṃ sevanto khāraparissāvane āsittaudakaṃ viya satataṃ samitaṃ hāyati parihāyati. Tulyasevīti attanā samānasevī. Seṭṭhamupanamanti seṭṭhaṃ [M 2.0094] puggalaṃ oṇamanto. Udeti khippanti khippameva vaḍḍhati. Tasmā attano uttariṃ bhajethāti yasmā seṭṭhaṃ puggalaṃ upanamanto udeti khippaṃ, tasmā attano uttaritaraṃ visiṭṭhataraṃ bhajetha.

‘The aggregate of virtue’ refers to the mass of virtue. In this passage, ‘I will support it with wisdom here and there,’ it means that by avoiding qualities unsuitable and unbeneficial to virtue and cultivating qualities that are suitable and beneficial, one thereby supports the aggregate of virtue with wisdom in each and every instance. The same principle applies to the aggregates of concentration and wisdom. ‘One declines’ means that by associating with a person inferior to oneself, one constantly and continually diminishes and deteriorates, like water poured into a salt-filtering vessel. ‘Associating with an equal’ means associating with someone equal to oneself. ‘Approaching the superior’ means bowing down to a superior person. ‘One rises quickly’ means one grows swiftly. Therefore, ‘one should associate with one better than oneself’ means that since one who approaches a superior person rises quickly, one should associate with one even more excellent and distinguished than oneself.

7. Jigucchitabbasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Jigucchitabba Sutta

27. Sattame jigucchitabboti gūthaṃ viya jigucchitabbo. Atha kho nanti atha kho assa. Kittisaddoti kathāsaddo. Evameva khoti ettha gūthakūpo viya dussīlyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gūthakūpe patitvā ṭhito dhammaniahi viya dussīlapuggalo. Gūthakūpato uddhariyamānena tena ahinā purisassa sarīraṃ āruḷhenāpi adaṭṭhabhāvo viya dussīlaṃ sevamānassāpi tassa kiriyāya akaraṇabhāvo. Sarīraṃ gūthena makkhetvā [P 2.0198] ahinā gatakālo viya dussīlaṃ sevamānassa pāpakittisaddaabbhuggamanakālo veditabbo.

27. In the seventh discourse, 'one should be disgusted with' means one should be disgusted as with feces. 'Atha kho naṃ' means 'atha kho assa'. 'The sound of reputation' refers to the sound of talk. In this passage, 'Just so indeed,' unvirtuousness should be seen as like a cesspool. An unvirtuous person should be seen as like a dhamani snake standing, having fallen into a cesspool. Just as there is the state of not being bitten by that snake that has climbed onto a person's body while being pulled out of a cesspool, so too should be seen the state of not performing the actions of that unvirtuous person, even while associating with them. The time when a bad reputation arises for one who associates with an unvirtuous person should be understood to be like the time of seizing a snake after smearing one's body with feces.

Tindukālātanti tindukarukkhaalātaṃ. Bhiyyosomattāya cicciṭāyatīti taṃ hi jhāyamānaṃ pakatiyāpi [V 2.0096] papaṭikāyo muñcantaṃ cicciṭāti “ciṭiciṭā”ti saddaṃ karoti, ghaṭṭitaṃ pana adhimattaṃ karotīti attho. Evameva khoti evamevaṃ kodhano attano dhammatāyapi uddhato caṇḍikato hutvā carati, appamattakaṃ pana vacanaṃ sutakāle “mādisaṃ nāma evaṃ vadati evaṃ vadatī”ti atirekataraṃ uddhato caṇḍikato hutvā carati. Gūthakūpoti gūthapuṇṇakūpo, gūtharāsiyeva vā. Opammasaṃsandanaṃ panettha purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tasmā evarūpo puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabboti yasmā kodhano atiseviyamāno atiupasaṅkamiyamānopi kujjhatiyeva, “kiṃ iminā”ti paṭikkamantepi kujjhatiyeva. Tasmā palālaggi viya ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo hi palālaggiṃ atiupasaṅkamitvā tappati, tassa sarīraṃ jhāyati. Yo atipaṭikkamitvā tappati, tassa sītaṃ na vūpasammati. Anupasaṅkamitvā apaṭikkamitvā pana majjhattabhāvena tappantassa sītaṃ vūpasammati, tasmā palālaggi viya kodhano puggalo majjhattabhāvena [M 2.0095] ajjhupekkhitabbo, na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.

‘Tindukālāta’ means a firebrand of tinduka wood. ‘It crackles excessively’ means that when burning, that firebrand, even by its nature, releases sparks and makes a ‘ciṭiciṭā’ sound; but when struck, it makes an even more excessive sound—this is the meaning. ‘Just so’ means that in the same way, an irascible person, even by their own nature, behaves arrogantly and fiercely. But upon hearing even a slight word, thinking, ‘They speak thus to one such as I, they speak thus,’ they act with even greater arrogance and ferocity. ‘Gūthakūpa’ means a pit full of excrement, or just a heap of excrement. The connection of the simile here should be understood in the same way as before. Therefore, ‘such a person should be regarded with indifference, not associated with’ means that because an irascible person gets angry when excessively associated with or excessively approached, and also gets angry when one withdraws thinking, ‘What is the use of this person?’ Therefore, like a straw fire, they should be regarded with indifference—not associated with, not befriended. What is meant? For whoever warms themselves by approaching a straw fire too closely, their body is burned. For whoever warms themselves by withdrawing too far, the cold is not allayed. But for one who warms themselves with a neutral attitude, neither approaching nor withdrawing, the cold subsides. Therefore, like a straw fire, an irascible person should be regarded with equanimity from a neutral position; not associated with, not befriended, not attended upon.

Kalyāṇamittoti sucimitto. Kalyāṇasahāyoti sucisahāyo. Sahāyā nāma sahagāmino saddhiṃcarā. Kalyāṇasampavaṅkoti kalyāṇesu sucipuggalesu sampavaṅko, tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāramānasoti attho.

‘A good friend’ means a pure friend. ‘A good companion’ means a pure companion. Companions are those who go together, those who associate together. ‘Inclination towards the good’ means being inclined towards good, pure individuals, having a mind that inclines towards, slopes towards, and tends towards them—this is the meaning.

8. Gūthabhāṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Gūthabhāṇī Sutta

28. Aṭṭhame gūthabhāṇīti yo gūthaṃ viya duggandhakathaṃ katheti. Pupphabhāṇīti [P 2.0199] yo pupphāni viya sugandhakathaṃ katheti. Madhubhāṇīti yo madhu viya madhurakathaṃ katheti. Sabhaggatoti sabhāya ṭhito. Parisaggatoti gāmaparisāya ṭhito. Ñātimajjhagatoti ñātīnaṃ majjhe ṭhito. Pūgamajjhagatoti seṇīnaṃ majjhe ṭhito. Rājakulamajjhagatoti rājakulassa majjhe mahāvinicchaye ṭhito. Abhinītoti pucchanatthāyānīto. Sakkhipuṭṭhoti sakkhiṃ katvā pucchito. Ehambho purisāti ālapanametaṃ. Attahetu vā parahetu vāti attano vā parassa vā hatthapādādihetu vā dhanahetu vā. Āmisakiñcikkhahetu vāti ettha āmisanti lañjo adhippeto. Kiñcikkhanti yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattakaṃ antamaso tittiriyavaṭṭakasappipiṇḍanavanītapiṇḍādimattakassa lañjassa hetūti attho. Sampajānamusā bhāsitā hotīti jānantoyeva musāvādaṃ kattā hoti.

28. In the eighth sutta, 'one who speaks filth' (gūthabhāṇī) means a person who speaks speech that is foul-smelling like excrement. 'One who speaks of flowers' (puppabhāṇī) means a person who speaks speech that is fragrant like flowers. 'One who speaks of honey' (madhubhāṇī) means a person who speaks speech that is sweet like honey. 'Gone to an assembly' (sabhaggato) means standing in an assembly. 'Gone to a gathering' (parisaggato) means standing in a village gathering. 'Gone into the midst of relatives' (ñātimajjhagato) means standing in the midst of relatives. 'Gone into the midst of a guild' (pūgamajjhagato) means standing in the midst of a guild of perfumers. 'Gone into the midst of a royal family' (rājakulamajjhagato) means standing in the midst of a royal family during a great judgment. 'Brought forward' (abhinīto) means brought for the purpose of questioning. 'Questioned as a witness' (sakkhipuṭṭho) means questioned after being made a witness. 'Hey, man!' (ehambho purisa) is a term of address. 'For one's own sake or for another's sake' (attahetu vā parahetu vā) means for one's own sake, or for another's sake, or for the sake of wealth. 'For the sake of some material trifle' (āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā): Herein, by 'āmisa', gain is intended. By 'kiñcikkha' is meant any insignificant gain whatsoever. The meaning is: for the sake of a gain at least as small as a partridge, a quail, a lump of ghee, or a lump of fresh butter. 'A falsehood is spoken with full awareness' (sampajānamusā bhāsitā hoti) means one knowingly becomes a speaker of falsehood.

Nelāti [V 2.0097] elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssa elanti nelā, niddosāti attho. “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti (udā. 65) ettha vuttasīlaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati appaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī. Pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī. Purassa esāti nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino [P 2.0200] hi yuttakathā honti[M 2.0096], pitimattaṃ pitāti, mātimattaṃ mātāti, bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuddhikarāti bahujanamanāpā.

Regarding `nelā`: a fault (`doso`) is called `elaṃ`. Because for this there is no `elaṃ`, it is `nelā`; the meaning is 'faultless'. This is like the virtue spoken of in the passage, 'Flawless, with a white covering' (`Nelaṅgo setapacchādo`). Regarding `kaṇṇasukhā` (pleasing to the ear): due to the sweetness of the expression, it is pleasant to the ears; it does not cause an ear-spike, like being pierced by a needle. Due to the sweetness of the meaning, it does not generate anger in the whole body but generates affection; thus, it is `pemanīyā` (endearing). It goes to the heart (`hadayaṃ gacchati`); unobstructed, it enters the mind with ease; thus, it is `hadayaṅgamā` (reaching the heart). Due to the completeness of its qualities, it is fit to be in a city (`pure`); thus, it is `porī` (urbane). It is also `porī` because it is very delicate, like a woman raised in a city. It is also `porī` as in `purassa esā` (this is of the city), which means it is the speech of city-dwellers. Indeed, city-dwellers have suitable speech; they call one who is like a father, 'father'; one who is like a mother, 'mother'; and one who is like a brother, 'brother'. Such speech is beloved by many people; thus, it is `bahujanakantā` (beloved by the multitude). Precisely because it is beloved, it is pleasing to many people and causes the mind to grow; thus, it is `bahujanamanāpā` (pleasing to the multitude).

9. Andhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Andha Sutta

29. Navame cakkhu na hotīti paññācakkhu na hoti. Phātiṃ kareyyāti phītaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ kareyya. Sāvajjānavajjeti sadosaniddose. Hīnappaṇīteti adhamuttame. Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgeti kaṇhasukkāyeva aññamaññaṃ paṭibāhanato paṭipakkhavasena sappaṭibhāgāti vuccanti. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – kusale dhamme “kusalā dhammā”ti jāneyya, akusale dhamme “akusalā dhammā”ti jāneyya. Sāvajjādīsupi eseva nayo. Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgesu pana kaṇhadhamme “sukkasappaṭibhāgā”ti jāneyya, sukkadhamme “kaṇhasappaṭibhāgā”ti yena paññācakkhunā jāneyya, tathārūpampissa cakkhu na hotīti. Iminā nayena sesavāresupi attho veditabbo.

29. In the ninth sutta, `cakkhu na hoti` (there is no eye) means there is no wisdom-eye. `Phātiṃ kareyya` (may he make it prosper) means one should make it prosperous and developed. `Sāvajjānavajje` refers to things with fault and without fault. `Hīnappaṇīte` refers to the inferior and the superior.
