Regarding `kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge` (having black and white counterparts): they are called `sappaṭibhāgā` (having counterparts) because the black and white themselves obstruct each other, by way of being opposites. Here, this is the summary: one should know wholesome states as 'wholesome states,' and one should know unwholesome states as 'unwholesome states.' This same method applies to things with fault, and so on. However, regarding states with black and white counterparts: the wisdom-eye by which one would know black states as 'states with a white counterpart' and white states as 'states with a black counterpart'—even such an eye that person does not possess. By this method, the meaning in the remaining instances should also be understood.

Na ceva bhogā tathārūpāti tathājātikā bhogāpissa na honti. Na ca puññāni kubbatīti puññāni ca na karoti. Ettāvatā bhoguppādanacakkhuno ca puññakaraṇacakkhuno ca abhāvo vutto. Ubhayattha kaliggāhoti idhaloke ca paraloke cāti ubhayasmimpi aparaddhaggāho, parājayaggāho hotīti attho. Atha vā ubhayattha kaliggāhoti ubhayesampi diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ atthānaṃ kaliggāho, parājayaggāhoti attho. Dhammādhammenāti dasakusalakammapathadhammenapi dasaakusalakammapathaadhammenapi. Saṭhoti kerāṭiko. Bhogāni pariyesatīti bhoge gavesati. Theyyena [P 2.0201] kūṭakammena, musāvādena cūbhayanti theyyādīsu ubhayena pariyesatīti attho. Kathaṃ? Theyyena kūṭakammena ca pariyesati, theyyena musāvādena ca pariyesati[V 2.0098], kūṭakammena musāvādena ca pariyesati. Saṅghātunti saṅgharituṃ. Dhammaladdhehīti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ akopetvā laddhehi. Uṭṭhānādhigatanti vīriyena [M 2.0097] adhigataṃ. Abyagghamānasoti nibbicikicchacitto. Bhaddakaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṃ devaṭṭhānaṃ. Na socatīti yasmiṃ ṭhāne antosokena na socati.

‘Nor are there possessions of such a kind’ (na ceva bhogā tathārūpāti) means possessions of such a nature do not exist for him. ‘Nor does he perform merits’ (na ca puññāni kubbatīti) means he does not perform merits. By this much, the absence of the eye for producing possessions and the eye for performing merits is stated. ‘He grasps what is faulty in both respects’ (ubhayattha kaliggāhoti) means in both this world and the next, he grasps what is faulty, he grasps defeat; this is the meaning. Alternatively, ‘he grasps what is faulty in both respects’ means he grasps what is faulty, he grasps defeat, regarding the benefits pertaining to both the present life and the future life; this is the meaning. ‘By what is righteous and unrighteous’ (dhammādhammenāti) means by both the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of kamma and the Adhamma of the ten unwholesome courses of kamma. ‘Deceitful’ (saṭhoti) means fraudulent. ‘He seeks riches’ (bhogāni pariyesatīti) means he searches for wealth. ‘By theft, by fraudulent action, and by false speech—by a combination of two’ (theyyena kūṭakammena, musāvādena cūbhayanti) means he seeks by a combination of two among theft and so on; this is the meaning. How so? He seeks by theft and by fraudulent action; he seeks by theft and by false speech; and he seeks by fraudulent action and by false speech. ‘To accumulate’ (saṅghātunti) means to gather. ‘Righteously gained’ (dhammaladdhehīti) means obtained without violating the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of kamma. ‘Acquired by exertion’ (uṭṭhānādhigatanti) means acquired through effort. ‘With an unagitated mind’ (abyagghamānasoti) means with a mind free from doubt. ‘A fortunate state’ (bhaddakaṃ ṭhānanti) means the best place, the celestial realm. ‘He does not grieve’ (na socatīti) means in that place, he does not grieve with inward sorrow.

10. Avakujjasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Avakujjasutta

30. Dasame avakujjapaññoti adhomukhapañño. Ucchaṅgapaññoti ucchaṅgasadisapañño. Puthupaññoti vitthārikapañño. Ādikalyāṇantiādīsu ādīti pubbapaṭṭhapanā. Majjhanti kathāvemajjhaṃ. Pariyosānanti sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Itissa te dhammaṃ kathentā pubbapaṭṭhapanepi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā kathenti, vemajjhepi pariyosānepi. Ettha ca atthi desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānāni, atthi sāsanassa. Tattha desanāya tāva catuppadikagāthāya paṭhamapadaṃ ādi, dve padāni majjhaṃ, avasānapadaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Ekānusandhikassa suttassa nidānaṃ ādi, anusandhi majjhaṃ, idamavocāti appanā pariyosānaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa paṭhamo anusandhi ādi, tato paraṃ eko vā aneke vā majjhaṃ, pacchimo pariyosānaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva desanāya nayo. Sāsanassa pana sīlaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhaṃ, vipassanā pariyosānaṃ. Samādhi vā ādi, vipassanā majjhaṃ, maggo pariyosānaṃ. Vipassanā vā ādi, maggo majjhaṃ, phalaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Maggo vā ādi, phalaṃ majjhaṃ, nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Dve dve vā kayiramāne sīlasamādhayo ādi, vipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ.

30. In the tenth sutta, `avakujjapañño` means a person with downward-turned wisdom. `Ucchaṅgapañño` means a person with wisdom like a treasure carried in the lap. `Puthupañño` means a person with expansive wisdom. Regarding “excellent in the beginning” and so on, “beginning” means the initial setting forth. “Middle” means the middle of the discourse. “Conclusion” means the completion. Thus, when they teach the Dhamma to that person, they teach it having made it good, excellent, and blameless in the initial setting forth, in the middle, and in the conclusion. And in this regard, there is a beginning, middle, and conclusion for the teaching, and there is for the dispensation. Among these, regarding the teaching, firstly: in a four-lined verse, the first line is the beginning, the two lines are the middle, and the final line is the conclusion. In a discourse with a single connection, the introduction is the beginning, the connection is the middle, and the concluding summation “idam avoca” is the conclusion. In a discourse with multiple connections, the first connection is the beginning, one or more that follow are the middle, and the last is the conclusion. This, firstly, is the method regarding the teaching. As for the dispensation: virtue is the beginning, concentration is the middle, and insight is the conclusion. Or, concentration is the beginning, insight is the middle, and the path is the conclusion. Or, insight is the beginning, the path is the middle, and the fruit is the conclusion. Or, the path is the beginning, the fruit is the middle, and Nibbāna is the conclusion. Or, when taken in pairs, virtue and concentration are the beginning, insight and the path are the middle, and the fruit and Nibbāna are the conclusion.

Sātthanti [P 2.0202] sātthakaṃ katvā desenti. Sabyañjananti akkharapāripūriṃ katvā desenti. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti sakalaparipuṇṇaṃ anūnaṃ katvā desenti. Parisuddhanti parisuddhaṃ nijjaṭaṃ niggaṇṭhiṃ katvā desenti. Brahmacariyaṃ pakāsentīti evaṃ desentā ca seṭṭhacariyabhūtaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ pakāsenti. Neva ādiṃ manasi karotīti neva pubbapaṭṭhapanaṃ manasi karoti.

`With meaning` means they teach having made it meaningful. `With the phrasing` means they teach having made the wording complete with all its syllables. `Entirely complete` means they teach having made it entirely complete and without deficiency. `Pure` means they teach having made it pure, free from entanglements and knots. `They make known the holy life` means that by teaching thus, they make known the noble eightfold path, which is the supreme course of conduct, comprised of the threefold training. `He does not attend to the beginning` means he does not attend to the initial setting forth.

Kumbhoti ghaṭo. Nikujjoti adhomukho ṭhapito. Evameva khoti ettha kumbho nikujjo viya avakujjapañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo, udakāsiñcanakālo [M 2.0098] viya dhammadesanāya laddhakālo, udakassa [V 2.0099] vivaṭṭanakālo viya tasmiṃ āsane nisinnassa uggahetuṃ asamatthakālo, udakassa asaṇṭhānakālo viya vuṭṭhahitvā asallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo.

A pot means a jar. 'Overturned' means placed face down. In this very way, a person with downward-turned wisdom should be understood as being like an overturned pot. The time when the Dhamma teaching is received should be known as being like the time of pouring water; the time when a person sitting in that seat is unable to learn should be known as being like the time when water flows away; the time of being unable to remember after having risen should be known as being like the time when water does not stay.

Ākiṇṇānīti pakkhittāni. Satisammosāya pakireyyāti muṭṭhassatitāya vikireyya. Evameva khoti ettha ucchaṅgo viya ucchaṅgapañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo, nānākhajjakāni viya nānappakāraṃ buddhavacanaṃ, ucchaṅge nānākhajjakāni khādantassa nisinnakālo viya tasmiṃ āsane nisinnassa uggaṇhanakālo, vuṭṭhahantassa satisammosā pakiraṇakālo viya tasmā āsanā vuṭṭhāya gacchantassa asallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo.

'Filled' means placed in. 'One might scatter due to lapsed mindfulness' means one might scatter due to forgetfulness. In this very way, a person with lap-like wisdom should be understood as being like a lap; the diverse word of the Buddha should be known as being like various kinds of food. The time of learning for a person sitting in that seat should be known as being like the time of sitting for one eating various foods in their lap; the time of being unable to remember for a person who, having risen from that seat, is leaving, should be known as being like the time of scattering due to lapsed mindfulness for one who is rising.

Ukkujjoti uparimukho ṭhapito. Saṇṭhātīti patiṭṭhahati. Evameva khoti ettha uparimukho ṭhapito kumbho viya puthupañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo, udakassa āsittakālo viya desanāya [P 2.0203] laddhakālo, udakassa saṇṭhānakālo viya tattha nisinnassa uggaṇhanakālo, no vivaṭṭanakālo viya vuṭṭhāya gacchantassa sallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo.

'Set upright' means placed face up. 'It stays' means it is established. In this very way, a person with broad wisdom should be understood as being like a pot placed face up. The time when the teaching is received should be understood as being like the time when water is poured in; the time of learning for a person sitting there should be understood as being like the time when water settles; the time of being able to remember for a person who, having risen, is leaving, should be known as being like the time when it does not flow away.

Dummedhoti nippañño. Avicakkhaṇoti saṃvidahanapaññāya rahito. Gantāti gamanasīlo. Seyyo etena vuccatīti etasmā puggalā uttaritaroti vuccati. Dhammānudhammappaṭipannoti navalokuttaradhammassa anudhammaṃ saha sīlena pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Antakaro siyāti koṭikaro paricchedakaro parivaṭumakaro bhaveyyāti.

'Of dull wisdom' means without wisdom. 'Undiscerning' means devoid of organizing wisdom. 'A goer' means one whose nature is to go. 'He is called superior to this one' means he is called more excellent than that person. 'One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma' means one who has entered upon the preliminary practice, which is the Dhamma conforming to the nine supramundane Dhammas, together with virtue. 'Of suffering' means of the suffering of the round of existence. 'He might be a maker of the end' means he might be a maker of the tip, a maker of the limit, a maker of the boundary.

Puggalavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on Persons.

4. Devadūtavaggo

4. The Chapter on the Divine Messengers

1. Sabrahmakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sabrahmaka Sutta

31. Catutthassa [V 2.0100] paṭhame ajjhāgāreti sake ghare. Pūjitā hontīti yaṃ ghare atthi, tena paṭijaggitā gopitā honti. Iti mātāpitupūjakāni kulāni mātāpitūhi sabrahmakānīti pakāsetvā idāni nesaṃ [M 2.0099] sapubbācariyakādibhāvaṃ pakāsento sapubbācariyakānītiādimāha. Tattha brahmātiādīni tesaṃ brahmādibhāvasādhanatthaṃ vuttāni. Bahukārāti puttānaṃ bahūpakārā. Āpādakāti jīvitassa āpādakā. Puttakānaṃ hi mātāpitūhi jīvitaṃ āpāditaṃ pālitaṃ ghaṭitaṃ anuppabandhena pavattitaṃ. Posakāti hatthapāde vaḍḍhetvā hadayalohitaṃ pāyetvā posetāro. Imassa lokassa dassetāroti puttānaṃ hi imasmiṃ loke iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇassa [P 2.0204] dassanaṃ nāma mātāpitaro nissāya jātanti imassa lokassa dassetāro nāma.

31. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, `ajjhāgāre` means 'in one's own home.' 'They are honored' means they are cared for and protected with whatever is available in the home. Thus, having shown that families who honor their parents are, through their parents, with Brahmā, now, wishing to show their state of being first teachers and so forth, he says the words beginning with `sapubbācariyakāni`. Therein, the words beginning with `brahmā` are spoken for the purpose of establishing their state of being Brahmā and so forth. `Bahukārā` means they are of great benefit to their children. `Āpādakā` means producers of life. For the life of children is brought into being, protected, fostered, and made to continue in sequence by their parents. `Posakā` means they are nourishers, having caused the hands and feet to develop and having caused them to drink the blood of the heart. `Imassa lokassa dassetāro` means that for children, the seeing of desirable and undesirable objects in this world arises in dependence on their parents; therefore, they are called 'showers of this world'.

Brahmāti mātāpitaroti seṭṭhādhivacanaṃ. Yathā brahmuno catasso bhāvanā avijahitā honti mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhāti, evameva mātāpitūnaṃ puttakesu catasso bhāvanā avijahitā honti. Tā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle veditabbā – kucchigatasmiṃ hi dārake “kadā nu kho puttakaṃ arogaṃ paripuṇṇaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ passissāmā”ti mātāpitūnaṃ mettacittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā panesa mando uttānaseyyako ūkāhi vā maṅkulādīhi pāṇakehi daṭṭho dukkhaseyyāya vā pana pīḷito parodati viravati, tadāssa saddaṃ sutvā mātāpitūnaṃ kāruññaṃ uppajjati, ādhāvitvā vidhāvitvā kīḷanakāle pana lobhanīyavayasmiṃ vā ṭhitakāle dārakaṃ oloketvā mātāpitūnaṃ cittaṃ sappimaṇḍe pakkhittasatavihatakappāsapicupaṭalaṃ viya mudukaṃ hoti āmoditaṃ pamoditaṃ, tadā tesaṃ muditā labbhati. Yadā panesa putto dārābharaṇaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā pāṭiyekkaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, tadā mātāpitūnaṃ “sakkoti dāni no puttako attano dhammatāya yāpetu”nti majjhattabhāvo uppajjati, tasmiṃ kāle upekkhā labbhatīti iminā kāraṇena “brahmāti mātāpitaro”ti vuttaṃ.

'Parents are Brahmā' is a designation of the highest. Just as for a Brahmā the four divine abidings are not abandoned—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—in just the same way, for parents, these four divine abidings towards their young children are not abandoned. These are to be understood at their respective times. For when a child is in the womb, a mind of loving-kindness arises in the parents, who think: 'When, indeed, will we see our young child, healthy and with complete major and minor limbs?' Then, when this child, being helpless and lying on his back, is bitten by lice or insects such as bedbugs, or is afflicted by uncomfortable lying, and he cries and wails, upon hearing his sound, compassion arises in the parents. Then, when looking at the young child running here and there, either at the time of playing or when at a charming age, the parents' minds become soft—like a layer of cotton wool, carded a hundred times and placed in ghee—delighted and overjoyed. At that time, sympathetic joy is obtained by them. Then, when this son, having taken on the maintenance of a wife, lives in a separate household, a state of neutrality arises in the parents, who think: 'Now our young son is able to live by his own means.' At that time, equanimity is obtained. For this reason, it is said, 'Parents are Brahmā.'

Pubbācariyāti [V 2.0101] vuccareti mātāpitaro hi jātakālato paṭṭhāya “evaṃ nisīda, evaṃ tiṭṭha, evaṃ gaccha, evaṃ saya, evaṃ khāda, evaṃ bhuñja, ayaṃ te, tātāti vattabbo, ayaṃ bhātikāti, ayaṃ bhaginīti, idaṃ nāma kātuṃ vaṭṭati, idaṃ na vaṭṭati, asukaṃ nāma upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati, asukaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti gāhāpenti sikkhāpenti. Athāparabhāge [P 2.0205] aññe ācariyā hatthisippaassasipparathasippadhanusippatharusippamuddāgaṇanādīni sikkhāpenti. Añño [M 2.0100] saraṇāni deti, añño sīlesu patiṭṭhāpeti, añño pabbājeti, añño buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhāpeti, añño upasampādeti, añño sotāpattimaggādīni pāpeti. Iti sabbepi te pacchācariyā nāma honti, mātāpitaro pana sabbapaṭhamā, tenāha – “pubbācariyāti vuccare”ti. Tattha vuccareti vuccanti kathiyanti. Āhuneyyā ca puttānanti puttānaṃ āhutaṃ pāhutaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ annapānādiṃ arahanti, anucchavikā taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ. Tasmā “āhuneyyā ca puttāna”nti vuttaṃ. Pajāya anukampakāti paresaṃ pāṇe acchinditvāpi attano pajaṃ paṭijagganti gopāyanti. Tasmā “pajāya anukampakā”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding the phrase 'They are called the first teachers': Indeed, from the time of birth, parents cause them to take up and train them, saying: 'Sit thus, stand thus, go thus, sleep thus, chew thus, eat thus. This is your father, this is your brother, this is your sister. It is proper to do such-and-such a thing; it is not proper. It is proper to approach such-and-such a person; it is not proper.' Then, later on, other teachers train them in the arts of the elephant, horse, chariot, bow, and sword; accounting, calculation, and so on. Another teacher gives the refuges, another establishes them in the precepts, another gives the going forth, another teaches the word of the Buddha, another confers the higher ordination, and another causes them to attain the path of stream-entry and so on. Thus, all of these are called 'later teachers', but parents are the very first. Therefore, He said: 'They are called the first teachers.' Therein, 'are called' means they are spoken of, they are said to be. 'And worthy of offerings from their children' means they are worthy of what is brought (`āhuta`), what is offered as a gift (`pāhuta`), and what is specially prepared (`abhisaṅkhata`), such as food and drink, from their children; they are fit to receive it. Therefore, it was said: 'And worthy of offerings from their children.' 'Compassionate toward their offspring' means that even by taking the lives of others, they tend to and protect their own offspring. Therefore, it was said: 'Compassionate toward their offspring.'

Namasseyyāti namo kareyya. Sakkareyyāti sakkārena paṭimāneyya. Idāni taṃ sakkāraṃ dassento “annenā”tiādimāha. Tattha annenāti yāgubhattakhādanīyena. Pānenāti aṭṭhavidhapānena. Vatthenāti nivāsanapārupanakena vatthena. Sayanenāti mañcapīṭhānuppadānena. Ucchādanenāti duggandhaṃ paṭivinodetvā sugandhakaraṇucchādanena. Nhāpanenāti sīte uṇhodakena, uṇhe sītodakena gattāni parisiñcitvā nhāpanena. Pādānaṃ dhovanenāti uṇhodakasītodakehi pādadhovanena ceva telamakkhanena ca. Peccāti paralokaṃ gantvā. Sagge pamodatīti idha tāva mātāpitūsu pāricariyaṃ disvā pāricariyakāraṇā taṃ paṇḍitamanussā idheva pasaṃsanti[P 2.0206], paralokaṃ pana gantvā sagge ṭhito so mātāpituupaṭṭhāko dibbasampattīhi āmodati pamodatīti.

'They should pay homage' means they should make obeisance. 'They should honor' means they should treat with respect. Now, to show that honor, he said, 'with food,' etc. Here, 'with food' means with rice-gruel, cooked rice, and edibles. 'With drink' means with the eight kinds of drink. 'With clothing' means with clothing for wearing and covering. 'With bedding' means providing couches and chairs. 'With ointment' means removing bad smells and applying fragrant ointment. 'With bathing' means cleansing the body by bathing with hot water in cold weather and cool water in hot weather. 'With washing the feet' means washing the feet with hot or cold water, and also anointing them with oil. 'Having passed away' means having gone to the other world. 'Rejoices in heaven' means that here, having seen the service to mother and father, wise people praise that person even in this very life on account of that service; but having gone to the other world and dwelling in heaven, that attendant of parents delights and rejoices with divine prosperity.

2. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

32. Dutiye tathārūpoti tathājātiko. Samādhipaṭilābhoti cittekaggatālābho. Imasmiṃ ca saviññāṇaketi ettha attano ca parassa cāti ubhayesampi kāyo saviññāṇakaṭṭhena ekato katvā imasminti vutto. Ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayāti ahaṅkāradiṭṭhi ca mamaṅkārataṇhā ca mānānusayo [V 2.0102] cāti attano ca parassa [M 2.0101] ca kilesā. Nāssūti na bhaveyyuṃ. Bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesūti rūpanimittaṃ, saddanimittaṃ, gandhanimittaṃ, rasanimittaṃ, phoṭṭhabbanimittaṃ, sassatādinimittaṃ, puggalanimittaṃ dhammanimittanti evarūpesu ca bahiddhā sabbanimittesu. Cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttinti phalasamādhiñceva phalañāṇañca. Siyāti bhaveyya.

32. In the second sutta, 'of such a kind' means 'of such a nature.' 'Attainment of concentration' means the attainment of one-pointedness of mind. And regarding 'in this conscious body,' here, having unified both one's own and another's body by virtue of their being conscious, the phrase 'in this' is used. 'The underlying tendencies of I-making, my-making, and conceit' means the defilements of oneself and another: the wrong view of 'I', the craving for 'mine', and the underlying tendency of conceit. 'They would not be' means they would not arise. And 'externally, in all signs' refers to signs of form, signs of sound, signs of smell, signs of taste, signs of touch, signs of eternalism and so on, signs of a person, and signs of phenomena—in all such external signs. 'Liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom' refers to fruition concentration and fruition knowledge. 'There would be' means there could be.

Idhānanda, bhikkhunoti, ānanda, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhuno. Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītanti nibbānaṃ dassento āha. Nibbānaṃ hi kilesānaṃ santatāya santaṃ nāma, nibbānaṃ santanti samāpattiṃ appetvāva divasampi nisinnassa cittuppādo santanteva pavattatītipi santaṃ. Paṇītanti samāpattiṃ appetvā nisinnassāpi cittuppādo paṇītanteva pavattatīti nibbānaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādīnipi tasseva vevacanāni. “Sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti samāpattiṃ appetvā nisinnassa hi divasabhāgampi cittuppādo sabbasaṅkhārasamathoteva pavattati…pe… tathā tīsu bhavesu vānasaṅkhātāya taṇhāya abhāvena nibbānanti laddhanāme tasmiṃ samāpattiṃ [P 2.0207] appetvā nisinnassa cittuppādo nibbānaṃ nibbānanteva pavattatīti sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādīni nāmāni labhati. Imasmiṃ pana aṭṭhavidhe ābhogasamannāhāre imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekopi labbhati, dvepi sabbepi labbhanteva.

'Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu,' means, Ānanda, for a bhikkhu in this Dispensation. Wishing to show Nibbāna by the text, 'This is peaceful, this is sublime,' He said. Indeed, Nibbāna is called 'peaceful' because of the peacefulness of the defilements. Nibbāna is peaceful—having entered into absorption, for one who is sitting even for a whole day, the arising of consciousness proceeds just as peaceful; for this reason also, it is 'peaceful'. 'Sublime'—for one who is sitting having entered into absorption, the arising of consciousness proceeds just as sublime; therefore, Nibbāna is called 'sublime'. The terms beginning with 'the stilling of all formations' are also synonyms for that very Nibbāna. Indeed, 'the stilling of all formations'—for one who is sitting having entered into absorption even for a part of the day, the arising of consciousness proceeds just as 'the stilling of all formations'... and so on... Similarly, in that which has obtained the name 'Nibbāna' due to the absence of craving, called 'vāna', in the three existences, for one who is sitting having entered into absorption, the arising of consciousness proceeds just as Nibbāna; therefore, it obtains names such as 'the stilling of all formations'. Furthermore, in this case of this eightfold directing of the mind, even one is obtained, two are obtained, and indeed all are obtained.

Saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena jānitvā. Paroparānīti parāni ca oparāni ca. Paraattabhāvasakaattabhāvāni hi parāni ca oparāni cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yassāti yassa arahato. Iñjitanti rāgiñjitaṃ dosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesaduccaritiñjitanti imāni satta iñjitāni calitāni phanditāni. Natthi kuhiñcīti katthaci ekārammaṇepi natthi. Santoti paccanīkakilesānaṃ santatāya santo. Vidhūmoti kāyaduccaritādidhūmavirahito. Anīghoti rāgādiīghavirahito. Nirāsoti nittaṇho. Atārīti tiṇṇo uttiṇṇo samatikkanto. Soti so arahaṃ khīṇāsavo. Jātijaranti ettha jātijarāgahaṇeneva byādhimaraṇampi gahitamevāti veditabbaṃ. Iti suttantepi gāthāyapi arahattaphalasamāpattiyeva kathitāti.

'Having comprehended' means having known by wisdom. 'Of others and of one's own' means both things pertaining to others and things pertaining to oneself. Indeed, the personal existences of others and one's own personal existence are called 'of others' and 'of one's own'; thus it is said. 'Of whom' means of which Arahant. 'Agitation' means the agitation of lust, and the agitation of hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, defilements, and misconduct—these seven agitations, stirrings, and tremblings. 'There is none anywhere' means there is none in any single object whatsoever. 'Peaceful' means peaceful due to the peacefulness of the opposing defilements. 'Smokeless' means free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and so forth. 'Untroubled' means free from the suffering of lust and so forth. 'Without hope' means without craving. 'Has crossed over' means has crossed, gone beyond, completely overcome. 'He' means that Arahant whose cankers are destroyed. 'Birth and aging'—here, by the taking up of 'birth and aging', sickness and death are also certainly included; thus it should be understood. Thus, in both the Sutta and the verse, only the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is spoken of.

3. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

33. Tatiye [M 2.0102] saṃkhittenāti mātikāṭhapanena. Vitthārenāti ṭhapitamātikāvibhajanena. Saṃkhittavitthārenāti [V 2.0103] kāle saṃkhittena kāle vitthārena. Aññātāro ca dullabhāti paṭivijjhanakapuggalā pana dullabhā. Idaṃ bhagavā “sāriputtattherassa ñāṇaṃ ghaṭṭemī”ti adhippāyena kathesi. Taṃ sutvā thero kiñcāpi “ahaṃ, bhante, ājānissāmī”ti na vadati, adhippāyena pana “vissatthā tumhe, bhante, desetha, ahaṃ tumhehi desitaṃ dhammaṃ nayasatena nayasahassena paṭivijjhissāmi, mamesa bhāro hotū”ti satthāraṃ desanāya ussāhento etassa bhagavā kālotiādimāha.

33. In the third sutta, 'in brief' means by the establishment of the mātikā. 'In detail' means by the analysis of the established mātikā. 'In brief and in detail' means at times in brief, at times in detail. 'And knowers are difficult to find' means: persons who have penetrated are difficult to find. The Blessed One spoke this with the intention, 'I shall test the knowledge of the Elder Sāriputta.' Hearing that, although the Elder did not say, 'Venerable Sir, I will understand,' he, encouraging the Teacher to teach, spoke the words beginning, 'Now is the time, O Blessed One,' with the intention: 'Venerable Sir, may you teach with confidence. I will penetrate the Dhamma taught by you by a hundred methods and by a thousand methods. Let this be my burden.'

Athassa satthā tasmātihāti desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha imasmiñca saviññāṇaketiādi vuttanayameva. Acchecchi [P 2.0208] taṇhanti maggañāṇasatthena taṇhaṃ chindi. Vivattayi saṃyojananti dasavidhampi saṃyojanaṃ samūlakaṃ ubbattetvā chaḍḍesi. Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassāti sammā upāyena sammā paṭipattiyā navavidhassa mānassa pahānābhisamayena vaṭṭadukkhassa antamakāsi. Idañca pana metaṃ, sāriputta, sandhāya bhāsitanti, sāriputta, mayā pārāyane udayapañhe idaṃ phalasamāpattimeva sandhāya etaṃ bhāsitaṃ.

Then the Teacher began the teaching to him with the words, 'Therefore...' Herein, the passage beginning 'imasmiñca saviññāṇake' is just according to the method already stated. 'He cut off craving' means: he cut off craving with the weapon of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. 'He turned away from the fetter' means: he uprooted and abandoned the tenfold fetter together with its root. 'Through right comprehension of conceit, he made an end of suffering' means: by the right means and the right practice, through the comprehension of the abandoning of the ninefold conceit, he made an end to the suffering of the round. 'And this, Sāriputta, was spoken by me in reference to this' means: Sāriputta, in the Pārāyana, in Udaya's Question, this was spoken by me in reference to this very attainment of fruition.

Idāni yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, taṃ dassento pahānaṃ kāmasaññānantiādi āraddhaṃ. Udayapañhe ca etaṃ padaṃ “pahānaṃ kāmacchandāna”nti (su. ni. 1112; cūḷani. udayamāṇavapucchāniddeso 75) āgataṃ, idha pana aṅguttarabhāṇakehi “kāmasaññāna”nti āropitaṃ. Tattha byañjanameva nānaṃ, attho pana ekoyeva. Kāmasaññānanti kāme ārabbha uppannasaññānaṃ, aṭṭhahi vā lobhasahagatacittehi sahajātasaññānaṃ. Domanassāna cūbhayanti etāsañca kāmasaññānaṃ cetasikadomanassānañcāti ubhinnampi pahānaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaphalaṃ aññāvimokkhaṃ pabrūmīti attho. Niddese pana “kāmacchandassa ca domanassassa ca ubhinnaṃ pahānaṃ vūpasamaṃ paṭinissaggaṃ paṭippassaddhiṃ amataṃ nibbāna”nti (cūḷani. udayamāṇavapucchāniddeso 75) vuttaṃ, taṃ atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ. Pahānanti hi khīṇākārasaṅkhāto vūpasamopi vuccati, kilese paṭinissajjanto maggopi, kilesapaṭippassaddhisaṅkhātaṃ phalampi[M 2.0103], yaṃ āgamma kilesā pahīyanti, taṃ amataṃ nibbānampi. Tasmā tattha tāni padāni āgatāni. “Aññāvimokkhaṃ pabrūmī”ti vacanato pana arahattaphalameva adhippetaṃ. Thinassa [P 2.0209] ca panūdanantipi thinassa ca panūdanante uppannattā arahattaphalameva adhippetaṃ[V 2.0104]. Kukkuccānaṃ nivāraṇanti kukkuccanivāraṇassa maggassa anantaraṃ uppannattā phalameva adhippetaṃ.

Now, to show what was spoken by the Blessed One, the exposition begins with 'the abandoning of sensual perceptions,' and so on. In Udaya's Question, this phrase appears as 'the abandoning of sensual desires,' but here it is rendered as 'sensual perceptions' by the Aṅguttara reciters. Here, the wording differs, but the meaning is the same. 'Sensual perceptions' refers to perceptions arisen in relation to sensual pleasures, or the perceptions associated with the eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness. 'And of displeasure, both' means the abandoning of both these sensual perceptions and mental displeasures—that is, the abandonment reckoned as calming, which is the fruit of Arahantship, the liberation of final knowledge, I declare. In the Niddesa, however, it is said: 'the abandoning, pacification, relinquishment, calming, deathlessness, and Nibbāna of both sensual desire and displeasure.' This was stated by way of extracting the meaning. For 'abandoning' can also refer to pacification in the sense of destruction, the path that relinquishes defilements, the fruit which is the calming of defilements, and the deathless Nibbāna, relying on which defilements are abandoned. Thus, those terms are used there. However, from the phrase 'I declare the liberation of final knowledge,' it is the fruit of Arahantship that is intended. 'And the dispelling of sloth' also refers to the fruit of Arahantship, as it arises at the conclusion of the path that dispels sloth. 'The restraining of remorse' refers to the fruit, as it arises immediately after the path that restrains remorse.

Upekkhāsatisaṃsuddhanti catutthajjhānike phale uppannāya upekkhāya ca satiyā ca saṃsuddhaṃ. Dhammatakkapurejavanti dhammatakko vuccati sammāsaṅkappo, so ādito hoti, purato hoti, pubbaṅgamo hoti aññāvimokkhassāti dhammatakkapurejavo. Taṃ dhammatakkapurejavaṃ. Aññāvimokkhanti aññindriyapariyosāne uppannaṃ vimokkhaṃ, aññāya vā vimokkhaṃ aññāvimokkhaṃ, paññāvimuttanti attho. Avijjāya pabhedananti avijjāya pabhedanante uppannattā, avijjāya pabhedanasaṅkhātaṃ vā nibbānaṃ ārabbha uppannattā evaṃladdhanāmaṃ arahattaphalameva. Iti sabbehipi imehi pahānantiādīhi padehi arahattaphalameva pakāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

“Purified by equanimity and mindfulness” means purified by the equanimity and mindfulness that arise in the fruit of the fourth jhāna. “Preceded by thought on the Dhamma”: here, right thought is called ‘thought on the Dhamma’; it is at the beginning, it is in front, and it is a forerunner of the liberation through final knowledge, thus it is ‘preceded by thought on the Dhamma’. “The liberation of final knowledge” is the liberation that arises at the culmination of the faculty of final knowledge, or it is liberation through final knowledge, meaning ‘liberated by wisdom’. “The breaking of ignorance” refers only to the fruit of Arahantship, which has obtained this name because it arises at the conclusion of the breaking of ignorance, or because it arises taking as its object Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the breaking of ignorance. Thus, it should be understood that by all these terms beginning with ‘abandoning’, only the fruit of Arahantship is indicated.

4. Nidānasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta

34. Catutthe nidānānīti kāraṇāni. Kammānanti vaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ. Lobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāyāti lubbhanapalubbhanasabhāvo lobho vaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ samudayāya piṇḍakaraṇatthāya nidānaṃ kāraṇaṃ paccayoti attho. Dosoti dussanapadussanasabhāvo doso. Mohoti muyhanapamuyhanasabhāvo moho.

34. In the fourth, ‘causes’ means reasons. ‘Of kamma’ means of kamma that leads to the round of existence. ‘Greed is a cause for the arising of kamma’: The meaning is that greed, which has the nature of craving and intense craving, is a cause, a reason, and a condition for the arising of kamma that leads to the round of existence, for the purpose of accumulation. ‘Hatred’ means hatred, which has the nature of corrupting and intensely corrupting. ‘Delusion’ means delusion, which has the nature of being bewildered and intensely bewildered.

Lobhapakatanti lobhena pakataṃ, lobhābhibhūtena luddhena hutvā katakammanti attho. Lobhato jātanti lobhajaṃ. Lobho nidānamassāti lobhanidānaṃ. Lobho samudayo assāti lobhasamudayaṃ. Samudayoti paccayo, lobhapaccayanti attho. Yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattatīti yasmiṃ ṭhāne assa lobhajakammavato [P 2.0210] puggalassa attabhāvo nibbattati, khandhā pātubhavanti. Tattha taṃ kammaṃ vipaccatīti tesu khandhesu taṃ kammaṃ vipaccati. Diṭṭhe vā dhammetiādi yasmā taṃ kammaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ vā hoti upapajjavedanīyaṃ vā aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ vā, tasmā taṃ pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

‘Produced by greed’ means done by greed; the meaning is an action done by one who, having become greedy, is overwhelmed by greed. ‘It is born from greed’, thus it is ‘greed-born’. ‘Greed is its cause’, thus it is ‘greed-caused’. ‘Greed is its origin’, thus it is ‘greed-originated’. ‘Origin’ means condition; the meaning is ‘having greed as its condition’. ‘Where his existence arises’ means in whatever place the existence of that person—whose kamma is born of greed—arises, the aggregates manifest. ‘There that kamma ripens’ means that kamma ripens in those aggregates. ‘In this very life or…’ and so forth, is stated to show the distinctions, because that kamma may be one to be experienced in this very life, one to be experienced in the next existence, or one to be experienced in subsequent existences. The same method applies to the remaining two.

Akhaṇḍānīti [M 2.0104] abhinnāni. Apūtīnīti pūtibhāvena abījattaṃ appattāni. Avātātapahatānīti [V 2.0105] na vātena na ca ātapena hatāni. Sārādānīti gahitasārāni sāravantāni na nissārāni. Sukhasayitānīti sannicayabhāvena sukhaṃ sayitāni. Sukhetteti maṇḍakhette. Suparikammakatāya bhūmiyāti naṅgalakasanena ceva aṭṭhadantakena ca suṭṭhu parikammakatāya khettabhūmiyā. Nikkhittānīti ṭhapitāni ropitāni. Anuppaveccheyyāti anuppaveseyya. Vuddhintiādīsu uddhaggamanena vuddhiṃ, heṭṭhā mūlappatiṭṭhānena virūḷhiṃ, samantā vitthārikabhāvena vepullaṃ.

‘Unbroken’ means not split. ‘Unspoiled’ means not having lost their seed potential through being rotten. ‘Not damaged by wind or sun’ means not harmed by wind or by the sun’s heat. ‘With substance’ means having absorbed essence, possessing essence, not without essence. ‘Well-stored’ means comfortably placed due to being accumulated. ‘In a good field’ means in a clear field. ‘In well-prepared soil’ means in field-soil thoroughly prepared by plowing and by harrowing with an eight-tined harrow. ‘Planted’ means placed, sown. ‘Would cause to enter’ means would cause to enter. In ‘growth,’ etc., growth is increase by upward movement, development is firm rooting below, and abundance is expansion in all directions.

Yaṃ panettha diṭṭhe vā dhammetiādi vuttaṃ, tattha asammohatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kammavibhatti nāma kathetabbā. Suttantikapariyāyena hi ekādasa kammāni vibhattāni. Seyyathidaṃ – diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ, yaggarukaṃ yabbahulaṃ yadāsannaṃ kaṭattā vā pana kammaṃ, janakaṃ upatthambhakaṃ upapīḷakaṃ upaghātakanti. Tattha ekajavanavīthiyaṃ sattasu cittesu kusalā vā akusalā vā paṭhamajavanacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti [P 2.0211] kākavaḷiyapuṇṇaseṭṭhīnaṃ viya kusalaṃ, nandayakkhanandamāṇavakanandagoghātakakokāliyasuppabuddhadevadattaciñcamāṇavikānaṃ viya ca akusalaṃ. Tathā asakkontaṃ pana ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti, avipākaṃ sampajjati. Taṃ migaluddakopamāya sādhetabbaṃ. Yathā hi migaluddakena migaṃ disvā dhanuṃ ākaḍḍhitvā khitto saro sace na virajjhati, taṃ migaṃ tattheva pāteti, atha naṃ migaluddako niccammaṃ katvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chetvā maṃsaṃ ādāya puttadāraṃ tosento gacchati. Sace pana virajjhati, migo palāyitvā puna taṃ disaṃ na oloketi. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sarassa avirajjhitvā migavijjhanaṃ viya hi diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassa kammassa vipākavārapaṭilābho, avijjhanaṃ viya avipākabhāvāya sampajjananti.

Furthermore, regarding what is stated here as ‘in this very life,’ etc., for the sake of non-bewilderment, the classification of kamma should be explained in this place. Indeed, according to the Suttanta method, eleven types of kamma are distinguished. They are as follows: kamma to be experienced in this very life, kamma to be experienced in the next life, kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives; weighty kamma, habitual kamma, proximate kamma, and kamma that is merely done; productive kamma, supportive kamma, obstructive kamma, and destructive kamma. Therein, in a single impulsion-process, the volition of the first impulsion among the seven mind-moments, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is called kamma to be experienced in this very life. It gives its result in this very life-existence, like the wholesome kamma of Kākavaḷiya and the millionaire Puṇṇa, and like the unwholesome kamma of the yakkha Nanda, the young man Nanda, the cow-killer Nanda, Kokāliya, Suppabuddha, Devadatta, and the young woman Ciñcā. However, when it is unable to do so, it becomes what is called ‘ineffective kamma’; it comes to have no result. This should be explained by the simile of the deer hunter. For it is as when a deer hunter, having seen a deer, draws his bow and shoots an arrow. If it does not miss, it causes the deer to fall right there. Then the deer hunter, having skinned it and cut it into pieces, takes the meat and goes, delighting his children and wife. But if it misses, the deer flees and does not look in that direction again. The application of this simile should be understood thus: The striking of the deer by the arrow that does not miss is like the obtaining of the opportunity for the fruition of kamma to be experienced in this very life, while the missing of the arrow is like its failure to bear fruit.

Atthasādhikā pana sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ anantare attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Taṃ panetaṃ kusalapakkhe aṭṭhasamāpattivasena, akusalapakkhe pañcānantariyakammavasena veditabbaṃ. Tattha aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī ekāya samāpattiyā brahmaloke nibbattati. Pañcannampi ānantariyānaṃ kattā ekena kammena niraye nibbattati, sesasamāpattiyo [M 2.0105] ca kammāni ca ahosikammabhāvaṃyeva āpajjanti, avipākāni honti. Ayampi attho purimaupamāyayeva dīpetabbo.

Furthermore, the volition of the seventh impulsion, which accomplishes the purpose, is called kamma to be experienced in the next existence. It yields its result in the immediately following existence. This should be understood by way of the eight attainments on the wholesome side, and by way of the five deeds of immediate retribution on the unwholesome side. In this regard, one who has obtained the eight attainments is reborn in the Brahma world through one attainment. The doer of the five deeds of immediate retribution is reborn in hell through one kamma; the remaining attainments and deeds reach the state of ineffective kamma and become fruitless. This meaning, too, should be explained by the previous simile.

Ubhinnaṃ [V 2.0106] antare pana pañcajavanacetanā aparapariyāyavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ anāgate yadā okāsaṃ labhati, tadā vipākaṃ deti. Sati saṃsārappavattiyā ahosikammaṃ nāma na hoti. Taṃ sabbaṃ sunakhaluddakena dīpetabbaṃ. Yathā hi sunakhaluddakena migaṃ disvā sunakho vissajjito migaṃ anubandhitvā yasmiṃ ṭhāne pāpuṇāti, tasmiṃ yeva ḍaṃsati; evamevaṃ [P 2.0212] idaṃ kammaṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne okāsaṃ labhati, tasmiṃyeva vipākaṃ deti, tena mutto satto nāma natthi.

Furthermore, the five impulsion-volitions in between the two are called kamma to be experienced in subsequent existences. When it finds an opportunity in a future existence, it yields its result. As long as the process of saṃsāra exists, it does not become what is called ineffective kamma. All this should be explained by the simile of the dog-hunter. Indeed, just as a dog, released by a dog-hunter upon seeing a deer, chases the deer and bites it at whatever place it catches up; in this very same way, this kamma yields its result at whatever place it gets an opportunity, and there is no being so-called who is free from it.

Kusalākusalesu pana garukāgarukesu yaṃ garukaṃ hoti, taṃ yaggarukaṃ nāma. Tadetaṃ kusalapakkhe mahaggatakammaṃ, akusalapakkhe pañcānantariyakammaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ sati sesāni kusalāni vā akusalāni vā vipaccituṃ na sakkonti, tadeva duvidhampi paṭisandhiṃ deti. Yathā hi sāsapappamāṇāpi sakkharā vā ayaguḷikā vā udakarahade pakkhittā udakapiṭṭhe uplavituṃ na sakkoti, heṭṭhāva pavisati; evameva kusalepi akusalepi yaṃ garukaṃ, tadeva gaṇhitvā gacchati.

Furthermore, among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, the weighty and the unweighty, whichever is weighty is called weighty kamma. This should be understood as exalted kamma on the wholesome side, and the five deeds of immediate retribution on the unwholesome side. When that exists, the remaining wholesome or unwholesome kammas are not able to ripen; only that weighty kamma, of either kind, gives rebirth-linking. Indeed, just as a piece of gravel or an iron ball, even if only the size of a mustard seed, when thrown into a lake, is not able to float on the water's surface but only sinks down; in this very same way, among wholesome and unwholesome kamma, whichever is weighty, only that takes hold and proceeds.

Kusalākusalesu pana yaṃ bahulaṃ hoti, taṃ yabbahulaṃ nāma. Taṃ dīgharattaṃ laddhāsevanavasena veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ vā balavakusalakammesu somanassakaraṃ, akusalakammesu santāpakaraṃ, etaṃ yabbahulaṃ nāma. Tadetaṃ yathā nāma dvīsu mallesu yuddhabhūmiṃ otiṇṇesu yo balavā, so itaraṃ pātetvā gacchati; evameva itaraṃ dubbalakammaṃ avattharitvā yaṃ āsevanavasena vā bahulaṃ, āsannavasena vā balavaṃ, taṃ vipākaṃ deti, duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayarañño kammaṃ viya.

However, among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, that which is much practiced is called habitual kamma. This should be understood by way of its being cultivated through repeated practice for a long time. Or, among strong wholesome kammas, that which produces joy, and among unwholesome kammas, that which produces torment, is called habitual kamma. Just as when two wrestlers have entered the wrestling ground, the one who is stronger, having thrown the other, goes on his way; even so, having overwhelmed the other, weaker kamma, that kamma which is much practiced by way of repetition or is strong by way of proximity, gives its result—like the kamma of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya.

So kira cūḷaṅgaṇiyayuddhe parājito vaḷavaṃ āruyha palāyi. Tassa cūḷupaṭṭhāko tissāmacco nāma ekakova pacchato ahosi. So ekaṃ aṭaviṃ pavisitvā nisinno jighacchāya bādhayamānāya – “bhātika tissa, ativiya no jighacchā bādhati, kiṃ karissāmā”ti āha[M 2.0106]. Atthi, deva, mayā sāṭakantare ṭhapetvā ekaṃ suvaṇṇasarakabhattaṃ ābhatanti. Tena hi āharāti. So nīharitvā rañño purato ṭhapesi. Rājā disvā, “tāta, cattāro koṭṭhāse karohī”ti āha. Mayaṃ tayo janā, kasmā devo cattāro koṭṭhāse kārayatīti? Bhātika [P 2.0213] tissa, yato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ attānaṃ sarāmi, na me ayyānaṃ adatvā āhāro paribhuttapubbo atthi, svāhaṃ ajjapi adatvā na paribhuñjissāmīti. So cattāro koṭṭhāse akāsi. Rājā “kālaṃ ghosehī”ti āha. Chaḍḍitāraññe kuto, ayye, labhissāma devāti[V 2.0107]. “Nāyaṃ tava bhāro. Sace mama saddhā atthi, ayye, labhissāma, vissattho kālaṃ ghosehī”ti āha. So “kālo, bhante, kālo, bhante”ti tikkhattuṃ ghosesi.

It is said that he, defeated in the battle of Cūḷaṅgaṇī, mounted a mare and fled. His young attendant, the minister named Tissa, was the only one following behind. Having entered a forest, he sat down, and being tormented by hunger, said: 'Elder brother Tissa, we are extremely tormented by hunger. What shall we do?' 'Your Majesty, there is one small golden bowl of rice that I have brought, having placed it in the fold of my garment.' 'In that case, bring it.' He took it out and placed it before the king. The king, seeing it, said: 'Minister, make four portions.' 'We are three people. Why does Your Majesty have four portions made?' 'Elder brother Tissa, from the time I can remember myself, there has been no food eaten by me without first giving to the noble ones. Even today, I will not eat without giving.' So he made four portions. The king said: 'Announce the time.' 'Your Majesty, in this abandoned forest, from where shall we find the noble ones?' 'This is not your burden. If my faith exists, we shall find the noble ones. Announce the time with confidence.' He then announced three times: 'It is time, venerable sir! It is time, venerable sir!'

Athassa bodhimātumahātissatthero taṃ saddaṃ dibbāya sotadhātuyā sutvā ‘katthāyaṃ saddo’ti taṃ āvajjento “ajja duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayamahārājā yuddhaparājito aṭaviṃ pavisitvā nisinno ekaṃ sarakabhattaṃ cattāro koṭṭhāse kāretvā ‘ekakova na paribhuñjissāmī’ti kālaṃ ghosāpesī”ti ñatvā “ajja mayā rañño saṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti manogatiyā āgantvā rañño purato aṭṭhāsi. Rājā disvā pasannacitto “passa, bhātika, tissā”ti vatvā theraṃ vanditvā “pattaṃ, bhante, dethā”ti āha. Thero pattaṃ nīhari. Rājā attano koṭṭhāsena saddhiṃ therassa koṭṭhāsaṃ patte pakkhipitvā, “bhante, āhāraparissayo nāma mā kadāci hotū”ti vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Tissāmaccopi “mama ayyaputte passante bhuñjituṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti attano koṭṭhāsaṃ therasseva patte ākiri. Vaḷavāpi cintesi – “mayhampi koṭṭhāsaṃ therasseva dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā vaḷavaṃ oloketvā “ayampi attano koṭṭhāsaṃ therasseva patte pakkhipanaṃ paccāsīsatī”ti ñatvā tampi tattheva pakkhipitvā theraṃ vanditvā uyyojesi. Thero taṃ bhattaṃ ādāya gantvā ādito paṭṭhāya bhikkhusaṅghassa ālopasaṅkhepena adāsi.

Then the Elder Bodhimātu Mahātissa, hearing that sound with the divine ear-element and reflecting, 'Whose sound is this?', understood: 'Today, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, being defeated in battle, has entered the forest and is seated. Having had a single meal in a small bowl made into four portions, he caused the time to be proclaimed, thinking, "I will not eat all alone."' Having known this, he thought, 'Today, it is proper for me to render assistance to the king.' And having come by the speed of mind, he stood before the king. The king, seeing him, with a confident mind, said, 'Look, brother Tissa!' and having paid homage to the elder, said, 'Venerable sir, give me your bowl.' The elder brought forth his bowl. The king, having placed his own portion together with the elder's portion into the bowl, paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, may there never be for me any danger on account of food,' and stood by. The minister Tissa also, thinking, 'I will not be able to eat while my young lord is watching,' poured his own portion into the elder's bowl. The mare also thought, 'It is proper for me also to give my portion only to the elder.' The king, looking at the mare and knowing, 'She also hopes to have her portion placed in the elder's bowl,' placed that portion there as well. Then, having paid homage to the elder, he sent him away. The elder, taking that alms-food and going, gave it to the community of monks, starting from the head of the assembly, in portions the size of a morsel.

Rājāpi cintesi – “ativiyamhā jighacchitā, sādhu vatassa sace atirekabhattasitthāni [P 2.0214] pahiṇeyyā”ti. Thero rañño cittaṃ ñatvā atirekabhattaṃ [M 2.0107] etesaṃ yāpanamattaṃ katvā pattaṃ ākāse khipi, patto āgantvā rañño hatthe patiṭṭhāsi. Bhattaṃ tiṇṇampi janānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ ahosi. Atha rājā pattaṃ dhovitvā “tucchapattaṃ na pesissāmī”ti uttarisāṭakaṃ mocetvā udakaṃ puñchitvā sāṭakaṃ patte ṭhapetvā “patto gantvā mama ayyassa hatthe patiṭṭhātū”ti ākāse khipi. Patto gantvā therassa hatthe patiṭṭhāsi.

The king also thought: 'We are extremely hungry. It would be good indeed if he would send the leftover grains of rice.' The elder, knowing the king's mind, made the leftover rice just enough to sustain these three persons and threw the bowl into the sky. The bowl came and stood in the king's hand. The rice was also sufficient for the three persons, as much as they desired. Then the king, having washed the bowl and thinking, 'I will not send an empty bowl,' removed his upper garment, made it a cloth for wiping water, placed it in the bowl, and having made the resolution, 'Let the bowl go and stand in my lord's hand,' threw it into the sky. The bowl went and stood in the elder's hand.

Aparabhāge rañño tathāgatassa sarīradhātūnaṃ aṭṭhamabhāgaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā vīsaratanasatikaṃ mahācetiyaṃ kārentassa apariniṭṭhiteyeva cetiye kālakiriyāsamayo anuppatto. Athassa mahācetiyassa dakkhiṇapasse nipannassa pañcanikāyavasena bhikkhusaṅghe sajjhāyaṃ karonte chahi devalokehi cha rathā āgantvā purato ākāse aṭṭhaṃsu. Rājā “puññapotthakaṃ āharathā”ti ādito paṭṭhāya puññapotthakaṃ vācāpesi. Atha naṃ kiñci kammaṃ na paritosesi. So “parato [V 2.0108] vācethā”ti āha. Potthakavācako “cūḷaṅgaṇiyayuddhe parājitena te deva aṭaviṃ pavisitvā nisinnena ekaṃ sarakabhattaṃ cattāro koṭṭhāse kāretvā bodhimātumahātissattherassa bhikkhā dinnā”ti āha. Rājā “ṭhapehī”ti vatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi, “bhante, kataro devaloko ramaṇīyo”ti? Sabbabodhisattānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ tusitabhavanaṃ mahārājāti. Rājā kālaṃ katvā tusitabhavanato āgataratheva patiṭṭhāya tusitabhavanaṃ agamāsi. Idaṃ balavakammassa vipākadāne vatthu.

Later, while the king, having enshrined the eighth part of the Tathāgata's bodily relics, was causing a great cetiya of one hundred and twenty cubits to be made, the time of his death arrived even before the cetiya was finished. Then, as he was lying on the southern side of the great cetiya, while the Saṅgha of monks was making recitation according to the five Nikāyas, six chariots from the six deva worlds came and stood in the sky before him. The king said, 'Bring the register-book of meritorious deeds,' and had the register-book of meritorious deeds read from the beginning. Then, no meritorious deed pleased him. He said, 'Read further on.' The reader of the book said, 'When defeated in the battle of Cūḷaṅgaṇiya, Your Majesty, having entered that very forest and while seated, caused a single meal of rice brought in a small bowl to be made into four portions, and alms were given to the elder Bodhimātu Mahātissa.' The king, saying, 'Stop,' asked the Saṅgha of monks, 'Venerable sirs, which deva world is delightful?' 'O great king, the Tusita abode, which is the dwelling place of all Bodhisattas, is delightful.' The king, having died, established himself in the very chariot that had come from the Tusita abode and went to the Tusita abode. This is the story regarding the rendering of the result of a powerful kamma.

Yaṃ pana kusalākusalesu āsannamaraṇe anussarituṃ sakkoti, taṃ yadāsannaṃ nāma. Tadetaṃ yathā nāma gogaṇaparipuṇṇassa vajassa dvāre vivaṭe parabhāge dammagavabalavagavesu [P 2.0215] santesupi yo vajadvārassa āsanno hoti antamaso dubbalajaraggavopi, so eva paṭhamataraṃ nikkhamati, evameva aññesu kusalākusalesu santesupi maraṇakālassa āsannattā vipākaṃ deti.

Now, whatever wholesome or unwholesome deed one is able to recollect at the approach of death, that is called 'death-proximate'. Just as, for example, when the gate of a pen full of cattle is opened, even though there are trainable and strong oxen in the back, the one that is near the gate—even if it is a weak, old ox—is the very one to go out first; in this very way, even though other wholesome and unwholesome deeds exist, it gives its result on account of its proximity to the time of death.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – madhuaṅgaṇagāme kira eko damiḷadovāriko pātova baḷisaṃ ādāya gantvā macche vadhitvā tayo koṭṭhāse katvā [M 2.0108] ekena taṇḍulaṃ gaṇhāti, ekena dadhiṃ, ekaṃ pacati. Iminā nīhārena paññāsa vassāni pāṇātipātakammaṃ katvā aparabhāge mahallako anuṭṭhānaseyyaṃ upagacchati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe girivihāravāsī cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissatthero “mā ayaṃ satto mayi passante nassatū”ti gantvā tassa gehadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Athassa bhariyā, “sāmi, thero āgato”ti ārocesi. Ahaṃ paññāsa vassāni therassa santikaṃ na gatapubbo, katarena me guṇena thero āgamissati, gacchāti naṃ vadathāti. Sā “aticchatha, bhante”ti āha. Thero “upāsakassa kā sarīrappavattī”ti pucchi. Dubbalo, bhanteti. Thero gharaṃ pavisitvā satiṃ uppādetvā “sīlaṃ gaṇhissasī”ti āha. Āma, bhante, dethāti. Thero tīṇi saraṇāni datvā pañca sīlāni dātuṃ ārabhi. Tassa pañca sīlānīti vacanakāleyeva jivhā papati. Thero “vaṭṭissati ettaka”nti nikkhamitvā gato. Sopi kālaṃ katvā cātumahārājikabhavane nibbatti. Nibbattakkhaṇeyeva ca “kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā mayā idaṃ laddha”nti āvajjento theraṃ nissāya laddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā devalokato āgantvā theraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. “Ko eso”ti ca vutte “ahaṃ, bhante, damiḷadovāriko”ti āha. Kuhiṃ nibbattosīti? Cātumahārājikesu, bhante, sace me ayyo pañca sīlāni adassa, upari [V 2.0109] devaloke nibbatto assaṃ. Ahaṃ kiṃ karissāmi, tvaṃ gaṇhituṃ nāsakkhi, puttakāti. So theraṃ vanditvā devalokameva gato. Idaṃ tāva kusalakamme vatthu.

Here are the stories: In the village of Madhuaṅgaṇa, there was a Tamil gatekeeper who, very early in the morning, would take a fishhook, go out, kill fish, and make three portions. With one portion he would obtain rice, with another curd, and one portion he would cook. In this manner, for fifty years he committed the act of taking life. In the later part of his life, he became elderly and was confined to his bed. At that moment, the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa, a resident of Girivihāra, thinking, 'Let this being not perish while I am watching,' went and stood at his house door. Then the man's wife announced, 'My lord, the Elder has come.' He replied, 'For fifty years, I have never gone to the Elder's presence. Due to what quality of mine would the Elder come? Tell him to go away!' She said, 'Pardon us, venerable sir.' The Elder asked, 'What is the lay follower’s bodily condition?' 'He is weak, venerable sir.' The Elder entered the house, aroused mindfulness, and said, 'Will you take the precepts?' 'Yes, venerable sir, please give them.' The Elder, having administered the three refuges, began to administer the five precepts. But at the very moment the words 'the five precepts' were spoken, the man's tongue failed him. The Elder, thinking, 'This much will suffice,' departed and went on his way. That man passed away and was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings. At the very moment of his rebirth, while reflecting, 'By what kamma, I wonder, have I obtained this?' he realized that it was obtained by relying on the Elder. Coming from the heavenly realm, he paid homage to the Elder and stood to one side. When asked, 'Who are you?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, I am the Tamil gatekeeper.' 'Where were you reborn?' 'In the realm of the Four Great Kings, venerable sir. If my lord had administered the five precepts to me, I would have been reborn in a higher heavenly realm.' The Elder replied, 'What could I do, my son? You were unable to receive them.' He paid homage to the Elder and returned to the heavenly realm. This, for now, is the story concerning a wholesome action.

Antaragaṅgāya [P 2.0216] pana mahāvācakālaupāsako nāma ahosi. So tiṃsa vassāni sotāpattimaggatthāya dvattiṃsākāraṃ sajjhāyitvā “ahaṃ evaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ sajjhāyanto obhāsamattampi nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, buddhasāsanaṃ aniyyānikaṃ bhavissatī”ti diṭṭhivipallāsaṃ patvā kālakiriyaṃ katvā mahāgaṅgāya navausabhiko susumārapeto hutvā nibbatti. Ekaṃ samayaṃ kacchakatitthena saṭṭhi pāsāṇatthambhasakaṭāni agamaṃsu. So sabbepi te goṇe ca pāsāṇe ca khādi. Idaṃ akusalakamme vatthu.

Furthermore, in the region between the Ganges, there was a lay follower named Mahāvācakāla. For thirty years, for the sake of the path of stream-entry, he recited the thirty-two aspects of the body. Then, having fallen into a perversion of view, thinking, 'While reciting the thirty-two aspects in this way, I was not able to produce even a mere glimmer of light; the Buddha’s dispensation must not be that which leads out [of saṃsāra],' he died and was reborn in the great Ganges as a crocodile-peta, nine usabhas in size. On one occasion, sixty carts with stone pillars went by way of the Kacchaka ford. He devoured all those oxen and those stones. This is the story concerning unwholesome kamma.

Etehi [M 2.0109] pana tīhi muttaṃ aññāṇavasena kataṃ kaṭattā vā pana kammaṃ nāma. Taṃ yathā nāma ummattakena khittadaṇḍaṃ yattha vā tattha vā gacchati, evameva tesaṃ abhāve yattha katthaci vipākaṃ deti.

Furthermore, kamma that is done by way of ignorance, or that which is called 'kamma that is merely done', is freed from these three [types]. Just as a stick thrown by a madman goes wherever it may, even so, in the absence of those [other kammas], it gives its result in some existence or other.

Janakaṃ nāma ekaṃ paṭisandhiṃ janetvā pavattiṃ na janeti, pavatte aññaṃ kammaṃ vipākaṃ nibbatteti. Yathā hi mātā janetiyeva, dhātiyeva pana jaggati; evamevaṃ mātā viya paṭisandhinibbattakaṃ janakakammaṃ, dhāti viya pavatte sampattakammaṃ. Upatthambhakaṃ nāma kusalepi labbhati akusalepi. Ekacco hi kusalaṃ katvā sugatibhave nibbattati. So tattha ṭhito punappunaṃ kusalaṃ katvā taṃ kammaṃ upatthambhetvā anekāni vassasatasahassāni sugatibhavasmiṃyeva vicarati. Ekacco akusalaṃ katvā duggatibhave nibbattati. So tattha ṭhito punappunaṃ akusalaṃ katvā taṃ kammaṃ upatthambhetvā bahūni vassasatasahassāni duggatibhavasmiṃyeva vicarati.

That which is called 'generative kamma', having produced one rebirth-linking, does not produce [the results in] the course of existence; in the course of existence, another kamma produces the result. Indeed, just as a mother only gives birth, and a nurse only nurtures; even so, like a mother, the kamma that produces rebirth-linking is generative kamma; like a nurse, in the course of existence, is the kamma that brings about accomplishment. That which is called 'supportive kamma' is found in the wholesome and also in the unwholesome. Indeed, a certain person, having done a wholesome deed, is reborn in a happy existence. Established there, doing wholesome deeds again and again, and having supported that kamma, he wanders only in a happy existence for many hundreds of thousands of years. A certain person, having done an unwholesome deed, is reborn in an unhappy existence. Established there, doing unwholesome deeds again and again, and having supported that kamma, he wanders only in an unhappy existence for many hundreds of thousands of years.

Aparo nayo – janakaṃ nāma kusalampi hoti akusalampi. Taṃ paṭisandhiyampi pavattepi rūpārūpavipākakkhandhe janeti. Upatthambhakaṃ pana vipākaṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti, aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavatteti. Upapīḷakaṃ [P 2.0217] nāma aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjanakasukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādheti, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na deti. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – kusalakamme vipaccamāne akusalakammaṃ [V 2.0110] upapīḷakaṃ hutvā tassa vipaccituṃ na deti. Akusalakamme vipaccamāne kusalakammaṃ upapīḷakaṃ hutvā tassa vipaccituṃ na deti. Yathā vaḍḍhamānakaṃ rukkhaṃ vā gacchaṃ vā lataṃ vā kocideva daṇḍena vā satthena vā bhindeyya vā chindeyya vā, atha so rukkho vā gaccho vā latā vā vaḍḍhituṃ na sakkuṇeyya; evamevaṃ kusalaṃ vipaccamānaṃ akusalena upapīḷitaṃ, akusalaṃ vā pana vipaccamānaṃ kusalena upapīḷitaṃ vipaccituṃ na sakkoti. Tattha sunakkhattassa akusalakammaṃ kusalaṃ upapīḷesi, coraghātakassa kusalakammaṃ akusalaṃ upapīḷesi.

Another method: generative kamma can be either wholesome or unwholesome. It generates the material and immaterial resultant aggregates at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence. Supportive kamma, however, is unable to generate a result; rather, it supports the pleasure and pain that are to arise in the result generated by another kamma that gave rebirth-linking, causing it to continue for a long time. Obstructive kamma obstructs and afflicts the pleasure and pain that are to arise in the result generated by another kamma that gave rebirth-linking, preventing its continuation for a long time. Here is the principle: when a wholesome kamma is ripening, an unwholesome kamma acts as an obstructive kamma, preventing it from ripening. When an unwholesome kamma is ripening, a wholesome kamma acts as an obstructive kamma, preventing it from ripening. Just as if someone were to break or cut a growing tree, bush, or vine with a stick or a weapon, that tree, bush, or vine would be unable to grow; in the same way, a ripening wholesome kamma obstructed by an unwholesome one, or a ripening unwholesome kamma obstructed by a wholesome one, is unable to ripen. In this context, Sunakkhatta’s unwholesome kamma obstructed the wholesome kamma, and the executioner's wholesome kamma obstructed the unwholesome kamma.

Rājagahe kira vātakāḷako paññāsa vassāni coraghātakammaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ rañño ārocesuṃ – “deva, vātakāḷako mahallako core ghātetuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Apanetha naṃ tasmā [M 2.0110] ṭhānantarāti. Amaccā naṃ apanetvā aññaṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapayiṃsu. Vātakāḷakopi yāva taṃ kammaṃ akāsi, tāva ahatavatthāni vā acchādituṃ surabhipupphāni vā piḷandhituṃ pāyāsaṃ vā bhuñjituṃ ucchādananhāpanaṃ vā paccanubhotuṃ nālattha. So “dīgharattaṃ me kiliṭṭhavesena carita”nti “pāyāsaṃ me pacāhī”ti bhariyaṃ āṇāpetvā nhānīyasambhārāni gāhāpetvā nhānatitthaṃ gantvā sīsaṃ nhatvā ahatavatthāni acchādetvā gandhe vilimpitvā pupphāni piḷandhitvā gharaṃ āgacchanto sāriputtattheraṃ disvā “saṃkiliṭṭhakammato camhi apagato, ayyo ca me diṭṭho”ti tuṭṭhamānaso theraṃ gharaṃ netvā navasappisakkaracuṇṇābhisaṅkhatena pāyāsena parivisi. Thero tassa anumodanamakāsi. So anumodanaṃ sutvā anulomikakhantiṃ paṭilabhitvā [P 2.0218] theraṃ anugantvā nivattamāno antarāmagge taruṇavacchāya gāviyā madditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpito gantvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti. Bhikkhū tathāgataṃ pucchiṃsu – “bhante, coraghātako ajjeva kiliṭṭhakammato apanīto, ajjeva kālaṅkato, kahaṃ nu kho nibbatto”ti? Tāvatiṃsabhavane, bhikkhaveti. Bhante, coraghātako dīgharattaṃ purise ghātesi, tumhe ca evaṃ vadetha, natthi nu kho pāpakammassa phalanti. Mā, bhikkhave, evaṃ avacuttha, balavakalyāṇamittūpanissayaṃ labhitvā dhammasenāpatissa piṇḍapātaṃ datvā anumodanaṃ sutvā anulomikakhantiṃ paṭilabhitvā so tattha nibbattoti.

In Rājagaha, it is said, an executioner named Vātakāḷaka performed the work of an executioner for fifty years. Then they reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, Vātakāḷaka is old; he is not able to execute thieves.' The king said: 'Remove him from that position.' The ministers removed him and appointed another in his place. As long as Vātakāḷaka performed that work, he never had the opportunity to wear new clothes, adorn himself with fragrant flowers, eat milk-rice, or enjoy anointing and bathing. Thinking, 'For a long time I have lived with a defiled appearance,' he ordered his wife, 'Cook milk-rice for me.' Having had bathing requisites brought, he went to the bathing place, bathed from the head down, put on new clothes, anointed himself with perfumes, and adorned himself with flowers. While returning home, he saw the Elder Sāriputta. With a delighted mind, he thought, 'I am freed from my defiled work, and I have seen the noble one.' He led the Elder to his house and served him milk-rice prepared with fresh ghee and powdered sugar. The Elder gave him a discourse of appreciation. Hearing the discourse of appreciation, he gained conformity-patience. Having accompanied the Elder for a distance, while he was returning on the way, he was trampled by a cow with a young calf and met his death. He was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. The monks asked the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the executioner was removed from his defiled work just today, and he passed away just today. Where was he reborn?' 'In the Tāvatiṃsa realm, monks.' 'Venerable sir, the executioner killed men for a long time, and yet you speak thus. Is there then no fruit of an evil deed?' 'Monks, do not speak thus. Having obtained the powerful support of a good friend, having given alms-food to the General of the Dhamma, having heard the discourse of appreciation, and having gained conformity-patience, he was reborn there.'

“Subhāsitaṃ suṇitvāna, nāgariyo coraghātako;

Anulomakhantiṃ laddhāna, modatī tidivaṃ gato”ti.

Having heard what was well-spoken, the executioner from the city, having obtained conformity-patience, rejoices, having gone to the celestial realm.

Upaghātakaṃ [V 2.0111] pana sayaṃ kusalampi akusalampi samānaṃ aññaṃ dubbalakammaṃ ghātetvā tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti. Evaṃ pana kammena kate okāse taṃ vipākaṃ uppannaṃ nāma vuccati. Upacchedakantipi etasseva nāmaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – kusalakammassa vipaccanakāle ekaṃ akusalakammaṃ uṭṭhāya taṃ kammaṃ chinditvā pāteti. Akusalakammassapi vipaccanakāle ekaṃ kusalakammaṃ uṭṭhāya taṃ kammaṃ chinditvā pāteti. Idaṃ upacchedakaṃ nāma. Tattha ajātasattuno kammaṃ kusalacchedakaṃ [M 2.0111] ahosi, aṅgulimālattherassa akusalacchedakanti. Evaṃ suttantikapariyāyena ekādasa kammāni vibhattāni.

Destructive kamma, being itself either wholesome or unwholesome, destroys another, weaker kamma; and having prevented its result, it creates an opportunity for its own result. When the opportunity has thus been made by the kamma, that result is said to have 'arisen.' 'Cutting-off kamma' is also a name for this very kamma. Here is the principle: at the time when a wholesome kamma is about to ripen, an unwholesome kamma may arise, cut off that kamma, and cause it to fall. Similarly, when an unwholesome kamma is about to ripen, a wholesome kamma may arise, cut off that kamma, and cause it to fall. This is called 'cutting-off kamma.' Herein, the kamma of Ajātasattu was one that cut off the wholesome, while that of the Elder Aṅgulimāla was one that cut off the unwholesome. Thus, according to the Suttanta method, eleven kammas are distinguished.

Abhidhammapariyāyena pana soḷasa kammāni vibhattāni, seyyathidaṃ – “atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti, atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni upadhisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti, atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni kālasampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti, atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni payogasampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti[P 2.0219]. Atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni gativipattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti, upadhivipattiṃ, kālavipattiṃ, payogavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti. Atthekaccāni kalyāṇāni kammasamādānāni gativipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti, upadhivipatti, kālavipatti, payogavipattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccanti. Atthekaccāni kalyāṇāni kammasamādānāni gatisampattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti, upadhisampattiṃ, kālasampattiṃ, payogasampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantī”ti (vibha. 810).

Furthermore, by the method of the Abhidhamma, sixteen kammas are distinguished, as follows: 'There are certain evil undertakings of kamma that do not ripen, being obstructed by the excellence of destiny. There are certain evil undertakings of kamma that do not ripen, being obstructed by the excellence of the physical basis. There are certain evil undertakings of kamma that do not ripen, being obstructed by the excellence of time. There are certain evil undertakings of kamma that do not ripen, being obstructed by the excellence of effort. There are certain evil undertakings of kamma that ripen on account of the failure of destiny, the failure of the physical basis, the failure of time, or the failure of effort. There are certain wholesome undertakings of kamma that do not ripen, being obstructed by the failure of destiny, the failure of the physical basis, the failure of time, or the failure of effort. There are certain wholesome undertakings of kamma that ripen on account of the excellence of destiny, the excellence of the physical basis, the excellence of time, or the excellence of effort.'

Tattha pāpakānīti lāmakāni. Kammasamādānānīti kammaggahaṇāni. Gahitasamādinnānaṃ kammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantītiādīsu aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanārahe kamme vijjamāneyeva sugatibhave nibbattassa taṃ kammaṃ gatisampattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Gatisampattiyā patibāhitaṃ hutvā na vipaccatīti attho. Yo pana pāpakammena dāsiyā vā kammakāriyā vā kucchiyaṃ nibbattitvā upadhisampanno hoti, attabhāvasamiddhiyaṃ tiṭṭhati. Athassa sāmikā tassa rūpasampattiṃ disvā “nāyaṃ kiliṭṭhakammassānucchaviko”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā attano jātaputtaṃ viya bhaṇḍāgārikādiṭṭhānesu ṭhapetvā sampattiṃ yojetvā pariharanti. Evarūpassa kammaṃ upadhisampattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Yo pana paṭhamakappikakālasadise sulabhasampannarasabhojane subhikkhakāle [V 2.0112] nibbattati, tassa vijjamānampi pāpakammaṃ kālasampattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Yo pana sammāpayogaṃ nissāya jīvati, upasaṅkamitabbayuttakāle upasaṅkamati, paṭikkamitabbayuttakāle paṭikkamati, palāyitabbayuttakāle palāyati. Lañjadānayuttakāle lañjaṃ deti, corikayuttakāle corikaṃ [M 2.0112] karoti, evarūpassa pāpakammaṃ payogasampattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma.

Therein, 'pāpakāni' means base. 'Kammasamādānāni' means the taking up of actions. This is a designation for actions that have been taken up and undertaken. In passages such as, 'obstructed by the excellence of destination, they do not ripen,' for one who is reborn in a good destination, even when there exists kamma that is fit to be experienced as an undesirable object, that kamma, being obstructed by the excellence of destination, is said not to ripen. The meaning is that, having been obstructed by the excellence of destination, it does not ripen. Furthermore, as for one who, due to bad kamma, is reborn in the womb of a female slave or a female worker, but becomes endowed with excellent physical attributes and is established in the prosperity of their individual existence; then their masters, seeing their excellence of form, give rise to the thought, 'This one is not suitable for sordid work,' and like their own born child, they place them in positions such as treasurer, provide them with wealth, and look after them. For such a person, their kamma, being obstructed by the excellence of physical attributes, is said not to ripen. Furthermore, as for one who is reborn in a time of abundance with easily obtainable food of excellent flavor, similar to the time of the first aeon; for them, even existing bad kamma, being obstructed by the excellence of the time, is said not to ripen. Furthermore, as for one who lives relying on right application: they approach at a time when it is proper to approach, withdraw at a time when it is proper to withdraw, and flee at a time when it is proper to flee. They give a bribe at a time when it is proper to give a bribe and commit theft at a time when it is proper to commit theft. For such a person, their bad kamma, being obstructed by the excellence of application, is said not to ripen.

Duggatibhave [P 2.0220] nibbattassa pana pāpakammaṃ gativipattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Yo pana dāsiyā vā kammakāriyā vā kucchismiṃ nibbatto dubbaṇṇo hoti dussaṇṭhāno, “yakkho nu kho manusso nu kho”ti vimatiṃ uppādeti. So sace puriso hoti, atha naṃ “nāyaṃ aññassa kammassa anucchaviko”ti hatthiṃ vā rakkhāpenti assaṃ vā goṇe vā, tiṇakaṭṭhādīni vā āharāpenti, kheḷasarakaṃ vā gaṇhāpenti. Sace itthī hoti, atha naṃ hatthiassādīnaṃ bhattamāsādīni vā pacāpenti, kacavaraṃ vā chaḍḍāpenti, aññaṃ vā pana jigucchanīyakammaṃ kārenti. Evarūpassa pāpakammaṃ upadhivipattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Yo pana dubbhikkhakāle vā parihīnasampattikāle vā antarakappe vā nibbattati, tassa pāpakammaṃ kālavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Yo pana payogaṃ sampādetuṃ na jānāti, upasaṅkamitabbayuttakāle upasaṅkamituṃ na jānāti…pe… corikayuttakāle corikaṃ kātuṃ na jānāti, tassa pāpakammaṃ payogavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma.

Moreover, for one born in a woeful state, unwholesome kamma ripens on account of a failure of destination. Furthermore, if someone is born in the womb of a female slave or a female worker, they are ugly and deformed, causing the doubt—'Is this a yakkha or a human?' If it is a man, then thinking, 'He is unfit for any other work,' they make him guard elephants, horses, or cattle, or bring grass and firewood, or carry the spittoon. If it is a woman, they make her cook food such as cooked rice and beans for elephants, horses, and the like, or discard rubbish, or perform other disgusting tasks. For such a person, unwholesome kamma ripens on account of a failure of physical condition. Furthermore, if someone is born during a famine, a time of declining prosperity, or an intermediate kappa, their unwholesome kamma ripens on account of a failure of time. Furthermore, if someone does not know how to accomplish an undertaking, does not know how to approach at the proper time... or does not know how to commit theft at the proper time for theft, their unwholesome kamma ripens on account of a failure of application.

Yo pana iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanārahe kamme vijjamāneyeva gantvā duggatibhave nibbattati, tassa taṃ kammaṃ gativipattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Yo pana puññānubhāvena rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ gehe nibbattitvā kāṇo vā hoti kuṇī vā khañjo vā pakkhahato vā, tassa oparajjasenāpatibhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānādīni na anucchavikānīti na denti. Iccassa taṃ puññaṃ upadhivipattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Yo pana dubbhikkhakāle vā parihīnasampattikāle vā antarakappe vā manussesu nibbattati, tassa taṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ kālavipattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma. Yo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva payogaṃ sampādetuṃ na jānāti, tassa kalyāṇakammaṃ payogavipattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati nāma.

One who, while possessing wholesome kamma fit for experiencing a desirable object, goes on to be born in a state of woe—that kamma of theirs does not ripen, being counteracted by a defective destination. Furthermore, one who, by the power of merit, is born in the households of kings, great ministers, or the like, but is blind, or crooked-limbed, or lame, or paralyzed—positions such as viceroy, general, or treasurer are not considered suitable for them, and so they are not given. Thus, that merit of theirs does not ripen, being counteracted by a defective physical condition. One who is born among humans during a time of famine, a time of declining prosperity, or an intermediate eon—that wholesome kamma of theirs does not ripen, being counteracted by a defective time. One who does not know how to properly apply effort, according to the manner stated above—that wholesome kamma of theirs does not ripen, being counteracted by a defective application.

Kalyāṇakammena pana sugatibhave nibbattassa taṃ kammaṃ gatisampattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma[V 2.0113]. Rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ [P 2.0221] kule nibbattitvā upadhisampattiṃ pattassa [M 2.0113] attabhāvasamiddhiyaṃ ṭhitassa devanagare samussitaratanatoraṇasadisaṃ attabhāvaṃ disvā “imassa oparajjasenāpatibhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānādīni anucchavikānī”ti daharasseva sato tāni ṭhānantarāni denti, evarūpassa kalyāṇakammaṃ upadhisampattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Yo paṭhamakappikesu vā sulabhannapānakāle vā nibbattati, tassa kalyāṇakammaṃ kālasampattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Yo vuttanayeneva payogaṃ sampādetuṃ jānāti, tassa kammaṃ payogasampattiṃ āgamma vipaccati nāma. Evaṃ abhidhammapariyāyena soḷasa kammāni vibhattāni.

Moreover, for one reborn in a fortunate existence, that wholesome kamma ripens by reason of a perfection of destination. For one born into a royal or high official family, having attained a perfection of physical condition, standing in the splendor of their own being, seeing their splendid body like a jeweled archway raised in a celestial city, and thinking, 'These positions of viceroy, general, or treasurer are suitable for him,' even while young, they are given those higher positions—for such a person, wholesome kamma ripens by reason of a perfection of physical condition. For one born in the early ages of the world or at a time when food and drink are easily obtained, their wholesome kamma ripens by reason of a perfection of time. For one who knows how to successfully apply effort in the aforementioned manner, their kamma ripens by reason of a perfection of application. Thus, in the Abhidhamma method, sixteen types of kamma are classified.

Aparānipi paṭisambhidāmaggapariyāyena dvādasa kammāni vibhattāni. Seyyathidaṃ – “ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko, bhavissati kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko, bhavissati kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.234).

Furthermore, twelve kammas are distinguished by the method of the discourse on the Path of Discriminations. Namely: “There was kamma, there was the result of kamma; there was kamma, there was no result of kamma; there was kamma, there is the result of kamma; there was kamma, there is no result of kamma; there was kamma, there will be the result of kamma; there was kamma, there will be no result of kamma; there is kamma, there is the result of kamma; there is kamma, there is no result of kamma; there is kamma, there will be the result of kamma; there is kamma, there will be no result of kamma; there will be kamma, there will be the result of kamma; there will be kamma, there will be no result of kamma.”

Tattha yaṃ kammaṃ atīte āyūhitaṃ atīteyeva vipākavāraṃ labhi, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ janesi, rūpajanakaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhi, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janetuṃ nāsakkhi, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana atīte āyūhitaṃ etarahi laddhavipākavāraṃ paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ janetvā rūpajanakaṃ rūpaṃ janetvā ṭhitaṃ, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ aladdhavipākavāraṃ paṭisandhijanakaṃ vā paṭisandhiṃ [P 2.0222] rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janetuṃ nāsakkhi, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana atīte āyūhitaṃ anāgate vipākavāraṃ labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ rūpaṃ janetuṃ sakkhissati, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ anāgate vipākavāraṃ na labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janetuṃ na sakkhissati, taṃ ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ.
