Among these, whatever kamma was accumulated in the past and obtained its opportunity for fruition in the past itself—the kamma that generates rebirth-linking generated rebirth-linking, and the kamma that generates materiality generated materiality—that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there was the result of kamma.’ Furthermore, whatever kamma did not obtain its opportunity for fruition, and the kamma that generates rebirth-linking was unable to generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality was unable to generate materiality, that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there was no result of kamma.’ Furthermore, whatever kamma was accumulated in the past and has now, in the present, obtained its opportunity for fruition—the kamma that generates rebirth-linking having generated rebirth-linking, and the kamma that generates materiality having generated materiality, it remains—that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there is the result of kamma.’ Whatever kamma has not obtained its opportunity for fruition, and the kamma that generates rebirth-linking was unable to generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality was unable to generate materiality, that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there is no result of kamma.’ Furthermore, whatever kamma was accumulated in the past and will obtain its opportunity for fruition in the future—the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will be able to generate rebirth-linking, and the kamma that generates materiality will be able to generate materiality—that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there will be the result of kamma.’ Whatever kamma will not obtain its opportunity for fruition in the future, and the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will be unable to generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality will be unable to generate materiality, that is said to be: ‘There was kamma, there will be no result of kamma.’

Yaṃ [V 2.0114][M 2.0114] pana etarahi āyūhitaṃ etarahiyeva vipākavāraṃ labhati, taṃ atthi kammaṃ atthi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana etarahi vipākavāraṃ na labhati, taṃ atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana etarahi āyūhitaṃ anāgate vipākavāraṃ labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ rūpaṃ janetuṃ sakkhissati, taṃ atthi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janetuṃ sakkhissati, taṃ atthi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, whatever kamma is accumulated in the present and obtains its opportunity for fruition in this very present, is said to be: 'There is kamma, there is the result of kamma.' Furthermore, whatever kamma in the present does not obtain its opportunity for fruition, is said to be: 'There is kamma, there is no result of kamma.' Furthermore, whatever kamma is accumulated in the present and will obtain its opportunity for fruition in a future existence—the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will be able to generate rebirth-linking, and the kamma that generates materiality will be able to generate materiality—is said to be: 'There is kamma, there will be the result of kamma.' Furthermore, whatever kamma will not obtain its opportunity for fruition, and the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will be unable to generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality will be unable to generate materiality, is said to be: 'There is kamma, there will not be the result of kamma.'

Yaṃ panānāgate āyūhissati, anāgateyeva vipākavāraṃ labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janessati, taṃ bhavissati kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhissati, paṭisandhijanakaṃ paṭisandhiṃ rūpajanakaṃ vā rūpaṃ janetuṃ na sakkhissati, taṃ bhavissati kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipākoti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāmaggapariyāyena dvādasa kammāni vibhattāni.

Furthermore, whatever kamma will be accumulated in the future and will obtain its opportunity for fruition in that very future—the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality will generate materiality—is said to be: 'There will be kamma, there will be the result of kamma.' Furthermore, whatever kamma will not obtain its opportunity for fruition in the future, and the kamma that generates rebirth-linking will be unable to generate rebirth-linking, or the kamma that generates materiality will be unable to generate materiality, is said to be: 'There will be kamma, there will not be the result of kamma.' Thus, by the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, twelve kammas are classified.

Iti imāni ceva dvādasa abhidhammapariyāyena vibhattāni ca soḷasa kammāni attano ṭhānā osakkitvā suttantikapariyāyena vuttāni ekādasa kammāniyeva bhavanti. Tānipi tato osakkitvā tīṇiyeva kammāni honti diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ, upapajjavedanīyaṃ[P 2.0223], aparapariyāyavedanīyanti. Tesaṃ saṅkamanaṃ natthi, yathāṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhanti. Yadi hi diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ kammaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ vā aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ vā bhaveyya, “diṭṭhe vā dhamme”ti satthā na vadeyya. Sacepi upapajjavedanīyaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ vā aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ vā bhaveyya, “upapajja vā”ti satthā na vadeyya. Athāpi aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ vā upapajjavedanīyaṃ vā bhaveyya, “apare vā pariyāye”ti satthā na vadeyya.

Thus, both these twelve kammas and the sixteen kammas classified by way of the Abhidhamma, having withdrawn from their own positions, become only the eleven kammas spoken of by way of the Suttanta. Even these, having withdrawn from that, become only three kammas: that to be experienced in this very life, that to be experienced in the next life, and that to be experienced in a subsequent course. There is no transference among them; they remain just in their own place. Indeed, if kamma to be experienced in this very life were to become kamma to be experienced in the next life or kamma to be experienced in a subsequent course, the Teacher would not have said, “in this very life.” And if kamma to be experienced in the next life were to become kamma to be experienced in this very life or kamma to be experienced in a subsequent course, the Teacher would not have said, “in the next life.” Furthermore, if kamma to be experienced in a subsequent course were to become kamma to be experienced in this very life or kamma to be experienced in the next life, the Teacher would not have said, “in a subsequent course.”

Sukkapakkhepi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Ettha pana lobhe vigateti lobhe apagate niruddhe. Tālavatthukatanti tālavatthu viya kataṃ, matthakacchinnatālo viya puna aviruḷhisabhāvaṃ katanti attho. Anabhāvaṃ katanti anuabhāvaṃ kataṃ, yathā puna nuppajjati, evaṃ katanti attho. Evassūti evaṃ bhaveyyuṃ. Evameva khoti ettha bījāni viya kusalākusalaṃ [M 2.0115] kammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tāni agginā ḍahanapuriso viya yogāvacaro, aggi viya maggañāṇaṃ[V 2.0115], aggiṃ datvā bījānaṃ ḍahanakālo viya maggañāṇena kilesānaṃ daḍḍhakālo, masikatakālo viya pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ chinnamūlake katvā ṭhapitakālo, mahāvāte opunitvā nadiyā vā pavāhetvā appavattikatakālo viya upādinnakasantānassa nirodhena chinnamūlakānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ appaṭisandhikabhāvena nirujjhitvā puna bhavasmiṃ paṭisandhiṃ aggahitakālo veditabbo.

In the wholesome side also, the meaning should be understood by this very method. Here, however, 'when greed has vanished' means when greed has departed and ceased through the knowledge of the path to Arahantship. 'Made like a palm stump' means made like the base of a palm tree; the meaning is that it is made to have the nature of not sprouting again, like a palm tree with its crown cut off. 'Made non-existent' means made into a state of subsequent non-existence; the meaning is that it is made in such a way that it does not arise again. 'Evassu' means 'may they be thus.' Here, in the phrase 'Evameva kho,' wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be regarded as seeds; the yogī should be regarded as a man who burns them with fire; the knowledge of the path should be regarded as fire. Like the time of burning the seeds by applying fire, so should the time of burning the defilements with the knowledge of the path be regarded. Like the time of reducing to charcoal, so should the time of establishing the five aggregates as having their root-cause cut off be regarded. Like the time of making them non-recurrent by winnowing them in a great wind or floating them away in a river, so should be understood the time of not grasping rebirth-linking again in a future existence, when the five aggregates whose root-cause has been cut off cease with the state of no rebirth-linking, due to the cessation of the continuum of clung-to aggregates.

Mohajañcāpaviddasūti mohajañcāpi aviddasu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ so avidū andhabālo lobhajañca dosajañca mohajañcāti kammaṃ karoti, evaṃ karontena yaṃ tena pakataṃ kammaṃ appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ. Idheva taṃ vedaniyanti [P 2.0224] taṃ kammaṃ tena bālena idha sake attabhāveyeva vedanīyaṃ, tasseva taṃ attabhāve vipaccatīti attho. Vatthuṃ aññaṃ na vijjatīti tassa kammassa vipaccanatthāya aññaṃ vatthu natthi. Na hi aññena kataṃ kammaṃ aññassa attabhāve vipaccati. Tasmā lobhañca dosañca, mohajañcāpi viddasūti tasmā yo vidū medhāvī paṇḍito taṃ lobhajādibhedaṃ kammaṃ na karoti, so vijjaṃ uppādayaṃ bhikkhu, sabbā duggatiyo jahe, arahattamaggavijjaṃ uppādetvā taṃ vā pana vijjaṃ uppādento sabbā duggatiyo jahati. Desanāsīsamevetaṃ, sugatiyopi pana so khīṇāsavo jahatiyeva. Yampi cetaṃ “tasmā lobhañca dosañcā”ti vuttaṃ, etthāpi lobhadosasīsena lobhajañca dosajañca kammameva niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ suttantesupi gāthāyapi vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitanti.

“And that which is born of delusion, for the ignorant one” means: and the unwholesome kamma born of delusion, for the one who does not know. This is what is meant: whatever kamma that ignorant, blind fool performs—born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion—and in so doing, whatever kamma, whether minor or major, is done by that person. “It is to be experienced right here” means that kamma is to be experienced by that fool right here in his own state of existence; the meaning is that it ripens in his very own state of existence. “No other ground exists” means there is no other ground for the ripening of that kamma. For kamma done by one does not ripen in the state of existence of another. “Therefore, greed and hatred, and that which is born of delusion, for the wise one” means: therefore, whatever person is wise, intelligent, and discerning does not perform that kamma which is distinguished as being born of greed and so forth. “That bhikkhu, generating knowledge, would abandon all miserable destinations”: having generated the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, or while generating that very knowledge, one abandons all miserable destinations. This is merely the heading of the teaching; indeed, that one whose cankers are destroyed abandons even the happy destinations. And as for that which was said, “Therefore, greed and hatred…,” here too it should be understood that only kamma born of greed and born of hatred is indicated, with greed and hatred as the heading. Thus, in both the suttas and the verses, only the round of existence and the cessation of the round are discussed.

5. Hatthakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta

35. Pañcame āḷaviyanti āḷaviraṭṭhe. Gomaggeti gunnaṃ gamanamagge. Paṇṇasanthareti sayaṃ patitapaṇṇasanthare. Athāti evaṃ gunnaṃ gamanamaggaṃ ujuṃ mahāpathaṃ nissāya siṃsapāvane sayaṃ patitapaṇṇāni saṅkaḍḍhitvā katasanthare sugatamahācīvaraṃ pattharitvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinne tathāgate. Hatthako āḷavakoti hatthato hatthaṃ gatattā evaṃladdhanāmo āḷavako rājaputto. Etadavocāti etaṃ “kacci, bhante[M 2.0116], bhagavā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Kasmā pana sammāsambuddho taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā nisinno, kasmā rājakumāro tattha gatoti? Sammāsambuddho tāva aṭṭhuppattikāya dhammadesanāya samuṭṭhānaṃ disvā tattha nisinno, rājakumāropi pātova uṭṭhāya pañcahi upāsakasatehi parivuto buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto [P 2.0225] mahāmaggā okkamma gopathaṃ gahetvā “buddhānaṃ [V 2.0116] pūjanatthāya missakamālaṃ ocinissāmī”ti gacchanto satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, evaṃ so tattha gatoti. Sukhamasayitthāti sukhaṃ sayittha.

35. In the fifth sutta, 'at Āḷavī' (āḷaviyaṃ) means in the Āḷavī country. 'On the cow path' (gomagge) means on the path for the cows' movement. 'On a bed of leaves' (paṇṇasanthare) means on a bed of leaves that have fallen by themselves. Then (atha): thus, when the Tathāgata was seated in the Siṃsapā forest—having relied on the straight main road, the path for the cows' movement, on a bed made by sweeping together leaves that had fallen by themselves, having spread the Sugata's great robe, and having folded his legs cross-legged. 'Hatthaka of Āḷavī' (hatthako āḷavako) means the royal prince of Āḷavī, so named because he had gone from hand to hand. 'He spoke thus' (etadavoca) means he spoke this utterance beginning with, “I hope, venerable sir, the Blessed One…” Why, then, did the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One go to that place and sit down, and why did the royal prince go there? The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, for his part, seeing the arising of a reason for a Dhamma teaching, sat there. The royal prince, too, rising early in the morning, surrounded by five hundred lay followers, was going to attend upon the Buddha. Leaving the main road, he took a cow path, thinking, “I will gather a mixed garland to honor the Buddhas.” As he was going, he saw the Teacher, approached, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Thus he went there. 'Did you sleep comfortably?' (sukhamasayittha) means 'Did you sleep well?'

Antaraṭṭhakoti māghaphagguṇānaṃ antare aṭṭhadivasaparimāṇo kālo. Māghassa hi avasāne cattāro divasā, phagguṇassa ādimhi cattāroti ayaṃ “antaraṭṭhako”ti vuccati. Himapātasamayoti himassa patanasamayo. Kharāti pharusā kakkhaḷā vā. Gokaṇṭakahatāti navavuṭṭhe deve gāvīnaṃ akkantakkantaṭṭhāne khurantarehi kaddamo uggantvā tiṭṭhati, so vātātapena sukkho kakacadantasadiso hoti dukkhasamphasso. Taṃ sandhāyāha – “gokaṇṭakahatā bhūmī”ti. Gunnaṃ khurantarehi chinnātipi attho. Verambho vāto vāyatīti catūhi disāhi vāyanto vāto vāyati. Ekāya disāya vā dvīhi vā disāhi tīhi vā disāhi vāyanto vāto verambhoti na vuccati.

‘Mid-season’ (antaraṭṭhako) means the period of eight days between Māgha and Phagguna. Indeed, there are four days at the end of Māgha and four at the beginning of Phagguna; this is called the ‘mid-season.’ ‘The time of snowfall’ (himapātasamayo) means the time of snow falling. ‘Harsh’ (kharā) means rough or hard. ‘Afflicted by cow-hoof prints’ (gokaṇṭakahatā) means that when it has just rained, in places repeatedly trampled by cows, mud rises up from between their hooves and stands there; that mud, having dried in the wind and sun, becomes like the teeth of a saw and is painful to the touch. Referring to this, the Blessed One said: ‘The ground is afflicted by cow-hoof prints.’ It also has the meaning: ‘cut by the spaces between the hooves of cattle.’ ‘The Verambha wind blows’ (verambho vāto vāyati) means the wind blows from the four directions. A wind blowing from one, two, or three directions is not called a Verambha wind.

Tena hi rājakumārāti idaṃ satthā “ayaṃ rājakumāro lokasmiṃ neva sukhavāsino, na dukkhavāsino jānāti, jānāpessāmi na”nti upari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento āha. Tattha yathā te khameyyāti yathā tuyhaṃ rucceyya. Idhassāti imasmiṃ loke assa. Gonakatthatoti caturaṅgulādhikalomena kāḷakojavena atthato. Paṭikatthatoti uṇṇāmayena setattharaṇena atthato. Paṭalikatthatoti ghanapupphena uṇṇāmayaattharaṇena atthato. Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇoti [P 2.0226] kadalimigacammamayena uttamapaccattharaṇena atthato. Taṃ kira paccattharaṇaṃ setavatthassa upari kadalimigacammaṃ attharitvā sibbitvā karonti. Sauttaracchadoti saha uttaracchadena, upari baddhena rattavitānena saddhinti attho. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānoti sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti pallaṅkassa ubhato ṭhapitalohitakūpadhāno. Pajāpatiyoti bhariyāyo. Manāpena [M 2.0117] paccupaṭṭhitā assūti manāpena upaṭṭhānavidhānena paccupaṭṭhitā bhaveyyuṃ.

‘Then, young nobleman’ (tena hi rājakumāra) — the Teacher said this, extending the discourse, thinking: ‘This royal prince does not know those who dwell in happiness in the world, nor those who dwell in suffering; I will cause him to know.’ Therein, ‘as it might please you’ (yathā te khameyya) means as you would wish. ‘For one here’ (idhassa) means for one in this world. ‘With a long-fleeced coverlet’ (gonakatthatoti) means spread with a black coverlet with fleece more than four fingers long. ‘With a woolen coverlet’ (paṭikatthatoti) means spread with a white woolen covering. ‘With a floral-patterned coverlet’ (paṭalikatthatoti) means spread with a woolen covering with a thick floral pattern. ‘With the finest covering of kadali-deer hide’ (kadali-migapavarapaccattharaṇoti) means spread with a superior covering made of kadali-deer hide. It is said that they make this covering by spreading kadali-deer hide over white cloth and stitching it. ‘With a canopy’ (sauttaracchadoti) means together with an upper covering; the meaning is, together with a red canopy fastened above. ‘With red cushions at both ends’ (ubhatolohitakūpadhānoti) means having red cushions placed at both ends of the couch: a head-pillow and a foot-pillow. ‘Wives’ (pajāpatiyoti) means consorts. ‘They would be attended by what is pleasing’ (manāpena paccupaṭṭhitā assūti) means they would be attended upon with a pleasing manner of service.

Kāyikāti pañcadvārakāyaṃ khobhayamānā. Cetasikāti manodvāraṃ khobhayamānā. So rāgo tathāgatassa pahīnoti tathārūpo rāgo tathāgatassa pahīnoti attho. Yo pana tassa rāgo, na so tathāgatassa pahīno nāma. Dosamohesupi eseva nayo.

'Bodily' (kāyikā) means agitating the body of consciousness arising through the five sense doors. 'Mental' (cetasikā) means agitating the mind-door. 'That lust has been abandoned by the Tathāgata' (so rāgo tathāgatassa pahīno) means lust of that sort has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. But as for the lust of that person, it is not called 'abandoned by the Tathāgata'. The same method applies to hatred and delusion as well.

Brāhmaṇoti bāhitapāpo khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo. Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto[V 2.0117]. Na limpati kāmesūti vatthukāmesu ca kilesakāmesu ca taṇhādiṭṭhilepehi na limpati. Sītibhūtoti abbhantare tāpanakilesānaṃ abhāvena sītibhūto. Nirūpadhīti kilesūpadhīnaṃ abhāvena nirūpadhi. Sabbā āsattiyo chetvāti āsattiyo vuccanti taṇhāyo, tā sabbāpi rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu āsattavisattā āsattiyo chinditvā. Vineyya hadaye daranti hadayanissitaṃ darathaṃ vinayitvā vūpasametvā. Santiṃ pappuyya cetasoti cittassa kilesanibbānaṃ pāpuṇitvā. Karaṇavacanaṃ vā etaṃ “sabbacetaso samannāharitvā”tiādīsu viya, cetasā nibbānaṃ pāpuṇitvāti attho.

'A brahmin' (brāhmaṇoti) means an Arahant who has banished evil, a brahmin whose taints are destroyed. 'Fully extinguished' (parinibbutoti) means fully extinguished by the extinction of defilements. 'He is not stained by sensual pleasures' (na limpati kāmesūti) means he is not stained by the defilements of craving and views regarding both object-based sensual pleasures and defilement-based sensual pleasures. 'Become cool' (sītibhūtoti) means he has become cool internally due to the absence of defilements that cause burning. 'Without acquisitions' (nirūpadhīti) means without acquisitions due to the absence of the acquisitions that are defilements. In 'having cut off all attachments' (sabbā āsattiyo chetvāti), cravings are called 'attachments'; because they attach and cling in various ways to objects such as forms, it means having cut off all those attachments. 'Having removed the distress in the heart' (vineyya hadaye daranti) means having removed and calmed the distress that is based in the heart. 'Having attained peace of mind' (santiṃ pappuyya cetasoti) means having attained the stilling of the defilements of the mind. Or, this word `cetaso` is in the instrumental case, as in such phrases as 'having brought together the whole mind' (sabbacetaso samannāharitvā); the meaning is: having attained Nibbāna with the mind.

6. Devadūtasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Messengers

36. Chaṭṭhe [P 2.0227] devadūtānīti devadūtā. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – devoti maccu, tassa dūtāti devadūtā. Jiṇṇabyādhimatā hi saṃvegajananaṭṭhena “idāni te maccusamīpaṃ gantabba”nti codenti viya, tasmā devadūtāti vuccanti. Devā viya dūtātipi devadūtā. Yathā hi alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya devatāya ākāse ṭhatvā “tvaṃ asukadivase marissasī”ti vutte tassā vacanaṃ saddhātabbaṃ hoti; evamevaṃ jiṇṇabyādhimatāpi dissamānā “tvampi evaṃdhammo”ti codenti viya, tesañca taṃ vacanaṃ anaññathābhāvitāya devatāya byākaraṇasadisameva hotīti devā viya dūtāti devadūtā. Visuddhidevānaṃ dūtātipi devadūtā. Sabbabodhisattā hi jiṇṇabyādhimatapabbajite disvāva saṃvegaṃ āpajjitvā nikkhamma pabbajiṃsu. Evaṃ visuddhidevānaṃ dūtātipi devadūtā. Idha pana liṅgavipallāsena “devadūtānī”ti vuttaṃ.

36. In the sixth sutta, `devadūtāni` means `devadūtā`. Here, this is the meaning of the word: `deva` is said to mean `maccu`, death; `dūtā` are his messengers, thus `devadūtā`. For the old, the sick, and the dead, by reason of causing a sense of spiritual urgency, are as if admonishing, saying, "Now it is time for you to go into the presence of death." Therefore, they are called `devadūtā`. Also, `devadūtā` means "messengers like devas." For just as when an adorned and prepared deity, standing in the sky, says, "You will die on such-and-such a day," her word is to be believed; in the very same way, the old, the sick, and the dead, when seen, are as if admonishing, saying, "You too are of such a nature." And their word, because of its unalterable nature, is just like the declaration of a deity. Thus, "messengers like devas" means `devadūtā`. Also, `devadūtā` means "messengers of the Visuddhidevas (pure devas)." For all Bodhisattas, upon seeing the old, the sick, the dead, and the renunciant, attained a sense of spiritual urgency, went forth from home, and became renunciants. Thus, they are also called `devadūtā` as "messengers of the Visuddhidevas." But here, it is said as `devadūtāni` through a change of gender from masculine to neuter.

Kāyena [M 2.0118] duccaritantiādi kasmā āraddhaṃ? Devadūtānuyuñjanaṭṭhānupakkamakammadassanatthaṃ. Iminā hi kammena ayaṃ satto niraye nibbattati, atha naṃ tattha yamo rājā devadūte samanuyuñjati. Tattha kāyena duccaritaṃ caratīti kāyadvārena tividhaṃ duccaritaṃ carati. Vācāyāti vacīdvārena catubbidhaṃ duccaritaṃ carati. Manasāti manodvārena tividhaṃ duccaritaṃ carati.

Why was the passage beginning with 'misconduct by body' undertaken? For the purpose of showing the kamma that is the cause for being questioned about the divine messengers. For by this kamma, this being is reborn in hell, and there King Yama questions him about the divine messengers. Therein, 'he practices misconduct by body' means he practices the threefold misconduct through the body-door. 'By speech' means he practices the fourfold misconduct through the speech-door. 'By mind' means he practices the threefold misconduct through the mind-door.

Tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālāti ettha ekacce therā “nirayapālā nāma natthi, yantarūpaṃ viya kammameva kāraṇaṃ kāretī”ti vadanti. Taṃ “atthi niraye nirayapālāti, āmantā. Atthi [V 2.0118] ca kāraṇikā”tiādinā nayena abhidhamme (kathā. 866) paṭisedhitameva. Yathā hi manussaloke kammakāraṇakārakā atthi, evameva niraye nirayapālā atthīti. Yamassa [P 2.0228] raññoti yamarājā nāma vemānikapetarājā. Ekasmiṃ kāle dibbavimāne dibbakapparukkhadibbauyyānadibbanāṭakādisabbasampattiṃ anubhavati, ekasmiṃ kāle kammavipākaṃ, dhammiko rājā, na cesa ekova hoti, catūsu pana dvāresu cattāro janā honti. Amatteyyoti mātu hito matteyyo, mātari sammā paṭipannoti attho. Na matteyyoti amatteyyo, mātari micchā paṭipannoti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Abrahmaññoti ettha ca khīṇāsavā brāhmaṇā nāma, tesu micchā paṭipanno abrahmañño nāma.

Then, monks, regarding the hell-wardens, some elders say, 'There are no beings called hell-wardens; like a mechanical figure, it is kamma alone that causes the punishment.' This has been refuted in the Abhidhamma by the method stating, 'Are there hell-wardens in hell? Yes. And there are tormentors,' and so on. For just as in the human world there are those who inflict punishment for deeds, even so in hell there are hell-wardens. Regarding 'of King Yama': King Yama is a king of the Vimanika Petas. At one time, he enjoys all prosperity in a divine mansion—divine wish-fulfilling trees, divine parks, divine dancers, and so on; at another time, he experiences the result of his kamma. He is a righteous king. And he is not the only one; rather, at the four gates, there are four persons. Regarding 'amatteyya': 'Matteyya' is one who is for the welfare of his mother, meaning one who behaves rightly towards his mother. Not 'matteyya' is 'amatteyya', meaning one who behaves wrongly towards his mother. This is the same method for the remaining terms. And regarding 'abrahmañña': those whose taints are destroyed are called 'brahmins'. One who behaves wrongly towards them is called 'abrahmañña'.

Samanuyuñjatīti anuyogavattaṃ āropento pucchati, laddhiṃ patiṭṭhāpento pana samanuggāhati nāma, kāraṇaṃ pucchanto samanubhāsati nāma. Nāddasanti attano santike pahitassa kassaci devadūtassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vadati.

'He questions' means he asks, imposing the course of inquiry. One who, however, is establishing a view is said to 'firmly uphold' it. One who asks for a reason is said to 'discuss appropriately'. He says this, 'I did not see,' with reference to the absence of any divine messenger having been sent to his presence.

Atha naṃ yamo “nāyaṃ bhāsitassa atthaṃ sallakkhetī”ti ñatvā atthaṃ sallakkhāpetukāmo ambhotiādimāha. Tattha jiṇṇanti jarājiṇṇaṃ. Gopānasivaṅkanti gopānasī viya vaṅkaṃ. Bhogganti bhaggaṃ. Imināpissa vaṅkabhāvameva dīpeti. Daṇḍaparāyaṇanti daṇḍapaṭisaraṇaṃ daṇḍadutiyaṃ. Pavedhamānanti kampamānaṃ. Āturanti jarāturaṃ. Khaṇḍadantanti jarānubhāvena khaṇḍitadantaṃ. Palitakesanti paṇḍarakesaṃ. Vilūnanti luñcitvā gahitakesaṃ viya [M 2.0119] khallāṭaṃ. Khalitasiranti mahākhallāṭasīsaṃ. Valitanti sañjātavaliṃ. Tilakāhatagattanti [P 2.0229] setatilakakāḷatilakehi vikiṇṇasarīraṃ. Jarādhammoti jarāsabhāvo, aparimutto jarāya, jarā nāma mayhaṃ abbhantareyeva pavattatīti. Parato byādhidhammo maraṇadhammoti padadvayepi eseva nayo.

Then Yama, knowing, “This one does not mark the meaning of what was said,” and wishing to make him mark the meaning, spoke the words beginning with ‘Ambho’. Herein, ‘aged’ means aged and worn out. ‘Bent like a rafter’ means bent like a rafter. ‘Broken’ means shattered. By this, it also reveals his bent state. ‘Dependent on a staff’ means relying on a staff, having a staff as a second. ‘Trembling’ means shaking. ‘Afflicted’ means afflicted by old age. ‘With broken teeth’ means having teeth broken by the power of age. ‘With gray hair’ means having white hair. ‘Vilūna’ means like hair that has been plucked out. ‘Khalitasira’ means having a bald head. ‘Wrinkled’ means having well-formed wrinkles. ‘With a body marked by spots’ means a body scattered with white and black moles. ‘Subject to aging’ means having the nature of aging, not freed from aging; aging indeed operates right within me. Further on, for the two phrases, ‘subject to sickness’ and ‘subject to death’, this is the same method.

Paṭhamaṃ devadūtaṃ samanuyuñjitvāti ettha jarājiṇṇasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya taruṇo ahosiṃ ūrubalī bāhubalī javasampanno, tassa me tā balajavasampattiyo antarahitā, vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, jarāyamhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi jarāya aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi jarā āgamissati. Iti tassā pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti[V 2.0119]. Tenevesa devadūto nāma jāto. Ābādhikanti bādhikaṃ. Dukkhitanti dukkhappattaṃ. Bāḷhagilānanti adhimattagilānaṃ.

In the phrase, ‘Having questioned the first divine messenger,’ the aged, worn-out being speaks thus in essence: ‘Look, sirs, I too was young like you, strong in thighs, strong in arms, and endowed with speed. For me, those accomplishments of strength and speed have vanished. Though my hands and feet exist, they do not perform the function of hands and feet. Due to not being freed from aging, I have become like this. It is not only I; you too are not freed from aging. For just as aging has come to me, so too will aging come to you. Therefore, before its arrival, do what is wholesome.’ For that very reason, this one has become known as a divine messenger. ‘Ābādhikaṃ’ means having an affliction. ‘Dukkhitaṃ’ means having reached suffering. ‘Bāḷhagilānaṃ’ means exceedingly ill.

Dutiyaṃ devadūtanti etthapi gilānasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “passatha, bho, ahampi tumhe viya nirogo ahosiṃ, somhi etarahi byādhinā abhihato, sake muttakarīse palipanno, uṭṭhātumpi na sakkomi. Vijjamānāpi me hatthapādā hatthapādakiccaṃ na karonti, byādhitomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi byādhito aparimuttāva. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi byādhi āgamissati. Iti tassa pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenevesa devadūto nāma jāto.

Here too, regarding the second divine messenger, the sick being, in essence, is said to speak thus: 'Behold, sirs, I too was once healthy like you, but now I am afflicted by illness, wallowing in my own urine and feces, unable even to rise. Though my hands and feet exist, they do not perform their functions; due to not being free from illness, I have become like this. It is not only I, for you too are not free from illness. Truly, just as illness has come to me, so too will illness come to you. Therefore, before it arrives, do what is wholesome.' For that very reason, this is called a divine messenger.

Ekāhamatantiādīsu ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamato, taṃ ekāhamataṃ. Parato [P 2.0230] padadvayepi eseva nayo. Bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathākkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātakaṃ. Vinīlo vuccati viparibhinnavaṇṇo, vinīlova vinīlako, taṃ vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Vipubbakanti vissandamānapubbakaṃ, paribhinnaṭṭhāne hi paggharitena pubbena palimakkhitanti attho.

Regarding 'ekāhamata' and so on: 'For one who is dead, one day has passed,' thus it is 'ekāhamata'; this refers to that 'ekāhamata'. For the two terms that follow, the method is the same. Like a leather bag inflated by wind, it is called 'uddhumātaka' (bloated) because of the state of swelling that arises progressively from the exhaustion of the life faculty. A corpse of spoiled, dark color is called 'vinīla' (livid). 'Vinīla' itself is 'vinīlaka'; this refers to that 'vinīlaka'. Alternatively, because of its repulsiveness, it is a repulsive, spoiled, dark-colored corpse; therefore, it is 'vinīlaka'. 'Vipubbaka' (festering) means having oozing pus; the meaning is that it is smeared with pus that has flowed out from where it has burst.

Tatiyaṃ [M 2.0120] devadūtanti ettha matakasatto atthato evaṃ vadati nāma – “passatha, bho, maṃ āmakasusāne chaḍḍitaṃ uddhumātakādibhāvappattaṃ, maraṇatomhi aparimuttatāya ediso jāto. Na kho panāhameva, tumhepi maraṇato aparimuttā. Yatheva hi mayhaṃ, evaṃ tumhākampi maraṇaṃ āgamissati. Iti tassa pure āgamanāva kalyāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Tenevassa devadūto nāma jāto.

Here, regarding the third divine messenger, the dead being, in essence, is said to speak thus: 'Behold me, sirs, cast into the charnel ground, having reached the state of being bloated and so on. Due to not being free from death, I have become like this. Indeed, it is not only I; you too are not free from death. Truly, just as death has come to me, so too will death come to you. Therefore, before it arrives, do what is wholesome.' For that very reason, this one has become known as a divine messenger.

Imaṃ pana devadūtānuyogaṃ ko labhati, ko na labhati? Yena tāva bahuṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ, so gantvā niraye nibbattatiyeva. Yena pana parittaṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ, so labhati. Yathā hi sabhaṇḍaṃ coraṃ gahetvā kattabbameva karonti na vinicchinanti. Anuvijjitvā gahitaṃ pana vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ nayanti, so vinicchayaṃ labhati. Evaṃsampadametaṃ. Parittapāpakammā hi attano dhammatāyapi saranti, sārīyamānāpi saranti.

Furthermore, who obtains this interrogation by the divine messengers, and who does not? One by whom much evil has been done, having gone to hell, is certainly reborn there. But one by whom little evil has been done obtains it. Indeed, it is just as when they catch a thief with the stolen goods, they only carry out what must be done; they do not hold a trial. But one who is caught after investigation, they lead to a place of judgment, and that person obtains a judgment. This analogy should be understood thus. For those with little evil kamma remember by their own nature, and they also remember when reminded.

Tattha [V 2.0120] dīghajayantadamiḷo nāma attano dhammatāya sari. So kira damiḷo sumanagirimahāvihāre ākāsacetiyaṃ rattapaṭena pūjesi, atha niraye ussadasāmante nibbatto aggijālasaddaṃ sutvāva attanā pūjitapaṭaṃ anussari, so gantvā sagge nibbatto. Aparopi puttassa daharabhikkhuno khalisāṭakaṃ dento pādamūle ṭhapesi, maraṇakālamhi paṭapaṭāti sadde nimittaṃ gaṇhi[P 2.0231], sopi ussadasāmante nibbatto jālasaddena taṃ sāṭakaṃ anussaritvā sagge nibbatto. Evaṃ tāva attano dhammatāya kusalaṃ kammaṃ saritvā sagge nibbattatīti.

Among them, a Tamil named Dīghajayanta remembered by his own nature. It is said that this Tamil made an offering at the open-air cetiya in the Sumanagiri Mahāvihāra with a red cloth. Then, having been reborn in the vicinity of an Ussada hell, just upon hearing the sound of the flames of hell-fire, he remembered the cloth he had offered. Having gone from there, he was reborn in heaven. Another person also, while giving a coarse cloth to his son who was a young bhikkhu, placed it at his feet; at the time of death, he took the sound 'paṭapaṭa' as a sign. He too, having been reborn in the vicinity of an Ussada hell, remembered that cloth upon hearing the sound of the flames and was reborn in heaven. Thus, by remembering wholesome kamma by one's own nature, one is reborn in heaven.

Attano dhammatāya asarante pana tayo devadūte pucchati. Tattha koci paṭhamena devadūtena sarati, koci dutiyatatiyehi, koci tīhipi nassarati. Taṃ yamo rājā disvā sayaṃ sāreti. Eko kira amacco sumanapupphakumbhena mahācetiyaṃ pūjetvā yamassa pattiṃ adāsi, taṃ akusalakammena niraye nibbattaṃ yamassa santikaṃ nayiṃsu. Tasmiṃ tīhipi devadūtehi kusalaṃ asarante yamo sayaṃ olokento disvā – “nanu tvaṃ mahācetiyaṃ sumanapupphakumbhena pūjetvā mayhaṃ pattiṃ adāsī”ti sāresi, so tasmiṃ kāle saritvā devalokaṃ gato[M 2.0121]. Yamo pana sayaṃ oloketvāpi apassanto – “mahādukkhaṃ nāma anubhavissati ayaṃ satto”ti tuṇhī ahosi.

But as for those who do not remember by their own nature, he questions them about the three divine messengers. There, some remember by means of the first divine messenger, some by means of the second and third, and some do not remember even by means of all three. Seeing him, King Yama himself reminds him. It is said that a certain minister, having worshipped the Great Stupa with a pot of sumana flowers, gave a share of merit to Yama. Having been reborn in hell due to unwholesome kamma, they led him into Yama's presence. When he did not remember the wholesome deed even with the three divine messengers, Yama himself, looking and seeing, reminded him: 'Did you not worship the Great Stupa with a pot of sumana flowers and give a share of merit to me?' Remembering at that moment, he went to the divine realm. But Yama, even after looking himself and not seeing, remained silent, thinking, 'This being will indeed experience great suffering.'

Tattaṃ ayokhilanti tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ sampajjalitāya lohapathaviyā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā dakkhiṇahatthe tālappamāṇaṃ ayasūlaṃ pavesenti, tathā vāmahatthādīsu. Yathā ca taṃ uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā, evaṃ urenapi vāmapassenapi dakkhiṇapassenapi nipajjāpetvā te taṃ kammakāraṇaṃ karontiyeva. Saṃvesetvāti jalitāya lohapathaviyā tigāvutaṃ attabhāvaṃ nipajjāpetvā. Kuṭhārīhīti mahatīhi gehassa ekapakkhacchadanamattāhi kuṭhārīhi tacchanti, lohitaṃ nadī hutvā sandati, lohapathavito jālā uṭṭhahitvā tacchitaṭṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti, mahādukkhaṃ uppajjati. Tacchantā pana suttāhataṃ karitvā dāruṃ viya aṭṭhaṃsampi chaḷaṃsampi karonti. Vāsīhīti mahāsuppappamāṇāhi vāsīhi. Rathe yojetvāti saddhiṃ yugayottapakkharathacakkakubbarapājanehi sabbato pajjalite rathe yojetvā. Mahantanti [P 2.0232] mahākūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ. Āropentīti sampajjalitehi ayamuggarehi pothentā āropenti. Sakimpi uddhanti supakkuthitāya ukkhaliyā pakkhittataṇḍulā viya uddhamadhotiriyañca gacchati. Mahānirayeti avīcimahānirayamhi.

Regarding 'a heated iron stake': They make the three-gāvuta-long body lie face-up on the blazing iron ground and drive an iron stake the size of a palm-tree trunk into the right hand, and likewise into the left hand and other limbs. Just as they make it lie face-up, so too they make it lie on its chest, on its left side, and on its right side, and they perform that very act of torment. Regarding 'having driven in': It means making the three-gāvuta-long body lie on the blazing iron ground. Regarding 'with axes': They chop with great axes the size of one side of a house's roof; blood flows like a river; flames rise from the iron ground and seize the chopped places, and great suffering arises. While chopping, having marked it as with a chalk line, they make it eight-cornered or six-cornered like timber. Regarding 'with adzes': It means with adzes the size of large winnowing baskets. Regarding 'harnessing to a chariot': It means harnessing to a chariot blazing on all sides, complete with yoke, straps, chariot fittings, chariot wheels, pole, and goad. Regarding 'great': It means the size of a great gabled house. Regarding 'they place upon': Beating with blazing iron mallets, they place him upon it. Regarding 'even once upwards': Like rice grains thrown into a well-boiling cooking pot, he goes upwards, downwards, and sideways. Regarding 'in the great hell': It means in the Avīci great hell.

Bhāgaso [V 2.0121] mitoti bhāge ṭhapetvā vibhatto. Pariyantoti parikkhitto. Ayasāti upari ayapaṭṭena chādito. Samantā yojanasataṃ, pharitvā tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati, yathā taṃ samantā yojanasate ṭhatvā olokentassa akkhīni yamakagoḷakā viya nikkhamanti.

Regarding 'measured out in portions': It means divided by being placed into portions. Regarding 'bounded': It means enclosed all around. Regarding 'covered with iron': It means covered above with an iron plate. Regarding 'it stands pervading a hundred yojanas all around': It stands pervading in such a way that when one looks at it from a hundred yojanas around, one's eyes bulge out like a pair of balls.

Hīnakāyūpagāti hīnaṃ kāyaṃ upagatā hutvā. Upādāneti taṇhādiṭṭhiggahaṇe. Jātimaraṇasambhaveti jātiyā ca maraṇassa ca kāraṇabhūte. Anupādāti catūhi upādānehi anupādiyitvā. Jātimaraṇasaṅkhayeti jātimaraṇasaṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne vimuccanti. Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutāti diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve sabbakilesanibbānena nibbutā. Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccagunti sakalavaṭṭadukkhaṃ atikkantā.

Regarding 'gone to an inferior group of beings': It means having gone to an inferior group of beings. Regarding 'in clinging': It means in the grasping by craving and wrong views. Regarding 'in what is a cause of birth and death': It means in what is the cause of both birth and death. Regarding 'without clinging': It means without clinging by means of the four kinds of clinging. Regarding 'in the destruction of birth and death': It means they are liberated in Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of birth and death. Regarding 'quenched in this very life': It means quenched in this very life, in this very existence, by the quenching of all defilements. Regarding 'they have overcome all suffering': It means they have transcended all the suffering of the round of existence.

7. Catumahārājasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse of the Four Great Kings

37. Sattame [M 2.0122] amaccā pārisajjāti paricārikadevatā. Imaṃ lokaṃ anuvicarantīti aṭṭhamīdivase kira sakko devarājā cattāro mahārājāno āṇāpeti – “tātā, ajja aṭṭhamīdivase manussalokaṃ anuvicaritvā puññāni karontānaṃ nāmagottaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgacchathā”ti. Te gantvā attano paricārake pesenti – “gacchatha, tātā, manussalokaṃ vicaritvā puññakārakānaṃ nāmagottāni suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhitvā ānethā”ti. Te tathā karonti. Tena vuttaṃ – “imaṃ lokaṃ anuvicarantī”ti. Kacci [P 2.0233] bahūtiādi tesaṃ upaparikkhākāradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ upaparikkhantā hi te anuvicaranti. Tattha uposathaṃ upavasantīti māsassa aṭṭhavāre uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhahanti. Paṭijāgarontīti paṭijāgarauposathakammaṃ nāma karonti. Taṃ karontā ekasmiṃ addhamāse catunnaṃ uposathadivasānaṃ paccuggamanānuggamanavasena karonti. Pañcamīuposathaṃ paccuggacchantā catutthiyaṃ uposathikā honti, anugacchantā chaṭṭhiyaṃ. Aṭṭhamīuposathaṃ paccuggacchantā sattamiyaṃ, anugacchantā navamiyaṃ. Cātuddasiṃ paccuggacchantā terasiyaṃ, pannarasīuposathaṃ anugacchantā pāṭipade uposathikā honti. Puññāni karontīti saraṇagamananiccasīlapupphapūjādhammassavanapadīpasahassaāropanavihārakaraṇādīni nānappakārāni puññāni karonti. Te evaṃ anuvicaritvā puññakammakārakānaṃ nāmagottāni sovaṇṇamaye paṭṭe likhitvā āharitvā catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ denti. Puttā imaṃ lokaṃ anuvicarantīti catūhi mahārājehi [V 2.0122] purimanayeneva pahitattā anuvicaranti. Tadahūti taṃdivasaṃ. Uposatheti uposathadivase.

37. In the seventh discourse, 'ministers and attendants' means attendant deities. Regarding 'They roam this world': It is said that on the eighth day, Sakka, the king of the devas, commands the Four Great Kings: 'My good sirs, today, on the eighth day, roam the human world, collect the names and clans of those performing meritorious deeds, and return.' They go and send their own attendants, saying: 'Go, my good sirs, wander the human world, write the names and clans of the merit-makers on a golden plate, and bring it back.' They do so. Therefore, it is said: 'They roam this world.' The passage beginning 'Are there many?' is said to show their manner of investigation, for they roam while investigating in this way. Therein, 'observing the Uposatha' means they undertake the Uposatha factors eight times a month. 'Keeping vigil' means they perform what is called the Uposatha-observance of keeping vigil. While doing so, in one half-month, they perform it with respect to the four Uposatha days by way of anticipating and following up. Those anticipating the fifth-day Uposatha observe it on the fourth, and those following up observe it on the sixth. Those anticipating the eighth-day Uposatha observe it on the seventh, and those following up observe it on the ninth. Those anticipating the fourteenth-day Uposatha observe it on the thirteenth, and those following up the fifteenth-day Uposatha observe it on the first day of the next fortnight. 'Performing meritorious deeds' means they perform various kinds of meritorious deeds, such as going for refuge, constant virtue, offering flowers, listening to the Dhamma, lighting a thousand lamps, building monasteries, and so on. Having roamed thus, they write the names and clans of the makers of meritorious deeds on a golden plate, bring it, and give it to the Four Great Kings. Regarding 'The sons roam this world': They roam because they are sent by the Four Great Kings in the same manner as before. Regarding 'on that day': It means on that day. Regarding 'on the Uposatha': It means on the Uposatha day.

Sace, bhikkhave, appakā hontīti catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ amaccā pārisajjā tā tā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo upasaṅkamanti, tato taṃ upanissāya adhivatthā devatā “mahārājānaṃ amaccā āgatā”ti paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gacchanti. Te paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā “kacci nu kho mārisā bahū manussā matteyyā”ti vuttanayena manussānaṃ puññapaṭipattiṃ pucchitvā “āma, mārisa, imasmiṃ gāme asuko ca asuko ca puññāni karontī”ti vutte tesaṃ nāmagottaṃ likhitvā aññattha [M 2.0123] gacchanti. Atha cātuddasiyaṃ catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ puttāpi tameva suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ gahetvā teneva nayena anuvicarantā nāmagottāni likhanti. Tadahuposathe [P 2.0234] pannarase cattāropi mahārājāno teneva nayena tasmiṃyeva suvaṇṇapaṭṭe nāmagottāni likhanti. Te suvaṇṇapaṭṭaparimāṇeneva – “imasmiṃ kāle manussā appakā, imasmiṃ kāle bahukā”ti jānanti. Taṃ sandhāya “sace, bhikkhave, appakā honti manussā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānanti paṭhamaṃ abhinibbatte tettiṃsa devaputte upādāya evaṃladdhanāmānaṃ. Tesaṃ pana uppattikathā dīghanikāye sakkapañhasuttavaṇṇanāya vitthāritā. Tenāti tena ārocanena, tena vā puññakārakānaṃ appakabhāvena. Dibbā vata, bho, kāyā parihāyissantīti navanavānaṃ devaputtānaṃ apātubhāvena devakāyā parihāyissanti, ramaṇīyaṃ dasayojanasahassaṃ devanagaraṃ suññaṃ bhavissati. Paripūrissanti asurakāyāti cattāro apāyā paripūrissanti. Iminā “mayaṃ paripuṇṇe devanagare devasaṅghamajjhe nakkhattaṃ kīḷituṃ na labhissāmā”ti anattamanā honti. Sukkapakkhepi imināva upāyena attho veditabbo.

Regarding 'If, monks, there are few': the ministers and retinues of the Four Great Kings approach those villages, towns, and royal cities. Then, relying on that, the deities dwelling there take an offering and go to their presence. Taking the offering, they ask about the virtuous practice of humans in the manner already stated. When it is said, 'Yes, good sirs, in this village, so-and-so and so-and-so perform meritorious deeds,' they write down their name and clan and go elsewhere. Then, on the fourteenth day, the sons of the Four Great Kings also take that same golden slate and, wandering about in the same way, write down names and clans. On that Uposatha day, the fifteenth, the Four Great Kings themselves, in the same way, write down the names and clans on that very golden slate. By the measure of the golden slate itself, they know: 'At this time, humans are few; at this time, they are many.' With reference to this, the passage beginning 'If, monks, there are few humans...' was spoken. Regarding 'of the Tāvatiṃsa devas': this name was obtained on account of the thirty-three devas who first arose. Their origin story is detailed in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya. 'Therefore' means by that announcement, or by the scarcity of those who perform meritorious deeds. 'Indeed, sirs, the divine hosts will decline' means that due to the non-appearance of new devas, the divine hosts will decline, and the delightful celestial city of ten thousand yojanas will become empty. 'The hosts of asuras will be filled' means the four states of deprivation will be filled. By this, they are displeased, thinking, 'We will not be able to enjoy a festival in the midst of the divine assembly in a fully populated celestial city.' Regarding the bright fortnight also, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindoti attano sakkadevarājakālaṃ sandhāya katheti. Ekassa vā sakkassa ajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā kathetīti vuttaṃ. Anunayamānoti anubodhayamāno. Tāyaṃ velāyanti tasmiṃ kāle.

“In the past, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas”: he spoke with reference to his own time as Sakka, king of the devas. Or, it is said that he spoke having grasped the inclination of a certain Sakka. Anunayamāno means making understand fittingly. Tāyaṃ velāyaṃ means at that time of so understanding fittingly.

Pāṭihāriyapakkhañcāti ettha pāṭihāriyapakkho nāma antovasse temāsaṃ nibaddhuposatho, taṃ asakkontassa dvinnaṃ pavāraṇānaṃ antare ekamāsaṃ nibaddhuposatho, tampi asakkontassa paṭhamapavāraṇato paṭṭhāya eko addhamāso pāṭihāriyapakkhoyeva nāma. Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgatanti aṭṭhahi [V 2.0123] guṇaṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Yopissa [P 2.0235] mādiso naroti yopi satto mādiso bhaveyya. Sakkopi kira vuttappakārassa uposathakammassa guṇaṃ jānitvā dve devalokasampattiyo pahāya māsassa aṭṭha vāre uposathaṃ upavasati. Tasmā evamāha. Aparo nayo – yopissa mādiso naroti yopi satto mādiso assa, mayā pattaṃ [M 2.0124] sampattiṃ pāpuṇituṃ iccheyyāti attho. Sakkā hi evarūpena uposathakammena sakkasampattiṃ pāpuṇitunti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Herein, regarding 'and the pāṭihāriyapakkha': the pāṭihāriyapakkha is the Uposatha observed uninterruptedly for three months within the rains-retreat. For one unable to do so, it is the Uposatha observed uninterruptedly for one month between the two Pavāraṇās. For one unable to do that either, a single half-month starting from the first Pavāraṇā is also called the pāṭihāriyapakkha. Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ means endowed with the eight factors which are virtuous qualities. Yopi'ssa mādiso naro means whatever being might be like me. It is said that Sakka, knowing the virtue of the Uposatha observance of the aforesaid kind, having abandoned two heavenly attainments, observes the Uposatha eight times a month. Therefore, he spoke thus. Another interpretation: Yopi'ssa mādiso naro means 'whatever being should be like me and should wish to attain the accomplishment that I have attained'—this is the meaning. For indeed, by such an act of observing the Uposatha, it is possible to attain the splendor of Sakka. This is the intention of Sakka herein.

Vusitavāti vutthavāso. Katakaraṇīyoti catūhi maggehi kattabbakiccaṃ katvā ṭhito. Ohitabhāroti khandhabhārakilesabhāraabhisaṅkhārabhāre otāretvā ṭhito. Anuppattasadatthoti sadattho vuccati arahattaṃ, taṃ anuppatto. Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanoti yena saṃyojanena baddho bhavesu ākaḍḍhīyati, tassa khīṇattā parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano. Sammadaññā vimuttoti hetunā nayena kāraṇena jānitvā vimutto. Kallaṃ vacanāyāti yuttaṃ vattuṃ.

Vusitavā means one who has lived the life, which is the noble path that has been practiced. Katakaraṇīyo means one who, having done the task to be done—such as full understanding—by means of the four noble paths, is established. Ohitabhāro means one who, having laid down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of the defilements, and the burden of volitional formations—which are wholesome and unwholesome kamma—is established. Anuppattasadattho: sadattha (one's own welfare) is said to be the fruit of Arahantship, and he has duly attained it. Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano means one whose fetter of becoming is destroyed because of the destruction of that fetter by which, being bound, one is dragged into states of existence. Sammadaññā vimutto means one who is liberated by knowing with cause, with method, and with reason. Kallaṃ vacanāya means it is suitable to say.

Yopissa mādiso naroti yopi mādiso khīṇāsavo assa, sopi evarūpaṃ uposathaṃ upavaseyyāti uposathakammassa guṇaṃ jānanto evaṃ vadeyya. Aparo nayo yopissa mādiso naroti yopi satto mādiso assa, mayā pattaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇituṃ iccheyyāti attho. Sakkā hi evarūpena uposathakammena khīṇāsavasampattiṃ pāpuṇitunti ayamettha adhippāyo. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva.

‘And whoever is a person like me’: one who knows the virtue of the Uposatha observance would speak thus: ‘Whoever is an Arahant like me should also observe such an Uposatha.’ Another interpretation of ‘And whoever is a person like me’ is: ‘Whatever being is like me and would wish to attain the accomplishment I have attained’—this is the meaning. For it is indeed possible to attain the accomplishment of one whose cankers are destroyed through such an Uposatha observance—this is the intention herein. The eighth sutta has a clear meaning.

9. Sukhumālasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sukhumāla Sutta

39. Navame sukhumāloti niddukkho. Paramasukhumāloti paramaniddukkho. Accantasukhumāloti satataniddukkho. Imaṃ [P 2.0236] bhagavā kapilapure nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya niddukkhabhāvaṃ gahetvā āha, cariyakāle pana tena anubhūtadukkhassa anto natthīti. Ekatthāti ekissā pokkharaṇiyā. Uppalaṃ vappatīti uppalaṃ ropeti. Sā nīluppalavanasañchannā hoti. Padumanti paṇḍarapadumaṃ. Puṇḍarīkanti rattapadumaṃ. Evaṃ itarāpi dve padumapuṇḍarīkavanehi sañchannā honti. Bodhisattassa kira sattaṭṭhavassikakāle rājā amacce pucchi – “taruṇadārakā katarakīḷikaṃ piyāyantī”ti? Udakakīḷikaṃ devāti. Tato rājā kuddālakammakārake sannipātetvā pokkharaṇiṭṭhānāni gaṇhāpesi. Atha sakko devarājā āvajjento taṃ pavattiṃ [V 2.0124] ñatvā – “na yutto mahāsattassa mānusakaparibhogo, dibbaparibhogo yutto”ti vissakammaṃ āmantetvā – “gaccha, tāta, mahāsattassa kīḷābhūmiyaṃ pokkharaṇiyo māpehī”ti āha. Kīdisā hontu[M 2.0125], devāti? Apagatakalalakaddamā hontu vippakiṇṇamaṇimuttapavāḷikā sattaratanamayapākāraparikkhittā pavāḷamayauṇhīsehi maṇimayasopānabāhukehi suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimayaphalakehi sopānehi samannāgatā. Suvaṇṇarajatamaṇipavāḷamayā cettha nāvā hontu, suvaṇṇanāvāya rajatapallaṅko hotu, rajatanāvāya suvaṇṇapallaṅko, maṇināvāya pavāḷapallaṅko, pavāḷanāvāya maṇipallaṅko, suvaṇṇarajatamaṇipavāḷamayāva udakasecananāḷikā hontu, pañcavaṇṇehi ca padumehi sañchannā hontūti. “Sādhu, devā”ti vissakammadevaputto sakkassa paṭissutvā rattibhāge otaritvā rañño gāhāpitapokkharaṇiṭṭhānesuyeva teneva niyāmena pokkharaṇiyo māpesi.

39. In the ninth sutta. 'Delicate' means free from suffering. 'Supremely delicate' means exceedingly free from suffering. 'Extremely delicate' means perpetually free from suffering. The Blessed One said this, taking into account the state of being free from suffering starting from the time of his birth in Kapilapura. However, during the time of his practice, there was no end to the suffering experienced by him; thus it should be understood. 'In one place' means in one pond. 'A water lily is sown' means he plants a water lily. That pond was covered with a grove of blue water lilies. 'Paduma' means a white lotus. 'Puṇḍarīka' means a red lotus. Similarly, the other two ponds were covered with groves of paduma and puṇḍarīka lotuses. It is said that when the Bodhisatta was seven or eight years old, the king asked his ministers, "What kind of games do young boys delight in?" "Water games, Your Majesty." Thereupon, the king, having assembled workers with hoes, had them select sites for the ponds. Then Sakka, king of the devas, reflecting and knowing of that matter, thought, "Human requisites are not suitable for the Great Being; divine requisites are suitable." Having addressed Vissakamma, he said, "Go, my dear, and create ponds in the Great Being's pleasure ground." "Of what kind should they be, lord?" "Let them be free of slime and mud; let them have jewels, pearls, and coral scattered about; let them be enclosed by a wall made of the seven kinds of gems, and be endowed with stairways having coral crests, jeweled handrails, and planks of gold, silver, and jewels. And herein, let there be boats made of gold, silver, jewels, and coral. In a golden boat, let there be a silver couch; in a silver boat, a golden couch; in a jeweled boat, a coral couch; and in a coral boat, a jeweled couch. Let the water-sprinkling tubes be made of gold, silver, jewels, and coral. And let the ponds be covered with lotuses of five colors." "Very well, lord," said Vissakamma, the deva's son. Having assented to Sakka, he descended in the night and created the ponds in the very sites that the king had caused to be selected, and according to that same plan.

Nanu cetā [P 2.0237] apagatakalalakaddamā, kathamettha padumāni pupphiṃsūti? So kira tāsu pokkharaṇīsu tattha tattha suvaṇṇarajatamaṇipavāḷamayā khuddakanāvāyo māpetvā “etā kalalakaddamapūritā ca hontu, pañcavaṇṇāni cettha padumāni pupphantū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ pañcavaṇṇāni padumāni pupphiṃsu, reṇuvaṭṭiyo uggantvā udakapiṭṭhaṃ ajjhottharitvā vicaranti. Pañcavidhā bhamaragaṇā upakūjantā vicaranti. Evaṃ tā māpetvā vissakammo devapurameva gato. Tato vibhātāya rattiyā mahājano disvā “mahāpurissassa māpitā bhavissantī”ti gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā mahājanaparivāro gantvā pokkharaṇiyo disvā “mama puttassa puññiddhiyā devatāhi māpitā bhavissantī”ti attamano ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya mahāpuriso udakakīḷikaṃ agamāsi.

But are not these ponds free of slime and mud? How then did lotuses bloom here? It is said that in those ponds, Vissakamma, having created small boats made of gold, silver, jewels, and coral here and there, made a resolution: 'Let these boats be filled with slime and mud, and let five-colored lotuses bloom here.' Thus, five-colored lotuses bloomed. Whorls of pollen, having risen up, moved about, covering the surface of the water. Swarms of bees of five kinds moved about, humming. Having created them thus, Vissakamma went to the celestial city itself. Then, when the night had dawned, the great populace saw them and, thinking, 'They must have been created for the Great Being,' went and informed the king. The king, surrounded by the great populace, went and saw the ponds. He became delighted, thinking, 'These must have been created through the meritorious power of my son.' From then on, the Great Being went to play in the water.

Yāvadeva mamatthāyāti ettha yāvadevāti payojanāvadhiniyāmavacanaṃ, yāva mameva atthāya, natthettha aññaṃ kāraṇanti attho. Na kho panassāhanti na kho panassa ahaṃ. Akāsikaṃ candananti asaṇhaṃ candanaṃ. Kāsikaṃ, bhikkhave, su me taṃ veṭhananti, bhikkhave, veṭhanampi me kāsikaṃ hoti. Ettha hi suiti ca tanti ca nipātamattaṃ, meti sāmivacanaṃ. Veṭhanampi me saṇhameva hotīti dasseti. Kāsikā kañcukāti pārupanakañcukopi saṇhakañcukova. Setacchattaṃ dhārīyatīti mānusakasetacchattampi dibbasetacchattampi uparidhāritameva hoti. Mā naṃ phusi sītaṃ vāti [M 2.0126] mā etaṃ bodhisattaṃ sītaṃ vā uṇhādīsu vā aññataraṃ phusatūti attho.

Regarding `Yāvadeva mamatthāya`: here `yāvadeva` is a word that defines the limit of a purpose. The meaning is: 'for my benefit alone; there is no other reason for this.' `Na kho panassāhaṃ` is to be divided as `na kho pana assa ahaṃ`. `Akāsikaṃ candanaṃ` means sandalwood that is not fine. Regarding `Kāsikaṃ, bhikkhave, su me taṃ veṭhanaṃ`: 'Bhikkhus, my turban is also of Kāsi cloth.' Herein, `su` and `taṃ` are mere particles; `me` is the genitive. It shows: 'My turban is also fine.' `Kāsikā kañcukā` means the tunic worn as an outer garment is also a fine tunic. `Setacchattaṃ dhārīyati` means both a human white parasol and a divine white parasol were held above him. `Mā naṃ phusi sītaṃ vā` means: 'May cold not afflict this Bodhisatta, or may any other among heat and so on not afflict him.' This is the meaning.

Tayo [V 2.0125] pāsādā ahesunti bodhisatte kira soḷasavassuddesike jāte [P 2.0238] suddhodanamahārājā “puttassa vasanakapāsāde kāressāmī”ti vaḍḍhakino sannipātāpetvā bhaddakena nakkhattamuhuttena navabhūmikataparikammaṃ kāretvā tayo pāsāde kārāpesi. Te sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Hemantikotiādīsu yattha sukhaṃ hemante vasituṃ, ayaṃ hemantiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – hemante vāso hemantaṃ, hemantaṃ arahatīti hemantiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo.

‘There were three palaces’—it is said that when the Bodhisatta was sixteen years of age, the great king Suddhodana, thinking, “I will have dwelling palaces made for my son,” summoned carpenters and, at a favorable constellation and moment, had the preparation of the new ground done, and had three palaces built. This was said in reference to them. Regarding ‘Hemantiko’ and so forth: that wherein it is pleasant to dwell in winter, this is the ‘hemantiko’. In the others too, this is the same method. Herein, this is the meaning of the word: dwelling in winter is ‘hemantaṃ’; because it is suitable for ‘hemantaṃ’, it is ‘hemantiko’. In the others too, this is the same method.

Tattha hemantiko pāsādo navabhūmako ahosi, bhūmiyo panassa uṇhautuggāhāpanatthāya nīcā ahesuṃ. Tattha dvāravātapānāni suphusitakavāṭāni ahesuṃ nibbivarāni. Cittakammampi karontā tattha tattha pajjalite aggikkhandheyeva akaṃsu. Bhūmattharaṇaṃ panettha kambalamayaṃ, tathā sāṇivitānanivāsanapārupanaveṭhanāni. Vātapānāni uṇhaggāhāpanatthaṃ divā vivaṭāni rattiṃ pihitāni honti.

Among them, the winter palace was nine-storied, and its stories were low for the purpose of taking in the warm air. Therein, the doors and windows had well-fitted shutters and were without openings. Those who did the painted work made them in various places only in the likeness of blazing masses of fire. Herein, the floor covering was made of wool; likewise the curtains, canopies, lower garments, upper garments, and head-wraps. The windows were opened during the day for the purpose of taking in the warmth, and were closed at night.

Gimhiko pana pañcabhūmako ahosi. Sītautuggāhāpanatthaṃ panettha bhūmiyo uccā asambādhā ahesuṃ. Dvāravātapānāni nātiphusitāni savivarāni sajālāni ahesuṃ. Cittakamme uppalāni padumāni puṇḍarīkāniyeva akaṃsu. Bhūmattharaṇaṃ panettha dukūlamayaṃ, tathā sāṇivitānanivāsanapārupanaveṭhanāni. Vātapānasamīpesu cettha nava cāṭiyo ṭhapetvā udakassa pūretvā nīluppalādīhi sañchādenti. Tesu tesu padesesu udakayantāni karonti, yehi deve vassante viya udakadhārā nikkhamanti. Antopāsāde tattha tattha kalalapūrā doṇiyo ṭhapetvā pañcavaṇṇāni padumāni ropayiṃsu. Pāsādamatthake sukkhamahiṃsacammaṃ bandhitvā yantaṃ parivattetvā yāva chadanapiṭṭhiyā pāsāṇe āropetvā tasmiṃ vissajjenti. Tesaṃ camme pavaṭṭantānaṃ saddo meghagajjitaṃ viya hoti. Dvāravātapānāni [P 2.0239] panettha divā pihitāni honti rattiṃ vivaṭāni.

Furthermore, the summer palace had five stories. To induce a cool temperature, the stories in this palace were high and spacious. The doors and windows were not too tightly fitted, but had openings and were fitted with lattices. For the decorative painting, they made images of blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses. The floor covering in this palace was made of fine white cloth; likewise were the curtains, canopies, lower garments, upper garments, and head-wraps. Near the windows, they placed new large jars, filled them with water, and covered them with blue lotuses and so forth. In various places, they installed water-machines from which streams of water issued forth, as if the sky were raining. Inside the palace, in various places, they placed troughs filled with mud and planted lotuses of five colors. On top of the palace, they stretched a dry buffalo hide, operated a machine to raise stones to the roof's surface, and released them onto the hide. The sound of those stones rolling on the hide was like the roar of thunder. The doors and windows in this palace were closed during the day and open at night.

Vassiko [M 2.0127] sattabhūmako ahosi. Bhūmiyo panettha dvinnampi utūnaṃ gāhāpanatthāya nātiuccā nātinīcā akaṃsu. Ekaccāni dvāravātapānāni suphusitāni, ekaccāni savivarāni. Tattha cittakammampi kesuci ṭhānesu pajjalitaaggikkhandhavasena, kesuci jātassaravasena kataṃ. Bhūmattharaṇādīni panettha kambaladukūlavasena ubhayamissakāni. Ekacce dvāravātapānā [V 2.0126] rattiṃ vivaṭā divā pihitā, ekacce divā vivaṭā rattiṃ pihitā. Tayopi pāsādā ubbedhena samappamāṇā. Bhūmikāsu pana nānattaṃ ahosi.

The rainy-season palace had seven stories. To be suitable for both seasons, the stories in this palace were made neither too high nor too low. Some doors and windows were well-fitted, while others had openings. The decorative painting there was also done; in some places resembling a blazing mass of fire, and in other places resembling the five kinds of lotuses born in water. The floor coverings and so forth were a mixture of both woolen cloth and fine white cloth. Some doors and windows were open at night and closed during the day, while others were open during the day and closed at night. All three palaces were of equal height, but there was a difference in their stories.

Evaṃ niṭṭhitesu pāsādesu rājā cintesi – “putto me vayappatto, chattamassa ussāpetvā rajjasiriṃ passissāmī”ti. So sākiyānaṃ paṇṇāni pahiṇi – “putto me vayappatto, rajje naṃ patiṭṭhāpessāmi, sabbe attano attano gehesu vayappattā, dārikā imaṃ gehaṃ pesentū”ti. Te sāsanaṃ sutvā – “kumāro kevalaṃ dassanakkhamo rūpasampanno, na kiñci sippaṃ jānāti, dārabharaṇaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissati, na mayaṃ dhītaro dassāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā puttassa santikaṃ gantvā ārocesi. Bodhisatto “kiṃ sippaṃ dassetuṃ vaṭṭati, tātā”ti āha. Sahassathāmadhanuṃ āropetuṃ vaṭṭati, tātāti. Tena hi āharāpethāti. Rājā āharāpetvā adāsi. Dhanuṃ purisasahassaṃ āropeti, purisasahassaṃ oropeti. Mahāpuriso dhanuṃ āharāpetvā pallaṅke nisinnova jiyaṃ pādaṅguṭṭhake veṭhetvā kaḍḍhanto pādaṅguṭṭhakeneva dhanuṃ āropetvā vāmena hatthena daṇḍe gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena kaḍḍhitvā jiyaṃ pothesi. Sakalanagaraṃ uppatanākārappattaṃ ahosi. “Kiṃ saddo eso”ti ca vutte “devo gajjatī”ti āhaṃsu. Athaññe “tumhe na jānātha, na devo gajjati, aṅgīrasassa kumārassa sahassathāmadhanuṃ āropetvā jiyaṃ pothentassa jiyappahārasaddo eso”ti [P 2.0240] āhaṃsu. Sākiyā tāvatakeneva āraddhacittā ahesuṃ.

When the palaces were completed, the king thought: 'My son has come of age. Having raised the white umbrella for him, I shall behold his royal glory.' He sent letters to the Sakyans, saying: 'My son has come of age. I shall establish him in the kingdom. Let all who have daughters of age in their respective homes send them to this house.' Having heard the message, they said: 'The prince is merely fit to be looked at and endowed with beauty; he knows no skill whatsoever and will not be able to support a wife. We will not give our daughters.' The king, having heard that report, went to his son's presence and informed him. The Bodhisatta asked: 'Father, what skill is it fitting to demonstrate?' 'It is fitting to string the bow of a thousand men's strength, dear son.' 'If so, have it brought.' The king had it brought and gave it to him. A thousand men string the bow, and a thousand men unstring it. The Great Being had the bow brought, and while still seated on the couch, he wrapped the bowstring on his big toe and, while pulling, strung the bow with his big toe alone. Then, holding the bow-staff with his left hand and drawing with his right hand, he twanged the bowstring. The entire city became as if it were about to fly up. And when it was asked, 'What sound is this?' they replied, 'A deva thunders.' Then others said: 'You do not know. It is not a deva thundering. This is the sound of the striking of the bowstring of Prince Aṅgīrasa, who, having strung the bow of a thousand men's strength, is twanging the string.' By that alone, the Sakyans were pleased in mind.

Mahāpuriso “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Aṭṭhaṅgulamattabahalaṃ ayopaṭṭaṃ kaṇḍena vinivijjhituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Taṃ vinivijjhitvā “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Caturaṅgulabahalaṃ asanaphalakaṃ vinivijjhituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Taṃ vinivijjhitvā “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Vidatthibahalaṃ udumbaraphalakaṃ vinivijjhituṃ [M 2.0128] vaṭṭatīti. Taṃ vinivijjhitvā “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Yante baddhaṃ phalakasataṃ vinivijjhituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Taṃ vinivijjhitvā “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Saṭṭhipaṭalaṃ sukkhamahiṃsacammaṃ vinivijjhituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Tampi vinivijjhitvā “aññaṃ kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Tato vālikasakaṭādīni ācikkhiṃsu. Mahāsatto vālikasakaṭampi palālasakaṭampi vinivijjhitvā udake ekusabhappamāṇaṃ kaṇḍaṃ pesesi, thale aṭṭhausabhappamāṇaṃ. Atha naṃ “idāni vātiṅgaṇasaññāya vālaṃ vijjhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. Tena hi bandhāpethāti. Saddantare bajjhatu, tātāti. Purato gacchantu, gāvutantare bandhantūti. Purato gacchantu, addhayojane bandhantūti[V 2.0127]. Purato gacchantu yojane bandhantūti. Bandhāpetha, tātāti yojanamatthake vātiṅgaṇasaññāya vālaṃ bandhāpetvā rattandhakāre meghapaṭalacchannāsu disāsu kaṇḍaṃ khipi, taṃ gantvā yojanamatthake vālaṃ phāletvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Na kevalañca ettakameva, taṃ divasaṃ pana mahāsatto loke vattamānasippaṃ sabbameva sandassesi. Sakyarājāno attano attano dhītaro alaṅkaritvā pesayiṃsu, cattālīsasahassanāṭakitthiyo ahesuṃ. Mahāpuriso tīsu pāsādesu devo maññe paricārento mahāsampattiṃ anubhavati.

The Great Being said, 'What else is it fitting to do?' It was said that an iron plate eight finger-widths thick should be pierced with an arrow. Having pierced it, he asked, 'What else is it fitting to do?' It was said that an asana wood plank four finger-widths thick should be pierced. Having pierced it, he asked, 'What else is it fitting to do?' It was said that an udumbara wood plank a span thick should be pierced. Having pierced it, he asked, 'What else is it fitting to do?' It was said that a hundred planks bound in a frame should be pierced. Having pierced it, he asked, 'What else is it fitting to do?' It was said that a dry buffalo hide of sixty layers should be pierced. Having pierced that also, he asked, 'What else is it fitting to do?' Then they pointed out things such as sand-carts. The Great Being, having pierced a sand-cart and also a straw-cart, sent an arrow a distance of one usabha into the water, and eight usabhas on land. Then they said to him, 'Now it is fitting to shoot a horsehair with the mark of an eggplant.' 'If so, have it tied,' he said. 'O sirs, let it be tied at the distance of a call's sound.' 'Let them go forward and tie it within a gāvuta.' 'Let them go forward and tie it at half a yojana.' 'Let them go forward and tie it at a yojana.' When he said, 'O sirs, have it tied,' they had the horsehair tied with the mark of an eggplant at a yojana's distance. In the darkness of night, when the directions were covered by a veil of clouds, he shot the arrow. It went and, at a yojana's distance, split the horsehair and entered the earth. And not only this much, but on that day, the Great Being displayed all the skills existing in the world. The Sakyan kings adorned their own daughters and sent them; there were forty thousand dancing women. The Great Being, being attended upon in the three palaces as if he were a deva, enjoyed great prosperity.

Nippurisehīti purisavirahitehi. Na kevalaṃ cettha tūriyāneva nippurisāni, sabbaṭṭhānānipi nippurisāneva. Dovārikāpi itthiyova, nhāpanādiparikammakarāpi itthiyova[P 2.0241]. Rājā kira “tathārūpaṃ issariyasukhasampattiṃ anubhavamānassa purisaṃ disvā parisaṅkā uppajjati, sā me puttassa mā ahosī”ti sabbakiccesu itthiyova ṭhapesi. Paricārayamānoti modamāno. Na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohāmīti pāsādato heṭṭhā na otarāmi. Iti maṃ cattāro māse añño sikhābaddho puriso nāma passituṃ nālattha. Yathāti yena niyāmena. Dāsakammakaraporisassāti dāsānañceva devasikabhattavetanābhatānaṃ kammakarānañca nissāya jīvamānapurisānañca. Kaṇājakanti sakuṇḍakabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgadutiyanti kañjikadutiyaṃ.

Nippurisehi: that is, devoid of men. Not only were the musical instruments here without men, but all places were also without men. Even the gatekeepers were women, and those who performed services such as bathing were also women. The king, it seems, thinking, "For one experiencing such sovereign happiness, anxiety might arise upon seeing a man; may that not happen to my son," appointed only women for all duties. Paricārayamāno: that is, delighting. Na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohāmi: I do not descend to the ground floor of the palace; that is, I do not come down from the palace. Thus, for four months, no other man with a topknot was able to see me. Yathā: that is, in the manner that. Dāsakammakaraporisassa: that is, of slaves, of laborers maintained by daily food and wages, and of men who live in dependence. Kaṇājakaṃ: that is, rice with broken grains. Bilaṅgadutiyaṃ: that is, accompanied by sour gruel.

Evarūpāya iddhiyāti evaṃjātikāya puññiddhiyā samannāgatassa. Evarūpena ca sukhumālenāti evaṃjātikena ca niddukkhabhāvena. Sokhumālenātipi [M 2.0129] pāṭho. Evaṃ tathāgato ettakena ṭhānena attano sirisampattiṃ kathesi. Kathento ca na uppilāvitabhāvatthaṃ kathesi, “evarūpāyapi pana sampattiyā ṭhito pamādaṃ akatvā appamattova ahosi”nti appamādalakkhaṇasseva dīpanatthaṃ kathesi. Teneva assutavā kho puthujjanotiādimāha. Tattha paranti parapuggalaṃ. Jiṇṇanti jarājiṇṇaṃ. Aṭṭīyatīti aṭṭo pīḷito hoti. Harāyatīti hiriṃ karoti lajjati. Jigucchatīti asuciṃ viya disvā jigucchaṃ uppādeti. Attānaṃyeva atisitvāti jarādhammampi samānaṃ attānaṃ atikkamitvā aṭṭīyati harāyatīti attho. Jarādhammoti jarāsabhāvo. Jaraṃ anatītoti jaraṃ anatikkanto, anto jarāya vattāmi. Iti paṭisañcikkhatoti evaṃ paccavekkhantassa. Yobbanamadoti yobbanaṃ nissāya uppajjanako mānamado. Sabbaso [P 2.0242] pahīyīti sabbākārena pahīno. Maggena pahīnasadiso katvā dassito. Na panesa maggena pahīno, paṭisaṅkhānena pahīnova kathitoti veditabbo. Bodhisattassa hi devatā [V 2.0128] jarāpattaṃ dassesuṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattā antarā mahāsattassa yobbanamado nāma na uppajjati. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ettha pana ārogyamadoti ahaṃ nirogoti ārogyaṃ nissāya uppajjanako mānamado. Jīvitamadoti ahaṃ ciraṃ jīvīti taṃ nissāya uppajjanako mānamado. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāyāti sikkhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā. Hīnāyāvattatīti hīnāya lāmakāya gihibhāvāya āvattati.

Evarūpāya iddhiyā: that is, endowed with power of merit of such a kind. Evarūpena ca sukhumālena: that is, with such a kind of freedom from suffering. There is also the reading Sokhumālena. Thus, the Tathāgata described his own glorious prosperity to this extent. And in describing it, he did so not for the sake of showing off, but for the purpose of illustrating the characteristic of heedfulness, saying, “Furthermore, even while established in such prosperity, I did not become heedless; I was indeed heedful.” For that very reason, he said the words beginning with, “The uninstructed worldling…” Therein, paraṃ means another person. Jiṇṇaṃ means worn out with age. Aṭṭīyati means he is distressed, oppressed. Harāyati means he feels shame, is embarrassed. Jigucchati means, seeing as if impure, he produces disgust. Attānaṃyeva atisitvā: the meaning is that although being oneself subject to the nature of aging, one overlooks oneself and is afflicted and ashamed. Jarādhammo means of the nature of aging. Jaraṃ anatīto means not having overcome aging, ‘I exist within aging.’ Iti paṭisañcikkhato: that is, for me who was contemplating in this way. Yobbanamadoti means the conceit arising dependent on youth. Sabbaso pahīyi means completely abandoned. It is shown as if abandoned by the path. However, it should be understood that this was not abandoned by the path, but was spoken of as being abandoned only through reflection. For, deities showed the Bodhisatta a person subject to aging. From that time onwards, in the period up until Arahantship, what is called the intoxication of youth did not arise for the Great Being. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. Herein, ārogyamado, ‘intoxication with health,’ means the conceit arising dependent on health, thinking, “I am free from disease.” Jīvitamado, ‘intoxication with life,’ means the conceit arising dependent on life, thinking, “I will live long.” Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya means having rejected the training. Hīnāyāvattati means he returns to the inferior, base household life.

Yathādhammāti byādhiādīhi yathāsabhāvā. Tathāsantāti yathā santā eva aviparītabyādhiādisabhāvāva hutvāti attho. Jigucchantīti parapuggalaṃ jigucchanti. Mama evaṃ vihārinoti mayhaṃ evaṃ jigucchāvihārena viharantassa evaṃ jigucchanaṃ nappatirūpaṃ bhaveyya nānucchavikaṃ. Sohaṃ evaṃ viharantoti so ahaṃ evaṃ paraṃ jigucchamāno viharanto, evaṃ vā iminā paṭisaṅkhānavihārena viharanto. Ñatvā dhammaṃ nirūpadhinti sabbūpadhivirahitaṃ nibbānadhammaṃ ñatvā. Sabbe made abhibhosmīti sabbe tayopi made abhibhaviṃ samatikkamiṃ. Nekkhamme daṭṭhu khematanti nibbāne khemabhāvaṃ disvā. Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khematotipi pāṭho, nibbānaṃ khemato disvāti attho. Tassa [M 2.0130] me ahu ussāhoti tassa mayhaṃ taṃ nekkhammasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ abhipassantassa ussāho ahu, vāyāmo ahosīti attho. Nāhaṃ [P 2.0243] bhabbo etarahi, kāmāni paṭisevitunti ahaṃ dāni duvidhepi kāme paṭisevituṃ abhabbo. Anivatti bhavissāmīti pabbajjato ca sabbaññutaññāṇato ca na nivattissāmi, anivattako bhavissāmi. Brahmacariyaparāyaṇoti maggabrahmacariyaparāyaṇo jātosmīti attho. Iti imāhi gāthāhi mahābodhipallaṅke attano āgamanīyavīriyaṃ kathesi.

Yathādhammā: that is, according to their inherent nature, such as illnesses. Tathāsantā: that is, being just as they are, of an undistorted nature of illness and so forth—this is the meaning. Jigucchanti: that is, they feel disgust toward another person. Mama evaṃ vihārino: that is, for me, living with such disgust, such disgust would not be fitting, not appropriate. Sohaṃ evaṃ viharanto: that is, I, living thus, feeling disgust toward another; or, living thus with this reflective contemplation. Ñatvā dhammaṃ nirūpadhiṃ: that is, having known the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is free from all substrates of existence. Sabbe made abhibhosmi: that is, I have overcome, I have transcended all three intoxications. Nekkhamme daṭṭhu khemataṃ: that is, having seen the state of security in renunciation. There is also the reading Nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato, meaning: having seen renunciation as security. Tassa me ahu ussāho: that is, for me, beholding that Nibbāna, which is called renunciation, exertion arose; that is, effort arose—this is the meaning. Nāhaṃ bhabbo etarahi kāmāni paṭisevituṃ: that is, I am now incapable of indulging in the two kinds of sensual pleasures. Anivatti bhavissāmi: that is, I will not turn back from the going forth and from the knowledge of omniscience; I will be one who does not turn back. Brahmacariyaparāyaṇo: that is, I have become one for whom the holy life of the path is the final goal—this is the meaning. Thus, with these verses, while at the great Bodhi-seat, he spoke of his own energy leading to attainment.

10. Ādhipateyyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Ādhipateyya Sutta

40. Dasame ādhipateyyānīti jeṭṭhakakāraṇato nibbattāni. Attādhipateyyantiādīsu attānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā nibbattitaṃ guṇajātaṃ attādhipateyyaṃ. Lokaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā nibbattitaṃ lokādhipateyyaṃ. Navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā nibbattitaṃ dhammādhipateyyaṃ. Na iti bhavābhavahetūti iti bhavo, iti bhavoti evaṃ āyatiṃ, na tassa tassa sampattibhavassa hetu. Otiṇṇoti anupaviṭṭho. Yassa hi jāti antopaviṭṭhā, so jātiyā otiṇṇo nāma. Jarādīsupi eseva nayo. Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassāti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkharāsissa. Antakiriyā [V 2.0129] paññāyethāti antakaraṇaṃ paricchedaparivaṭumakaraṇaṃ paññāyeyya. Ohāyāti pahāya. Pāpiṭṭhatareti lāmakatare. Āraddhanti paggahitaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, āraddhattāva asallīnaṃ. Upaṭṭhitāti catusatipaṭṭhānavasena upaṭṭhitā. Upaṭṭhitattāva asammuṭṭhā. Passaddho kāyoti nāmakāyo ca karajakāyo ca passaddho vūpasantadaratho. Passaddhattāva asāraddho. Samāhitaṃ cittanti ārammaṇe cittaṃ sammā āhitaṃ suṭṭhu ṭhapitaṃ. Sammā āhitattāva ekaggaṃ. Adhipatiṃ karitvāti jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā. Suddhaṃ [P 2.0244] attānaṃ pariharatīti suddhaṃ nimmalaṃ katvā attānaṃ pariharati paṭijaggati, gopāyatīti attho. Ayañca yāva arahattamaggā pariyāyena suddhamattānaṃ pariharati nāma, phalappattova pana nippariyāyena suddhamattānaṃ pariharati.

40. In the tenth, `ādhipateyyāni` (sovereignties) are so called because they arise from the cause of being foremost. Among these, `attādhipateyya` (self-sovereignty) refers to the collection of qualities that arises from making oneself foremost. `Lokādhipateyya` (world-sovereignty) refers to what arises from making the world foremost. `Dhammādhipateyya` (Dhamma-sovereignty) refers to what arises from making the ninefold supramundane Dhamma foremost. `Na iti bhavābhavahetu` (not for the cause of this or that existence) means that it is not for the cause of any particular prosperous existence in the future, based on thinking, 'Thus there is being, thus there is non-being.' `Otiṇṇa` (overcome) means entered. For one who is internally entered by birth is said to be overcome by birth.
