The same method applies to aging and so on. `Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa` (of the entire mass of suffering) means of the whole heap of suffering in the round of existence. `Antakiriyā paññāyetha` (the ending should be discerned) means the making of an end, the making of the absence of limitation, should be discerned. `Ohāya` means `pahāya` (having abandoned). `Pāpiṭṭhatare` means `lāmakatare` (more inferior). `Āraddha` (aroused) means taken up, fully complete; because it is aroused, it is not sluggish. `Upaṭṭhitā` (established) means established by way of the four foundations of mindfulness; because it is established, it is unconfused. `Passaddho kāyo` (calmed body) means both the mental body and the physical body are calmed, with distress pacified; because it is calmed, it is unagitated. `Samāhitaṃ cittaṃ` (concentrated mind) means the mind is well placed and properly fixed on its object; because it is well placed, it is one-pointed. `Adhipatiṃ karitvā` means `jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā` (having made it foremost). `Suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharati` (he maintains himself purified) means he, having made himself pure and stainless, maintains, looks after, and protects himself; this is the meaning. And this one, up to the path of Arahantship, is said to maintain himself purified in a figurative sense, but one who has attained the fruit maintains himself purified in a direct sense.

Svākkhātotiādīni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.147) vitthāritāni. Jānaṃ passaṃ viharantīti taṃ dhammaṃ jānantā passantā viharanti. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, tīṇi ādhipateyyānīti [M 2.0131] ettāvatā tīṇi ādhipateyyāni lokiyalokuttaramissakāni kathitāni.

`Svākkhāto` (well-expounded) and other such terms are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. `Jānaṃ passaṃ viharanti` (they dwell knowing and seeing) means they dwell knowing and seeing that Dhamma. With the passage, 'These, bhikkhus, are the three sovereignties,' the three sovereignties, being a mixture of mundane and supramundane, have been spoken of.

Pakubbatoti karontassa. Attā te purisa jānāti, saccaṃ vā yadi vā musāti yaṃ tvaṃ karosi, taṃ yadi vā yathāsabhāvaṃ yadi vā no yathāsabhāvanti tava attāva jānāti. Iminā ca kāraṇena veditabbaṃ “pāpakammaṃ karontassa loke paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Kalyāṇanti sundaraṃ. Atimaññasīti atikkamitvā maññasi. Attānaṃ parigūhasīti yathā me attāpi na jānāti, evaṃ naṃ parigūhāmīti vāyamasi. Attādhipateyyakoti attajeṭṭhako. Lokādhipoti lokajeṭṭhako. Nipakoti paññavā. Jhāyīti jhāyanto. Dhammādhipoti dhammajeṭṭhako. Saccaparakkamoti thiraparakkamo bhūtaparakkamo. Pasayha māranti māraṃ pasahitvā. Abhibhuyya antakanti idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Yo ca phusī jātikkhayaṃ padhānavāti yo jhāyī padhānavā māraṃ abhibhavitvā jātikkhayaṃ arahattaṃ phusi. So [P 2.0245] tādisoti so tathāvidho tathāsaṇṭhito. Lokavidūti tayo loke vidite pākaṭe katvā ṭhito. Sumedhoti supañño. Sabbesu dhammesu atammayo munīti sabbe tebhūmakadhamme taṇhāsaṅkhātāya tammayatāya abhāvena atammayo khīṇāsavamuni kadāci katthaci na hīyati na parihīyatīti vuttaṃ hotīti.

`Pakubbato` (of one who acts) means of one who does. `Attā te purisa jānāti, saccaṃ vā yadi vā musā` (Your self, O person, knows whether it is true or false) means: what you do, whether it is in accordance with its true nature or not, your own self knows. And for this reason, it should be understood that “for one who does an evil deed, there is no such thing as a hidden place in the world.” `Kalyāṇaṃ` (beautiful) means lovely. `Atimaññasi` (you despise) means you think, having transgressed. `Attānaṃ parigūhasi` (you conceal yourself) means you strive, thinking: “I will conceal it in such a way that even my own self does not know.” `Attādhipateyyako` (self-sovereign) means one for whom the self is foremost. `Lokādhipo` (world-sovereign) means one for whom the world is foremost. `Nipako` (wise) means possessing wisdom. `Jhāyī` (one who burns) means one who burns up evil. `Dhammādhipo` (Dhamma-sovereign) means one for whom the Dhamma is foremost. `Saccaparakkamo` (resolute in truth) means one with true effort. `Pasayha māraṃ` (having conquered Māra) means having subdued Māra. `Abhibhuyya antakaṃ` (having overcome the Ender) is a synonym for that very phrase. `Yo ca phusī jātikkhayaṃ padhānavā` (And one who, striving, has reached the destruction of birth) means: the one who burns up evil, who is striving, having overcome Māra, has reached the destruction of birth, which is Arahantship. `So tādiso` (such a one) means one of such a kind, so constituted. `Lokavidū` (knower of the world) means one who stands having made the three worlds known and manifest. `Sumedho` (wise) means possessing good wisdom. `Sabbesu dhammesu atammayo munī` (the sage not made of that in regard to all things) means: the sage whose taints are destroyed, who is 'not made of that' due to the absence of 'being made of that,' which is called craving, with regard to all things of the three realms, is never diminished or falls away anywhere at any time; this is what is said.

Devadūtavaggo catuttho.

The Devadūta Chapter is the fourth.

5. Cūḷavaggo

5. The Minor Chapter

1. Sammukhībhāvasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Presence

41. Pañcamassa [V 2.0130] paṭhame sammukhībhāvāti sammukhībhāvena, vijjamānatāyāti attho. Pasavatīti paṭilabhati. Saddhāya sammukhībhāvāti yadi hi saddhā na bhaveyya, deyyadhammo na bhaveyya, dakkhiṇeyyasaṅkhātā paṭiggāhakapuggalā na bhaveyyuṃ, kathaṃ puññakammaṃ kareyya. Tesaṃ pana sammukhībhāvena sakkā kātunti tasmā “saddhāya sammukhībhāvā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca dve [M 2.0132] dhammā sulabhā deyyadhammā ceva dakkhiṇeyyā ca, saddhā pana dullabhā. Puthujjanassa hi saddhā athāvarā padavārena nānā hoti, teneva mahāmoggallānasadisopi aggasāvako pāṭibhogo bhavituṃ asakkonto āha – “dvinnaṃ kho te ahaṃ, āvuso, dhammānaṃ pāṭibhogo bhogānañca jīvitassa ca, saddhāya pana tvaṃyeva pāṭibhogo”ti (udā. 18).

41. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, `sammukhībhāvā` means by being present; that is, by being existent. `Pasavati` means one obtains. Regarding ‘Through the presence of faith’: indeed, if there were no faith, if there were no gift-object, if there were no recipient individuals reckoned as worthy of a noble offering, how could one perform a meritorious act? But through their presence, it is possible to do so. Therefore, he said, “Through the presence of faith,” and so on. And herein, two things are easy to obtain: gift-objects and worthy recipients, but faith is difficult to obtain. Indeed, for a worldling, faith is unstable; it changes with every footstep. For that very reason, even a chief disciple like Mahāmoggallāna, being unable to become a guarantor, said: “Friend, I am a guarantor for two of your things: for possessions and for life, but for faith, you yourself are the guarantor.”

2. Tiṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Tiṭhāna Sutta

42. Dutiye vigatamalamaccherenāti vigatamacchariyamalena. Muttacāgoti vissaṭṭhacāgo. Payatapāṇīti dhotahattho. Assaddho hi satakkhattuṃ hatthe dhovitvāpi malinahatthova hoti, saddho pana dānābhiratattā malinahatthopi dhotahatthova. Vossaggaratoti [P 2.0246] vossaggasaṅkhāte dāne rato. Yācayogoti yācituṃ yutto, yācakehi vā yogo assātipi yācayogo. Dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti dānaṃ dadanto saṃvibhāgañca karonto dānasaṃvibhāgarato nāma hoti.

42. In the second sutta, `vigatamalamaccherena` means with the stain of miserliness gone. `Muttacāgo` means one whose giving is released. `Payatapāṇi` means one with washed hands. Indeed, a faithless person, even after washing their hands a hundred times, still has stained hands, but a faithful person, because of delighting in giving, even with stained hands, has hands as if washed. `Vossaggarato` means one who delights in giving, which is called relinquishment. `Yācayogo` means suitable to be asked; or, one has a connection with those who ask, thus they are `yācayogo`. `Dānasaṃvibhāgarato` means one who gives a gift and makes a distribution is called ‘one who delights in giving and sharing’.

Dassanakāmo sīlavatanti dasapi yojanāni vīsampi tiṃsampi yojanasatampi gantvā sīlasampanne daṭṭhukāmo hoti pāṭaliputtakabrāhmaṇo viya saddhātissamahārājā viya ca. Pāṭaliputtassa kira nagaradvāre sālāya nisinnā dve brāhmaṇā kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsimahānāgattherassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā “amhehi taṃ bhikkhuṃ daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dvepi janā nikkhamiṃsu. Eko antarāmagge kālamakāsi. Eko samuddatīraṃ patvā nāvāya mahātitthapaṭṭane oruyha anurādhapuraṃ [V 2.0131] āgantvā “kāḷavallimaṇḍapo kuhi”nti pucchi. Rohaṇajanapadeti. So anupubbena therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā cūḷanagaragāme dhuraghare nivāsaṃ gahetvā therassa āhāraṃ sampādetvā pātova vuṭṭhāya therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā gantvā janapariyante ṭhito theraṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā sakiṃ tattheva ṭhito vanditvā puna upasaṅkamitvā gopphakesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā vandanto “uccā, bhante, tumhe”ti āha. Thero ca nātiucco nātirasso pamāṇayuttova, tena naṃ puna āha – “nātiuccā tumhe, tumhākaṃ [M 2.0133] pana guṇā mecakavaṇṇassa samuddassa matthakena gantvā sakalajambudīpatalaṃ ajjhottharitvā gatā, ahampi pāṭaliputtanagaradvāre nisinno tumhākaṃ guṇakathaṃ assosi”nti. So therassa bhikkhāhāraṃ datvā attano ticīvaraṃ paṭiyādetvā therassa santike pabbajitvā tassovāde patiṭṭhāya katipāheneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

“Desiring to see the virtuous” means that one is desirous of seeing persons endowed with virtue, traveling ten, twenty, thirty, or even a hundred yojanas to do so, like the brahmin of Pāṭaliputta or King Saddhātissa. It is said that two brahmins, sitting in a hall at the city gate of Pāṭaliputta, heard praises of the Elder Mahānāga of Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa and thought, “We should see that monk,” and both set out. One died along the way. The other reached the seacoast, and disembarking from a ship at the port of Mahātittha, went to Anurādhapura and asked, “Where is Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa?” They replied, “In the Rohaṇa country.” He gradually reached the elder’s dwelling place, took up residence in a main house in the village of Cūḷanagara, prepared food for the elder, and rising early, inquired about the elder’s dwelling place. He went there and stood at the edge of the inhabited area. Seeing the elder approaching from afar, he stood right there and paid respects once. Then, approaching again, he firmly grasped the elder’s ankles and, while paying respects, said, “Venerable sir, you are tall.” The elder was neither too tall nor too short, but of proper proportion. Therefore, the brahmin said to him again, “You are not too tall, venerable sir, but your virtues, having traveled over the surface of the dark-hued ocean, have spread and overwhelmed the entire land of Jambudīpa. I too, sitting at the city gate of Pāṭaliputta, heard praises of your virtues.” He offered almsfood to the elder, prepared his own triple robe, and went forth in the elder’s presence. Established in the elder’s instruction, he attained Arahantship within a few days.

Saddhātissamahārājāpi, “bhante, mayhaṃ vanditabbayuttakaṃ [P 2.0247] ekaṃ ayyaṃ ācikkhathā”ti pucchi. Bhikkhū “maṅgalavāsī kuṭṭatissatthero”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā mahāparivārena pañcayojanamaggaṃ agamāsi. Thero “kiṃ saddo eso, āvuso”ti bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi. “Rājā, bhante, tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgato”ti. Thero cintesi – “kiṃ mayhaṃ mahallakakāle rājagehe kamma”nti divāṭṭhāne mañce nipajjitvā bhūmiyaṃ lekhaṃ likhanto acchi. Rājā “kahaṃ thero”ti pucchitvā “divāṭṭhāne”ti sutvā tattha gacchanto theraṃ bhūmiyaṃ lekhaṃ likhantaṃ disvā “khīṇāsavassa nāma hatthakukkuccaṃ natthi, nāyaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti avanditvāva nivatti. Bhikkhusaṅgho theraṃ āha – “bhante, evaṃvidhassa saddhassa pasannassa rañño kasmā vippaṭisāraṃ karitthā”ti. “Āvuso, rañño pasādarakkhanaṃ na tumhākaṃ bhāro, mahallakattherassa bhāro”ti vatvā aparabhāge anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyanto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ āha – “mayhaṃ kūṭāgāramhi aññampi pallaṅkaṃ attharathā”ti. Tasmiṃ atthate thero – “idaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ antare appatiṭṭhahitvā raññā diṭṭhakāleyeva bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhātū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā parinibbāyi. Kūṭāgāraṃ pañcayojanamaggaṃ ākāsena agamāsi. Pañcayojanamagge dhajaṃ dhāretuṃ samatthā rukkhā dhajapaggahitāva ahesuṃ. Gacchāpi gumbāpi sabbe kūṭāgārābhimukhā hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

King Saddhātissa also asked, “Venerable sirs, please point out a worthy elder whom I should pay respects to.” The monks replied, “The Elder Kuṭṭatissa, who dwells in Maṅgala.” The king, with a great retinue, traveled a distance of five yojanas. The elder asked the monastic community, “Friends, what is this noise?” They answered, “Venerable sir, the king has come to see you.” The elder thought, “What business does an old man like me have with the royal palace?” and, in the day quarters, lay down on his couch, writing on the ground. The king, asking, “Where is the elder?” and hearing he was in the day quarters, went there. Seeing the elder writing on the ground, he thought, “One who is a perfected one has no restlessness of hand; this one is not a perfected one,” and turned back without paying respects. The monastic community said to the elder, “Venerable sir, why did you cause such a faithful and devoted king to have regret?” The elder replied, “Friends, protecting the king’s faith is not your burden; it is the burden of an old elder.” Later, while passing away into the nibbāna-element without remainder, he addressed the monastic community: “In my peaked house, spread out another couch.” When it was spread, the elder resolved, “May this peaked house, without stopping in the intervening space, be established on the ground at the very moment the king sees it,” and then passed into final nibbāna. The peaked house traveled five yojanas through the sky. Trees along the five-yojana path, capable of bearing flags, stood as if holding raised flags. All shrubs and thickets turned toward the peaked house and stood still.

Raññopi paṇṇaṃ pahiṇiṃsu “thero parinibbuto, kūṭāgāraṃ ākāsena āgacchatī”ti. Rājā na saddahi. Kūṭāgāraṃ ākāsena gantvā thūpārāmaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā silācetiyaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Cetiyaṃ saha vatthunā uppatitvā kūṭāgāramatthake aṭṭhāsi, sādhukārasahassāni pavattiṃsu[V 2.0132]. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahābyagghatthero nāma lohapāsāde sattamakūṭāgāre nisinno bhikkhūnaṃ vinayakammaṃ karonto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ saddo [M 2.0134] eso”ti paṭipucchi. Bhante, maṅgalavāsī kuṭṭatissatthero parinibbuto, kūṭāgāraṃ pañcayojanamaggaṃ ākāsena āgataṃ, tattha so sādhukārasaddoti. Āvuso, puññavante nissāya [P 2.0248] sakkāraṃ labhissāmāti antevāsike khamāpetvā ākāseneva āgantvā taṃ kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā dutiyamañce nisīditvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Rājā gandhapupphacuṇṇāni ādāya gantvā ākāse ṭhitaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ disvā kūṭāgāraṃ pūjesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kūṭāgāraṃ otaritvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ. Rājā mahāsakkārena sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ akāsi. Evarūpā sīlavantānaṃ dassanakāmā nāma honti.

They sent a message to the king: “The Elder has attained Parinibbāna, and the pinnacled pavilion is coming through the sky.” The king did not believe it. The pinnacled pavilion, having traveled through the sky, circumambulated the Thūpārāma to the right and went to the site of the Silācetiya. The cetiya, together with its base, rose up and stood on top of the pinnacled pavilion, and thousands of acclamations arose. At that moment, the elder named Mahābyaggha, seated in the seventh pinnacled chamber of the Lohapāsāda, heard that sound and asked in return, “What is this sound?” They replied, “Venerable Sir, the Elder Kuṭṭatissa of Maṅgalavāsa has attained Parinibbāna; the pinnacled pavilion has come a distance of five yojanas through the sky, and that is the sound of acclamation there.” He said, “Friends, by relying on the meritorious one, we shall receive honor.” Having asked forgiveness of his resident pupils, he came through the sky itself, entered that pinnacled pavilion, sat on the second couch, and attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element that has no residue remaining. The king, taking perfumes, flowers, and fragrant powders, went and saw the pinnacled pavilion standing in the sky and honored it. At that moment, the pinnacled pavilion descended and was established on the ground. The king had the funeral rites performed with great honor, took the relics, and built a cetiya. Such, indeed, are those who desire to see the virtuous.

Saddhammaṃ sotumicchatīti tathāgatappaveditaṃ saddhammaṃ sotukāmo hoti piṇḍapātikattherādayo viya. Gaṅgāvanavāliaṅgaṇamhi kira tiṃsa bhikkhū vassaṃ upagatā anvaddhamāsaṃ uposathadivase catupaccayasantosabhāvanārāmamahāariyavaṃsañca (a. ni. 4.28) kathenti. Eko piṇḍapātikatthero pacchābhāgena āgantvā paṭicchannaṭṭhāne nisīdi. Atha naṃ eko gonaso jaṅghapiṇḍimaṃsaṃ saṇḍāsena gaṇhanto viya ḍaṃsi. Thero olokento gonasaṃ disvā “ajja dhammassavanantarāyaṃ na karissāmī”ti gonasaṃ gahetvā thavikāya pakkhipitvā thavikāmukhaṃ bandhitvā avidūre ṭhāne ṭhapetvā dhammaṃ suṇantova nisīdi. Aruṇuggamanañca visaṃ vikkhambhetvā therassa tiṇṇaṃ phalānaṃ pāpuṇanañca visassa daṭṭhaṭṭhāneneva otaritvā pathavipavisanañca dhammakathikattherassa dhammakathāniṭṭhāpanañca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Tato thero āha – “āvuso eko me coro gahito”ti thavikaṃ muñcitvā gonasaṃ vissajjesi. Bhikkhū disvā “kāya velāya daṭṭhattha, bhante”ti pucchiṃsu. Hiyyo sāyanhasamaye, āvusoti. Kasmā, bhante, evaṃ bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ karitthāti. Āvuso, sacāhaṃ dīghajātikena daṭṭhoti vadeyyaṃ, nayimaṃ ettakaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ [P 2.0249] labheyyanti. Idaṃ tāva piṇḍapātikattherassa vatthu.

“One who wishes to hear the good Dhamma”—this means one becomes desirous of hearing the good Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata, like the Elder Piṇḍapātika and others. It is said that thirty monks entered upon the rains-residence in the open space of Gaṅgāvanavāli. Every half-month, on the Uposatha day, they would speak on the great noble tradition of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. A certain Elder Piṇḍapātika arrived after the talk had begun and sat in a concealed place. Then, a viper bit him on the flesh of his calf, as if seizing it with pincers. The Elder, looking and seeing the viper, thought, “Today, I will not create an obstacle to my hearing of the Dhamma.” Having caught the viper, he put it into a bag, tied the mouth of the bag, placed it in a spot not far away, and sat, continuing to listen to the Dhamma. The rising of the dawn; the Elder's attainment of the three fruits by suppressing the poison with the power of insight; the poison's descent into the earth from the very place he was bitten; and the conclusion of the Dhamma talk by the preaching elder—all occurred in the very same moment. Then the Elder said, “Friends, a certain thief has been caught by me.” Untying the bag, he released the viper. The monks, seeing this, asked, “Venerable sir, at what time were you bitten?” “Yesterday evening, friends.” “Venerable sir, why did you perform such a difficult deed?” “Friends, if I had said, ‘I have been bitten by a long-bodied creature,’ I would not have obtained this much benefit.” This, for now, is the story of the Elder Piṇḍapātika.

Dīghavāpiyampi “mahājātakabhāṇakatthero gāthāsahassaṃ mahāvessantaraṃ kathessatī”ti tissamahāgāme tissamahāvihāravāsī eko [M 2.0135] daharo sutvā tato nikkhamitvā ekāheneva navayojanamaggaṃ āgato. Tasmiṃyeva khaṇe thero dhammakathaṃ ārabhi. Daharo dūramaggāgamanena sañjātakāyadarathattā paṭṭhānagāthāya saddhiṃ avasānagāthaṃyeva vavatthapesi. Tato therassa “idamavocā”ti [V 2.0133] vatvā uṭṭhāya gamanakāle “mayhaṃ āgamanakammaṃ moghaṃ jāta”nti rodamāno aṭṭhāsi. Eko manusso taṃ kathaṃ sutvā gantvā therassa ārocesi, “bhante, ‘tumhākaṃ dhammakathaṃ sossāmī’ti eko daharabhikkhu tissamahāvihārā āgato, so ‘kāyadarathabhāvena me āgamanaṃ moghaṃ jāta’nti rodamāno ṭhito”ti. Gacchatha saññāpetha naṃ “puna sve kathessāmā”ti. So punadivase therassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi.

Also in Dīghavāpi, a certain young monk residing in Tissamahāvihāra in Tissamahāgāma, having heard, “The Elder, an expert in the great Khuddaka Nikāya, will preach the Mahāvessantara, which has a thousand verses,” set out from there and in just one day arrived after a journey of nine yojanas. At that very moment, the Elder began the Dhamma talk. The young monk, due to bodily affliction arising from the long journey, was able to grasp only the concluding verse along with the introductory verse. After that, when the Elder, having said, “Thus was it said,” rose and was leaving, the young monk stood weeping, thinking, “My act of coming has become fruitless.” A certain man, hearing that sound, went and informed the Elder, “Venerable sir, a young monk came from Tissamahāvihāra, thinking, ‘I will listen to your Dhamma talk.’ He is standing weeping, thinking, ‘Due to bodily affliction, my coming has become fruitless.’” “Go and inform him, saying, ‘We will preach again tomorrow.’” On the next day, having listened to the Elder’s Dhamma talk, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Aparāpi ullakolikaṇṇivāsikā ekā itthī puttakaṃ pāyamānā “dīghabhāṇakamahāabhayatthero nāma ariyavaṃsapaṭipadaṃ kathetī”ti sutvā pañcayojanamaggaṃ gantvā divākathikattherassa nisinnakāleyeva vihāraṃ pavisitvā bhūmiyaṃ puttaṃ nipajjāpetvā divākathikattherassa ṭhitakāva dhammaṃ assosi. Sarabhāṇake there uṭṭhite dīghabhāṇakamahāabhayatthero catupaccayasantosabhāvanārāmamahāariyavaṃsaṃ ārabhi. Sā ṭhitakāva paggaṇhāti. Thero tayo eva paccaye kathetvā uṭṭhānākāraṃ akāsi. Sā upāsikā āha – “ayyo, ‘ariyavaṃsaṃ kathessāmī’ti siniddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā madhurapānakaṃ pivitvā yaṭṭhimadhukatelādīhi bhesajjaṃ katvā kathetuṃ [P 2.0250] yuttaṭṭhāneyeva uṭṭhahatī”ti. Thero “sādhu, bhaginī”ti vatvā upari bhāvanārāmaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Aruṇuggamanañca therassa “idamavocā”ti vacanañca upāsikāya sotāpattiphaluppatti ca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi.

Also, a certain woman from Ullakolikaṇṇivāsa, while carrying her young son, heard, “An Elder named Mahāabhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, teaches the practice of the Ariyavaṃsa.” Having traveled a distance of five yojanas, she entered the monastery at the very time the Elder who preaches during the day was seated. She laid her son on the ground and, while standing, listened to the Dhamma. When the Elder who recites the Pāḷi had risen, the Elder Mahāabhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, began the great Ariyavaṃsa of contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. She, while standing, absorbed it. The Elder, having spoken of only three requisites, made a gesture of rising. That laywoman said: “Venerable sir, having declared, ‘I will teach the Ariyavaṃsa,’ and having eaten rich food, drunk a sweet drink, and prepared medicine with things such as ghee, honey, and oil, you are now rising at the very moment it is suitable to teach.” The Elder, saying, “Very well, sister,” proceeded to expound upon the delight in meditation. The rising of the dawn, the Elder’s concluding words, “Thus was it said,” and the laywoman’s attainment of the fruit of stream-entry all occurred in the very same moment.

Aparāpi kaḷamparavāsikā itthī aṅkena puttaṃ ādāya “dhammaṃ sossāmī”ti cittalapabbataṃ gantvā ekaṃ rukkhaṃ nissāya dārakaṃ nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ ṭhitakāva dhammaṃ suṇāti. Rattibhāgasamanantare eko dīghajātiko tassā [M 2.0136] passantiyāyeva samīpe nipannadārakaṃ catūhi dāṭhāhi ḍaṃsitvā agamāsi. Sā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ ‘putto me sappena daṭṭho’ti vakkhāmi, dhammassa antarāyo bhavissati. Anekakkhattuṃ kho pana me ayaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭe vaṭṭantiyā putto ahosi, dhammameva carissāmī”ti tiyāmarattiṃ ṭhitakāva dhammaṃ paggaṇhitvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya aruṇe uggate saccakiriyāya puttassa visaṃ nimmathetvā puttaṃ gahetvā gatā. Evarūpā puggalā dhammaṃ sotukāmā nāma honti.

Also, another woman, a resident of Kaḷampara, taking her son in her arms, went to Cittalapabbata thinking, “I will listen to the Dhamma.” Leaning against a tree, she laid the child down and, while standing, listened to the Dhamma. In the course of the night, a long-bodied snake, while she was watching, bit the child lying near her with its four fangs and went away. She thought: “If I were to say, ‘My son has been bitten by a snake,’ there will be an obstacle to the Dhamma. Indeed, many times while I was revolving in the round of existence, this one has been my son; I will practice only the Dhamma.” Standing for the three watches of the night, she took up the Dhamma well and became established in the fruit of stream-entry. When dawn had broken, by an act of truth, she subdued the poison for her son and, taking him, went away. Such persons are called those who are desirous of hearing the Dhamma.

3. Atthavasasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Grounds for the Goal

43. Tatiye [V 2.0134] tayo, bhikkhave, atthavase sampassamānenāti tayo atthe tīṇi kāraṇāni passantena. Alamevāti yuttameva. Yo dhammaṃ desetīti yo puggalo catusaccadhammaṃ pakāseti. Atthappaṭisaṃvedīti aṭṭhakathaṃ ñāṇena paṭisaṃvedī. Dhammappaṭisaṃvedīti pāḷidhammaṃ paṭisaṃvedī.

43. In the third sutta, “Monks, by one who sees three grounds for the goal…” means: by one who sees three benefits, three reasons. “It is enough” means: it is indeed suitable. “One who teaches the Dhamma” means: a person who reveals the Dhamma of the Four Truths. “One who is sensitive to the meaning” means: one who repeatedly experiences the commentary with wisdom. “One who is sensitive to the Dhamma” means: one who repeatedly experiences the Dhamma of the Pāḷi text.

4. Kathāpavattisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Course of Discussion

44. Catutthe ṭhānehīti kāraṇehi. Pavattinīti appaṭihatā niyyānikā.

44. In the fourth sutta, “by grounds” means: by causes. “Proceeding” means: unhindered, leading to liberation.

5. Paṇḍitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Wise One

45. Pañcame paṇḍitapaññattānīti paṇḍitehi paññattāni kathitāni pasatthāni. Sappurisapaññattānīti sappurisehi mahāpurisehi paññattāni kathitāni pasatthāni. Ahiṃsāti karuṇā ceva karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca. Saṃyamoti sīlasaṃyamo. Damoti [P 2.0251] indriyasaṃvaro, uposathavasena vā attadamanaṃ, puṇṇovāde (ma. ni. 3.395 ādayo; saṃ. ni. 4.88 ādayo) damoti vuttā khantipi āḷavake (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 183 ādayo) vuttā paññāpi imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭatiyeva. Mātāpitu upaṭṭhānanti mātāpitūnaṃ rakkhanaṃ gopanaṃ paṭijagganaṃ. Santānanti aññattha buddhapaccekabuddhaariyasāvakā santo nāma, idha pana mātāpituupaṭṭhākā adhippetā. Tasmā uttamaṭṭhena santānaṃ[M 2.0137], seṭṭhacariyaṭṭhena brahmacārīnaṃ. Idaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ sabbhi upaññātanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sataṃ etāni ṭhānānīti santānaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ etāni ṭhānāni kāraṇāni. Ariyo dassanasampannoti idha imesaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ ṭhānānaṃ kāraṇena ariyo ceva dassanasampanno ca veditabbo, na buddhādayo na sotāpannā. Atha vā sataṃ etāni ṭhānānīti mātupaṭṭhānaṃ pitupaṭṭhānanti etāni ṭhānāni santānaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ kāraṇānīti evaṃ mātāpituupaṭṭhākavasena imissā gāthāya attho veditabbo. Mātāpituupaṭṭhākoyeva hi idha “ariyo dassanasampanno”ti vutto. Sa lokaṃ bhajate sivanti so khemaṃ devalokaṃ gacchatīti.

45. In the fifth sutta, 'prescribed by the wise' means prescribed, spoken, and praised by the wise. 'Prescribed by the good' means prescribed, spoken, and praised by good and great people. 'Non-harming' means both compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion. 'Restraint' means restraint of moral virtue. 'Taming' means restraint of the faculties; or, by way of the Uposatha observance, the taming of oneself. Also, the patience spoken of as 'taming' in the Puṇṇovāda Sutta, and the wisdom spoken of in the Āḷavaka Sutta, are indeed applicable in this sutta. 'Attending to mother and father' means the protecting, guarding, and looking after of one's parents. 'Of the good': elsewhere, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples are called 'the good', but here it is intended to mean those who attend to their parents. Therefore, 'santānaṃ' is meant in the highest sense, and 'brahmacārīnaṃ' in the sense of the best conduct. Thus the meaning here should be understood as: 'This attending to mother and father is prescribed by the good.' 'These are the grounds of the good' means these grounds are the causes for the good, the highest persons. 'Noble and endowed with vision': here, one should be understood as noble and endowed with vision because of performing these very three grounds, not the Buddhas and others, nor stream-enterers. Alternatively, 'these are the grounds of the good' means that these grounds—attending to mother and attending to father—are the causes for the good, the highest persons. Thus, the meaning of this verse should be understood in terms of one who attends to parents. Indeed, here it is only the one who attends to parents who is called 'noble and endowed with vision.' 'He resorts to a secure world' means he goes to the secure world of the devas.

6. Sīlavantasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sutta on the Virtuous

46. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0135] tīhi ṭhānehīti tīhi kāraṇehi. Kāyenātiādīsu bhikkhū āgacchante disvā paccuggamanaṃ karontā gacchante anugacchantā āsanasālāya sammajjanaupalepanādīni karontā āsanāni paññāpentā pānīyaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpentā kāyena puññaṃ pasavanti nāma. Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā “yāguṃ detha, bhattaṃ detha, sappinavanītādīni detha, gandhapupphādīhi pūjetha, uposathaṃ upavasatha, dhammaṃ suṇātha, cetiyaṃ vandathā”tiādīni vadantā vācāya puññaṃ pasavanti nāma. Bhikkhū piṇḍāya carante disvā “labhantū”ti cintentā manasā puññaṃ pasavanti nāma. Pasavantīti paṭilabhanti. Puññaṃ [P 2.0252] panettha lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ kathitaṃ.

46. In the sixth sutta, 'by three grounds' means by three causes. In the text beginning with 'by body,' etc., those who, upon seeing monks approaching, go to meet them; who accompany them when they depart; who perform tasks such as sweeping and smearing with cow-dung in the dining hall; who prepare seats; and who set out drinking water—these are said to generate merit by body. Those who, upon seeing the community of monks going for alms, say such things as, 'Give gruel, give rice, give ghee, fresh butter, etc.; worship with perfumes, flowers, etc.; observe the Uposatha; listen to the Dhamma; pay homage to the cetiya'—these are said to generate merit by speech. Those who, upon seeing monks going for alms, think, 'May they obtain it'—these are said to generate merit by mind. 'They generate' means they obtain. Herein, merit is spoken of as a mixture of worldly and supramundane.

7. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sutta on the Characteristics of the Conditioned

47. Sattame saṅkhatassāti paccayehi samāgantvā katassa. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇānīti saṅkhataṃ etanti sañjānanakāraṇāni nimittāni. Uppādoti jāti. Vayoti bhedo. Ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ nāma jarā. Tattha saṅkhatanti tebhūmakā dhammā. Maggaphalāni pana asammasanūpagattā idha na kathīyanti. Uppādādayo saṅkhatalakkhaṇā nāma. Tesu uppādakkhaṇe uppādo, ṭhānakkhaṇe jarā, bhedakkhaṇe vayo. Lakkhaṇaṃ na saṅkhataṃ, saṅkhataṃ na lakkhaṇaṃ[M 2.0138], lakkhaṇena pana saṅkhataṃ paricchinnaṃ. Yathā hatthiassagomahiṃsādīnaṃ sattisūlādīni sañjānanalakkhaṇāni na hatthiādayo, napi hatthiādayo lakkhaṇāneva, lakkhaṇehi pana te “asukassa hatthī, asukassa asso, asukahatthī, asukaasso”ti vā paññāyanti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

47. In the seventh sutta, 'of the conditioned' means of that which is made by the coming together of conditions. 'Characteristics of the conditioned' means the signs, the causes for knowing thus: 'This is conditioned.' 'Arising' is birth. 'Passing away' is dissolution. The alteration of that which persists is called aging. Therein, 'the conditioned' refers to the phenomena of the three planes of existence. However, the paths and fruits are not spoken of here because they are not subject to comprehension. Arising and so on are called the characteristics of the conditioned. Among them, at the moment of arising, there is arising; at the moment of presence, there is aging; at the moment of dissolution, there is passing away. The characteristic is not the conditioned; the conditioned is not the characteristic. But by the characteristic, the conditioned is defined. Just as for elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, and so on, spears, pikes, and so on are the signs for recognition, but they are not the elephants, etc., nor are the elephants, etc., the characteristics themselves; yet by these characteristics they are known as 'so-and-so's elephant,' 'so-and-so's horse,' 'such-and-such an elephant,' or 'such-and-such a horse'—in such a way is this accomplishment of the simile to be understood.

8. Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sutta on the Characteristics of the Unconditioned

48. Aṭṭhame asaṅkhatassāti paccayehi samāgantvā akatassa. Asaṅkhatalakkhaṇānīti asaṅkhataṃ etanti sañjānanakāraṇāni nimittāni. Na uppādo paññāyatītiādīhi uppādajarābhaṅgānaṃ abhāvo vutto. Uppādādīnañhi abhāvena asaṅkhatanti paññāyati.

48. In the eighth sutta, 'of the unconditioned' means of that which is not made by conditions coming together. 'Characteristics of the unconditioned' means the signs, the causes for recognizing thus, 'This is unconditioned.' By the text beginning with 'no arising is discerned,' the absence of arising, aging, and dissolution is stated. Indeed, through the absence of arising and so on, it is known as 'unconditioned.'

9. Pabbatarājasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta of the Mountain King

49. Navame [V 2.0136] mahāsālāti mahārukkhā. Kulapatinti kulajeṭṭhakaṃ. Seloti silāmayo. Araññasminti agāmakaṭṭhāne. Brahmāti mahanto. Vaneti aṭaviyaṃ. Vanappatīti vanajeṭṭhakā. Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, maggaṃ sugatigāminanti sugatigāmikamaggasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ caritvā.

49. In the ninth sutta, 'great sāl trees' means great trees. 'A clan leader' means the chief of the clan. 'A rock' means made of stone. 'In the wilderness' means in a place without a village. 'Great' means large. 'In the forest' means in the woods. 'Lords of the forest' means the chiefs of the forest. "Having practiced the Dhamma here, the path leading to a good destination" means having practiced the Dhamma which is reckoned as the path leading to a good destination.

10. Ātappakaraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sutta on What Should Be Done with Ardency

50. Dasame [P 2.0253] ātappaṃ karaṇīyanti vīriyaṃ kātuṃ yuttaṃ. Anuppādāyāti anuppādatthāya, anuppādaṃ sādhessāmīti iminā kāraṇena kattabbanti attho. Paratopi eseva nayo. Sārīrikānanti sarīrasambhavānaṃ. Dukkhānanti dukkhamānaṃ. Tibbānanti bahalānaṃ, tāpanavasena vā tibbānaṃ. Kharānanti pharusānaṃ. Kaṭukānanti tikhiṇānaṃ. Asātānanti amadhurānaṃ. Amanāpānanti manaṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ asamatthānaṃ. Pāṇaharānanti jīvitaharānaṃ. Adhivāsanāyāti adhivāsanatthāya sahanatthāya khamanatthāya.

50. In the tenth sutta, 'ardency is to be done' means it is proper to make an effort. 'For non-arising' means for the purpose of non-arising; the meaning is that it is to be done for this reason: 'I will prevent unarisen states from arising.' This same method applies also to what follows. 'Bodily' means arisen in the body. 'Painful' means difficult to endure. 'Severe' means intense, or alternatively, fierce by way of tormenting. 'Harsh' means rough. 'Sharp' means sharp. 'Unpleasant' means not sweet. 'Disagreeable' means unable to gladden the mind. 'Life-taking' means life-destroying. 'For endurance' means for the purpose of endurance, for the purpose of bearing, for the purpose of forbearance.

Ettake [M 2.0139] ṭhāne satthā āṇāpetvā āṇattiṃ pavattetvā idāni samādapento yato kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha yatoti yadā. Ātāpīti vīriyavā. Nipakoti sappañño. Satoti satiyā samannāgato. Dukkhassa antakiriyāyāti vaṭṭadukkhassa paricchedaparivaṭumakiriyāya. Ime ca pana ātāpādayo tayopi lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā.

In this much of the passage, the Teacher, having given a command and issued the instruction, and now wishing to encourage them, spoke the words beginning with 'When, monks...' Therein, 'when' means when. 'Ardent' means possessing energy. 'Prudent' means wise. 'Mindful' means endowed with mindfulness. 'For making an end of suffering' means for making an end to the cycle, which is the boundary of the suffering of the round. Furthermore, these three, beginning with ardency, are taught as being mixed, mundane and supramundane.

11. Mahācorasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Sutta of the Great Thief

51. Ekādasame mahācoroti mahanto balavacoro. Sandhinti gharasandhiṃ. Nillopanti mahāvilopaṃ. Ekāgārikanti ekameva gehaṃ parivāretvā vilumpanaṃ. Paripanthepi tiṭṭhatīti panthadūhanakammaṃ karoti. Nadīvidugganti nadīnaṃ duggamaṭṭhānaṃ antaradīpakaṃ, yattha sakkā hoti dvīhipi tīhipi jaṅghasahassehi saddhiṃ nilīyituṃ. Pabbatavisamanti [P 2.0254] pabbatānaṃ visamaṭṭhānaṃ pabbatantaraṃ, yattha sakkā hoti sattahi vā aṭṭhahi vā jaṅghasahassehi saddhiṃ nilīyituṃ. Tiṇagahananti tiṇena vaḍḍhitvā sañchannaṃ dvattiyojanaṭṭhānaṃ. Rodhanti ghanaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṃsaṭṭhasākhaṃ ekābaddhaṃ [V 2.0137] mahāvanasaṇḍaṃ. Pariyodhāya atthaṃ bhaṇissantīti pariyodahitvā taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ pakkhipitvā atthaṃ kathayissanti. Tyāssāti te assa. Pariyodhāya atthaṃ bhaṇantīti kismiñci kiñci vattuṃ āraddheyeva “mā evaṃ avacuttha, mayaṃ etaṃ kulaparamparāya jānāma, na esa evarūpaṃ karissatī”ti taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ pakkhipitvā mahantampi dosaṃ harantā atthaṃ bhaṇanti. Atha vā pariyodhāyāti paṭicchādetvātipi attho. Te hi tassapi dosaṃ paṭicchādetvā atthaṃ bhaṇanti. Khataṃ upahatanti guṇakhananena khataṃ, guṇupaghātena upahataṃ. Visamena kāyakammenāti sampakkhalanaṭṭhena visamena kāyadvārikakammena. Vacīmanokammesupi eseva nayo. Antaggāhikāyāti dasavatthukāya antaṃ gahetvā ṭhitadiṭṭhiyā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

51. In the eleventh, 'great thief' means a great, powerful thief. 'Breach' means a house-breach. 'Plundering' means great plunder. 'Single-house raiding' means looting by surrounding just one house. 'Stands on the highway' means he commits the act of highway robbery. 'A difficult river-crossing' means a place among rivers that is difficult to access, an island, where it is possible to hide with two or three thousand horsemen. 'Uneven mountain terrain' means an uneven place among mountains, a mountain pass, where it is possible to hide with seven or eight thousand horsemen. 'A thicket of grass' means a place of two or three yojanas overgrown and covered by grass. 'A dense thicket' means a great forest grove that is dense, with branches intertwined with each other, connected as one. 'They will speak for his benefit, having bolstered his case' means they will speak for his benefit after having embellished it, inserting this and that reason. 'Tyāssa' is to be divided as 'te assa' (they for him). 'They speak for his benefit, having bolstered his case' means that as soon as someone starts to say anything against him, they speak for his benefit, inserting this and that reason, saying, ‘Do not speak thus! We know him through his family lineage; he would not do such a thing!’ Thus, while removing even a great fault, they speak for his benefit. Alternatively, the meaning of 'pariyodhāya' is also 'having concealed.' For they speak for his benefit by concealing his fault. 'Undermined and damaged' means undermined by the digging up of virtues, and damaged by the destruction of virtues. 'By unrighteous bodily action' means by bodily action that is unrighteous in the sense of being erroneous. The same method applies to verbal and mental actions. 'With a view that grasps at extremes' means with a wrong view that is established by grasping an extreme, a view which has ten grounds. The rest has a clear meaning throughout.

Cūḷavaggo pañcamo.

The Minor Division, the Fifth.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is completed.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Brāhmaṇavaggo

(6) 1. The Chapter on Brahmins

1. Paṭhamadvebrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Sutta on the First Two Brahmins

52. Brāhmaṇavaggassa [V 2.0138][M 2.0140][P 2.0255] paṭhame jiṇṇāti jarājiṇṇā. Vuddhāti vayovuddhā. Mahallakāti jātimahallakā. Addhagatāti tayo addhe atikkantā. Vayoanuppattāti tatiyaṃ vayaṃ anuppattā. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti puttadāre attano vacanaṃ akaronte disvā “samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gantvā niyyānikamaggaṃ gavesissāmā”ti cintetvā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Mayamassu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇāti; bho gotama, mayaṃ brāhmaṇā na khattiyā nāmaccā na gahapatikāti brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā jiṇṇātiādimāhaṃsu. Akatabhīruttāṇāti akatabhayaparittāṇā. Avassayabhūtaṃ patiṭṭhākammaṃ amhehi na katanti dassenti. Tagghāti ekaṃsatthe nipāto, sampaṭicchanatthe vā. Ekantena tumhe evarūpā, ahampi kho etaṃ sampaṭicchāmīti ca dasseti. Upanīyatīti upasaṃharīyati. Ayaṃ hi jātiyā jaraṃ upanīyati, jarāya byādhiṃ, byādhinā maraṇaṃ, maraṇena puna jātiṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “upanīyatī”ti.

52. In the first discourse of the Brāhmaṇa Chapter, 'jiṇṇā' means decrepit with old age. 'Vuddhā' means advanced in age. 'Mahallakā' means great by birth. 'Addhagatā' means having traversed the three periods of life. 'Vayoanuppattā' means having reached the last stage of life. 'Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu' means that, seeing their sons and wives not heeding their words, they thought, 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and seek the path of escape,' and so they approached. 'Mayamassu, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā' means: having made known their brahmin status by saying, 'Venerable Gotama, we are brahmins, not khattiyas, not ministers, not householders,' they then spoke the words beginning with 'jiṇṇā.' 'Akatabhīruttāṇā' means having not made a protection from fear. By this, they show: 'A wholesome action that serves as a firm support, a reliable refuge, has not been done by us.' 'Taggha' is a particle in the sense of certainty, or in the sense of acceptance. It shows: 'Certainly, you are of such a nature, and I, too, accept this statement.' 'Upanīyati' means it is brought near. For this world is led by birth to old age, by old age to sickness, by sickness to death, and by death again to birth. Therefore, it is said: 'upanīyati.'

Idāni yasmā te brāhmaṇā mahallakattā pabbajitvāpi vattaṃ pūretuṃ na sakkhissanti, tasmā ne pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpento bhagavā yodha kāyena saṃyamotiādimāha. Tattha kāyena saṃyamoti kāyadvārena saṃvaro. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Taṃ tassa petassāti taṃ puññaṃ tassa paralokaṃ gatassa tāyanaṭṭhena tāṇaṃ, nilīyanaṭṭhena leṇaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena dīpo, avassayanaṭṭhena saraṇaṃ, uttamagativasena parāyaṇañca hotīti dasseti. Gāthā uttānatthāyeva. Evaṃ [P 2.0256] te brāhmaṇā tathāgatena pañcasu sīlesu samādapitā yāvajīvaṃ pañca sīlāni rakkhitvā sagge nibbattiṃsu.

Now, because those brahmins, due to their great age, would not be able to fulfill the duties even if they went forth, the Blessed One, wishing to establish them in the five precepts, said, 'Here, there is restraint with the body,' and so on. Therein, 'restraint with the body' means restraint through the body-door. This same method applies to the remaining phrases. 'Taṃ tassa petassa' shows this: that merit, for that being who has gone to the next world, is a protection in the sense of protecting, a shelter in the sense of a hiding place, an island in the sense of a support, a refuge in the sense of a resort, and also a final destination by way of a supreme destination. The verses are clear in meaning. Thus, those brahmins, having been caused to undertake the five precepts by the Tathāgata, guarded the five precepts for as long as they lived and were reborn in the heavenly world.

2. Dutiyadvebrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Two Brahmins

53. Dutiye [V 2.0139][M 2.0141] bhājananti yaṃkiñci bhaṇḍakaṃ. Sesaṃ paṭhame vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

53. In the second discourse, 'bhājanaṃ' means any kind of article. The rest should be understood by the very same method as was explained in the first discourse.

3. Aññatarabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Sutta on a Certain Brahmin

54. Tatiye sammodanīyanti sammodajananiṃ. Sāraṇīyanti saritabbayuttakaṃ. Vītisāretvāti pariyosāpetvā. Kittāvatāti kittakena. Sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hotīti sāmaṃ passitabbo hoti. Akālikoti na kālantare phaladāyako. Ehipassikoti “ehi passā”ti evaṃ dassetuṃ sakkāti āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ pucchati. Opaneyyikoti attano cittaṃ upanetabbo. Paccattaṃ veditabboti sāmaṃyeva jānitabbo. Viññūhīti paṇḍitehi. Pariyādinnacittoti ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhacitto hutvā. Cetetīti cinteti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imasmiṃ pana sutte brāhmaṇena lokuttaramaggo pucchito, satthārāpi soyeva kathito. So hi sāmaṃ passitabbattā sandiṭṭhiko nāmāti.

54. In the third sutta, 'sammodanīyaṃ' means engendering cordiality. 'Sāraṇīyaṃ' means fit to be remembered. 'Vītisāretvā' means having concluded. 'Kittāvatā' means by how much. 'The Dhamma is sandiṭṭhika' means it is to be seen by oneself. 'Akāliko' means it is not fruit-bearing at a later time. 'Ehipassiko' means it is possible to show it by saying, 'Come and see'; by this, he asks about the practice that leads to attainment. 'Opaneyyiko' means it is to be brought into one's own mind. 'To be personally experienced' means it is to be known by oneself alone. 'By the wise' means by the wise, the noble ones. 'Pariyādinnacitto' means having a mind seized, grasped, and clung to. 'Ceteti' means he thinks. The rest here is self-explanatory. Furthermore, in this sutta, the supramundane path was asked about by the brahmin, and that very path was explained by the Teacher. Indeed, because it is to be seen by oneself, it is called 'sandiṭṭhika.'

4. Paribbājakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Sutta on Wanderers

55. Catutthe brāhmaṇaparibbājakoti brāhmaṇajātiko paribbājako, na khattiyādijātiko. Attatthampīti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ attano atthaṃ.

55. In the fourth sutta, 'brāhmaṇaparibbājako' means a wanderer of brahmin birth, not of khattiya or other birth. 'Attatthampi' means one's own benefit, which pertains to the present life and the future life, and is a mixture of worldly and supramundane.

5. Nibbutasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Sutta on Nibbāna

56. Pañcame akālikanti na kālantare pattabbaṃ. Opaneyyikanti paṭipattiyā upagantabbaṃ.

56. In the fifth sutta, 'akālikaṃ' means not to be attained after some time. 'Opaneyyikaṃ' means to be approached through practice.

6. Palokasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Sutta on the Other World

57. Chaṭṭhe ācariyapācariyānanti ācariyānañceva ācariyācariyānañca. Avīci maññe phuṭo ahosīti yathā avīci mahānirayo nirantaraphuṭo nerayikasattehi paripuṇṇo, manussehi [V 2.0140] evaṃ paripuṇṇo hoti. Kukkuṭasaṃpātikāti ekagāmassa chadanapiṭṭhito uppatitvā itaragāmassa [M 2.0142][P 2.0257] chadanapiṭṭhe patanasaṅkhāto kukkuṭasaṃpāto etāsu atthīti kukkuṭasaṃpātikā. Kukkuṭasaṃpādikātipi pāṭho, gāmantarato gāmantaraṃ kukkuṭānaṃ padasā gamanasaṅkhāto kukkuṭasaṃpādo etāsu atthīti attho. Ubhayampetaṃ ghananivāsataṃyeva dīpeti. Adhammarāgarattāti rāgo nāma ekanteneva adhammo, attano parikkhāresu pana uppajjamāno na adhammarāgoti adhippeto, paraparikkhāresu uppajjamānova adhammarāgoti. Visamalobhābhibhūtāti lobhassa samakālo nāma natthi, ekantaṃ visamova esa. Attanā pariggahitavatthumhi pana uppajjamāno samalobho nāma, parapariggahitavatthumhi uppajjamānova visamoti adhippeto. Micchādhammaparetāti avatthupaṭisevanasaṅkhātena micchādhammena samannāgatā. Devo na sammā dhāraṃ anuppavecchatīti vassitabbayutte kāle vassaṃ na vassati. Dubbhikkhanti dullabhabhikkhaṃ. Dussassanti vividhasassānaṃ asampajjanena dussassaṃ. Setaṭṭhikanti sasse sampajjamāne pāṇakā patanti, tehi daṭṭhattā nikkhantanikkhantāni sālisīsāni setavaṇṇāni honti nissārāni. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “setaṭṭhika”nti. Salākāvuttanti vapitaṃ vapitaṃ sassaṃ salākāmattameva sampajjati, phalaṃ na detīti attho. Yakkhāti yakkhādhipatino. Vāḷe amanusse ossajjantīti caṇḍayakkhe manussapathe vissajjenti, te laddhokāsā mahājanaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti.

57. In the sixth sutta, `ācariyapācariyānaṃ` means: of the first teachers and of the teachers' teachers. `Avīci maññe phuṭo ahosi` means: just as the great Avīci hell is continuously filled with hell-beings and completely full, so too is this place filled with people. `Kukkuṭasaṃpātikā` refers to villages where a chicken, flying up from the roof of one house, can land on the roof of another; such villages are called `kukkuṭasaṃpātikā`. There is also the reading `kukkuṭasaṃpādikā`, meaning that chickens walk from one village to another. Both these terms indicate a dense settlement. `Adhammarāgarattā`: lust is, indeed, exclusively unrighteous, but lust that arises toward one's own requisites is not intended as 'unrighteous lust'; it is intended as 'unrighteous lust' only when it arises toward others' requisites. `Visamalobhābhibhūtā`: for greed, there is no such thing as a balanced time; it is exclusively unbalanced. But when it arises toward one's own possessions, it is intended as 'balanced greed'; it is intended as 'unbalanced greed' only when it arises toward others' possessions. `Micchādhammaparetā`: they are endowed with wrong practice, namely, engaging in what is unsuitable. `Devo na sammā dhāraṃ anuppavecchati`: when rain is fit to fall, it does not fall. `Dubbhikkhaṃ`: a scarcity of food. `Dussassaṃ`: a poor harvest, due to the failure of various crops to mature. `Setaṭṭhikaṃ`, the 'white-boned' disease: when the crop is maturing, insects fall upon it; because they are bitten by them, the emerging rice-ears become white and without substance. Referring to this, it is so called. `Salākāvuttaṃ`, the 'stalk-only' growth: the sown crop matures only to a stalk; it does not produce fruit. This is the meaning. `Yakkhā`: the yakkha chieftains. `Vāḷe amanusse ossajjanti`: they release fierce yakkhas onto human paths, and when they get the opportunity, they cause the destruction of life of the masses.

7. Vacchagottasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vacchagotta Sutta.

58. Sattame mahapphalanti mahāvipākaṃ. Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontīti ettha dhammo nāma kathitakathā, anudhammo nāma kathitassa paṭikathanaṃ. Sahadhammikoti sakāraṇo sahetuko. Vādānupātoti vādassa anupāto, anupatanaṃ pavattīti attho. Gārayhaṃ [P 2.0258] ṭhānanti garahitabbayuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhotā gotamena vuttā sakāraṇā vādappavatti kiñcipi gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ na āgacchatīti. Atha vā tehi parehi vuttā sakāraṇā vādappavatti kiñci gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ na āgacchatīti pucchati.

58. In the seventh sutta, `mahapphalaṃ` means great result. In the passage `dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākaronti`, 'they explain the Dhamma and what is in accordance with the Dhamma': here, `dhammo` means the spoken word, and `anudhammo` means speaking in imitation of what has been spoken. `Sahadhammiko`, 'with reason,' means with cause, with a basis. `Vādānupāto`, 'following the argument,' means the following of the speech, the sequence, the occurrence; this is the meaning. `Gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ`, 'a blameworthy position,' means a reason connected with what is blameworthy. This is what is meant: 'The occurrence of speech spoken by the venerable Gotama, which is with reason, does not lead to any blameworthy reason whatsoever.' Alternatively, he asks: 'Does the occurrence of speech spoken by those others, which is with reason, not lead to any blameworthy reason?'

Antarāyakaro [M 2.0143] hotīti antarāyaṃ vināsaṃ kicchalābhakaṃ vilomakaṃ karoti. Pāripanthikoti panthadūhanacoro. Khato ca hotīti guṇakhananena khato hoti. Upahatoti guṇupaghāteneva upahato.

`Antarāyakaro hoti`, 'creates obstacles,' means it causes obstruction, destruction, difficult acquisition, or opposition. `Pāripanthiko`, 'a highway robber,' means a thief who destroys on the path. `Khato ca hoti`, 'is undermined,' means one is undermined by the undermining of virtues. `Upahato`, 'is ruined,' means one is ruined by the very destruction of virtues.

Candanikāyāti [V 2.0141] asucikalalakūpe. Oligalleti niddhamanakalale. So cāti so sīlavāti vuttakhīṇāsavo. Sīlakkhandhenāti sīlarāsinā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ vuccati paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ, taṃ asekkhassa pavattattā asekkhanti vuttaṃ. Itarāni sikkhāpariyosānappattatāya sayampi asekkhāneva. Tāni ca pana lokuttarāni, paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ.

`Candanikāya`, 'in a cesspit,' means in a mire-pit of filth. `Oligalleti`, 'plunges,' means into the mud discharged from a drain. `So ca`, 'and he,' refers to that aforementioned destroyer of taints who is called `sīlavā`, 'virtuous.' `Sīlakkhandhena`, 'by the aggregate of virtue,' means by the mass of virtue. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here, reviewing knowledge is called the knowledge and vision of liberation. Because it occurs for one beyond training, it is called `asekkhaṃ`, 'beyond training.' The others, because they have reached the conclusion of the training, are themselves also 'beyond training.' Furthermore, those are supramundane, while reviewing knowledge is mundane.

Rohiṇīsūti rattavaṇṇāsu. Sarūpāsūti attano vacchakehi samānarūpāsu. Pārevatāsūti kapotavaṇṇāsu. Dantoti nibbisevano. Puṅgavoti usabho. Dhorayhoti dhuravāho. Kalyāṇajavanikkamoti kalyāṇena ujunā javena gantā. Nāssa vaṇṇaṃ parikkhareti assa goṇassa sarīravaṇṇaṃ na upaparikkhanti, dhuravahanakammameva pana upaparikkhanti. Yasmiṃ kasmiñci jātiyeti yattha katthaci kulajāte. Yāsu kāsuci etāsūti etāsu khattiyādippabhedāsu yāsu kāsuci jātīsu.

`Rohiṇīsu`, 'among the red cows,' means among the reddish-colored ones. `Sarūpāsu`, 'among those of similar form,' means among those similar in form to their own calves. `Pārevatāsu`, 'among the dove-colored,' means among the dove-colored ones. `Danto`, 'tamed,' means free from opposition. `Puṅgavo`, 'a lead bull,' means a bull. `Dhorayho`, 'a beast of burden,' means a bearer of the yoke. `Kalyāṇajavanikkamo`, 'of fine speed and gait,' means one who goes with a good, straight speed. `Nāssa vaṇṇaṃ parikkhare`, 'they do not examine its appearance,' means they do not examine the body-color of that ox, but they only examine the work of bearing the yoke. `Yasmiṃ kasmiñci jātiye`, 'in whatever birth,' means born in whatever family. `Yāsu kāsuci etāsu`, 'among whichever of these,' means among whichever of these castes, which are divided into the warrior class, etc.

Brahmacariyassa kevalīti brahmacariyassa kevalena samannāgato, paripuṇṇabhāvena yuttoti attho. Khīṇāsavo hi sakalabrahmacārī nāma hoti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pannabhāroti [P 2.0259] oropitabhāro, khandhabhāraṃ kilesabhāraṃ kāmaguṇabhārañca oropetvā ṭhitoti attho. Katakiccoti catūhi maggehi kiccaṃ katvā ṭhito. Pāragū sabbadhammānanti sabbadhammā vuccanti pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, tesaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ abhiññāpāraṃ, pariññāpāraṃ, pahānapāraṃ, bhāvanāpāraṃ, sacchikiriyāpāraṃ, samāpattipārañcāti chabbidhaṃ pāraṃ gatattā pāragū. Anupādāyāti aggahetvā. Nibbutoti kilesasantāparahito. Virajeti rāgadosamoharajarahite.

`Brahmacariyassa kevalī`, 'perfect in the holy life,' means endowed with the entirety of the holy life, meaning joined with the state of completeness. For one whose taints are destroyed is indeed called a `sakalabrahmacārī`, 'a complete practitioner of the holy life.' Hence, this was said. `Pannabhāro`, 'one whose burden is laid down,' means one whose burden is cast off; this means one who stands having cast off the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of sensual pleasures. `Katakicco`, 'one who has done what had to be done,' means one who stands having done the sixteen tasks by means of the four paths. `Pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ`, 'gone beyond all phenomena': all phenomena are said to be the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements; having gone to the six kinds of far shore in regard to all those phenomena—the far shore of direct knowledge, the far shore of full understanding, the far shore of abandoning, the far shore of development, the far shore of realization, and the far shore of attainment—one is `pāragū`, 'gone beyond.' `Anupādāya`, 'without grasping,' means not taking up. `Nibbuto`, 'extinguished,' means devoid of the fever of defilements. `Viraje`, 'in the stainless,' means in that which is devoid of the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion.

Avijānantāti [M 2.0144] khettaṃ ajānantā. Dummedhāti nippaññā. Assutāvinoti khettavinicchayasavanena rahitā. Bahiddhāti imamhā sāsanā bahiddhā. Na hi sante upāsareti buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsave uttamapurise na upasaṅkamanti. Dhīrasammateti paṇḍitehi sammate sambhāvite. Mūlajātā patiṭṭhitāti iminā sotāpannassa saddhaṃ dasseti. Kule vā idha jāyareti idha vā manussaloke khattiyabrāhmaṇavessakule jāyanti. Ayameva hi tividhā kulasampatti nāma. Anupubbena nibbānaṃ, adhigacchantīti sīlasamādhipaññāti ime guṇe pūretvā anukkamena nibbānaṃ adhigacchantīti.

'Not knowing' means not knowing the field. 'Foolish' means lacking wisdom. 'Unlearned' means lacking the hearing that discerns the field. 'Outsiders' means those outside this Dispensation. 'They do not approach the virtuous ones' means they do not draw near to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and arahants—the supreme persons. 'Esteemed by the wise' means esteemed and honored by the wise. 'Rooted and established': by this, the faith of a stream-enterer is shown. 'Born in a family here' means they are born in a khattiya, brāhmaṇa, or vessa family in this human world. This indeed is called the threefold accomplishment in family. 'Gradually attaining Nibbāna' means that having fulfilled these qualities—morality, concentration, and wisdom—they progressively attain Nibbāna.

8. Tikaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Tikaṇṇa Sutta

59. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0142] tikaṇṇoti tassa nāmaṃ. Upasaṅkamīti “samaṇo kira gotamo paṇḍito, gacchissāmi tassa santika”nti cintetvā bhuttapātarāso mahājanaparivuto upasaṅkami. Bhagavato sammukhāti dasabalassa purato nisīditvā. Vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti kasmā bhāsati? So kira ito pubbe tathāgatassa santikaṃ agatapubbo. Athassa etadahosi – “buddhā nāma durāsadā, mayi paṭhamataraṃ akathente katheyya vā na vā. Sace na kathessati, atha maṃ samāgamaṭṭhāne kathentaṃ [P 2.0260] evaṃ vakkhanti ‘tvaṃ idha kasmā kathesi, yena te samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gantvā vacanamattampi na laddha’nti. Tasmā ‘evaṃ me ayaṃ garahā muccissatī’”ti maññamāno bhāsati. Kiñcāpi brāhmaṇānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tathāgatassa pana ñāṇaṃ ghaṭṭessāmīti adhippāyeneva bhāsati. Evampi tevijjā brāhmaṇāti tevijjakabrāhmaṇā evaṃpaṇḍitā evaṃdhīrā evaṃbyattā evaṃbahussutā evaṃvādino, evaṃsammatāti attho. Itipīti iminā tesaṃ paṇḍitādiākāraparicchedaṃ dasseti. Ettakena kāraṇena paṇḍitā…pe… ettakena kāraṇena sammatāti ayañhi ettha attho.

59. In the eighth sutta, Tikaṇṇa is his name. 'He approached' means that, having thought, “The ascetic Gotama, it is said, is wise; I will go to his presence,” and after eating his morning meal, surrounded by a great crowd, he approached. 'In the presence of the Blessed One' means having sat down in front of the Ten-Powered One. As for 'He speaks praise'—why does he speak? It is said that he had never before come into the presence of the Tathāgata. Then this thought occurred to him: “Buddhas are indeed difficult to approach. If I do not speak first, he may or may not speak. If he does not speak, then in the assembly they will say this to me as I am speaking, ‘Why do you speak here? You went to the ascetic Gotama and did not get even a word.’ Therefore, thinking, ‘In this way I will be freed from this blame,’ he speaks.” Although he speaks the praise of the brahmins, he speaks with the sole intention of testing the Tathāgata’s knowledge. 'Thus also are the three-Veda brahmins' means that the three-Veda brahmins are so wise, so steadfast, so competent, so learned, so eloquent, and so esteemed. By this phrase `iti pi` (`thus also`), it shows the delimitation of their qualities, beginning with wisdom. “For such-and-such a reason they are wise… for such-and-such a reason they are esteemed”—this indeed is the meaning here.

Yathā kathaṃ pana brāhmaṇāti ettha yathāti kāraṇavacanaṃ, kathaṃ panāti pucchāvacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kathaṃ pana, brāhmaṇa, brāhmaṇā tevijjaṃ [M 2.0145] paññāpenti. Yathā evaṃ sakkā hoti jānituṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ vadehīti. Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo “jānanaṭṭhāneyeva maṃ sammāsambuddho pucchi, no ajānanaṭṭhāne”ti attamano hutvā idha, bho gotamātiādimāha. Tattha ubhatoti dvīhipi pakkhehi. Mātito ca pitito cāti yassa mātā brāhmaṇī, mātu mātā brāhmaṇī, tassāpi mātā brāhmaṇī. Pitā brāhmaṇo, pitu pitā brāhmaṇo, tassāpi pitā brāhmaṇo, so ubhato sujāto mātito ca pitito ca. Saṃsuddhagahaṇikoti yassa saṃsuddhā mātu gahaṇī, kucchīti attho. “Samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā”ti pana ettha kammajatejodhātu gahaṇīti vuccati.

In 'Yathā kathaṃ pana brāhmaṇa,' 'yathā' is a term for reason, and 'kathaṃ pana' is a term for questioning. This is what is meant: 'How then, O brahmin, do the brahmins declare the threefold Veda? By what reason it is possible to know this, state that reason.' Hearing that, the brahmin, thinking, 'The Perfectly Enlightened One has asked me only on a point that I know, not on a point that I do not know,' became pleased in mind and said, 'Here, venerable Gotama,' and so on. Therein, 'from both' means from both sides. 'From the mother's side and from the father's side' means: he whose mother is a brahmin woman, whose mother's mother is a brahmin woman, and her mother is also a brahmin woman; whose father is a brahmin, whose father's father is a brahmin, and his father is also a brahmin—he is well-born on both sides, from his mother's side and from his father's side. 'Of pure conception' means he whose mother's conception, that is, womb, is pure. But in the phrase 'samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā,' 'gahaṇī' is said to be the heat-element born of kamma.

Yāva sattamā pitāmahayugāti ettha pitu pitā pitāmaho, pitāmahassa yugaṃ pitāmahayugaṃ. Yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ vuccati. Abhilāpamattameva cetaṃ, atthato pana pitāmahoyeva pitāmahayugaṃ. Tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā. Evaṃ yāva sattamo puriso, tāva saṃsuddhagahaṇiko, atha [P 2.0261] vā akkhitto anupakkuṭṭho jātivādenāti [V 2.0143] dasseti. Akkhittoti “apanetha etaṃ, kiṃ iminā”ti evaṃ akkhitto anavakkhitto. Anupakkuṭṭhoti na upakkuṭṭho, na akkosaṃ vā nindaṃ vā pattapubbo. Kena kāraṇenāti? Jātivādena. “Itipi hīnajātiko eso”ti evarūpena vacanenāti attho.

In 'Up to the seventh grandfather-generation': here, the father's father is the grandfather, and the grandfather's generation is the grandfather-generation. By 'generation' is meant the measure of a lifespan. This is merely a term, but in meaning, the grandfather himself is the grandfather-generation. Beyond him, all previous ancestors are included by the term 'grandfather'. Thus, as far as the seventh man, so far is he of pure conception; or else, it shows that he is unrejected and unreviled on account of talk about birth. 'Unrejected' means not cast out thus: 'Remove this one! What is the use of him?'—in this way he is not cast out, not disparaged. 'Unreviled' means not reviled, never having encountered abuse or blame. For what reason? On account of talk about birth. The meaning is: by words of this kind, 'This one is of low birth.'

Ajjhāyakoti idaṃ “na dānime jhāyanti, na dānime jhāyantīti kho, vāseṭṭha, ajjhāyakā ajjhāyakāteva tatiyaṃ akkharaṃ upanibbatta”nti (dī. ni. 3.132) evaṃ paṭhamakappikakāle jhānavirahitānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ garahavacanaṃ uppannaṃ. Idāni pana taṃ ajjhāyatīti ajjhāyako, mante parivattetīti iminā atthena pasaṃsāvacanaṃ katvā voharanti. Mante dhāretīti mantadharo.

Regarding 'Ajjhāyaka': This arose as a term of reproach in the primordial age for brahmins devoid of jhāna: 'Now these do not meditate, now these do not meditate; thus, Vāseṭṭha, the term 'ajjhāyaka' was formed, the third letter having been brought into being.' But now, having made it a term of praise, they use it with this meaning: one is an 'ajjhāyaka' because one recites, and because one repeats the mantras. One who retains the mantras is a 'mantadhara'.

Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti irubbedayajubbedasāmabbedānaṃ. Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasena pāraṃ gatoti pāragū. Saha nighaṇḍunā ca keṭubhena ca sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ. Nighaṇḍūti nāmanighaṇḍurukkhādīnaṃ vevacanapakāsakasatthaṃ. Keṭubhanti kiriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ upakārāya satthaṃ. Saha akkharappabhedena [M 2.0146] sākkharappabhedānaṃ. Akkharappabhedoti sikkhā ca nirutti ca. Itihāsapañcamānanti āthabbaṇavedaṃ catutthaṃ katvā itiha āsa, itiha āsāti īdisavacanapaṭisaṃyutto purāṇakathāsaṅkhāto khattavijjāsaṅkhāto vā itihāso pañcamo etesanti itihāsapañcamā. Tesaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ vedānaṃ.

'Of the three Vedas' means of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. A 'pāragū' is one who has gone to the further shore, having mastered them by means of oral recitation. The Vedas are mastered 'together with the Nighaṇḍu and the Keṭubha.' 'Nighaṇḍu' is the text that explains the synonyms of names, trees, and so on. 'Keṭubha' is a text that aids poets in the arrangement and variation of compositions. They are also mastered 'together with the Akkharappabheda,' which comprises phonetics (sikkhā) and etymology (nirutti). 'With the Itihāsa as the fifth' refers to those Vedas where, having made the Āthabbaṇa Veda the fourth, the Itihāsa is the fifth. The Itihāsa is connected with sayings such as 'thus it was here, thus it was here,' and is known as ancient lore or, alternatively, the science of the warrior class. The full phrase is 'of those Vedas which have the Itihāsa as the fifth'.

Padaṃ tadavasesañca byākaraṇaṃ adhīyati vedeti cāti padako veyyākaraṇo. Lokāyataṃ vuccati vitaṇḍavādasatthaṃ. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇanti mahāpurisānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇadīpakaṃ dvādasasahassaganthapamāṇaṃ satthaṃ, yattha soḷasasahassagāthāpadaparimāṇā buddhamantā nāma ahesuṃ, yesaṃ vasena “iminā lakkhaṇena samannāgatā buddhā nāma honti[P 2.0262], iminā paccekabuddhā, dve aggasāvakā, asīti mahāsāvakā, buddhamātā, buddhapitā, aggupaṭṭhākā, aggupaṭṭhāyikā, rājā cakkavattī”ti ayaṃ viseso ñāyati. Anavayoti imesu lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anūno paripūrakārī, avayo na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Avayo nāma yo tāni atthato ca ganthato ca sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Atha vā anavayoti anu avayo, sandhivasena ukāralopo. Anu avayo paripuṇṇasippoti attho.

He studies and knows the padas and the remaining grammar; therefore, he is called a padaka (one versed in the texts) and a veyyākaraṇa (grammarian). Lokāyata is the name for the treatise on sophistry. 'The Marks of a Great Man' is a treatise that illuminates the characteristics of great beings such as the Buddhas, having a measure of twelve thousand sections. In it, there were what are called 'Buddha-mantras', measuring sixteen thousand verse-pādas, by means of which this distinction is known: 'Those endowed with this mark are called Buddhas; with this, Paccekabuddhas; the two chief disciples; the eighty great disciples; the Buddha's mother; the Buddha's father; the chief male attendants; the chief female attendants; and a wheel-turning monarch.' 'Without deficiency' means that in these treatises on Lokāyata and the Marks of a Great Man, he is not lacking, one who makes them complete; he is not deficient—this is what is meant. 'Deficient' refers to one who is unable to master them in both meaning and text. Alternatively, anavayo is parsed as anu avayo, with the elision of the 'u' due to sandhi. The meaning is: anu (thoroughly) not deficient, that is, one whose skill is complete.

Tena [V 2.0144] hīti idaṃ bhagavā naṃ āyācantaṃ disvā “idānissa pañhaṃ kathetuṃ kālo”ti ñatvā āha. Tassattho – yasmā maṃ āyācasi, tasmā suṇāhīti. Vivicceva kāmehītiādi visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.70) vitthāritameva. Idha panetaṃ tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipattidassanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha dvinnaṃ vijjānaṃ anupadavaṇṇanā ceva bhāvanānayo ca visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.402 ādayo) vitthāritova.

“Therefore” — seeing him entreating, the Blessed One, knowing that it was the time to answer his question, said this. Its meaning is: “Since you entreat me, therefore listen.” The passage beginning, “Secluded from sensual pleasures,” etc., is indeed elaborated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, however, it should be understood that this is stated to show the preliminary practice for the three knowledges. Therein, the word-by-word explanation for the two knowledges and the method of cultivation are indeed elaborated in the Visuddhimagga.

Paṭhamā vijjāti paṭhamaṃ uppannāti paṭhamā, viditakaraṇaṭṭhena vijjā. Kiṃ viditaṃ karoti? Pubbenivāsaṃ. Avijjāti tasseva pubbenivāsassa aviditakaraṇaṭṭhena tappaṭicchādako moho vuccati. Tamoti sveva moho paṭicchādakaṭṭhena tamoti vuccati. Ālokoti sāyeva vijjā obhāsakaraṇaṭṭhena ālokoti vuccati. Ettha ca vijjā adhigatāti ayaṃ attho[M 2.0147]. Sesaṃ pasaṃsāvacanaṃ. Yojanā panettha ayamassa vijjā adhigatā, athassa adhigatavijjassa avijjā vihatā vinaṭṭhāti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā vijjā uppannā. Itarasmimpi padadvaye eseva nayo. Yathā tanti ettha yathāti opammaṃ, tanti nipātamattaṃ. Satiyā avippavāsena appamattassa. Vīriyātāpena ātāpino. Kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pahitattassa. Pesitattassāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato avijjā vihaññeyya, vijjā uppajjeyya. Tamo vihaññeyya, āloko uppajjeyya, evameva tassa avijjā vihatā[P 2.0263], vijjā uppannā. Tamo vihato, āloko uppanno. Etassa tena padhānānuyogassa anurūpameva phalaṃ laddhanti.

The first knowledge is called ‘first’ because it arises first; it is called ‘knowledge’ because of its characteristic of making known. What does it make known? Past lives. Ignorance is said to be the delusion that conceals those very past lives, due to its characteristic of not making them known. That very delusion is called ‘darkness’ because of its characteristic of concealing. That very knowledge is called ‘light’ because of its characteristic of illuminating. And here, 'knowledge has been attained'—this is the essential meaning. The rest is a statement of praise. The construction of the meaning here is this: For this person, knowledge has been attained; then, for him who has attained knowledge, ignorance is dispelled, destroyed. This is the meaning. Why? Because knowledge has arisen. The same method applies to the other pair of terms. In the phrase 'yathā taṃ', 'yathā' is a simile; 'taṃ' is merely a particle. 'Of the heedful one' (appamattassa) is through not being parted from mindfulness. 'Of the ardent one' (ātāpino) is through the ardour of energy. 'Of one who has sent forth his mind' (pahitattassa) is through lack of regard for body and life; the meaning is 'one who has dispatched his mind' (pesitattassa). This is what is said: Just as for one who dwells heedful, ardent, and with mind sent forth, ignorance would be dispelled and knowledge would arise, darkness would be dispelled and light would arise—even so, for that person, ignorance is dispelled, knowledge has arisen, darkness is dispelled, and light has arisen. A fitting fruit, appropriate to this application to the endeavor, has been obtained.

Cutūpapātakathāyaṃ vijjāti dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjā. Avijjāti sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhippaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

In the discourse on passing away and rebirth, 'knowledge' is the knowledge of the divine eye. Ignorance is the ignorance that conceals the passing away and rebirth of beings. The rest is as previously explained.

Tatiyavijjāya so evaṃ samāhite citteti vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti arahattamaggañāṇatthāya. Arahattamaggo hi āsavavināsanato āsavānaṃ khayoti vuccati, tatra cetaṃ ñāṇaṃ tattha pariyāpannattāti. Cittaṃ abhininnāmetīti vipassanācittaṃ abhinīharati. So idaṃ dukkhanti evamādīsu ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyoti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇappaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti paṭivijjhati, tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti, tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati[V 2.0145], taṃ tesaṃ apavattiṃ nibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti. Tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti sarasalakkhaṇappaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti paṭivijjhatīti evamattho veditabbo.

For the third knowledge, with the mind thus concentrated, the fourth jhāna consciousness that is the basis for insight should be understood. 'For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints' is for the purpose of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. For the path of Arahantship is called 'the destruction of the taints' because it destroys the taints, and this knowledge is included therein because it is part of it. 'He directs the mind' means he brings forth the insight-mind. In reference to such passages as 'He... "this is suffering,"' he knows and penetrates all the truth of suffering as it really is by penetrating its own characteristic, understanding that 'suffering is just this much, and no more than this.' He also knows and penetrates the craving that produces that suffering as 'This is the origin of suffering.' He also knows and penetrates the state, having reached which both of these cease, as 'This is the cessation of suffering.' And he knows and penetrates the Noble Path that leads to it as 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering'—by penetrating its own characteristic as it really is. Thus, the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā idāni kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento ime āsavātiādimāha. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passatoti tassa bhikkhuno evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa. Saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathesi. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccatīti iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Maggakkhaṇe hi cittaṃ vimuccati, phalakkhaṇe [M 2.0148] vimuttaṃ hoti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ dasseti. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ. Tena hi ñāṇena so paccavekkhanto khīṇā jātītiādīni pajānāti. Katamā panassa [P 2.0264] jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ pajānātīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiappaṭisandhikaṃ hotīti jānanto pajānāti.

Having thus shown the truths in their own nature, now, wishing to show them by way of an alternative method through the power of the defilements, he spoke the words beginning with 'these are the taints'. The phrase 'For one who knows thus, who sees thus' refers to that monk who knows thus and sees thus. He speaks of the path that, together with insight, has reached its culmination. The word `kāmāsavā` is used in the sense of the ablative, `kāmāsavato` (from the taint of sensual desire). By the word 'is liberated' (`vimuccati`), he indicates the moment of the path. For at the moment of the path, the mind is being liberated; at the moment of fruition, it has become liberated. By the phrase 'the knowledge "liberated" in what is liberated,' he indicates the reviewing knowledge. By the phrases beginning with 'Birth is destroyed,' he indicates its ground. Indeed, with that reviewing knowledge, he who is reviewing understands the things beginning with 'birth is destroyed'. But what birth is destroyed for him, and how does he understand it? Not his past birth, for it was already destroyed before; not the future, because there is no striving in the future; not the present, because it is existing. But that birth—differentiated into one, four, or five aggregates—which would arise in the one-, four-, or five-constituent planes of existence due to the path not having been developed, that birth is destroyed by reaching the state of a non-arising nature due to the path having been developed. He understands this by reviewing the defilements abandoned through the development of the path, knowing thus: 'When there is an absence of defilements, even existing kamma becomes incapable of producing a future linking-consciousness.'

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso. Tasmā so attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti pajānāti. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā so attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti puna itthabhāvāya, evaṃ soḷasavidhakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato, imasmā evaṃ pakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi, ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya. Te carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissantīti pajānāti. Idha [V 2.0146] vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇavijjā. Avijjāti catusaccappaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

“The holy life has been lived” means it has been lived, thoroughly lived, done, practiced, and completed. This is the meaning. “The holy practice” means the holy practice of the path. Indeed, while the seven trainees together with the virtuous worldling are dwelling in the holy practice, the one whose taints are destroyed has completed the dwelling. Therefore, reflecting on his own dwelling in the holy practice, he knows distinctly, “The holy practice has been lived.” “What had to be done has been done” means the sixteenfold duty regarding the four truths—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development through the four paths—has been completed. This is the meaning. Indeed, virtuous worldlings and others are performing that duty, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed has done what was to be done. Therefore, reflecting on his own duty, he knows distinctly, “What had to be done has been done.” “There is no further for this state” means he knows distinctly that for him there is no further task of developing the path, either for this state of the sixteenfold duty or for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, “for this state” means: from this state of being, that is, from this present continuum of aggregates, there is no other continuum of aggregates for me. But these five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain like trees with their roots cut. He knows distinctly that with the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel. Here, “true knowledge” is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. “Ignorance” is the ignorance that conceals the four truths. The remainder is just as has been explained.

Anuccāvacasīlassāti yassa sīlaṃ kālena hāyati, kālena vaḍḍhati, so uccāvacasīlo nāma hoti. Khīṇāsavassa pana sīlaṃ [P 2.0265] ekantavaḍḍhitameva. Tasmā so anuccāvacasīlo nāma hoti. Vasībhūtanti [M 2.0149] vasippattaṃ. Susamāhitanti suṭṭhu samāhitaṃ, ārammaṇamhi suṭṭhapitaṃ. Dhīranti dhitisampannaṃ. Maccuhāyinanti maccuṃ jahitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sabbappahāyinanti sabbe pāpadhamme pajahitvā ṭhitaṃ. Buddhanti catusaccabuddhaṃ. Antimadehinanti sabbapacchimasarīradhārinaṃ. Taṃ namassanti gotamanti taṃ gotamagottaṃ buddhasāvakā namassanti. Atha vā gotamabuddhassa sāvakopi gotamo, taṃ gotamaṃ devamanussā namassantīti attho.

As for ‘one of unwavering virtue’: one whose virtue declines at times and grows at times is called ‘one of fluctuating virtue.’ But the virtue of one whose taints are destroyed only ever grows. Therefore, he is called ‘one of unwavering virtue.’ ‘Mastered’ means having attained mastery. ‘Well-composed’ means thoroughly composed, well-established on the object. ‘Wise’ means endowed with fortitude. ‘Having abandoned death’ means having abandoned death and being established. ‘Having abandoned all’ means having abandoned all evil qualities and being established. ‘Awakened’ means one who has understood the Four Truths. ‘Final-body bearer’ means one who bears the very last body. ‘They venerate that Gotama’ means the disciples of the Buddha venerate that one of the Gotama clan. Alternatively, a disciple of the Buddha Gotama is also called a Gotama, and the meaning is that devas and humans venerate that Gotama.
