Pubbenivāsanti pubbenivutthakkhandhaparamparaṃ. Yovetīti yo aveti avagacchati. Yovedītipi pāṭho. Yo avedi, viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā ṭhitoti attho. Saggāpāyañca passatīti cha kāmāvacare nava brahmaloke cattāro ca apāye passati. Jātikkhayaṃ pattoti arahattaṃ patto. Abhiññāvositoti jānitvā kiccavosānena vosito. Munīti moneyyena samannāgato khīṇāsavamuni. Etāhīti heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhāhi pubbenivāsañāṇādīhi. Nāññaṃ lapitalāpananti yo panañño tevijjoti aññehi lapitavacanamattameva lapati, tamahaṃ tevijjoti na vadāmi, attapaccakkhato ñatvā parassapi tisso vijjā kathentamevāhaṃ tevijjoti vadāmīti attho. Kalanti koṭṭhāsaṃ. Nāgghatīti na pāpuṇāti. Idāni brāhmaṇo bhagavato kathāya pasanno pasannākāraṃ karonto abhikkantantiādimāha.

‘Past abodes’ means the succession of aggregates previously dwelt in. ‘He who knows’ means he who knows and understands. There is also the reading ‘he has known,’ and the meaning is: he stands having made manifest what has been known. ‘He sees heaven and the states of deprivation’ means he sees the six sense-sphere heavens, the nine Brahmā realms, and the four states of deprivation. ‘Attained the destruction of birth’ means he has attained Arahantship. ‘Perfected in higher knowledge’ means having known, he is perfected through the completion of the task. ‘Sage’ means the sage whose taints are destroyed, who is endowed with sagacity. ‘By these’ means by the knowledge of past abodes and so on, which are pointed out below. ‘Not by other talk and chatter’ means: as for any other person who merely repeats the words spoken by others, saying ‘I am one with the threefold knowledge,’ I do not call him one with the threefold knowledge. Only one who, having known for himself directly, can also speak to another of the three knowledges, do I call ‘one with the threefold knowledge.’ This is the meaning. ‘A fraction’ means a portion. ‘Is not worth’ means does not attain. Now the brahmin, pleased by the Blessed One’s discourse and making a gesture of pleasure, said the words beginning with ‘Excellent.’

9. Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta

60. Navame yassassūti yassa bhaveyyuṃ. Yaññotiādīsu yajitabboti yañño, deyyadhammassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Saddhanti [P 2.0266] matakabhattaṃ. Thālipākoti varapurisānaṃ dātabbayuttaṃ bhattaṃ. Deyyadhammanti vuttāvasesaṃ yaṃkiñci deyyadhammaṃ nāma. Tevijjesu brāhmaṇesu dānaṃ dadeyyāti sabbametaṃ dānaṃ tevijjesu dadeyya, tevijjā brāhmaṇāva paṭiggahetuṃ yuttāti dasseti. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

60. In the ninth sutta, `yassassu` means `yassa bhaveyyuṃ` (for whom there would be). In passages such as `yañño`, because it is to be offered, it is called a sacrifice; this is a name for a gift-offering. `Saddha` means food offered in dedication to the deceased. `Thālipāka` means food suitable to be given to excellent men. `Deyyadhamma` means whatever gift-offering so-called remains, other than what has been mentioned. By the passage, ‘One should give a gift to brahmins possessed of the three knowledges,’ it shows that all this gift-offering should be given to those possessed of the three knowledges, and that only brahmins possessed of the three knowledges are fit to receive it. The remainder here is by the same method as stated above.

10. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

61. Dasame [V 2.0147] saṅgāravoti evaṃnāmako rājagahanagare jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇakārako āyuttakabrāhmaṇo. Upasaṅkamīti bhuttapātarāso hutvā mahājanaparivuto upasaṅkami. Mayamassūti ettha assūti [M 2.0150] nipātamattaṃ, mayaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇā nāmāti idameva atthapadaṃ. Yaññaṃ yajāmāti bāhirasamaye sabbacatukkena sabbaṭṭhakena sabbasoḷasakena sabbadvattiṃsāya sabbacatusaṭṭhiyā sabbasatena sabbapañcasatenāti ca evaṃ pāṇaghātapaṭisaṃyutto yañño nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Anekasārīrikanti anekasarīrasambhavaṃ. Yadidanti yā esā. Yaññādhikaraṇanti yajanakāraṇā ceva yājanakāraṇā cāti attho. Ekasmiñhi bahūnaṃ dadantepi dāpentepi bahūsupi bahūnaṃ dentesupi dāpentesupi puññapaṭipadā anekasārīrikā nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tuyhañca tuyhañca yajāmīti vadantassāpi tvañca tvañca yajāhīti āṇāpentassāpi ca anekasārīrikāva hoti. Tampi sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa vā tassa vāti yasmā vā tasmā vā. Ekamattānaṃ dametīti attano indriyadamanavasena ekaṃ attānameva dameti. Ekamattānaṃ sametīti attano rāgādisamanavasena ekaṃ attānameva sameti. Parinibbāpetīti [P 2.0267] rāgādiparinibbāneneva parinibbāpeti. Evamassāyanti evaṃ santepi ayaṃ.

61. In the tenth sutta, ‘Saṅgārava’ is a brahmin of that name in the city of Rājagaha, who undertook the repairing of what was dilapidated, a brahmin engaged in the king's affairs. ‘He approached’ means he approached after having eaten his morning meal, surrounded by a large crowd. In ‘mayamassu,’ ‘assu’ is merely a particle; ‘We, O Gotama, are brahmins by name’—this alone is the meaningful phrase. ‘We perform a sacrifice’ means: in the external doctrine, a sacrifice connected with the killing of living beings is performed with a group of all four creatures, a group of all eight, a group of all sixteen, a group of all thirty-two, a group of all sixty-four, a group of all one hundred, and a group of all five hundred. With reference to this, he spoke thus. ‘Anekasārīrikaṃ’ means arising from many bodies. ‘Yadidaṃ’ means that which is. ‘Yaññādhikaraṇaṃ’ means because of sacrificing and because of causing to sacrifice. For when one person gives to many or causes others to give, or when many people give to many or cause others to give, the practice of merit is called ‘arising from many bodies.’ With reference to this, it was said. Also, for one who says, ‘I sacrifice for you and for you,’ and for one who commands, ‘You and you, sacrifice,’ it is indeed ‘arising from many bodies.’ With reference to this also, it was said. ‘Yassa vā tassa vā’ means from any person whatsoever. ‘Ekamattānaṃ dameti’ means one tames only one's own self by means of restraining one's faculties. ‘Ekamattānaṃ sameti’ means one pacifies only one's own self by means of pacifying lust and so on. ‘Parinibbāpeti’ means one brings to complete quenching through the complete quenching of lust and so on. ‘Evamassāyaṃ’ means: although it is so, this…

Evamidaṃ brāhmaṇassa kathaṃ sutvā satthā cintesi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo pasughātakasaṃyuttaṃ mahāyaññaṃ anekasārīrikaṃ puññapaṭipadaṃ vadeti, pabbajjāmūlakaṃ pana puññuppattipaṭipadaṃ ekasārīrikanti vadeti. Nevāyaṃ ekasārīrikaṃ jānāti, na anekasārīrikaṃ, handassa ekasārīrikañca anekasārīrikañca paṭipadaṃ desessāmī”ti upari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento tena hi brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha yathā te khameyyāti yathā tuyhaṃ rucceyya. Idha tathāgato loke uppajjatītiādi visuddhimagge vitthāritameva. Ethāyaṃ maggoti etha tumhe, ahamanusāsāmi, ayaṃ maggo. Ayaṃ paṭipadāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Yathā paṭipannoti yena maggena paṭipanno. Anuttaraṃ brahmacariyogadhanti arahattamaggasaṅkhātassa brahmacariyassa anuttaraṃ ogadhaṃ uttamapatiṭṭhābhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ. Iccāyanti iti ayaṃ.

Having heard this discourse of the brahmin, the Teacher thought: 'This brahmin speaks of the great sacrifice connected with the slaughter of animals, a practice involving many bodies, as the path of merit; but he speaks of the path for the arising of merit, which is rooted in renunciation, as a practice involving a single body. This one knows neither the practice involving a single body nor the practice involving many bodies. Well now, I shall teach him the path involving a single body and the path involving many bodies.' Thus, extending the discourse further, He said, 'Then, O brahmin...' and so on. Therein, 'as you would approve' means 'as it would please you.' 'Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world,' and so on, is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Come, this is the path' means 'Come, you all, I shall instruct you; this is the path.' 'This is the practice' is a synonym for that very phrase. 'As practiced' means 'by which path one has practiced.' 'The unsurpassed immersion in the holy life' means Nibbāna, the unsurpassed foundation, the supreme establishment for the holy life called the Arahantship-path. The word `iccāyaṃ` is to be divided as `iti ayaṃ`.

Appaṭṭhatarāti yattha bahūhi veyyāvaccakarehi vā upakaraṇehi vā attho natthi. Appasamārambhatarāti yattha bahūnaṃ kammacchedavasena pīḷāsaṅkhāto [M 2.0151] samārambho natthi. Seyyathāpi bhavaṃ gotamo[V 2.0148], bhavaṃ cānando, ete me pujjāti yathā bhavaṃ gotamo, bhavañcānando, evarūpā mama pūjitā, tumheyeva dve janā mayhaṃ pujjā ca pāsaṃsā cāti imamatthaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vadati. Tassa kira evaṃ ahosi – “ānandatthero maṃyeva imaṃ pañhaṃ kathāpetukāmo, attano kho pana vaṇṇe vutte padussanako nāma natthī”ti. Tasmā pañhaṃ akathetukāmo vaṇṇabhaṇanena vikkhepaṃ karonto evamāha.

'Less burdensome' means where there is no need for many attendants or implements. 'Of less undertaking' means where there is no undertaking, which is defined as the oppression of many by way of interrupting their work. 'Just as the Venerable Gotama and the Venerable Ānanda, these are revered by me' means: he says this with the following meaning in mind: 'Just as the Venerable Gotama and the Venerable Ānanda are revered, so too are persons of such a nature revered by me. You two persons alone are revered and praised by me.' It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'The Elder Ānanda wishes to make me, and no other, answer this question. Indeed, when one's own praise is spoken, there is no one who is not pleased.' Therefore, not wishing to answer the question, he created a diversion by speaking praise, and said thus.

Na [P 2.0268] kho tyāhanti na kho te ahaṃ. Theropi kira cintesi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo pañhaṃ akathetukāmo parivattati, imaṃ pañhaṃ etaṃyeva kathāpessāmī”ti. Tasmā naṃ evamāha.

The phrase `Na kho tyāhaṃ` is to be divided as `na kho te ahaṃ`, meaning: 'Indeed, that is not what I asked you.' The Elder, it is said, also thought: 'This brahmin, not wishing to answer the question, is being evasive. I will make this very person answer this question.' Therefore, he said this to him.

Sahadhammikanti sakāraṇaṃ. Saṃsādetīti saṃsīdāpeti. No vissajjetīti na katheti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ parimoceyyanti yaṃnūnāhaṃ ubhopete vihesato parimoceyyaṃ. Brāhmaṇo hi ānandena pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ akathento viheseti, ānandopi brāhmaṇaṃ akathentaṃ kathāpento. Iti ubhopete vihesato mocessāmīti cintetvā evamāha. Kā nvajjāti kā nu ajja. Antarākathā udapādīti aññissā kathāya antarantare katarā kathā uppajjīti pucchati. Tadā kira rājantepure tīṇi pāṭihāriyāni ārabbha kathā udapādi, taṃ pucchāmīti satthā evamāha. Atha brāhmaṇo “idāni vattuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti rājantepure uppannaṃ kathaṃ ārocento ayaṃ khvajja, bho gotamātiādimāha. Tattha ayaṃ khvajjāti ayaṃ kho ajja. Pubbe sudanti ettha sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Uttari manussadhammāti dasakusalakammapathasaṅkhātā manussadhammā uttariṃ. Iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassesunti bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā ākāseneva gamiṃsu ceva āgamiṃsu cāti evaṃ pubbe pavattaṃ ākāsagamanaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Etarahi pana bahutarā ca bhikkhūti idaṃ so brāhmaṇo “pubbe bhikkhū ‘cattāro paccaye uppādessāmā’ti maññe evamakaṃsu, idāni paccayānaṃ uppannabhāvaṃ ñatvā soppena ceva pamādena ca vītināmentī”ti laddhiyā evamāha.

‘In accordance with the Dhamma’ means with a reason. ‘Confounds’ means causes to sink. ‘Does not reply’ means does not speak. ‘Perhaps I should release’ means ‘perhaps I should free both from harassment.’ For the brahmin is vexed by not answering the question asked by Ānanda, and Ānanda vexes by pressing the brahmin to answer. Thinking thus, ‘I will free both from harassment,’ he spoke thus. ‘What now?’ means ‘what indeed today?’ ‘A side discussion arose’ means he asks what other discussion arose in between the main one. At that time, it seems, a discussion arose in the king's palace concerning three miracles. Thinking, ‘I will ask about that,’ the Teacher spoke thus. Then the brahmin, thinking, ‘Now I will be able to speak,’ recounts the discussion that arose in the king's palace, saying, ‘This now, Venerable Gotama,’ etc. Here, ‘this now’ means ‘this indeed today.’ ‘Before, indeed’—here ‘indeed’ is merely a particle. ‘Superior to human states’ means superior to the ten wholesome courses of action, known as human states. ‘Show a miracle of psychic power’ refers to the past practice of going and returning through the air while going for alms; thus he speaks. ‘But now, many monks’—this the brahmin says with the view that: ‘Before, the monks perhaps thought, “We will obtain the four requisites,” and thus acted; now, knowing the availability of requisites, they pass their time in sleep and heedlessness.’

Pāṭihāriyānīti [M 2.0152] paccanīkapaṭiharaṇavasena pāṭihāriyāni. Iddhipāṭihāriyanti ijjhanavasena iddhi, paṭiharaṇavasena pāṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiyeva pāṭihāriyaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ. Itaresupi [P 2.0269] eseva nayo. Anekavihitaṃ iddhividhantiādīnaṃ attho ceva bhāvanānayo ca visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.365) vitthāritova.

‘Miracles’ are so called by way of dispelling what is contrary. ‘Miracle of psychic power’—by way of accomplishment it is psychic power, by way of dispelling what is contrary it is a miracle; psychic power itself is the miracle, the miracle of psychic power. The same method applies to the others. The meaning of ‘manifold psychic powers,’ etc., and the method of development are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Nimittena [V 2.0149] ādisatīti āgatanimittena vā gatanimittena vā ṭhitanimittena vā “idaṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti katheti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira rājā tisso muttā gahetvā purohitaṃ pucchi “kiṃ me, ācariya, hatthe”ti. So ito cito ca olokesi, tena ca samayena ekā sarabū “makkhikaṃ gahessāmī”ti pakkhantā, gahaṇakāle makkhikā palātā. So makkhikāya muttattā “muttā mahārājā”ti āha. Muttā tāva hontu, kati muttāti. So puna nimittaṃ olokesi. Athāvidūre kukkuṭo tikkhattuṃ saddaṃ nicchāresi. Brāhmaṇo “tisso mahārājā”ti āha. Evaṃ ekacco āgatanimittena katheti. Etenupāyena gataṭhitanimittehipi kathanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evampi te manoti evaṃ tava mano somanassito vā domanassito vā kāmavitakkādisaṃyutto vāti. Dutiyaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Itipi te cittanti itipi tava cittaṃ, imañca imañca atthaṃ cintayamānaṃ pavattatīti attho. Bahuṃ cepi ādisatīti bahuṃ cepi katheti. Tatheva taṃ hotīti yathā kathitaṃ, tatheva hoti.

‘He foretells by a sign’ means he tells by a sign of coming, or by a sign of going, or by a sign of standing, saying, ‘Such-and-such a thing will come to be.’ Herein is the story: It is said that a certain king took three pearls and asked his royal chaplain, ‘Teacher, what is in my hand?’ He looked here and there, and at that moment, a house lizard, intending, ‘I will catch a fly,’ leapt forward, but at the moment of catching, the fly escaped. Because the fly was released (muttattā), he said, ‘Pearls (muttā), Your Majesty.’ ‘Let them be pearls, but how many pearls are there?’ He looked for a sign again. Then, not far away, a rooster made a sound three times. The brahmin said, ‘Three, Your Majesty.’ Thus, a certain person tells by a sign of coming. By this method, telling by signs of going and standing should also be understood. ‘So too is your mind’ means thus your mind is either joyful or sorrowful or associated with sensual thoughts, and so on. The second phrase is a synonym of that very one. ‘So too is your consciousness’ means so too your consciousness proceeds, thinking of this and that matter; this is the meaning. ‘Even if he foretells much’ means even if he says much. ‘It is just so’ means it is just as it was said.

Amanussānanti yakkhapisācādīnaṃ. Devatānanti cātumahārājikādīnaṃ. Saddaṃ sutvāti aññassa cittaṃ ñatvā kathentānaṃ sutvā. Vitakkavipphārasaddanti vitakkavipphāravasena uppannaṃ vippalapantānaṃ suttappamattādīnaṃ saddaṃ. Sutvāti taṃ sutvā. Yaṃ vitakkayato tassa so saddo uppanno, tassa vasena “evampi te mano”tiādisati.

‘Of non-humans’ means of yakkhas, pisācas, and the like. ‘Of deities’ means of the devas of the Cātumahārājika realm and the like. The phrase ‘having heard the sound’ refers to hearing the sound of those who speak and thereby knowing another’s mind. ‘The sound of the diffusion of thought’ means the sound, arisen through the power of the diffusion of thought, of those who are muttering, such as those who are asleep, heedless, and so on. ‘Having heard’ means having heard that. For a person who is thinking a certain thought, that sound arises. By means of that, he foretells, ‘So too is your mind.’

Tatrimāni vatthūni – eko kira manusso “aṭṭaṃ karissāmī”ti gāmā nagaraṃ gacchanto [P 2.0270] nikkhantaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya “vinicchayasabhāyaṃ rañño ca rājamahāmattānañca idaṃ kathessāmi idaṃ kathessāmī”ti vitakkento rājakulaṃ gato viya rañño purato ṭhito viya aṭṭakārakena saddhiṃ [M 2.0153] kathento viya ca ahosi, tassa taṃ vitakkavipphāravasena niccharantaṃ saddaṃ sutvā eko puriso “kenaṭṭhena gacchasī”ti āha. Aṭṭakammenāti. Gaccha, jayo te bhavissatīti. So gantvā aṭṭaṃ katvā jayameva pāpuṇi.

In this regard, these are the stories. It is said that a certain man, thinking, 'I will attend to a legal matter,' was going from a village to a city. From the moment he set out, he was thinking, 'In the hall of justice, I will say this to the king and the king's great ministers, and I will say that.' While thinking thus, he was as if he had gone to the royal court, as if he stood before the king, and as if he were speaking with the opposing litigant. Hearing the sound that issued forth by the power of the expansion of his thought, a man asked, 'For what purpose are you going?' 'For a legal case.' 'Go, victory will be yours,' he said. That man went, presented his case, and attained victory indeed.

Aparopi thero moḷiyagāme piṇḍāya cari. Atha naṃ nikkhamantaṃ ekā dārikā aññavihitā na addasa. So gāmadvāre ṭhatvā nivattitvā oloketvā taṃ disvā vitakkento agamāsi. Gacchantoyeva ca “kiṃ nu kho kurumānā dārikā na addasā”ti vacībhedaṃ akāsi. Passe ṭhito eko puriso sutvā “tumhe, bhante, moḷiyagāme caritthā”ti āha.

Another elder, too, wandered for alms in Moḷiyagāma. Then, as he was departing, a certain girl, her mind directed elsewhere, did not see him. He, having stood at the village gate, turned back, looked, and seeing her, went on his way thinking. And even while going, he made a verbal utterance, 'What, I wonder, was the girl doing that she did not see me?' A man standing nearby heard this and said, 'Venerable sir, you have wandered for alms in Moḷiyagāma.'

Manosaṅkhārā [V 2.0150] paṇihitāti cittasaṅkhārā suṭṭhapitā. Vitakkessatīti vitakkayissati pavattayissatīti pajānāti. Pajānanto ca āgamanena jānāti, pubbabhāgena jānāti, antosamāpattiyaṃ cittaṃ apaloketvā jānāti. Āgamanena jānāti nāma kasiṇaparikammakāleyeva “yenākārenesa kasiṇabhāvanaṃ āraddho paṭhamajjhānaṃ vā…pe… catutthajjhānaṃ vā aṭṭha vā samāpattiyo nibbattessatī”ti jānāti. Pubbabhāgena jānāti nāma paṭhamavipassanāya āraddhāyayeva jānāti, “yenākārena esa vipassanaṃ āraddho sotāpattimaggaṃ vā nibbattessati…pe… arahattamaggaṃ vā nibbattessatī”ti jānāti. Antosamāpattiyaṃ cittaṃ oloketvā jānāti nāma – “yenākārena imassa manosaṅkhārā suṭṭhapitā, imassa nāma cittassa anantarā imaṃ nāma vitakkaṃ vitakkessati, ito vuṭṭhitassa etassa hānabhāgiyo vā samādhi bhavissati [P 2.0271] ṭhitibhāgiyo vā visesabhāgiyo vā nibbedhabhāgiyo vā, abhiññāyo vā nibbattessatī”ti jānāti. Tattha puthujjano cetopariyañāṇalābhī puthujjanānaṃyeva cittaṃ jānāti, na ariyānaṃ. Ariyesupi heṭṭhimo uparimassa cittaṃ na jānāti, uparimo pana heṭṭhimassa jānāti. Etesu ca sotāpanno sotāpattiphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati…pe… arahā arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Uparimo heṭṭhimaṃ na samāpajjati. Tesañhi heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā samāpatti tatravattiyeva hoti. Tatheva taṃ [M 2.0154] hotīti etaṃ ekaṃsena tatheva hoti. Cetopariyañāṇavasena ñātañhi aññathābhāvi nāma natthi.

The mental formations are well-directed—this means the formations of the mind are well-established. 'He will think'—this means he will reflect, he will cause to proceed—thus he understands. And understanding, he knows through the approach, he knows through the preliminary stage, he knows by observing the mind within the attainment. To know through the approach means that even during the preparatory work of the kasiṇa, he knows: 'By this manner, having undertaken the kasiṇa meditation, he will produce the first jhāna... up to the fourth jhāna or the eight attainments.' To know through the preliminary stage means that from the very beginning of insight meditation, he knows: 'By this manner, having undertaken insight, he will produce the path of stream-entry... up to the path of arahantship.' To know by observing the mind within the attainment means he knows: 'By this manner are this person's mental formations well-established. Immediately after such-and-such a mind of his, he will think such-and-such a thought. For one who emerges from this, the concentration will be one that partakes of decline, or partakes of stability, or partakes of distinction, or partakes of penetration, or he will produce the higher knowledges.' Here, an ordinary person who has attained the knowledge of others' minds knows only the minds of ordinary people, not those of the noble ones. Even among the noble ones, a lower one does not know the mind of a higher one, but a higher one knows the mind of a lower one. And among these, a stream-enterer attains the fruition attainment of stream-entry... up to an arahant attains the fruition attainment of arahantship. A higher one does not attain a lower attainment. For them, the lower attainments occur only for those at the respective lower levels. The phrase 'It is just so' means that this is definitely just so. For what is known by means of the knowledge of others' minds, there is no such thing as becoming otherwise.

Evaṃ vitakkethāti evaṃ nekkhammavitakkādayo pavattentā vitakketha. Mā evaṃ vitakkayitthāti evaṃ kāmavitakkādayo pavattentā mā vitakkayittha. Evaṃ manasi karothāti evaṃ aniccasaññameva, dukkhasaññādīsu vā aññataraṃ manasi karotha. Mā evanti niccantiādinā nayena mā manasā karittha. Idanti idaṃ pañcakāmaguṇarāgaṃ pajahatha. Idañca upasampajjāti idaṃ catumaggaphalappabhedaṃ lokuttaradhammameva upasampajja pāpuṇitvā nipphādetvā viharatha.

'Think thus' means: thus, causing thoughts of renunciation and the like to arise, you should think. 'Do not think thus' means: thus, causing thoughts of sensuality and the like to arise, you should not think. 'Direct your mind thus' means: thus, you should direct your mind to the perception of impermanence itself, or to any one among the perceptions of suffering and the like. 'Do not do so' means: you should not mentally formulate in the manner of 'it is permanent,' and so on. 'This' means: you should abandon this lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'And having attained this' means: having approached, reached, and accomplished this supramundane Dhamma itself, which is distinguished by the four paths and fruits, you should dwell.

Māyāsahadhammarūpaṃ viya khāyatīti māyāya samānakāraṇajātikaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Māyākāropi hi udakaṃ gahetvā telaṃ karoti, telaṃ gahetvā udakanti evaṃ anekarūpaṃ māyaṃ dasseti. Idampi pāṭihāriyaṃ tathārūpamevāti. Idampi me, bho gotama, pāṭihāriyaṃ māyāsahadhammarūpaṃ viya khāyatīti cintāmaṇikavijjāsarikkhakataṃ sandhāya evaṃ āha. Cintāmaṇikavijjaṃ [V 2.0151] jānantāpi hi āgacchantameva disvā “ayaṃ idaṃ nāma vitakkento āgacchatī”ti jānanti. Tathā “idaṃ nāma vitakkento ṭhito, idaṃ nāma vitakkento nisinno, idaṃ nāma vitakkento nipanno”ti jānanti.

'It appears to be of a nature similar to magic' means: it appears as if it has a nature with a cause similar to a magical illusion. Indeed, a magician, taking water, makes oil; taking oil, he makes water—thus he displays magic of various kinds. 'This miracle, too, is of such a nature.' 'This miracle, too, Venerable Gotama, appears to me to be of a nature similar to magic'—he said this referring to it having been made similar to the art called Cintāmaṇi. Indeed, those who know the Cintāmaṇi art, upon seeing someone approaching, know, 'This person is coming thinking such-and-such.' Similarly, they know, 'This person is standing thinking such-and-such, is sitting thinking such-and-such, is lying down thinking such-and-such.'

Abhikkantataranti [P 2.0272] sundarataraṃ. Paṇītataranti uttamataraṃ. Bhavañhi gotamo avitakkaṃ avicāranti idha brāhmaṇo avasesaṃ ādesanāpāṭihāriyaṃ bāhirakanti na gaṇhi. Idañca pana sabbaṃ so brāhmaṇo tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ kathentoyeva āha. Addhā kho tyāyanti ekaṃseneva tayā ayaṃ. Āsajja upanīya vācā bhāsitāti mama guṇe ghaṭṭetvā mameva guṇānaṃ santikaṃ upanītā vācā bhāsitā. Apica tyāhaṃ byākarissāmīti apica te ahameva kathessāmīti. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

'More splendid' means more beautiful. 'More excellent' means more supreme. In the passage 'For the Venerable Gotama is without applied thought and sustained thought,' here the brahmin did not regard the miracle of teaching without remainder as something external. And furthermore, that brahmin said all this only while intending to speak of the Tathāgata's qualities. 'Certainly by you... me...' means: it is certainly by you that I have been addressed. 'A challenging and insinuating speech was spoken' means: a speech was spoken that touched upon my qualities and was brought near to my very own qualities. 'And moreover, I will explain to you' means: 'Moreover, I myself will declare it to you.' The rest has an obvious meaning.

Brāhmaṇavaggo paṭhamo.

The Brahmin Chapter, the First.

(7) 2. Mahāvaggo

(7) 2. The Great Chapter

1. Titthāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Titthāyatana Sutta

62. Dutiyassa [V 2.0152][M 2.0155] paṭhame titthāyatanānīti titthabhūtāni āyatanāni, titthiyānaṃ vā āyatanāni. Tattha titthaṃ jānitabbaṃ, titthakarā jānitabbā, titthiyā jānitabbā, titthiyasāvakā jānitabbā. Titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Titthikarā nāma tāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ uppādakā. Titthiyā nāma yesaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo ruccanti khamanti. Titthiyasāvakā nāma tesaṃ paccayadāyakā. Āyatananti “kambojo assānaṃ āyatanaṃ, gunnaṃ dakkhiṇāpatho āyatana”nti ettha sañjātiṭṭhānaṃ āyatanaṃ nāma.

62. In the first sutta of the second chapter: `titthāyatanāni` (sectarian grounds) means grounds that have become sectarian fords, or the grounds of sectarians. Therein, the sectarian ford should be understood, the founders of sectarian fords should be understood, the sectarians should be understood, and the disciples of sectarians should be understood. 'Sectarian ford' refers to the sixty-two views. 'Founders of sectarian fords' refers to the originators of those views. 'Sectarians' refers to those for whom those views are pleasing and acceptable. 'Disciples of sectarians' refers to their providers of requisites. `Āyatana` (ground), as in 'Kamboja is the ground for horses, Dakkhinapatha is the ground for cattle,' here means the place of arising.

“Manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā;

Chāyaṃ chāyatthino yanti, phalatthaṃ phalabhojino”ti. (a. ni. 5.38) –

In a delightful abode, birds frequent it; those desiring shade go for shade, fruit-eaters for fruit.

Ettha samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, vimuttāyatanānī”ti (a. ni. 5.26) ettha kāraṇaṃ. Taṃ [P 2.0273] idha sabbampi labbhati. Sabbepi hi diṭṭhigatikā sañjāyamānā imesuyeva tīsu ṭhānesu sañjāyanti, samosaraṇamānāpi etesuyeva tīsu ṭhānesu samosaranti sannipatanti, diṭṭhigatikabhāve ca nesaṃ etāneva tīṇi kāraṇānīti titthabhūtāni sañjātiādinā atthena āyatanānītipi titthāyatanāni. Tenevatthena titthiyānaṃ āyatanānītipi titthāyatanāni. Samanuyuñjiyamānānīti kā nāmetā diṭṭhiyoti evaṃ pucchiyamānāni. Samanugāhiyamānānīti kiṃkāraṇā etā diṭṭhiyo uppannāti evaṃ sammā anuggāhiyamānāni. Samanubhāsiyamānānīti paṭinissajjetha etāni pāpakāni diṭṭhigatānīti evaṃ sammā anusāsiyamānāni. Apica tīṇipi etāni anuyogapucchāvevacanāneva. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “samanuyuñjatīti vā samanuggāhatīti vā samanubhāsatīti vā esese ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge tajjāte taññevā”ti.

Here, it means a place of assembly. In the passage, 'Monks, these are the five grounds for liberation,' it means cause. All of these meanings are obtained here. For indeed, all who hold wrong views, when arising, arise only in these three grounds; and when assembling, they assemble and gather only in these three grounds. And in their state of being holders of wrong views, these three alone are the causes. Therefore, because they are grounds (in the sense of arising, etc.) that have become sectarian fords, they are called `titthāyatanāni`. For this same reason, because they are the grounds of sectarians, they are also called `titthāyatanāni`. `Samanuyuñjiyamānāni` means being questioned thus: 'What are these views?' `Samanugāhiyamānāni` means being properly investigated thus: 'For what reason have these views arisen?' `Samanubhāsiyamānāni` means being properly admonished thus: 'Abandon these evil views!' Moreover, all three of these terms are simply synonyms for inquiry and questioning. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: 'Whether one says `samanuyuñjati`, `samanuggāhati`, or `samanubhāsati`, it is the same, of one meaning, equal, of the same share, of that same nature, that very thing.'

Parampi [V 2.0153] gantvāti ācariyaparamparā laddhiparamparā attabhāvaparamparāti etesu yaṃkiñci paramparaṃ gantvāpi. Akiriyāya saṇṭhahantīti akiriyamatte saṃtiṭṭhanti. “Amhākaṃ ācariyo pubbekatavādī, amhākaṃ pācariyo pubbekatavādī, amhākaṃ ācariyapācariyo pubbekatavādī. Amhākaṃ ācariyo issaranimmānavādī[M 2.0156], amhākaṃ pācariyo issaranimmānavādī, amhākaṃ ācariyapācariyo issaranimmānavādī. Amhākaṃ ācariyo ahetuapaccayavādī, amhākaṃ pācariyo ahetuapaccayavādī, amhākaṃ ācariyapācariyo ahetuapaccayavādī”ti evaṃ gacchantāni hi etāni ācariyaparamparaṃ gacchanti nāma. “Amhākaṃ ācariyo pubbekataladdhiko, amhākaṃ pācariyo…pe… amhākaṃ ācariyapācariyo ahetuapaccayaladdhiko”ti evaṃ gacchantāni laddhiparamparaṃ gacchanti nāma. “Amhākaṃ ācariyassa attabhāvo pubbekatahetu, amhākaṃ pācariyassa…pe… [P 2.0274] amhākaṃ ācariyapācariyassa attabhāvo ahetu apaccayo”ti evaṃ gacchantāni attabhāvaparamparaṃ gacchanti nāma. Evaṃ pana suvidūrampi gacchantāni akiriyamatteyeva saṇṭhahanti, ekopi etesaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ kattā vā kāretā vā na paññāyati.

As to 'Having gone beyond': this means having gone to any one of these lineages—a lineage of teachers, a lineage of doctrines, or a lineage of personal existences. As to 'they are established in inaction': this means they are established in mere inaction. For instance: 'Our teacher is a proponent of past-action theory; our teacher's teacher is a proponent of past-action theory; our teacher's teacher's teacher is a proponent of past-action theory. Our teacher is a proponent of creation by a supreme being; our teacher's teacher is a proponent of creation by a supreme being; our teacher's teacher's teacher is a proponent of creation by a supreme being. Our teacher is a proponent of causelessness; our teacher's teacher is a proponent of causelessness; our teacher's teacher's teacher is a proponent of causelessness.' In this way, these tenets are said to proceed through a lineage of teachers. 'Our teacher holds the doctrine of past actions; our teacher's teacher… and so on… our teacher's teacher's teacher holds the doctrine of causelessness.' In this way, these tenets are said to proceed through a lineage of doctrines. 'Our teacher's personal existence has a past-action cause; our teacher's teacher's… and so on… our teacher's teacher's teacher's personal existence is without cause and without condition.' In this way, these tenets are said to proceed through a lineage of personal existences. Furthermore, even when these tenets go very far, they are established only in mere inaction; not even one doer or instigator is apparent among those who hold these views.

Purisapuggaloti satto. Kāmañca purisotipi vutte puggalotipi vutte sattoyeva vutto hoti, ayaṃ pana sammutikathā nāma yo yathā jānāti, tassa tathā vuccati. Paṭisaṃvedetīti attano santāne uppannaṃ jānāti paṭisaṃviditaṃ karoti, anubhavati vā. Pubbekatahetūti pubbekatakāraṇā, pubbekatakammapaccayeneva paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Iminā kammavedanañca kiriyavedanañca paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ vipākavedanameva sampaṭicchanti. Ye vā ime pittasamuṭṭhānā ābādhā semhasamuṭṭhānā vātasamuṭṭhānā sannipātikā utupariṇāmajā visamaparihārajā opakkamikā ābādhā kammavipākajā ābādhāti aṭṭha rogā vuttā, tesu satta paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ vipākavedanaṃyeva sampaṭicchanti. Yepime diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ aparapariyāyavedanīyanti tayo kammarāsayo vuttā, tesupi dve paṭibāhitvā ekaṃ aparapariyāyakammaṃyeva sampaṭicchanti. Yepime diṭṭhadhammavedanīyo vipāko upapajjavedanīyo aparapariyāyavedanīyoti tayo vipākarāsayo vuttā, tesupi dve paṭibāhitvā ekaṃ aparapariyāyavipākameva sampaṭicchanti. Yepime kusalacetanā akusalacetanā vipākacetanā kiriyacetanāti cattāro cetanārāsayo vuttā, tesupi tayo paṭibāhitvā ekaṃ vipākacetanaṃyeva sampaṭicchanti.

A person is a being. Although when it is said 'a man' or 'a person,' it is only a being that is spoken of, this, however, is called conventional speech; it is spoken of for someone according to how they know. 'Experiences' means one knows what has arisen in one's own continuity, makes it manifest, or undergoes it. 'Due to what was done previously' means due to a cause made previously; the meaning is that one experiences solely through the condition of kamma done previously. By this, they reject both feeling associated with kamma and feeling associated with functional consciousness, and accept only feeling associated with result. And as for these eight kinds of diseases that are mentioned—diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, those from a combination of these, those born of climatic change, those born of improper conduct, those that are externally inflicted, and diseases born of the result of kamma—rejecting seven among them, they accept only the one born of the result of kamma. And as for these three categories of kamma that are mentioned—kamma to be experienced in the present life, kamma to be experienced in the next life, and kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life—having rejected two among them, they accept only kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life. And as for these three categories of result that are mentioned—result to be experienced in the present life, result to be experienced in the next life, and result to be experienced in a subsequent life—having rejected two among them, they accept only the result to be experienced in a subsequent life. And as for these four categories of volition that are mentioned—wholesome volition, unwholesome volition, resultant volition, and functional volition—having rejected three among them, they accept only resultant volition.

Issaranimmānahetūti [V 2.0154] issaranimmānakāraṇā, issarena nimmitattā paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Ayaṃ hi tesaṃ adhippāyo [P 2.0275] – imā tisso vedanā [M 2.0157] paccuppanne attanā katamūlakena vā āṇattimūlakena vā pubbekatena vā ahetuapaccayā vā paṭisaṃvedituṃ nāma na sakkā, issaranimmānakāraṇāyeva pana imā paṭisaṃvedetīti. Evaṃvādino panete heṭṭhā vuttesu aṭṭhasu rogesu ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbe paṭibāhanti, heṭṭhā vuttesu ca tīsu kammarāsīsu tīsu vipākarāsīsu catūsu cetanārāsīsu ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbepi paṭibāhanti.

The cause of creation by a sovereign being means due to the cause of creation by a sovereign being; because one experiences it as created by a sovereign being—this is the meaning. For this is their intention: these three feelings cannot be experienced in the present through a cause made by oneself, or through a cause based on command, or through a past action, or without a cause or condition; rather, they are experienced solely due to the cause of creation by a sovereign being. Furthermore, those who hold such a view, without accepting even one of the eight diseases mentioned previously, reject them all; and without accepting even one of the three groups of kamma, the three groups of resultants, or the four groups of volition mentioned previously, they reject them all.

Ahetuapaccayāti hetuñca paccayañca vinā, akāraṇeneva paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Ayañhi nesaṃ adhippāyo – imā tisso vedanā paccuppanne attanā katamūlakena vā āṇattimūlakena vā pubbekatena vā issaranimmānahetunā vā paṭisaṃvedituṃ nāma na sakkā, ahetuapaccayāyeva pana imā paṭisaṃvedetīti. Evaṃvādino panete heṭṭhā vuttesu rogādīsu ekampi asampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ paṭibāhanti.

“Without cause and condition” means experiencing without a generative cause and a supporting condition, simply without a reason—this is the meaning. For this is their intention: these three feelings cannot be experienced in the present due to a cause made by oneself, or a cause based on command, or a past action, or the cause of creation by a sovereign being; rather, they are experienced only without cause and without condition. Furthermore, those who hold such a view, without accepting even one of the previously mentioned diseases and so on, reject them all.

Evaṃ satthā mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā idāni taṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ tatra, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha evaṃ vadāmīti laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ evaṃ vadāmīti dasseti. Laddhiñhi appatiṭṭhāpetvā niggayhamānā laddhito laddhiṃ saṅkamanti, bho gotama, na mayaṃ pubbekatavādaṃ vadāmātiādīni vadanti. Laddhiyā pana patiṭṭhāpitāya saṅkamituṃ alabhantā suniggahitā honti, iti nesaṃ laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ evaṃ vadāmīti āha. Tenahāyasmantoti tena hi āyasmanto. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi etaṃ saccaṃ, evaṃ sante tena tumhākaṃ vādena. Pāṇātipātino bhavissanti pubbekatahetūti ye keci loke pāṇaṃ atipātenti, sabbe te pubbekatahetu pāṇātipātino bhavissanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Na hi pāṇātipātakammaṃ attanā katamūlakena na āṇattimūlakena na issaranimmānahetunā [P 2.0276] na ahetuapaccayā sakkā paṭisaṃvedetuṃ, pubbekatahetuyeva paṭisaṃvedetīti ayaṃ vo laddhi. Yathā ca pāṇātipātino, evaṃ pāṇātipātā viramantāpi pubbekatahetuyeva viramissantīti. Iti bhagavā tesaṃyeva laddhiṃ gahetvā tesaṃ niggahaṃ āropeti. Iminā nayena adinnādāyinotiādīsupi yojanā veditabbā.

Thus the Teacher, having laid down the matrix, now, in order to analyze and explain it, spoke the passage beginning with, 'Therein, O monks...'. Therein, He shows that He says, 'Thus I say,' for the purpose of establishing their doctrine. Indeed, without having established their own view, when pressed, they shift from one view to another, saying such things as, 'Venerable Gotama, we do not advocate the doctrine of past actions.' But when their view has been established, being unable to shift, they are thoroughly rebuked. Therefore, for the purpose of establishing their view, He said, 'Thus I say.' The phrase 'Then, venerable ones' means this: If this is true, this being so, then by your doctrine, people will be destroyers of life because of past actions. That is, whoever in the world destroys life, all of them will be destroyers of life because of past actions. For what reason? For the kamma of destroying life cannot be experienced as rooted in what is done by oneself, nor as rooted in a command, nor due to the creation of a sovereign being, nor as being without cause or condition; one experiences it only because of what was done in the past. This is your view. And just as they are destroyers of life because of past actions, so too those who refrain from destroying life will refrain only because of past actions. Thus, the Blessed One, taking their own view, applies the censure to them. By this method, the application should also be understood for 'taking what is not given,' and so on.

Sārato [M 2.0158] paccāgacchatanti sārabhāvena gaṇhantānaṃ. Chandoti kattukamyatāchando. Idaṃ vā karaṇīyaṃ [V 2.0155] idaṃ vā akaraṇīyanti ettha ayaṃ adhippāyo – idaṃ vā karaṇīyanti kattabbassa karaṇatthāya, idaṃ vā akaraṇīyanti akattabbassa akaraṇatthāya kattukamyatā vā paccattapurisakāro vā na hoti. Chandavāyāmesu vā asantesu “idaṃ kattabba”ntipi “idaṃ na kattabba”ntipi na hoti. Iti karaṇīyākaraṇīye kho pana saccato thetato anupalabbhiyamāneti evaṃ kattabbe ca akattabbe ca bhūtato thirato apaññāyamāne alabbhamāne. Yadi hi kattabbaṃ kātuṃ akattabbato ca viramituṃ labheyya, karaṇīyākaraṇīyaṃ saccato thetato upalabbheyya. Yasmā pana ubhayampi taṃ esa nupalabbhati, tasmā taṃ saccato thetato na upalabbhati, evaṃ tasmiṃ ca anupalabbhiyamāneti attho. Muṭṭhassatīnanti naṭṭhassatīnaṃ vissaṭṭhassatīnaṃ. Anārakkhānaṃ viharatanti chasu dvāresu nirārakkhānaṃ viharantānaṃ. Na hoti paccattaṃ sahadhammiko samaṇavādoti evaṃ bhūtānaṃ tumhākaṃ vā aññesaṃ vā mayaṃ samaṇāti paccattaṃ sakāraṇo samaṇavādo na hoti na ijjhati. Samaṇāpi hi pubbekatakāraṇāyeva honti, assamaṇāpi pubbekatakāraṇāyevāti. Sahadhammikoti sakāraṇo. Niggaho [P 2.0277] hotīti mama niggaho hoti, te pana niggahitā hontīti.

The phrase sārato paccāgacchataṃ means: of those who grasp it as essential. Chando is the desire to act. Regarding 'This should be done, or this should not be done,' the intention here is this: for the purpose of doing what should be done and for the purpose of not doing what should not be done, there is neither a desire to act nor personal effort. And when desire and effort are absent, neither 'This should be done' nor 'This should not be done' exists. Thus, the phrase 'when what should be done and what should not be done are not found to be true and firm' means: when what should be done and what should not be done are not discerned or obtained as real and stable. For if one could obtain the ability to do what should be done and to refrain from what should not be done, then what should be done and what should not be done would be obtained as true and firm. But since one does not obtain that pair, it is therefore not obtained as true and firm. This is the meaning of 'when that is not being obtained.' Muṭṭhassatīnaṃ means: of those with lost mindfulness, of those with lapsed mindfulness. Anārakkhānaṃ viharataṃ means: of those dwelling unguarded at the six doors. 'There is no personal, well-founded claim to being an ascetic' means: for those who are thus, whether yourselves or others, the personal, reasoned assertion 'We are ascetics' does not exist, it is not successful. For ascetics become so only because of a cause made in the past, and non-ascetics also become so only because of a cause made in the past. Sahadhammiko means with reason. 'There is a censure' means that my censure is established, and they are censured.

Evaṃ pubbekatavādino niggahetvā idāni issaranimmānavādino niggahetuṃ tatra, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tassattho pubbekatavāde vuttanayeneva veditabbo, tathā ahetukavādepi.

Having thus refuted those who hold the doctrine of past actions, now, in order to refute those who hold the doctrine of creation by a sovereign being, He spoke the words beginning with, 'Therein, O monks...'. Its meaning should be understood in the very same way as was stated in the section on the doctrine of past actions; likewise also in the section on the doctrine of no-cause.

Evaṃ imesaṃ titthāyatanānaṃ parampi gantvā akiriyāya saṇṭhahanabhāvena tucchabhāvaṃ aniyyānikabhāvaṃ, asārabhāvena thusakoṭṭanasadisataṃ āpajjanabhāvena aggisaññāya dhamamānakhajjupanakasarikkhataṃ taṃdiṭṭhikānaṃ purimassapi majjhimassapi pacchimassapi atthadassanatāya abhāvena andhaveṇūpamataṃ saddamatteneva tāni gahetvā sāradiṭṭhikānaṃ pathaviyaṃ patitassa beluvapakkassa daddabhāyitasaddaṃ sutvā “pathavī saṃvaṭṭamānā āgacchatī”ti saññāya palāyantena sasakena sarikkhabhāvañca dassetvā idāni attanā desitassa dhammassa sārabhāvañceva niyyānikabhāvañca dassetuṃ ayaṃ [M 2.0159] kho pana, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha aniggahitoti aññehi aniggahito niggahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Asaṃkiliṭṭhoti nikkileso parisuddho, “saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ naṃ karissāmā”ti pavattehipi tathā kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Anupavajjoti upavādavinimutto. Appaṭikuṭṭhoti “kiṃ iminā haratha na”nti evaṃ appaṭibāhito[V 2.0156], anupakkuṭṭho vā. Viññūhīti paṇḍitehi. Apaṇḍitānañhi ajānitvā kathentānaṃ vacanaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Tasmā viññūhīti āha.

Thus, having shown that even as these sectarian tenets are followed up through further successions, they are void due to being established in inaction and are not a means of deliverance; that due to being without essence, they are like the pounding of chaff; that due to arriving at the perception of 'fire', they are like a fanned firefly; that due to the absence of seeing the meaning for their proponents—the earlier, middle, and later—they are like a line of blind men; and for those holding the view of substance who have grasped these tenets merely by sound, they are like the hare that, upon hearing the 'thud' of a ripe wood-apple fruit falling to the ground, flees with the perception, 'The earth is breaking up and coming!'; now, in order to show the essential nature and the deliverance-leading nature of the Dhamma taught by himself, he spoke the passage beginning, 'This, O bhikkhus...'. Therein, 'unrefuted' means unable to be refuted by others. 'Unstained' means without defilements, pure; it cannot be made so even by those who set out thinking, 'We will make it stained.' 'Blameless' means free from reproach. 'Unrejected' means not prohibited thus: 'What is the use of this? Get rid of it!', or, not reviled. 'By the wise' means by the learned. For the word of the unwise, who speak without knowing, is no authority. Therefore, he said, 'by the wise'.

Idāni tassa dhammassa dassanatthaṃ “katamo ca, bhikkhave”ti pañhaṃ pucchitvā “imā cha dhātuyo”tiādinā nayena mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā yathāpaṭipāṭiyā vibhajitvā dassento puna imā cha dhātuyotiādimāha. Tattha dhātuyoti sabhāvā. Nijjīvanissattabhāvappakāsako hi sabhāvaṭṭho dhātvaṭṭho nāma. Phassāyatanānīti [P 2.0278] vipākaphassānaṃ ākaraṭṭhena āyatanāni. Manopavicārāti vitakkavicārapādehi aṭṭhārasasu ṭhānesu manassa upavicārā.

Now, for the purpose of showing that Dhamma, having asked the question, 'And which, O bhikkhus...?' and having laid down the matrix by the method beginning with 'these six elements,' while showing it by analyzing it according to its sequence, he again spoke the passage beginning, 'these six elements...'. Therein, 'elements' means intrinsic natures. For the meaning of 'element' is the meaning of intrinsic nature, which makes known the state of being without a life-principle and without a being. 'Bases for contact' means they are bases in the sense of being a source for resultant contacts. 'Mental explorations' are the mind's explorations in the eighteen instances by means of the 'feet' of initial thought and sustained thought.

Pathavīdhātūti patiṭṭhādhātu. Āpodhātūti ābandhanadhātu. Tejodhātūti paripācanadhātu. Vāyodhātūti vitthambhanadhātu. Ākāsadhātūti asamphuṭṭhadhātu. Viññāṇadhātūti vijānanadhātu. Evamidaṃ dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ kho panetaṃ saṅkhepato āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhepatopi vitthāratopi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vitthārato āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhepato kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati, vitthāratova vaṭṭati. Imasmiṃ pana titthāyatanasutte idaṃ saṅkhepato chadhātuvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ ubhayathāpi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

The earth element is the element of foundation. The water element is the element of cohesion. The fire element is the element of maturing. The air element is the element of support. The space element is the element of non-contact. The consciousness element is the element of cognition. Thus has this meditation subject on the elements come down. Furthermore, where this has come down in brief, it is fitting to speak of it both in brief and in detail. Where it has come down in detail, it is not fitting to speak of it in brief; it is fitting to speak of it only in detail. In this Discourse on the Bases of Sectarianism, however, this meditation subject has come down in brief by way of the six elements. It is fitting to speak of it in both ways.

Saṅkhepato chadhātuvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggaṇhantopi evaṃ pariggaṇhāti – pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātūti imāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, ākāsadhātu upādārūpaṃ. Ekasmiṃ ca upādārūpe diṭṭhe sesāni tevīsati diṭṭhānevāti sallakkhetabbāni. Viññāṇadhātūti cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandho hoti, tena sahajātā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandhoti ime cattāro arūpakkhandhā nāma. Cattāri pana mahābhūtāni catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādārūpaṃ [M 2.0160] rūpakkhandho nāma. Tattha cattāro arūpakkhandhā nāmaṃ, rūpakkhandho rūpanti nāmañca rūpañcāti dveyeva dhammā honti, tato uddhaṃ satto vā jīvo vā natthīti evaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno saṅkhepato chadhātuvasena arahattasampāpakaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

When taking up the meditation subject in brief by way of the six elements, one comprehends it thus: the earth element, water element, fire element, and air element—these are the four great primary elements; the space element is derived matter. And it should be noted that when one derived matter is seen, the remaining twenty-three are also seen. The consciousness element is the mind, which is the consciousness aggregate; co-arisen with it, feeling is the feeling aggregate, perception is the perception aggregate, and contact and volition are the formations aggregate—these four are called the immaterial aggregates. Furthermore, the four great primary elements and the matter derived from the four great primary elements are called the material aggregate. Therein, the four immaterial aggregates are 'name,' and the material aggregate is 'form'—thus, there are only these two phenomena: name and form. Beyond these, there is no being or life-principle. In this way, the meditation subject that leads to Arahantship should be understood by a monk in brief by way of the six elements.

Vitthārato pariggaṇhanto pana cattāri mahābhūtāni pariggaṇhitvā ākāsadhātupariggahānusārena tevīsati upādārūpāni pariggaṇhāti. Atha nesaṃ paccayaṃ upaparikkhanto [V 2.0157] puna cattāreva mahābhūtāni disvā tesu pathavīdhātu [P 2.0279] vīsatikoṭṭhāsā, āpodhātu dvādasa, tejodhātu cattāro, vāyodhātu chakoṭṭhāsāti koṭṭhāsavasena samodhānetvā dvācattālīsa mahābhūtāni ca vavatthapetvā tesu tevīsati upādārūpāni pakkhipitvā pañcasaṭṭhi rūpāni vavatthapeti. Tāni ca vatthurūpena saddhiṃ chasaṭṭhi hontīti chasaṭṭhi rūpāni passati. Viññāṇadhātu pana lokiyacittavasena ekāsīti cittāni. Tāni sabbānipi viññāṇakkhandho nāma hoti. Tehi sahajātā vedanādayopi tattakāyevāti ekāsīti vedanā vedanākkhandho, ekāsīti saññā saññākkhandho, ekāsīti cetanā saṅkhārakkhandhoti ime cattāro arūpakkhandhā tebhūmakavasena gayhamānā catuvīsādhikāni tīṇi dhammasatāni hontīti iti ime ca arūpadhammā chasaṭṭhi ca rūpadhammāti sabbepi samodhānetvā nāmañca rūpañcāti dveva dhammā honti, tato uddhaṃ satto vā jīvo vā natthīti nāmarūpavasena pañcakkhandhe vavatthapetvā tesaṃ paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjāpaccayā taṇhāpaccayā kammapaccayā āhārapaccayāti evaṃ paccayaṃ disvā “atītepi imehi paccayehi idaṃ vaṭṭaṃ pavattittha, anāgatepi etehi paccayehi pavattissati, etarahipi etehiyeva pavattatī”ti tīsu kālesu kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā anukkamena paṭipajjamāno arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Evaṃ vitthāratopi chadhātuvasena arahattasampāpakaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

When comprehending in detail, one first comprehends the four great elements and then, in accordance with the comprehension of the space element, comprehends the twenty-three derived materialities. Then, investigating their condition, one again sees the four great elements. Among them, the earth element has twenty portions, the water element has twelve, the fire element has four, and the air element has six portions. Thus, combining them by way of portions, one defines the forty-two great elements. Adding the twenty-three derived materialities to them, one defines sixty-five materialities. And these, together with the base-materiality, become sixty-six; thus, one sees sixty-six materialities. As for the consciousness element, by way of mundane consciousness, there are eighty-one consciousnesses. All of these are called the consciousness aggregate. The co-nascent feelings and so forth are also of that same number. Thus, eighty-one feelings are the feeling aggregate, eighty-one perceptions are the perception aggregate, and eighty-one volitions are the formations aggregate. These four immaterial aggregates, when taken by way of the three planes, become three hundred and twenty-four phenomena. Thus, these immaterial phenomena and the sixty-six material phenomena, when combined, become only two things: name and form. Beyond that, there is no being or life. Having thus defined the five aggregates by way of name and form, while searching for their condition, one sees the condition thus: from ignorance as condition, from craving as condition, from kamma as condition, and from nutriment as condition, name-and-form arises. Seeing the condition in this way: 'In the past, too, this round of existence arose from these conditions; in the future, too, it will arise from these conditions; and at present, it occurs only because of these same conditions.' In this way, having crossed over doubt concerning the three times, and practicing in sequence, one attains Arahantship. Thus, the meditation subject that leads to Arahantship by way of the six elements should be understood in detail as well.

Cakkhu phassāyatananti suvaṇṇādīnaṃ suvaṇṇādiākaro viya dve cakkhuviññāṇāni dve sampaṭicchanāni tīṇi santīraṇānīti imehi sattahi viññāṇehi sahajātānaṃ sattannaṃ phassānaṃ samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaroti āyatanaṃ. Sotaṃ phassāyatanantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Mano phassāyatananti [M 2.0161] ettha pana dvāvīsati vipākaphassā yojetabbā. Iti [P 2.0280] hidaṃ chaphassāyatanānaṃ vasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ saṅkhepatopi vitthāratopi kathetabbaṃ. Saṅkhepato tāva – ettha hi purimāni pañca āyatanāni upādārūpaṃ, tesu diṭṭhesu avasesaṃ upādārūpaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Chaṭṭhaṃ āyatanaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ viññāṇakkhandho hoti, tena sahajātā vedanādayo sesā tayo arūpakkhandhāti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca arahattasampāpakaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The eye-contact-base: Just as a mine is a source of gold and so forth, so too, because it is a source in the sense of being the place of arising for the seven contacts that are co-nascent with these seven consciousnesses—namely, the two eye-consciousnesses, the two receiving-consciousnesses, and the three investigating-consciousnesses—it is called a base. This same method applies to the ear-contact-base and so on. In the case of the mind-contact-base, however, twenty-two resultant contacts should be connected. Thus, this meditation subject is presented by way of the six contact-bases. It should be explained both in brief and in detail. First, in brief: Herein, the first five bases are derived material form; when these are seen, the remaining derived material form is indeed seen. The sixth base is the mind; that is the consciousness aggregate. Feeling and so forth, which are co-nascent with it, are the remaining three immaterial aggregates. Thus, in the manner already stated previously, the meditation subject that leads to the attainment of Arahantship should be understood both in brief and in detail.

Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ passitvā. Somanassaṭṭhāniyanti somanassassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ. Upavicaratīti tattha manaṃ cārento upavicarati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo[V 2.0158]. Ettha ca iṭṭhaṃ vā hotu aniṭṭhaṃ vā, yaṃ rūpaṃ disvā somanassaṃ uppajjati, taṃ somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ nāma. Yaṃ disvā domanassaṃ uppajjati, taṃ domanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ nāma. Yaṃ disvā upekkhā uppajjati, taṃ upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Saddādīsupi eseva nayo. Iti idaṃ saṅkhepato kammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ kho panetaṃ saṅkhepato āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhepatopi vitthāratopi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vitthārato āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhepato kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Imasmiṃ pana titthāyatanasutte idaṃ saṅkhepato aṭṭhārasamanopavicāravasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ. Taṃ saṅkhepatopi vitthāratopi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

‘Having seen a form with the eye’ means having perceived a form with eye-consciousness. ‘A basis for joy’ means it is a cause for joy. ‘Dwells upon’ means one engages with it by directing the mind toward it. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Herein, whether it is a desirable or an undesirable object, whatever form, having been seen, gives rise to joy is called ‘a basis for joy.’ Whatever form, having been seen, gives rise to displeasure is called ‘a basis for displeasure.’ Whatever form, having been seen, gives rise to equanimity is called ‘a basis for equanimity’; thus it should be understood. This same method applies to sounds and so forth. Thus, this meditation subject is presented in brief. Furthermore, that which is presented in brief, it is fitting to explain both in brief and in detail. That which is presented in detail, it is not fitting to explain in brief. In this Titthāyatana Sutta, however, this meditation subject is presented in brief by way of the eighteen mental inspections. It is fitting to explain it both in brief and in detail.

Tattha saṅkhepato tāva – cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo, rūpaṃ saddo gandho rasoti imāni nava upādārūpāni, tesu diṭṭhesu sesaṃ upādārūpaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ tīṇi mahābhūtāni, tehi diṭṭhehi catutthaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Mano viññāṇakkhandho, tena sahajātā vedanādayo tayo arūpakkhandhāti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca arahattasampāpakaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, first, in brief: eye-sensitivity, ear-sensitivity, nose-sensitivity, tongue-sensitivity, body-sensitivity; visible form, sound, odor, and taste—these nine are derived materiality. When these are seen, the remaining derived materiality is also seen. The tangible object consists of three great elements; when these are seen, the fourth is also seen. The mind is the consciousness aggregate; feeling and so forth, which are co-nascent with it, are the three immaterial aggregates. Thus, in the manner already stated previously, the meditation subject that leads to the fruit of Arahantship should be understood both concisely and in detail.

Ariyasaccānīti [P 2.0281] ariyabhāvakarāni, ariyapaṭividdhāni vā saccāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panetaṃ padaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.529) pakāsitaṃ. Channaṃ, bhikkhave, dhātūnanti idaṃ kimatthaṃ āraddhaṃ? Sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ. Yassa hi tathāgato dvādasapadaṃ paccayāvaṭṭaṃ kathetukāmo hoti, tassa gabbhāvakkanti vaṭṭaṃ dasseti. Gabbhāvakkanti vaṭṭasmiṃ hi dassite kathetumpi sukhaṃ hoti [M 2.0162] paraṃ avabodhe utumpīti sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ idamāraddhanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha channaṃ dhātūnanti heṭṭhā vuttānaṃyeva pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ. Upādāyāti paṭicca. Etena paccayamattaṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “chadhātupaccayā gabbhassāvakkanti hotī”ti. Kassa channaṃ dhātūnaṃ paccayena, kiṃ mātu, udāhu pitūti? Na mātu na pitu, paṭisandhiggaṇhanakasattasseva pana channaṃ dhātūnaṃ paccayena gabbhassāvakkanti nāma hoti. Gabbho ca nāmesa nirayagabbho tiracchānayonigabbho pettivisayagabbho manussagabbho devagabbhoti nānappakāro hoti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne manussagabbho adhippeto. Avakkanti hotīti okkanti nibbatti pātubhāvo hoti, kathaṃ hotīti? Tiṇṇaṃ sannipātena. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The Noble Truths (ariyasaccāni) are truths that make one noble, or truths that are penetrated by the noble ones. This is the summary here; but in detail, this term has been explained in the Visuddhimagga. 'Bhikkhus, of the six elements...'—for what purpose was this undertaken? For the purpose of easy understanding. Indeed, for whomever the Tathāgata wishes to teach the twelve-factored cycle of conditions, to that person he shows the cycle of conception. For when the cycle of conception is shown, it is easy to teach and easy for others to understand. Therefore, it should be known that this was undertaken for the purpose of easy understanding. Therein, 'of the six elements' refers to the earth element and so on, which were already mentioned previously. 'Dependent on' (upādāya) means 'conditioned by' (paṭicca). By this, he shows mere conditionality. This is what is meant: 'Due to the six elements as a condition, the descent of the embryo occurs.' Due to whose six elements as a condition—the mother's, or the father's? Not the mother's, nor the father's; rather, it is due to the six elements of the very being who takes up rebirth-linking that the so-called descent of the embryo occurs. And this so-called conception is of various kinds: conception in hell, conception in the animal realm, conception in the realm of ghosts, human conception, and divine conception. But in this context, human conception is intended. 'Descent occurs' (avakkanti hoti) means entry, coming into being, manifestation occurs. How does it occur? Through the conjunction of three things. For this was said:

“Tiṇṇaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, sannipātā gabbhassāvakkanti hoti. Katamesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ[V 2.0159]? Idha mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā honti, mātā ca na utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca na paccupaṭṭhito hoti. Neva tāva gabbhassāvakkanti hoti. Idha mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā honti, mātā ca utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca na paccupaṭṭhito hoti, neva tāva gabbhassāvakkanti hoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, mātāpitaro ca sannipatitā honti, mātā ca utunī hoti, gandhabbo ca paccupaṭṭhito hoti. Evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sannipātā gabbhassāvakkanti hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.408).

“Bhikkhus, the descent of an embryo occurs through the concurrence of three things. Which three? Here, the mother and father have come together, but the mother is not in her fertile season, and the gandhabba is not present. In that case, there is no descent of an embryo. Here, the mother and father have come together, and the mother is in her fertile season, but the gandhabba is not present; still, there is no descent of an embryo. But when, bhikkhus, the mother and father have come together, and the mother is in her fertile season, and the gandhabba is present—then, through the concurrence of these three, the descent of an embryo occurs.”

Okkantiyā [P 2.0282] sati nāmarūpanti “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṭṭhāne vatthudasakaṃ kāyadasakaṃ bhāvadasakaṃ tayo arūpino khandhāti tettiṃsa dhammā gahitā, imasmiṃ pana “okkantiyā sati nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṭṭhāne viññāṇakkhandhampi pakkhipitvā gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe catuttiṃsa dhammā gahitāti veditabbā. Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanantiādīhi yatheva okkantiyā sati nāmarūpapātubhāvo dassito, evaṃ nāmarūpe sati saḷāyatanapātubhāvo, saḷāyatane sati phassapātubhāvo, phasse sati vedanāpātubhāvo dassito.

Regarding 'When there is descent, there is mentality-materiality': in the passage that states 'With consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality,' thirty-three phenomena are taken: the heart-base decad (vatthu-dasaka), the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), and the three immaterial aggregates. However, in this passage, 'When there is descent, there is mentality-materiality,' the consciousness aggregate is also included, and it should be known that at the moment of rebirth-linking for beings in the womb, thirty-four phenomena are taken. Just as the manifestation of mentality-materiality is shown when there is descent, so too, when mentality-materiality is present, the manifestation of the six sense bases is shown; when the six sense bases are present, the manifestation of contact is shown; and when contact is present, the manifestation of feeling is shown.

Vediyamānassāti [M 2.0163] ettha vedanaṃ anubhavantopi vediyamānoti vuccati jānantopi. “Vediyāmahaṃ, bhante, vediyatīti maṃ saṅgho dhāretū”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 102) ettha hi anubhavanto vediyamāno nāma, “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmīti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.113; dī. ni. 2.380; vibha. 363) ettha jānanto. Idhāpi jānantova adhippeto. Idaṃ dukkhanti paññapemīti evaṃ jānantassa sattassa “idaṃ dukkhaṃ ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, natthi ito uddhaṃ dukkha”nti paññapemi bodhemi jānāpemi. Ayaṃ dukkhasamudayotiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Regarding “one who feels” (vediyamānassa), here, one who experiences feeling is also called “one who feels,” and so is one who knows. For in the passage, “I feel, venerable sir, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who feels,” the one who experiences is called “one who feels.” In the passage, “While feeling a pleasant feeling, he understands, ‘I am feeling a pleasant feeling,’” it refers to the one who knows. Here too, it is the one who knows that is intended. Regarding the statement, “I declare that this is suffering,” it means: to the being who knows thus, I declare, make understand, and make known, “This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is no suffering beyond this.” This same method also applies to the statements beginning with, “This is the origin of suffering.”

Tattha dukkhādīsu ayaṃ sanniṭṭhānakathā – ṭhapetvā hi taṇhaṃ tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā dukkhaṃ nāma, tasseva pabhāvikā pubbataṇhā dukkhasamudayo nāma, tesaṃ dvinnampi saccānaṃ anuppattinirodho dukkhanirodho nāma, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā nāma. Iti bhagavā okkantiyā sati nāmarūpanti kathentopi vediyamānassa jānamānasseva kathesi, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti kathentopi, saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti kathentopi, phassapaccayā vedanāti kathentopi, vediyamānassa kho panāhaṃ, bhikkhave, idaṃ dukkhanti paññapemīti [V 2.0160] kathentopi[P 2.0283], ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti paññapemīti kathentopi vediyamānassa jānamānasseva kathesi.

Herein, this is the definitive statement concerning suffering and so on: Indeed, setting aside craving, the five aggregates belonging to the three realms are called suffering. The previous craving that is their source is called the origin of suffering. The non-recurrent cessation of both these truths is called the cessation of suffering. The Noble Eightfold Path is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus, even when the Blessed One taught, “When there is descent, there is mentality-materiality,” he spoke only to one who knows. And even when teaching, “With mentality-materiality as condition, the six sense bases,” and “With the six sense bases as condition, contact,” and “With contact as condition, feeling,” and when declaring, “To one who feels, O bhikkhus, I make known that this is suffering,” and when declaring, “This is the origin of suffering,” “This is the cessation of suffering,” and “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering”—he spoke only to one who knows.

Idāni tāni paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitāni saccāni vitthārento katamañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.537) vitthāritameva. Tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha “dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā”ti (ma. ni. 1.133; dī. ni. 2.400; vibha. 203) imāya tantiyā āgataṃ, idha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti paccayākāravasena. Tattha ca dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ “yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho”ti (ma. ni. 1.134; dī. ni. 2.401; vibha. 204) imāya tantiyā āgataṃ, idha “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā”ti paccayākāranirodhavasena.

Now, wishing to elaborate upon those truths that were established in sequence, He spoke the passage beginning with, 'And what, O bhikkhus...'. All of that has indeed been elaborated upon in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga. It should be understood by the very method stated there. This, however, is the distinction: there, the noble truth of the origin of suffering is presented by the textual passage, 'that craving which leads to renewed existence', whereas here it is presented by way of the mode of conditionality as, 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise.' And there, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is presented by the textual passage, 'the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving', whereas here it is presented by way of the cessation of the mode of conditionality as, 'with the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance.'

Tattha asesavirāganirodhāti asesavirāgena ca asesanirodhena ca. Ubhayampetaṃ aññamaññavevacanameva. Saṅkhāranirodhoti saṅkhārānaṃ anuppattinirodho [M 2.0164] hoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Imehi pana padehi yaṃ āgamma avijjādayo nirujjhanti, atthato taṃ nibbānaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti. Nibbānañhi avijjānirodhotipi saṅkhāranirodhotipi evaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ nirodhanāmena kathīyati. Kevalassāti sakalassa. Dukkhakkhandhassāti vaṭṭadukkharāsissa. Nirodho hotīti appavatti hoti. Tattha yasmā avijjādīnaṃ nirodho nāma khīṇākāropi vuccati arahattampi nibbānampi, tasmā idha khīṇākāradassanavasena dvādasasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ, dvādasasuyeva nibbānaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatīti ettha nibbānameva sandhāya idanti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgikoti na aṭṭhahi aṅgehi vinimutto añño maggo nāma atthi. Yathā pana pañcaṅgikaṃ tūriyanti vutte pañcaṅgamattameva [P 2.0284] tūriyanti vuttaṃ hoti, evamidhāpi aṭṭhaṅgikamattameva maggo hotīti veditabbo. Aniggahitoti na niggahito. Niggaṇhanto hi hāpetvā vā dasseti vaḍḍhetvā vā taṃ parivattetvā vā. Tattha yasmā cattāri ariyasaccāni “na imāni cattāri, dve vā tīṇi vā”ti evaṃ hāpetvāpi “pañca vā cha vā”ti evaṃ vaḍḍhetvāpi “na imāni cattāri ariyasaccāni, aññāneva cattāri ariyasaccānī”ti dassetuṃ na sakkā. Tasmā ayaṃ dhammo aniggahito nāma. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Herein, asesavirāganirodhāti means: by the remainderless fading away and by the remainderless cessation. Both these terms are simply synonyms for one another. Saṅkhāranirodho means the cessation of formations by way of their non-re-arising. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Furthermore, by these terms, that Nibbāna, depending on which ignorance and so forth cease, is in meaning revealed. Indeed, Nibbāna is spoken of by the name 'cessation' of those respective phenomena, such as 'the cessation of ignorance' and 'the cessation of formations'. Kevalassa means 'of the whole'. Dukkhakkhandhassa means 'of the mass of suffering in the cycle of existence'. Nirodho hoti means 'there is non-occurrence'. Herein, since the cessation of ignorance and so forth is called the state of destruction, is called Arahantship, and is called Nibbāna, therefore, here it should be understood that by way of showing the state of destruction, in the twelve instances Arahantship is spoken of, and in those same twelve instances Nibbāna is spoken of. In the phrase idaṃ vuccati, the word idaṃ is spoken with reference to Nibbāna itself. Aṭṭhaṅgiko means: there is no other path apart from the eight factors. Just as when 'a five-factored musical instrument' is said, it is meant that only the five factors are the instrument, so too here it should be understood that only the eight factors are the path. Aniggahito means 'not assailed'. Indeed, one who assails shows it by diminishing it, or by exaggerating it, or by distorting it. Herein, because it is not possible to show the four noble truths by diminishing them, saying, 'These are not four, but two or three,' nor by exaggerating them, saying, 'They are five or six,' nor by distorting them, saying, 'These are not the four noble truths; the four noble truths are different ones,' therefore this Dhamma is called 'unassailable'. The remainder is clear in every respect.

2. Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta

63. Dutiye [V 2.0161] amātāputtikānīti mātā ca putto ca mātāputtaṃ, parittātuṃ samatthabhāvena natthi ettha mātāputtanti amātāputtikāni. Yanti yasmiṃ samaye. Tattha mātāpi puttaṃ nappaṭilabhatīti tasmiṃ aggibhaye uppanne mātāpi puttaṃ passituṃ na labhati, puttopi mātaraṃ passituṃ na labhatīti attho. Bhayaṃ hotīti cittutrāsabhayaṃ hoti. Aṭavisaṅkopoti aṭaviyā saṅkopo. Aṭavīti cettha aṭavivāsino corā veditabbā. Yadā hi te aṭavito janapadaṃ otaritvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo paharitvā vilumpanti, tadā aṭavisaṅkopo nāma hoti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Cakkasamārūḷhāti ettha iriyāpathacakkampi vaṭṭati yānacakkampi. Bhayasmiṃ hi sampatte yesaṃ yānakāni atthi, te attano parikkhārabhaṇḍaṃ tesu āropetvā palāyanti. Yesaṃ natthi[M 2.0165], te kājena vā ādāya sīsena vā ukkhipitvā palāyantiyeva. Te cakkasamārūḷhā nāma honti. Pariyāyantīti ito cito ca gacchanti. Kadācīti kismiñcideva kāle. Karahacīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Mātāpi puttaṃ paṭilabhatīti āgacchantaṃ vā gacchantaṃ vā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīnaṃ vā passituṃ labhati. Udakavāhakoti [P 2.0285] nadīpūro. Mātāpi puttaṃ paṭilabhatīti kulle vā uḷumpe vā mattikābhājane vā dārukkhaṇḍe vā laggaṃ vuyhamānaṃ passituṃ paṭilabhati, sotthinā vā puna uttaritvā gāme vā araññe vā ṭhitaṃ passituṃ labhatīti.

63. In the second Sutta, amātāputtikāni ('motherless and childless') means that there is no mother and child (mātāputtaṃ) present, in the sense that they are unable to protect each other, hence amātāputtikāni. Yanti means yasmiṃ samaye ('at which time'). There, mātāpi puttaṃ nappaṭilabhati ('a mother does not find her child') means that when that danger of fire arises, a mother does not get to see her child, and a child does not get to see its mother—this is the meaning. Bhayaṃ hoti ('there is fear') means there is fear that is terror of the mind. Aṭavisaṅkopo ('peril from the forest') means destruction on account of the forest. Here, by aṭavī ('forest'), the thieves dwelling in the forest should be understood. For when they descend from the forest into the inhabited country, attack and plunder villages, towns, and royal cities, then it is called 'peril from the forest'—this was said in reference to that. Cakkasamārūḷhā ('mounted on wheels'): here, both the wheel of postures and the wheel of a vehicle are suitable. For when danger has arrived, those who have vehicles load their requisite goods onto them and flee. Those who do not have them, taking their goods either with a carrying-pole or carrying them on their heads, flee just the same. They are called 'mounted on wheels.' Pariyāyanti ('they wander about') means they go here and there. Kadāci ('sometimes') means at some particular time. Karahaci ('at any time') is a synonym for that very word. Mātāpi puttaṃ paṭilabhati ('a mother finds her child') means she gets to see the child whether coming or going, or hidden in a certain place. Udakavāhako ('carried by water') means a river in flood. Mātāpi puttaṃ paṭilabhati ('a mother finds her child') means she gets to see the child clinging to a bamboo raft, a log-raft, an earthen pot, or a piece of wood, being carried along; or, having crossed over safely, she gets to see him standing in a village or in the forest.

Evaṃ pariyāyato amātāputtikāni bhayāni dassetvā idāni nippariyāyena dassento tīṇimānītiādimāha. Tattha jarābhayanti jaraṃ paṭicca uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “jaraṃ paṭicca uppajjati bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃso cetaso utrāso. Byādhiṃ paṭicca, maraṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjati bhayaṃ bhayānakaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃso cetaso utrāso”ti (vibha. 921). Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Having thus shown the dangers named amātāputtikāni figuratively, now, desiring to show them directly, He spoke the words beginning with tīṇimāni. Therein, jarābhayaṃ ('the danger of old age') is the fear that arises in dependence on old age. This same method applies to the others as well. And this was also stated: 'Dependent on old age arises fear, terror, stupefaction, horripilation, and dread of mind. Dependent on sickness... Dependent on death... arises fear, terror, stupefaction, horripilation, and dread of mind.' The remainder is clear in every respect.

3. Venāgapurasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Venāgapura Sutta

64. Tatiye kosalesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Cārikaṃ caramānoti addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto. Cārikā ca nāmesā bhagavato duvidhā hoti turitacārikā ca aturitacārikā cāti. Tattha dūrepi bodhaneyyapuggalaṃ disvā tassa bodhanatthāya sahasā gamanaṃ turitacārikā nāma[V 2.0162]. Sā mahākassapapaccuggamanādīsu daṭṭhabbā. Yaṃ pana gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā devasikaṃ yojanaaddhayojanavasena piṇḍapātacariyādīhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhantassa gamanaṃ, ayaṃ aturitacārikā nāma. Imaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “cārikaṃ caramāno”ti. Vitthārena pana cārikākathā sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.254) vuttā. Brāhmaṇagāmoti brāhmaṇānaṃ samosaraṇagāmopi brāhmaṇagāmoti vuccati, brāhmaṇānaṃ bhogagāmopi. Idha samosaraṇagāmo brāhmaṇavasanagāmoti adhippeto. Tadavasarīti tattha avasari, sampattoti attho. Vihāro panettha [P 2.0286] aniyāmito. Tasmā tassa avidūre buddhānaṃ [M 2.0166] anucchaviko eko vanasaṇḍo atthi, satthā taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ gatoti veditabbo.

64. In the third sutta, kosalesu ('in Kosala') means in the country with that name. Cārikaṃ caramāno ('wandering on a journey') means going on a long journey. And this journey of the Blessed One is of two kinds: a swift journey and an unhurried journey. Therein, having seen, even at a distance, a person capable of being awakened, the journey undertaken swiftly for the purpose of awakening that person is called a 'swift journey'. This is to be seen in instances such as the going out to meet Mahākassapa. But the journey of one who is benefiting the world through the alms-round and so on, going daily in succession through villages and towns, covering a yojana or half a yojana—this is called an 'unhurried journey'. With reference to this it was said: cārikaṃ caramāno. The discourse on journeying, however, is told in detail in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, in the explanation of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Brāhmaṇagāmo ('a brahmin village') is said of a village of assembly for brahmins, and also a fief-village of brahmins. Here, a village of assembly for brahmins is intended. Tadavasari ('he arrived there') means: there he arrived, he reached. Here, the monastery was not specified. Therefore, it should be understood that not far from there is a forest grove suitable for Buddhas, and the Teacher went to that forest grove.

Assosunti suṇiṃsu upalabhiṃsu, sotadvārasampattavacananigghosānusārena jāniṃsu. Khoti avadhāraṇatthe, padapūraṇamatte vā nipāto. Tattha avadhāraṇatthena “assosuṃ eva, na tesaṃ koci savanantarāyo ahosī”ti ayamattho veditabbo. Padapūraṇena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattameva.

`Assosuṃ` means: they heard, they perceived; they knew by following the sound of speech that reached the ear-door. The word `kho` is a particle that occurs in the sense of emphasis, or merely for filling out the phrase. Therein, by its sense of emphasis, this meaning should be understood: 'They indeed heard; there was no obstacle to their hearing.' As a mere filler of the phrase, it is only for the smoothness of the expression.

Idāni yamatthaṃ assosuṃ, taṃ pakāsetuṃ samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha samitapāpattā samaṇoti veditabbo. Khalūti anussavatthe nipāto. Bhoti tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ ālapanamattaṃ. Gotamoti bhagavato gottavasena paridīpanaṃ, tasmā “samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo”ti ettha samaṇo kira, bho, gotamagottoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sakyaputtoti idaṃ pana bhagavato uccākulaparidīpanaṃ. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti saddhāpabbajitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ, kenaci pārijuññena anabhibhūto aparikkhīṇaṃyeva taṃ kulaṃ pahāya saddhāya pabbajitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ kho panāti itthambhūtākhyānatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho. Kalyāṇoti kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato, seṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kittisaddoti kittiyeva, thutighoso vā. Abbhuggatoti sadevakaṃ lokaṃ ajjhottharitvā uggato. Kinti? Itipi so bhagavā…pe… buddho bhagavāti. Tatrāyaṃ padasambandho – so bhagavā itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavāti. Iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, to make known what they heard, the words beginning with 'The ascetic `khalu`, sirs, Gotama' were spoken. Therein, it should be understood that he is an 'ascetic' (`samaṇa`) because of having pacified evil. The word `khalu` is a particle in the sense of hearsay. The word `bho` is merely a term of mutual address for them. The word `gotamo` is an indication of the Blessed One by way of his clan name. Therefore, herein in 'The ascetic `khalu`, sirs, Gotama,' the meaning should be seen thus: 'Sirs, the ascetic of the Gotama clan, it is said, is coming.' This word `sakyaputto` ('son of the Sakyans'), however, indicates the Blessed One's high lineage. The phrase `sakyakulā pabbajito` ('gone forth from the Sakyan clan') indicates the state of having gone forth out of faith; it means that he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that clan which was not overcome by any decline and was undiminished.
