The phrase `taṃ kho pana` is a term used in the sense of specifying a particular quality; the meaning is 'of that Honorable Gotama.' `Kalyāṇo` ('good') means endowed with good qualities; it means excellent. `Kittisaddo` ('sound of fame') is the sound of fame itself, or the sound of praise. `Abbhuggato` ('has gone up') means it has arisen after having pervaded the world with its devas. How so? 'For this reason, that Blessed One is an Arahant... a Buddha, a Bhagavā.' Therein, this is the connection of the words: That Blessed One is, for this reason, an Arahant; for this reason, a Sammāsambuddha... for this reason, a Bhagavā. This means: 'for this reason and for this reason.'

Tattha “ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi kāraṇehi so bhagavā arahanti [P 2.0287] veditabbo”tiādinā nayena mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā [V 2.0163] sabbāneva etāni padāni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.125-127) buddhānussatiniddese vitthāritānīti tato nesaṃ vitthāro gahetabbo.

Therein, having laid down the matrix by the method beginning with, “Because of being far away, because of having destroyed the enemies and the spokes of the wheel, because of being worthy of requisites, and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil—for these reasons, that Blessed One is to be known as an Arahant,” all these terms have been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga in the Exposition of the Recollection of the Buddha. Therefore, their detailed explanation should be understood from there.

So [M 2.0167] imaṃ lokanti so bhavaṃ gotamo imaṃ lokaṃ, idāni vattabbaṃ nidasseti. Sadevakanti saha devehi sadevakaṃ. Evaṃ saha mārena samārakaṃ. Saha brahmunā sabrahmakaṃ. Saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehi sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ. Pajātattā pajā, taṃ pajaṃ. Saha devamanussehi sadevamanussaṃ. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, samārakavacanena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇivacanena sāsanassa paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ, samitapāpabāhitapāpasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca, pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ, sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi padehi okāsalokena saddhiṃ sattaloko, dvīhi pajāvasena sattalokova gahitoti veditabbo.

As for 'this world,' that venerable Gotama indicates this spatial world, which is now to be spoken of. As for 'with its devas,' it is together with the devas. Likewise, 'with its Māra' is together with Māra. 'With its Brahmā' is together with Brahmā. 'With its ascetics and brahmins' is together with ascetics and brahmins. Because they are variously born (`pajātattā`), they are a 'generation' (`pajā`); that generation. 'With its devas and humans' is together with devas and humans. Therein, by the expression 'with its devas,' the inclusion of the five sense-sphere deva realms should be understood; by the expression 'with its Māra,' the inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere deva realm; by the expression 'with its Brahmā,' the inclusion of the Brahmā worlds beginning with the Brahmakāyika; by the expression 'with its ascetics and brahmins,' the inclusion of ascetics and brahmins who are opponents and enemies of the Teaching, and also of ascetics and brahmins who have pacified and banished evil; by the expression 'generation,' the inclusion of the world of beings; by the expression 'with its devas and humans,' the inclusion of conventional devas (i.e., kings) and the remaining humans. Thus, herein, it should be understood that by three terms, the world of beings together with the spatial world is included, and by two terms, by way of 'generation,' only the world of beings is included.

Aparo nayo – sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaraloko gahito, samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaradevaloko, sabrahmakaggahaṇena rūpībrahmaloko, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādiggahaṇena catuparisavasena, sammutidevehi vā saha manussaloko, avasesasabbasattaloko vā. Porāṇā panāhu – sadevakanti devatāhi saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Samārakanti mārena saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Sabrahmakanti brahmehi saddhiṃ avasesalokaṃ. Evaṃ sabbepi tibhavūpage satte tīhākārehi tīsu padesu pakkhipitvā puna dvīhi padehi pariyādātuṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussanti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pañcahi padehi tena tenākārena tedhātukameva pariyādinnanti.

Another method—by the inclusion of 'with the devas,' the formless-sphere world is included; by the inclusion of 'with Māra,' the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included; by the inclusion of 'with Brahmā,' the form-sphere Brahmā world is included; by the inclusion of 'with ascetics and brahmins,' etc., by way of the fourfold assembly, the human world together with conventional devas, or the remaining world of all beings, is included. Furthermore, the ancients say: by 'with the devas' is included the remaining world together with the deities. By 'with Māra' is included the remaining world together with Māra. By 'with Brahmā' is included the remaining world together with the Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings who resort to the three states of existence in three terms by three aspects, in order to encompass them again with two terms, it is said: 'the generation with its ascetics and brahmins' and 'with its devas and humans.' In this way, by these five terms, in their respective aspects, just the three realms are fully encompassed.

Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetīti sayanti sāmaṃ, aparaneyyo hutvā. Abhiññāti abhiññāya, adhikena ñāṇena ñatvāti attho. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā[P 2.0288], etena anumānādipaṭikkhepo kato. Pavedetīti bodheti ñāpeti pakāseti.

“Having realized by direct knowledge, he makes it known”—`sayaṃ` ('himself') means personally, being not led by another. `Abhiññā` ('by direct knowledge') means by special knowledge, having known with superior knowledge; this is the meaning. `Sacchikatvā` ('having realized') means having made it directly present—by this, inference and the like are rejected. `Pavedeti` ('makes it known') means he causes to know, causes to perceive, and makes manifest.

So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… pariyosānakalyāṇanti so bhagavā sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca hitvāpi anuttaraṃ vivekasukhaṃ dhammaṃ [M 2.0168] deseti. Tañca kho appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desento ādikalyāṇādippakārameva deseti, ādimhipi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā [V 2.0164] deseti, majjhepi, pariyosānepi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā desetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“He teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning… good in the end”—that Blessed One, on account of compassion for beings, teaches the Dhamma, having relinquished even the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion. And when teaching that Dhamma, whether a little or a lot, he teaches only that which has the quality of being good in the beginning and so on; he teaches, making it good, excellent, and only blameless in the beginning, and likewise in the middle and in the end. Thus it is said.

Tattha atthi desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ, atthi sāsanassa. Desanāya tāva catuppadikāyapi gāthāya paṭhamapādo ādi nāma, tato dve majjhaṃ nāma, ante eko pariyosānaṃ nāma. Ekānusandhikassa suttassa nidānaṃ ādi, idamavocāti pariyosānaṃ, ubhinnaṃ antarā majjhaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa suttassa paṭhamānusandhi ādi, ante anusandhi pariyosānaṃ, majjhe eko vā dve vā bahū vā majjhameva.

Here, there is a beginning, a middle, and an end to the teaching; there is also a beginning, a middle, and an end to the Dispensation. With regard to the teaching, firstly, even in a four-line verse, the first line is called the beginning, the two lines after that are called the middle, and the one line at the end is called the culmination. For a discourse with a single connection, the introduction is the beginning, the words “Thus he spoke” are the culmination, and what is between the two is the middle. For a discourse with multiple connections, the first connection is the beginning, the connection at the end is the culmination, and one, two, or many connections in the middle are simply the middle.

Sāsanassa sīlasamādhivipassanā ādi nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ diṭṭhi ca ujukā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.369). “Atthi, bhikkhave, majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā”ti evaṃ vutto pana ariyamaggo majjhaṃ nāma. Phalañceva nibbānañca pariyosānaṃ nāma. “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyaṃ etaṃpāraṃ etaṃpariyosāna”nti ettha phalaṃ pariyosananti vuttaṃ. “Nibbānogadhañhi, āvuso visākha, brahmacariyaṃ vussati nibbānaparāyaṇaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.466) ettha nibbānaṃ pariyosānanti vuttaṃ. Idha [P 2.0289] pana desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento ādimhi sīlaṃ dassetvā majjhe maggaṃ pariyosāne nibbānaṃ dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ – “so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇa”nti. Tasmā aññopi dhammakathiko dhammaṃ kathento –

Of the Dispensation, virtue, concentration, and insight are called the beginning. And this was said: “What is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue that is well-purified and view that is straight.” The Noble Path, spoken of thus, “There is, bhikkhus, a Middle Way fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,” is called the middle. Both the fruit and Nibbāna are called the culmination. In the passage, “This holy life, Brahmin, has this as its further shore, this as its culmination,” the fruit is said to be the culmination. In the passage, “The holy life, friend Visākha, is plunged into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, and has Nibbāna as its culmination,” Nibbāna is said to be the culmination. Here, however, the beginning, middle, and culmination of the teaching are intended. For the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, having presented virtue at the beginning, shows the path in the middle and Nibbāna at the culmination. Therefore, it is said: “He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the culmination.” Therefore, any other Dhamma speaker, when expounding the Dhamma—

“Ādimhi sīlaṃ dasseyya, majjhe maggaṃ vibhāvaye;

Pariyosānamhi nibbānaṃ, esā kathikasaṇṭhitī”ti.

“At the beginning, one should show virtue; in the middle, one should make clear the path; at the culmination, one should make clear Nibbāna—this is the well-established method of a speaker.”

Sātthaṃ sabyañjananti yassa hi yāgubhattaitthipurisādivaṇṇanānissitā desanā hoti, na so sātthaṃ deseti. Bhagavā pana tathārūpaṃ desanaṃ pahāya catusatipaṭṭhānādinissitaṃ desanaṃ deseti. Tasmā “sātthaṃ desetī”ti [M 2.0169] vuccati. Yassa pana desanā ekabyañjanādiyuttā vā sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā vā sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjanā vā sabbaniggahitabyañjanā vā, tassa damiḷakirātayavanādimilakkhānaṃ [V 2.0165] bhāsā viya byañjanapāripūriyā abhāvato abyañjanā nāma desanā hoti. Bhagavā pana –

Herein, regarding 'with meaning and with phrasing': For one whose teaching is based on praising things like gruel, rice, women, men, and so on, he does not teach a teaching with meaning. The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such a teaching, teaches a teaching based on the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'He teaches with meaning.' But for one whose teaching is endowed with only one kind of letter, or has all letters recited without touching the lips, or has all letters recited by releasing completely, or has all letters checked, his teaching, like the languages of the Tamils, Kirātas, Yavanas, and other barbarians, is called 'without phrasing' due to the lack of completeness of the sounds. The Blessed One, however—

“Sithilaṃ dhanitañca dīgharassaṃ, lahukaṃ garukañca niggahītaṃ;

Sambandhaṃ vavatthitaṃ vimuttaṃ, dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedo”ti. –

“Lax and tense, long and short, light and heavy, and checked; connected, separated, and released—thus tenfold is the distinction of the understanding of articulation.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ dasavidhaṃ byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā paripuṇṇabyañjanameva katvā dhammaṃ deseti. Tasmā “sabyañjanaṃ katvā desetī”ti vuccati. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti ettha kevalanti sakalādhivacanaṃ. Paripuṇṇanti anūnādhikavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sakalaparipuṇṇameva deseti, ekadesanāpi aparipuṇṇā natthīti. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Yo hi “imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ nissāya lābhaṃ vā sakkāraṃ vā labhissāmī”ti deseti, tassa aparisuddhā desanā nāma hoti. Bhagavā pana lokāmisanirapekkho [P 2.0290] hitapharaṇeneva mettābhāvanāya muduhadayo ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitena cittena deseti. Tasmā parisuddhaṃ desetīti vuccati. Brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti ettha brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ. Tasmā brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… parisuddhaṃ, evaṃ desento ca sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalasāsanabrahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtaṃ cariyaṃ, brahmabhūtānaṃ vā buddhādīnaṃ cariyanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Without disregarding the tenfold phrasing thus spoken, He teaches the Dhamma, making it complete in phrasing. Therefore, it is said, 'He teaches it complete with phrasing.' In the phrase 'entirely complete,' the word 'entirely' (kevala) is a term for 'whole.' The word 'complete' (paripuṇṇa) is a term for 'without deficiency or excess.' This is what is meant: He teaches the Dhamma that is only entirely complete; not even a single teaching is incomplete. 'Pure' means without defilements. For whoever teaches thinking, 'Relying on this teaching of the Dhamma, I will obtain gain or honor,' his teaching is called impure. But the Blessed One, being unconcerned with worldly gain, with a tender heart, teaches solely through the development of loving-kindness that brings about welfare, with a mind established in the nature of uplifting. Therefore, it is said, 'He teaches what is pure.' Regarding 'He makes manifest the holy life,' here 'holy life' means the entire Dispensation comprised of the threefold training. Therefore, the meaning of 'He makes manifest the holy life' should be understood thus: He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... and so on... pure, and in so teaching, He makes manifest the holy life of the entire Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training. 'Holy life' means the conduct that is supreme in the sense of being excellent, or the conduct of those who have become supreme, such as the Buddhas and others. This is what is meant.

Sādhu kho panāti sundaraṃ kho pana, atthāvahaṃ sukhāvahanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathārūpānaṃ arahatanti yathārūpo so bhavaṃ gotamo, evarūpānaṃ anekehipi kappakoṭisatasahassehi dullabhadassanānaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhittehi asītianubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavarehi samākiṇṇamanoramasarīrānaṃ anappakadassanānaṃ atimadhuradhammanigghosānaṃ yathābhūtaguṇādhigamena loke arahantoti laddhasaddānaṃ arahataṃ. Dassanaṃ hotīti pasādasommāni akkhīni ummīletvā dassanamattampi sādhu hoti. Sace pana aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena brahmassarena dhammaṃ desentassa ekapadampi sotuṃ labhissāma, sādhutaraṃyeva bhavissatīti [M 2.0170] evaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ katvā. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti sabbakiccāni pahāya tuṭṭhamānasā agamaṃsu. Añjaliṃ paṇāmetvāti ete ubhatopakkhikā, te evaṃ cintesuṃ – “sace no micchādiṭṭhikā codessanti ‘kasmā tumhe samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vanditthā’ti, tesaṃ ‘kiṃ añjalikaraṇamattenāpi vanditaṃ hotī’ti vakkhāma[V 2.0166]. Sace no sammādiṭṭhikā codessanti ‘kasmā bhagavantaṃ na vanditthā’ti, ‘kiṃ sīsena bhūmiṃ paharanteneva vanditaṃ hoti. Nanu añjalikammampi vandanā evā’ti vakkhāmā”ti.

“Good indeed!”—this means it is excellent indeed, beneficial, and brings happiness. “Of such Arahants” means: of Arahants of such a nature as the venerable Gotama, whose sight is difficult to obtain even over many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons; who are surrounded by a fathom-wide aura; adorned with the eighty minor characteristics; whose delightful bodies are perfectly endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man; whose appearance is dazzling; whose voice, which is the sound of the Dhamma teaching, is exceedingly sweet; and who, through the attainment of true qualities, have gained the fame in the world as “Arahants”. “To see them is” means: opening one's clear and serene eyes, even the mere sight of them is good. But if we can hear even a single word from him teaching the Dhamma with his voice endowed with the eight qualities of Brahma, it will be even better. Having formed this intention, they approached the Blessed One, leaving all duties behind, their hearts content. “Having raised the joined palms in reverence”—these who belonged to two factions thought thus: “If those of wrong view should reproach us, asking, 'Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?', we will say to them, 'Is it considered homage merely by the act of joining the palms?' And if those of right view should reproach us, asking, 'Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?', we will say, 'Is homage paid only by striking the ground with one's head? Is not the act of joining the palms also indeed a form of homage?'”

Nāmagottanti[P 2.0291], “bho gotama, ahaṃ asukassa putto datto nāma mitto nāma idhāgato”ti vadantā nāmaṃ sāventi nāma. “Bho gotama, ahaṃ vāseṭṭho nāma kaccāno nāma idhāgato”ti vadantā gottaṃ sāventi nāma. Ete kira daliddā jiṇṇakulaputtā “parisamajjhe nāmagottavasena pākaṭā bhavissāmā”ti evaṃ akaṃsu. Ye pana tuṇhībhūtā nisīdiṃsu, te kerāṭikā ceva andhabālā ca. Tattha kerāṭikā “ekaṃ dve kathāsallāpe karonte vissāsiko hoti, atha vissāse sati ekaṃ dve bhikkhā adātuṃ na yutta”nti tato attānaṃ mocentā tuṇhībhūtā nisīdanti. Andhabālā aññāṇatāyeva avakkhittamattikāpiṇḍā viya yattha katthaci tuṇhībhūtā nisīdanti.

As for 'name and clan': saying, “Venerable Gotama, I am the son of so-and-so, named Datta, named Mitta, and have come here,” they announce their name. Saying, “Venerable Gotama, I am named Vāseṭṭha, named Kaccāna, and have come here,” they announce their clan. It is said that these were poor, worn-out sons of good families who thought, “In the midst of the assembly, we will become known by name and clan,” and so they did. But those who sat silently were either deceitful or utterly foolish. Among them, the deceitful ones thought, “If one engages in even a little conversation, familiarity arises, and once there is familiarity, it is not proper not to give alms on one or two occasions.” Wishing to free themselves from this, they sat silently. The utterly foolish, out of sheer ignorance, sat silently wherever they might be, like lumps of clay thrown down.

Venāgapurikoti venāgapuravāsī. Etadavocāti pādantato paṭṭhāya yāva kesaggā tathāgatassa sarīraṃ olokento asītianubyañjanasamujjalehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ sarīrā nikkhamitvā samantato asītihatthappadesaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitāhi chabbaṇṇāhi ghanabuddharaṃsīhi samparivāritaṃ tathāgatassa sarīraṃ disvā sañjātavimhayo vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanto etaṃ “acchariyaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

“Venāgapurika” means a resident of Venāgapura. “He spoke thus” means: observing the Tathāgata’s body from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair—a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by dense, six-colored Buddha-rays which, having emerged from his body, stood pervading the area of eighty cubits all around—and seeing the Tathāgata’s body, he became amazed and, wishing to speak his praise, spoke these words beginning with, “Marvelous, Venerable Gotama!”

Tattha yāvañcidanti adhimattappamāṇaparicchedavacanametaṃ. Tassa vippasannapadena saddhiṃ sambandho. Yāvañca vippasannāni adhimattavippasannānīti attho. Indriyānīti cakkhādīni cha indriyāni. Tassa hi pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsassa vippasannataṃ disvā tesaṃ vippasannatā pākaṭā ahosi. Yasmā pana sā mane vippasanneyeva hoti, avippasannacittānañhi indriyappasādo nāma natthi, tasmāssa manindriyappasādopi pākaṭo ahosi. Taṃ esa vippasannataṃ [M 2.0171] gahetvā “vippasannāni indriyānī”ti āha. Parisuddhoti nimmalo. Pariyodātoti pabhassaro. Sāradaṃ [P 2.0292] badarapaṇḍunti saradakāle jātaṃ nātisuparipakkaṃ badaraṃ. Tañhi parisuddhañceva hoti pariyodātañca. Tālapakkanti suparipakkatālaphalaṃ. Sampati bandhanā pamuttanti taṃkhaṇaññeva bandhanā pamuttaṃ. Tassa hi bandhanamūlaṃ apanetvā paramukhaṃ katvā phalake ṭhapitassa caturaṅgulamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ olokentānaṃ parisuddhaṃ pariyodātaṃ hutvā khāyati. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha[V 2.0167]. Nekkhaṃ jambonadanti surattavaṇṇassa jambonadasuvaṇṇassa ghaṭikā. Dakkhakammāraputtasuparikammakatanti dakkhena suvaṇṇakāraputtena suṭṭhu kataparikammaṃ. Ukkāmukhe sukusalasampahaṭṭhanti suvaṇṇakārauddhane pacitvā sukusalena suvaṇṇakārena ghaṭṭanaparimajjanahaṃsanena suṭṭhu pahaṭṭhaṃ suparimadditanti attho. Paṇḍukambale nikkhittanti agginā pacitvā dīpidāṭhāya ghaṃsitvā gerukaparikammaṃ katvā rattakambale ṭhapitaṃ. Bhāsateti sañjātaobhāsatāya bhāsate. Tapateti andhakāraviddhaṃsanatāya tapate. Virocatīti vijjotamānaṃ hutvā virocati, sobhatīti attho.

Herein, yāvañcidaṃ is a term indicating an excessive measure or limit. It should be connected with the word vippasanna. The meaning is: yāva ca vippasannāni means serene to an excessive degree. Indriyāni means the six faculties beginning with the eye. Indeed, for him, having seen the serenity of the location where the five faculties are established, their serenity became manifest. Furthermore, since that serenity exists only when the mind is serene—for indeed, for those with an unserene mind, there is no such thing as serenity of the faculties—therefore, the serenity of his mind-faculty also became manifest. Taking that serenity, he said, “The faculties are serene.” Parisuddho means stainless. Pariyodāto means radiant. Sāradaṃ badarapaṇḍu means a not very well-ripened jujube fruit from the autumn season; indeed, it is both pure and radiant. Tālapakkaṃ means a well-ripened palm fruit. Sampati bandhanā pamuttaṃ means just at that moment freed from its stalk. Indeed, of that fruit, when the root of its binding is removed and it is placed face-up on a board, an area of about four finger-breadths appears pure and radiant to those who look at it. It was with reference to this that he spoke thus. Nekkhaṃ jambonadaṃ means an ingot of Jambūnada gold, which has a bright red color. Dakkhakammāraputtasuparikammakataṃ means well-finished by a skilled goldsmith’s son. Ukkāmukhe sukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ means, having been smelted in a goldsmith’s furnace, it is well-burnished and well-rubbed by a very skilled goldsmith by means of striking, rubbing, and burnishing. Paṇḍukambale nikkhittaṃ means placed on a red blanket after being smelted with fire, rubbed with a leopard's fang, and finished with red ochre. Bhāsateti means it shines because of its arisen luster. Tapateti means it glows because it dispels darkness. Virocati means, becoming effulgent, it shines splendidly; the meaning is that it is beautiful.

Uccāsayanamahāsayanānīti ettha atikkantappamāṇaṃ uccāsayanaṃ nāma, āyatavitthataṃ akappiyabhaṇḍaṃ mahāsayanaṃ nāma. Idāni tāni dassento seyyathidaṃ, āsandītiādimāha. Tattha āsandīti atikkantappamāṇaṃ āsanaṃ. Pallaṅkoti pādesu vāḷarūpāni ṭhapetvā kato. Gonakoti dīghalomako mahākojavo. Caturaṅgulādhikāni kira tassa lomāni. Cittakoti vānacittaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Paṭikāti uṇṇāmayo setattharako. Paṭalikāti [P 2.0293] ghanapuppho uṇṇāmayattharako, yo āmalakapaṭṭotipi vuccati. Tūlikāti tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ aññatarapuṇṇā tūlikā. Vikatikāti sīhabyagghādirūpavicitro uṇṇāmayattharako. Uddalomīti ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Keci ekato uggatapupphanti vadanti. Ekantalomīti ekatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Keci ubhato uggatapupphanti vadanti. Kaṭṭissanti ratanaparisibbitaṃ koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ. Koseyyanti ratanaparisibbitameva kosiyasuttamayaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ. Kuttakanti soḷasannaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ ṭhatvā naccanayoggaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ. Hatthattharādayo hatthipiṭṭhādīsu attharaṇakaattharakā ceva [M 2.0172] hatthirūpādīni dassetvā kataattharakā ca. Ajinappaveṇīti ajinacammehi mañcappamāṇena sibbitvā katappaveṇī. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

In the phrase 'high beds and luxurious beds,' that which exceeds the prescribed measurement is called a 'high bed'; a long and wide item that is unsuitable is called a 'luxurious bed.' Now, to illustrate these, he begins with 'āsandī' and so on. Therein, an 'āsandī' is a seat exceeding the prescribed measurement. A 'pallaṅka' is one made by placing figures of beasts of prey on its legs. A 'gonaka' is a large, long-fleeced rug. It is said that its fleece exceeds four finger-breadths in length. A 'cittaka' is a woolen spread variegated with gems. A 'paṭikā' is a white woolen spread. A 'paṭalikā' is a woolen spread with a solid floral pattern, which is also called 'āmalakapaṭṭa'. A 'tūlikā' is a mattress filled with one of the three kinds of cotton. A 'vikatikā' is a woolen spread variegated with figures of lions, tigers, and so on. An 'uddalomī' is a woolen spread with fringes on both sides. Some say it is a spread with raised flowers on one side. An 'ekantalomī' is a woolen spread with a fringe on one side. Some say it is a spread with raised flowers on both sides. A 'kaṭṭissa' is a covering sewn with gems, made of a silk-blend fabric. A 'koseyya' is a covering sewn with gems, made of silk thread. A 'kuttaka' is a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing women to stand and dance upon. 'Hatthatthara' and so on are both spreads laid out on the backs of elephants and other such animals, and spreads made displaying the figures of elephants and so on. An 'ajinappaveṇī' is a layered spread made by stitching together skins of the black antelope to the size of a couch. The rest have the same meaning as previously stated.

Nikāmalābhīti atikāmalābhī icchiticchitalābhī. Akicchalābhīti adukkhalābhī. Akasiralābhīti vipulalābhī mahantalābhī, uḷāruḷārāneva labhati maññeti sandhāya vadati. Ayaṃ kira brāhmaṇo sayanagaruko, so bhagavato vippasannindriyāditaṃ disvā “addhā esa evarūpesu uccāsayanamahāsayanesu nisīdati ceva nipajjati ca. Tenassa vippasannāni indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto”ti maññamāno imaṃ senāsanavaṇṇaṃ kathesi.

“‘He obtains at will’ means he obtains exceedingly as desired, obtaining whenever he desires. ‘He obtains without trouble’ means he obtains without suffering. ‘He obtains without difficulty’ means he obtains abundantly, he obtains greatly. He speaks with reference to this; I think he means that he obtains only the most excellent things. This brahmin, it seems, gave importance to beds and seats. Having seen the Blessed One’s especially serene faculties, he thought, ‘Without a doubt, this one sits and also lies down on such high seats and great seats. That is why his faculties are especially serene, and his skin-complexion is pure and exceedingly bright.’ Thinking thus, he spoke this praise of the lodging.

Laddhā [V 2.0168] ca pana na kappantīti ettha kiñci kiñci kappati. Suddhakoseyyañhi mañcepi attharituṃ vaṭṭati, gonakādayo ca bhūmattharaṇaparibhogena, āsandiyā pāde chinditvā, pallaṅkassa [P 2.0294] vāḷe bhinditvā, tūlikaṃ vijaṭetvā “bimbohanañca kātu”nti (cūḷava. 297) vacanato imānipi ekena vidhānena kappanti. Akappiyaṃ pana upādāya sabbāneva na kappantīti vuttāni.

Regarding the statement, ‘And yet, though obtained, they are not allowable,’ here, some things are indeed allowable. For a pure silk covering is suitable to be spread even on a couch, and long-fleeced rugs and the like are suitable for use as a ground-covering. And since it is said, ‘Having cut the legs of a long chair, having broken the frame of a couch, having unraveled a cotton mattress, a bolster may also be made,’ these too are allowable by a certain procedure. However, on account of what is unallowable, it is said that all of them are not allowable.

Vanantaññeva pavisāmīti araññaṃyeva pavisāmi. Yadevāti yāniyeva. Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādento ujuṃ kāyaṃ ṭhapetvā. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapetvā, pariggahitaniyyānaṃ vā katvāti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “parīti pariggahaṭṭho. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho. Satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.164). Upasampajja viharāmīti paṭilabhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā viharāmi. Evaṃbhūtoti evaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī hutvā. Dibbo me eso tasmiṃ samaye caṅkamo hotīti cattāri hi rūpajjhānāni samāpajjitvā caṅkamantassa caṅkamo dibbacaṅkamo nāma hoti, samāpattito vuṭṭhāya caṅkamantassāpi caṅkamo dibbacaṅkamoyeva. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo. Tathā itaresu dvīsu vihāresu.

“I shall enter the wilderness alone,” means I enter the forest alone. ‘Yadeva’ means ‘yāniyeva’ (whatever indeed). “Having folded my legs cross-legged” means having bound the legs firmly in the lotus position. “Setting my body upright” means aligning the eighteen vertebrae, joint by joint, keeping the body straight. “Establishing mindfulness in front” means establishing mindfulness directed towards the meditation object, or having made it a well-grasped means of escape. As it is said: “‘Pari’ means ‘encompassing’; ‘mukha’ means ‘the means of exit’; and ‘sati’ means ‘establishment.’ Therefore, it is called ‘establishing mindfulness in front.’” “Dwelling, having attained” means dwelling, having attained and directly realized it. “Being thus” refers to being endowed with one of the first jhānas or other such attainment. “This walk of mine is divine at that time” means, indeed, the walk of one who, having attained the four form jhānas, then walks, is called a divine walk; even the walk of one who walks after emerging from the attainment is a divine walk. The same principle applies to standing and the other postures, as well as to the other two dwellings.

So [M 2.0173] evaṃ pajānāmi “rāgo me pahīno”ti mahābodhipallaṅke arahattamaggena pahīnarāgameva dassento “so evaṃ pajānāmi rāgo me pahīno”ti āha. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Iminā pana kiṃ kathitaṃ hotīti? Paccavekkhaṇā kathitā, paccavekkhaṇāya phalasamāpatti kathitā. Phalasamāpattiñhi samāpannassapi samāpattito vuṭṭhitassāpi caṅkamādayo ariyacaṅkamādayo honti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

“Thus, I understand: ‘Greed is abandoned in me’”—showing that greed has been abandoned by the path of arahantship while seated on the great enlightenment seat, he says: “Thus, I understand: ‘Greed is abandoned in me.’” The same principle applies to the remaining phrases. But what is being spoken about with this? Reviewing is spoken about, and by means of reviewing, the fruition-attainment is spoken about. For one who has attained fruition, both while experiencing the attainment and after rising from it, walking and other activities are noble walking and the like. The rest here is self-explanatory.

4. Sarabhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Sarabha Sutta

65. Catutthe [P 2.0295] rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare. Gijjhakūṭe pabbateti gijjhasadisānissa kūṭāni, gijjhā vā tassa kūṭesu vasantīti gijjhakūṭo, tasmiṃ gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Etenassa rājagahaṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā viharantassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ. Gijjhakūṭasmiñhi tathāgataṃ [V 2.0169] uddissa vihāro kārito, gijjhakūṭavihārotvevassa nāmaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ tasmiṃ samaye viharatīti. Sarabho nāma paribbājako acirapakkanto hotīti sarabhoti evaṃnāmako paribbājako imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā nacirasseva pakkanto hoti, adhunā vibbhantoti attho. Sammāsambuddhe hi loke uppanne titthiyā naṭṭhalābhasakkārā ahesuṃ, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. Yathāha –

65. In the fourth sutta, in the city named Rājagaha. On Vulture Peak Mountain: its peaks are like vultures, or vultures dwell on its peaks, hence it is Vulture Peak; on that Vulture Peak Mountain. By this, his dwelling place is shown, as he dwelt having made Rājagaha his alms-resort village. For on Vulture Peak, a monastery was built dedicated to the Tathāgata, and its name was indeed Vulture Peak Monastery. There, at that time, he was dwelling. The wanderer named Sarabha had recently departed: the wanderer named Sarabha, having gone forth in this Dispensation, had not long after departed, meaning he had now returned to the lay state. For when the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One arose in the world, the sectarians suffered loss of gains and honor, while great gains and honor arose for the Three Jewels. As it is said:

“Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. Aññatitthiyā pana paribbājakā asakkatā honti agarukatā amānitā apūjitā na lābhino cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti (udā.14; saṃ.ni.1.2.70).

“At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, esteemed, revered, and venerated, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But the other sectarian wanderers were not honored, not respected, not esteemed, not revered, nor were they recipients of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”

Te evaṃ parihīnalābhasakkārā pañcasatamattā ekasmiṃ paribbājakārāme sannipatitvā sammantayiṃsu – “bho, mayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya hatalābhasakkārā jātā, samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakānañcassa ekaṃ avaṇṇaṃ upadhāretha, avaṇṇaṃ pattharitvā etassa [M 2.0174] sāsanaṃ garahitvā amhākaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ uppādessāmā”ti. Te vajjaṃ olokentā – “tīsu dvāresu ājīve cāti catūsupi ṭhānesu samaṇassa gotamassa vajjaṃ passituṃ na sakkā, imāni cattāri ṭhānāni muñcitvā aññattha olokethā”ti [P 2.0296] āhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ antare eko evamāha – “ahaṃ aññaṃ na passāmi, ime anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ sannipatitvā dvāravātapānāni pidhāya sāmaṇerānampi pavesanaṃ na denti. Jīvitasadisāpi upaṭṭhākā daṭṭhuṃ na labhanti, āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ osāretvā osāretvā janaṃ āvaṭṭetvā āvaṭṭetvā khādanti. Sace taṃ mayaṃ āharituṃ sakkhissāma, evaṃ no lābhasakkārauḷāro bhavissatī”ti. Aparopi evameva vadanto uṭṭhāsi. Sabbe ekavādā ahesuṃ. Tato āhaṃsu – “yo taṃ āharituṃ sakkhissati, taṃ mayaṃ amhākaṃ samaye jeṭṭhakaṃ karissāmā”ti.

They, thus deprived of gains and honor, about five hundred in number, gathered in a certain wanderers’ park and consulted: “Sirs, from the time the ascetic Gotama arose, we have been deprived of gains and honor. Let us find some point of dispraise concerning the ascetic Gotama and his disciples. Having spread the dispraise and censured his Dispensation, we will cause gain and honor to arise for ourselves.” Looking for a fault, they said: “It is not possible to see any fault in the ascetic Gotama in the three doors of action and in his livelihood—in these four areas. Having set aside these four areas, look elsewhere.” Then one among them spoke thus: “I see nothing else. These monks gather every half-month, close the doors and windows, and do not allow even novices to enter. Even attendants who are like their very life are not permitted to see them. Having repeatedly employed the Āvaṭṭanī magic and having repeatedly enticed the people, they consume them. If we are able to bring this up, our gain and honor will surely be abundant.” Another also rose and spoke similarly. All were in agreement. Then they said: “Whoever is able to bring this up, we will make him our elder in our community.”

Tato koṭito paṭṭhāya “tvaṃ sakkhissasi, tvaṃ sakkhissasī”ti pucchitvā “ahaṃ na sakkhissāmi, ahaṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti bahūhi vutte sarabhaṃ pucchiṃsu – “tvaṃ sakkhissasi ācariyā”ti. So āha – “agaru etaṃ āharituṃ, sace tumhe attano kathāya ṭhatvā maṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ [V 2.0170] karissathā”ti. Agaru etamācariya āhara, tvaṃ katoyevāsi amhehi jeṭṭhakoti. So āha – “taṃ āharantena thenetvā vā vilumpitvā vā āharituṃ na sakkā, samaṇassa pana gotamassa sāvakasadisena hutvā tassa sāvake vanditvā vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā tesaṃ patte bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā āharituṃ sakkā. Ruccati vo etassa ettakassa kiriyā”ti. Yaṃkiñci katvā āharitvā ca no dehīti. Tena hi maṃ disvā apassantā viya bhaveyyāthāti paribbājakānaṃ saññaṃ datvā dutiyadivase pātova uṭṭhāya gijjhakūṭamahāvihāraṃ gantvā diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena pāde vandi. Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “aññe paribbājakā caṇḍā pharusā, ayaṃ pana saddho bhavissati pasanno”ti. Bhante, tumhe ñatvā yuttaṭṭhānasmiṃyeva pabbajitā, mayaṃ pana anupadhāretvā atittheneva pakkhantā aniyyānikamagge vicarāmāti. So evaṃ vatvā diṭṭhe diṭṭhe bhikkhū punappunaṃ vandati, nhānodakādīni paṭiyādeti, dantakaṭṭhaṃ kappiyaṃ karoti, pāde dhovati makkheti, atirekabhattaṃ labhitvā bhuñjati.

Thereafter, starting from the least capable one, they asked, “Will you be able? Will you be able?” When it was said by many, “I will not be able, I will not be able,” they asked Sarabha, “Teacher, will you be able?” He said, “It is no great burden to bring this, if you will stand by your agreement and make me the chief.” “Teacher, that is no great burden. Bring it. It is for that very reason that you are our chief,” they said. He said, “It is not possible for one bringing it to bring it by stealing or by plundering. However, it is possible to bring it by becoming like a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, paying homage to his disciples, performing the major and minor duties, and eating the food in their bowls. Is the performance of this much agreeable to you?” “Having done whatsoever, and having brought it, give it to us,” they said. “In that case, having seen me, be as if you do not see me.” Thus, having given this signal to the wanderers, on the second day, having arisen very early in the morning and gone to the Gijjhakūṭa Mahāvihāra, he paid homage at the feet of every bhikkhu he saw with the five-point prostration. The bhikkhus said, “Other wanderers are fierce and harsh, but this one must be faithful and devout.” “Venerable sirs,” he said, “you, having understood, have gone forth in a suitable place indeed. But we, without proper investigation, have plunged into what is not a true ford and wander on a path that does not lead out.” Having spoken thus, he repeatedly paid homage to every bhikkhu he saw. He prepared bathing water and so forth, made the tooth-sticks allowable, washed and anointed their feet. Having received leftover food, he ate it.

Taṃ [M 2.0175] iminā nīhārena vasantaṃ eko mahāthero disvā, “paribbājaka, tvaṃ saddho pasanno, kiṃ [P 2.0297] na pabbajasī”ti. Ko maṃ, bhante, pabbājessati. Mayañhi cirakālaṃ bhadantānaṃ paccatthikā hutvā vicarimhāti. Thero “sace tvaṃ pabbajitukāmo, ahaṃ taṃ pabbājessāmī”ti vatvā pabbājesi. So pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ vattapaṭivattamakāsi. Atha naṃ thero vatte pasīditvā nacirasseva upasampādesi. So uposathadivase bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ uposathaggaṃ pavisitvā bhikkhū mahantena ussāhena pātimokkhaṃ paggaṇhante disvā “iminā nīhārena osāretvā osāretvā lokaṃ khādanti, katipāhena harissāmī”ti cintesi. So pariveṇaṃ gantvā upajjhāyaṃ vanditvā, “bhante, ko nāmo ayaṃ dhammo”ti pucchi. Pātimokkho nāma, āvusoti. Uttamadhammo esa, bhante, bhavissatīti. Āma, āvuso, sakalasāsanadhāraṇī ayaṃ sikkhāti. Bhante, sace esa sikkhādhammo uttamo, imameva paṭhamaṃ gaṇhāmīti. Gaṇhāvusoti thero sampaṭicchi. So gaṇhanto paribbājake passitvā “kīdisaṃ ācariyā”ti pucchito, “āvuso, mā cintayittha, katipāhena āharissāmī”ti vatvā nacirasseva uggaṇhitvā upajjhāyaṃ āha – “ettakameva, bhante, udāhu aññampi atthī”ti. Ettakameva, āvusoti.

A certain great elder, seeing him living in this manner, said to him: “Wanderer, you are faithful and devoted. Why do you not go forth?” “Who, venerable sir, would give me the going forth? For we have long been adversaries of the venerable ones.” The elder said: “If you wish to go forth, I will give you the going forth,” and so he ordained him. From the time of his going forth, he performed the major and minor duties without interruption. Then the elder, pleased with his performance of the duties, gave him the higher ordination not long after. On the Uposatha day, he entered the Uposatha hall together with the monks and saw them reciting the Pātimokkha with great effort. He thought: “By this method, gathering and gathering, they devour the world. In a few days, I will take it away.” He went to his monastic dwelling, paid respects to his preceptor, and asked: “Venerable sir, what is the name of this Dhamma?” “It is called the Pātimokkha, friend.” “This must be the supreme Dhamma, venerable sir.” “Yes, friend, this training is the foundation of the entire Dispensation.” “Venerable sir, if this Dhamma of the training is supreme, I will learn it first.” “Learn it, friend,” the elder consented. While he was learning, he was seen by some wanderers who asked him, “Teacher, how is it?” He replied: “Friends, do not worry; in a few days, I will bring it.” Having mastered it before long, he said to his preceptor: “Is this all, venerable sir, or is there more?” “This is all, friend.”

So punadivase yathānivatthapārutova gahitanīhāreneva pattaṃ gahetvā gijjhakūṭā nikkhamma paribbājakārāmaṃ agamāsi. Paribbājakā disvā “kīdisaṃ, ācariya, nāsakkhittha maññe āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ [V 2.0171] āharitu”nti taṃ parivārayiṃsu. Mā cintayittha, āvuso, āhaṭā me āvaṭṭanimāyā, ito paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ lābhasakkāro mahā bhavissati. Tumhe aññamaññaṃ samaggā hotha, mā vivādaṃ akatthāti. Sace te, ācariya, suggahitā, amhepi naṃ vācehīti. So ādito paṭṭhāya pātimokkhaṃ osāresi. Atha te sabbepi – “etha, bho, nagare vicarantā samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ kathessāmā”ti anugghāṭitesuyeva nagaradvāresu dvārasamīpaṃ gantvā vivaṭena dvārena [P 2.0298] sabbapaṭhamaṃ pavisiṃsu. Evaṃ saliṅgeneva apakkantaṃ taṃ paribbājakaṃ sandhāya – “sarabho nāma paribbājako acirapakkanto hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

On the following day, just as he was dressed and robed, and with the very appearance he had adopted, he took his bowl, departed from Gijjhakūṭa, and went to the wanderers' park. Seeing him, the wanderers surrounded him, saying: “Teacher, how was it? It seems you were able to bring the Āvaṭṭanī illusion!” “Do not worry, friends, the Āvaṭṭanī illusion has been brought by me. From this day onwards, our gain and honor will be great. Be united among one another; do not quarrel,” he said. “Teacher, if it has been well learned by you, then teach it to us also,” they said. He, starting from the beginning, recited the Pātimokkha in full. Then all of them said, “Come, sirs! Wandering in the city, let us speak dispraise of the ascetic Gotama.” While the city gates were still unopened, they went near a gate, and when it was opened, they were the very first to enter. Thus, it was said with reference to that wanderer who had departed still in his own guise: “The wanderer named Sarabha has not long departed.”

Taṃ [M 2.0176] divasaṃ pana bhagavā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento idaṃ addasa – “ajja sarabho paribbājako nagare vicaritvā pakāsanīyakammaṃ karissati, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kathento visaṃ siñcitvā paribbājakārāmaṃ gamissati, ahampi tattheva gamissāmi, catassopi parisā tattheva osarissanti. Tasmiṃ samāgame caturāsīti pāṇasahassāni amatapānaṃ pivissantī”ti. Tato “tassa okāso hotu, yathāruciyā avaṇṇaṃ pattharatū”ti cintetvā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “ānanda, aṭṭhārasasu mahāvihāresu bhikkhusaṅghassa mayā saddhiṃyeva piṇḍāya carituṃ ārocehī”ti. Thero tathā akāsi. Bhikkhū pattacīvaramādāya satthārameva parivārayiṃsu. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ādāya dvāragāmasamīpeyeva piṇḍāya cari. Sarabhopi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ nagaraṃ paviṭṭho tattha tattha parisamajjhe rājadvāravīthicatukkādīsu ca gantvā “aññāto mayā samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ dhammo”tiādīni abhāsi. Taṃ sandhāya so rājagahe parisati evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsatītiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha aññātoti ñāto avabuddho, pākaṭaṃ katvā uggahitoti dīpeti. Aññāyāti jānitvā. Apakkantoti saliṅgeneva apakkanto. Sace hi samaṇassa gotamassa sāsane koci sāro abhavissa, nāhaṃ apakkamissaṃ. Tassa pana sāsanaṃ asāraṃ nissāraṃ, āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ osāretvā samaṇā lokaṃ khādantīti evamatthaṃ dīpento evamāha.

On that day, at dawn, the Blessed One surveyed the world and saw this: “Today, the wanderer Sarabha, after wandering through the city, will make a public denunciation; speaking ill of the Three Jewels and spreading poison, he will go to the wanderers’ park. I too will go there, and the fourfold assembly will also converge there. At that gathering, eighty-four thousand beings will drink the nectar of immortality.” Then, thinking, “Let him have the opportunity; let him spread slander as he wishes,” he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, announce to the Saṅgha of monks in the eighteen great monasteries that they are to go for alms together with me.” The Elder did so. The monks, taking their bowls and robes, surrounded the Teacher. The Teacher, accompanied by the Saṅgha of monks, went for alms in the vicinity of the gate-village. Sarabha, too, having entered the city with other wanderers, went here and there into the midst of assemblies—at the royal gate, on main roads, at crossroads, and so on—and declared such things as, “The Dhamma of the ascetics, the Sakyan sons, is known to me!” In reference to this, it was said: “He speaks such words in the assembly at Rājagaha,” and so on. Therein, ‘known’ (aññāto) means he explains it as ‘known,’ ‘understood,’ and ‘grasped after making it manifest.’ ‘Having known’ (aññāya) means ‘having known.’ ‘Departed’ (apakkanto) means ‘he departed in his very own appearance.’ Indeed, if there had been any essence in the ascetic Gotama’s dispensation, I would not have departed. But his dispensation is without essence, devoid of essence; having resorted to the Āvaṭṭani magic, the ascetics devour the world.” Explaining this meaning, he spoke thus.

Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhūti atha evaṃ tasmiṃ paribbājake bhāsamāne araññavāsino pañcasatā bhikkhū “asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma satthā piṇḍāya carituṃ gato”ti ajānantā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Te sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Assosunti suṇiṃsu. Yena [P 2.0299] bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti “imaṃ kāraṇaṃ dasabalassa ārocessāmā”ti upasaṅkamiṃsu.

Now, while that wanderer was speaking thus, five hundred forest-dwelling monks, unaware that the Teacher had gone for alms to such and such a place, entered Rājagaha for alms at the time for the alms-round. It was with reference to them that this was said. ‘They heard’ (assosuṃ) means they heard. ‘They approached the Blessed One’ (yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu) means they approached thinking, ‘We will report this matter to the One with Ten Powers.’

Sippinikātīranti [V 2.0172] sippinikāti evaṃnāmikāya nadiyā tīraṃ. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvenāti kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā abbhantare khantiṃ dhāretvā citteneva adhivāsesīti attho. Evaṃ adhivāsetvā puna cintesi – “kiṃ nu kho ajja mayā sarabhassa vādaṃ maddituṃ gacchantena ekakena gantabbaṃ[M 2.0177], udāhu bhikkhusaṅghaparivutenā”ti. Athassa etadahosi – sacāhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gamissāmi, mahājano evaṃ cintessati – “samaṇo gotamo vāduppattiṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto pakkhaṃ ukkhipitvā gantvā parisabalena uppannaṃ vādaṃ maddati, paravādīnaṃ sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na detī”ti. Na kho pana mayhaṃ uppanne vāde paraṃ gahetvā maddanakiccaṃ atthi, ahameva gantvā maddissāmi. Anacchariyaṃ cetaṃ yvāhaṃ idāni buddhabhūto attano uppannaṃ vādaṃ maddeyyaṃ, cariyaṃ caraṇakāle ahetukapaṭisandhiyaṃ nibbattenāpi hi mayā vahitabbaṃ dhuraṃ añño vahituṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Imassa panatthassa sādhanatthaṃ –

‘The bank of the Sippinikā’ (Sippinikātīraṃ) means the bank of the river named Sippinikā. ‘The Blessed One endured in silence’ (adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena) means that without moving his limbs or speech, maintaining patience inwardly, he endured by means of the mind alone; this is the meaning. Having endured thus, he then considered: “Today, as I go to crush Sarabha’s doctrine, should I go alone, or should I go surrounded by the community of monks?” Then it occurred to him: “If I go surrounded by the community of monks, the great populace will think: ‘The ascetic Gotama, going to a place where a debate has arisen, raises his own faction and, having gone, crushes the arisen doctrine with the strength of his retinue; he does not allow the heads of his opponents to be raised.’ But for me, when a debate has arisen, there is no need to take another to crush it; I alone will go and crush it. It is no wonder that I, now having become a Buddha, should crush a doctrine that has arisen concerning myself. For indeed, even during the time of practicing the perfections, when I was reborn with a rootless rebirth-linking, there was no one else capable of bearing the burden that had to be borne by me. To establish this meaning—

“Yato yato garu dhuraṃ, yato gambhīravattanī;

Tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjenti, svāssu taṃ vahate dhura”nti. (jā. 1.1.29) –

“Wherever the burden is heavy, wherever the track is deep; then they yoke the black one, and he indeed bears that burden.”

Idaṃ kaṇhajātakaṃ āharitabbaṃ. Atīte kira eko satthavāho ekissā mahallikāya gehe nivāsaṃ gaṇhi. Athassa ekissā dhenuyā rattibhāgasamanantare gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Sā ekaṃ vacchakaṃ vijāyi. Mahallikāya vacchakaṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya puttasineho udapādi. Punadivase satthavāhaputto – “tava gehavetanaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. Mahallikā “mayhaṃ aññena kiccaṃ na atthi, imameva vacchakaṃ dehī”ti āha. Gaṇha, ammāti. Sā taṃ gaṇhitvā khīraṃ pāyetvā yāgubhattatiṇādīni dadamānā [P 2.0300] posesi. So vuddhimanvāya paripuṇṇarūpo balavīriyasampanno ahosi sampannācāro, kāḷako nāma nāmena. Athekassa satthavāhassa pañcahi sakaṭasatehi āgacchantassa udakabhinnaṭṭhāne sakaṭacakkaṃ laggi. So dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi yojetvā nīharāpetuṃ asakkonto kāḷakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “tāta, tava vetanaṃ dassāmi, sakaṭaṃ me ukkhipitvā dehī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā taṃ ādāya – “añño iminā saddhiṃ dhuraṃ vahituṃ samattho natthī”ti dhurasakaṭe yottaṃ bandhitvā taṃ ekakaṃyeva yojesi. So taṃ sakaṭaṃ ukkhipitvā thale patiṭṭhāpetvā eteneva nihārena pañca sakaṭasatāni nīhari. So sabbapacchimasakaṭaṃ nīharitvā mociyamāno “su”nti katvā sīsaṃ ukkhipi.

This Kaṇha Jātaka should be related. In the past, it is said, a caravan leader took up residence in the house of an elderly woman. Then, just after the night had passed, one of his cows gave birth. She bore a single calf. For the elderly woman, from the moment she saw the calf, an affection as for a son arose. The next day, the caravan leader’s son said, “Take your payment for the house.” The elderly woman replied, “I have no need for anything else; just give me this very calf.” “Take him, mother,” he said. She took him, had him drink milk, and raised him, giving him gruel, rice, grass, and other things. Having attained growth, he became complete in form, endowed with strength and energy, and possessed of good conduct; by name, he was called Kāḷaka. Then, as a certain caravan leader was approaching with five hundred carts, a cart wheel got stuck in a place where the road was broken by water. Unable to have it pulled out even after yoking ten, twenty, or thirty oxen, he approached Kāḷaka and said: “My good fellow, I will give you a wage; please lift up my cart for me.” And having said this, he took him and, thinking, “No other is able to bear the yoke with this one,” tied the traces to the yoke of the cart and yoked him all alone. He lifted that cart, set it on dry ground, and in that very same way, pulled out the five hundred carts. Having pulled out the very last cart, as he was being unyoked, he snorted and raised his head.

Satthavāho [V 2.0173][M 2.0178] “ayaṃ ettakāni sakaṭāni ukkhipanto evaṃ na akāsi, vetanatthaṃ maññe karotī”ti sakaṭagaṇanāya kahāpaṇe gahetvā pañcasatabhaṇḍikaṃ tassa gīvāya bandhāpesi. So aññesaṃ attano santikaṃ allīyituṃ adento ujukaṃ gehameva agamāsi. Mahallikā disvā mocetvā kahāpaṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā “kasmā, putta, evamakāsi, mā tvaṃ ‘mayā kammaṃ katvā ābhatena ayaṃ jīvissatī’ti saññamakāsī”ti vatvā goṇaṃ uṇhodakena nhāpetvā telena abbhañjitvā “ito paṭṭhāya puna mā evamakāsī”ti ovadi. Evaṃ satthā “cariyaṃ caraṇakāle ahetukapaṭisandhiyaṃ nibbattenāpi hi mayā vahitabbadhuraṃ añño vahituṃ samattho nāma nāhosī”ti cintetvā ekakova agamāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitotiādi vuttaṃ.

The caravan leader, thinking, “This black bull, while lifting so many carts, did not act like this; I think he is doing it for wages,” took kahāpaṇas according to the number of carts and had a bundle of five hundred tied around his neck. That black bull, not allowing others to approach him, went straight home. The mistress of the house, seeing this, untied the bundle, and knowing them to be kahāpaṇas, said, “Why, my son, did you do this? You must not think, ‘This mistress of the house will live on the wealth brought by me, having done the work.’” Having said this, she bathed the bull with warm water, anointed it with oil, and advised, “From now on, do not do so again.” Thus the Teacher, reflecting, “Even when I was reborn with a rootless rebirth-linking at the time of practicing the conduct, there was no other who was capable of carrying the burden that had to be carried by me,” went alone. To show this, it was said: “Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having arisen from seclusion in the evening time…” and so on.

Tattha paṭisallānāti puthuttārammaṇehi cittaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā sallānato, phalasamāpattitoti attho. Tenupasaṅkamīti paribbājakesu sakalanagare pakāsanīyakammaṃ katvā nagarā nikkhamma paribbājakārāme sannipatitvā “sace, āvuso sarabha, samaṇo gotamo āgamissati, kiṃ [P 2.0301] karissasī”ti. Samaṇe gotame ekaṃ karonte ahaṃ dve karissāmi, dve karonte cattāri, cattāri karonte pañca, pañca karonte dasa, dasa karonte vīsati, vīsati karonte tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsaṃ karonte cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsaṃ karonte paññāsaṃ, paññāsaṃ karonte sataṃ, sataṃ karonte sahassaṃ karissāmīti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ sīhanādakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā nisinnesu upasaṅkami.

Herein, as for `paṭisallāna` (seclusion): the meaning is seclusion, which is the withdrawal of the mind from various objects, and the attainment of fruition. As for `tenupasaṅkami` (He approached them): He approached the wanderers as they were seated, after they had made a proclamation throughout the entire city, gone out from the city, gathered in the wanderers' park, and raised a mutual discussion that was a lion's roar, saying: “Friend Sarabha, if the ascetic Gotama comes, what will you do?” “If the ascetic Gotama speaks one phrase, I will speak two; if he speaks two, I will speak four; if he speaks four, I will speak five; if he speaks five, I will speak ten; if he speaks ten, I will speak twenty; if he speaks twenty, I will speak thirty; if he speaks thirty, I will speak forty; if he speaks forty, I will speak fifty; if he speaks fifty, I will speak a hundred; if he speaks a hundred, I will speak a thousand.”

Upasaṅkamanto pana yasmā paribbājakārāmassa nagaramajjheneva maggo, tasmā surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā sugatamahācīvaraṃ pārupitvā vissaṭṭhabalo rājā viya ekakova nagaramajjhena agamāsi. Micchādiṭṭhikā disvā “paribbājakā samaṇassa gotamassa pakāsanīyakammaṃ karontā avaṇṇaṃ patthariṃsu, so ete anuvattitvā saññāpetuṃ gacchati maññe”ti anubandhiṃsu. Sammādiṭṭhikāpi “sammāsambuddho pattacīvaraṃ ādāya ekakova nikkhanto, ajja sarabhena saddhiṃ mahādhammasaṅgāmo bhavissati. Mayampi tasmiṃ samāgame kāyasakkhino bhavissāmā”ti anubandhiṃsu. Satthā passantasseva mahājanassa paribbājakārāmaṃ upasaṅkami.

Now, as the path to the wanderers’ park lay right through the middle of the city, he, having worn a well-dyed, double-layered undergarment and donned the great robe of the Sugata, went alone through the middle of the city like a king whose forces have been dismissed. Those of wrong view, upon seeing him, thought, “The wanderers, performing a conspicuous act against the ascetic Gotama, have spread dispraise. He is going after them to make them understand, it seems,” and they followed him. Those of right view also thought, “The Perfectly Enlightened One has taken his bowl and robe and gone forth alone. Today there will be a great Dhamma battle with Sarabha. We too shall be bodily witnesses at that assembly,” and they followed him. The Teacher approached the wanderers’ park while the great crowd was watching.

Paribbājakā [M 2.0179] rukkhānaṃ khandhaviṭapasākhantarehi samuggacchantā chabbaṇṇaghanabuddharasmiyo disvā “aññadā evarūpo obhāso nāma natthi, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti ulloketvā “samaṇo [V 2.0174] gotamo āgacchatī”ti āhaṃsu. Taṃ sutvāva sarabho jāṇukantare sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā adhomukho nisīdi. Evaṃ tasmiṃ samaye bhagavā taṃ ārāmaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Tathāgato hi jambudīpatale aggakule jātattā aggāsanārahotissa sabbattha āsanaṃ paññattameva hoti. Evaṃ paññatte mahārahe buddhāsane nisīdi.

The wanderers, seeing the six-hued, dense Buddha-rays emanating from the gaps between the tree trunks, boughs, and branches, looked up, thinking, “At other times, there is no radiance such as this. What could this be?” and said, “The ascetic Gotama is coming.” Just on hearing this, Sarabha placed his head between his knees and sat with his face downcast. Thus, at that time, the Blessed One approached that park and sat down on the prepared seat. Indeed, the Tathāgata, due to being born into the foremost family on the surface of Jambudīpa, is worthy of the foremost seat; for him, a seat is always prepared everywhere. Thus, he sat on the great and precious Buddha-seat that had been prepared.

Te paribbājakā sarabhaṃ paribbājakaṃ etadavocunti sammāsambuddhe kira sarabhena saddhiṃ ettakaṃ kathenteyeva [P 2.0302] bhikkhusaṅgho satthu padānupadiko hutvā paribbājakārāmaṃ sampāpuṇi, catassopi parisā paribbājakārāmeyeva osariṃsu. Tato te paribbājakā “acchariyaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa kammaṃ, sakalanagaraṃ vicaritvā avaṇṇaṃ pattharitvā pakāsanīyakammaṃ katvā āgatānaṃ verīnaṃ paṭisattūnaṃ paccāmittānaṃ santikaṃ āgantvā thokampi viggāhikakathaṃ na kathesi, āgatakālato paṭṭhāya satapākatelena makkhento viya amatapānaṃ pāyento viya madhurakathaṃ kathetī”ti sabbepi sammāsambuddhaṃ anuvattantā etadavocuṃ.

Regarding 'Those wanderers said this to Sarabha the wanderer': While the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One was speaking with Sarabha for just that long, the community of monks, following in the Teacher's footsteps, reached the wanderers' park; the four assemblies also descended into the wanderers' park. Then those wanderers reflected: 'Wonderful is the deed of the ascetic Gotama! Having wandered through the entire city, spread dispraise, and performed a conspicuous act, he has come into the presence of his arrived enemies, adversaries, and foes, yet he does not speak even a little contentious talk. From the moment of his arrival, as if anointing with oil boiled a hundred times or as if giving the deathless drink, he speaks sweet words.' Thus, all of them, following the example of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, said this.

Yāceyyāsīti āyāceyyāsi pattheyyāsi piheyyāsi. Tuṇhībhūtoti tuṇhībhāvaṃ upagato. Maṅkubhūtoti nittejataṃ āpanno. Pattakkhandhoti onatagīvo. Adhomukhoti heṭṭhāmukho. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sabbe dhammā mayā abhisambuddhā”ti evaṃ paṭijānato tava. Anabhisambuddhāti ime nāma dhammā tayā anabhisambuddhā. Tatthāti tesu anabhisambuddhāti evaṃ dassitadhammesu. Aññena vā aññaṃ paṭicarissatīti aññena vā vacanena aññaṃ vacanaṃ paṭicchādessati, aññaṃ pucchito aññaṃ kathessatīti adhippāyo. Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmessatīti bahiddhā aññaṃ āgantukakathaṃ āharanto purimakathaṃ apanāmessati. Appaccayanti anabhiraddhiṃ atuṭṭhākāraṃ pātukarissatīti pākaṭaṃ karissati. Ettha ca appaccayena domanassaṃ vuttaṃ, purimehi dvīhi mandabalavabhedo kodhoyeva.

'You should request' means you should ask, you should aspire, you should yearn. 'Having become silent' means having reached a state of silence. 'Having become crestfallen' means having reached a state of being without splendor. 'With shoulders drooping' means with neck stooped. 'With face downcast' means with face lowered. 'Of you who claims to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' means of you who claims thus: 'I am a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully awakened to by me.' 'Not fully awakened to' means 'these phenomena have not been fully awakened to by you.' 'Therein' means in those phenomena thus pointed out as 'not fully awakened to.' 'Or he will evade one matter with another' means he will cover up one statement with another statement, or when asked one thing, he will speak of another; this is the intention. 'He will divert the talk externally' means by bringing in another, external topic, he will set aside the previous topic. 'He will show displeasure' means he will make manifest displeasure, an appearance of dissatisfaction; he will make it apparent. And here, by 'displeasure,' unhappiness is stated; by the previous two terms, only anger, with its division into weak and strong, is stated.

Evaṃ [M 2.0180] bhagavā paṭhamavesārajjena sīhanādaṃ naditvā puna dutiyādīhi nadanto yo kho maṃ paribbājakātiādimāha. Tattha yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desitoti yassa maggassa [P 2.0303] vā phalassa vā atthāya tayā catusaccadhammo desito. So na niyyātīti so dhammo na niyyāti na niggacchati, na taṃ atthaṃ sādhetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Takkarassāti yo naṃ karoti, tassa paṭipattipūrakassa puggalassāti attho. Sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti hetunā nayena kāraṇena sakalassa [V 2.0175] vaṭṭadukkhassa khayāya. Atha vā yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desitoti yassa te atthāya dhammo desito. Seyyathidaṃ – rāgapaṭighātatthāya asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, dosapaṭighātatthāya mettābhāvanā, mohapaṭighātatthāya pañca dhammā, vitakkupacchedāya ānāpānassati. So na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti so dhammo yo naṃ yathādesitaṃ karoti, tassa takkarassa sammā hetunā nayena kāraṇena vaṭṭadukkhakkhayāya na niyyāti na niggacchati, taṃ atthaṃ na sādhetīti ayamettha attho. Seyyathāpi sarabho paribbājakoti yathā ayaṃ sarabho paribbājako pajjhāyanto appaṭibhāno nisinno, evaṃ nisīdissatīti.

Thus, having uttered the lion's roar with the first assurance, the Blessed One, wishing to utter it again with the second and subsequent assurances, spoke the words beginning, 'O wanderers, whoever...'. Therein, 'for whose benefit the Dhamma was taught by you' means: the Dhamma of the Four Truths was taught by you for the benefit of whichever path or whichever fruit. ‘It does not lead out’ means that Dhamma does not lead out, does not go forth; it does not accomplish that benefit—this is what is meant. ‘For the one who does it’ means for that person who fulfills the practice; this is the meaning. ‘For the right destruction of suffering’ means for the destruction of all the suffering of the round by cause, method, and reason. Alternatively, ‘for whose benefit the Dhamma was taught by you’ means the Dhamma was taught by you for the benefit of... Namely: the meditation subject of foulness for the purpose of destroying lust, the development of loving-kindness for the purpose of destroying hatred, the five dhammas for the purpose of destroying delusion, and mindfulness of breathing for cutting off thoughts. ‘It does not lead out for the one who does it, for the right destruction of suffering’ means: that Dhamma of practice, for one who practices it as it was taught, does not lead out, does not go forth, for that practitioner for the destruction of the suffering of the round by right cause, method, and reason; it does not accomplish that benefit. This is the meaning here. ‘Just like the wanderer Sarabha’ means: just as this wanderer Sarabha is seated, brooding and unresponsive, so too will he sit.

Evaṃ tīhi padehi sīhanādaṃ naditvā desanaṃ nivattentasseva tathāgatassa tasmiṃ ṭhāne sannipatitā caturāsītipāṇasahassaparimāṇā parisā amatapānaṃ pivi, satthā parisāya amatapānassa pītabhāvaṃ ñatvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pakkāmi. Tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ atha kho bhagavātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sīhanādanti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ appaṭinādaṃ. Vehāsaṃ pakkāmīti abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Evaṃ pakkhando ca pana taṃkhaṇaññeva gijjhakūṭamahāvihāre patiṭṭhāsi.

Thus, having uttered the lion's roar with these three statements, just as the Tathāgata was bringing the discourse to a close, an assembly of eighty-four thousand living beings gathered in that place drank the deathless nectar. Knowing that the assembly had drunk the deathless nectar, the Teacher rose into the air and departed. To illustrate this matter, it is said: “Then the Blessed One…” and so on. Therein, ‘lion's roar’ means the supreme roar, the fearless roar, the unrivaled roar. ‘Departed into the air’ means that having attained the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge, having emerged and made a resolution, he rose into the sky together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. And having risen up in this way, at that very moment he was established at the great monastery on Vulture Peak.

Vācāya sannitodakenāti vacanapatodena. Sañjambharimakaṃsūti [P 2.0304] sambharitaṃ nirantaraphuṭaṃ akaṃsu, upari vijjhiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Brahāraññeti mahāraññe. Sīhanādaṃ nadissāmīti sīhassa nadato ākāraṃ disvā “ayampi tiracchānagato, ahampi, imassa cattāro pādā, mayhampi, ahampi evameva sīhanādaṃ nadissāmī”ti cintesi. So sīhassa sammukhā nadituṃ asakkonto [M 2.0181] tasmiṃ gocarāya pakkante ekako nadituṃ ārabhi. Athassa siṅgālasaddoyeva nicchari. Tena vuttaṃ – siṅgālakaṃyeva nadatīti. Bheraṇḍakanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Apica bhinnassaraṃ amanāpasaddaṃ nadatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evameva kho tvanti iminā opammena paribbājakā tathāgataṃ sīhasadisaṃ katvā sarabhaṃ siṅgālasadisaṃ akaṃsu. Ambukasañcarīti khuddakakukkuṭikā. Purisakaravitaṃ ravissāmīti mahākukkuṭaṃ ravantaṃ disvā “imassapi dve pādā dve pakkhā, mayhampi tatheva, ahampi evarūpaṃ ravitaṃ ravissāmī”ti sā tassa sammukhā ravituṃ asakkontī tasmiṃ pakkante ravamānā kukkuṭikāravaṃyeva ravi. Tena vuttaṃ – ambukasañcariravitaṃyeva ravatīti. Usabhoti goṇo. Suññāyāti tucchāya jeṭṭhakavasabhehi virahitāya[V 2.0176]. Gambhīraṃ naditabbaṃ maññatīti jeṭṭhakavasabhassa nādasadisaṃ gambhīranādaṃ naditabbaṃ maññati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

‘With the goad of speech’ means with the goad that is speech. ‘They made it completely filled and pervaded without interval’; it is meant that they pierced upwards. ‘In the great forest’ means in the great forest. ‘I will roar a lion’s roar’: having seen the manner of a roaring lion, he thought, “This one is an animal, and so am I. It has four feet, and so do I. I too will roar a lion’s roar just like this.” He, being unable to roar in the lion’s presence, began to roar alone when that lion had gone away to its feeding ground. Then, only the sound of a jackal came forth from him. Therefore it is said: he howls only as a jackal. ‘Bheraṇḍaka’ is a synonym for that. Moreover, it is meant that he utters a broken, unpleasant sound. By this simile of ‘Just so, you...’, the wanderers, having made the Tathāgata like a lion, made Sarabha like a jackal. ‘A wandering hen’ means a small hen. ‘I will crow a man's crowing’: having seen a great rooster crowing, she thought, “This one has two feet and two wings, and so do I. I too will crow a crowing like this.” She, being unable to crow in its presence, crowed only a hen’s crow when it had gone away. Therefore it is said: she merely cackles like a wandering hen. ‘An ox’ means a bull. ‘Empty’ means empty, devoid of the chief bulls. ‘He thinks a deep roar should be roared’ means he thinks a deep roar like the roar of a chief bull should be roared. The rest everywhere has a clear meaning.

5. Kesamuttisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Kesamutti Sutta

66. Pañcame kālāmānaṃ nigamoti kālāmā nāma khattiyā, tesaṃ nigamo. Kesamuttiyāti kesamuttanigamavāsino. Upasaṅkamiṃsūti sappinavanītādibhesajjāni ceva aṭṭhavidhapānakāni ca gāhāpetvā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Sakaṃyeva vādaṃ dīpentīti attanoyeva laddhiṃ kathenti. Jotentīti pakāsenti. Khuṃsentīti ghaṭṭenti. Vambhentīti [P 2.0305] avajānanti. Paribhavantīti lāmakaṃ karonti. Omakkhiṃ karontīti ukkhittakaṃ karonti, ukkhipitvā chaḍḍenti. Aparepi, bhanteti so kira aṭavimukhe gāmo, tasmā tattha aṭaviṃ atikkantā ca atikkamitukāmā ca vāsaṃ kappenti. Tesupi paṭhamaṃ āgatā attano laddhiṃ dīpetvā pakkamiṃsu, pacchā āgatā “kiṃ te jānanti, amhākaṃ antevāsikā te, amhākaṃ santike kiñci kiñci sippaṃ uggaṇhiṃsū”ti attano laddhiṃ dīpetvā pakkamiṃsu. Kālāmā ekaladdhiyampi saṇṭhahituṃ na sakkhiṃsu. Te etamatthaṃ dīpetvā bhagavato evamārocetvā tesaṃ no, bhantetiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha hoteva kaṅkhāti hotiyeva kaṅkhā. Vicikicchāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Alanti yuttaṃ.

66. In the fifth (section), 'the town of the Kālāmas' means the town of the Kālāmas, who were Khattiyas. 'Kesamutti' refers to the residents of the town of Kesamutta. 'They approached' means they approached, having brought medicines such as ghee and fresh butter, and also the eight kinds of drinks. 'Proclaiming their own doctrine' means they state their own views. 'They illuminate' means they make clear. 'They revile' means they censure. 'They despise' means they look down upon. 'They belittle' means they make it inferior. 'They treat with contempt' means they make it something to be cast aside; having lifted it up, they abandon it. 'Others also, Venerable Sir' – it is said that that village was at the entrance to the forest; therefore, those who had passed through the forest and those who wished to pass through it stayed there. Among them, those who arrived first proclaimed their own views and departed. Those who arrived later, proclaiming their own views, departed, saying: 'What do they know? They are our resident pupils; they learned some little skill from us.' The Kālāmas were not able to be established in even a single view. Having explained this matter, they reported it thus to the Blessed One and said, 'Venerable Sir, for us...' and so forth. Herein, 'doubt indeed arises' means doubt indeed arises. 'Vicikicchā' is just another term for it. 'It is fitting' means it is suitable.

Mā [M 2.0182] anussavenāti anussavakathāyapi mā gaṇhittha. Mā paramparāyāti paramparakathāyapi mā gaṇhittha. Mā itikirāyāti evaṃ kira etanti mā gaṇhittha. Mā piṭakasampadānenāti amhākaṃ piṭakatantiyā saddhiṃ sametīti mā gaṇhittha. Mā takkahetūti takkaggāhenapi mā gaṇhittha. Mā nayahetūti nayaggāhenapi mā gaṇhittha. Mā ākāraparivitakkenāti sundaramidaṃ kāraṇanti evaṃ kāraṇaparivitakkenapi mā gaṇhittha. Mā diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyāti amhākaṃ nijjhāyitvā khamitvā gahitadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ sametītipi mā gaṇhittha. Mā bhabbarūpatāyāti ayaṃ bhikkhu bhabbarūpo, imassa kathaṃ gahetuṃ yuttantipi mā gaṇhittha. Mā samaṇo no garūti ayaṃ samaṇo amhākaṃ garu, imassa kathaṃ gahetuṃ yuttantipi mā gaṇhittha. Samattāti paripuṇṇā. Samādinnāti [P 2.0306] gahitā parāmaṭṭhā. Yaṃsa hotīti yaṃ kāraṇaṃ tassa puggalassa hoti. Alobhādayo [V 2.0177] lobhādipaṭipakkhavasena veditabbā. Vigatābhijjhotiādīhi mettāya pubbabhāgo kathito.

‘Do not accept by mere hearsay’ (mā anussavena) means do not accept even by hearsay talk. ‘Do not accept by mere tradition’ (mā paramparāya) means do not accept even by traditional talk. ‘Do not accept by mere rumor’ (mā itikirāya) means do not accept thinking ‘it is said thus.’ ‘Do not accept by mere scriptural transmission’ (mā piṭakasampadānena) means do not accept thinking ‘it agrees with our textual tradition.’ ‘Do not accept by mere logic’ (mā takkahetu) means do not accept even by logical grasping. ‘Do not accept by mere inference’ (mā nayahetu) means do not accept even by inferential grasping. ‘Do not accept by mere reflection on reasons’ (mā ākāraparivitakkena) means do not accept even by reflection on reasons, thinking ‘this is a good reason.’ ‘Do not accept by mere agreement with a considered view’ (mā diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā) means do not accept even because it agrees with a view that you have considered and accepted. ‘Do not accept because the speaker seems competent’ (mā bhabbarūpatāya) means do not accept thinking ‘this monk is competent, so it is fitting to accept his words.’ ‘Do not accept because the ascetic is our teacher’ (mā samaṇo no garu) means do not accept thinking ‘this ascetic is our teacher, so it is fitting to accept his words.’ ‘Fully’ (samattā) means complete. ‘Taken up’ (samādinnā) means grasped and misapprehended. ‘Whatever is for one’ (yaṃsa hoti) refers to whatever reason there is for that individual. Non-greed and the like should be understood as the opposites of greed and the like. By the words beginning with ‘Free from covetousness,’ the preliminary stage of loving-kindness is taught.

Idāni mettādikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento mettāsahagatenātiādimāha. Tattha kammaṭṭhānakathāya vā bhāvanānaye vā pāḷivaṇṇanāya vā yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.240) vuttameva. Evaṃ averacittoti evaṃ akusalaverassa ca puggalaverino ca natthitāya averacitto. Abyābajjhacittoti kodhacittassa abhāvena niddukkhacitto. Asaṃkiliṭṭhacittoti kilesassa natthitāya asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto. Visuddhacittoti kilesamalābhāvena visuddhacitto hotīti attho. Tassāti tassa evarūpassa ariyasāvakassa. Assāsāti avassayā patiṭṭhā. Sace kho pana atthi paro lokoti yadi imamhā lokā paraloko nāma atthi. Athāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā parammaraṇā…pe… upapajjissāmīti atthetaṃ kāraṇaṃ, yenāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā parammaraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmīti evaṃ sabbattha nayo veditabbo. Anīghanti niddukkhaṃ. Sukhinti sukhitaṃ. Ubhayeneva visuddhaṃ attānaṃ samanupassāmīti yañca pāpaṃ na karomi, yañca karotopi na karīyati, iminā ubhayenāpi visuddhaṃ attānaṃ samanupassāmi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Now, desiring to teach the meditation subject beginning with loving-kindness, He spoke the words beginning with `mettāsahagatena`. Therein, whatever should be said in the discourse on the meditation subject, by the method of development, or by way of explaining the Pāḷi, all that has already been said by me in the Visuddhimagga. `Evaṃ averacitto` means: thus, one has a mind without enmity due to the absence of both the enmity that is unwholesome and enmity towards persons. `Abyābajjhacitto` means: one has a mind without suffering due to the absence of a mind of anger. `Asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto` means: due to the absence of defilement, one has an undefiled mind. `Visuddhacitto` means: one has a purified mind due to the absence of the stain of defilements; this is the meaning. `Tassāti` refers to that noble disciple of such a nature. `Assāsāti` means: supports and foundations. `Sace kho pana atthi paro loko`ti means: if from this present world there is indeed what is called a world beyond. The meaning of `Athāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā parammaraṇā… upapajjissāmi` is: Then, with the breakup of the body, after death, I will arise. The full phrase means: There is that reason by which I, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, the method should be understood in all sentences. `Anīghanti` means without suffering. `Sukhinti` means endowed with happiness. `Ubhayeneva visuddhaṃ attānaṃ samanupassāmīti` means: I clearly see myself as pure by both these two means: by the evil that I do not do, and by the evil that, even if one does it, is not considered done. By both these reasons, I clearly see myself as pure. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

6. Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta

67. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0183] migāranattāti migāraseṭṭhino nattā. Sekhuniyanattāti sekhuniyaseṭṭhino nattā. Upasaṅkamiṃsūti bhuttapātarāsā dāsakammakaraparivutā [P 2.0307] upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tesaṃ kira purebhatte pubbaṇhasamayeyeva gehe eko pañho samuṭṭhito, taṃ pana kathetuṃ okāso nāhosi. Te “taṃ pañhaṃ sossāmā”ti therassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā tuṇhī nisīdiṃsu. Thero “gāme taṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ pañhaṃ sotuṃ āgatā bhavissantī”ti tesaṃ manaṃ ñatvā tameva pañhaṃ ārabhanto etha tumhe sāḷhātiādimāha. Tattha atthi lobhoti lubbhanasabhāvo lobho nāma atthīti pucchati. Abhijjhāti kho ahaṃ sāḷhā etamatthaṃ vadāmīti etaṃ lobhasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ ahaṃ “abhijjhā”ti vadāmi, “taṇhā”ti vadāmīti samuṭṭhitapañhassa atthaṃ dīpento āha. Evaṃ sabbavāresu nayo netabbo.

67. In the sixth. 'Migāranattā' means the grandson of Migāra the wealthy man. 'Sekhuniyanattā' means the grandson of Sekhuniya the wealthy man. 'Upasaṅkamiṃsu' means: they approached, having eaten their morning meal, accompanied by servants and workers. It is said that for them, a question had arisen in their house before the meal, in the forenoon itself, but there was no opportunity to resolve it. Thinking, 'We shall hear that question,' they went to the elder, paid homage, and sat down silently. The elder, knowing their minds and thinking, 'They must have come to hear the question that arose in the village,' took up that very question and spoke the words beginning with, 'Come, you Sāḷha.' Herein, by 'Atthi lobho,' he asks: 'Does there exist a state with the nature of coveting, called greed?' He spoke the words, "Sāḷha, I say this meaning is covetousness," in order to explain the meaning of the question that had arisen. This means: "That thing which is designated as greed, I call ‘covetousness’; I call it ‘craving’.” Thus, the method should be applied in all instances.

So [V 2.0178] evaṃ pajānātīti so cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā ṭhito ariyasāvako samāpattito vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ ārabhanto evaṃ pajānāti. Atthi idanti atthi dukkhasaccasaṅkhātaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ nāmarūpavasena paricchinditvā pajānanto esa “evaṃ pajānāti atthi ida”nti vutto. Hīnanti samudayasaccaṃ. Paṇītanti maggasaccaṃ. Imassa saññāgatassa uttari nissaraṇanti imassa vipassanāsaññāsaṅkhātassa saññāgatassa uttari nissaraṇaṃ nāma nibbānaṃ, tamatthīti iminā nirodhasaccaṃ dasseti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ kathitaṃ. Ahu pubbe lobhoti pubbe me lobho ahosi. Tadahu akusalanti taṃ akusalaṃ nāma ahosi, tadā vā akusalaṃ nāma ahosi. Iccetaṃ kusalanti iti etaṃ kusalaṃ, tasseva akusalassa natthibhāvaṃ kusalaṃ khemanti sandhāya vadati. Nicchātoti nittaṇho. Nibbutoti [P 2.0308] abbhantare santāpakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena nibbuto. Sītibhūtoti sītalībhūto. Sukhappaṭisaṃvedīti kāyikacetasikassa sukhassa paṭisaṃveditā. Brahmabhūtenāti seṭṭhabhūtena. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

“He understands thus” means: that noble disciple, established after having developed the four divine abidings, having arisen from attainment and begun insight, understands thus. “There is this” means: this person, who understands by delineating the five aggregates designated as the truth of suffering in terms of name-and-form, is said to “understand thus: there is this.” “Inferior” means the truth of origin. “Superior” means the truth of the path. “Beyond this state of perception there is an escape” means: beyond this state of perception designated as insight-perception, the escape is Nibbāna; by stating ‘that exists,’ he indicates the truth of cessation. By “The knowledge: ‘In the liberated, it is liberated,’” are taught the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge. “There was greed before” means: “Before, greed existed in me.” “That was unwholesome” means: “That was called unwholesome.” “This is wholesome” means: “Thus, this is wholesome”; he speaks with reference to the wholesome and safe state of the non-existence of that very unwholesome. “Free from craving” means: without craving. “Quenched” means: quenched due to the absence of internal defilements that cause burning. “Cooled” means: become cool. “Experiencing bliss” means: experiencing bodily and mental bliss. “Become divine” means: become excellent. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

7. Kathāvatthusuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Subjects of Discourse

68. Sattame [M 2.0184] kathāvatthūnīti kathākāraṇāni, kathāya bhūmiyo patiṭṭhāyoti attho. Atītaṃ vā, bhikkhave, addhānanti atītamaddhānaṃ nāma kālopi vaṭṭati khandhāpi. Anāgatapaccuppannesupi eseva nayo. Tattha atīte kassapo nāma sammāsambuddho ahosi, tassa kikī nāma kāsikarājā aggupaṭṭhāko ahosi, vīsati vassasahassāni āyu ahosīti iminā nayena kathento atītaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheti nāma. Anāgate metteyyo nāma buddho bhavissati, tassa saṅkho nāma rājā aggupaṭṭhāko bhavissati, asīti vassasahassāni āyu bhavissatīti iminā nayena kathento anāgataṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheti nāma. Etarahi asuko nāma rājā dhammikoti iminā nayena kathento paccuppannaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheti nāma.

68. In the seventh sutta, kathāvatthūni means the causes for talk, the grounds for talk, and the bases for talk. In the phrase 'Past time, O monks,' the term 'past time' refers to both time and the aggregates. The same principle applies to the future and the present.
