Therein, one who speaks in this way, 'In the past, there was a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kassapa, whose chief supporter was King Kikī of Kāsi, and whose lifespan was twenty thousand years,' is said to be speaking about the past. One who speaks in this way, 'In the future, there will be a Buddha named Metteyya, whose chief supporter will be King Saṅkha, and whose lifespan will be eighty thousand years,' is said to be speaking about the future. One who speaks in this way, 'At present, such-and-such a king is righteous,' is said to be speaking about the present.

Kathāsampayogenāti kathāsamāgamena. Kacchoti kathetuṃ yutto. Akacchoti kathetuṃ na yutto. Ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyaṃ pañhantiādīsu, “cakkhu, anicca”nti puṭṭhena, “āma, anicca”nti ekaṃseneva byākātabbaṃ. Eseva nayo sotādīsu. Ayaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Aniccaṃ nāma cakkhū”ti puṭṭhena pana “na cakkhumeva, sotampi aniccaṃ, ghānampi anicca”nti evaṃ vibhajitvā [V 2.0179] byākātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Yathā cakkhu, tathā sotaṃ. Yathā sotaṃ, tathā cakkhū”ti puṭṭhena “kenaṭṭhena pucchasī”ti paṭipucchitvā “dassanaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte “na hī”ti byākātabbaṃ. “Aniccaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte, “āmā”ti byākātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”ntiādīni [P 2.0309] puṭṭhena pana “abyākatametaṃ bhagavatā”ti ṭhapetabbo, esa pañho na byākātabbo. Ayaṃ ṭhapanīyo pañho.

Kathāsampayogena means by coming together for talk. Kaccho means suitable to speak. Akaccho means not suitable to speak. In the case of a question to be answered categorically, such as when asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?' one should answer categorically, 'Yes, it is impermanent.' The same method applies to the ear and so on. This is a question to be answered categorically. But when asked, 'Is that which is called "impermanent" the eye?' one should answer analytically, 'Not only the eye is impermanent; the ear is also impermanent, and the nose is also impermanent.' This is a question to be answered analytically. When asked, 'As is the eye, so is the ear; as is the ear, so is the eye?' one should counter-question, 'In what sense do you ask?' If the reply is, 'In the sense of seeing,' one should answer, 'No.' If the reply is, 'In the sense of impermanence,' one should answer, 'Yes.' This is a question to be answered by counter-question. But when asked such questions as, 'Is the life principle the same as the body?' one should set it aside, saying, 'This has not been declared by the Blessed One.' This question is not to be answered. This is a question to be set aside.

Ṭhānāṭhāne na saṇṭhātīti kāraṇākāraṇe na saṇṭhāti. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – sassatavādī yuttena kāraṇena pahoti ucchedavādiṃ niggahetuṃ, ucchedavādī tena niggayhamāno “kiṃ panāhaṃ ucchedaṃ vadāmī”ti sassatavādibhāvameva dīpeti, attano vāde patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Evaṃ ucchedavādimhi pahonte sassatavādī, puggalavādimhi pahonte suññatavādī, suññatavādimhi pahonte puggalavādīti evaṃ ṭhānāṭhāne na saṇṭhāti nāma.

'One does not stand firm in what is a ground and what is not a ground' means one does not stand firm in what is a cause and what is not a cause. Herein, this is the method: an eternalist, with a suitable reason, is able to refute an annihilationist. The annihilationist, being refuted by him, considers, 'Why, then, should I speak of annihilation?' and reveals only the state of being an eternalist, being unable to stand in his own view. Likewise, when the annihilationist is able, the eternalist does not stand firm; when the personalist is able, the advocate of emptiness does not stand firm; and when the advocate of emptiness is able, the personalist does not stand firm. Thus, it is said that one 'does not stand firm in what is a ground and what is not a ground.'

Parikappe [M 2.0185] na saṇṭhātīti idaṃ pañhapucchanepi pañhakathanepi labbhati. Kathaṃ? Ekacco hi “pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti kaṇṭhaṃ sodheti, so itarena “idaṃ nāma tvaṃ pucchissasī”ti vutto ñātabhāvaṃ ñatvā “na etaṃ, aññaṃ pucchissāmī”ti vadati. Pañhaṃ puṭṭhopi “pañhaṃ kathessāmī”ti hanuṃ saṃsodheti, so itarena “idaṃ nāma kathessasī”ti vutto ñātabhāvaṃ ñatvā “na etaṃ, aññaṃ kathessāmī”ti vadati. Evaṃ parikappe na saṇṭhāti nāma.

'One does not stand firm in deliberation'—this is found both in the asking of questions and in the answering of them. How so? For instance, a certain person, thinking, 'I will ask a question,' clears his throat. When he is told by another, 'You are about to ask this particular question,' he, knowing that his intention has been discovered, says, 'Not that one; I will ask another.' Also, one who has been asked a question, thinking, 'I will answer the question,' adjusts his jaw. When he is told by another, 'You are about to say this particular thing,' he, knowing that his intention has been discovered, says, 'Not that; I will say something else.' Thus, it is said that one 'does not stand firm in deliberation.'

Aññātavāde na saṇṭhātīti aññātavāde jānitavāde na saṇṭhāti. Kathaṃ? Ekacco pañhaṃ pucchati, taṃ itaro “manāpo tayā pañho pucchito, kahaṃ te esa uggahito”ti vadati. Itaro pucchitabbaniyāmeneva pañhaṃ pucchitvāpi tassa kathāya “apañhaṃ nu kho pucchita”nti vimatiṃ karoti. Aparo pañhaṃ puṭṭho katheti, tamañño “suṭṭhu te pañho kathito, kattha te uggahito, pañhaṃ kathentena nāma evaṃ kathetabbo”ti vadati. Itaro kathetabbaniyāmeneva pañhaṃ kathetvāpi tassa kathāya “apañho nu kho mayā kathito”ti vimatiṃ karoti.

'One does not stand firm in a known matter' means one does not stand firm in a matter that is known, that is recognized. How so? A certain person asks a question, and another says to him, 'The question you asked is pleasing; where did you learn it?' The former, even having asked the question in the proper manner of asking, becomes doubtful because of that person's speech, thinking, 'Have I indeed asked an improper question?' Another person, having been asked a question, answers it. Someone else says to him, 'Your answer to the question was excellent; where did you learn it? One who answers a question should indeed answer it like this.' The former, even having answered the question in the proper manner of answering, becomes doubtful because of that person's speech, thinking, 'Was what I answered in fact an improper answer?'

Paṭipadāya na saṇṭhātīti paṭipattiyaṃ na tiṭṭhati, vattaṃ ajānitvā apucchitabbaṭṭhāne pucchatīti attho. Ayaṃ pañho [P 2.0310] nāma cetiyaṅgaṇe pucchitena na kathetabbo, tathā bhikkhācāramagge [V 2.0180] gāmaṃ piṇḍāya caraṇakāle. Āsanasālāya nisinnakāle yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā gahetvā nisinnakāle paribhuñjitvā nisinnakāle divāvihāraṭṭhānagamanakālepi. Divāṭṭhāne nisinnakāle pana okāsaṃ kāretvāva pucchantassa kathetabbo, akāretvā pucchantassa na kathetabbo. Idaṃ vattaṃ ajānitvā pucchanto paṭipadāya na saṇṭhāti nāma. Evaṃ santāyaṃ, bhikkhave, puggalo akaccho hotīti, bhikkhave, etaṃ imasmiṃ ca kāraṇe sati ayaṃ puggalo na kathetuṃ yutto nāma hoti.

'He does not stand firm in the practice' means he does not abide in the proper conduct; not knowing the proper procedure, he asks in an inappropriate place—this is the meaning. A question should not be answered by one who is asked in the stupa courtyard; likewise on the alms-round path, while wandering in the village for alms, while seated in the assembly hall, while seated having received gruel or food, while seated after having eaten, and also while going to the place for the day's abiding. However, when one is seated in the place for the day's abiding, a question should be answered for one who asks after having been given an opportunity; it should not be answered for one who asks without having been given an opportunity. One who asks without knowing this proper procedure is said to be one who 'does not stand firm in the practice'. 'Thus, monks, such a person is unfit for discussion' means: Monks, when this reason is present, this person is indeed not fit for discussion.

Ṭhānāṭhāne saṇṭhātīti sassatavādī yuttena kāraṇena pahoti ucchedavādiṃ niggahetuṃ, ucchedavādī tena niggayhamānopi “ahaṃ tayā satakkhattuṃ niggayhamānopi ucchedavādīyevā”ti vadati. Iminā nayena sassatapuggalasuññatavādādīsupi nayo netabbo. Evaṃ ṭhānāṭhāne saṇṭhāti [M 2.0186] nāma. Parikappe saṇṭhātīti “pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti kaṇṭhaṃ sodhento “tvaṃ imaṃ nāma pucchissasī”ti vutte, “āma, etaṃyeva pucchissāmī”ti vadati. Pañhaṃ kathessāmīti hanuṃ saṃsodhentopi “tvaṃ imaṃ nāma kathessasī”ti vutte, “āma, etaṃyeva kathessāmī”ti vadati. Evaṃ parikappe saṇṭhāti nāma.

'He stands firm in what is appropriate and inappropriate' means: an eternalist is able to refute an annihilationist with proper reasoning. Even when being refuted, the annihilationist says, “Though I am refuted by you a hundred times, I am still an annihilationist.” In this way, the same method should be applied to those who hold views of eternalism, personal identity, emptiness, and so on. Thus, it is said that one 'stands firm in what is appropriate and inappropriate'. 'He stands firm in anticipation' means: when clearing his throat to ask a question, if told, “You will ask such-and-such,” he replies, “Yes, I will ask just that.” Or when adjusting his jaw to answer a question, if told, “You will answer such-and-such,” he replies, “Yes, I will answer just that.” Thus, it is said that one 'stands firm in anticipation.'

Aññātavāde saṇṭhātīti imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchitvā “suṭṭhu te pañho pucchito, pucchantena nāma evaṃ pucchitabba”nti vutte sampaṭicchati, vimatiṃ na uppādeti. Pañhaṃ kathetvāpi “suṭṭhu te pañho kathito, kathentena nāma evaṃ kathetabba”nti vutte sampaṭicchati, vimatiṃ na uppādeti. Paṭipadāya saṇṭhātīti gehe nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakādīni datvā yāva bhattaṃ niṭṭhāti, tasmiṃ antare nisinno pañhaṃ pucchati[P 2.0311]. Sappiādīni bhesajjāni aṭṭhavidhāni pānakāni vatthacchādanamālāgandhādīni vā ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā tāni datvā divāṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā okāsaṃ kāretvā pañhaṃ pucchati. Evañhi vattaṃ ñatvā pucchanto paṭipadāya saṇṭhāti nāma. Tassa pañhaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

He stands firm in the acknowledged statement: having asked this question, if it is said, “Your question is well asked; one who asks should ask thus,” he accepts it and does not give rise to doubt. Having answered a question, if it is said, “Your answer is well given; one who answers should answer thus,” he accepts it and does not give rise to doubt. He stands firm in the proper conduct: having seated someone in a house and given rice gruel, hard food, and so on, he asks the question while seated during the interval until the meal is finished. Or, having taken medicines such as ghee, the eight kinds of drinks, or robes, coverings, garlands, perfumes, and so on, and having gone to the monastery, given them, entered the day-quarters, and requested permission, he asks the question. Indeed, one who asks, knowing the proper conduct thus, is called one who stands firm in the proper conduct. It is fitting to answer his question.

Aññenaññaṃ paṭicaratīti aññena vacanena aññaṃ paṭicchādeti, aññaṃ vā pucchito aññaṃ katheti. Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmetīti āgantukakathaṃ otārento purimakathaṃ bahiddhā apanāmeti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – bhikkhū kira sannipatitvā ekaṃ daharaṃ, “āvuso, tvaṃ imañcimañca āpattiṃ āpanno”ti āhaṃsu. So āha – “bhante, nāgadīpaṃ gatomhī”ti. Āvuso[V 2.0181], na mayaṃ tava nāgadīpagamanena atthikā, āpattiṃ pana āpannoti pucchāmāti. Bhante, nāgadīpaṃ gantvā macche khādinti. Āvuso, tava macchakhādanena kammaṃ natthi, āpattiṃ kirasi āpannoti. So “nātisupakko maccho mayhaṃ aphāsukamakāsi, bhante”ti. Āvuso, tuyhaṃ phāsukena vā aphāsukena vā kammaṃ natthi, āpattiṃ āpannosīti. Bhante, yāva tattha vasiṃ, tāva me aphāsukameva jātanti. Evaṃ āgantukakathāvasena bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmetīti veditabbaṃ.

He conceals one thing with another: with one statement, he conceals another; or, when asked about one thing, he speaks of another. He leads the talk outside: by introducing extraneous talk, he pushes aside the original talk. Herein is the story: It is said that monks, having assembled, said to a certain young monk, “Friend, you have fallen into this and that offense.” He said, “Venerable sirs, I have gone to Nāgadīpa.” They said, “Friend, we have no interest in your going to Nāgadīpa; rather, we ask if you have fallen into an offense.” He said, “Venerable sirs, having gone to Nāgadīpa, I ate fish.” They said, “Friend, there is no issue with your eating fish; have you fallen into an offense?” He said, “Venerable sirs, the fish, not being well-cooked, caused me discomfort.” They said, “Friend, there is no issue with your comfort or discomfort; have you fallen into an offense?” He said, “Venerable sirs, for as long as I lived there, only discomfort arose for me.” Thus it should be understood how, by means of extraneous talk, he leads the talk outside.

Abhiharatīti ito cito ca suttaṃ āharitvā avattharati. Tepiṭakatissatthero viya. Pubbe kira bhikkhū mahācetiyaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā saṅghakiccaṃ katvā bhikkhūnaṃ ovādaṃ datvā aññamaññaṃ pañhasākacchaṃ karonti. Tatthāyaṃ thero tīhi piṭakehi tato tato suttaṃ āharitvā divasabhāge ekampi pañhaṃ niṭṭhāpetuṃ na deti. Abhimaddatīti kāraṇaṃ [M 2.0187] āharitvā maddati. Anupajagghatīti parena pañhe pucchitepi kathitepi pāṇiṃ paharitvā mahāhasitaṃ hasati, yena parassa “apucchitabbaṃ nu kho pucchiṃ, akathetabbaṃ nu kho kathesi”nti vimati uppajjati. Khalitaṃ gaṇhātīti appamattakaṃ mukhadosamattaṃ gaṇhāti[P 2.0312], akkhare vā pade vā byañjane vā durutte “evaṃ nāmetaṃ vattabba”nti ujjhāyamāno vicarati. Saupanisoti saupanissayo sapaccayo.

Overwhelming: bringing in a sutta from here and there and spreading it over. Like the elder Tepiṭaka Tissa: It is said that in the past, monks would gather in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, attend to monastic duties, give advice to the monks, and engage in question-and-answer discussions with each other. There, this elder, drawing a sutta from here and there in the three baskets, would not allow even a single question to be settled during the day. Crushing: bringing up a reason and crushing. Mocking: when a question is asked or answered by another, striking one’s hand and laughing loudly, making the other doubt, “Did I perhaps ask what should not be asked? Did I perhaps say what should not be said?” Seizing upon a slip: taking hold of even a minor verbal fault—merely a fault of the mouth—whether in a syllable, word, or expression that is badly said, and wandering about finding fault, saying, “This should be said in this way.” With a proximate cause: with dependence, with a cause.

Ohitasototi ṭhapitasoto. Abhijānāti ekaṃ dhammanti ekaṃ kusaladhammaṃ abhijānāti ariyamaggaṃ. Parijānāti ekaṃ dhammanti ekaṃ dukkhasaccadhammaṃ tīraṇapariññāya parijānāti. Pajahati ekaṃ dhammanti ekaṃ sabbākusaladhammaṃ pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti. Sacchikaroti ekaṃ dhammanti ekaṃ arahattaphaladhammaṃ nirodhameva vā paccakkhaṃ karoti. Sammāvimuttiṃ phusatīti sammā hetunā nayena kāraṇena arahattaphalavimokkhaṃ ñāṇaphassena phusati.

With attentive ear: with ear set ready. Understands one thing: understands one wholesome quality—the noble path. Understands one thing thoroughly: understands one truth of suffering by way of scrutinizing comprehension. Abandons one thing: abandons, dispels, and eliminates all unwholesome qualities. Realizes one thing: directly experiences the quality of the fruit of arahantship or even cessation itself. Touches right liberation: touches the liberation of the fruit of arahantship with the touch of knowledge, by means of the right reason, method, and cause.

Etadatthā, bhikkhave, kathāti, bhikkhave, yā esā kathāsampayogenāti kathā dassitā, sā etadatthā, ayaṃ tassā kathāya bhūmi patiṭṭhā. Idaṃ vatthu yadidaṃ anupādā cittassa vimokkhoti evaṃ sabbapadesu yojanā veditabbā. Etadatthā mantanāti yā ayaṃ kacchākacchesu puggalesu kacchena saddhiṃ mantanā, sāpi etadatthāyeva. Etadatthā upanisāti ohitasoto saupanisoti evaṃ vuttā upanisāpi etadatthāyeva. Etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānanti tassā upanisāya sotāvadhānaṃ[V 2.0182], tampi etadatthameva. Anupādāti catūhi upādānehi aggahetvā. Cittassa vimokkhoti arahattaphalavimokkho. Arahattaphalatthāya hi sabbametanti suttantaṃ vinivattetvā upari gāthāhi kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto ye viruddhātiādimāha.

Monks, this is the purpose of talk: monks, the talk that has been presented is for this purpose. The liberation of the mind through non-clinging is the ground, the foundation, and the subject matter of that talk. Thus should the application in all passages be understood. This is the purpose of deliberation: that deliberation which is held with a suitable person from among those suitable and unsuitable for it, that too is for this very purpose. This is the purpose of the proximate cause: that proximate cause spoken of thus, 'with attentive ear, with a proximate cause,' is also for this very purpose. This is the purpose of paying attention: the paying attention to that proximate cause is also for this very purpose. Non-clinging: not grasping with the four kinds of clinging. The liberation of the mind: the liberation which is the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, all this was said for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, having concluded the Sutta and bringing it to a climax with the following verses, he said, 'Those who are at variance...' and so on.

Tattha viruddhāti virodhasaṅkhātena kopena viruddhā. Sallapantīti sallāpaṃ karonti. Viniviṭṭhāti abhiniviṭṭhā hutvā. Samussitāti [P 2.0313] mānussayena suṭṭhu ussitā. Anariyaguṇamāsajjāti anariyaguṇakathaṃ guṇamāsajja kathenti. Guṇaṃ ghaṭṭetvā kathā hi anariyakathā nāma, na ariyakathā, taṃ [M 2.0188] kathentīti attho. Aññoññavivaresinoti aññamaññassa chiddaṃ aparādhaṃ gavesamānā. Dubbhāsitanti dukkathitaṃ. Vikkhalitanti appamattakaṃ mukhadosakhalitaṃ. Sampamohaṃ parājayanti aññamaññassa appamattena mukhadosena sampamohañca parājayañca. Abhinandantīti tussanti. Nācareti na carati na katheti. Dhammaṭṭhapaṭisaṃyuttāti yā ca dhamme ṭhitena kathitakathā, sā dhammaṭṭhā ceva hoti tena ca dhammena paṭisaṃyuttāti dhammaṭṭhapaṭisaṃyuttā. Anunnatena manasāti anuddhatena cetasā. Apaḷāsoti yugaggāhapaḷāsavasena apaḷāso hutvā. Asāhasoti rāgadosamohasāhasānaṃ vasena asāhaso hutvā.

Herein, `hostile` means: hostile with anger, which is known as opposition. `They converse` means: they make conversation. `Obstinate` means: being firmly established. `Puffed up` means: well exalted by the influence of conceit. `Engaging in unworthy qualities` means: having resorted to the quality that is the talk characteristic of the ignoble, they speak. Indeed, talk connected with one's own qualities is called unworthy talk, not noble talk; it is this that they speak—this is the meaning. `Seeking each other’s openings` means: seeking each other’s flaws and offenses. `Badly spoken` means: badly spoken. `A slip` means: a slight slip which is an offense of speech. `They delight in confusion and defeat` means: they delight in each other's confusion and defeat due to a slight offense of speech. `They delight` means: they are pleased. `One should not engage in` means: one does not practice, does not speak. `Connected with the Dhamma and grounded` means: whatever talk is spoken by one established in the Dhamma, that is both grounded in the Dhamma and connected with that Dhamma—thus, it is called 'connected with the Dhamma and grounded'. `With a mind not elated` means: with a mind that is not agitated. `Without contentiousness` means: being without contentiousness by way of partisan spite. `Without aggression` means: being without aggression by way of the aggressions of lust, hatred, and delusion.

Anusūyāyamānoti na usūyamāno. Dubbhaṭṭhe nāpasādayeti dukkathitasmiṃ na apasādeyya. Upārambhaṃ na sikkheyyāti kāraṇuttariyalakkhaṇaṃ upārambhaṃ na sikkheyya. Khalitañca na gāhayeti appamattakaṃ mukhakhalitaṃ “ayaṃ te doso”ti na gāhayeyya. Nābhihareti nāvatthareyya. Nābhimaddeti ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ āharitvā na maddeyya. Na [P 2.0314] vācaṃ payutaṃ bhaṇeti saccālikapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vācaṃ na bhaṇeyya. Aññātatthanti jānanatthaṃ. Pasādatthanti pasādajananatthaṃ. Na samusseyya mantayeti na mānussayena samussito bhaveyya. Na hi mānussitā hutvā paṇḍitā kathayanti, mānena pana anussitova hutvā mantaye katheyya bhāseyyāti.

`Not being envious` means: not being envious. `One should not disparage in what is poorly spoken` means: one should not disparage in what is badly spoken. `One should not train in reproach` means: one should not train in reproach, which is characterized by excessive rejoinder. `And one should not have a slip seized upon` means: one should not have a slight slip of the tongue seized upon, saying, 'This is your fault.' `One should not bring against` means: one should not overwhelm. `One should not crush` means: one should not crush by bringing up a single point. `One should not speak contrived words` means: one should not speak words connected with deceitfulness. `For the sake of knowing` means: for the purpose of knowing. `For the sake of confidence` means: for the purpose of generating confidence. `One should not be puffed up while one discusses` means: one should not be puffed up with conceit. Indeed, the wise do not speak being puffed up with conceit; but rather, being not puffed up with conceit, one should discuss, speak, and talk.

8. Aññatitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on Other Sectarians

69. Aṭṭhame bhagavaṃmūlakāti bhagavā mūlaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃmūlakā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime, bhante, amhākaṃ dhammā pubbe kassapasammāsambuddhena uppāditā, tasmiṃ parinibbute ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ime dhamme uppādetuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi, bhagavato [V 2.0183] pana no ime dhammā uppāditā. Bhagavantañhi nissāya mayaṃ ime dhamme ājānāma paṭivijjhāmāti evaṃ bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammāti. Bhagavaṃnettikāti bhagavā dhammānaṃ netā vinetā anunetā yathāsabhāvato pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ gahetvāva dassetāti dhammā bhagavaṃnettikā nāma [M 2.0189] honti. Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇāti catubhūmakadhammā sabbaññutaññāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchamānā bhagavati paṭisaranti nāmāti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Paṭisarantīti osaranti samosaranti. Apica mahābodhimaṇḍe nisinnassa bhagavato paṭivedhavasena phasso āgacchati – “ahaṃ bhagavā kinnāmo”ti. Tvaṃ phusanaṭṭhena phasso nāma. Vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇaṃ āgacchati – “ahaṃ bhagavā kinnāma”nti. Tvaṃ vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇaṃ nāmāti. Evaṃ catubhūmakadhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvato pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇhanto bhagavā dhamme paṭisaratīti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātūti bhagavatova etassa bhāsitassa attho upaṭṭhātu, tumheyeva no kathetvā dethāti attho.

69. In the eighth sutta. 'Rooted in the Blessed One' means the Blessed One is the root of these dhammas; thus, they are rooted in the Blessed One. This is what is said: 'Venerable sir, these dhammas of ours were formerly brought into being by the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa. When he attained final Nibbāna, for a whole Buddha-interval, no other ascetic or brahmin was capable of bringing these dhammas into being. But for us, these dhammas were brought into being by the Blessed One. Indeed, it is by relying on the Blessed One that we know and penetrate these dhammas. Thus, venerable sir, our dhammas are rooted in the Blessed One.' 'Guided by the Blessed One' means the Blessed One is the guide, the special guide, and the one who guides fittingly of the dhammas, showing them by taking each name individually according to its own nature; thus, the dhammas are called 'guided by the Blessed One.' 'Having the Blessed One as their resort' means that the dhammas of the four planes, as they come into the range of the omniscient knowledge, are said to resort to the Blessed One; thus, they have the Blessed One as their resort. 'They resort to' means they come together, they assemble. Furthermore, for the Blessed One seated at the site of great awakening, by way of penetrative understanding, contact comes, asking: 'Blessed One, what is my name?' 'You are named "contact" (phassa) because of the characteristic of touching.' Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness come, asking: 'Blessed One, what is my name?' 'You are named "consciousness" (viññāṇa) because of the characteristic of cognizing.' In this way, the Blessed One, taking the individual name of each of the dhammas of the four planes according to its own nature, penetratively understands the dhammas. Therefore, the Blessed One is the one who penetratively understands them. 'Let it be clear to the Blessed One alone' means: let the meaning of what has been said become clear to the Blessed One alone; you alone should explain it to us. This is the meaning.

Rāgo [P 2.0315] khoti rajjanavasena pavattarāgo. Appasāvajjoti lokavajjavasenapi vipākavajjavasenapīti dvīhipi vajjehi appasāvajjo, appadosoti attho. Kathaṃ? Mātāpitaro hi bhātibhaginiādayo ca puttabhātikānaṃ āvāhavivāhamaṅgalaṃ nāma kārenti. Evaṃ tāveso lokavajjavasena appasāvajjo. Sadārasantosamūlikā pana apāye paṭisandhi nāma na hotīti evaṃ vipākavajjavasena appasāvajjo. Dandhavirāgīti virajjamāno panesa saṇikaṃ virajjati, na sīghaṃ muccati. Telamasirāgo viya ciraṃ anubandhati, dve tīṇi bhavantarāni gantvāpi nāpagacchatīti dandhavirāgī.

Lust, indeed, is the lust that occurs by way of attachment. 'Of little fault' means it is of little fault by way of worldly fault and also by way of resultant fault; thus, by both these faults, it is of little fault. The meaning is 'of little blemish.' How so? For parents, elder brothers, elder sisters, and others arrange the auspicious ceremony of marriage for their sons and younger brothers. Thus, firstly, this lust is of little fault by way of worldly fault. However, lust that is rooted in contentment with one's own wife does not lead to rebirth in the woeful states; thus, it is of little fault by way of resultant fault. 'Slow to fade' means that while this lust is fading, it fades slowly; it is not quickly released. Like a stain of oil and soot, it follows for a long time; even after passing through two or three existences, it does not depart. Therefore, it is called 'slow to fade'.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira puriso bhātu jāyāya micchācāraṃ carati. Tassāpi itthiyā attano sāmikato soyeva piyataro ahosi. Sā tamāha – “imasmiṃ kāraṇe pākaṭe jāte mahatī garahā bhavissati, tava bhātikaṃ ghātehī”ti. So “nassa, vasali, mā evaṃ puna avacā”ti apasādesi. Sā tuṇhī hutvā katipāhaccayena puna kathesi, tassa cittaṃ dvajjhabhāvaṃ agamāsi. Tato tatiyavāraṃ kathito “kinti katvā okāsaṃ labhissāmī”ti āha. Athassa sā upāyaṃ kathentī “tvaṃ mayā vuttameva karohi, asukaṭṭhāne mahākakudhasamīpe titthaṃ atthi, tattha tikhiṇaṃ daṇḍakavāsiṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhāhī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Jeṭṭhabhātāpissa araññe kammaṃ katvā gharaṃ āgato. Sā tasmiṃ muducittā viya hutvā “ehi [M 2.0190] sāmi[V 2.0184], sīse te olikhissāmī”ti olikhantī “upakkiliṭṭhaṃ te sīsa”nti āmalakapiṇḍaṃ datvā “gaccha asukaṭṭhāne sīsaṃ dhovitvā āgacchāhī”ti pesesi. So tāya vuttatitthameva gantvā āmalakakakkena sīsaṃ makkhetvā udakaṃ oruyha onamitvā sīsaṃ [P 2.0316] dhovi. Atha naṃ itaro rukkhantarato nikkhamitvā khandhaṭṭhike paharitvā jīvitā voropetvā gehaṃ agamāsi.

Here is the story: A certain man was committing misconduct with his brother’s wife. That woman also loved him more than her own husband. She said to him, 'If this matter becomes known, there will be great reproach. Kill your brother.' He rebuked her, saying, 'Begone, wretch! Do not speak like that again.' She remained silent, but after a few days she spoke again, and his mind became ambivalent. Then, when she spoke for the third time, he said, 'How can I get an opportunity?' Then she, explaining the plan, said: 'You must do exactly as I say. At such-and-such a place, near a great kakudha tree, there is a bathing-place. Take a sharp adze and wait there.' He did so. His elder brother, having worked in the forest, returned home. The woman, pretending to be affectionate towards him, said, 'Come, my lord, I will comb your head.' While combing, she said, 'Your head is dirty,' gave him a lump of āmalaka, and sent him, saying, 'Go to such-and-such a place, wash your head, and return.' He went to the very bathing-place she had mentioned, smeared his head with the āmalaka paste, went down into the water, bent down, and washed his head. Then the other man emerged from between the trees, struck him on the collarbone, deprived him of life, and went home.

Itaro bhariyāya sinehaṃ pariccajitumasakkonto tasmiṃyeva gehe mahādhammani hutvā nibbatti. So tassā ṭhitāyapi nisinnāyapi gantvā sarīre patati. Atha naṃ sā “soyeva ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti ghātāpesi. So puna tassā sinehena tasmiṃyeva gehe kukkuro hutvā nibbatti. So padasā gamanakālato paṭṭhāya tassā pacchato pacchato carati. Araññaṃ gacchantiyāpi saddhiṃyeva gacchati. Taṃ disvā manussā “nikkhanto sunakhaluddako, kataraṭṭhānaṃ gamissatī”ti uppaṇḍenti. Sā puna taṃ ghātāpesi.

Unable to relinquish his affection for his wife, the other man was reborn as a large house lizard right in that very house. It would go and fall upon her body whether she was standing or sitting. Then, thinking, 'This must be him,' she had it killed. Again, due to his affection for her, he was reborn in that same house as a dog. From the time it could walk, it followed closely behind her. Even when she went to the forest, it went right along with her. Seeing this, people mocked, saying, 'The dog-hunter has set out! To what place will he go?' She then had it killed once more.

Sopi puna tasmiṃyeva gehe vacchako hutvā nibbatti. Tatheva tassā pacchato pacchato carati. Tadāpi naṃ manussā disvā “nikkhanto gopālako, kattha gāviyo carissantī”ti uppaṇḍenti. Sā tasmimpi ṭhāne taṃ ghātāpesi. So tadāpi tassā upari sinehaṃ chindituṃ asakkonto catutthe vāre tassāyeva kucchiyaṃ jātissaro hutvā nibbatti. So paṭipāṭiyā catūsu attabhāvesu tāya ghātitabhāvaṃ disvā “evarūpāya nāma paccatthikāya kucchismiṃ nibbattosmī”ti tato paṭṭhāya tassā hatthena attānaṃ phusituṃ na deti. Sace naṃ sā phusati, kandati rodati. Atha naṃ ayyakova paṭijaggati. Taṃ aparabhāge vuddhippattaṃ ayyako āha – “tāta, kasmā tvaṃ mātu hatthena attānaṃ phusituṃ na desi. Sacepi taṃ phusati, mahāsaddena rodasi kandasī”ti. Ayyakena puṭṭho “na esā mayhaṃ mātā, paccāmittā esā”ti taṃ pavattiṃ sabbaṃ ārocesi. So taṃ āliṅgitvā roditvā “ehi, tāta, kiṃ amhākaṃ [P 2.0317] īdise ṭhāne nivāsakicca”nti taṃ ādāya nikkhamitvā ekaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā pabbajitvā ubhopi tattha vasantā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

He also was again reborn as a calf in that very house. Just as before, it followed closely behind her. Even then, people, seeing him, would mock, saying: “The cowherd has come out! Where will he have the cows graze?” In that place also, she had him killed. Even then, being unable to sever his affection for her, on the fourth occasion, he was reborn in her very womb, having become one who remembers past lives. He, having seen in succession that he had been killed by her in four existences, reflected: “I have been born in the womb of such an enemy!” From then on, he did not allow her to touch him with her hand. If she touched him, he would wail and weep. Then, only the grandfather cared for him. Later, when he had grown up, the grandfather asked: “Dear child, why do you not allow your mother to touch you with her hand? And if she touches you, you weep and wail with a loud voice.” Being asked by the grandfather, he replied, “She is not my mother; she is an enemy,” and recounted the entire story. The grandfather, embracing and weeping over him, said: “Come, dear child, what business is there for us to live in such a place?” Taking him, he departed, went to a monastery, and they both went forth. Dwelling there, they both attained Arahantship.

Mahāsāvajjoti [M 2.0191] lokavajjavasenapi vipākavajjavasenapīti dvīhipi kāraṇehi mahāsāvajjo. Kathaṃ? Dosena hi duṭṭho hutvā mātaripi aparajjhati, pitaripi bhātibhaginiādīsupi [V 2.0185] pabbajitesupi. So gatagataṭṭhānesu “ayaṃ puggalo mātāpitūsupi aparajjhati, bhātibhaginiādīsupi, pabbajitesupī”ti mahatiṃ garahaṃ labhati. Evaṃ tāva lokavajjavasena mahāsāvajjo. Dosavasena pana katena ānantariyakammena kappaṃ niraye paccati. Evaṃ vipākavajjavasena mahāsāvajjo. Khippavirāgīti khippaṃ virajjati. Dosena hi duṭṭho mātāpitūsupi cetiyepi bodhimhipi pabbajitesupi aparajjhitvā “mayhaṃ khamathā”ti. Accayaṃ deseti. Tassa saha khamāpanena taṃ kammaṃ pākatikameva hoti.

'Of great fault' is so called for two reasons: by way of worldly fault and also by way of resultant fault; thus, it is of great fault for both reasons. How so? For, being corrupted by hatred, one offends against one's mother, one's father, one's brothers, sisters, and others, and the ordained. In every place one goes, such a person incurs great blame: 'This person offends against his mother and father, his brothers, sisters, and others, and the ordained.' Thus, firstly, it is of great fault by way of worldly blame. Furthermore, by an action with immediate result done through hatred, one is cooked in hell for an eon. Thus, it is of great fault by way of resultant fault. 'Quickly fading' means it quickly fades. For one corrupted by hatred, having offended against one's mother and father, a cetiya, the Bodhi tree, and the ordained, confesses the transgression, saying, 'Forgive me.' Through their forgiveness, that kamma becomes just as it was before.

Mohopi dvīheva kāraṇehi mahāsāvajjo. Mohena hi mūḷho hutvā mātāpitūsupi cetiyepi bodhimhipi pabbajitesupi aparajjhitvā gatagataṭṭhāne garahaṃ labhati. Evaṃ tāva lokavajjavasena mahāsāvajjo. Mohavasena pana katena ānantariyakammena kappaṃ niraye paccati. Evaṃ vipākavajjavasenapi mahāsāvajjo. Dandhavirāgīti saṇikaṃ virajjati. Mohena mūḷhena hi katakammaṃ saṇikaṃ muccati. Yathā hi acchacammaṃ satakkhattumpi dhoviyamānaṃ na paṇḍaraṃ hoti, evameva mohena mūḷhena katakammaṃ sīghaṃ na muccati, saṇikameva muccatīti. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

Delusion is also of great fault for two reasons. For, being deluded by delusion, one offends against one's mother and father, a cetiya, the Bodhi tree, and the ordained, and incurs blame in every place one goes. Thus, firstly, it is of great fault by way of worldly blame. Furthermore, by an action with immediate result done through delusion, one is cooked in hell for an eon. Thus, it is also of great fault by way of resultant fault. 'Slow to fade' means it fades slowly. For the kamma done by one who is deluded by delusion is slowly released. Just as a bear's hide, even when washed a hundred times, does not become white, in the same way, the kamma done by one who is deluded by delusion is not quickly released; it is released only slowly. The rest here is self-evident.

9. Akusalamūlasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Unwholesome Roots

70. Navame akusalamūlānīti akusalānaṃ mūlāni, akusalāni ca tāni mūlāni cāti vā akusalamūlāni. Yadapi, bhikkhave, lobhoti yopi, bhikkhave, lobho. Tadapi [P 2.0318] akusalamūlanti sopi akusalamūlaṃ. Akusalamūlaṃ vā sandhāya idha tampīti attho vaṭṭatiyeva. Etenupāyena sabbattha nayo netabbo. Abhisaṅkharotīti āyūhati sampiṇḍeti rāsiṃ karoti. Asatā dukkhaṃ uppādayatīti abhūtena avijjamānena yaṃkiñci tassa abhūtaṃ dosaṃ vatvā dukkhaṃ uppādeti. Vadhena vātiādi yenākārena dukkhaṃ uppādeti, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha jāniyāti dhanajāniyā. Pabbājanāyāti gāmato vā raṭṭhato vā pabbājanīyakammena[M 2.0192]. Balavamhīti ahamasmi balavā. Balattho itipīti balena me attho itipi, bale vā ṭhitomhītipi vadati.

70. In the ninth sutta, 'unwholesome roots' means the roots of unwholesome states; or, they are unwholesome and they are roots, thus they are 'unwholesome roots'. 'Whatever, bhikkhus, is greed' means: whatever greed there is, bhikkhus. 'That too is an unwholesome root' means: that greed is also an unwholesome root. Alternatively, referring to 'unwholesome root', the meaning 'that too' is indeed appropriate here. By this method, the principle should be applied everywhere. 'He fabricates' means he strives, collects, and heaps up. 'He produces suffering with the untrue' means that by speaking of some untrue, non-existent fault of another, he produces suffering. The passage beginning 'By killing, or...' is stated to show the manner in which he produces suffering. Therein, 'by loss' means by loss of wealth. 'By banishment' means by an act of banishment from a village or a country. 'I am strong' means 'I am strong'. As for 'for the purpose of strength', he says either 'I have need of strength' or 'I am established in strength'.

Akālavādīti kālasmiṃ na vadati, akālasmiṃ vadati nāma. Abhūtavādīti bhūtaṃ na vadati[V 2.0186], abhūtaṃ vadati nāma. Anatthavādīti atthaṃ na vadati, anatthaṃ vadati nāma. Adhammavādīti dhammaṃ na vadati, adhammaṃ vadati nāma. Avinayavādīti vinayaṃ na vadati, avinayaṃ vadati nāma.

'One who speaks out of season' means one does not speak in season, but speaks out of season. 'One who speaks untruth' means one does not speak truth, but speaks untruth. 'One who speaks unprofitably' means one does not speak profitably, but speaks unprofitably. 'One who speaks against the Dhamma' means one does not speak according to the Dhamma, but speaks against the Dhamma. 'One who speaks against the Vinaya' means one does not speak according to the Vinaya, but speaks against the Vinaya.

Tathā hāyanti tathā hi ayaṃ. Na ātappaṃ karoti tassa nibbeṭhanāyāti tassa abhūtassa nibbeṭhanatthāya vīriyaṃ na karoti. Itipetaṃ atacchanti imināpi kāraṇena etaṃ atacchaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ.

'Thus it declines' is to be divided as 'thus indeed this is'. 'He does not make effort for its removal' means he does not make effort for the removal of that which is untrue. 'Therefore, this is false' means 'for this reason too, this is false.' The other term is just a synonym for that.

Duggati pāṭikaṅkhāti nirayādikā duggati icchitabbā, sā assa avassabhāvinī, tatthānena nibbattitabbanti attho. Uddhastoti upari dhaṃsito. Pariyonaddhoti samantā onaddho. Anayaṃ āpajjatīti avuḍḍhiṃ āpajjati. Byasanaṃ [P 2.0319] āpajjatīti vināsaṃ āpajjati. Gimhakālasmiñhi māluvāsipāṭikāya phalitāya bījāni uppatitvā vaṭarukkhādīnaṃ mūle patanti. Tattha yassa rukkhassa mūle tīsu disāsu tīṇi bījāni patitāni honti, tasmiṃ rukkhe pāvussakena meghena abhivaṭṭhe tīhi bījehi tayo aṅkurā uṭṭhahitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ allīyanti. Tato paṭṭhāya rukkhadevatāyo sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Tepi aṅkurā vaḍḍhamānā latābhāvaṃ āpajjitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā sabbaviṭapasākhāpasākhā saṃsibbitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ upari pariyonandhanti. So māluvālatāhi saṃsibbito ghanehi mahantehi māluvāpattehi sañchanno deve vā vassante vāte vā vāyante tattha tattha palujjitvā khāṇumattameva avasissati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

'A bad destination is to be expected' means: a bad destination, such as hell, is to be expected; for that person, it is an unavoidable destination, and he is to be reborn there. This is the meaning. 'Uddhasto' means 'overthrown from above.' 'Pariyonaddho' means 'completely enveloped.' 'He meets with ruin' means he meets with decline. 'He meets with destruction' means he meets with ruin. Indeed, in the hot season, when the māluvā creeper's seed pods burst, the seeds fly up and fall at the roots of banyan trees and the like. There, if three seeds fall at the roots of a tree in three directions, when a heavy rain from a monsoon cloud pours down, three sprouts arise from those seeds and cling to that tree. From then on, the tree deities are no longer able to maintain their own natural state. Those sprouts, growing larger, become creepers, climb the tree, entwine every branch and sub-branch, and completely envelop the tree from above. Entwined by the māluvā creepers and covered by their dense, large leaves, that tree, whether it rains or the wind blows, breaks apart here and there until only a stump remains. It was in reference to this that it was said.

Evameva khoti ettha pana idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – sālādīsu aññatararukkho viya hi ayaṃ satto daṭṭhabbo, tisso māluvālatā viya tīṇi akusalamūlāni, yāva rukkhasākhā asampattā, tāva tāsaṃ latānaṃ ujukaṃ rukkhārohanaṃ viya lobhādīnaṃ dvāraṃ asampattakālo, sākhānusārena [M 2.0193] gamanakālo viya dvāravasena gamanakālo, pariyonaddhakālo viya lobhādīhi pariyuṭṭhitakālo, khuddakasākhānaṃ palujjanakālo viya dvārappattānaṃ kilesānaṃ vasena khuddānukhuddakā āpattiyo āpannakālo, mahāsākhānaṃ palujjanakālo viya garukāpattiṃ āpannakālo, latānusārena otiṇṇena udakena mūlesu tintesu rukkhassa bhūmiyaṃ patanakālo viya kamena cattāri pārājikāni āpajjitvā catūsu apāyesu nibbattanakālo daṭṭhabbo.

Even so, here, this is the connection of the simile: This being should be seen like a certain tree among sāla trees and so on. The three māluvā creepers are like the three unwholesome roots. As long as the tree branches have not been reached, the creepers' straight ascent of the tree is like the time before the doors of greed, etc., have been reached. The time of proceeding along the branches is like the time of proceeding by way of the doors. The time when the tree is enveloped is like the time when one is assailed by greed, etc. The time when the small branches break is like the time when, through the power of the defilements that have reached the doors, minor and very minor offenses are committed. The time when the main branches break is like the time when a grave offense is committed. The time when the tree, with its roots soaked by the water that has flowed down along the creepers, falls to the ground is like the time when, having sequentially committed the four pārājika offenses, one is reborn in the four states of woe. This should be understood.

Sukkapakkho [V 2.0187] vuttavipallāsena veditabbo. Evameva khoti ettha pana idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – sālādīsu aññatararukkho viya ayaṃ satto daṭṭhabbo, tisso māluvālatā viya tīṇi akusalamūlāni, tāsaṃ appavattiṃ kātuṃ āgatapuriso viya yogāvacaro, kuddālo viya paññā, kuddālapiṭakaṃ viya saddhāpiṭakaṃ, palikhananakhaṇitti viya [P 2.0320] vipassanāpaññā, khaṇittiyā mūlacchedanaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇena avijjāmūlassa chindanakālo, khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chindanakālo viya khandhavasena diṭṭhakālo, phālanakālo viya maggañāṇena kilesānaṃ samugghātitakālo, masikaraṇakālo viya dharamānakapañcakkhandhakālo, mahāvāte opuṇitvā appavattanakālo viya upādinnakakkhandhānaṃ appaṭisandhikanirodhena nirujjhitvā punabbhave paṭisandhiaggahaṇakālo daṭṭhabboti. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

The bright side should be understood by the reversal of what has been said. Even so, here, this is the connection of the simile: this being should be seen like a certain tree among sāla trees and so on; the three māluvā creepers are like the three unwholesome roots; the yogāvacara practitioner is like a person who comes to prevent their growth; wisdom is like a hoe; the basket of faith is like a work basket; insight-wisdom is like a digging tool for digging all around; severing the root with the digging tool is like the time when the root of ignorance is severed by insight-knowledge; the time of cutting into pieces is like the time of seeing in terms of the aggregates; the time of splitting is like the time when defilements are eradicated by path-knowledge; the time of reducing to charcoal is like the time of the presently existing five aggregates; the time of non-occurrence after being scattered by a great wind is like the time when the appropriated aggregates, having ceased through cessation without rebirth-linking, do not take up rebirth-linking again in a future existence. In this sutta, the round of existence and the turning away from the round are explained.

10. Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

71. Dasame tadahuposatheti tasmiṃ ahu uposathe taṃ divasaṃ uposathe, pannarasikauposathadivaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamīti uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya gandhamālādihatthā upasaṅkami. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Divā divassāti divasassa divā nāma majjhanho, imasmiṃ ṭhite majjhanhike kāleti attho. Kuto nu tvaṃ āgacchasīti kiṃ karontī vicarasīti pucchati. Gopālakuposathoti gopālakehi saddhiṃ upavasanauposatho. Nigaṇṭhuposathoti nigaṇṭhānaṃ upavasanauposatho. Ariyuposathoti ariyānaṃ upavasanauposatho. Seyyathāpi visākheti yathā nāma, visākhe. Sāyanhasamaye [M 2.0194] sāmikānaṃ gāvo niyyātetvāti gopālakā hi devasikavetanena vā pañcāhadasāhaaddhamāsamāsachamāsasaṃvaccharaparicchedena vā gāvo gahetvā rakkhanti. Idha pana devasikavetanena rakkhantaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – niyyātetvāti paṭicchāpetvā “etā vo gāvo”ti datvā. Iti [P 2.0321] paṭisañcikkhatīti attano gehaṃ gantvā bhuñjitvā mañce nipanno evaṃ paccavekkhati. Abhijjhāsahagatenāti taṇhāya sampayuttena. Evaṃ kho, visākhe, gopālakuposatho hotīti ariyuposathova ayaṃ, aparisuddhavitakkatāya pana gopālakauposathaṭṭhāne ṭhito. Na mahapphaloti vipākaphalena na mahapphalo. Na mahānisaṃsoti vipākānisaṃsena na mahānisaṃso. Na mahājutikoti vipākobhāsena na mahāobhāso. Na mahāvipphāroti vipākavipphārassa amahantatāya na mahāvipphāro.

71. In the tenth sutta, “on that Uposatha day” means on that day called the Uposatha, on that day which is the Uposatha; it is meant to be the fifteenth-day Uposatha day. “Approached” means: having undertaken the Uposatha factors, she approached with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, in hand. “Handa” is a particle in the sense of relinquishing. “Divā divassa” (during the day) means the ‘day’ of the day, namely midday; the meaning is “at the time of established midday.” “Whence do you come?” he asks, meaning “What were you doing, wandering about?” “The cowherd’s Uposatha” means an Uposatha observed in comparison with cowherds. “The Nigaṇṭha’s Uposatha” means the Uposatha of observance of the Nigaṇṭhas. “The Noble One’s Uposatha” means the Uposatha of observance of the Noble Ones. “Just as, Visākha” means just as, Visākha. Regarding “In the evening, having returned the cattle to their owners”: Cowherds indeed guard cattle, having taken them for daily wages, or for wages fixed for periods of five days, ten days, half a month, a month, six months, or a year. Here, however, this is said with reference to one who guards for daily wages. “Having returned” means having made the owners accept them, saying, “These are your cattle.” “Thus he reflects” means: having gone to his own home, eaten, and lying on a bed, he reflects thus. “Accompanied by covetousness” means associated with craving. Regarding “Thus, Visākha, is the cowherd’s Uposatha”: This is indeed the Noble One’s Uposatha, but due to impure thinking, it stands in the place of the cowherd’s Uposatha. “Not of great fruit” means not of great fruit in terms of resultant fruit. “Not of great benefit” means not of great benefit in terms of resultant benefit. “Not of great radiance” means not of great radiance in terms of resultant splendor. “Not of great pervasiveness” means not of great pervasiveness because of the insignificance of the result’s pervasiveness.

Samaṇajātikāti [V 2.0188] samaṇāyeva. Paraṃ yojanasatanti yojanasataṃ atikkamitvā tato paraṃ. Tesu daṇḍaṃ nikkhipāhīti tesu yojanasatato parabhāgesu ṭhitesu sattesu daṇḍaṃ nikkhipa, nikkhittadaṇḍo hohi. Nāhaṃ kvacani kassaci kiñcanatasminti ahaṃ katthaci kassaci parassa kiñcanatasmiṃ na homi. Kiñcanaṃ vuccati palibodho, palibodho na homīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na ca mama kvacani katthaci kiñcanatatthīti mamāpi kvacani anto vā bahiddhā vā katthaci ekaparikkhārepi kiñcanatā natthi, palibodho natthi, chinnapalibodhohamasmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhogeti mañcapīṭhayāgubhattādayo. Adinnaṃyeva paribhuñjatīti punadivase mañce nipajjantopi pīṭhe nisīdantopi yāguṃ pivantopi bhattaṃ bhuñjantopi te bhoge adinneyeva paribhuñjati. Na mahapphaloti nipphalo. Byañjanameva hi ettha sāvasesaṃ, attho pana niravaseso. Evaṃ upavutthassa hi uposathassa appamattakampi vipākaphalaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā nipphalotveva veditabbo. Sesapadesupi [P 2.0322] eseva nayo.

“Of the ascetic-kind” means ascetics themselves. “Beyond a hundred leagues” means having gone beyond a hundred leagues, and then further. “Lay down the rod among them” means: lay down the rod among those beings dwelling in the regions beyond the hundred leagues; become one who has laid down the rod. “I am not an affliction to anyone anywhere” means: I am not an affliction to any other person anywhere. An affliction (palibodho) is called ‘kiñcana’; it is said, ‘I am not an affliction.’ “And for me there is no anxiety about anything anywhere” means: For me also, there is no anxiety (kiñcanatā) regarding anything, whether internal or external, in any place, not even regarding a single requisite; there is no anxiety (palibodho). It is said, ‘I am one whose anxiety is cut off.’ “Possessions” refers to beds, chairs, gruel, meals, and so on. “He makes use of what is not given” means on the next day, even when lying on a bed, sitting on a chair, drinking gruel, or eating a meal, he makes use of those possessions only as what is not given. “Not of great fruit” means fruitless. For in this case, only the expression has a remainder, but the meaning is without remainder. Indeed, for an Uposatha observed in this way, there is not even a small resultant fruit that is desirable, pleasing, or agreeable. Therefore, it should be known as simply fruitless. This same method applies to the remaining phrases.

Upakkiliṭṭhassa cittassāti idaṃ kasmā āha? Saṃkiliṭṭhena hi cittena upavuttho uposatho na mahapphalo hotīti dassitattā visuddhena cittena upavutthassa mahapphalatā anuññātā hoti. Tasmā yena kammaṭṭhānena cittaṃ visujjhati, taṃ cittavisodhanakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ idamāha[M 2.0195]. Tattha upakkamenāti paccattapurisakārena, upāyena vā. Tathāgataṃ anussaratīti aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi tathāgataguṇe anussarati. Ettha hi itipi so bhagavāti so bhagavā itipi sīlena, itipi samādhināti sabbe lokiyalokuttarā buddhaguṇā saṅgahitā. Arahantiādīhi pāṭiyekkaguṇāva niddiṭṭhā. Tathāgataṃ anussarato cittaṃ pasīdatīti lokiyalokuttare tathāgataguṇe anussarantassa cittuppādo pasanno hoti.

Why did he say this: “of a defiled mind”? Because it has been shown that the Uposatha observed with a defiled mind is not of great fruit, the great fruitfulness of one observed with a purified mind is thus acknowledged. Therefore, to show the meditation subject by which the mind is purified, he said this. Therein, “by striving” means by individual effort, or by a method. “Recollecting the Tathāgata” means one recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata for eight reasons. For herein, by “Thus indeed is the Blessed One,” all the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Buddha, such as “thus by virtue,” “thus by concentration,” are included. By the terms beginning with “Arahaṃ,” only the individual qualities are pointed out. As for “the mind of one recollecting the Tathāgata becomes serene,” it means the mind-moment of one recollecting the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Tathāgata becomes serene.

Cittassa upakkilesāti pañca nīvaraṇā. Kakkanti āmalakakakkaṃ. Tajjaṃ vāyāmanti tajjātikaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ kakkena makkhanaghaṃsanadhovanavāyāmaṃ. Pariyodapanā hotīti suddhabhāvakaraṇaṃ hoti. Kiliṭṭhasmiṃ hi sīse pasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamāno na sobhati, parisuddhe pana tasmiṃ pasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamāno sobhati, evameva kiliṭṭhacittena uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya uposatho upavuttho na mahapphalo hoti, parisuddhena pana cittena uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya upavuttho uposatho mahapphalo hotīti adhippāyena evamāha. Brahmuposathaṃ upavasatīti brahmā vuccati sammāsambuddho, tassa guṇānussaraṇavasena ayaṃ uposatho brahmuposatho [V 2.0189] nāma, taṃ upavasati. Brahmunā saddhiṃ saṃvasatīti sammāsambuddhena saddhiṃ saṃvasati. Brahmañcassa [P 2.0323] ārabbhāti sammāsambuddhaṃ ārabbha.

“The defilements of the mind” are the five hindrances. “Paste” means āmalaka paste. “Appropriate effort” means the effort of anointing, rubbing, and washing with the paste, which is of that kind and suitable for it. “There is purification” means there is the making of a pure state. Indeed, when the head is dirty, one adorning it with an ornament and playing at a festival does not look beautiful; but when that head is pure, one adorning it with an ornament and playing at a festival looks beautiful. In the same way, the Uposatha observed by undertaking the Uposatha factors with a defiled mind is not of great fruit; but the Uposatha observed by undertaking the Uposatha factors with a purified mind is of great fruit. With this intention, he spoke thus. As for “He observes the Brahma Uposatha”: the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is called “Brahmā.” By virtue of recollecting his qualities, this Uposatha is named the Brahma Uposatha; he observes it. “He dwells together with Brahmā” means he dwells together with the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. “And having made Brahmā the object” means having made the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One the object.

Dhammaṃ anussaratīti sahatantikaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ anussarati. Sottinti kuruvindakasottiṃ. Kuruvindakapāsāṇacuṇṇena hi saddhiṃ lākhaṃ yojetvā maṇike katvā vijjhitvā suttena āvuṇitvā taṃ maṇi kalāpapantiṃ ubhato gahetvā piṭṭhiṃ ghaṃsenti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “sottiñca paṭiccā”ti. Cuṇṇanti nhānīyacuṇṇaṃ. Tajjaṃ vāyāmanti ubbaṭṭanaghaṃsanadhovanādikaṃ tadanurūpavāyāmaṃ. Dhammuposathanti sahatantikaṃ navalokuttaradhammaṃ ārabbha upavutthattā ayaṃ uposatho “dhammuposatho”ti vutto. Idhāpi pariyodapanāti pade ṭhatvā purimanayeneva yojanā kātabbā.

‘He recollects the Dhamma’ means he recollects the supramundane Dhamma together with the scripture. ‘The polishing paste’ means the corundum polishing paste. For, having mixed lac with corundum stone powder, made it into beads, pierced them, and strung them with a thread, they take that string of beads at both ends and rub a surface. Referring to this, it is said: ‘and depending on the polishing paste.’ ‘The powder’ means bathing powder. ‘Effort suitable for that’ means effort appropriate to that, such as scrubbing, rubbing, and washing. ‘The Dhamma Uposatha’ is so called because this Uposatha is observed in relation to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with the scripture. Here too, standing on the word ‘purification’, the connection should be made in the same way as before.

Saṅghaṃ anussaratīti aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ guṇe anussarati. Usmañca paṭiccāti dve tayo vāre gāhāpitaṃ usumaṃ paṭicca. Usañcātipi pāṭho, ayamevattho[M 2.0196]. Khāranti chārikaṃ. Gomayanti gomuttaṃ vā ajalaṇḍikā vā. Pariyodapanāti idhāpi purimanayeneva yojanā kātabbā. Saṅghuposathanti aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ guṇe ārabbha upavutthattā ayaṃ uposatho “saṅghuposatho”ti vutto.

‘Recollecting the Sangha’ means recollecting the qualities of the eight noble individuals. ‘And depending on steam’ means depending on steam that has been applied two or three times. There is also the reading ‘usañca’; this is the very same meaning. ‘Alkali’ means ash. ‘Cow-dung’ means cow urine or goat-dung. Here too, standing on the word ‘purification’, the connection should be made in the same way as before. ‘The Sangha Uposatha’ is so called because this Uposatha is observed in relation to the qualities of the eight noble individuals.

Sīlānīti gahaṭṭho gahaṭṭhasīlāni, pabbajito pabbajitasīlāni. Akhaṇḍānītiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.21) vitthāritova. Vālaṇḍupakanti assavālehi vā makacivālādīhi vā kataṃ aṇḍupakaṃ. Tajjaṃ [P 2.0324] vāyāmanti telena temetvā malassa tintabhāvaṃ ñatvā chārikaṃ pakkhipitvā vālaṇḍupakena ghaṃsanavāyāmo. Idha pariyodapanāti pade ṭhatvā evaṃ yojanā kātabbā kiliṭṭhasmiñhi ādāse maṇḍitapasādhitopi attabhāvo olokiyamāno na sobhati, parisuddhe sobhati. Evameva kiliṭṭhena cittena upavuttho uposatho na mahapphalo hoti, parisuddhena pana mahapphalo hotīti. Sīluposathanti attano sīlānussaraṇavasena upavuttho uposatho sīluposatho nāma. Sīlena saddhinti attano pañcasīladasasīlena saddhiṃ. Sīlañcassa ārabbhāti pañcasīlaṃ dasasīlañca ārabbha.

‘Precepts’ means a householder observes the householder’s precepts, a renunciant observes the renunciant’s precepts. The meaning of ‘unbroken’ and so on is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. A ‘horsehair scrubber’ is a scrubber made of horsehair or fibers such as those from makaci grass. ‘The effort suitable for that’ is the effort of scrubbing with a horsehair scrubber after having moistened the object with oil, and, knowing the dirt has become soaked, applying ash. Here, standing on the word ‘purification,’ the connection should be made thus: for when a mirror is dirty, one’s own person, even though adorned and beautified, does not look beautiful when seen in it; when the mirror is clean, it looks beautiful. In the same way, an Uposatha observed with a defiled mind does not bear great fruit, but when observed with a purified mind, it bears great fruit. ‘The Sīla Uposatha’ is the Uposatha observed by way of recollecting one’s own precepts. ‘Together with virtue’ means together with one’s own five or ten precepts. ‘And concerning his virtue’ refers to the five precepts and the ten precepts.

Devatā anussaratīti devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano saddhādiguṇe anussarati. Ukkanti [V 2.0190] uddhanaṃ. Loṇanti loṇamattikā. Gerukanti gerukacuṇṇaṃ. Nāḷikasaṇḍāsanti dhamananāḷikañceva parivattanasaṇḍāsañca. Tajjaṃ vāyāmanti uddhane pakkhipanadhamanaparivattanādikaṃ anurūpaṃ vāyāmaṃ. Idha pariyodapanāti pade ṭhatvā evaṃ yojanā veditabbā – saṃkiliṭṭhasuvaṇṇamayena hi pasādhanabhaṇḍena pasādhitā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamānā na sobhanti, parisuddhasuvaṇṇamayena sobhanti. Evameva saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa uposatho na mahapphalo hoti, parisuddhacittassa mahapphalo. Devatuposathanti devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano guṇe anussarantena upavutthauposatho devatuposatho nāma. Sesaṃ imesu buddhānussatiādīsu kammaṭṭhānesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.123 ādayo) vuttameva.

‘Recollection of deities’ means recollecting one's own qualities such as faith, and so on, after establishing deities in the place of witnesses. ‘Ukkā’ means a furnace. ‘Loṇa’ means salty earth. ‘Geruka’ means red ochre powder. ‘Nāḷikasaṇḍāsa’ means the blowing tube and the turning tongs. ‘Effort suitable for that’ means the appropriate effort for purification, such as putting into the furnace, blowing, and turning. Here, standing on the word ‘purification’, the connection should be understood thus: For, those adorned with ornaments made of impure gold do not shine while playing at festivals, whereas they shine with those made of pure gold. In the same way, the Uposatha is not of great fruit for one with a defiled mind, but is of great fruit for one with a pure mind. ‘The Uposatha of deities’ means the Uposatha observed by one who recollects one's own qualities after establishing deities in the place of witnesses. As for the rest, whatever should be said concerning these meditation subjects such as the recollection of the Buddha and so on, all that has been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Pāṇātipātanti [M 2.0197] pāṇavadhaṃ. Pahāyāti taṃ pāṇātipātacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ pajahitvā. Paṭiviratāti [P 2.0325] pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya tato dussīlyato oratā viratāva. Nihitadaṇḍā nihitasatthāti parūpaghātatthāya daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā ādāya avattanato nikkhittadaṇḍā ceva nikkhittasatthā cāti attho. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā daṇḍaṃ sabbampi avasesaṃ upakaraṇaṃ sattānaṃ vihiṃsanabhāvato satthanti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana bhikkhū kattaradaṇḍaṃ vā dantakaṭṭhavāsiṃ vā pipphalakaṃ vā gahetvā vicaranti, na taṃ parūpaghātatthāya. Tasmā nihitadaṇḍā nihitasatthātveva saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Lajjīti pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya lajjāya samannāgatā. Dayāpannāti dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpannā. Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti sabbe pāṇabhūte hitena anukampakā, tāya eva dayāpannatāya sabbesaṃ pāṇabhūtānaṃ hitacittakāti attho. Ahampajjāti ahampi ajja. Imināpi aṅgenāti imināpi guṇaṅgena. Arahataṃ anukaromīti yathā purato gacchantaṃ pacchato gacchanto anugacchati nāma, evaṃ ahampi arahantehi paṭhamaṃ kataṃ imaṃ guṇaṃ pacchā karonto tesaṃ arahantānaṃ anukaromi. Uposatho ca me upavuttho bhavissatīti evaṃ karontena mayā arahatañca anukataṃ bhavissati, uposatho ca upavuttho bhavissati.

‘Taking life’ means the volition for killing a living being. ‘Having abandoned’ means: having abandoned that immoral conduct designated as the volition for taking life. ‘Abstaining’ means: from the time of its abandonment onwards, they have abstained, they have verily abstained from that immoral conduct. ‘Having laid down the rod, having laid down the weapon’ means: because they do not proceed having taken up a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others, they have laid down the rod and laid down the weapon; this is the meaning. And here, it should be understood that, setting aside the rod, all other remaining implements are called a ‘weapon’ because they are a cause for harming beings. Furthermore, whatever walking stick, tooth-stick adze, or razor that monks take up and wander with, is not for the purpose of harming others. Therefore, they are indeed counted as ‘those who have laid down the rod and laid down the weapon’. ‘Shameful’ means: endowed with shame, which has the characteristic of revulsion towards evil. ‘Compassionate’ means: having attained compassion, the state of a mind of loving-kindness. ‘Sympathetic for the welfare of all living beings’ means: they are compassionate towards all living beings for their welfare; that is, precisely because of that state of being endowed with compassion, they have a mind concerned with the welfare of all living beings; this is the meaning. ‘Ahampajja’ is to be parsed as ‘ahampi ajja’ (I too, today). ‘By this factor as well’ means: by this virtuous quality as well. ‘I emulate the Arahants’ means: just as one going behind is said to follow one going in front, so too do I, by practicing afterwards this virtue first practiced by the Arahants, emulate those Arahants. ‘And the Uposatha will have been observed by me’ means: by me, acting thus, the Arahants will have been emulated, and the Uposatha will have been observed.

Adinnādānanti adinnassa parapariggahitassa ādānaṃ, theyyaṃ corikanti attho. Dinnameva ādiyantīti dinnādāyī. Cittenapi dinnameva paṭikaṅkhantīti dinnapāṭikaṅkhī. Thenetīti theno, na thenena athenena. Athenattāyeva sucibhūtena. Attanāti attabhāvena, athenaṃ [P 2.0326] sucibhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā viharantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Taking what is not given’ means: the taking of what is not given and is possessed by another; that is, theft, the act of a thief; this is the meaning. They take only what is given, hence they are ‘takers of what is given’. Even with the mind, they desire only what is given, hence they are ‘expectant of what is given’. One who steals (theneti) is a thief (theno). Not by a thievish [self], but by a non-thievish one. By a self that has become pure precisely through the state of being a non-thief. ‘By a self’ (attanā) means by one's being (attabhāvena); it is said that they dwell having made their being non-thievish and pure.

Abrahmacariyanti [V 2.0191] aseṭṭhacariyaṃ. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ carantīti brahmacārī. Ārācārīti abrahmacariyato dūrācārī. Methunāti rāgapariyuṭṭhānavasena sadisattā methunakāti laddhavohārehi paṭisevitabbato methunoti saṅkhaṃ gatā asaddhammā. Gāmadhammāti gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammā.

Abrahmacariya means ignoble conduct. They practice noble conduct (brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ), therefore they are called brahmacārī (celibates). Ārācārī means one whose conduct is far from ignoble conduct. Methunā refers to the practices of the ignoble, which have come to be designated as 'methuna' because they are to be engaged in by those who are designated as 'methunakā' (those who couple) due to their similarity by the power of the arising of lust. Gāmadhammā means the practices of village-dwellers.

Musāvādāti alikavacanā tucchavacanā. Saccaṃ vadantīti saccavādī. Saccena saccaṃ saṃdahanti ghaṭṭentīti saccasandhā, na antarantarā musā vadantīti attho[M 2.0198]. Yo hi puriso kadāci musāvādaṃ vadati, kadāci saccaṃ. Tassa musāvādena antaritattā saccaṃ saccena na ghaṭīyati. Tasmā na so saccasandho. Ime pana na tādisā, jīvitahetupi musā avatvā saccena saccaṃ saṃdahantiyevāti saccasandhā. Thetāti thirā, ṭhitakathāti attho. Eko puggalo haliddirāgo viya thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇu viya assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍamiva ca na ṭhitakatho hoti. Eko pāsāṇalekhā viya indakhīlo viya ca ṭhitakatho hoti, asinā sīsaṃ chindantepi dve kathā na katheti. Ayaṃ vuccati theto. Paccayikāti pattiyāyitabbakā, saddhāyikāti attho. Ekacco hi puggalo na paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukena nāmā”ti vutte “mā tassa vacanaṃ saddahathā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Eko paccayiko hoti, “idaṃ kena vuttaṃ, asukenā”ti vutte “yadi tena vuttaṃ, idameva pamāṇaṃ, idāni paṭikkhipitabbaṃ natthi, evamevaṃ ida”nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati paccayiko. Avisaṃvādakā [P 2.0327] lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādentīti attho.

Musāvādā means false speech, empty speech. They speak the truth, therefore they are called truth-speakers. They connect truth with truth, therefore they are called saccasandhā (truth-binders); the meaning is that they do not speak falsehoods in between. For a certain person sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes truth. His truth is not connected with truth because it is interrupted by falsehood. Therefore, he is not a saccasandho. But these noble ones are not like that; not speaking a falsehood even for the sake of their life, they connect truth with truth. Therefore, they are called saccasandhā. Thetā means firm; the meaning is one of established speech. One person is not of established speech, like the stain of turmeric, like a post driven into a heap of chaff, and like a gourd placed on a horse's back. Another is of established speech, like an inscription on stone and like a city gate-post; even if his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not speak two kinds of speech. This one is called theto (steadfast). Paccayikā means trustworthy; the meaning is reliable. For a certain person is not trustworthy. When it is said, “Who said this?” “So-and-so,” he becomes one of whom it is said, “Do not believe his word.” Another is trustworthy. When it is said, “Who said this?” “So-and-so,” he becomes one of whom it is said, “If it was said by him, this itself is the authority. Now there is nothing to be rejected. This is exactly so.” This one is called trustworthy. Avisaṃvādakā lokassa (not deceiving the world) means that because of that truthfulness, they do not deceive the world.

Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānanti surāmerayamajjānaṃ pānacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ pamādakāraṇaṃ. Ekabhattikāti pātarāsabhattaṃ sāyamāsabhattanti dve bhattāni. Tesu pātarāsabhattaṃ antomajjhanhikena paricchinnaṃ, itaraṃ majjhanhikato uddhaṃ antoaruṇena. Tasmā antomajjhanhike dasakkhattuṃ bhuñjamānāpi ekabhattikāva honti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “ekabhattikā”ti. Rattibhojanaṃ ratti, tato uparatāti rattūparatā. Atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāma, tato viratattā viratā vikālabhojanā.

As for `surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāna`, it is the cause of heedlessness, described as the volition to drink distilled liquor, fermented liquor, and intoxicants. As for `ekabhattikā`, there are two meals: the morning meal and the night meal. Among these, the morning meal is defined by the period within midday, and the other is from midday upwards, within dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within midday, they are still considered to be one who eats a single meal. With reference to this, it is said, 'one who eats a single meal'. As for `rattūparatā`: `ratti` refers to eating at night; they are `uparatā` (abstained) from that, hence they are `rattūparatā`. When midday has passed, eating until sunset is called eating at the wrong time (`vikālabhojana`); because of abstaining from that, they are ones who refrain from eating at the wrong time.

Sāsanassa ananulomattā visūkaṃ paṭāṇibhūtaṃ dassananti visūkadassanaṃ, attanā naccananaccāpanādivasena naccañca gītañca vāditañca, antamaso mayūranaccanādivasenāpi pavattānaṃ naccādīnaṃ visūkabhūtaṃ dassanañcāti naccagītavāditavisūkadassanaṃ. Naccādīni hi attanā [V 2.0192] payojetuṃ vā parehi payojāpetuṃ vā payuttāni passituṃ vā neva bhikkhūnaṃ, na bhikkhunīnaṃ vaṭṭanti.

A seeing that is contrary and like a thorn because of its unsuitability for the Dispensation is `visūkadassana`. And the contrary seeing of dancing and so on that occurs by means of dancing and causing to dance, singing and causing to sing, and playing instruments and causing to play instruments oneself—or at the very least, by means of peacock dancing and so on—is `naccagītavāditavisūkadassana`. Indeed, it is not allowable for monks or for nuns to engage in dancing and so on themselves, to cause others to engage in them, or to watch them when engaged in by others.

Mālādīsu [M 2.0199] mālāti yaṃkiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhanti yaṃkiñci gandhajātaṃ. Vilepananti chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Tattha piḷandhanto dhāreti nāma, ūnaṭṭhānaṃ pūrento maṇḍeti nāma, gandhavasena chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanto vibhūseti nāma. Ṭhānaṃ vuccati kāraṇaṃ, tasmā yāya dussīlyacetanāya tāni mālādhāraṇādīni mahājano karoti, tato paṭiviratāti attho. Uccāsayanaṃ vuccati pamāṇātikkantaṃ, mahāsayanaṃ akappiyattharaṇaṃ, tato paṭiviratāti attho.

In `mālā`, etc., `mālā` is any flower. `Gandha` is any kind of perfume. `Vilepana` is that which creates desire for the skin's complexion. Therein, one who adorns with them is called 'one who wears'; one who fills a deficient place is called 'one who decorates'; one who takes pleasure by means of fragrance and desire for the skin's complexion is called 'one who beautifies'. The cause is called `ṭhāna` (basis). Therefore, the meaning is this: one abstains from that unvirtuous volition by which the great populace does those things, such as wearing garlands. `Uccāsayana` (a high bed) is said to be that which exceeds the proper measure; `mahāsayana` (a great bed) is an unsuitable covering. The meaning is that one abstains from these.

Kīvamahapphaloti kittakaṃ mahapphalo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Pahūtarattaratanānanti pahūtena rattasaṅkhātena ratanena samannāgatānaṃ, sakalajambudīpatalaṃ bheritalasadisaṃ [P 2.0328] katvā kaṭippamāṇehi sattahi ratanehi pūritānanti attho. Issariyādhipaccanti issarabhāvena vā issariyameva vā ādhipaccaṃ, na ettha sāhasikakammantipi issariyādhipaccaṃ. Rajjaṃ kāreyyāti evarūpaṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ kāreyya. Aṅgānantiādīni tesaṃ janapadānaṃ nāmāni. Kalaṃ nāgghati soḷasinti ekaṃ ahorattaṃ upavutthauposathe puññaṃ soḷasabhāge katvā tato ekaṃ bhāgañca na agghati. Ekarattuposathassa soḷasiyā kalāya yaṃ vipākaphalaṃ, taṃyeva tato bahutaraṃ hotīti attho. Kapaṇanti parittakaṃ.

“How great is the fruit?” means how great is the fruit. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. “Abounding in much impassioned treasure” means endowed with an abundance of treasure designated as ‘impassioned,’ having made the entire surface of Jambudīpa like the surface of a great drum and filled it with the seven treasures up to the measure of the waist; this is the meaning. “Lordship and sovereignty” means sovereignty by way of being a lord, or sovereignty that is simply lordship itself. Herein, there is no forceful action; for that reason also, it is called lordship and sovereignty. “Would rule a kingdom” means he would rule such a wheel-turning kingdom. “Aṅga” and so on are the names of those districts. “A sixteenth part is not worth” means that all that sovereignty is not worth even one part of the merit of observing the Uposatha for a single day and night, after that merit has been divided into sixteen parts. Whatever resultant fruit there is from a sixteenth part of the Uposatha observed for one night, that very fruit is much greater than that sovereignty; this is the meaning. “Kapaṇa” means trifling.

Abrahmacariyāti aseṭṭhacariyato. Rattiṃ na bhuñjeyya vikālabhojananti uposathaṃ upavasanto rattibhojanañca divāvikālabhojanañca na bhuñjeyya. Mañce chamāyaṃva sayetha santhateti muṭṭhihatthapādake kappiyamañce vā sudhādiparikammakatāya bhūmiyaṃ vā tiṇapaṇṇapalālādīni santharitvā kate santhate vā sayethāti attho. Etaṃ hi aṭṭhaṅgikamāhuposathanti evaṃ pāṇātipātādīni asamācarantena upavutthaṃ uposathaṃ aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgatattā aṭṭhaṅgikanti vadanti. Taṃ pana upavasantena “sve uposathiko bhavissāmī”ti ajjeva “idañca idañca kareyyāthā”ti āhārādividhānaṃ vicāretabbaṃ. Uposathadivase pātova bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā dasasīlalakkhaṇaññuno upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā santike vācaṃ bhinditvā [M 2.0200] uposathaṅgāni samādātabbāni. Pāḷiṃ ajānantena pana “buddhapaññattaṃ uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Aññaṃ alabhantena attanāpi adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, vacībhedo pana kātabboyeva[V 2.0193]. Uposathaṃ upavasantena parūparodhapaṭisaṃyuttā kammantā na vicāretabbā, āyavayagaṇanaṃ [P 2.0329] karontena na vītināmetabbaṃ, gehe pana āhāraṃ labhitvā niccabhattikabhikkhunā viya paribhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā dhammo vā sotabbo, aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu aññataraṃ vā manasikātabbaṃ.

“Abrahmacariya” (unchastity) means ignoble conduct. “One should not eat at night or at the wrong time” means one observing the Uposatha should not eat night-time meals or daytime meals at improper hours. “One should lie down on a bed or on the ground on a spread” means one should lie down either on a permissible bed with legs of a cubit and a fist in height, or on ground prepared with plaster and so on, or on a spread made with grass, leaves, straw, and so on; this is the meaning. “This is called the eight-factored Uposatha.” Thus, the Uposatha, observed by one not engaging in killing living beings and so on, is called eight-factored because it is endowed with eight factors. One who intends to observe it should, on the day before, determine, “Tomorrow I will observe the Uposatha,” and arrange for food and other things, thinking, “This and that should be done.” On the Uposatha day, early in the morning, one should undertake the Uposatha factors by uttering the words in the presence of a monk, a nun, or a male or female lay follower who knows the characteristics of the ten precepts. If one does not know the Pāli formula, one should resolve by saying, “I undertake the Uposatha prescribed by the Buddha.” If no one else is available, one may undertake it by oneself, but a verbal declaration must certainly be made. While observing the Uposatha, one should not manage work connected with oppressing others, nor should one pass the time counting income and expenditure. Rather, having received and eaten food at home, one should then go to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma, just as a monk with a regular meal would do; or one should pay attention to one of the thirty-eight meditation objects.

Sudassanāti sundaradassanā. Obhāsayanti obhāsayamānā. Anupariyantīti vicaranti. Yāvatāti yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Antalikkhagāti ākāsaṅgamā. Pabhāsantīti jotanti pabhā muñcanti. Disāvirocanāti sabbadisāsu virocamānā. Atha vā pabhāsantīti disāhi disā obhāsanti. Virocanāti virocamānā. Veḷuriyanti maṇīti vatvāpi iminā jātimaṇibhāvaṃ dasseti. Ekavassikaveḷuvaṇṇañhi veḷuriyaṃ jātimaṇi nāma. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Bhaddakanti laddhakaṃ. Siṅgīsuvaṇṇanti gosiṅgasadisaṃ hutvā uppannattā evaṃ nāmakaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ. Kañcananti pabbateyyaṃ pabbate jātasuvaṇṇaṃ. Jātarūpanti satthuvaṇṇasuvaṇṇaṃ. Haṭakanti kipillikāhi nīhaṭasuvaṇṇaṃ. Nānubhavantīti na pāpuṇanti. Candappabhāti sāmiatthe paccattaṃ, candappabhāyāti attho. Upavassuposathanti upavasitvā uposathaṃ. Sukhudrayānīti sukhaphalāni sukhavedanīyāni. Saggamupenti ṭhānanti saggasaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ upagacchanti, kenaci aninditā hutvā devaloke uppajjantīti attho. Sesamettha yaṃ antarantarā na vuttaṃ, taṃ vuttānusāreneva veditabbanti.

“Sudassanā” means having a beautiful appearance. “Obhāsayanti” means illuminating. “Anupariyanti” means they wander about. “Yāvatā” means as far as a place. “Antalikkhagā” means traveling in the sky. “Pabhāsanti” means they shine, they emit radiance. “Disāvirocanā” means shining in all directions. Alternatively, “pabhāsanti” means they illuminate from direction to direction. “Virocanā” means shining. By this word “veḷuriya,” even after saying “maṇi” (gem), it shows the state of being a natural gem. Indeed, a veḷuriya having the color of a one-year-old bamboo is called a natural gem. With reference to that, he spoke thus. “Bhaddakaṃ” means excellent. “Siṅgīsuvaṇṇaṃ” is gold so-named because it arises resembling a cow's horn. “Kañcanaṃ” is mountain-gold, gold born on a mountain. “Jātarūpaṃ” is gold the color of the Teacher. “Haṭakaṃ” is gold extracted by ants and other such creatures. “Nānubhavanti” means they do not reach. “Candappabhā” is a nominative in the sense of the possessive; the meaning is 'of the moon's radiance.' “Upavassuposathaṃ” means having observed the Uposatha. “Sukhudrayāni” means having pleasant results, having pleasant feeling as a result. “Saggamupenti ṭhānaṃ” means they approach the place called heaven; the meaning is: being uncensured by anyone, they are born in the world of devas. Herein, whatever remaining word has not been stated in between, that should be understood only in accordance with the method already stated.

Mahāvaggo dutiyo.

The Great Chapter, the Second.

(8) 3. Ānandavaggo

3. The Ānanda Chapter

1. Channasuttavaṇṇanā

1. 1. Commentary on the Channa Sutta

72. Tatiyassa [V 2.0194][P 2.0330] paṭhame channoti evaṃnāmako channaparibbājako. Tumhepi, āvusoti, āvuso, yathā mayaṃ rāgādīnaṃ pahānaṃ paññāpema, kiṃ evaṃ tumhepi paññāpethāti pucchati. Tato thero “ayaṃ paribbājako amhe rāgādīnaṃ pahānaṃ paññāpemāti vadati, natthi panetaṃ [M 2.0201] bāhirasamaye”ti taṃ paṭikkhipanto mayaṃ kho, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha khoti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto, mayameva paññāpemāti attho. Tato paribbājako cintesi “ayaṃ thero bāhirasamayaṃ luñcitvā haranto ‘mayamevā’ti āha. Kiṃ nu kho ādīnavaṃ disvā ete etesaṃ pahānaṃ paññāpentī”ti. Atha theraṃ pucchanto kiṃ pana tumhetiādimāha. Thero tassa byākaronto ratto khotiādimāha. Tattha attatthanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ lokiyalokuttaraṃ attano atthaṃ. Paratthaubhayatthesupi eseva nayo.

72. In the first sutta of the third vagga, 'Channo' refers to the wanderer so-named Channa. 'Tumhepi, āvuso' means: he asks, 'Friend, just as we declare the abandoning of lust and so forth, what do you also declare?' Then the Elder, rejecting this with the thought, 'This wanderer says that we declare the abandoning of lust and so forth, but this does not exist in the external doctrine,' said, 'We, friend,' and so on. Therein, 'kho' is a particle in the sense of emphasis; the meaning is, 'we alone declare.' Then the wanderer thought, 'This Elder, having rejected and dismissed the external doctrine, said, “we alone.” Seeing what danger, I wonder, do they declare the abandoning of these things?' Then, questioning the Elder, he said, 'But what about you?' and so on. The Elder, explaining to him, said, 'One who is impassioned, indeed...' and so on. Therein, 'attatthaṃ' means one's own welfare—of the present life and the life to come, worldly and supramundane. This same method applies also to the welfare of others and the welfare of both.

Andhakaraṇotiādīsu yassa rāgo uppajjati, taṃ yathābhūtadassananivāraṇena andhaṃ karotīti andhakaraṇo. Paññācakkhuṃ na karotīti acakkhukaraṇo. Ñāṇaṃ na karotīti aññāṇakaraṇo. Kammassakatapaññā jhānapaññā vipassanāpaññāti imā tisso paññā appavattikaraṇena nirodhetīti paññānirodhiko. Aniṭṭhaphaladāyakattā dukkhasaṅkhātassa vighātasseva pakkhe vattatīti vighātapakkhiko. Kilesanibbānaṃ na saṃvattetīti anibbānasaṃvattaniko. Alañca panāvuso ānanda, appamādāyāti, āvuso ānanda, sace evarūpā paṭipadā atthi, alaṃ tumhākaṃ appamādāya yuttaṃ anucchavikaṃ, appamādaṃ karotha, āvusoti therassa vacanaṃ anumoditvā pakkāmi. Imasmiṃ sutte ariyamaggo lokuttaramissako kathito. Sesamettha [P 2.0331] uttānatthamevāti.

In the passage beginning 'Andhakaraṇo' and so on: for whomever lust arises, by preventing the vision of things as they truly are, it makes one blind; therefore, it is 'a maker of blindness' (andhakaraṇo). It does not produce the eye of wisdom; therefore, it is 'a maker of no-eye' (acakkhukaraṇo). It does not produce knowledge; therefore, it is 'a maker of ignorance' (aññāṇakaraṇo).
