The wisdom of kamma as one's own property, jhāna-wisdom, and insight-wisdom—by causing the non-occurrence of these three kinds of wisdom, it obstructs them; therefore, it is 'an obstructor of wisdom' (paññānirodhiko). Because it gives an undesirable result, it exists on the side of destruction, which is designated as suffering; therefore, it is 'on the side of destruction' (vighātapakkhiko). It does not conduce to the stilling of defilements; therefore, it is 'not conducive to Nibbāna' (anibbānasaṃvattaniko). 'And it is enough, friend Ānanda, for diligence...' means: having rejoiced in the Elder's words, 'Friend Ānanda, if such a practice exists, it is enough for your diligence, it is proper, it is suitable; practice diligence, friend,' he departed. In this sutta, the noble path mixed with the supramundane is taught. The rest here has a plain meaning.

2. Ājīvakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. 2. Commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta

73. Dutiye [V 2.0195] tena hi gahapatīti thero kira cintesi – “ayaṃ idha āgacchanto na aññātukāmo hutvā āgami, pariggaṇhanatthaṃ pana āgato. Iminā pucchitapañhaṃ imināva kathāpessāmī”ti. Iti taṃyeva kathaṃ kathāpetukāmo tena hītiādimāha. Tattha tena hīti kāraṇāpadeso. Yasmā tvaṃ evaṃ pucchasi, tasmā taññevettha paṭipucchāmīti. Kesaṃ noti katamesaṃ nu. Sadhammukkaṃsanāti attano laddhiyā ukkhipitvā ṭhapanā. Paradhammāpasādanāti paresaṃ laddhiyā ghaṭṭanā vambhanā avakkhipanā. Āyataneva dhammadesanāti kāraṇasmiṃyeva dhammadesanā. Attho ca vuttoti mayā pucchitapañhāya attho ca pakāsito[M 2.0202]. Attā ca anupanītoti amhe evarūpāti evaṃ attā ca na upanīto. Nupanītotipi pāṭho.

73. In the second sutta, it is said the Elder thought: 'This householder, in coming here, did not come wishing to know, but rather came for the purpose of testing wisdom. I will make this very person answer the question he has asked.' Thus, wishing to make him speak on that very matter, he spoke the words beginning with 'Tena hi'. Therein, 'tena hi' is a word indicating a reason. It means: 'Because you ask thus, therefore I will in turn question you yourself in this matter.' 'Kesaṃ no' means 'of which persons?' 'Exaltation of the good Dhamma' is the exalting and establishing of one's own view. 'Disparagement of another's Dhamma' is the attacking, reviling, and belittling of the views of others. 'Teaching the Dhamma only on the basis of a reason' is teaching the Dhamma only when there is a suitable reason. 'And the meaning was stated' means the meaning of the question I asked was also made clear. 'And the self was not brought forward' means the self was not brought forward thus: 'We are of such a nature.' The reading is also 'nupanīto'.

3. Mahānāmasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahānāmasakka Sutta

74. Tatiye gilānā vuṭṭhitoti gilāno hutvā vuṭṭhito. Gelaññāti gilānabhāvato. Upasaṅkamīti bhuttapātarāso mālāgandhādīni ādāya mahāparivāraparivuto upasaṅkami. Bāhāyaṃ gahetvāti na bāhāyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhi, nisinnāsanato vuṭṭhāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā dakkhiṇabāhāyaṃ aṅguṭṭhakena saññaṃ datvā ekamantaṃ apanesīti veditabbo. Athassa “sekhampi kho, mahānāma, sīla”ntiādinā nayena sattannaṃ sekhānaṃ sīlañca samādhiñca paññañca kathetvā upari arahattaphalavasena asekhā sīlasamādhipaññāyo kathento – “sekhasamādhito sekhaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ asekhañca phalañāṇaṃ pacchā, sekhavipassanāñāṇato ca asekhaphalasamādhi pacchā uppajjatī”ti dīpesi. Yāni pana sampayuttāni samādhiñāṇāni, tesaṃ apacchā apure uppatti veditabbāti.

74. In the third sutta, 'recovered from illness' means having been ill, he had recovered. 'From the illness' means from the state of being ill. 'He approached' means: having eaten his morning meal, taking flowers, perfumes, and so on, surrounded by a large retinue, he approached. 'Taking by the arm' should be understood as follows: he did not take him by the arm and drag him, but rather, rising from his seat, going to his presence, and giving a sign on his right arm with his thumb, he led him aside. Then, having explained the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the seven trainees by the method beginning with 'Mahānāma, there is the trainee's virtue...', and above that, explaining the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the non-trainees by way of the fruit of Arahantship, he showed that: 'After the trainee's concentration, the trainee's insight-knowledge and the non-trainee's fruition-knowledge arise; and after the trainee's insight-knowledge, the non-trainee's fruition-concentration arises.' Furthermore, as for those concentration-knowledges that are associated, their arising should be known as neither before nor after.

4. Nigaṇṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nigaṇṭha Sutta

75. Catutthe [P 2.0332] kūṭāgārasālāyanti dve kaṇṇikā gahetvā haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena katāya gandhakuṭiyā. Aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātīti appamattakampi asesetvā sabbaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti. Satataṃ samitanti sabbakālaṃ nirantaraṃ. Ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitanti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [V 2.0196] mayhaṃ upaṭṭhitamevāti dasseti. Purāṇānaṃ kammānanti āyūhitakammānaṃ. Tapasā byantībhāvanti dukkaratapena vigatantakaraṇaṃ. Navānaṃ kammānanti idāni āyūhitabbakammānaṃ. Akaraṇāti anāyūhanena. Setughātanti padaghātaṃ paccayaghātaṃ katheti. Kammakkhayā dukkhakkhayoti kammavaṭṭakkhayena dukkhakkhayo. Dukkhakkhayā vedanākkhayoti dukkhavaṭṭakkhayena vedanākkhayo. Dukkhavaṭṭasmiñhi khīṇe vedanāvaṭṭampi khīṇameva hoti. Vedanākkhayā sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatīti vedanākkhayena pana sakalavaṭṭadukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇameva bhavissati. Sandiṭṭhikāyāti sāmaṃ passitabbāya paccakkhāya. Nijjarāya visuddhiyāti [M 2.0203] kilesajīraṇakapaṭipadāya kilese vā nijjīraṇato nijjarāya sattānaṃ visuddhiyā. Samatikkamo hotīti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa atikkamo hoti. Idha, bhante, bhagavā kimāhāti, bhante, bhagavā imāya paṭipattiyā kimāha, kiṃ etaṃyeva kilesanijjīraṇakapaṭipadaṃ paññapeti, udāhu aññanti pucchati.

75. In the fourth sutta, 'in the hall with a peaked roof' means in the fragrant hut made by taking two pinnacles and covered with a roof thatched in the pattern of a circling swan's wing. 'He declares complete knowledge and vision' means he declares all knowledge and vision without leaving out even a trifle. 'Constantly, continuously' means at all times, without interruption. 'Knowledge and vision are present' means he shows that omniscient knowledge is indeed present in him. 'Of past deeds' means of accumulated actions. 'Through austerity, their cessation' means making an end through difficult ascetic practices. 'Of new deeds' means of actions to be accumulated now. 'By not doing' means by not accumulating. 'Breaking the bridge' means he speaks of destroying the cause. 'Through the destruction of actions, the destruction of suffering' means the destruction of suffering through the destruction of the cycle of actions. 'Through the destruction of suffering, the destruction of feelings' means the destruction of feelings through the destruction of the cycle of suffering. For when the cycle of suffering is exhausted, the cycle of feelings is also exhausted. 'Through the destruction of feelings, all suffering will be worn away' means through the destruction of feelings, all suffering in the entire cycle will indeed be worn away. 'Visible here and now' means to be seen for oneself, directly. 'For purification through wearing away' means by the practice of wearing away defilements, or by the purification of beings through the wearing away of defilements. 'There is transcendence' means there is the transcendence of all suffering in the cycle. 'Here, venerable sir, what does the Blessed One say?' means, 'Venerable sir, what does the Blessed One say about this practice? Does he prescribe this very path of wearing away defilements, or something else?'—he asks.

Jānatāti anāvaraṇañāṇena jānantena. Passatāti [P 2.0333] samantacakkhunā passantena. Visuddhiyāti visuddhisampāpanatthāya. Samatikkamāyāti samatikkamanatthāya. Atthaṅgamāyāti atthaṃ gamanatthāya. Ñāyassa adhigamāyāti saha vipassanāya maggassa adhigamanatthāya. Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyāti apaccayanibbānassa sacchikaraṇatthāya. Navañca kammaṃ na karotīti navaṃ kammaṃ nāyūhati. Purāṇañca kammanti pubbe āyūhitakammaṃ. Phussa phussa byantī karotīti phusitvā phusitvā vigatantaṃ karoti, vipākaphassaṃ phusitvā phusitvā taṃ kammaṃ khepetīti attho. Sandiṭṭhikāti sāmaṃ passitabbā. Akālikāti na kālantare kiccakārikā. Ehipassikāti “ehi passā”ti evaṃ dassetuṃ yuttā. Opaneyyikāti upanaye yuttā allīyitabbayuttā. Paccattaṃ veditabbā viññūhīti paṇḍitehi attano attano santāneyeva jānitabbā, bālehi pana dujjānā. Iti sīlavasena dve maggā, dve ca phalāni kathitāni. Sotāpannasakadāgāmino hi sīlesu paripūrakārinoti. Vivicceva kāmehītiādikāya pana samādhisampadāya tayo maggā, tīṇi ca phalāni kathitāni. Anāgāmī ariyasāvako hi samādhimhi paripūrakārīti vutto. Āsavānaṃ khayātiādīhi arahattaphalaṃ kathitaṃ. Keci pana sīlasamādhayopi arahattaphalasampayuttāva idha adhippetā. Ekekassa pana vasena paṭipattidassanatthaṃ visuṃ visuṃ tanti āropitāti.

'Knowing' means knowing with unobstructed knowledge. 'Seeing' means seeing with the all-seeing eye. 'For purification' means for the purpose of attaining purification. 'For transcendence' means for the purpose of transcending. 'For passing away' means for the purpose of going to an end. 'For the attainment of the method' means for the attainment of the path together with insight. 'For the realization of Nibbāna' means for the realization of unconditioned Nibbāna. 'And does not do new deeds' means he does not accumulate new kamma. 'And old deeds' means previously accumulated kamma. 'Contacting again and again, he makes an end' means contacting again and again, he brings them to an end; having contacted the resultant contact again and again, he exhausts that kamma—this is the meaning. 'Visible here and now' means to be seen for oneself. 'Timeless' means not yielding their results at a later time. 'Inviting inspection' means fit to be shown with the words, "Come and see." 'Leading onward' means fit to be approached, fit to be adhered to. 'To be experienced individually by the wise' means to be known by the wise each in their own mind-stream, but difficult for fools to know. Thus, by way of virtue, two paths and two fruits are spoken of. For stream-enterers and once-returners are indeed fulfillers in virtues. But by the accomplishment of concentration beginning with the passage, 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures,' three paths and three fruits are spoken of. For the non-returning noble disciple is said to be a fulfiller in concentration. By the passages beginning with, 'With the destruction of the taints,' the fruit of arahantship is spoken of. Some, however, hold that even virtue and concentration associated with the fruit of arahantship are intended here. But for the purpose of showing the practice in each case, the text is set down separately.

5. Nivesakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Nivesaka Sutta

76. Pañcame [V 2.0197] amaccāti suhajjā. Ñātīti sassusasurapakkhikā. Sālohitāti samānalohitā bhātibhaginiādayo. Aveccappasādeti guṇe avecca jānitvā uppanne acalappasāde. Aññathattanti bhāvaññathattaṃ[M 2.0204]. Pathavīdhātuyātiādīsu vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu thaddhākārabhūtāya [P 2.0334] pathavīdhātuyā, dvādasasu koṭṭhāsesu yūsagatāya ābandhanabhūtāya āpodhātuyā, catūsu koṭṭhāsesu paripācanabhūtāya tejodhātuyā, chasu koṭṭhāsesu vitthambhanabhūtāya vāyodhātuyā siyā aññathattaṃ. Na tvevāti imesaṃ hi catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ aññamaññabhāvūpagamanena siyā aññathattaṃ, ariyasāvakassa pana na tveva siyāti dasseti. Ettha ca aññathattanti pasādaññathattañca gatiaññathattañca. Tañhi tassa na hoti, bhāvaññathattaṃ pana hoti. Ariyasāvako hi manusso hutvā devopi hoti brahmāpi. Pasādo panassa bhavantarepi na vigacchati, na ca apāyagatisaṅkhātaṃ gatiaññathattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Satthāpi tadeva dassento tatridaṃ aññathattantiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

76. In the fifth sutta, 'amaccā' means those with a good heart. 'Ñātī' means those on the side of one's mother-in-law and father-in-law. 'Sālohitā' means those of the same blood, such as brothers, sisters, and so on. 'Aveccappasāde' means in the unwavering confidence that has arisen from having thoroughly known the virtues. 'Aññathattaṃ' means alteration of state. Regarding the text beginning 'of the earth element,' there might be an alteration of the earth element, which has become rigid in form in twenty parts; of the water element, which has become fluid and cohesive in twelve parts; of the fire element, which has become digestive in four parts; and of the wind element, which has become supportive in six parts. As for 'na tveva' (not so), this shows that while there might be an alteration of these four great elements through their mutual transformation, for a noble disciple, there is certainly no such alteration. And here, 'aññathattaṃ' means alteration of confidence and alteration of destiny. For that does not happen to him, but alteration of state does happen. For a noble disciple, having been a human, also becomes a deva or a Brahmā. But his confidence does not vanish even in another existence, and he does not reach an alteration of destiny known as going to the woeful states. The Teacher, showing that very thing, said the passage beginning, 'Here, this alteration...'. The rest here is clear in meaning.

6. Paṭhamabhavasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Discourse on Existence

77. Chaṭṭhe kāmadhātuvepakkanti kāmadhātuyā vipaccanakaṃ. Kāmabhavoti kāmadhātuyaṃ upapattibhavo. Kammaṃ khettanti kusalākusalakammaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena khettaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ bījanti sahajātaṃ abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ viruhanaṭṭhena bījaṃ. Taṇhā snehoti paggaṇhanānubrūhanavasena taṇhā udakaṃ nāma. Avijjānīvaraṇānanti avijjāya āvaritānaṃ. Taṇhāsaṃyojanānanti taṇhābandhanena baddhānaṃ. Hīnāya dhātuyāti kāmadhātuyā. Viññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhitanti abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ. Majjhimāya dhātuyāti rūpadhātuyā. Paṇītāya dhātuyāti arūpadhātuyā. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

77. In the sixth sutta, 'kāmadhātuvepakkaṃ' means that which ripens in the desire realm. 'Kāmabhavo' means rebirth-existence in the desire realm. 'Kamma is the field' means wholesome and unwholesome kamma is the field in the sense of being a place of growth. 'Consciousness is the seed' means the conascent conditioning consciousness is the seed in the sense of sprouting. 'Craving is moisture' means craving is called water, by way of moistening and promoting growth. 'Of those with the hindrance of ignorance' means of those obstructed by ignorance. 'Of those with the fetter of craving' means of those bound by the bond of craving. 'In the inferior element' means in the desire element. 'Consciousness is established' means the conditioning consciousness is established. 'In the intermediate element' means in the form element. 'In the superior element' means in the formless element. The rest here is clear in meaning.

7. Dutiyabhavasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Existence

78. Sattame cetanāti kammacetanā. Patthanāpi kammapatthanāva. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

78. In the seventh sutta, 'cetanā' is kamma-volition. 'Patthanā' is also kamma-aspiration. The remainder is just like the previous explanation.

8. Sīlabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue and Observance

79. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0198][P 2.0335] sīlabbatanti sīlañceva vatañca. Jīvitanti dukkarakārikānuyogo. Brahmacariyanti brahmacariyavāso. Upaṭṭhānasāranti upaṭṭhānena sāraṃ[M 2.0205], “idaṃ varaṃ idaṃ niṭṭhā”ti evaṃ upaṭṭhitanti attho. Saphalanti saudrayaṃ savaḍḍhikaṃ hotīti pucchati. Na khvettha, bhante, ekaṃsenāti, bhante, na kho ettha ekaṃsena byākātabbanti attho. Upaṭṭhānasāraṃ sevatoti idaṃ sāraṃ varaṃ niṭṭhāti evaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ sevamānassa. Aphalanti iṭṭhaphalena aphalaṃ. Ettāvatā kammavādikiriyavādīnaṃ pabbajjaṃ ṭhapetvā seso sabbopi bāhirakasamayo gahito hoti. Saphalanti iṭṭhaphalena saphalaṃ saudrayaṃ. Ettāvatā imaṃ sāsanaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbāpi kammavādikiriyavādīnaṃ pabbajjā gahitā. Na ca panassa sulabharūpo samasamo paññāyāti evaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā pañhaṃ kathento assa ānandassa paññāya samasamo na sulabhoti dasseti. Imasmiṃ sutte sekkhabhūmi nāma kathitāti.

79. In the eighth sutta, 'sīlabbata' means both virtue and observance. 'Jīvita' means the pursuit of difficult practices. 'Brahmacariya' means living the holy life. 'Upaṭṭhānasāra' means essential through dedication; the meaning is that which is established thus: 'This is excellent, this is the culmination.' 'Saphalaṃ' asks: 'Is it fruitful, with increase, with growth?' 'Na kho ettha, bhante, ekaṃsena' means: 'Venerable sir, in this matter it should not be answered categorically.' 'Upaṭṭhānasāraṃ sevato' means for one who cultivates that which is established thus: 'This is the essence, this is excellent, this is the culmination.' 'Aphalaṃ' means fruitless of the desired fruit. By this much, having set aside the going forth of the proponents of kamma and action, all the remaining external doctrines are included. 'Saphalaṃ' means fruitful with the desired fruit, with increase. By this much, beginning with this Dispensation, all the goings forth of the proponents of kamma and action are included. 'Na ca panassa sulabharūpo samasamo paññāyāti' shows that while explaining the question standing in the trainee's stage, a person exactly equal in wisdom to that Ānanda is not easy to find. In this discourse, what is called the stage of the trainee is explained.

9. Gandhajātasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Kinds of Fragrance

80. Navame etadavocāti pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto dasabalassa vattaṃ dassetvā attano divāvihāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “imasmiṃ loke mūlagandho nāma atthi, sāragandho nāma atthi, pupphagandho nāma atthi. Ime pana tayopi gandhā anuvātaṃyeva gacchanti, na paṭivātaṃ. Atthi nu kho kiñci, yassa paṭivātampi gandho gacchatī”ti cintetvā aṭṭhannaṃ varānaṃ gahaṇakāleyeva kaṅkhuppattisamaye upasaṅkamanavarassa gahitattā takkhaṇaṃyeva divāṭṭhānato vuṭṭhāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno uppannāya kaṅkhāya vinodanatthaṃ etaṃ “tīṇimāni, bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha gandhajātānīti gandhajātiyo. Mūlagandhoti [P 2.0336] mūlavatthuko gandho, gandhasampannaṃ vā mūlameva mūlagandho. Tassa hi gandho anuvātaṃ gacchati. Gandhassa pana gandho nāma natthi. Sāragandhapupphagandhesupi eseva nayo. Atthānanda, kiñci gandhajātanti ettha saraṇagamanādayo guṇavaṇṇabhāsanavasena disāgāmitāya gandhasadisattā gandhā, tesaṃ vatthubhūto puggalo gandhajātaṃ nāma. Gandho gacchatīti vaṇṇabhāsanavasena gacchati. Sīlavāti pañcasīlena vā dasasīlena vā sīlavā. Kalyāṇadhammoti teneva sīladhammena kalyāṇadhammo sundaradhammo. Vigatamalamaccherenātiādīnaṃ [V 2.0199] attho visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.160) vitthāritova. Disāsūti catūsu disāsu catūsu anudisāsu[M 2.0206]. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti samitapāpabāhitapāpā samaṇabrāhmaṇā.

80. In the ninth sutta, 'he said this' means: After returning from the alms-round after the meal, having performed his duties for the Ten-Powered One, he went to his daytime dwelling place and thought, 'In this world, there is what is called root fragrance, heartwood fragrance, and flower fragrance. However, these three fragrances travel only with the wind, not against it. Is there anything whose fragrance travels against the wind?' Reflecting thus, because the boon of approaching the Teacher when doubt arose had been taken at the very time of receiving the eight boons, he immediately rose from his daytime dwelling, approached the Teacher, paid homage, sat down to one side, and to dispel the arisen doubt, spoke these words beginning with, 'There are these three, Venerable Sir.' Herein, 'gandhajātāni' means types of fragrances. 'Mūlagandho' refers to fragrance based on roots, or the root itself that is rich in fragrance is called root fragrance. Its fragrance travels with the wind. But there is no such thing as a fragrance of a fragrance. The same principle applies to heartwood fragrance and flower fragrance. Regarding the phrase 'Is there, Ānanda, any kind of fragrance?': here, qualities such as going for refuge are called 'fragrances' because, like fragrance, they travel to all directions by means of proclaiming their virtues. The person who is the basis for these is called a 'gandhajāta' (a kind of fragrance). 'The fragrance travels' means it travels by means of praise. 'Virtuous' means one endowed with the five or ten precepts. 'Of good qualities' means of good and beautiful qualities through that same virtue. The meaning of 'free from stains and stinginess,' etc., has been extensively explained by me in the Visuddhimagga. 'In all directions' means in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions. 'Ascetics and brahmins' means ascetics and brahmins who have calmed and banished evil.

Na pupphagandho paṭivātametīti vassikapupphādīnaṃ gandho paṭivātaṃ na gacchati. Na candanaṃ tagaramallikā vāti candanatagaramallikānampi gandho paṭivātaṃ na gacchatīti attho. Devalokepi phuṭasumanā nāma hoti, tassā pupphitadivase gandho yojanasataṃ ajjhottharati. Sopi paṭivātaṃ vidatthimattampi ratanamattampi gantuṃ na sakkotīti vadanti. Satañca gandho paṭivātametīti satañca paṇḍitānaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhaputtānaṃ sīlādiguṇagandho paṭivātaṃ gacchati. Sabbā disā sappuriso pavāyatīti sappuriso paṇḍito sīlādiguṇagandhena sabbā disā pavāyati, sabbā disā gandhena avattharatīti attho.

“The scent of a flower does not travel against the wind”: The scent of flowers such as jasmine and so on does not travel against the wind. “Neither sandalwood, tagara, nor jasmine”: the scent of sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine also does not travel against the wind—this is the meaning. In the deva world, there is a flower named Sumanā; on the day it blooms, its scent pervades a hundred yojanas. Even that, they say, is not able to travel against the wind even a span or a cubit. “But the scent of the good travels against the wind”: The scent of the virtue and other qualities of the good and wise—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and sons of the Buddha—travels against the wind. “The good person pervades all directions”: The good person, the wise one, pervades all directions with the scent of virtue and other qualities; he pervades all directions with his scent—this is the meaning.

10. Cūḷanikāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Cūḷanika Sutta

81. Dasamassa duvidho nikkhepo atthuppattikopi pucchāvasikopi. Kataraatthuppattiyaṃ kassa pucchāya kathitanti ce? Aruṇavatisuttantaatthuppattiyaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.185 ādayo) ānandattherassa pucchāya kathitaṃ. Aruṇavatisuttanto kena kathitoti? Dvīhi [P 2.0337] buddhehi kathito sikhinā ca bhagavatā amhākañca satthārā. Imasmā hi kappā ekatiṃsakappamatthake aruṇavatinagare aruṇavato rañño pabhāvatiyā nāma mahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattitvā paripakke ñāṇe mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā sikhī bhagavā bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko aruṇavatiṃ nissāya viharanto ekadivasaṃ pātova sarīrappaṭijagganaṃ katvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro “aruṇavatiṃ piṇḍāya pavisissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā vihāradvārakoṭṭhakasamīpe ṭhito abhibhuṃ nāma aggasāvakaṃ āmantesi – “atippago kho, bhikkhu, aruṇavatiṃ piṇḍāya pavisituṃ, yena aññataro brahmaloko tenupasaṅkamissāmā”ti. Yathāha –

81. The tenth has a twofold exposition: one based on the origination of the matter and one based on a question. If it is asked, 'Based on which origination of the matter and in response to whose question was it spoken?' The answer is: It was spoken based on the origination of the Aruṇavatī Sutta and in response to the question of the Elder Ānanda. By whom was the Aruṇavatī Sutta spoken? It was spoken by two Buddhas: by the Blessed One Sikhī and by our Teacher. For, thirty-one aeons prior to this one, in the city of Aruṇavatī, the Blessed One Sikhī was born in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the chief consort of King Aruṇavata. When his knowledge had matured, he went forth in the Great Renunciation. Having penetrated to omniscient knowledge at the Bodhi-seat and set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, he was dwelling near Aruṇavatī. One day, early in the morning, having attended to his bodily needs, surrounded by a great community of monks, he went forth thinking, 'I will enter Aruṇavatī for alms.' Having gone out, he stood near the monastery gatehouse and addressed his chief disciple named Abhibhū: 'Monk, it is still too early to enter Aruṇavatī for alms. Let us approach a certain Brahmā world.' As it is said:

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, sikhī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho abhibhuṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – ‘āyāma, brāhmaṇa, yena aññataro brahmaloko [M 2.0207] tenupasaṅkamissāma, na tāva bhattakālo bhavissatī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bhante’ti kho, bhikkhave, abhibhū bhikkhu sikhissa [V 2.0200] bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa paccassosi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, sikhī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho abhibhū ca bhikkhu yena aññataro brahmaloko tenupasaṅkamiṃsū”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185).

“Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū: ‘Come, brahmin, let us approach a certain Brahmā world; the time for the meal has not yet arrived.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ replied the monk Abhibhū to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the monk Abhibhū approached a certain Brahmā world.”

Tattha mahābrahmā sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā attamano paccuggamanaṃ katvā brahmāsanaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi, therassāpi anucchavikaṃ āsanaṃ paññāpayiṃsu. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane, theropi attano paññattāsane nisīdi. Mahābrahmāpi dasabalaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

There, the Great Brahmā, seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One, was delighted and went forward to greet him. Having had a Brahmā seat prepared, he offered it. They also prepared a suitable seat for the elder. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat, and the elder also sat on his own prepared seat. The Great Brahmā, having paid homage to the One with Ten Powers, sat down to one side.

Atha kho, bhikkhave, sikhī bhagavā abhibhuṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “paṭibhātu taṃ, brāhmaṇa, brahmuno ca brahmaparisāya ca brahmapārisajjānañca dhammīkathāti. ‘Evaṃ, bhante’ti kho, bhikkhave, abhibhū bhikkhu sikhissa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa paṭissuṇitvā brahmuno ca brahmaparisāya ca brahmapārisajjānañca dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. There dhammaṃ kathente brahmagaṇā ujjhāyiṃsu [P 2.0338] – “cirassañca mayaṃ satthu brahmalokāgamanaṃ labhimha, ayañca bhikkhu ṭhapetvā satthāraṃ sayaṃ dhammakathaṃ ārabhī”ti.

“Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī addressed the monk Abhibhū: ‘Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, brahmin, for Brahmā, his assembly, and his retinue.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the monk Abhibhū replied, and having hearkened to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, he gave a Dhamma talk to Brahmā, his assembly, and his retinue.” While the elder was giving the Dhamma talk, the assembly of Brahmās complained: “Only after a long time have we obtained the Teacher's arrival in the Brahmā world, yet this monk, setting aside the Teacher, has himself begun a Dhamma talk!”

Satthā tesaṃ anattamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā abhibhuṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “ujjhāyanti kho te, brāhmaṇa, brahmā ca brahmaparisā ca brahmapārisajjā ca. Tena hi tvaṃ – brāhmaṇa, bhiyyosomattāya saṃvejehī”ti. Thero satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā anekavihitaṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ katvā sahassilokadhātuṃ sarena viññāpento “ārambhatha nikkamathā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185) gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi. Kiṃ pana katvā thero sahassilokadhātuṃ viññāpesīti? Nīlakasiṇaṃ tāva samāpajjitvā sabbattha andhakāraṃ phari, tato “kimidaṃ andhakāra”nti sattānaṃ ābhoge uppanne ālokaṃ dassesi. “Kiṃ āloko aya”nti vicinantānaṃ attānaṃ dassesi, sahassacakkavāḷe devamanussā añjaliṃ paggaṇhitvā paggaṇhitvā theraṃyeva namassamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Thero “mahājano mayhaṃ dhammaṃ desentassa saraṃ suṇātū”ti imā [M 2.0208] gāthā abhāsi. Sabbe osaṭāya parisāya majjhe nisīditvā dhammaṃ desentassa viya saddaṃ assosuṃ. Atthopi nesaṃ pākaṭo ahosi.

The Teacher, knowing their state of displeasure, spoke these words to the monk Abhibhū: “Brahmin, the Brahmās, the Brahmā assembly, and the Brahmā attendants look down upon you. Therefore, Brahmin, stir them up even more.” The elder, having accepted the Teacher’s word, performed various miraculous transformations and, making his voice known throughout the thousandfold world-system, recited the pair of verses beginning, “Strive, go forth…” But how did the elder make the thousandfold world-system know? First, having entered into the blue kasiṇa, he spread darkness everywhere. Then, when the thought, “What is this darkness?” arose in the beings, he showed them light. To those who were investigating, “What is this light?” he showed himself. In the thousandfold universe, gods and humans stood paying homage to the elder himself, having raised their joined hands. The elder, thinking, “Let the great multitude hear my voice as I teach the Dhamma,” recited these verses. All heard the sound as if they were sitting in the midst of a gathered assembly, hearing one who was teaching the Dhamma. The meaning also became clear to them.

Atha kho bhagavā saddhiṃ therena aruṇavatiṃ paccāgantvā piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto [V 2.0201] bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi – “assuttha no tumhe, bhikkhave, abhibhussa bhikkhuno brahmaloke ṭhitassa gāthāyo bhāsamānassā”ti. Te “āma, bhante”ti paṭijānitvā sutabhāvaṃ āvikarontā tadeva gāthādvayaṃ udāhariṃsu. Satthā “sādhu sādhū”ti sādhukāraṃ datvā desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Evaṃ tāva idaṃ suttaṃ ito ekatiṃsakappamatthake sikhinā bhagavatā kathitaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, returning with the elder to Aruṇavatī, after going for alms and returning from the alms-round after his meal, asked the Saṅgha of monks: "Monks, did you hear the verses spoken by the monk Abhibhū while standing in the Brahmā world?" They acknowledged, "Yes, Venerable Sir," and, making it clear that they had heard them, recited the same two verses. The Teacher, giving his approval with "Good, good," concluded the discourse. Thus, this sutta was spoken by the Blessed One Sikhī thirty-one aeons ago.

Amhākaṃ pana bhagavā sabbaññutaṃ patto pavattitavaradhammacakko sāvatthiṃ upanissāya jetavane viharanto jeṭṭhamūlamāsapuṇṇamadivase bhikkhū āmantetvā imaṃ aruṇavatisuttaṃ [P 2.0339] paṭṭhapesi. Ānandatthero bījaniṃ gahetvā bījayamāno ṭhitakova ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā ekabyañjanampi ahāpetvā sakalasuttaṃ uggaṇhi. So punadivase piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto dasabalassa vattaṃ dassetvā attano divāvihāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā saddhivihārikantevāsikesu vattaṃ dassetvā pakkantesu hiyyo kathitaṃ aruṇavatisuttaṃ āvajjento nisīdi. Athassa sabbaṃ suttaṃ vibhūtaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So cintesi – “sikhissa bhagavato aggasāvako brahmaloke ṭhatvā cakkavāḷasahasse andhakāraṃ vidhametvā sarīrobhāsaṃ dassetvā attano saddaṃ sāvento dhammakathaṃ kathesīti hiyyo satthārā kathitaṃ, sāvakassa tāva visayo evarūpo, dasa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ patto pana sammāsambuddho kittakaṃ ṭhānaṃ sarena viññāpeyyā”ti. So evaṃ uppannāya vimatiyā vinodanatthaṃ taṅkhaṇeyeva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ pucchi. Etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ atha kho āyasmā ānandoti vuttaṃ.

Now, our Blessed One, having attained omniscience and set rolling the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, while dwelling near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, on the full-moon day of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, addressed the monks and established this Aruṇavatī Sutta. The elder Ānanda, taking a fan, stood fanning the Blessed One and learned the entire sutta from beginning to end without omitting a single syllable. The next day, after returning from the alms-round and performing his duties to the One with Ten Powers, he went to his day-quarters; and when his co-residents and pupils, having been shown their duties, had departed, he sat down reflecting on the Aruṇavatī Sutta spoken the previous day. Then the entire sutta appeared clearly to him. He thought: 'Yesterday the Teacher said: "The chief disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī, standing in the Brahmā world, having dispelled the darkness in the thousandfold world-system, having revealed his bodily radiance, and making his voice heard, taught the Dhamma." Such is the scope of a disciple. But a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience—how vast an area could he make known with his voice?' To dispel the doubt that had thus arisen, he immediately approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter. To show this matter, it is said: 'Then the Venerable Ānanda...'

Tattha sammukhāti sammukhībhūtena mayā etaṃ sutaṃ, na anussavena, na dūtaparamparāyāti iminā adhippāyena evamāha. Kīvatakaṃ pahoti sarena viññāpetunti kittakaṃ ṭhānaṃ sarīrobhāsena vihatandhakāraṃ katvā sarena viññāpetuṃ sakkoti. Sāvako so, ānanda, appameyyā tathāgatāti [M 2.0209] idaṃ bhagavā iminā adhippāyenāha – ānanda, tvaṃ kiṃ vadesi, so padesañāṇe ṭhito sāvako. Tathāgatā pana dasa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pattā appameyyā. So tvaṃ nakhasikhāya paṃsuṃ gahetvā mahāpathavipaṃsunā saddhiṃ upamento viya kiṃ nāmetaṃ vadesi. Añño hi sāvakānaṃ visayo, añño buddhānaṃ. Añño sāvakānaṃ gocaro, añño buddhānaṃ. Aññaṃ sāvakānaṃ balaṃ, aññaṃ buddhānanti. Iti bhagavā iminā adhippāyena appameyyabhāvaṃ vatvā tuṇhī ahosi.

Herein, as for 'in person' (sammukhā): 'This was heard by me face-to-face; it was not heard through hearsay, nor through a succession of messengers.' With this intention, he spoke thus. As for 'How far is one able to make things known by voice?': How large of an area, having dispelled the darkness with the radiance of the body, is one able to make things known by voice? As for the statement, 'He is a disciple, Ānanda; the Tathāgatas are immeasurable,' the Blessed One spoke this with the following intention: 'Ānanda, what are you saying? That one is a disciple established in partial knowledge. The Tathāgatas, on the other hand, having fulfilled the ten perfections and attained the knowledge of omniscience, are immeasurable. You, like one who takes dust on the tip of a fingernail and compares it with the dust of the great earth, for what reason do you say this? Indeed, the domain of disciples is one thing, and the domain of Buddhas is another. The range of disciples is one thing, and the range of Buddhas is another. The power of disciples is one thing, and the power of Buddhas is another.' Thus, with this intention, the Blessed One, after speaking of the state of being immeasurable, became silent.

Thero [V 2.0202][P 2.0340] dutiyampi pucchi. Satthā, “ānanda, tvaṃ tāḷacchiddaṃ gahetvā anantākāsena upamento viya, cātakasakuṇaṃ gahetvā diyaḍḍhayojanasatikena supaṇṇarājena upamento viya, hatthisoṇḍāya udakaṃ gahetvā mahāgaṅgāya upamento viya, caturatanike āvāṭe udakaṃ gahetvā sattahi sarehi upamento viya, nāḷikodanamattalābhiṃ manussaṃ gahetvā cakkavattiraññā upamento viya, paṃsupisācakaṃ gahetvā sakkena devaraññā upamento viya, khajjopanakappabhaṃ gahetvā sūriyappabhāya upamento viya kiṃ nāmetaṃ vadesīti dīpento dutiyampi appameyyabhāvameva vatvā tuṇhī ahosi. Tato thero cintesi – “satthā mayā pucchito na tāva kathesi, handa naṃ yāvatatiyaṃ yācitvā buddhasīhanādaṃ nadāpessāmī”ti. So tatiyampi yāci. Taṃ dassetuṃ tatiyampi khotiādi vuttaṃ. Athassa bhagavā byākaronto sutā te ānandātiādimāha. Thero cintesi – “satthā me ‘sutā te, ānanda, sahassī cūḷanikā lokadhātū’ti ettakameva vatvā tuṇhī jāto, idāni buddhasīhanādaṃ nadissatī”ti so satthāraṃ yācanto etassa bhagavā kālotiādimāha.

The Elder asked for a second time. The Teacher, wishing to illustrate, 'Ānanda, it is as if you, having taken the eye of a needle, were to compare it with the limitless sky; or as if, having taken a small cātaka bird, you were to compare it with the Supaṇṇa king who is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size; or as if, having taken water with an elephant's trunk, you were to compare it with the great Ganges; or as if, having taken water in a four-cubit pit, you were to compare it with the seven great lakes; or as if, having taken a poor person who receives only a measure of rice, you were to compare him with a wheel-turning monarch; or as if, having taken a dust-goblin, you were to compare it with Sakka, king of the devas; or as if, having taken the light of a firefly, you were to compare it with the light of the sun—why indeed do you say this?', for a second time, spoke only of the immeasurable nature and then became silent. Then the Elder thought: 'The Teacher, though asked by me, has not yet spoken. Come now, having requested him up to a third time, I will cause him to utter the Buddha's lion's roar.' So he requested for a third time. To show that, the words beginning with 'For a third time...' were said. Then the Blessed One, explaining to him, said the words beginning with 'Have you heard, Ānanda...'. The Elder thought: 'The Teacher, having said to me only this much, "Have you heard, Ānanda, of the thousandfold minor world-system?", has become silent. Now he will utter the Buddha's lion's roar.' So he, entreating the Teacher, said the words beginning with 'This is the time, Blessed One...'.

Bhagavāpissa vitthārakathaṃ kathetuṃ tena hānandātiādimāha. Tattha yāvatāti yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Candimasūriyāti candimā ca sūriyo ca. Pariharantīti vicaranti. Disā bhantīti sabbadisā obhāsanti. Virocanāti virocamānā. Ettāvatā ekacakkavāḷaṃ paricchinditvā dassitaṃ hoti. Idāni taṃ sahassaguṇaṃ katvā dassento tāva sahassadhā lokoti āha. Tasmiṃ sahassadhā loketi tasmiṃ sahassacakkavāḷe. Sahassaṃ cātumahārājikānanti [M 2.0210] sahassaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ devalokānaṃ. Yasmā pana ekekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe cattāro cattāro mahārājāno[P 2.0341], tasmā cattāri mahārājasahassānīti vuttaṃ. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Cūḷanikāti khuddikā. Ayaṃ sāvakānaṃ visayo. Kasmā panesā ānītāti? Majjhimikāya lokadhātuyā paricchedadassanatthaṃ.

The Blessed One, in order to give him a detailed discourse, spoke the words beginning with, 'Therefore, Ānanda...' Therein, 'as far as' means 'whatever extent of a place'. 'The moon and the sun' refers to the moon and the sun. 'They revolve' means they move around. 'They illuminate the directions' means they light up all directions. 'Radiant' means shining. By this much, one world-system has been demarcated and shown. Now, showing that multiplied a thousandfold, he says, “a thousandfold world.” In that ‘thousandfold world’ means in that thousand world-systems. ‘A thousand Cātumahārājika realms’ means a thousand Cātumahārājika deva-worlds. Since in each world-system there are four great kings, therefore it is said, “four thousand great kings.” By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere. Cūḷanikā means minor. This is the domain of the disciples. But why is this brought in? To show the demarcation of the middling world-system.

Yāvatāti yattakā. Tāva sahassadhāti tāva sahassabhāgena. Dvisahassī majjhimikā lokadhātūti ayaṃ sahassacakkavāḷāni sahassabhāgena gaṇetvā dasasatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇā dvisahassī majjhimikā nāma lokadhātu. Ayaṃ sāvakānaṃ avisayo, buddhānameva visayo. Ettakepi hi ṭhāne tathāgatā andhakāraṃ vidhametvā sarīrobhāsaṃ dassetvā sarena viññāpetuṃ sakkontīti dīpeti. Ettakena buddhānaṃ jātikkhettaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Bodhisattānañhi pacchimabhave [V 2.0203] devalokato cavitvā mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase ca kucchito nikkhamanadivase ca mahābhinikkhamanadivase ca sambodhidhammacakkappavattanaāyusaṅkhāravossajjanaparinibbānadivasesu ca ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ kampati.

“Yāvatā” means “as much as.” “Tāva sahassadhā” means “as much as a thousandfold.” “The middling two-thousandfold world-system” refers to this: counting a thousand world-systems as a thousandfold, this world-sphere, measuring a million world-systems, is called the middling two-thousandfold world-system. This is beyond the scope of disciples; it is only the domain of the Buddhas. For it is shown that even in such a place, the Tathāgatas are able to dispel the darkness, reveal their bodily radiance, and make themselves known with their voice. By this much, what is called the Buddhas' birth-range is shown. For, in the final existence of Bodhisattas, this much of a place trembles on the day of taking conception in the mother's womb after passing away from the deva-world, on the day of emerging from the womb, on the day of the Great Renunciation, and on the days of attaining complete enlightenment, setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, relinquishing the life-formations, and attaining Parinibbāna.

Tisahassī mahāsahassīti sahassito paṭṭhāya tatiyāti tisahassī, sahassaṃ sahassadhā katvā gaṇitaṃ majjhimikaṃ sahassadhā katvā gaṇitattā mahantehi sahassehi gaṇitāti mahāsahassī. Ettāvatā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇo loko dassito hoti. Bhagavā ākaṅkhamāno ettake ṭhāne andhakāraṃ vidhametvā sarīrobhāsaṃ dassetvā sarena viññāpeyyāti. Gaṇakaputtatissatthero pana evamāha – “na tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuyā evaṃ parimāṇaṃ. Idañhi ācariyānaṃ sajjhāyamuḷhakaṃ vācāya parihīnaṭṭhānaṃ, dasakoṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇaṃ pana ṭhānaṃ tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātu nāmā”ti. Ettāvatā hi bhagavatā āṇākkhettaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Etasmiñhi [P 2.0342] antare āṭānāṭiyaparittaisigiliparittadhajaggaparittabojjhaṅgaparittakhandhaparitta- moraparittamettaparittaratanaparittānaṃ āṇā pharati. Yāvatā pana ākaṅkheyyāti yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ iccheyya, iminā visayakkhettaṃ [M 2.0211] dasseti. Buddhānañhi visayakkhettassa pamāṇaparicchedo nāma natthi, natthikabhāve cassa imaṃ opammaṃ āharanti – koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷamhi yāva brahmalokā sāsapehi pūretvā sace koci puratthimāya disāya ekacakkavāḷe ekaṃ sāsapaṃ pakkhipanto āgaccheyya, sabbepi te sāsapā parikkhayaṃ gaccheyyuṃ, na tveva puratthimāya disāya cakkavāḷāni. Dakkhiṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha buddhānaṃ avisayo nāma natthi.

Regarding 'tisahassī mahāsahassī': 'Tisahassī' refers to the world-system counted by the third multiplication by a thousand, starting from a thousand. 'Mahāsahassī' is so called because it is counted by great thousands, being calculated by taking the middling thousandfold world-system a thousand times. By this, the world is shown to have the extent of one hundred thousand koṭi world-systems. The Blessed One, if he so wished, could in such an expanse dispel the darkness, display his bodily radiance, and make himself known by his voice. However, the Elder Gaṇakaputtatissa said thus: 'That is not the measure of the tisahassi-mahāsahassi world-system. For this is a point diminished by the speech of the teachers, which is confused by recitation. Rather, the extent of ten thousand koṭi world-systems is what is called the tisahassi-mahāsahassi world-system.' Indeed, by this the Blessed One has shown what is called the domain of authority. For within this expanse, the commanding power of the Āṭānāṭiya-paritta, Isigili-paritta, Dhajagga-paritta, Bojjhaṅga-paritta, Khandha-paritta, Mora-paritta, Mettā-paritta, and Ratana-paritta pervades. As for the phrase 'as far as he might wish,' this means 'whatever place he might desire.' By this, the domain of his range is shown. Indeed, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a measured limit to their domain of range. Regarding the fact that it has no limit, they bring forth this simile: If one were to fill one hundred thousand koṭi world-systems up to the Brahmā world with mustard seeds, and if a person, proceeding in the eastern direction, were to deposit one mustard seed in each world-system, all those mustard seeds would be exhausted, but the world-systems in the eastern direction would not be. The same method applies to the southern and other directions. Therein, there is no world-system that is not the domain of the Buddhas.

Evaṃ vutte thero cintesi – “satthā evamāha – ‘ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuṃ sarena viññāpeyya, yāvatā pana ākaṅkheyyā’ti. Visamo kho panāyaṃ loko, anantāni cakkavāḷāni, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sūriyo uggato hoti, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne majjhe ṭhito, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne atthaṅgato. Ekasmiṃ ṭhāne paṭhamayāmo hoti, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne majjhimayāmo, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne pacchimayāmo. Sattāpi kammappasutā, khiḍḍāpasutā, āhārappasutāti evaṃ tehi tehi kāraṇehi vikkhittā ca pamattā ca honti. Kathaṃ nu kho te satthā sarena viññāpeyyā”ti. So evaṃ cintetvā vimaticchedanatthaṃ tathāgataṃ pucchanto yathā kathaṃ panātiādimāha.

When this was said, the elder thought: “The Teacher has said, ‘Ānanda, if the Tathāgata wishes, he could make his voice known throughout the three-thousandfold great thousand world-system, as far as he desires.’ But this world is uneven, with countless world-systems. In one place the sun is rising, in another it is at its zenith, and in another it is setting. In one place it is the first watch of the night, in another the middle watch, and in another the last watch. Beings are intent on work, intent on play, or intent on food—thus they are scattered and heedless due to these various reasons. How then could the Teacher make his voice known to them?” Reflecting thus, to cut off his doubt, he questioned the Tathāgata, beginning with, “But how...?”

Athassa [V 2.0204] satthā byākaronto idhānanda, tathāgatotiādimāha. Tattha obhāsena phareyyāti sarīrobhāsena phareyya. Pharamāno panesa kiṃ kareyyāti? Yasmiṃ ṭhāne sūriyo paññāyati, tattha naṃ attano ānubhāvena atthaṃ gameyya. Yattha pana na paññāyati, tattha naṃ uṭṭhāpetvā majjhe ṭhapeyya[P 2.0343]. Tato yattha sūriyo paññāyati, tattha manussā “adhunāva sūriyo paññāyittha, so idāneva atthaṅgamito, nāgāvaṭṭo nu kho ayaṃ, bhūtāvaṭṭayakkhāvaṭṭadevatāvaṭṭānaṃ aññataro”ti vittakkaṃ uppādeyyuṃ. Yattha pana na paññāyati, tattha manussā “adhunāva sūriyo atthaṅgamito, svāyaṃ idāneva uṭṭhito, kiṃ nu kho ayaṃ nāgāvaṭṭabhūtāvaṭṭayakkhāvaṭṭadevatāvaṭṭānaṃ aññataro”ti vitakkaṃ uppādeyyuṃ. Tato tesu manussesu ālokañca andhakārañca āvajjitvā “kiṃ paccayā nu kho ida”nti pariyesamānesu satthā nīlakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā [M 2.0212] bahalandhakāraṃ patthareyya. Kasmā? Tesaṃ kammādippasutānaṃ sattānaṃ santāsajananatthaṃ. Atha nesaṃ santāsaṃ āpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā odātakasiṇasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā paṇḍaraṃ ghanabuddharasmiṃ vissajjento candasahassasūriyasahassauṭṭhānakālo viya ekappahāreneva sabbaṃ ekālokaṃ kareyya. Tañca kho tilabījamattena kāyappadesena obhāsaṃ muñcanto. Yo hi cakkavāḷapathaviṃ dīpakapallakaṃ katvā mahāsamudde udakaṃ telaṃ katvā sineruṃ vaṭṭiṃ katvā aññasmiṃ sinerumuddhani ṭhapetvā jāleyya, so ekacakkavāḷeyeva ālokaṃ kareyya. Tato paraṃ vidatthimpi obhāsetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Tathāgato pana tilaphalappamāṇena sarīrappadesena obhāsaṃ muñcitvā tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuṃ ekobhāsaṃ kareyya tato vā pana bhiyyo. Evaṃ mahantā hi buddhaguṇāti.

Then the Teacher, wishing to answer him, spoke the words beginning with, 'Here, Ānanda, a Tathāgata...' Therein, 'he would pervade with radiance' means he would pervade with bodily radiance. Furthermore, while pervading, what would he do? This is the question. In whatever world-system the sun appears, in that place he would cause it to set by means of his own radiance. But where it does not appear, he would cause it to turn back and place it in the middle. Thereupon, in the place where the sun appears, people would give rise to the thought: 'Just now the sun appeared, and now it has set for us. Could this be a turning of the nāgas? Could it be one of the turnings of spirits, yakkhas, or devas?' But in the place where the sun does not appear, people would give rise to the thought: 'Just now the sun had set, and now this very one has risen. Could this be a turning of the nāgas, spirits, yakkhas, or devas?' Thereupon, while those people, reflecting on the light and the darkness, were searching, thinking, 'Due to what cause has this arisen?', the Teacher, having entered the blue kasiṇa, would spread out dense darkness. Why? For the purpose of generating terror in those beings devoted to their occupations and so on. Then, having known that they had become terrified, he would enter the attainment based on the white kasiṇa and, while emitting a pure, dense Buddha-radiance, like the time of the rising of a thousand moons and a thousand suns, he would in a single instant make everything have a single light. And this he would do by releasing the radiance from a part of his body the size of a sesame seed. For indeed, if someone, having made the earth of a world-system into an oil lamp, having made the water in the great ocean into oil, having made Sineru into a wick, and having placed it on the peak of another Sineru, were to light it, that person could produce light in only one world-system. Beyond that, he would not be able to illuminate even a span. But the Tathāgata, releasing radiance from a part of his body the size of a sesame fruit, could make the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system have a single light, or even more than that. Indeed, so great are the qualities of a Buddha.

Taṃ ālokaṃ sañjāneyyunti taṃ ālokaṃ disvā “yena sūriyo atthañceva gamito uṭṭhāpito ca, bahalandhakārañca vissaṭṭhaṃ, esa so puriso idāni ālokaṃ katvā ṭhito, aho acchariyapuriso”ti añjaliṃ paggayha namassamānā nisīdeyyuṃ. Saddamanussāveyyāti [P 2.0344] dhammakathāsaddamanussāveyya. Yo hi ekaṃ cakkavāḷapabbataṃ bheriṃ katvā mahāpathaviṃ bhericammaṃ katvā sineruṃ daṇḍaṃ katvā aññasmiṃ sinerumatthake ṭhapetvā ākoṭeyya, so ekacakkavāḷeyeva taṃ saddaṃ sāveyya, parato vidatthimpi atikkāmetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Tathāgato pana pallaṅke vā pīṭhe vā nisīditvā tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuṃ sarena viññāpeti, tato vā pana bhiyyo, evaṃ mahānubhāvā tathāgatāti. Iti bhagavā iminā ettakena visayakkhettameva dasseti.

'They would recognize that light' means that, seeing that light, they would think: 'The one by whom the sun was caused to set and also caused to rise, and by whom dense darkness was sent forth—this is that person who now stands, having created light. Oh, what a marvelous person!' Raising their folded hands in reverence, they would sit down while paying homage. 'He would cause a sound to be heard' means he would cause the sound of a Dhamma talk to be heard. For if someone were to make one world-system mountain into a drum, the great earth into its drumhead, Mount Sineru into a drumstick, and then strike it while standing on another Mount Sineru, he would cause that sound to be heard only in one world-system; he would not be able to make it go beyond that, even by a span. But the Tathāgata, seated on a throne or a seat, makes his voice known throughout the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system, or even beyond. Thus, the Tathāgatas are of great power. In this way, the Blessed One shows just this much as the extent of his range.

Imañca [V 2.0205] pana buddhasīhanādaṃ sutvā therassa abbhantare balavapīti uppannā, so pītivasena udānaṃ udānento lābhā vata metiādimāha. Tattha yassa me satthā evaṃmahiddhikoti yassa mayhaṃ satthā evaṃmahiddhiko, tassa mayhaṃ evaṃmahiddhikassa satthu paṭilābho lābhā ceva suladdhañcāti attho. Atha vā yvāhaṃ evarūpassa satthuno pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vicarituṃ, pādaparikammaṃ piṭṭhiparikammaṃ kātuṃ, mukhadhovanaudakanhānodakāni dātuṃ, gandhakuṭipariveṇaṃ sammajjituṃ, uppannāya kaṅkhāya pañhaṃ pucchituṃ, madhuradhammakathañca [M 2.0213] sotuṃ labhāmi, ete sabbepi mayhaṃ lābhā ceva suladdhañcātipi sandhāya evamāha. Ettha ca bhagavato andhakārālokasaddasavanasaṅkhātānaṃ iddhīnaṃ mahantatāya mahiddhikatā, tāsaṃyeva anupharaṇena mahānubhāvatā veditabbā. Udāyīti lāḷudāyitthero. So kira pubbe upaṭṭhākatthere āghātaṃ bandhitvā carati. Tasmā idāni okāsaṃ labhitvā imasmiṃ buddhasīhanādapariyosāne jalamānaṃ dīpasikhaṃ nibbāpento viya carantassa goṇassa tuṇḍe pahāraṃ dento viya bhattabharitaṃ [P 2.0345] pātiṃ avakujjanto viya therassa pasādabhaṅgaṃ karonto evamāha.

And hearing this lion’s roar of the Buddha, strong joy arose within the elder. Filled with joy, he uttered this inspired saying: 'What a gain for me!' and so forth. Therein, 'For me, whose teacher possesses such great psychic power,' means: 'For me, whose teacher possesses such great psychic power, to have obtained such a teacher is indeed a gain and well-gained.' Alternatively, he spoke thus with this in mind: 'What a gain and well-gained it is for me that I am able to wander carrying the bowl and robes of such a teacher, to perform the duties of attending to his feet and back, to offer water for washing his face and bathing, to sweep his fragrant cell and surrounding area, to ask questions when doubts arise, and to listen to his sweet Dhamma talks! All these are gains for me and are well-gained.' And here, the Blessed One's great psychic power is due to the greatness of his powers, which are known as causing darkness, light, and sound to be heard. Through the pervading of these very powers, his great might should be understood. 'Udāyī' refers to the elder Lāḷudāyī. It is said that he had previously harbored resentment toward the attendant elder. Therefore, now, having gotten the opportunity at the conclusion of this lion’s roar of the Buddha, he spoke as if extinguishing a blazing lamp flame, as if striking a walking bull on the snout, or as if overturning a bowl full of food, thus shattering the elder’s serene confidence.

Evaṃ vutte bhagavāti evaṃ udāyittherena vutte bhagavā yathā nāma papātataṭe ṭhatvā pavedhamānaṃ purisaṃ ekamante ṭhito hitesī puriso “ito ehi ito ehī”ti punappunaṃ vadeyya, evamevaṃ udāyittheraṃ tasmā vacanā nivārento mā hevaṃ udāyi, mā hevaṃ udāyīti āha. Tattha hīti nipātamattaṃ, mā evaṃ avacāti attho. Mahārajjanti cakkavattirajjaṃ. Nanu ca satthā ekassa sāvakassa dhammadesanāya uppannapasādassa mahānisaṃsaṃ aparicchinnaṃ akāsi, so kasmā imassa buddhasīhanādaṃ ārabbha uppannassa pasādassa ānisaṃsaṃ paricchindatīti? Ariyasāvakassa ettakaattabhāvaparimāṇattā. Dandhapaññopi hi sotāpanno sattakkhattuṃ devesu ca manussesu ca attabhāvaṃ paṭilabhati, tenassa gatiṃ paricchindanto evamāha. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve ṭhatvā. Parinibbāyissatīti appaccayaparinibbānena parinibbāyissati. Iti nibbānena kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto imaṃ sīhanādasuttaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

When this was said by the Elder Udāyī, the Blessed One—just as a well-wishing person, standing to one side of a man who is standing on the edge of a cliff and trembling, might repeatedly say, 'Come this way, come this way!'—in the very same way, restraining the Elder Udāyī from that statement, said, 'Not so, Udāyī, not so, Udāyī.' Therein, the meaning is 'do not speak thus.' 'The great kingdom' means the kingdom of a wheel-turning monarch. But did not the Teacher make the great benefit for the faith that arose in one disciple through the teaching of the Dhamma unlimited? Why then does he limit the benefit of this faith that has arisen on account of the Buddha's lion's roar? Because for a noble disciple, there is such a measure to their states of existence. For even a dull-witted stream-enterer obtains a state of existence seven times among gods and humans; thus, limiting his destiny, he spoke thus. 'In this very life' means while remaining in this very existence. 'Will attain final Nibbāna' means he will attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna without any remaining condition for rebirth. Thus, taking Nibbāna as the pinnacle, he concluded this Lion's Roar Sutta.

Ānandavaggo tatiyo.

The Ānanda Chapter is the third.

(9) 4. Samaṇavaggo

(9) 4. The Chapter on Ascetics

1. Samaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Ascetics

82. Catutthassa [V 2.0206] paṭhame samaṇiyānīti samaṇasantakāni. Samaṇakaraṇīyānīti samaṇena kattabbakiccāni. Adhisīlasikkhāsamādānantiādīsu samādānaṃ vuccati gahaṇaṃ, adhisīlasikkhāya samādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ pūraṇaṃ [M 2.0214] adhisīlasikkhāsamādānaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca sīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ, cittaṃ adhicittaṃ, paññā adhipaññāti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha pañcasīlaṃ sīlaṃ [P 2.0346] nāma, taṃ upādāya dasasīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ nāma, tampi upādāya catupārisuddhisīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ nāma. Apica sabbampi lokiyasīlaṃ sīlaṃ nāma, lokuttarasīlaṃ adhisīlaṃ, tadeva sikkhitabbato sikkhāti vuccati. Kāmāvacaracittaṃ pana cittaṃ nāma, taṃ upādāya rūpāvacaraṃ adhicittaṃ nāma, tampi upādāya arūpāvacaraṃ adhicittaṃ nāma. Apica sabbampi lokiyacittaṃ cittameva, lokuttaraṃ adhicittaṃ. Paññāyapi eseva nayo. Tasmāti yasmā imāni tīṇi samaṇakaraṇīyāni, tasmā. Tibboti bahalo. Chandoti kattukamyatākusalacchando. Iti imasmiṃ suttante tisso sikkhā lokiyalokuttarā kathitāti.

82. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, `samaṇiyāni` means what belongs to an ascetic. `Samaṇakaraṇīyāni` means the duties to be performed by an ascetic. In phrases such as `adhisīlasikkhāsamādāna`, `samādāna` is said to be 'undertaking'; `adhisīlasikkhāsamādāna` is the undertaking and fulfilling of the training in higher virtue. For the remaining two terms as well, this is the method. And here, this division should be understood: virtue (`sīla`) and higher virtue (`adhisīla`); mind (`citta`) and higher mind (`adhicitta`); wisdom (`paññā`) and higher wisdom (`adhipaññā`). Therein, the five precepts are called `sīla`. In dependence on that, the ten precepts are called `adhisīla`. In dependence on that too, the fourfold purification virtue is called `adhisīla`. Furthermore, all worldly virtue is called `sīla`; supramundane virtue is `adhisīla`. That very thing, because it is to be trained in, is called `sikkhā`. Now, consciousness of the sensual sphere is called `citta`. In dependence on that, consciousness of the fine-material sphere is called `adhicitta`. In dependence on that too, consciousness of the immaterial sphere is called `adhicitta`. Furthermore, all worldly consciousness is just `citta`; supramundane consciousness is `adhicitta`. For wisdom too, this is the method. `Tasmā` means: because (`yasmā`) these three are the duties of an ascetic, therefore (`tasmā`). `Tibbo` means intense. `Chando` means wholesome desire, which is the wish to act. Thus, in this sutta, the three trainings are taught as worldly and supramundane.

2. Gadrabhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Gadrabha Sutta

83. Dutiye piṭṭhito piṭṭhitoti pacchato pacchato. Ahampi dammo ahampi dammoti ahampi “dammo dammamāno”ti vadamāno gāvīti. Seyyathāpi gunnanti yathā gāvīnaṃ. Gāvo hi kāḷāpi rattāpi setādivaṇṇāpi honti, gadrabhassa pana tādiso vaṇṇo nāma natthi. Yathā ca vaṇṇo, evaṃ saropi padampi aññādisameva. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Imasmimpi sutte tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitāti.

83. In the second sutta, `piṭṭhito piṭṭhito` means from behind, from behind. `Ahampi dammo ahampi dammo` means saying, “I too am a bull being tamed,” like cattle. `Seyyathāpi gunnaṃ` means just as for cattle. For cattle are black, red, and of colors such as white, but a donkey has no such color. And just as the color, so too the sound and the track are of a different kind. The rest has an obvious meaning. In this sutta too, the three trainings are taught as mixed.

3. Khettasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Khetta Sutta

84. Tatiye [V 2.0207] paṭikaccevāti paṭhamameva. Sukaṭṭhaṃ karotīti naṅgalena sukaṭṭhaṃ karoti. Sumatikatanti matiyā suṭṭhu samīkataṃ. Kālenāti vapitabbayuttakālena. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitā.

84. In the third discourse, 'paṭikacceva' means 'at the very first.' 'Sukaṭṭhaṃ karoti' means he makes it well-plowed with a plow. 'Sumatikatam' means made well-leveled with fine soil. 'Kālena' means at the appropriate time for sowing. The rest is clear. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of as mixed.

4. Vajjiputtasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Vajjiputta Sutta

85. Catutthe [M 2.0215] vajjiputtakoti vajjirājakulassa putto. Diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasatanti paṇṇāsādhikaṃ sikkhāpadasataṃ. Tasmiṃ samaye paññattāni sikkhāpadāneva sandhāyetaṃ [P 2.0347] vuttaṃ. So kira bhikkhu ajjavasampanno ujujātiko avaṅko akuṭilo, tasmā “ahaṃ ettakāni sikkhāpadāni rakkhituṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ vā na vā”ti cintetvā satthu ārocesi. Sakkomahanti sakkomi ahaṃ. So kira “ettakesu sikkhāpadesu sikkhantassa agaru tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhitu”nti maññamāno evamāha. Atha bhagavā yathā nāma paññāsa tiṇakalāpiyo ukkhipituṃ asakkontassa kalāpiyasataṃ bandhitvā sīse ṭhapeyya, evameva ekissāpi sikkhāya sikkhituṃ asakkontassa aparā dvepi sikkhā upari pakkhipanto tasmātiha tvaṃ bhikkhūtiādimāha. Sukhumālo kira uttaro nāma jānapadamanusso lohapāsādavihāre vasati. Atha naṃ daharabhikkhū āhaṃsu – “uttara, aggisālā ovassati, tiṇaṃ kappiyaṃ katvā dehī”ti. Taṃ ādāya aṭaviṃ gantvā tena lāyitaṃ tiṇaṃyeva karaḷe bandhitvā “paññāsa karaḷe gahetuṃ sakkhissasi uttarā”ti āhaṃsu. So “na sakkhissāmī”ti āha. Asītiṃ pana sakkhissasīti? Na sakkhissāmi, bhanteti. Ekaṃ karaḷasataṃ sakkhissasīti? Āma, bhante, gaṇhissāmīti. Daharabhikkhū karaḷasataṃ bandhitvā tassa sīse ṭhapayiṃsu. So ukkhipitvā nitthunanto gantvā aggisālāya samīpe pātesi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū “kilantarūposi uttarā”ti āhaṃsu. Āma, bhante, daharā bhikkhū maṃ vañcesuṃ, imaṃ ekampi karaḷasataṃ ukkhipituṃ asakkontaṃ maṃ “paṇṇāsa karaḷe ukkhipāhī”ti vadiṃsu. Āma, uttara, vañcayiṃsu tanti. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitā.

85. In the fourth Sutta, 'Vajjiputtaka' means a son of the Vajji royal family. 'Diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasata' refers to one hundred and fifty training rules. At that time, this was said referring only to the training rules that had been established. It is said that this monk was endowed with straightforwardness, upright by nature, not crooked, and not deceitful; therefore, considering, 'Might I be able to keep so many training rules, or not?' he informed the Teacher. 'Sakkomahaṃ' means 'I am able.' It is said that, thinking, 'For one training in so many training rules, it is not a burden to train in the three trainings,' he spoke thus. Then the Blessed One, just as for someone unable to lift fifty bundles of grass, one might bind a hundred bundles and place them on his head, in the very same way, for someone unable to train in even one training, he added the other two trainings on top, and therefore said, 'Therefore, monk,' and so on. It is said that a refined country-dweller named Uttara lived in the Lohapāsāda monastery. Then the young monks said to him, 'Uttara, the fire hall is leaking; make some grass allowable and give it to us.' Taking him to the forest, they tied the grass he had cut into bundles and asked, 'Uttara, will you be able to take fifty bundles?' He said, 'I will not be able.' 'But will you be able to take eighty?' they asked. 'I will not be able, venerable sirs.' 'Will you be able to take one hundred bundles?' 'Yes, venerable sirs, I will take them.' The young monks tied a hundred bundles and placed them on his head. He lifted them and, groaning as he went, dropped them near the fire hall. Then the monks asked him, 'Uttara, you look tired.' 'Yes, venerable sirs, the young monks deceived me. They told me, who am unable to lift even this one hundred bundles, to lift fifty bundles!' 'Yes, Uttara, they deceived you.' Thus should this example be understood. Here too, the three trainings are taught as being mixed.

5. Sekkhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Sekha Sutta

86. Pañcame [V 2.0208] ujumaggānusārinoti ujumaggo vuccati ariyamaggo, taṃ anussarantassa paṭipannakassāti attho. Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇanti paṭhamameva maggañāṇaṃ uppajjati. Maggo hi kilesānaṃ khepanato khayo nāma, taṃsampayuttaṃ [M 2.0216] ñāṇaṃ khayasmiṃ ñāṇaṃ nāma. Tato [P 2.0348] aññā anantarāti tato catutthamaggañāṇato anantarā aññā uppajjati, arahattaphalaṃ uppajjatīti attho. Aññāvimuttassāti arahattaphalavimuttiyā vimuttassa. Ñāṇaṃ ve hotīti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ hoti. Iti suttepi gāthāsupi satta sekhā kathitā. Avasāne pana khīṇāsavo dassitoti.

86. In the fifth sutta: Regarding 'following the straight path,' the straight path is called the Noble Path; the meaning is 'for one who practices by following along it.' Regarding 'the first knowledge in destruction,' it means that first, the path-knowledge itself arises. For the path is called destruction because of destroying the defilements; the knowledge associated with it is called 'knowledge in destruction.' Regarding 'Then immediately after, final knowledge,' it means that immediately after that fourth path-knowledge, final knowledge arises—the meaning is, the fruition of arahantship arises. Regarding 'of one liberated by final knowledge,' it means of one liberated by the liberation that is the fruition of arahantship. Regarding 'There is indeed knowledge,' it means reviewing knowledge arises. Thus, in both the sutta and the verses, seven learners are spoken of. At the end, however, the one whose taints are destroyed is shown.

6. Paṭhamasikkhāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Training Discourse

87. Chaṭṭhe attakāmāti attano hitakāmā. Yatthetaṃ sabbaṃ samodhānaṃ gacchatīti yāsu sikkhāsu sabbametaṃ diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasataṃ saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Paripūrakārī hotīti samattakārī hoti. Mattaso kārīti pamāṇena kārako, sabbena sabbaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti attho. Khuddānukhuddakānīti cattāri pārājikāni ṭhapetvā sesasikkhāpadāni. Tatrāpi saṅghādisesaṃ khuddakaṃ, thullaccayaṃ anukhuddakaṃ nāma. Thullaccayañca khuddakaṃ, pācittiyaṃ anukhuddakaṃ nāma, pācittiyañca khuddakaṃ, pāṭidesaniyadukkaṭadubbhāsitāni anukhuddakāni nāma. Ime pana aṅguttaramahānikāyavaḷañjanakaācariyā “cattāri pārājikāni ṭhapetvā sesāni sabbānipi khuddānukhuddakānī”ti vadanti. Tāni āpajjatipi vuṭṭhātipīti ettha pana khīṇāsavo tāva lokavajjaṃ nāpajjati, paṇṇattivajjameva āpajjati. Āpajjanto ca kāyenapi vācāyapi cittenapi āpajjati. Kāyena āpajjanto kuṭikārasahaseyyādīni āpajjati, vācāya āpajjanto sañcarittapadasodhammādīni, cittena āpajjanto rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇaṃ āpajjati. Sekkhesupi eseva nayo. Na hi mettha, bhikkhave, abhabbatā vuttāti, bhikkhave, na hi mayā ettha evarūpaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjane ca vuṭṭhāne ca ariyapuggalassa abhabbatā kathitā. Ādibrahmacariyakānīti [P 2.0349] maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāni cattāri mahāsīlasikkhāpadāni. Brahmacariyasāruppānīti tāniyeva catumaggabrahmacariyassa sāruppāni anucchavikāni. Tatthāti tesu sikkhāpadesu. Dhuvasīloti nibaddhasīlo. Ṭhitasīloti patiṭṭhitasīlo. Sotāpannoti sotasaṅkhātena [V 2.0209] maggena phalaṃ [M 2.0217] āpanno. Avinipātadhammoti catūsu apāyesu apatanasabhāvo. Niyatoti sotāpattimagganiyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti uparimaggattayasambodhiparāyaṇo.

6. In the sixth sutta: 'Attakāmā' means desiring one's own welfare. 'Yatthetaṃ sabbaṃ samodhānaṃ gacchati' means: in which trainings all these one hundred and fifty training rules are included. 'Paripūrakārī hoti' means one who fulfills completely. 'Mattaso kārī' means one who acts by measure, unable to do everything in every way; this is the meaning. 'Khuddānukhuddakāni' means the training rules remaining after setting aside the four pārājikas. Among them, the saṅghādisesa is minor, and the thullaccaya is called very minor. The thullaccaya is also minor, while the pācittiya is called very minor. The pācittiya is also minor, whereas the pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita are called very minor. However, the teachers who use the Aṅguttara Mahānikāya say, 'Setting aside the four pārājikas, all the remaining training rules are minor and very minor (khuddānukhuddakāni).' 'Tāni āpajjatipi vuṭṭhātipi': In this regard, a taint-destroyer (khīṇāsava) does not commit an offense that is blameworthy in the world; he commits only an offense established by rule. And when committing an offense, he commits it through body, speech, or mind. Committing through the body, one commits offenses such as those concerning building a hut and lying down together; committing through speech, one commits offenses such as those concerning acting as a go-between and teaching Dhamma word-by-word; committing through the mind, one commits the offense of accepting gold and silver. For trainees (sekkhas) also, this is the same method. 'Na hi mettha, bhikkhave, abhabbatā vuttā' means: 'Bhikkhus, it has not been stated by me that in this regard a noble person is incapable of committing such an offense or of rising from it.' 'Ādibrahmacariyakāni' means the four training rules of great virtue, which are the beginning of the noble practice of the path (maggabrahmacariya). 'Brahmacariyasāruppāni' means those very same rules are suitable and appropriate for the noble practice of the four paths. 'Tattha' means in those training rules. 'Dhuvasīlo' means of constant virtue. 'Ṭhitasīlo' means of established virtue. 'Sotāpanno' means one who has attained the fruit by means of the path designated as the stream. 'Avinipātadhammo' means having the nature of not falling into the four woeful states. 'Niyato' means one who is fixed by the certainty of the stream-entry path. 'Sambodhiparāyaṇo' means one whose destination is the enlightenment of the three higher paths.

Tanuttāti tanubhāvo. Sakadāgāmino hi rāgādayo abbhapaṭalaṃ viya macchikāpattaṃ viya ca tanukā honti, na bahalā. Orambhāgiyānanti heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ. Saṃyojanānanti bandhanānaṃ. Parikkhayāti parikkhayena. Opapātiko hotīti uppannako hoti. Tattha parinibbāyīti heṭṭhā anotaritvā upariyeva parinibbānadhammo. Anāvattidhammoti yonigativasena anāgamanadhammo.

87. ‘Tanuttā’ means the state of being subtle. Indeed, for the once-returner, defilements beginning with lust are subtle, like a layer of cloud and like a fly's wing; they are not thick. ‘Orambhāgiyānaṃ’ means of the lower part. ‘Saṃyojanānaṃ’ means of the fetters. ‘Parikkhayā’ means due to complete destruction. ‘Opapātiko hoti’ means he is spontaneously born. ‘Tattha parinibbāyī’ means, not having descended to the lower part, he is of the nature to attain parinibbāna only in the upper realm. ‘Anāvattidhammo’ means he is of the nature not to return by way of womb-birth.

Padesaṃ padesakārītiādīsu padesakārī puggalo nāma sotāpanno ca sakadāgāmī ca anāgāmī ca, so padesameva sampādeti. Paripūrakārī nāma arahā, so paripūrameva sampādeti. Avañjhānīti atucchāni saphalāni saudrayānīti attho. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missakāva kathitā.

In phrases such as ‘padesaṃ padesakārī,’ the person called a doer of a part is the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner; he accomplishes only a part. The one called a doer of the whole is the Arahant; he accomplishes the whole. ‘Avañjhāni’ means not empty, fruitful, and with increase; this is the meaning. Here also, the three trainings are taught as mixed.

7. Dutiyasikkhāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Training Discourse

88. Sattame kolaṃkoloti kulā kulaṃ gamanako. Kulanti cettha bhavo adhippeto, tasmā “dve vā tīṇi vā kulānī”ti etthapi dve vā tayo vā bhaveti attho veditabbo. Ayañhi dve vā bhave sandhāvati tayo vā, uttamakoṭiyā cha vā. Tasmā dve vā tīṇi vā cattāri vā pañca vā cha vāti evamettha vikappo daṭṭhabbo. Ekabījīti ekasseva bhavassa bījaṃ etassa atthīti ekabījī. Uddhaṃsototiādīsu atthi uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī, atthi [P 2.0350] uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī, atthi na uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī, atthi na uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī. Tattha yo idha anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā avihādīsu nibbatto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā uparūpari nibbattitvā akaniṭṭhaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana avihādīsu nibbatto tattheva aparinibbāyitvā akaniṭṭhampi appatvā uparimabrahmaloke parinibbāyati, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo ito cavitvā [M 2.0218] akaniṭṭheyeva nibbattati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana avihādīsu catūsu aññatarasmiṃ nibbattitvā tattheva parinibbāyati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma.

In the seventh sutta, 'kolaṃkola' means 'one who goes from family to family.' And here, by 'family' (kula), existence (bhava) is intended; therefore, in the phrase 'two or three families,' the meaning should be understood as 'two or three existences.' For this person transmigrates through two or three existences, or up to six in the highest case. Therefore, the variation here should be understood as two, three, four, five, or six existences. 'Ekabījī' means one for whom there is the seed for only a single existence. In the case of 'uddhaṃsota' (upward-flowing) and so on, there is: one who is upward-flowing, heading for Akaniṭṭha; one who is upward-flowing, not heading for Akaniṭṭha; one who is not upward-flowing, heading for Akaniṭṭha; and one who is not upward-flowing, not heading for Akaniṭṭha. Therein, one who, having attained the fruition of non-returning in this world, is reborn in the Avihā realm and so on, and having remained there for the full lifespan, is reborn in successively higher realms until reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, is called 'one who is upward-flowing, heading for Akaniṭṭha.' But one who, having been reborn in the Avihā realm and so on, without attaining final Nibbāna there and without reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains final Nibbāna in a higher brahma world, is called 'one who is upward-flowing, not heading for Akaniṭṭha.' One who, having passed away from here, is reborn directly in the Akaniṭṭha realm, is called 'one who is not upward-flowing, heading for Akaniṭṭha.' But one who, having been reborn in one of the four realms beginning with Avihā, attains final Nibbāna there itself, is called 'one who is not upward-flowing, not heading for Akaniṭṭha'.

Yattha [V 2.0210] katthaci uppanno pana sasaṅkhārena sappayogena arahattaṃ patto sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī nāma. Asaṅkhārena appayogena patto asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī nāma. Yo pana kappasahassāyukesu avihesu nibbattitvā pañcamaṃ kappasataṃ atikkamitvā arahattaṃ patto, ayaṃ upahaccaparinibbāyī nāma. Atappādīsupi eseva nayo. Antarāparinibbāyīti yo āyuvemajjhaṃ anatikkamitvā parinibbāyati, so tividho hoti. Kappasahassāyukesu tāva avihesu nibbattitvā eko nibbattadivaseyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce nibbattadivase pāpuṇāti, paṭhamassa pana kappasatassa matthake pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ paṭhamo antarāparinibbāyī. Aparo evaṃ asakkonto dvinnaṃ kappasatānaṃ matthake pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ dutiyo. Aparo evampi asakkonto catunnaṃ kappasatānaṃ matthake pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ tatiyo antarāparinibbāyī. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Furthermore, one who, having been reborn anywhere, attains Arahantship with exertion, with effort, is called one who attains parinibbāna with exertion. One who attains it without exertion, without effort, is called one who attains parinibbāna without exertion. Now, one who, having been reborn in the Aviha realms with a lifespan of a thousand eons, attains Arahantship after surpassing five hundred eons, is called an Upahacca-parinibbāyī. In the Atappa realms and so on, this is the same principle. An Antarā-parinibbāyī is one who attains parinibbāna without surpassing the middle of the lifespan; he is of three kinds. Firstly, having been reborn in the Aviha realms with a lifespan of a thousand eons, one attains Arahantship on the very day of rebirth. If he does not attain it on the day of rebirth, he then attains it at the end of the first hundred eons; this is the first Antarā-parinibbāyī. Another, being unable to do so, attains it at the end of two hundred eons; this is the second. Yet another, being unable to do so even thus, attains it at the end of four hundred eons; this is the third Antarā-parinibbāyī. The remainder is as has been stated.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā catuvīsati sotāpannā, dvādasa sakadāgāmino, aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāmino, dvādasa ca arahanto kathetabbā. Imasmiṃ hi sāsane saddhādhuraṃ paññādhuranti [P 2.0351] dve dhurāni, dukkhapaṭipadādandhābhiññādayo catasso paṭipadā. Tattheko saddhādhurena abhinivisitvā sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā ekameva bhavaṃ nibbattitvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayameko ekabījī. So paṭipadāvasena catubbidho hoti. Yathā cesa, evaṃ paññādhurena abhiniviṭṭhopīti aṭṭha ekabījino. Tathā kolaṃkolā sattakkhattuparamā cāti ime catuvīsati sotāpannā nāma. Tīsu pana vimokkhesu suññatavimokkhena sakadāgāmibhūmiṃ pattā catunnaṃ paṭipadānaṃ vasena cattāro sakadāgāmino, tathā animittavimokkhena pattā cattāro, appaṇihitavimokkhena pattā cattāroti ime dvādasa sakadāgāmino. Avihesu pana tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīti pañca anāgāmino, te asaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañca, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañcāti dasa honti, tathā atappādīsu. Akaniṭṭhesu pana uddhaṃsoto natthi[M 2.0219], tasmā tattha cattāro sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, cattāro asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti aṭṭha, ime aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāmino. Yathā pana sakadāgāmino, tatheva arahantopi dvādasa veditabbā. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitā.

Furthermore, in this connection, twenty-four stream-enterers, twelve once-returners, forty-eight non-returners, and twelve arahants should be spoken of. For in this Dispensation, there are two burdens—the burden of faith and the burden of wisdom—and four practices: painful practice with slow insight, and so forth. Therein, one who, having inclined by means of the burden of faith, having attained the fruit of stream-entry and being reborn in only one more existence, makes an end of suffering—this one is a one-seeder (`ekabījin`). He becomes fourfold by way of the practices. And just as this one is, so too one who has inclined by means of the burden of wisdom is also fourfold—thus, there are eight one-seeders. Likewise, the clan-to-clan (`kolaṅkola`) and the seven-times-at-most (`sattakkhattuparama`) are also eight each. Thus, these are the twenty-four named stream-enterers. Furthermore, among the three liberations, those who have attained the stage of a once-returner through the liberation of emptiness become four once-returners by way of the four practices; similarly, those who have attained through the signless liberation are four, and those who have attained through the desireless liberation are four—thus, these are the twelve once-returners. Furthermore, in the Aviha realms, there are three who attain parinibbāna in the interval (`antarāparinibbāyin`), one who attains parinibbāna upon landing (`upahaccaparinibbāyin`), and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (`uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmin`)—thus, there are five non-returners. They are five who attain parinibbāna without exertion (`asaṅkhāraparinibbāyin`) and five who attain parinibbāna with exertion (`sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyin`); thus, they are ten. It is similar in the Atappa and other realms. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realms, there is no one who goes upstream; therefore, there are four who attain parinibbāna with exertion and four who attain parinibbāna without exertion—thus, eight. These are the forty-eight non-returners. Furthermore, just as there are twelve once-returners, so too the arahants should be understood as twelve. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of as mixed.

8. Tatiyasikkhāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Third Discourse on the Trainings

89. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0211] taṃ vā pana anabhisambhavaṃ appaṭivijjhanti taṃ arahattaṃ apāpuṇanto appaṭivijjhanto. Iminā nayena sabbaṭṭhānesu attho veditabbo. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitā. Navamaṃ uttānatthameva. Idhāpi tisso sikkhā missikāva kathitā.

89. In the eighth discourse, 'not fully comprehending and not penetrating' means not attaining and not penetrating that fruit of arahantship. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of as mixed. The ninth discourse has a plain meaning. Here too, the three trainings are spoken of as mixed.

10. Dutiyasikkhattayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Three Trainings

91. Dasame āsavānaṃ khayāti ettha arahattamaggo adhipaññāsikkhā nāma. Phalaṃ pana sikkhitasikkhassa uppajjanato sikkhāti na vattabbaṃ.

91. In the tenth sutta, regarding the phrase 'from the destruction of the taints,' the path of Arahantship is called the training in higher wisdom. However, the fruit should not be called 'training,' because it arises for one whose training has been completed.

Yathā [P 2.0352] pure tathā pacchāti yathā paṭhamaṃ tīsu sikkhāsu sikkhati, pacchā tatheva sikkhatīti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Yathā adho tathā uddhanti yathā heṭṭhimakāyaṃ asubhavasena passati, uparimakāyampi tatheva pharati. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Yathā divā tathā rattinti yathā divā tisso sikkhā sikkhati, rattimpi tatheva sikkhatīti attho. Abhibhuyya disā sabbāti sabbā disā ārammaṇavasena abhibhavitvā. Appamāṇasamādhināti arahattamaggasamādhinā.
