'As before, so afterwards' means: just as one trains in the three trainings at first, so one trains in the same way afterwards. This is the meaning. The same method applies to the second phrase. 'As below, so above' means: just as one views the lower part of the body by way of unattractiveness, so too one views the upper part of the body. The same method applies to the second phrase. 'As by day, so by night' means: just as one trains in the three trainings by day, so one trains in the same way by night. This is the meaning. 'Having overcome all directions' means having overcome all directions by way of taking them as an object. 'With immeasurable concentration' means with the concentration associated with the path of Arahantship.

Sekkhanti sikkhamānaṃ sakaraṇīyaṃ. Paṭipadanti paṭipannakaṃ. Saṃsuddhacāriyanti saṃsuddhacaraṇaṃ parisuddhasīlaṃ. Sambuddhanti catusaccabuddhaṃ. Dhīraṃ paṭipadantagunti khandhadhīraāyatanadhīravasena dhīraṃ dhitisampannaṃ paṭipattiyā antaṃ gataṃ. Viññāṇassāti carimakaviññāṇassa. Taṇhākkhayavimuttinoti taṇhākkhayavimuttisaṅkhātāya arahattaphalavimuttiyā samannāgatassa. Pajjotasseva nibbānanti padīpanibbānaṃ viya. Vimokkho hoti cetasoti cittassa vimutti vimuccanā appavattibhāvo hoti. Taṇhākkhayavimuttino hi khīṇāsavassa carimakaviññāṇanirodhena [M 2.0220] parinibbānaṃ viya cetaso vimokkho hoti, na gataṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, apaṇṇattikabhāvūpagamoyeva hotīti attho.

'A learner' means one who is training, who has a task to be done. 'One on the path' means one who is practicing. 'Of pure conduct' means one of well-purified conduct, of perfectly pure morality. 'The Perfectly Enlightened One' means one who has awakened to the Four Truths. 'Steadfast, having reached the end of the practice' means one who is steadfast by way of steadfastness in the aggregates, sense bases, and elements; endowed with resolve; who has, by means of the practice, gone to the end, which is Nibbāna. 'Of consciousness' means of the final consciousness. 'Of one liberated by the destruction of craving' means of one endowed with the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, which is known as liberation by the destruction of craving. 'Like the extinguishing of a lamp' means like the extinguishing of a lamp. 'There is liberation of the mind' means there is the mind's liberation, its release, its state of non-recurrence. Indeed, for one liberated by the destruction of craving, an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, with the cessation of the final consciousness there is a liberation of the mind like Parinibbāna; a destination is not discerned, it is simply the attainment of a state beyond designation. This is the meaning.

11. Saṅkavāsuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Saṅkavā Sutta

92. Ekādasame [V 2.0212] saṅkavā nāma kosalānaṃ nigamoti saṅkavāti evaṃnāmako kosalaraṭṭhe nigamo. Āvāsikoti bhārahāro nave āvāse samuṭṭhāpeti, purāṇe paṭijaggati. Sikkhāpadapaṭisaṃyuttāyāti sikkhāsaṅkhātehi padehi paṭisaṃyuttāya, tīhi sikkhāhi samannāgatāyāti attho. Sandassetīti [P 2.0353] sammukhe viya katvā dasseti. Samādapetīti gaṇhāpeti. Samuttejetīti samussāheti. Sampahaṃsetīti paṭiladdhaguṇehi vaṇṇaṃ kathento vodāpeti. Adhisallikhateti ativiya sallikhati, ativiya sallikhitaṃ katvā saṇhaṃ saṇhaṃ kathetīti attho.

92. In the eleventh discourse, regarding 'Saṅkava, a market town of the Kosalans,' Saṅkava is a market town of that name in the Kosala country. 'Resident' (āvāsiko) means one who carries the burden, establishes new dwellings, and maintains old ones. 'Connected with the training rules' (sikkhāpadapaṭisaṃyuttāya) means connected with the items called 'training,' that is, endowed with the three trainings. 'He shows' (sandasseti) means he shows as if face to face. 'He encourages' (samādapeti) means he causes one to take it up. 'He inspires' (samuttejeti) means he urges on. 'He gladdens' (sampahaṃseti) means he purifies by speaking praise of the virtues attained. 'He polishes exceedingly' (adhisallikhateti) means he polishes exceedingly; having polished exceedingly, he speaks finely and subtly: this is the meaning.

Accayoti aparādho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma adhibhavitvā pavatto. Ahudeva akkhantīti ahosiyeva anadhivāsanā. Ahu appaccayoti ahosi atuṭṭhākāro. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti anāgate saṃvaratthāya, puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa khalitassa vā akaraṇatthāyāti attho. Tagghāti ekaṃsena. Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosīti yathā dhammo ṭhito, tathā karosi, khamāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ tava aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Vuddhihesā, kassapa, ariyassa vinayeti esā kassapa buddhassa bhagavato sāsane vuddhi nāma. Katamā? Yāyaṃ accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaritvā āyatiṃ saṃvarāpajjanā. Desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto “yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti āha. Na sikkhākāmoti tisso sikkhā na kāmeti na pattheti na piheti. Sikkhāsamādānassāti sikkhāparipūraṇassa. Na vaṇṇavādīti guṇaṃ na katheti. Kālenāti yuttappayuttakālena. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

‘Transgression’ (accayo) means offense. ‘He transgressed against me’ (maṃ accagamā) means he overstepped, overpowered, and proceeded against me. ‘There was indeed intolerance’ (ahudeva akkhantī) means there was indeed non-endurance. ‘There was resentment’ (ahu appaccayo) means there was a state of displeasure. ‘May he accept’ (paṭiggaṇhātu) means may he forgive. ‘For restraint in the future’ (āyatiṃ saṃvarāya) means for the sake of restraint in the future, so that such an offense, fault, or slip may not occur again: this is the meaning. ‘Certainly’ (taggha) means assuredly. ‘You make amends according to the Dhamma’ (yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi) means you act as the Dhamma stands, you seek forgiveness: this is what is meant. ‘We accept it from you’ (taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma) means we forgive that offense of yours. ‘This, Kassapa, is growth in the Noble One’s discipline’ (vuddhi hesā, kassapa, ariyassa vinaye) means this, Kassapa, is called growth in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What is it? It is this: seeing a transgression as a transgression, making amends according to the Dhamma, and undertaking future restraint. But when giving a teaching based on a person, he says: ‘One who sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint in the future.’ ‘Not desiring the training’ (na sikkhākāmo) means one does not desire, does not wish for, and does not long for the three trainings. ‘Of undertaking the training’ (sikkhāsamādānassa) means of one who perfects the training. ‘Not praising’ (na vaṇṇavādī) means one does not speak of qualities. ‘In time’ (kālena) means at a suitable and proper time. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Samaṇavaggo catuttho.

The Chapter on Ascetics is the fourth.

(10) 5. Loṇakapallavaggo

(10) 5. The Chapter on the Lump of Salt

1. Accāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Accāyika Sutta

93. Pañcamassa [V 2.0213][M 2.0221][P 2.0354] paṭhame accāyikānīti atipātikāni. Karaṇīyānīti avassakiccāni. Yañhi na avassaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ kiccanti vuccati. Avassaṃ kātabbaṃ karaṇīyaṃ nāma. Sīghaṃ sīghanti vegena vegena. Tassa kho tanti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ. Natthi sā iddhi vā ānubhāvo vāti sā vā iddhi so vā ānubhāvo natthi. Uttarasveti tatiyadivase. Utupariṇāminīti laddhautupariṇāmāni hutvā. Jāyantipīti tatiyadivase nikkhantasetaṅkurāni honti, sattāhe patte nīlaṅkurāni honti. Gabbhīnipi hontīti diyaḍḍhamāsaṃ patvā gahitagabbhāni honti. Paccantipīti tayo māse patvā paccanti. Idāni yasmā buddhānaṃ gahapatikena vā sassehi vā attho natthi, sāsane pana tappaṭirūpakaṃ puggalaṃ vā atthaṃ vā dassetuṃ taṃ taṃ opammaṃ āharanti. Tasmā yamatthaṃ dassetukāmena etaṃ ābhataṃ, taṃ dassento evameva khotiādimāha. Taṃ atthato uttānameva. Sikkhā pana idhāpi missikā eva kathitā.

93. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, 'urgent matters' (accāyikāni) means extremely pressing matters. 'Necessary tasks' (karaṇīyāni) means duties that must be done. For that which does not necessarily have to be done is called a 'duty' (kicca), whereas that which must necessarily be done is called a 'necessary task' (karaṇīya). 'Quickly, quickly' (sīghaṃ sīghaṃ) means with great speed. In the phrase 'tassa kho taṃ,' the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. 'There is no such power or influence' means that neither that power nor that influence exists. 'The day after tomorrow' (uttarasve) means on the third day. 'Subject to seasonal change' (utupariṇāminī) means having undergone seasonal change. 'They also sprout' (jāyanti pi) means that on the third day white sprouts emerge, and upon reaching the seventh day, they become green sprouts. 'They also become pregnant' (gabbhīni pi honti) means that after a month and a half, they have taken seed. 'They also ripen' (paccanti pi) means that after three months, they ripen. Now, since the Buddhas have no need for a householder or for crops, they bring forth a particular simile in the Teaching to illustrate a corresponding person or meaning. Therefore, showing the meaning for which this simile was brought, He said, 'Even so,' etc. The meaning of that is indeed clear. Here, too, the trainings are spoken of as mixed.

2. Pavivekasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Paviveka Sutta

94. Dutiye cīvarapavivekanti cīvaraṃ nissāya uppajjanakakilesehi vivittabhāvaṃ. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Sāṇānīti sāṇavākacelāni. Masāṇānīti missakacelāni. Chavadussānīti matasarīrato chaḍḍitavatthāni, erakatiṇādīni vā ganthetvā katanivāsanāni. Paṃsukūlānīti pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍitanantakāni. Tirīṭānīti rukkhatacavatthāni. Ajinānīti [P 2.0355] ajinamigacammāni. Ajinakkhipanti tadeva majjhe phālitaṃ, sahakhurakantipi vadanti. Kusacīranti kusatiṇāni ganthetvā katacīraṃ. Vākacīraphalakacīresupi eseva nayo. Kesakambalanti manussakesehi katakambalaṃ. Vālakambalanti assavālādīhi katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhikanti ulūkapattāni ganthetvā katanivāsanaṃ.

94. In the second discourse, 'seclusion regarding robes' (cīvarapaviveka) means the state of being secluded from the defilements that arise dependent on robes. This same method applies to the other two terms. 'Hempen cloths' (sāṇāni) means cloths woven from hemp fibre. 'Mixed-fibre cloths' (masāṇāni) means mixed cloths. 'Shroud cloths' (chavadussāni) means cloths discarded from a dead body, or lower garments made by weaving together eraka grass and so on. 'Rag-robes' (paṃsukūlāni) means ownerless cloths discarded on the ground. 'Bark garments' (tirīṭāni) means garments made from tree bark. 'Antelope hides' (ajināni) means black antelope skins. 'A hide garment' (ajinakkhipa) means that same skin, split in the middle; it is also said to be that same skin, complete with its hooves. 'Kusa-grass garment' (kusacīra) means a robe made by weaving kusa grass. This same method also applies to bark-fibre robes and wood-strip robes. 'A hair blanket' (kesakambala) means a blanket made from human hair. 'A horse-hair blanket' (vālakambala) means a blanket made from horse-tail hair and so on. 'An owl-feather garment' (ulūkapakkhika) means a lower garment made by weaving owl feathers.

Sākabhakkhāti [V 2.0214][M 2.0222] allasākabhakkhā. Sāmākabhakkhāti sāmākataṇḍulabhakkhā. Nīvārādīsu nīvārā nāma araññe sayaṃ jātavīhijāti. Daddulanti cammakārehi cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. Haṭaṃ vuccati silesopi sevālopi kaṇikārādirukkhaniyyāsopi. Kaṇanti kuṇḍakaṃ. Ācāmoti bhattaukkhalikāya laggo jhāmaodano. Taṃ chaḍḍitaṭṭhāne gahetvā khādanti, odanakañjiyantipi vadanti. Piññākādayo pākaṭāva. Pavattaphalabhojīti patitaphalabhojī. Bhusāgāranti khalasālaṃ.

'Eaters of greens' (sākabhakkhā) means eaters of fresh greens. 'Eaters of sāmāka' (sāmākabhakkhā) means eaters of sāmāka rice grains. Among 'wild rice' (nīvāra) and so on, 'nīvāra' is a species of grain that grows by itself in the forest. 'Scraps' (daddula) means the scrapings discarded by leather workers after scraping a hide. 'Haṭaṃ' is said of tree resin, algae, and also the resin of trees such as the kaṇikāra. 'Broken rice' (kaṇa) means rice bran. 'Scum' (ācāma) is the burnt scrap of rice sticking to the rice pot; they take and eat it from the place where it was discarded. It is also said to be rice gruel. 'Eaters of oil-seed cakes' (piññākādayo) and so on are well-known. 'One who eats fallen fruit' (pavattaphalabhojī) means one who eats fruit that has fallen by itself. 'A chaff-shed' (bhusāgāra) means a shed on a threshing floor.

Sīlavāti catupārisuddhisīlena samannāgato. Dussīlyañcassa pahīnaṃ hotīti pañca dussīlyāni pahīnāni honti. Sammādiṭṭhikoti yāthāvadiṭṭhiko. Micchādiṭṭhīti ayāthāvadiṭṭhi. Āsavāti cattāro āsavā. Aggappattoti sīlaggappatto. Sārappattoti sīlasāraṃ patto. Suddhoti parisuddho. Sāre patiṭṭhitoti sīlasamādhipaññāsāre patiṭṭhito.

'Virtuous' (sīlavā) means one who is endowed with the fourfold purity of virtue. 'And his immorality is abandoned' means that the five kinds of immorality are abandoned. 'One with right view' (sammādiṭṭhika) means one who sees things as they are. 'Wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi) means a view that is not as things are. 'Taints' (āsavā) means the four taints. 'One who has reached the peak' (aggappatta) means one who has reached the peak of virtue. 'One who has reached the essence' (sārappatta) means one who has attained the essence of virtue. 'Pure' (suddha) means purified. 'Established in the essence' (sāre patiṭṭhita) means established in the essence of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Seyyathāpīti yathā nāma. Sampannanti [P 2.0356] paripuṇṇaṃ paripakkasālibharitaṃ. Saṅgharāpeyyāti saṅkaḍḍhāpeyya. Ubbahāpeyyāti khalaṭṭhānaṃ āharāpeyya. Bhusikanti bhusaṃ. Koṭṭāpeyyāti udukkhale pakkhipāpetvā musalehi paharāpeyya. Aggappattānīti taṇḍulaggaṃ pattāni. Sārappattādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Yaṃ panettha “dussīlyañcassa pahīnaṃ micchādiṭṭhi cassa pahīnā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ sotāpattimaggena pahīnabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Seyyathāpi means just as. Sampannaṃ means full, filled with ripe rice. Saṅgharāpeyya means one should have it collected. Ubbahāpeyya means one should have it brought to the threshing floor. Bhusikaṃ means chaff. Koṭṭāpeyya means one should have it placed in a small mortar and have it struck with pestles. Aggappattāni means having reached the state of being the best of rice grains. In sārappatta, etc., this is the method. The remainder is just clear. As for what is said here, "his immorality is abandoned and his wrong view is abandoned," it should be known that this is said with reference to the state of being abandoned by the path of stream-entry.

3. Saradasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sarada Sutta.

95. Tatiye viddheti valāhakavigamena dūrībhūte. Deveti ākāse. Abhivihaccāti abhivihanitvā. Yatoti yasmiṃ kāle. Virajanti rāgarajādirahitaṃ. Tesaṃyeva malānaṃ vigatattā vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti catusaccadhammapariggāhakaṃ sotāpattimaggacakkhuṃ. Natthi taṃ saṃyojananti duvidhamevassa saṃyojanaṃ natthi, itarampi pana puna imaṃ lokaṃ ānetuṃ asamatthatāya natthīti vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte jhānānāgāmī nāma kathitoti.

95. In the third sutta, viddhe means having become distant due to the absence of clouds. Deve means in the sky. Abhivihacca means having dispelled. Yato means at which time. Virajaṃ means free from the dust of passion and so on. Vītamalaṃ means stainless, due to the departure of those very stains. Dhammacakkhuṃ means the eye of the stream-entry path, which comprehends the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Regarding 'there is no fetter for him,' for that person, there is no fetter of two kinds; furthermore, it is said that the other fetter is also non-existent because of its inability to bring him back to this world of sense-pleasures again. In this sutta, the one called a non-returner by way of jhāna is taught.

4. Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Assemblies Sutta.

96. Catutthe [V 2.0215] na bāhulikā hontīti paccayabāhullikā na honti. Na sāthalikāti tisso sikkhā sithilaṃ katvā na gaṇhanti. Okkamane nikkhittadhurāti [M 2.0223] okkamanaṃ vuccati avagamanaṭṭhena pañca nīvaraṇāni, tesu nikkhittadhurā. Paviveke pubbaṅgamāti kāyacittaupadhivivekasaṅkhāte tividhepi viveke pubbaṅgamā. Vīriyaṃ ārabhantīti duvidhampi vīriyaṃ paggaṇhanti. Appattassāti jhānavipassanāmaggaphalasaṅkhātassa appattavisesassa. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Pacchimā [P 2.0357] janatāti saddhivihārikaantevāsikādayo. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatīti ācariyupajjhāyehi kataṃ anukaroti. Yaṃ tāya janatāya ācariyupajjhāyesu diṭṭhaṃ, tassa anugatiṃ āpajjati nāma. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, aggavatī parisāti, bhikkhave, ayaṃ parisā aggapuggalavatī nāma vuccati.

96. In the fourth sutta, 'they are not indulgent' means they are not excessive in requisites. 'They are not negligent' means they do not hold the three trainings loosely. Regarding 'they have laid down the burden regarding obstacles,' 'obstacle' (okkamana) is said in the sense of 'going down,' referring to the five hindrances; they are those who have laid down the burden in those. 'They are foremost in seclusion' means they are foremost in all three kinds of seclusion, namely, seclusion of body, mind, and attachments. 'They arouse energy' means they exert both kinds of energy. 'For what is unattained' refers to the special unattained, described as jhāna, insight, path, and fruit. The remaining two phrases follow the same pattern. 'The later generation' refers to co-resident pupils, resident pupils, and so forth. 'They follow what they have seen' means they imitate what has been done by their teachers and preceptors. Whatever has been seen by that generation in their teachers and preceptors, they follow that. 'This, monks, is called the leading assembly' means, monks, this assembly is called the one possessing leading individuals.

Bhaṇḍanajātāti jātabhaṇḍanā. Kalahajātāti jātakalahā. Bhaṇḍananti cettha kalahassa pubbabhāgo, hatthaparāmāsādivasena vītikkamo kalaho nāma. Vivādāpannāti viruddhavādaṃ āpannā. Mukhasattīhīti guṇavijjhanaṭṭhena pharusā vācā “mukhasattiyo”ti vuccanti, tāhi mukhasattīhi. Vitudantā viharantīti vijjhantā vicaranti.

‘Bhaṇḍanajātā’ means that quarrels have arisen. ‘Kalahajātā’ means that contentions have arisen. And here, ‘bhaṇḍana’ is the preliminary stage of ‘kalaha’; ‘kalaha’ is transgression by way of physical contact and so on. ‘Vivādāpannā’ means having fallen into contradictory speech. ‘Mukhasattīhi’: harsh speech is called ‘mouth-darts’ in the sense of piercing good qualities; with those mouth-darts. ‘Vitudantā viharanti’ means they go about piercing.

Samaggāti sahitā. Sammodamānāti samappavattamodā. Khīrodakībhūtāti khīrodakaṃ viya bhūtā. Piyacakkhūhīti upasantehi mettacakkhūhi. Pīti jāyatīti pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajjati. Kāyo passambhatīti nāmakāyopi rūpakāyopi vigatadaratho hoti. Passaddhakāyoti asāraddhakāyo. Sukhaṃ vediyatīti kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ vediyati. Samādhiyatīti ārammaṇe sammā ṭhapīyati.

'United' means being together. 'Rejoicing together' means having joy that proceeds harmoniously. 'Having become like milk and water' means having become like milk and water. 'With kind eyes' means with calmed, loving eyes. 'Joy arises' means five kinds of joy arise. 'The body becomes tranquil' means both the mental body and the physical body become free from distress. 'One with a tranquil body' means one with an unperturbed body. 'They feel happiness' means they experience bodily and mental happiness. 'The mind becomes concentrated' means it is properly established on its object.

Thullaphusitaketi mahāphusitake. Pabbatakandarapadarasākhāti ettha kandaro nāma “ka”nti laddhanāmena udakena dārito udakabhinno pabbatappadeso, yo “nitambho”tipi “nadikuñjo”tipi vuccati. Padaraṃ nāma aṭṭha māse deve avassante phalito bhūmippadeso. Sākhāti kusobbhagāminiyo khuddakamātikāyo. Kusobbhāti khuddakaāvāṭā. Mahāsobbhāti mahāāvāṭā. Kunnadiyoti khuddakanadiyo. Mahānadiyoti [P 2.0358] gaṅgāyamunādikā mahāsaritā.

'Thullaphusitake' means having large raindrops. Regarding 'Pabbatakandarapadarasākhā': here, 'kandara' is a mountain region split by water that has received the name 'kaṃ', a region broken by water, which is also called 'nitambha' or 'nadikuñja.' 'Padara' is a region of land that has cracked when the sky has not rained for eight months. 'Sākhā' means small channels leading to small hollows. 'Kusobbhā' means small hollows. 'Mahāsobbhā' means large hollows. 'Kunnadiyo' means small rivers. 'Mahānadiyo' means great rivers such as the Ganges and Yamuna.

5-7. Paṭhamaājānīyasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-7. Commentary on the First Thoroughbred Sutta, etc.

97-99. Pañcame [V 2.0216][M 2.0224] aṅgehīti guṇaṅgehi. Rājārahoti rañño araho anucchaviko. Rājabhoggoti rañño upabhogabhūto. Rañño aṅganti rañño hatthapādādiaṅgasamatāya aṅganteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Vaṇṇasampannoti sarīravaṇṇena sampanno. Balasampannoti kāyabalena sampanno. Āhuneyyoti āhutisaṅkhātaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto. Pāhuneyyoti pāhunakabhattassa anucchaviko. Dakkhiṇeyyoti dasavidhadānavatthupariccāgavasena saddhādānasaṅkhātāya dakkhiṇāya anucchaviko. Añjalikaraṇīyoti añjalipaggahaṇassa anucchaviko. Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassāti sabbalokassa asadisaṃ puññaviruhanaṭṭhānaṃ.

In the fifth, 'aṅgehi' means with the factors that are virtues. 'Rājāraho' means worthy of a king, appropriate. 'Rājabhoggo' means fit for the king's use and enjoyment. 'Rañño aṅgaṃ' means it is reckoned as a very factor of the king, due to its similarity to the king's limbs such as his hands and feet. 'Vaṇṇasampanno' means endowed with beauty of form. 'Balasampanno' means endowed with physical strength. 'Āhuneyyo' means worthy of offerings brought from afar. 'Pāhuneyyo' means worthy of a meal for guests. 'Dakkhiṇeyyo' means worthy of a donation given in faith. 'Añjalikaraṇīyo' means worthy of reverential salutation. 'Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā' means the unsurpassed field of merit for the world; an incomparable place for the sprouting of merit for the entire world.

Vaṇṇasampannoti guṇavaṇṇena sampanno. Balasampannoti vīriyabalena sampanno. Javasampannoti ñāṇajavena sampanno. Thāmavāti ñāṇathāmena samannāgato. Daḷhaparakkamoti thiraparakkamo. Anikkhittadhuroti aṭṭhapitadhuro paggahitadhuro, aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ appatvā vīriyadhuraṃ na nikkhipissāmīti evaṃ paṭipanno. Imasmiṃ sutte catusaccavasena sotāpattimaggo, sotāpattimaggena ca ñāṇajavasampannatā kathitāti. Chaṭṭhe tīṇi ca maggāni tīṇi ca phalāni, tīhi maggaphalehi ca ñāṇajavasampannatā kathitā. Sattame arahattaphalaṃ, arahattaphaleneva ca maggakiccaṃ kathitaṃ. Phalaṃ pana javitajavena uppajjanato javoti ca vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

'Endowed with beauty' means endowed with the beauty that is virtue. 'Endowed with strength' means endowed with the strength that is effort. 'Endowed with swiftness' means endowed with the swiftness that is wisdom. 'Possessing stamina' means endowed with the stamina that is wisdom. 'Of firm exertion' means one of steadfast exertion. 'One who has not laid down the burden' means one who has not put down the yoke, who practices thus: "Until I attain the supreme fruit, Arahantship, I will not lay down the yoke that is effort." In this fifth sutta, by way of the four truths, the path of stream-entry is taught, and by the path of stream-entry itself, the state of being endowed with the swiftness that is wisdom is taught. In the sixth, the three paths and the three fruits are taught, and by the three paths and fruits, the state of being endowed with the swiftness that is wisdom is taught. In the seventh, the fruit of Arahantship is taught, and by the fruit of Arahantship itself, the function of the path is taught. But as for the fruit, because it arises with the swiftness of an impulsion, it is also fitting to be called 'swiftness'.

8. Potthakasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta.

100. Aṭṭhame [P 2.0359] navoti karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccati. Potthakoti vākamayavatthaṃ. Majjhimoti paribhogamajjhimo. Jiṇṇoti paribhogajiṇṇo. Ukkhaliparimajjananti ukkhaliparipuñchanaṃ dussīloti nissīlo. Dubbaṇṇatāyāti guṇavaṇṇābhāvena dubbaṇṇatāya. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjantīti tena kataṃ anukaronti. Na mahapphalaṃ hotīti vipākaphalena mahapphalaṃ na hoti. Na mahānisaṃsanti vipākānisaṃseneva na mahānisaṃsaṃ. Appagghatāyāti [M 2.0225] vipākagghena appagghatāya. Kāsikaṃ vatthanti tīhi kappāsaaṃsūhi suttaṃ kantitvā katavatthaṃ, tañca kho kāsiraṭṭheyeva uṭṭhitaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Sīlaṃ panettha missakaṃ kathitanti.

100. In the eighth, 'new' is said with reference to its making. 'A coarse cloth' means a garment made of bark fiber. 'Medium' means of medium use. 'Worn out' means worn out through use. 'A pot-wiper' means a cloth for wiping a rice-pot. 'Of bad virtue' means without virtue. 'Due to ugliness' means due to the absence of the beauty of virtue, due to having a bad appearance. 'They fall into imitation' means they imitate the deeds done by that person. 'It is not of great fruit' means with respect to the resultant fruit, it is not of great fruit. 'It is not of great benefit' means with respect to the resultant benefit, it is not of great benefit. 'Due to being of little value' means due to being of little value with respect to the price that is the result. 'Kāsi cloth' means a cloth made by spinning thread from three strands of cotton fiber, and that, indeed, is produced only in the Kāsi country. The rest is clear. Herein, mixed virtue—that is, mixed mundane and supramundane virtue—is taught.

9. Loṇakapallasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Loṇakapalla Sutta

101. Navame [V 2.0217] yathā yathāyanti yathā yathā ayaṃ. Tathā tathā tanti tathā tathā taṃ kammaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo evaṃ vadeyya – “yathā yathā kammaṃ karoti, tathā tathāssa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyateva. Na hi sakkā katassa kammassa vipākaṃ paṭisedhetuṃ. Tasmā yattakaṃ kammaṃ karoti, tattakassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyatevā”ti. Evaṃ santanti evaṃ sante. Brahmacariyavāso na hotīti yaṃ maggabhāvanato pubbe upapajjavedanīyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, tassa avassaṃ paṭisaṃvedanīyattā brahmacariyaṃ vutthampi avutthameva hoti. Okāso na paññāyati sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyāti yasmā ca evaṃ sante tena kammāyūhanañceva vipākānubhavanā ca hoti, tasmā hetunā nayena vaṭṭadukkhassa antakiriyāya okāso na paññāyati nāma.

101. In the ninth [sutta], yathā yathāyaṃ is to be parsed as yathā yathā ayaṃ (in whatever way this person...). Tathā tathā taṃ means 'in that very way that kamma...'. This is what is meant: whoever would say thus, 'In whatever way one performs kamma, in that very way one certainly experiences its result. For it is not possible to prevent the result of kamma that has been done. Therefore, whatever amount of kamma one performs, one certainly experiences the result of that amount.' If it is so, 'the living of the holy life does not occur' is because whatever kamma to be experienced in a subsequent rebirth was done before the development of the path, since it must inevitably be experienced, the holy life, even though lived, is as if not lived. 'An opportunity is not seen for the complete ending of suffering' is because, this being so, for that person there is both the accumulation of kamma and the experiencing of its result; therefore, by this reasoning, an opportunity for making an end of the suffering of the round is indeed not seen.

Yathā yathā vedanīyanti yena yenākārena veditabbaṃ. Tathā [P 2.0360] tathāssa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyatīti tena tenākārena assa vipākaṃ paccanubhoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadetaṃ sattasu javanesu paṭhamajavanakammaṃ sati paccaye vipākavāraṃ labhantameva diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ hoti, asati ahosikammaṃ nāma. Yañca sattamajavanakammaṃ sati paccaye upapajjavedanīyaṃ hoti, asati ahosikammaṃ nāma. Yañca majjhe pañcajavanakammaṃ yāva saṃsārappavatti, tāva aparapariyāyavedanīyaṃ nāma hoti. Etesu ākāresu yena yenākārena veditabbaṃ kammaṃ ayaṃ puriso karoti, tena tenevassa vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyati nāma. Aṭṭhakathāyañhi laddhavipākavārameva kammaṃ yathāvedanīyaṃ kammaṃ nāmāti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyavāso hotīti kammakkhayakarassa brahmacariyassa khepetabbakammasambhavato vāso nāma hoti, vutthaṃ suvutthameva hotīti [M 2.0226] attho. Okāso paññāyati sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyāti yasmā evaṃ sante tena tena maggena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena tesu tesu bhavesu āyatiṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ na uppajjati, tasmā okāso paññāyati sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya.

‘In whatever way it is to be experienced’ means: in whatever manner it is to be experienced. ‘In that very way one experiences its result’ means: in that very manner one experiences the result of that kamma. This is what is meant: Among the seven impulsions, the kamma of the first impulsion, when a condition is present, obtains its turn to give a result and is to be experienced in the present existence; when a condition is absent, it is called defunct kamma. And the kamma of the seventh impulsion, when a condition is present, is to be experienced in the next existence; when a condition is absent, it is called defunct kamma. And the kamma of the five impulsions in the middle, for as long as the round of saṃsāra continues, is called kamma to be experienced in successive existences. Among these manners, in whatever manner a person performs kamma that is to be experienced, in that very manner is it called that one experiences its result. For in the Commentary, it is said that only kamma which has obtained its turn to give a result is called 'kamma to be experienced in such and such a way'. ‘Thus, bhikkhus, there is the living of the holy life’ means: it is called a 'living' because of the possibility of kamma-to-be-exhausted through the holy life which brings about the destruction of kamma; the meaning is that the holy life, having been lived, is indeed well-lived. ‘An opportunity is discerned for the complete ending of suffering’ means: because, this being so, through the cessation of consciousness connected with formations by that noble path, the suffering of the round does not arise in the future in those various existences, therefore an opportunity is discerned for the complete ending of suffering.

Idāni taṃ yathāvedanīyakammasabhāvaṃ dassento idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassātiādimāha. Tattha appamattakanti parittaṃ thokaṃ mandaṃ lāmakaṃ. Tādisaṃyevāti taṃsarikkhakameva. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyanti tasmiṃ kammeyeva diṭṭhadhamme vipaccitabbaṃ vipākavāraṃ labhantaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ hoti. Nāṇupi khāyatīti dutiye attabhāve aṇupi na khāyati, aṇumattampi dutiye attabhāve [V 2.0218] vipākaṃ na detīti attho. Bahudevāti [P 2.0361] bahukaṃ pana vipākaṃ kimeva dassatīti adhippāyo. Abhāvitakāyotiādīhi kāyabhāvanārahito vaṭṭagāmī puthujjano dassito. Parittoti parittaguṇo. Appātumoti ātumā vuccati attabhāvo, tasmiṃ mahantepi guṇaparittatāya appātumoyeva. Appadukkhavihārīti appakenapi pāpena dukkhavihārī. Bhāvitakāyotiādīhi khīṇāsavo dassito. So hi kāyānupassanāsaṅkhātāya kāyabhāvanāya bhāvitakāyo nāma. Kāyassa vā vaḍḍhitattā bhāvitakāyo. Bhāvitasīloti vaḍḍhitasīlo. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Pañcadvārabhāvanāya vā bhāvitakāyo. Etena indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ, bhāvitasīloti iminā sesāni tīṇi sīlāni. Aparittoti na parittaguṇo. Mahattoti attabhāve parittepi guṇamahantatāya mahatto. Appamāṇavihārīti khīṇāsavassetaṃ nāmameva. So hi pamāṇakarānaṃ rāgādīnaṃ abhāvena appamāṇavihārī nāma.

Now, wishing to show the nature of that kamma to be experienced in a certain way, He said the words beginning with, 'Here, bhikkhus, for a certain person...'. Therein, 'a trifling kamma' means little, slight, feeble, inferior. 'Of such a kind indeed' means just like that kamma. 'To be experienced in this very life' means: the kamma that obtains the turn for its result to be ripened in this very life itself is called 'to be experienced in this very life'. 'Not even a little is seen' means: not even a little result appears in a second existence; it does not give even a slight result in a second existence—this is the meaning. 'Let alone much' implies: how then could it give a great result? By the words beginning with 'undeveloped in body', an ordinary person who goes to the round of existence, devoid of body-development, is shown. 'Limited' means of limited virtue. 'Of little self' means: 'existence' is called 'self'; even though that existence is great, due to the limitedness of his virtues, he is indeed 'of little self'. 'Dwelling in suffering from a little' means dwelling in suffering even due to a minor evil deed. By the words beginning with 'developed in body', one whose taints are destroyed is shown. For he is indeed called 'one with a developed body' by the body-development known as the contemplation of the body. Or, because of the development of the body, he is 'one with a developed body'. 'Developed in virtue' means increased in virtue. This is the method in the remaining two phrases as well. Or, he is 'one with a developed body' due to development at the five sense doors. By this, the virtue of restraint of the faculties is stated; by 'developed in virtue', the remaining three virtues are stated. 'Unlimited' means not of limited virtue. 'Great' means: even though his existence is limited, due to the greatness of his virtues, he is called 'great'. 'Dwelling without measure' is just a name for one whose taints are destroyed. For he is called 'one who dwells without measure' due to the absence of lust, etc., which create measure.

Paritteti khuddake. Udakamallaketi udakasarāve. Orabbhikoti urabbhasāmiko. Urabbhaghātakoti sūnakāro. Jāpetuṃ vāti dhanajāniyā jāpetuṃ. Jhāpetuntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Yathāpaccayaṃ vā kātunti yathā icchati, tathā kātuṃ. Urabbhadhananti eḷakaagghanakamūlaṃ. So panassa sace icchati, deti. No ce icchati, gīvāyaṃ gahetvā [M 2.0227] nikkaḍḍhāpeti. Sesaṃ [P 2.0362] vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti.

‘Paritta’ means small. ‘Udakamallaka’ means a water bowl. ‘Orabbhika’ means the owner of a ram. ‘Urabbhaghātaka’ means a butcher. ‘Jāpetuṃ’ means to cause to be diminished by the loss of wealth. There is also the reading ‘jhāpetuṃ’, which has this same meaning. ‘Yathāpaccayaṃ vā kātuṃ’ means to do as one wishes. ‘Urabbhadhana’ means the value of a ram. If that person wishes, he gives it to him; if he does not wish, he has him seized by the neck and thrown out. The remainder should be understood in the way already stated. In this sutta, however, the round of existence and that which is free from the round have been taught.

10. Paṃsudhovakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Paṃsudhovaka Sutta

102. Dasame dhovatīti vikkhāleti. Sandhovatīti suṭṭhu dhovati, punappunaṃ dhovati. Niddhovatīti niggaṇhitvā dhovati. Aniddhantakasāvanti anīhatadosaṃ anapanītakasāvaṃ. Pabhaṅgūti pabhijjanasabhāvaṃ, adhikaraṇīyaṃ ṭhapetvā muṭṭhikāya pahaṭamattaṃ bhijjati. Paṭṭikāyāti suvaṇṇapaṭṭakāya. Gīveyyaketi gīvālaṅkāre.

102. 'He washes' means he cleans. 'He washes thoroughly' means he washes well, he washes repeatedly. 'He scrubs' means he washes, having pressed it down. 'With unremoved defilements' means with fault not removed, with impurity not taken away. 'Fragile' means of a nature to break; having been placed on an anvil, it breaks merely upon being struck with a fist. 'With a sheet' means with a gold sheet. 'With a neck ornament' means with a neck decoration.

Adhicittanti samathavipassanācittaṃ. Anuyuttassāti bhāventassa. Sacetasoti cittasampanno. Dabbajātikoti paṇḍitajātiko. Kāmavitakkādīsu kāme ārabbha uppanno vitakko kāmavitakko. Byāpādavihiṃsasampayuttā vitakkā byāpādavihiṃsavitakkā nāma. Ñātivitakkādīsu “amhākaṃ ñātakā bahū puññavantā”tiādinā nayena ñātake ārabbha uppanno [V 2.0219] vitakko ñātivitakko. “Asuko janapado khemo subhikkho”tiādinā nayena janapadamārabbha uppanno vitakko janapadavitakko. “Aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyu”nti evaṃ uppanno vitakko anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nāma. Dhammavitakkāvasissantīti dhammavitakkā nāma dasavipassanupakkilesavitakkā. So hoti samādhi na ceva santoti so avasiṭṭhadhammavitakko vipassanāsamādhi avūpasantakilesattā santo na hoti. Na paṇītoti na atappako. Nappaṭippassaddhiladdhoti [P 2.0363] na kilesapaṭippassaddhiyā laddho. Na ekodibhāvādhigatoti na ekaggabhāvappatto. Sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagatoti sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilese niggaṇhitvā vāretvā vārito, na kilesānaṃ chinnante uppanno, kilese pana vāretvā uppanno.

'Higher mind' means the mind of serenity and insight. 'Of one who is devoted' means of one who develops it. 'Endowed with mind' means endowed with a mind. 'Of a competent nature' means of a wise nature. Regarding thoughts of sensuality and so on, a thought that has arisen concerning sensual objects is a thought of sensuality. Thoughts connected with ill will and harm are called thoughts of ill will and harm. Regarding thoughts of relatives and so on, a thought that has arisen concerning relatives in the manner of 'Our relatives are many and meritorious,' and so on, is a thought of relatives. A thought that has arisen concerning a country in the manner of 'Such-and-such a country is safe and has abundant food,' and so on, is a thought of a country. A thought that has arisen thus, 'Oh, may others not despise me,' is called a thought connected with not being despised. As for the remaining thoughts of Dhamma, thoughts called 'thoughts of Dhamma' are the ten thoughts that are corruptions of insight. That concentration is not peaceful; that remaining thought of Dhamma, the concentration of insight, is not peaceful because the defilements are not calmed. 'It is not excellent' means it is not soothing. 'Not obtained through tranquility' means not obtained by the calming of defilements. 'Not attained through unification' means it has not reached the state of one-pointedness. 'Attained by restraint through suppression with effort' means it is restrained with exertion, having suppressed and restrained the defilements; it has not arisen at the end of cutting off the defilements, but rather, it has arisen by restraining the defilements.

Hoti [M 2.0228] so, bhikkhave, samayoti ettha samayo nāma utusappāyaṃ āhārasappāyaṃ senāsanasappāyaṃ puggalasappāyaṃ dhammassavanasappāyanti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ sappāyānaṃ paṭilābhakālo. Yaṃ taṃ cittanti yasmiṃ samaye taṃ vipassanācittaṃ. Ajjhattaṃyeva santiṭṭhatīti attaniyeva tiṭṭhati. Niyakajjhattañhi idha ajjhattaṃ nāma. Gocarajjhattampi vaṭṭati. Puthuttārammaṇaṃ pahāya ekasmiṃ nibbānagocareyeva tiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sannisīdatīti suṭṭhu nisīdati. Ekodi hotīti ekaggaṃ hoti. Samādhiyatīti sammā ādhiyati. Santotiādīsu paccanīkakilesavūpasamena santo. Atappakaṭṭhena paṇīto. Kilesapaṭippassaddhiyā laddhattā paṭippassaddhaladdho. Ekaggabhāvaṃ gatattā ekodibhāvādhigato. Kilesānaṃ chinnante uppannattā na sappayogena kilese niggaṇhitvā vāretvā vāritoti na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Ettāvatā ayaṃ bhikkhu vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ patto nāma hoti.

“There comes a time, monks”—here, 'time' refers to the time when these five favorable conditions are obtained: a favorable season, favorable food, favorable lodging, favorable companionship, and a favorable opportunity to hear the Dhamma. “That mind”—at that time, that is the insight-mind. “It settles right inwardly” means it remains within oneself. For here, 'inwardly' means one's own inwardness. It is also suitable for the inwardness of the object-sphere. This is what is meant: having abandoned various objects, it remains only in the one object-sphere which is Nibbāna. “It becomes composed” means it sits well. “It becomes unified” means it becomes one-pointed. “It becomes concentrated” means it is rightly placed. In the text beginning with 'peaceful', it is 'peaceful' through the calming of opposing defilements. It is 'refined' in the sense of not causing agitation. Because it is obtained through the calming of defilements, it is 'obtained-through-calming'. Because it has reached a state of one-pointedness, it is 'attained-through-the-state-of-unification'. Because it arises at the end of cutting off the defilements, it is not restrained by suppressing and warding off defilements with effort; thus it has not reached the state of being restrained by suppression with exertion. To this extent, this monk, having turned away from the round of existence, is said to have attained Arahantship.

Idāni khīṇāsavassa sato abhiññāpaṭipadaṃ dassento yassa yassa cātiādimāha. Tattha abhiññā sacchikaraṇīyassāti abhijānitvā paccakkhaṃ kātabbassa. Sati satiāyataneti pubbahetusaṅkhāte ceva idāni ca paṭiladdhabbe abhiññāpādakajjhānādibhede ca sati satikāraṇe. Vitthārato [P 2.0364] pana ayaṃ abhiññākathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.365 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Āsavānaṃ khayātiādi cettha phalasamāpattivasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, wishing to show the path of direct knowledge of one who is an Arahant with taints destroyed, he spoke the words beginning with 'For whomsoever...'. Therein, 'to be realized by direct knowledge' means that which is to be made manifest after having directly known it. 'When there is a cause' means: when there is a cause, that is, both the cause designated as a prior cause, and the cause to be obtained now, of the various kinds beginning with the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge. However, this discussion on direct knowledge should be understood in detail in the way explained in the Visuddhimagga. And here, the text beginning with 'with the destruction of the taints' should be understood as spoken by way of the attainment of fruition.

11. Nimittasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Sutta on the Sign

103. Ekādasamepi [V 2.0220] adhicittaṃ samathavipassanācittameva. Tīṇi nimittānīti tīṇi kāraṇāni. Kālena kālanti kāle kāle, yuttakāleti attho. Kālena kālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ manasikātabbantiādīsu taṃ taṃ kālaṃ sallakkhetvā ekaggatāya yuttakāle ekaggatā manasikātabbā. Ekaggatā hi idha samādhinimittanti vuttā. Tatra vacanattho – samādhiyeva nimittaṃ samādhinimittaṃ. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Paggahoti pana vīriyassa nāmaṃ, upekkhāti majjhattabhāvassa. Tasmā [M 2.0229] vīriyassa yuttakāle vīriyaṃ manasikātabbaṃ, majjhattabhāvassa yuttakāle majjhattabhāve ṭhātabbanti. Ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyyāti kāraṇaṃ vijjati yena taṃ cittaṃ kosajjabhāve tiṭṭheyya. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Upekkhānimittaṃyeva manasi kareyyāti ettha ca ñāṇajavaṃ upekkheyyāti ayamattho. Āsavānaṃ khayāyāti arahattaphalatthāya.

103. In the eleventh sutta also, the higher mind is indeed the mind of serenity and insight. 'The three signs' means three causes. 'From time to time' means at various times, at a suitable time; this is the meaning. In such texts as 'the sign of concentration should be attended to from time to time,' having noted each suitable time, one-pointedness should be attended to at the time suitable for one-pointedness. Indeed, one-pointedness is here called the 'sign of concentration.' Therein, the meaning of the word is: concentration itself is the cause, hence 'sign of concentration.' This same method applies to the remaining two terms. Furthermore, 'exertion' is a name for energy, and 'equanimity' is for the state of neutrality. Therefore, at the time suitable for energy, energy should be attended to; and at the time suitable for the state of neutrality, one should be established in the state of neutrality. 'It is possible that the mind might lead to laziness' means there exists a reason for which that mind might stand in a state of laziness. This same method applies in the other cases also. And in the text 'one should attend only to the sign of equanimity,' the meaning is this: one should be equanimous towards the impulse of knowledge. 'For the destruction of the taints' means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship.

Ukkaṃ bandheyyāti aṅgārakapallaṃ sajjeyya. Ālimpeyyāti tattha aṅgāre pakkhipitvā aggiṃ datvā nāḷikāya dhamanto aggiṃ gāhāpeyya. Ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyyāti aṅgāre viyūhitvā aṅgāramatthake vā ṭhapeyya, mūsāya vā pakkhipeyya. Ajjhupekkhatīti pakkāpakkabhāvaṃ upadhāreti.

'One should prepare a firebrand' means one should prepare a charcoal pan. 'One should kindle it' means having put charcoal in it and applied fire, blowing with a tube, one should make the fire catch. 'One should place it in the mouth of the firebrand' means having spread out the charcoal, one should place it on top of the charcoal or put it in a crucible. 'One watches over it' means one observes the state of its cooking.

Sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāyāti arahattaphalatthāya sammā ṭhapīyati. Ettāvatā [P 2.0365] hi vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattappatto bhikkhu dassito. Idāni tassa khīṇāsavassa abhiññāya paṭipadaṃ dassento yassa yassa cātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'Is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints' means is rightly established for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, by this much, a bhikkhu who has developed insight and attained Arahantship has been shown. Now, wishing to show the path of direct knowledge of that one whose taints are destroyed, He spoke the words beginning with 'For whomsoever...'. That should be understood only in the way already stated above.

Loṇakapallavaggo pañcamo.

The Salt Crystal Chapter is the fifth.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is completed.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty

(11) 1. Sambodhavaggo

(11) 1. The Chapter on Awakening

1. Pubbevasambodhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse Before Enlightenment

104. Tatiyassa [V 2.0221][M 2.0230] paṭhame pubbeva sambodhāti sambodhito pubbeva, ariyamaggappattito aparabhāgeyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Anabhisambuddhassāti appaṭividdhacatusaccassa. Bodhisattasseva satoti bujjhanakasattasseva sato, sammāsambodhiṃ adhigantuṃ ārabhantasseva sato, sambodhiyā vā sattasseva laggasseva sato. Dīpaṅkarassa hi bhagavato pādamūle aṭṭhadhammasamodhānena abhinīhārasamiddhito pabhuti tathāgato sammāsambodhiṃ satto laggo “pattabbā mayā esā”ti tadadhigamāya parakkamaṃ amuñcantoyeva āgato, tasmā bodhisattoti vuccati. Ko nu khoti katamo nu kho. Lokoti saṅkhāraloko. Assādoti madhurākāro. Ādīnavoti anabhinanditabbākāro. Tassa mayhanti tassa evaṃ bodhisattasseva sato mayhaṃ. Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti nibbānaṃ āgamma ārabbha paṭicca chandarāgo vinayaṃ gacchati pahīyati, tasmā nibbānaṃ “chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahāna”nti vuccati. Idaṃ lokanissaraṇanti idaṃ nibbānaṃ lokato nissaṭattā lokanissaraṇanti vuccati. Yāvakīvanti [P 2.0366] yattakaṃ pamāṇaṃ kālaṃ. Abbhaññāsinti abhivisiṭṭhena ariyamaggañāṇena aññāsiṃ. Ñāṇañca pana me dassananti dvīhipi padehi paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

104. In the first sutta of the third fifty, 'before enlightenment' means before His enlightenment; this is said with reference only to the period after the attainment of the Noble Path. 'Not fully enlightened' refers to one who has not penetrated the Four Noble Truths. 'While being a Bodhisatta' means while being a being destined for awakening, or while striving to attain perfect enlightenment, or while being a being attached to, clinging to, enlightenment. For from the time the Tathāgata, at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, fulfilled his aspiration through the convergence of eight qualities, he was attached to and clung to perfect enlightenment, thinking, ‘This must be attained by me,’ and came thus, not abandoning effort for its attainment. Therefore, he is called a Bodhisatta. 'What indeed?' means 'what kind indeed?'. 'The world' refers to the world of formations. 'Gratification' means its pleasing aspect. 'Danger' means its undesirable aspect. 'For me' refers to 'for me, who was thus a Bodhisatta'. The terms 'the removal of desire and lust' and 'the abandonment of desire and lust' mean that in dependence on Nibbāna, desire and lust are removed and abandoned; therefore, Nibbāna is called 'the removal of desire and lust' and 'the abandonment of desire and lust'. 'This escape from the world' means this Nibbāna is called an escape from the world because it is a departure from the world. 'As long as' means for whatever length of time. 'I directly knew' means I knew with the distinguished knowledge of the Noble Path. 'And my knowledge and vision'—by both these phrases, reviewing knowledge is stated. The rest here is self-evident.

2. Paṭhamaassādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the First Discourse on Gratification

105. Dutiye assādapariyesanaṃ acarinti assādapariyesanatthāya acariṃ. Kuto paṭṭhāyāti? Sumedhakālato paṭṭhāya. Paññāyāti sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya. Sudiṭṭhoti suppaṭividdho. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Tatiyaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

105. In the second discourse, 'I wandered seeking gratification' means I wandered for the purpose of seeking gratification. 'From where did it begin?' means from the time of Sumedha. 'By wisdom' means by the wisdom of the path together with insight. 'Well seen' means thoroughly penetrated. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere. The third discourse is entirely clear.

4. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Recluses and Brahmins

107. Catutthe [M 2.0231][V 2.0222] sāmaññatthanti catubbidhaṃ ariyaphalaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sāmaññatthena vā cattāro maggā, brahmaññatthena cattāri phalāni. Imesu pana catūsupi suttesu khandhalokova kathito.

107. In the fourth discourse, 'the goal of recluseship' is the fourfold noble fruit. The other term is a synonym for it. Alternatively, by the term 'goal of recluseship' the four paths are taught, and by the term 'goal of brahminship' the four fruits are taught. However, in these four discourses, only the world of the aggregates is taught.

5. Ruṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Weeping

108. Pañcamaṃ atthuppattiyā nikkhittaṃ. Katarāya atthuppattiyā? Chabbaggiyānaṃ anācāre. Te kira gāyantā naccantā hasantā vicariṃsu. Bhikkhū dasabalassa ārocayiṃsu. Satthā te pakkosāpetvā tesaṃ ovādatthāya idaṃ suttaṃ ārabhi. Tattha ruṇṇanti roditaṃ. Ummattakanti ummattakakiriyā. Komārakanti kumārakehi kattabbakiccaṃ. Dantavidaṃsakahasitanti dante dassetvā pāṇiṃ paharantānaṃ mahāsaddena hasitaṃ. Setughāto gīteti gīte vo paccayaghāto hotu, sahetukaṃ gītaṃ pajahathāti dīpeti. Naccepi eseva nayo. Alanti yuttaṃ. Dhammappamoditānaṃ satanti ettha dhammo vuccati kāraṇaṃ, kenacideva kāraṇena pamuditānaṃ santānaṃ. Sitaṃ sitamattāyāti tasmiṃ sitakāraṇe sati yaṃ sitaṃ karotha, taṃ vo sitamattāya aggadante dassetvā pahaṭṭhākāramattadassanāyayeva [P 2.0367] yuttanti vuttaṃ hoti.

108. The fifth discourse was set forth due to an occasion. Due to what occasion? The misconduct of the group-of-six monks. It is said they wandered about singing, dancing, and laughing. The monks informed the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, having had them summoned, began this discourse for the purpose of admonishing them. Therein, 'weeping' is lamentation. 'Madness' is the conduct of a madman. 'Childishness' is a deed to be done by children. 'Laughing while showing the teeth' is laughing with a loud sound while clapping the hands and showing the teeth. 'A barrier to song' indicates this meaning: 'In singing, let there be for you a destruction of the cause; abandon singing that has a cause.' In dancing also, this is the same method. 'Enough' means it is suitable. In 'of those delighted by the Dhamma', here 'dhamma' is said to mean 'cause'; that is, of those who are delighted for some reason or other. 'A mere smile' means: when there is a cause for smiling, the smile that you make should be for you a mere smile, suitable only for showing the tips of the teeth and displaying a mere joyful demeanor. This is what is meant.

6. Atittisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Unsatisfaction

109. Chaṭṭhe soppassāti niddāya. Paṭisevanāya natthi tittīti yathā yathā paṭisevati, tathā tathā ruccatiyevāti titti nāma natthi. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Sace hi mahāsamudde udakaṃ surā bhaveyya, surāsoṇḍo ca maccho hutvā nibbatteyya, tassa tattha carantassapi sayantassapi titti nāma na bhaveyya. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

109. In the sixth discourse, 'sleepiness' means sleep. 'There is no satisfaction in partaking' means that in whatever way one partakes, in that way one only desires it; there is no such thing as satisfaction. In the remaining two terms also, this is the same method. Indeed, if the water in the great ocean were liquor, and a drunkard, having become a fish, were to arise there, for him, while moving about and sleeping there, there would be no such thing as satisfaction. In this discourse, only the round of existence is taught.

7. Arakkhitasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unguarded

110. Sattame avassutaṃ hotīti tintaṃ hoti. Na bhaddakaṃ maraṇaṃ hotīti apāye paṭisandhipaccayatāya na laddhakaṃ hoti. Kālakiriyāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sukkapakkhe sagge paṭisandhipaccayatāya [V 2.0223] bhaddakaṃ hoti [M 2.0232] laddhakaṃ. Taṃ pana ekantena sotāpannādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ariyasāvakānaṃyeva vaṭṭati. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

110. In the seventh discourse, 'is corrupt' means it is drenched. 'It is not a fortunate death' means that because it is a cause for rebirth in the lower realms, a fortunate death is not obtained. 'Making an end' is a synonym for that very word. On the bright side, because it is a cause for rebirth in heaven, a fortunate death is obtained. That, however, applies exclusively to the three noble disciples, beginning with the stream-enterer. The rest here is self-evident.

8. Byāpannasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Ill Will

111. Aṭṭhame byāpannanti pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasutte vuttanayameva.

111. In the eighth discourse, 'corrupted' means having abandoned the natural state, one remains. The rest is in the same way as was stated in the previous discourse.

9. Paṭhamanidānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Foundations

112. Navame nidānānīti kāraṇāni. Kammānaṃ samudayāyāti vaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ piṇḍakaraṇatthāya. Lobhapakatanti lobhena pakataṃ. Sāvajjanti sadosaṃ. Taṃ kammaṃ kammasamudayāya saṃvattatīti taṃ kammaṃ aññesampi vaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ samudayāya piṇḍakaraṇatthāya saṃvattati. Na taṃ kammaṃ kammanirodhāyāti taṃ pana kammaṃ vaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ nirodhatthāya na saṃvattati. Sukkapakkhe [P 2.0368] kammānaṃ samudayāyāti vivaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ samudayatthāya. Iminā nayena sabbaṃ atthato veditabbaṃ.

112. In the ninth discourse, 'foundations' means causes. 'For the arising of kamma' means for the purpose of accumulating kamma that leads to the round of rebirth. 'Produced by greed' means done by greed. 'Blameworthy' means with fault. 'That kamma conduces to the arising of kamma' means that kamma conduces to the arising and accumulation of other kamma that leads to the round. 'That kamma does not lead to the cessation of kamma' means that kamma, however, does not conduce to the cessation of kamma that leads to the round. On the bright side, 'for the arising of kamma' means for the purpose of the arising of kamma that leads out of the round. By this method, everything should be understood according to its meaning.

10. Dutiyanidānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Foundations

113. Dasame kammānanti vaṭṭagāmikammānameva. Chandarāgaṭṭhāniyeti chandarāgassa kāraṇabhūte. Ārabbhāti āgamma sandhāya paṭicca. Chandoti taṇhāchando. Yo cetaso sārāgoti yo cittassa rāgo rajjanā rajjitattaṃ, etamahaṃ saṃyojanaṃ vadāmi, bandhanaṃ vadāmīti attho. Sukkapakkhe kammānanti vivaṭṭagāmikammānaṃ. Tadabhinivattetīti taṃ abhinivatteti. Yadā vā tena vipāko ñāto hoti vidito, tadā te ceva dhamme tañca vipākaṃ abhinivatteti. Iminā ca padena vipassanā kathitā, tadabhinivattetvāti iminā maggo. Cetasā abhinivijjhitvāti iminā ca maggova. Paññāya ativijjha passatīti saha vipassanāya maggapaññāya nibbijjhitvā passati. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ pana sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti.

113. In the tenth discourse, 'kammānaṃ' refers to kamma that leads to the round of rebirth. 'Chandarāgaṭṭhāniye' means that which is a cause of desire and lust. 'Ārabbha' means having depended on, having referred to, and having approached. 'Chando' is the desire that is craving. 'Yo cetaso sārāgo' means: whatever lust of the mind, whatever passion, whatever state of being impassioned there is—this I call a fetter, I call a bondage. This is the meaning. In the bright portion, 'kammānaṃ' refers to kamma that leads out of the round. 'Tadabhinivatteti' means one develops it. Or, when the result is known and understood by that person, then one develops both those very phenomena and that result. By this word, insight is taught; by 'tadabhinivattetvā', the path is taught. And by 'cetasā abhinivijjhitvā' as well, the path itself is taught. 'Paññāya ativijjha passati' means one sees, having penetrated the defilements with the wisdom of the path together with insight. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances. In this discourse, however, the round and the release from the round are taught.

Sambodhavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Enlightenment.

(12) 2. Āpāyikavaggo

(12) 2. The Chapter on Those Destined for the States of Woe

1. Āpāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Those Destined for the States of Woe

114. Dutiyassa [V 2.0224][M 2.0233] paṭhame apāyaṃ gacchissantīti āpāyikā. Nirayaṃ gacchissantīti nerayikā. Idamappahāyāti idaṃ brahmacāripaṭiññatādiṃ pāpadhammattayaṃ avijahitvā. Brahmacāripaṭiññoti [P 2.0369] brahmacāripaṭirūpako, tesaṃ vā ākappaṃ avijahanena “ahampi brahmacārī”ti evaṃpaṭiñño. Anuddhaṃsetīti akkosati paribhāsati codeti. Natthi kāmesu dosoti kilesakāmena vatthukāme sevantassa natthi doso. Pātabyatanti pivitabbataṃ paribhuñjitabbataṃ nirāsaṅkena cittena pipāsitassa pānīyapivanasadisaṃ paribhuñjitabbataṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

114. In the first discourse of the second chapter, because 'they will go to the state of woe', they are called 'āpāyikā' (destined for the state of woe). Because 'they will go to hell', they are called 'nerayikā' (hell-bound). 'Not abandoning this' means not having abandoned this triad of evil phenomena, beginning with claiming to lead the holy life. 'Claiming to lead the holy life' means one who is a counterfeit of one who leads the holy life; or, by not abandoning their guise, one who professes, "I too lead the holy life." 'Anuddhaṃseti' means one reviles, threatens, or reproaches. 'There is no fault in sensual pleasures' means there is no fault for one who indulges in material sensual pleasures with defiling craving. 'Fit to be drunk' means the state of being fit to be drunk, fit to be consumed; to be consumed like the drinking of water for a thirsty person, with a mind free from hesitation. In this discourse, only the round of rebirth is spoken of.

2. Dullabhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on What is Difficult to Obtain

115. Dutiye kataññū katavedīti “iminā mayhaṃ kata”nti tena katakammaṃ ñatvā viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā paṭikaraṇakapuggalo.

115. In the second discourse, 'kataññū katavedī' refers to a person who, knowing the deed done by another, thinking 'this was done for me,' and making that deed known and evident, is one who repays the kindness.

3. Appameyyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Immeasurable Sutta

116. Tatiye sukhena metabboti suppameyyo. Dukkhena metabboti duppameyyo. Pametuṃ na sakkotīti appameyyo. Unnaḷoti uggatanaḷo, tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitoti attho. Capaloti pattamaṇḍanādinā cāpallena samannāgato. Mukharoti mukhakharo. Vikiṇṇavācoti asaññatavacano. Asamāhitoti cittekaggatārahito. Vibbhantacittoti bhantacitto bhantagāvibhantamigasappaṭibhāgo. Pākatindriyoti vivaṭindriyo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

116. In the third discourse, 'suppameyyo' means one who is easily measured (sukhena metabbo). 'Duppameyyo' means one who is measured with difficulty (dukkhena metabbo). 'Appameyyo' means one who cannot be measured (pametuṃ na sakko). 'Unnaḷo' means a reed that has risen up; the meaning is one who stands having raised up empty conceit. 'Capalo' means endowed with fickleness, such as by adorning one's bowl and so on. 'Mukharo' means harsh-mouthed. 'Vikiṇṇavāco' means having unrestrained speech. 'Asamāhito' means devoid of one-pointedness of mind. 'Vibbhantacitto' means having a bewildered mind, resembling a bewildered cow or a bewildered deer. 'Pākaṭindriyo' means having open faculties. The rest here is clear indeed.

4. Āneñjasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Imperturbable Sutta

117. Catutthe [V 2.0225] tadassādetīti taṃ jhānaṃ assādeti. Taṃ nikāmetīti tadeva pattheti. Tena ca vittiṃ āpajjatīti tena jhānena tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjati. Tatra ṭhitoti tasmiṃ jhāne ṭhito. Tadadhimuttoti tattheva adhimutto. Tabbahulavihārīti tena bahulaṃ viharanto. Sahabyataṃ upapajjatīti sahabhāvaṃ upapajjati, tasmiṃ devaloke nibbattatīti attho[M 2.0234]. Nirayampi gacchatītiādi nirayādīhi avippamuttattā aparapariyāyavasena tattha gamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na [P 2.0370] hi tassa upacārajjhānato balavataraṃ akusalaṃ atthi, yena anantaraṃ apāye nibbatteyya. Bhagavato pana sāvakoti sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmīnaṃ aññataro. Tasmiṃyeva bhaveti tattheva arūpabhave. Parinibbāyatīti appaccayaparinibbānena parinibbāyati. Adhippayāsoti adhikappayogo. Sesamettha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte puthujjanassa upapattijjhānaṃ kathitaṃ, ariyasāvakassa tadeva upapattijjhānañca vipassanāpādakajjhānañca kathitaṃ.

117. In the fourth discourse, 'tadassādeti' means: he delights in that jhāna. 'Taṃ nikāmeti' means: he longs for that very jhāna. 'Tena ca vittiṃ āpajjati' means: by that jhāna he reaches satisfaction. 'Tatra ṭhito' means: established in that jhāna. 'Tadadhimutto' means: intent on that very thing. 'Tabbahulavihārī' means: frequently abiding by means of that. 'Sahabyataṃ upapajjati' means: he is reborn into a state of companionship; the meaning is that he is born in that deva-world. The phrase 'nirayampi gacchati', etc., is said with reference to going there by the power of a subsequently effective kamma, due to not being freed from hell and so on. For that person, there is no unwholesome kamma more powerful than access concentration by which he would be reborn in a woeful state in the immediately following life. However, 'a disciple of the Blessed One' means one among the stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners. 'Tasmiṃyeva bhave' means: in that very formless existence. 'Parinibbāyati' means: he attains parinibbāna through the parinibbāna that is without causal condition. 'Adhippayāso' means: excessive application. The rest here should be understood in the way already stated. Furthermore, in this discourse, the jhāna that causes rebirth for an ordinary person is taught; and for a noble disciple, that same jhāna that causes rebirth and the jhāna that is the basis for insight are taught.

5. Vipattisampadāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sutta on Failure and Accomplishment

118. Pañcame sīlavipattīti sīlassa vipannākāro. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Natthi dinnanti dinnassa phalābhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yiṭṭhaṃ vuccati mahāyogo. Hutanti paheṇakasakkāro adhippeto. Tampi ubhayaṃ phalābhāvameva sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sukatadukkaṭānanti sukatadukkatānaṃ, kusalākusalānanti attho. Phalaṃ vipākoti yaṃ phalanti vā vipākoti vā vuccati, taṃ natthīti vadati. Natthi ayaṃ lokoti paraloke ṭhitassa ayaṃ loko natthi, natthi paro lokoti idha loke ṭhitassāpi paraloko natthi, sabbe tattha tattheva ucchijjantīti dasseti. Natthi mātā natthi pitāti tesu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ phalābhāvavasena vadati. Natthi sattā opapātikāti cavitvā uppajjanakasattā nāma natthīti vadati. Sampadāti pāripūriyo. Sīlasampadāti sīlassa paripuṇṇaavekallabhāvo. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Atthi dinnantiādi vuttapaṭipakkhanayena gahetabbaṃ.

118. In the fifth discourse, 'sīlavipatti' means the corrupted state of virtue. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. 'Natthi dinnaṃ' (there is nothing given) is said with reference to the absence of the fruit of giving. 'Yiṭṭhaṃ' (what is sacrificed) is called a great offering. 'Hutaṃ' (what is offered) is intended to mean honor and hospitality. He also rejects both of these, with reference to the absence of their fruits. 'Sukatadukkaṭānaṃ' means of well-done and ill-done deeds, that is, of wholesome and unwholesome deeds. 'Phalaṃ vipāko' (fruit and result) means whatever is called fruit or result; he says that does not exist. 'Natthi ayaṃ loko' (this world does not exist) means for one established in the other world, this world does not exist. 'Natthi paro loko' (the other world does not exist) means even for one established in this world, the other world does not exist; this shows that all beings are annihilated right there. 'Natthi mātā natthi pitā' (there is no mother, there is no father) is said with reference to the absence of fruit from right and wrong conduct towards them. 'Natthi sattā opapātikā' (there are no spontaneously arisen beings) means he says there are no beings who arise after passing away. 'Sampadā' means accomplishments. 'Sīlasampadā' means the complete, unbroken state of virtue. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. 'Atthi dinnaṃ' (there is what is given) and so on, should be understood in the way opposite to what was stated.

6. Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Incontrovertible Sutta

119. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0226][P 2.0371] apaṇṇako maṇīti chahi talehi samannāgato pāsako. Sugatiṃ sagganti cātumahārājikādīsu aññataraṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte sīlañca sammādiṭṭhi cāti ubhayampi missakaṃ kathitaṃ. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

119. In the sixth discourse, 'apaṇṇako maṇi' is a die endowed with six faces. 'A good destination, heaven' means a heavenly world such as that of the Four Great Kings and so forth. In this discourse, both virtue and right view are taught in combination. The seventh discourse is self-explanatory.

8. Paṭhamasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the First Sutta on Purity

121. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0235] soceyyānīti sucibhāvā. Kāyasoceyyanti kāyadvāre sucibhāvo. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Imesu pana paṭipāṭiyā catūsu suttesu agārikapaṭipadā kathitā. Sotāpannasakadāgāmīnampi vaṭṭati.

121. In the eighth sutta, 'soceyyāni' means states of purity. 'Kāyasoceyyaṃ' means purity at the body-door. The same method applies to the other two. Furthermore, in these four suttas, the practice for householders is taught in sequence. It is also suitable for stream-enterers and once-returners.

9. Dutiyasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Second Soceyya Sutta

122. Navame ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ. Kāmacchandanti kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ. Byāpādādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Gāthāya pana kāyasucinti kāyadvāre suciṃ, kāyena vā suciṃ. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Ninhātapāpakanti sabbe pāpe ninhāpetvā dhovitvā ṭhitaṃ. Iminā suttenapi gāthāyapi khīṇāsavova kathitoti.

122. In the ninth sutta, 'internal' means one's own internal state. 'Sensual desire' means the hindrance of sensual desire. The same method applies to malice and so forth. The rest here is according to the method stated below. In the verse, however, 'pure in body' means pure at the body-door, or pure by means of the body. The same method applies to the other two. 'Having washed away evil' means one who is established, having washed and cleansed away all evil. By this sutta and also by this verse, only the one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of.

10. Moneyyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Moneyya Sutta

123. Dasame moneyyānīti munibhāvā. Kāyamoneyyanti kāyadvāre munibhāvo sādhubhāvo paṇḍitabhāvo. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kāyamoneyyanti idaṃ tividhakāyaduccaritappahānaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ nāma. Apica tividhaṃ kāyasucaritampi kāyamoneyyaṃ, tathā kāyārammaṇaṃ [P 2.0372] ñāṇaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ, kāyapariññā kāyamoneyyaṃ, pariññāsahagato maggo kāyamoneyyaṃ, kāye chandarāgassa pahānaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ, kāyasaṅkhāranirodho catutthajjhānasamāpatti kāyamoneyyaṃ. Vacīmoneyyepi eseva nayo.

123. In the tenth sutta, 'sagehoods' (moneyyāni) means states of a sage (munibhāvā). 'Bodily sagehood' means the state of a sage, the nature of a good person, and the state of a wise person at the body-door. The same method applies to the other two. 'This, monks, is called bodily sagehood'—this means the abandonment of the threefold bodily misconduct is called bodily sagehood. Moreover, the threefold bodily good conduct is also bodily sagehood; likewise, knowledge with the body as its object is bodily sagehood; full understanding of the body is bodily sagehood; the path accompanied by full understanding is bodily sagehood; the abandonment of desire and lust for the body is bodily sagehood; the attainment of the fourth jhāna, which is the cessation of bodily formations, is bodily sagehood. The same method applies to verbal sagehood.

Ayaṃ [V 2.0227] panettha viseso – yathā idha catutthajjhānasamāpatti, evaṃ tattha vacīsaṅkhāranirodho dutiyajjhānasamāpatti vacīmoneyyanti veditabbā. Manomoneyyampi imināva nayena atthaṃ ñatvā cittasaṅkhāranirodho saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti manomoneyyanti veditabbā. Kāyamuninti kāyadvāre muniṃ uttamaṃ parisuddhaṃ, kāyena vā muniṃ. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Sabbappahāyinanti khīṇāsavaṃ. Khīṇāsavo hi sabbappahāyī nāmāti.

Herein is this distinction: just as here the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily sagehood, so there the attainment of the second jhāna, which is the cessation of verbal formations, is to be understood as verbal sagehood. As for mental sagehood, having understood the meaning by this same method, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which is the cessation of mental formations, is to be understood as mental sagehood. 'Bodily sage' means a sage at the body-door, supreme, and pure; or a sage by means of the body. The same method applies to the other two. 'One who has abandoned all' means the one whose taints are destroyed. For one whose taints are destroyed is indeed called 'one who has abandoned all.'

Āpāyikavaggo dutiyo.

The Āpāyika Chapter, the Second.

(13) 3. Kusināravaggo

(13) 3. The Kusinārā Chapter

1. Kusinārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Kusinārā Sutta

124. Tatiyassa [V 2.0228][M 2.0236] paṭhame kusinārāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Baliharaṇe vanasaṇḍeti evaṃnāmake vanasaṇḍe. Tattha kira bhūtabalikaraṇatthaṃ baliṃ haranti, tasmā baliharaṇanti vuccati. Ākaṅkhamānoti icchamāno. Sahatthāti sahatthena. Sampavāretīti alaṃ alanti vācāya ceva hatthavikārena ca paṭikkhipāpeti. Sādhu vata māyanti sādhu vata maṃ ayaṃ. Gathitoti taṇhāgedhena gathito. Mucchitoti [P 2.0373] taṇhāmucchanāyayeva mucchito. Ajjhopannoti taṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā pavatto. Anissaraṇapaññoti chandarāgaṃ pahāya saṃkaḍḍhitvā paribhuñjanto nissaraṇapañño nāma hoti, ayaṃ na tādiso, sacchandarāgo paribhuñjatīti anissaraṇapañño. Sukkapakkho vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo. Nekkhammavitakkādayo panettha missakā kathitāti veditabbā.

124. In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'in Kusinārā' means in a city of that name. 'In the Baliharaṇa grove' means in a forest grove of that name. There, it is said, they bring offerings for the purpose of making offerings to spirits; therefore, it is called 'Baliharaṇa.' 'Wishing' means desiring. 'With his own hand' means with his own hand. 'Sampavāreti' means he causes one to refuse by word and by gesture of the hand, saying, 'It is enough, it is enough.' The phrase 'Sādhu vata māyaṃ' is to be parsed as 'Sādhu vata maṃ ayaṃ'. 'Bound' means bound by the snare of craving. 'Infatuated' means infatuated solely by the infatuation of craving. 'Engrossed' means having been swallowed, brought to completion, and set in motion by craving. 'One without the wisdom of escape' means a monk who partakes after having abandoned and rooted out sensual desire is called 'one with the wisdom of escape'; this monk is not like that, he partakes with sensual desire, therefore he is 'one without the wisdom of escape.' The bright side should be understood in the reverse way of what was said. It should be understood that herein thoughts of renunciation and so forth are taught as mixed.

2. Bhaṇḍanasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sutta on Disputing

125. Dutiye pajahiṃsūti pajahanti. Bahulamakaṃsūti punappunaṃ karonti. Idhāpi tayo vitakkā missakāva kathitā.

125. In the second sutta, 'they abandoned' (pajahiṃsu) means they abandon (pajahanti). 'They frequently did' (bahulamakaṃsu) means they do repeatedly (punappunaṃ karonti). Here too, the three thoughts are stated as mixed.

3. Gotamakacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sutta on the Gotamaka Shrine

126. Tatiye gotamake cetiyeti gotamakayakkhassa bhavane. Tathāgato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsati vassāni kadāci cāpāle cetiye, kadāci sārandade, kadāci bahuputte, kadāci gotamaketi evaṃ yebhuyyena devakulesuyeva vihāsi. Imasmiṃ pana kāle vesāliṃ upanissāya gotamakassa yakkhassa bhavanaṭṭhāne vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “gotamake cetiye”ti. Etadavocāti etaṃ “abhiññāyāha”ntiādikaṃ suttaṃ avoca.

126. In the third sutta, 'at the Gotamaka shrine' (gotamake cetiye) means in the dwelling of the Gotamaka yakkha. Indeed, for twenty years during the first period of his enlightenment, the Tathāgata dwelt sometimes at the Cāpāla shrine, sometimes at the Sārandada shrine, sometimes at the Bahuputta shrine, and sometimes at the Gotamaka shrine—thus, for the most part, he dwelt only in the shrines of deities. At this time, however, relying on Vesālī, he dwelt at the site of the dwelling of the Gotamaka yakkha. Therefore it was said: 'at the Gotamaka shrine.' 'He said this' (etadavoca) means he spoke this sutta beginning with 'I, through direct knowledge...' (abhiññāyāhaṃ), and so forth.

Idañca [V 2.0229] bhagavatā suttaṃ atthuppattiyaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Kataraatthuppattiyanti? Mūlapariyāyaatthuppattiyaṃ (ma. ni. 1.1 ādayo). Sambahulā kira brāhmaṇapabbajitā attanā [M 2.0237] uggahitabuddhavacanaṃ nissāya jānanamadaṃ uppādetvā dhammassavanaggaṃ na gacchanti – “sammāsambuddho kathento amhehi ñātameva kathessati, no aññāta”nti. Bhikkhū tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ. Satthā te bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā mukhapaṭiññaṃ gahetvā mūlapariyāyaṃ desesi. Te bhikkhū desanāya neva āgataṭṭhānaṃ, na gataṭṭhānaṃ addasaṃsu. Apassantā “sammāsambuddho ‘mayhaṃ kathā niyyātī’ti mukhasampattameva kathetī”ti cintayiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ manaṃ jānitvā imaṃ suttantaṃ ārabhi.

And it should be understood that this sutta was spoken by the Blessed One in connection with an occasion. What occasion? The occasion of the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. It is said that a number of brahmin ascetics, relying on the Buddha’s words that they themselves had learned, generated conceit in their knowledge and did not go to hear the Dhamma, thinking, 'When the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One speaks, he will speak only what we already know, nothing unknown.' The bhikkhus reported this to the Tathāgata. The Teacher had those bhikkhus summoned, and after taking their verbal admission, taught the Mūlapariyāya. Through the teaching, those bhikkhus saw neither the place they had come from nor the place they had gone to. Not seeing, they thought, 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, saying, “My speech leads out,” only speaks of what has reached his mouth.' Knowing their minds, the Teacher began this sutta.

Tattha abhiññāyāti “ime pañcakkhandhā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa [P 2.0374] dhātuyo, bāvīsatindriyāni, cattāri saccāni, nava hetū, satta phassā, satta vedanā, satta cetanā, satta saññā, satta cittānī”ti jānitvā paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā, tathā – “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena te te dhamme jānitvā paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhameva katvāti attho. Sanidānanti sappaccayameva katvā kathemi, no appaccayaṃ. Sappāṭihāriyanti paccanīkapaṭiharaṇena sappāṭihāriyameva katvā kathemi, no appāṭihāriyaṃ. Alañca pana voti yuttañca pana tumhākaṃ. Tuṭṭhiyāti “sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti tīṇi ratanāni guṇato anussarantānaṃ tumhākaṃ yuttameva tuṭṭhiṃ kātunti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

Herein, 'having directly known' means knowing, penetrating, and directly realizing these: the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the four truths, the nine causes, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven volitions, the seven perceptions, and the seven consciousnesses. Similarly, by the method beginning with 'these are the four foundations of mindfulness,' it means knowing, penetrating, and directly realizing those various dhammas. This is the meaning. 'With a cause' means: I teach with a cause, not without a cause. 'With the removal of opposition' means: I teach by removing opposing states, not without removing them. 'It is indeed fitting for you' means: it is indeed fitting for you. 'For satisfaction' means: it is indeed proper for you to feel satisfaction, for those of you who recollect the virtues of the Three Jewels thus: 'The Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Sangha is of good conduct.' This same method applies to the remaining two phrases.

Akampitthāti chahi ākārehi akampittha. Evarūpo hi pathavikampo bodhimaṇḍepi ahosi. Bodhisatte kira dakkhiṇadisābhāgena bodhimaṇḍaṃ abhiruḷhe dakkhiṇadisābhāgo heṭṭhā avīciṃ pāpuṇanto viya ahosi, uttarabhāgo uggantvā bhavaggaṃ abhihananto viya. Pacchimadisaṃ gate pacchimabhāgo heṭṭhā avīciṃ pāpuṇanto viya ahosi, pācīnabhāgo uggantvā bhavaggaṃ abhihananto viya. Uttaradisaṃ gate uttaradisābhāgo heṭṭhā avīciṃ pāpuṇanto viya, dakkhiṇadisābhāgo uggantvā bhavaggaṃ abhihananto viya. Pācīnadisaṃ gate pācīnadisābhāgo heṭṭhā avīciṃ pāpuṇanto viya, pacchimabhāgo uggantvā bhavaggaṃ abhihananto viya. Bodhirukkhopi sakiṃ heṭṭhā avīciṃ pāpuṇanto viya, sakiṃ uggantvā bhavaggaṃ abhihananto viya. Tasmimpi divase evaṃ chahi ākārehi cakkavāḷasahassī mahāpathavī akampittha.

'It shook' means it shook in six ways. Indeed, an earthquake of this nature occurred even at the Bodhimaṇḍa. It is said that when the Bodhisatta ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa by the southern side, the southern part was as if reaching down to Avīci, while the northern part rose up as if striking the summit of existence. When he went to the western side, the western part was as if reaching down to Avīci, while the eastern part rose up as if striking the summit of existence. When he went to the northern side, the northern part was as if reaching down to Avīci, while the southern part rose up as if striking the summit of existence. When he went to the eastern side, the eastern part was as if reaching down to Avīci, while the western part rose up as if striking the summit of existence. The Bodhi tree also, at one time, was as if reaching down to Avīci, and at another time, rose up as if striking the summit of existence. On that day also, the great earth, extending to a thousand world-systems, shook in these six ways.

4. Bharaṇḍukālāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta

127. Catutthe [V 2.0230][M 2.0238] kevalakappanti sakalakappaṃ. Anvāhiṇḍantoti vicaranto. Nāddasāti kiṃ kāraṇā na addasa? Ayaṃ kira bharaṇḍu kālāmo sakyānaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ khādanto vicarati. Tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sampattakāle ekā dhammadesanā samuṭṭhahissatīti [P 2.0375] ñatvā bhagavā evaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi, yathā añño āvasatho na paññāyittha. Tasmā na addasa. Purāṇasabrahmacārīti porāṇako sabrahmacārī. So kira āḷārakālāmakāle tasmiṃyeva assame ahosi, taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Santharaṃ paññāpehīti santharitabbaṃ santharāhīti attho. Santharaṃ paññāpetvāti kappiyamañcake paccattharaṇaṃ paññāpetvā. Kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpetīti ettha pariññā nāma samatikkamo, tasmā kāmānaṃ samatikkamaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ paññāpeti. Na rūpānaṃ pariññanti rūpānaṃ samatikkamabhūtaṃ arūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ na paññāpeti. Na vedanānaṃ pariññanti vedanānaṃ samatikkamaṃ nibbānaṃ na paññāpeti. Niṭṭhāti gati nipphatti. Udāhu puthūti udāhu nānā.

127. In the fourth, `kevalakappaṃ` means the entire. `Anvāhiṇḍanto` means wandering about. Regarding `nāddasa` (he did not see): for what reason did he not see? It is said that this Bharaṇḍu Kālāma wanders about, eating the best alms-food of the Sakyans. Knowing that a Dhamma teaching would arise upon arrival at his dwelling place, the Blessed One resolved in such a way that no other lodging would appear. Therefore, he did not see. `Purāṇasabrahmacārī` means a former companion in the holy life.
