It is said that during the time of Āḷāra Kālāma, he was in that very hermitage; referring to that, he spoke thus. `Santharaṃ paññāpehi` (Prepare a seat) means 'Spread it out.' `Santharaṃ paññāpetvā` (Having prepared a seat) means having arranged a covering on a suitable couch. Regarding `kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti` (he declares the full understanding of sensual pleasures): here, `pariññā` (full understanding) means overcoming; therefore, he declares the first jhāna as the overcoming of sensual pleasures. `Na rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ` (Not the full understanding of forms) means he does not declare the formless-sphere attainment, which is the overcoming of forms. `Na vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ` (Not the full understanding of feelings) means he does not declare Nibbāna, which is the overcoming of feelings. `Niṭṭhā` (conclusion) means completion or accomplishment. `Udāhu puthu` means or diversely.

5. Hatthakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta

128. Pañcame abhikkantāya rattiyāti ettha abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanādīsu dissati. Tattha “abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho, uddisatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti evamādīsu khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

128. In the fifth, regarding `abhikkantāya rattiyā` (when the night was far advanced): here, the term `abhikkanta` is seen in the senses of passing away, beauty, surpassing form, and great approval, and so on. Among these, in the sense of passing away (`khaya`), it is seen in such phrases as: “Venerable sir, the night has passed, the first watch is over, the Sangha of monks has been seated for a long time; may the Blessed One, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha for the monks.” In the sense of beauty (`sundara`), it is seen in such phrases as: “This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons.”

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. (vi. va. 857) –

“Who is it that venerates my feet, blazing with power and glory, illuminating all directions with surpassing beauty?”

Evamādīsu abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamā”ti evamādīsu (pārā. 15) abbhanumodane. Idha pana sundare. Tena abhikkantāya rattiyāti iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya rattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhikkantavaṇṇāti idha abhikkantasaddo abhirūpe, vaṇṇasaddo [P 2.0376] pana chavithutikulavaggakāraṇasaṇṭhānapamāṇarūpāyatanādīsu dissati. Tattha “suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā”ti [V 2.0231][M 2.0239] evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 553) chaviyaṃ. “Kadā saññūḷhā pana te gahapati samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) thutiyaṃ. “Cattārome, bho gotama, vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 3.115) kulavagge. “Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhatthenoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.234) kāraṇe. “Mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.138) saṇṭhāne. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (pārā. 602) pamāṇe. “Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā”ti evamādīsu rūpāyatane. So idha chaviyā daṭṭhabbo. Tena abhikkantavaṇṇāti abhirūpacchavi, iṭṭhavaṇṇā manāpavaṇṇāti vuttaṃ hoti.

In such verses as this, it is seen in the sense of surpassing form. In such passages as, “Excellent, Master Gotama!”, it is in the sense of great approval. Here, however, it is in the sense of beautiful. Therefore, `abhikkantāya rattiyā` means on a desirable, lovely, and agreeable night; this is what is said. In `abhikkantavaṇṇā` (of excellent complexion), the word `abhikkanta` is in the sense of surpassing form, while the word `vaṇṇa` is seen in the senses of skin, praise, caste-group, cause, shape, size, the sphere of form, and so on. Among these: in “Golden-skinned is the Blessed One,” it refers to skin. In “When, householder, were the praises of the ascetic Gotama composed by you?”, it refers to praise. In “These four, Master Gotama, are the castes,” it refers to caste-group. In “Then by what cause is he called ‘Gandhatthena’?”, it refers to cause. In “Having manifested the form of a great elephant king,” it refers to shape. In “There are three sizes of the bowl,” it refers to size. In “Form, scent, taste, and nutritive essence,” it refers to the sphere of form. Here, it should be understood as skin. Therefore, `abhikkantavaṇṇā` means of beautiful skin, of a desirable complexion, of an agreeable complexion; this is what is said.

Kevalakappanti ettha kevalasaddo anavasesayebhuyyābyāmissānatirekadaḷhatthavisaṃyogādianekattho. Tathā hissa “kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariya”nti evamādīsu (pārā. 1) anavasesatā attho. “Kevalakappā ca aṅgamagadhā pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ ādāya upasaṅkamissantī”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 43) yebhuyyatā. “Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti evamādīsu (vibha. 225) abyāmissatā. “Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ nūna ayamāyasmā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 244) anatirekatā. “Āyasmato, bhante, anuruddhassa bāhiyo nāma saddhivihāriko kevalakappaṃ saṅghabhedāya ṭhito”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.243) daḷhatthatā. “Kevalī vusitavā uttamapurisoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.57) visaṃyogo. Idha [P 2.0377] pana anavasesatā atthoti adhippetā.

In the phrase 'kevalakappaṃ', the word 'kevala' has many meanings, such as entirety, predominance, unmixedness, not exceeding, firmness, and separation. Indeed, in phrases such as, “the holy life, entirely complete and pure,” the meaning is entirety. In phrases such as, “The majority of the people of Aṅga and Magadha will approach, bringing abundant hard and soft food,” the meaning is predominance. In phrases such as, “There is the arising of the entire mass of suffering,” the meaning is unmixedness. In phrases such as, “Surely this venerable one has mere faith,” the meaning is not exceeding. In phrases such as, “Venerable sir, the venerable Anuruddha’s co-resident disciple named Bāhiya is firmly intent on causing a schism in the Sangha,” the meaning is firmness. In phrases such as, “One who is perfected, who has lived the holy life, is called a supreme person,” the meaning is separation. Here, however, the intended meaning is entirety.

Kappasaddo panāyaṃ abhisaddahanavohārakālapaññattichedanavikappalesasamantabhāvādianekattho. Tathā hissa “okappaniyametaṃ bhoto gotamassa, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) abhisaddahanamattho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 250) vohāro. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kālo. “Iccāyasmā kappo”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 1098; cūḷani. kappamāṇavapucchā 117, kappamāṇavapucchāniddeso 61) paññatti[M 2.0240]. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”ti evamādīsu (jā. 2.22.1368; vi. va. 1094) chedanaṃ. “Kappati dvaṅgulakappo”ti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 446) vikappo. “Atthi kappo nipajjitu”nti evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.80) leso. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ [V 2.0232] obhāsetvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāvo. Idha panassa samantabhāvo attho adhippeto. Tasmā kevalakappaṃ jetavananti ettha anavasesaṃ samantato jetavananti attho.

Now, this term 'kappa' has many meanings, such as: conviction, usage, time, designation, cutting, contrivance, pretext, and all-encompassing. For instance, in passages such as, 'This is to be believed of the Venerable Gotama, as is fitting for the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' it has the meaning of conviction. In passages such as, 'Monks, I allow you to consume fruit with five ascetic allowances,' it means usage. In passages such as, 'Whereby I dwell for the entire duration,' it means time. In passages such as, 'Thus, the Venerable Kappa,' it means designation. In passages such as, 'Adorned, with hair and beard cut,' it means cutting. In passages such as, 'The two-finger-breadth allowance is permissible,' it means contrivance. In passages such as, 'There is a pretext for lying down,' it means pretext. And in passages such as, 'Having illuminated the Bamboo Grove all around,' it means all-encompassing. Here, however, its intended meaning is all-encompassing. Therefore, in the phrase 'kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ', the meaning is 'Jetavana all around, without remainder'.

Obhāsetvāti ābhāya pharitvā. Vālukāyāti saṇhāya vālukāya. Na saṇṭhātīti na patiṭṭhāti. Oḷārikanti brahmadevatāya hi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhānakāle attabhāvo oḷāriko māpetuṃ vaṭṭati pathavī vā, tasmā evamāha. Dhammāti iminā pubbe uggahitabuddhavacanaṃ dasseti. Nappavattino ahesunti sajjhāyamūḷhakā vācā parihīnāyeva ahesuṃ. Appaṭivānoti [P 2.0378] anivatto anukkaṇṭhito.

'Having illuminated' means having pervaded with radiance. 'On the sand' means on the fine sand. 'It does not stand' means it is not established. Regarding 'coarse': for when a Brahmā deva is establishing a footing on the earth, it is fitting to create a coarse physical body, or the earth itself; therefore, it is said thus. By 'Dhamma', it shows the word of the Buddha learned in a previous existence. 'They were not current' means the words rooted in recitation had simply declined. 'Not turning back' means not retreating, not discontented.

Dassanassāti cakkhuviññāṇena dassanassa. Upaṭṭhānassāti catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhānassa. Adhisīlanti dasavidhaṃ sīlaṃ. Tañhi pañcasīlaṃ upādāya adhisīlanti vuccati. Avihaṃ gatoti avihabrahmaloke nibbattosmīti dasseti.

'Of seeing' means of seeing with eye-consciousness. 'Of attending' means of attending with the four requisites. 'Higher virtue' means the tenfold virtue. For that, with reference to the five precepts, is called 'higher virtue.' 'Gone to Aviha' shows the meaning, 'I have been reborn in the Aviha Brahmā world.'

6. Kaṭuviyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta

129. Chaṭṭhe goyogapilakkhasminti gāvīnaṃ vikkayaṭṭhāne uṭṭhitapilakkhassa santike. Rittassādanti jhānasukhābhāvena rittassādaṃ. Bāhirassādanti kāmaguṇasukhavasena bāhirassādaṃ. Kaṭuviyanti ucchiṭṭhaṃ. Āmagandhenāti kodhasaṅkhātena vissagandhena. Avassutanti tintaṃ. Makkhikāti kilesamakkhikā. Nānupatissantīti uṭṭhāya na anubandhissanti. Nānvāssavissantīti anubandhitvā na khādissanti. Saṃvegamāpādīti sotāpanno jāto.

129. In the sixth: 'At the Goyoga Pilakkha tree' means: near the Pilakkha tree that stands in the place for buying and selling cattle. 'Devoid of taste' means: having an empty taste due to the absence of the bliss of jhāna. 'External taste' means: having an external taste by way of the bliss of sensual pleasures. 'Foul' means: like leftovers. 'With the stench of raw flesh' means: with the poisonous smell called anger. 'Dripping' means: soaked. 'Flies' means: the flies that are defilements. 'They will not fall upon' means: rising up, they will not pursue. 'They will not flow after' means: having pursued, they will not devour. 'He produced a sense of urgency' means: he became a stream-enterer.

Kaṭuviyakatoti ucchiṭṭhakato. Ārakā hotīti dūre hoti. Vighātasseva bhāgavāti dukkhasseva bhāgī. Caretīti carati gacchati. Dummedhoti duppañño. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭameva kathitaṃ, gāthāsu vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti. Sattame vaṭṭameva bhāsitaṃ.

'Made foul' means: made like leftovers. 'Is far away' means: is far. 'A partaker of distress' means: a partaker of suffering only. 'Wanders' means: goes. 'One of little wisdom' means: one without wisdom. In this sutta, only the round of existence is taught; in the verses, the round and the unbinding from the round are taught. In the seventh, only the round of existence is spoken of.

8. Dutiyaanuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta

131. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0233][M 2.0241] idaṃ te mānasminti ayaṃ te navavidhena vaḍḍhitamānoti attho. Idaṃ te uddhaccasminti idaṃ tava uddhaccaṃ cittassa uddhatabhāvo. Idaṃ [P 2.0379] te kukkuccasminti idaṃ tava kukkuccaṃ.

131. In the eighth: 'This is your conceit' means: 'this is your conceit that has increased in nine ways'. 'This is your restlessness' means: 'this is your restlessness, the agitated state of the mind'. 'This is your worry' means: 'this is your worry'.

9. Paṭicchannasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Paṭicchanna Sutta

132. Navame āvahantīti niyyanti. Paṭicchanno āvahatīti paṭicchannova hutvā niyyāti. Vivaṭo virocatīti ettha ekato ubhato attato sabbatthakatoti catubbidhā vivaṭatā veditabbā. Tattha ekato vivaṭaṃ nāma asādhāraṇasikkhāpadaṃ. Ubhato vivaṭaṃ nāma sādhāraṇasikkhāpadaṃ. Attato vivaṭaṃ nāma paṭiladdhadhammaguṇo. Sabbatthakavivaṭaṃ nāma tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ.

132. In the ninth: 'They bring' means: they proceed forth. 'Concealed, he brings' means: being concealed, he proceeds forth. 'Open, he shines'—here, openness should be understood as fourfold: open on one side, open on both sides, open in meaning, and open in all respects. Among these, 'open on one side' is the name for a training rule not held in common. 'Open on both sides' is the name for a training rule held in common. 'Open in meaning' is the name for the attained qualities of the Dhamma. 'Open in all respects' is the name for the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha.

10. Lekhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Lekha Sutta

133. Dasame abhiṇhanti abhikkhaṇaṃ nirantaraṃ. Āgāḷhenāti gāḷhena kakkhaḷena. Pharusenāti pharusavacanena. Gāḷhaṃ katvā pharusaṃ katvā vuccamānopīti attho. Amanāpenāti manaṃ anallīyantena avaḍḍhantena. Sandhiyatimevāti ghaṭiyatiyeva. Saṃsandatimevāti nirantarova hoti. Sammodatimevāti ekībhāvameva gacchati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

133. In the tenth, 'abhiṇhaṃ' means repeatedly, without interruption. 'Āgāḷhena' means severely, roughly. 'Pharusena' means with harsh speech. The meaning is: even when spoken to firmly and harshly. 'Amanāpena' means not adhering to the mind, not causing it to grow. 'Sandhiyatimeva' means he is indeed joined. 'Saṃsandatimeva' means he is indeed continuous. 'Sammodatimeva' means he indeed attains a state of unity. The rest is clear everywhere.

Kusināravaggo tatiyo.

The Kusināra Chapter, the Third.

(14) 4. Yodhājīvavaggo

(14) 4. The Yodhājīva Chapter

1. Yodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta

134. Catutthassa [V 2.0234] paṭhame yuddhaṃ upajīvatīti yodhājīvo. Rājārahoti rañño anucchaviko. Rājabhoggoti rañño upabhogaparibhogo. Aṅganteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti hattho viya pādo viya ca avassaṃ icchitabbattā aṅganti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Dūre pātī hotīti udake usabhamattaṃ[M 2.0242], thale aṭṭhusabhamattaṃ, tato vā uttarinti dūre kaṇḍaṃ pāteti. Duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayassa hi yodhājīvo navausabhamattaṃ kaṇḍaṃ pātesi, pacchimabhave bodhisatto yojanappamāṇaṃ. Akkhaṇavedhīti [P 2.0380] avirādhitavedhī, akkhaṇaṃ vā vijju vijjantarikāya vijjhituṃ samatthoti attho. Mahato kāyassa padāletāti ekatobaddhaṃ phalakasatampi mahiṃsacammasatampi aṅguṭṭhapamāṇabahalaṃ lohapaṭṭampi caturaṅgulabahalaṃ asanapadarampi vidatthibahalaṃ udumbarapadarampi dīghantena vālikasakaṭampi vinivijjhituṃ samatthoti attho. Yaṃkiñci rūpantiādi visuddhimagge vitthāritameva. Netaṃ mamātiādi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ. Sammappaññāya passatīti sammā hetunā kāraṇena sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya passati. Padāletīti arahattamaggena padāleti.

134. In the first of the fourth, a warrior (yodhājīvo) is so called because he lives by warfare (yuddhaṃ upajīvati). Rājāraho means suitable for the king. Rājabhoggo means for the king's use and enjoyment. Aṅganteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati means: because he is inevitably desired like a hand or a foot, he is counted as a limb. Dūre pātī hoti means: he makes an arrow fall a distance of one usabha in water and a distance of eight usabhas on land, or even further to a distant place. Indeed, the warrior of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya made an arrow fall a distance of nine usabhas; in his last life, the Bodhisatta was able to make an arrow fall a distance of a yojana. Akkhaṇavedhī means one who pierces without failure, or the meaning is: one who is able to shoot in the interval of a lightning flash. Mahato kāyassa padāletā means: he is able to pierce a hundred planks bound together, a hundred layers of buffalo hide, an iron plate eight fingers thick, an asana plank four fingers thick, an udumbara plank a span thick, or a cart of straw lengthwise. 'Whatever form...' and so on has been explained in detail by me in the Visuddhimagga. 'This is not mine...' and so on is said by way of rejecting craving, conceit, and wrong view. Sammappaññāya passati means: he sees rightly by cause and reason, with insight and path wisdom. Padāleti means: he splits with the path of Arahantship.

2. Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Parisā Sutta

135. Dutiye ukkācitavinītāti appaṭipucchitvā vinītā dubbinītaparisā. Paṭipucchāvinītāti pucchitvā vinītā suvinītaparisā. Yāvatāvinītāti pamāṇavasena vinītā, pamāṇaṃ ñatvā vinītaparisāti attho. “Yāvatajjhā”ti pāḷiyā pana yāva ajjhāsayāti attho, ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā vinītaparisāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatiyaṃ uttānameva.

135. In the second, ukkācitavinītā means an assembly that is difficult to discipline, being disciplined without being questioned. Paṭipucchāvinītā means an assembly that is easy to discipline, being disciplined after being questioned. Yāvatāvinītā means disciplined by way of a measure; the meaning is an assembly disciplined after knowing the measure. However, for the Pāli text 'yāvatajjhā', the meaning is 'as far as the disposition'; it is said to be an assembly disciplined after knowing the disposition. The third is self-evident.

4. Uppādāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Uppāda Sutta

137. Catutthe [V 2.0235] dhammaṭṭhitatāti sabhāvaṭṭhitatā. Dhammaniyāmatāti sabhāvaniyāmatā. Sabbe saṅkhārāti catubhūmakasaṅkhārā. Aniccāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Dukkhāti sampaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā. Anattāti avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā. Iti imasmiṃ sutte tīṇi lakkhaṇāni missakāni kathitāni.

137. In the fourth, dhammaṭṭhitatā means the stability of nature. Dhammaniyāmatā means the fixed nature of phenomena. Sabbe saṅkhārā means the conditioned things of the four planes. Aniccā means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. Dukkhā means suffering in the sense of oppression by arising and ceasing. Anattā means not-self in the sense of not being subject to one's will. Thus, in this sutta, the three characteristics are taught in combination.

5. Kesakambalasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Kesakambala Sutta

138. Pañcame tantāvutānaṃ vatthānanti paccatte sāmivacanaṃ, tantehi vāyitavatthānīti attho. Kesakambaloti [P 2.0381] manussakesehi vāyitakambalo[M 2.0243]. Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇavādānanti idampi paccatte sāmivacanaṃ. Paṭikiṭṭhoti pacchimako lāmako. Moghapurisoti tucchapuriso. Paṭibāhatīti paṭisedheti. Khippaṃ uḍḍeyyāti kuminaṃ oḍḍeyya. Chaṭṭhasattamāni uttānatthāneva.

138. In the fifth, tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ is a genitive used in the sense of the nominative; the meaning is 'cloths woven on looms'. Kesakambala means a blanket woven from human hair. The term vādānaṃ is also a genitive used in the sense of the nominative. Paṭikiṭṭha means the last, the inferior. Moghapurisa means a hollow man, that is, a man devoid of jhāna, path, and fruition. Paṭibāhati means rejects. Khippaṃ uḍḍeyya means one should set a fish-trap. The sixth and seventh are of self-evident meaning.

8. Assakhaḷuṅkasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta

141. Aṭṭhame assakhaḷuṅkoti assapoto. Idamassa javasmiṃ vadāmīti ayamassa ñāṇajavoti vadāmi. Idamassa vaṇṇasmiṃ vadāmīti ayamassa guṇavaṇṇoti vadāmi. Idamassa ārohapariṇāhasminti ayamassa uccabhāvo parimaṇḍalabhāvoti vadāmīti.

141. In the eighth, assakhaḷuṅka means a colt. 'I speak of this in regard to his speed' means: I say this—the knowing of the Four Noble Truths—is his swiftness of knowledge. 'I speak of this in regard to his appearance' means: I say this—the lack of coarseness in the Abhidhamma—is his fine appearance of virtue. 'I speak of this in regard to his height and girth' means: I say this—the receiving of the four requisites—is his tallness and well-roundedness.

9. Assaparassasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Assaparassa Sutta

142. Navame assaparasseti assesu parasse. Purisaparasseti purisesu parasse, purisapuriseti attho. Imasmiṃ sutte tīṇi maggaphalāni kathitāni. Tattha ayaṃ tīhi maggehi ñāṇajavasampannoti veditabbo.

142. In the ninth, assaparassa means another among horses. Purisaparassa means another among men; the meaning is man after man, in succession. In this sutta, three paths and fruits are taught. Therein, it should be understood that this person is endowed with the swiftness of knowledge through the three paths.

10. Assājānīyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Assājānīya Sutta

143. Dasame [V 2.0236] bhadreti bhaddake. Assājānīyeti kāraṇākāraṇaṃ jānanake asse. Purisājānīyesupi eseva nayo. Imasmiṃ sutte arahattaphalaṃ kathitaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ arahattamaggena ñāṇajavasampannoti veditabbo.

143. In the tenth, 'bhadra' means good. 'Assājānīya' means horses that know what is a cause and what is not a cause. This same method applies also to thoroughbred men. In this sutta, the fruit of Arahantship is taught. Therein, this one should be understood as endowed with the swiftness of knowledge by the path of Arahantship.

11. Paṭhamamoranivāpasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the First Moranivāpa Sutta

144. Ekādasame accantaniṭṭhoti antaṃ atikkantaniṭṭho, akuppaniṭṭho dhuvaniṭṭhoti attho. Sesaṃ sadisameva.

144. In the eleventh, 'accantaniṭṭha' means one who has an end that has been surpassed, one who has an unshakable end, one who has a permanent end; this is the meaning. The rest is just the same.

12. Dutiyamoranivāpasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Second Moranivāpa Sutta

145. Dvādasame iddhipāṭihāriyenāti ijjhanakapāṭihāriyena. Ādesanāpāṭihāriyenāti [P 2.0382] ādisitvā apadisitvā kathanaanukathanakathāpāṭihāriyena.

145. In the twelfth, 'iddhipāṭihāriyena' means by the miracle of accomplishment. 'Ādesanāpāṭihāriyena' means by the miracle of initial and subsequent discourse, after having pointed out and instructed.

13. Tatiyamoranivāpasuttavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Third Moranivāpa Sutta

146. Terasame [M 2.0244] sammādiṭṭhiyāti phalasamāpattatthāya sammādiṭṭhiyā. Sammāñāṇenāti phalañāṇena. Sammāvimuttiyāti sesehi phalasamāpattidhammehi. Imesu tīsupi suttesu khīṇāsavova kathitoti.

146. In the thirteenth sutta, 'sammādiṭṭhiyā' means by right view for the sake of attaining fruition. 'Sammāñāṇena' means by fruition-knowledge. 'Sammāvimuttiyā' means by the remaining factors of fruition attainment. In all these three suttas, only the one whose taints are destroyed is taught.

Yodhājīvavaggo catuttho.

The Yodhājīva Chapter is the fourth.

(15) 5. Maṅgalavaggo

(15) 5. The Chapter on Blessings

1-9. Akusalasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–9. Commentary on the Akusala Sutta and so forth.

147-155. Pañcamassa [V 2.0237] paṭhame yathābhataṃ nikkhittoti yathā ānetvā ṭhapito. Dutiye sāvajjenāti sadosena. Tatiye visamenāti sapakkhalanena. Samenāti apakkhalanena. Catutthe asucināti gūthasadisena aparisuddhena amejjhena. Sucināti parisuddhena mejjhena. Pañcamādīni uttānāneva.

147–155. In the first of the fifth chapter, 'yathābhataṃ nikkhitta' means placed just as it was brought. In the second, 'sāvajjenā' means with blemish. In the third, 'visamena' means with stumbling. 'Samena' means without stumbling. In the fourth, 'asucinā' means like excrement, impure, and unclean. 'Sucina' means pure and clean. The fifth and so forth are self-evident.

10. Pubbaṇhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Pubbaṇha Sutta

156. Dasame sunakkhattantiādīsu yasmiṃ divase tayo sucaritadhammā pūritā honti, so divaso laddhanakkhattayogo nāma, tenassa sadā sunakkhattaṃ nāma hotīti vuccati. Sveva divaso katamaṅgalo nāma hoti, tenassa sadā sumaṅgalanti vuccati. Pabhātampissa sadā suppabhātameva, sayanato uṭṭhānampi suhuṭṭhitameva, khaṇopi sukkhaṇova, muhuttopi sumuhuttova. Ettha ca dasaccharapamāṇo [P 2.0383] kālo khaṇo nāma, tena khaṇena dasakkhaṇo kālo layo nāma, tena layena ca dasalayo kālo khaṇalayo nāma, tena dasaguṇo muhutto nāma, tena dasaguṇo khaṇamuhutto nāmāti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Suyiṭṭhaṃ brahmacārisūti yasmiṃ divase tīṇi sucaritāni pūritāni, tadāssa seṭṭhacārīsu dinnadānaṃ suyiṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti[M 2.0245]. Padakkhiṇaṃ kāyakammanti taṃ divasaṃ tena kataṃ kāyakammaṃ vaḍḍhikāyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Padakkhiṇāni katvānāti vaḍḍhiyuttāni kāyakammādīni katvā. Labhantatthe padakkhiṇeti padakkhiṇe vaḍḍhiattheyeva labhati. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti.

156. In the tenth sutta, regarding 'an auspicious constellation' and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this way: The day on which the three principles of good conduct are fulfilled is called 'endowed with a good constellation.' Therefore, for that person, it is always called a 'good constellation,' so it is said. That very day is called 'one for which an auspicious ceremony has been performed'; therefore, for that person, it is always a 'good auspicious sign,' so it is said. For that person, the dawn is also always indeed a good dawn, rising from bed is indeed a good rising, the moment is also indeed a good moment, and the instant is also indeed a good instant. And here, a period of time the measure of ten finger-snaps is called a moment (khaṇa); a period of ten moments is called a laya; a period of ten layas is called a khaṇalaya; ten times that is called an instant (muhutta); and ten times that instant is called a khaṇamuhutta—this division should be understood. Regarding 'Well-offered to those practicing the holy life': on the day when the three good conducts are fulfilled, then, for that person, the gift given to those of excellent conduct is called 'well-offered.' Regarding 'Auspicious bodily action': the bodily action performed by that person on that day is called 'bodily action connected with growth.' In the remaining phrases, this is the method. Regarding 'having performed auspicious deeds': having performed bodily actions and so forth that are connected with growth. Regarding 'they attain the object in auspiciousness': they attain only the auspicious benefits of growth. The rest is clear.

Maṅgalavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Auspicious Signs is the fifth.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Third Fifty is finished.

(16) 6. Acelakavaggavaṇṇanā

(16) 6. Commentary on the Chapter on the Naked Ascetic

157-163. Ito [V 2.0238] paresu āgāḷhā paṭipadāti gāḷhā kakkhaḷā lobhavasena thiraggahaṇā. Nijjhāmāti attakilamathānuyogavasena suṭṭhu jhāmā santattā paritattā. Majjhimāti neva kakkhaḷā na jhāmā majjhe bhavā. Acelakoti niccelo naggo. Muttācāroti vissaṭṭhācāro, uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karoti, passāvaṃ karoti, khādati bhuñjati. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi niṭṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ [P 2.0384] apalekhati, uccārampi katvā hatthasmiṃyeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalekhati. Bhikkhāya gahaṇatthaṃ “ehi, bhadante”ti vutto na etīti na ehibhadantiko. “Tena hi tiṭṭha, bhante”ti vuttopi na tiṭṭhatīti na tiṭṭhabhadantiko. Tadubhayampi kira so “etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti na karoti. Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭabhikkhaṃ. Uddissakatanti idaṃ tumhe uddissa katanti evamārocitabhikkhaṃ. Nimantananti “asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthā”ti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyati na gaṇhāti. Na kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā dīyamānaṃ bhikkhampi na gaṇhāti. Na kaḷopimukhāti kaḷopīti ukkhali vā pacchi vā, tatopi na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? “Kumbhikaḷopiyo maṃ nissāya kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantī”ti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā dīyamānaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? “Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatī”ti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo. Dvinnanti [M 2.0246] dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti.

Hereafter, ‘an extreme practice’ (āgāḷhā paṭipadā) means a rigid, harsh practice, firmly grasped due to greed. ‘Scorched’ (nijjhāmā) means thoroughly scorched, heated, and burnt by the practice of self-mortification. ‘The middle way’ (majjhimā) means neither rigid nor scorched, existing in the middle. ‘Naked ascetic’ (acelaka) means one without clothes, naked. ‘Unrestrained in conduct’ (muttācāra) means loose in conduct, devoid of the behavior of ordinary householders; while standing, he defecates, urinates, eats, and consumes. ‘Licking the hands’ (hatthāpalekhana): when the morsel in his hand is finished, he licks his hand with his tongue; and after defecating, perceiving his hand as a cleansing stick, he scrapes with his hand. ‘Not a “Come here, venerable”’ (na ehibhadantiko): when told, “Come here, venerable,” he does not come. ‘Not a “Stay here, venerable”’ (na tiṭṭhabhadantiko): when told, “Stay here, venerable,” he does not stay. It is said that he does neither, thinking, “I will have followed his word.” ‘Brought beforehand’ (abhihaṭa): alms brought having been taken beforehand. ‘Made for a specific person’ (uddissakata): alms announced as, “This was made specifically for you.” ‘Invitation’ (nimantana): he does not accept or take even alms to which he has been invited, such as, “You should enter such-and-such family, street, or village.” ‘Not from a pot’s mouth’ (na kumbhimukhā): he does not take alms even when being given after being taken out from a pot. ‘Not from a basket’s mouth’ (na kaḷopimukhā): kaḷopī means a cooking pot or a basket; he does not take from that either. Why? “On account of me, the pot and the basket might receive a blow from a ladle.” ‘Not across a threshold’ (na eḷakamantara): he does not take alms being given after making a threshold the boundary. Why? “On account of me, this is made into a boundary.” The same principle applies to sticks and pestles. ‘Not between two’ (dvinnam): he does not take when one person, from among two who are eating, gets up and offers it. Why? Because it is an interruption to the morsel.

Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamati, pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hoti, purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotīti na gaṇhāti. Na saṅkittīsūti saṅkittetvā katabhattesu. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānaṃ atthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni [P 2.0385] samādapetvā bhattaṃ pacanti, ukkaṭṭhācelako tato na paṭiggaṇhāti. Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho “piṇḍaṃ labhissāmī”ti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti. Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī[V 2.0239]. Sace hi acelakaṃ disvā “imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā”ti manussā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti, tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti, tato āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? “Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jāto”ti.

Furthermore, regarding the phrases beginning with 'not from a pregnant woman': the child in the pregnant woman’s womb is distressed; for the child of a nursing mother, there is an interruption to the milk; and for a woman who has gone to another man, there is an interruption to her pleasure—therefore, he does not accept. 'Not from those who have made a proclamation' means from meals prepared after having made a proclamation. During a time of famine, it is said, the disciples of the naked ascetics, for the sake of the naked ascetics, having solicited rice and so on from here and there, cook a meal; the most eminent naked ascetic does not accept from that. 'Not where a dog is' means: he does not accept what has been brought from a place where a dog is present thinking, “I will get a lump of food,” without first giving to that dog. Why? Because for this dog, there is an interruption to its lump of food. 'Wandering in swarms' means wandering in groups. For if people, seeing a naked ascetic, enter a kitchen thinking, “We will give alms-food to this one,” and as they are entering, flies that were resting in rice pots, baskets, and so on, fly up and move about in swarms, he does not accept the alms-food brought from there. Why? Because he thinks, “On account of me, an interruption to the flies' feeding has occurred.”

Thusodakanti sabbasassasambhārehi katasovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbesu sāvajjasaññī. Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiṃyeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati. Ekālopikoti ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti. Ekāhikanti ekadivasantarikaṃ. Addhamāsikanti addhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ, ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena addhamāsavārenāti evaṃ divasavārena ābhatabhattabhojanaṃ. Sākabhakkhotiādīni vuttatthāneva.

'Thusodaka' refers to the sovīraka made with the ingredients of all grains. And herein, only the drinking of intoxicants is faulty, but this one is one who perceives fault in all of them. 'Ekāgārika' is one who, having received alms-food at only one house, returns. 'Ekālopika' is one who subsists on just one morsel. In the case of 'dvāgārika' and so on, this is the same method. 'Ekissāpi dattiyā' means with a single datti. A datti is a small bowl, wherein they place the first portion of the alms-food and keep it. 'Ekāhikaṃ' means every other day. 'Aḍḍhamāsikaṃ' means every half-month. 'Pariyāyabhattabhojanaṃ' means eating a meal by turns; that is, eating a meal brought by a turn of days, thus: by a turn of one day, or two days, or seven days, or a half-month. The terms beginning with 'sākabhakkho' have the meaning already stated.

Ubbhaṭṭhakoti uddhaṃ ṭhitako. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikavīriyamanuyutto, gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ [P 2.0386] koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karoti. Seyyanti [M 2.0247] sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappeti. Sāyaṃ tatiyamassāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. Pāto majjhanhike sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ “pāpaṃ pavāhessāmī”ti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharati.

Ubbhaṭṭhako means one who stands upright. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto means one who is devoted to the exertion of squatting; even when walking, being in a squatting posture, he proceeds by jumping repeatedly. Kaṇṭakāpassayiko is one who, having driven either iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground, and having spread a hide there, performs standing, walking, and so on. Regarding his lying down (seyyaṃ), even when sleeping, he prepares his bed right there. Sāyatatiyakaṃ means one for whom the evening is the third time. In the morning, at midday, and in the evening—thus three times a day—thinking, 'I will wash away evil,' he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water.

Kāye kāyānupassītiādīni heṭṭhā ekakanipātavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, majjhimā paṭipadāti, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogañca attakilamathānuyogañcāti dve ante anupagatā, sassatucchedantehi vā vimuttā majjhimā paṭipadāti veditabbā.

The phrases beginning with 'observing the body in the body' and so forth should be understood in the same way as has been stated below in the commentary on the Book of Ones. This, bhikkhus, is called the Middle Path. Bhikkhus, this path, not having approached the two extremes—namely, the devotion to indulgence in sensual pleasures and the devotion to self-mortification—and being free from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, should be understood as the Middle Path.

Acelakavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics is the sixth.

17-18. Peyyālavaggādivaṇṇanā

17-18. Commentary on the Chapter of Repetitions and so forth

164-184. Samanuññoti [V 2.0240] samānajjhāsayo. Rāgassāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa. Abhiññāyāti abhijānanatthaṃ. Suññato samādhītiādīhi tīhipi samādhīhi vipassanāva kathitā. Vipassanā hi niccābhinivesa-niccanimitta-niccapaṇidhiādīnaṃ abhāvā imāni nāmāni labhati. Pariññāyāti parijānanatthaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayoti.

164-184. Samanuñño means having a similar inclination. Rāgassa means of the lust that has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object. Abhiññāya means for the purpose of directly knowing. By the three concentrations beginning with 'suññato samādhi' (concentration on emptiness), only insight is spoken of. Indeed, insight, due to the absence of adherence to permanence, the sign of permanence, the aspiration for permanence, and so on, obtains these names. Pariññāya means for the purpose of full understanding. In the remaining passages as well, this same method is to be understood.

Peyyālavaggādi niṭṭhitā.

The Chapter of Repetitions and so forth is concluded.

Manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Tikanipātassa saṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of Threes is concluded.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Catukkanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Book of Fours

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Bhaṇḍagāmavaggo

1. The Chapter on Bhaṇḍagāma

1. Anubuddhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Anubuddha Sutta

1. Catukkanipātassa [V 2.0241][M 2.0249][P 3.0001] paṭhame ananubodhāti abujjhanena ajānanena. Appaṭivedhāti appaṭivijjhanena apaccakkhakiriyāya. Dīghamaddhānanti cirakālaṃ. Sandhāvitanti bhavato bhavaṃ gamanavasena sandhāvitaṃ. Saṃsaritanti punappunaṃ gamanāgamanavasena saṃsaritaṃ. Mamañceva tumhākañcāti mayā ca tumhehi ca. Atha vā sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritanti sandhāvanaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ mamañceva [V 2.0242] tumhākañca ahosīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Ariyassāti niddosassa. Sīlaṃ samādhi paññāti ime pana tayo dhammā maggaphalasampayuttāva veditabbā, vimuttināmena phalameva niddiṭṭhaṃ. Bhavataṇhāti bhavesu taṇhā. Bhavanettīti [P 3.0002] bhavarajju. Taṇhāya eva etaṃ nāmaṃ. Tāya hi sattā goṇā viya gīvāya bandhitvā taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ nīyanti, tasmā bhavanettīti vuccati.

1. In the first sutta of the Book of Fours: Ananubodhā means by not awakening, by not knowing. Appaṭivedhā means by not penetrating, by not realizing directly. Dīghamaddhānaṃ means for a long time. Sandhāvitaṃ means having roamed from existence to existence by way of going. Saṃsaritaṃ means having transmigrated by way of going and coming again and again. Mamañceva tumhākañca means by me and by you. Alternatively, in 'sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'the roaming and transmigration of both myself and you occurred.' Ariyassa means of the faultless one. Sīlaṃ, samādhi, paññā: these three qualities, however, should be understood as associated with the path and its fruition; by the name 'liberation,' only the fruition is indicated. Bhavataṇhā means craving for existences. Bhavanetti means the guide-rope of existence. This is indeed a name for craving. For by this, beings, like oxen tied by the neck, are led to this and that existence; therefore, it is called 'the guide-rope of existence.'

Anuttarāti lokuttarā. Dukkhassantakaroti vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaro. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Idamassa bodhimaṇḍe paṭhamaparinibbānaṃ, pacchā pana yamakasālānamantare anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutoti yathānusandhinā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Anuttarā means supramundane. Dukkhassantakaro means the end-maker of the suffering of the round of existence. Cakkhumā means possessing the five eyes. Parinibbuto means fully extinguished through the extinction of defilements. This was his first full extinguishment at the seat of Awakening. Later, however, between the twin sāla trees, he was fully extinguished in the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining—thus he concluded the discourse in accordance with its sequence.

2. Papatitasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Papatita Sutta

2. Dutiye papatitoti patito cuto. Appapatitoti apatito patiṭṭhito. Tattha lokiyamahājano patitoyeva nāma, sotāpannādayo kilesuppattikkhaṇe patitā nāma, khīṇāsavo ekantapatiṭṭhito nāma.

2. In the second sutta, papatito (fallen) means fallen, departed. Appapatito (not fallen) means not fallen, established. Therein, the great mass of worldlings are indeed called 'fallen.' Stream-enterers and the like are called 'fallen' at the moment of the arising of defilements. The one whose taints are destroyed is called 'utterly established.'

Cutā [M 2.0250] patantīti ye cutā, te patanti nāma. Patitāti ye patitā, te cutā nāma. Cutattā patitā, patitattā cutāti attho. Giddhāti rāgarattā. Punarāgatāti puna jātiṃ puna jaraṃ puna byādhiṃ puna maraṇaṃ āgatā nāma honti. Kataṃ kiccanti catūhi maggehi kattabbakiccaṃ kataṃ. Rataṃ rammanti ramitabbayuttake guṇajāte ramitaṃ. Sukhenānvāgataṃ sukhanti sukhena sukhaṃ anuāgataṃ sampattaṃ. Mānusakasukhena dibbasukhaṃ, jhānasukhena vipassanāsukhaṃ, vipassanāsukhena maggasukhaṃ, maggasukhena [P 3.0003] phalasukhaṃ, phalasukhena nibbānasukhaṃ sampattaṃ adhigatanti attho.

Cutā patanti (those who have shifted, fall) means: those who have shifted are called 'falling.' Patitā (fallen) means: those who have fallen are called 'shifted.' The meaning is: because of having shifted, they are fallen; because of having fallen, they have shifted. Giddhā (greedy) means: impassioned with lust. Punarāgatā (returned again) means: they are those who have come again to birth, again to aging, again to sickness, and again to death. Kataṃ kiccaṃ (the task is done) means: the task to be done by the four paths is done. Rataṃ rammaṃ (delighting in the delightful) means: delighting in the collection of qualities worthy of delight. Sukhenānvāgataṃ sukhaṃ (happiness followed by happiness) means: through one happiness, another happiness is successively reached, is attained. The meaning is: through human happiness, divine happiness is attained; through the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of insight; through the happiness of insight, the happiness of the path; through the happiness of the path, the happiness of fruition; and through the happiness of fruition, the happiness of Nibbāna is attained and realized.

3. Paṭhamakhatasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the First Khata Sutta

3. Tatiyaṃ dukanipātavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva. Gāthāsu pana nindiyanti ninditabbayuttakaṃ. Nindatīti garahati. Pasaṃsiyoti pasaṃsitabbayutto. Vicināti mukhena so kalinti yo evaṃ pavatto[V 2.0243], tena mukhena kaliṃ vicināti nāma. Kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindatīti tena ca kalinā sukhaṃ na paṭilabhati. Sabbassāpi sahāpi attanāti sabbenapi sakena dhanena ceva attanā ca saddhiṃ yo parājayo, so appamattakova kalīti attho. Yo sugatesūti yo pana sammaggatesu puggalesu cittaṃ padusseyya, ayaṃ cittapadosova tato kalito mahantataro kali. Idāni tassa mahantatarabhāvaṃ dassento sataṃ sahassānantiādimāha. Tattha sataṃ sahassānanti nirabbudagaṇanāya satasahassaṃ. Chattiṃsatīti aparāni ca chattiṃsati nirabbudāni. Pañca cāti abbudagaṇanāya ca pañca abbudāni. Yamariyagarahīti yaṃ ariye garahanto nirayaṃ upapajjati, tattha ettakaṃ āyuppamāṇanti.

3. The third [sutta] has already been explained in the commentary on the Dukanipāta. In the verses, however, the meaning should be understood thus: nindiyaṃ means a person worthy of blame. Nindati means he reproaches. Pasaṃsiyo means worthy of praise. Vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ means: a person who behaves thus acquires misfortune with his mouth. Kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindati means: through that misfortune he does not obtain happiness. Sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā means: the defeat that occurs together with all of one's own wealth and with oneself is called a minor misfortune. Yo sugatesu means: whoever should corrupt his mind towards well-gone persons, this very corruption of mind is a far greater misfortune than that. Now, wishing to show its state of being much greater, he spoke the words beginning with sataṃ sahassānaṃ. Therein, sataṃ sahassānaṃ means one hundred thousand by the Nirabbuda reckoning. Chattiṃsati means and another thirty-six Nirabbudas. Pañca ca means and five Abbudas by the Abbuda reckoning. Yamariyagarahī means: a person reproaching the noble ones is reborn in a certain hell; there, the measure of the lifespan is this much.

4. Dutiyakhatasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Khata Sutta

4. Catutthe [P 3.0004] mātari pitari cātiādīsu mittavindako mātari micchāpaṭipanno nāma, ajātasattu pitari micchāpaṭipanno nāma, devadatto tathāgate micchāpaṭipanno nāma, kokāliko tathāgatasāvake micchāpaṭipanno nāma. Bahuñcāti bahukameva. Pasavatīti paṭilabhati. Tāyāti tāya micchāpaṭipattisaṅkhātāya adhammacariyāya. Peccāti ito gantvā. Apāyaṃ gacchatīti nirayādīsu aññatarasmiṃ nibbattati. Sukkapakkhepi eseva nayo.

4. In the fourth sutta, regarding 'towards mother and father' and so on, Mittavindaka is one who has practiced wrongly towards his mother, Ajātasattu is one who has practiced wrongly towards his father, Devadatta is one who has practiced wrongly towards the Tathāgata, and Kokālika is one who has practiced wrongly towards a disciple of the Tathāgata. 'Much' means: very much indeed. 'Brings forth' means: obtains. 'By that' means: by that unrighteous conduct called wrong practice. 'After departing' means: having gone from here. 'Goes to a state of loss' means: is reborn in one or another of the hells and so on. This same method applies also to the bright division.

5. Anusotasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Downstream Sutta

5. Pañcame [M 2.0251] anusotaṃ gacchatīti anusotagāmī. Kilesasotassa paccanīkapaṭipattiyā paṭisotaṃ gacchatīti paṭisotagāmī. Ṭhitattoti ṭhitasabhāvo. Tiṇṇoti oghaṃ taritvā ṭhito. Pāraṅgatoti paratīraṃ gato. Thale tiṭṭhatīti nibbānathale tiṭṭhati. Brāhmaṇoti seṭṭho niddoso. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Kāme ca paṭisevatīti kilesakāmehi vatthukāme paṭisevati. Pāpañca kammaṃ karotīti pāpañca pāṇātipātādikammaṃ karoti. Pāpañca kammaṃ na karotīti pañcaverakammaṃ na karoti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ṭhitattoti ayaṃ anāgāmī puggalo tasmā lokā puna paṭisandhivasena anāgamanato ṭhitatto nāma.

5. In the fifth sutta, 'goes with the stream' means: one who goes with the stream. 'Goes against the stream' means: one who goes against the stream by the practice in opposition to the stream of defilements. 'One with a steadfast self' means: one whose nature is steadfast. 'Crossed over' means: having crossed over the four floods, one stands. 'Gone to the far shore' means: one has gone to the other shore. 'Stands on dry land' means: one stands on the dry land of Nibbāna. 'A brahmin' means: excellent, faultless. 'Here' means: in this world. 'And indulges in sensual pleasures' means: one indulges in objects of sensual pleasure by means of the defilements of sensual pleasure. 'And does an evil action' means: one does an evil action such as the destruction of life. 'And does not do an evil action' means: one does not do the action of the five enmities. As for 'This one, monks, is called one with a steadfast self': this non-returner is called 'one with a steadfast self' because of not coming again from that world by way of rebirth-linking.

Taṇhādhipannāti [P 3.0005] taṇhāya adhipannā ajjhotthaṭā, taṇhaṃ vā adhipannā ajjhogāḷhā. Paripuṇṇasekhoti [V 2.0244] sikkhāpāripūriyā ṭhito. Aparihānadhammoti aparihīnasabhāvo. Cetovasippattoti cittavasībhāvaṃ patto. Evarūpo khīṇāsavo hoti, idha pana anāgāmī kathito. Samāhitindriyoti samāhitachaḷindriyo. Paroparāti parovarā uttamalāmakā, kusalākusalāti attho. Sameccāti ñāṇena samāgantvā. Vidhūpitāti viddhaṃsitā jhāpitā vā. Vusitabrahmacariyoti maggabrahmacariyaṃ vasitvā ṭhito. Lokantagūti tividhassāpi lokassa antaṃ gato. Pāragatoti chahākārehi pāragato. Idha khīṇāsavova kathito. Iti suttepi gāthāsupi vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

‘Overcome by craving’ means: oppressed and overwhelmed by craving; or alternatively, having reached unto craving, they are immersed. ‘Fully accomplished in training’ means: established in the completion of the training. ‘Not subject to decline’ means: one whose nature does not decline. ‘Master of mind’ means: one who has attained mastery over the mind. Such a one is a perfected one, but here the Non-returner is spoken of. ‘With faculties composed’ means: with the six faculties well-composed. ‘Superior and inferior’ means: the highest and the lowest, that is, the wholesome and unwholesome. ‘Having fully understood’ means: having come together by means of knowledge. ‘Dispelled’ means: destroyed or burned away. ‘Lived the holy life’ means: having lived the noble life which is the path, one is established. ‘Gone to the end of the world’ means: having gone to the end of the threefold world. ‘Gone to the far shore’ means: gone to the far shore in six ways. Here, only the perfected one is spoken of. Thus, in the sutta and in the verses, both the round of existence and its cessation are spoken of.

6. Appassutasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Little-Learned Sutta

6. Chaṭṭhe anupapannoti anupāgato. Suttantiādīsu ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakhandhakaparivārasuttanipātamaṅgalasuttaratanasutta- nāḷakasuttatuvaṭakasuttāni, aññampi ca suttanāmakaṃ tathāgatavacanaṃ suttanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyanti veditabbaṃ, visesena saṃyuttake sakalopi sagāthāvaggo. Sakalampi abhidhammapiṭakaṃ, niggāthakasuttaṃ, yañca aññampi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi asaṅgahitaṃ [P 3.0006] buddhavacanaṃ, taṃ veyyākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Dhammapada-theragāthā-therigāthā suttanipāte nosuttanāmikā suddhikagāthā [M 2.0252] ca gāthāti veditabbā. Somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā dveasīti suttantā udānanti veditabbā. “Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā”tiādinayappavattā dasuttarasatasuttantā itivuttakanti veditabbā. Apaṇṇakajātakādīni paññāsādhikāni pañca jātakasatāni jātakanti veditabbāni. “Cattārome, bhikkhave, acchariyā abbhutā dhammā ānande”tiādinayappavattā sabbepi acchariyaabbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttā suttantā abbhutadhammanti veditabbā. Cūḷavedallamahāvedallasammādiṭṭhisakkapañhasaṅkhārabhājaniyamahāpuṇṇamasuttādayo sabbepi vedañca tuṭṭhiñca laddhā laddhā pucchitā suttantā vedallanti veditabbā. Na atthamaññāya na dhammamaññāyāti aṭṭhakathañca pāḷiñca ajānitvā. Dhammānudhammappaṭipannoti navalokuttaradhammassa anurūpadhammaṃ sahasīlaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ na paṭipanno hoti. Iminā upāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Paṭhamavāre panettha appassutadussīlo kathito, dutiye appassutakhīṇāsavo, tatiye bahussutadussīlo, catutthe bahussutakhīṇāsavo.

6. In the sixth, 'anupapanno' means 'not approached'. The Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, Parivāra, Suttanipāta, Maṅgalasutta, Ratanasutta, Nāḷakasutta, and Tuvaṭṭakasutta, and also any other word of the Tathāgata designated as a 'sutta', are to be known as 'Sutta'. All suttas with verses are to be known as 'Geyya'; especially, in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the entire Sagāthāvagga. The entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and whatever other word of the Buddha is not included in the other eight categories, are to be known as 'Veyyākaraṇa'. The Dhammapada, the Theragāthā, the Therīgāthā, and the pure verses in the Suttanipāta which are not designated as suttas, are to be known as 'Gāthā'. The eighty-two suttas connected with verses born of knowledge accompanied by joy are to be known as 'Udāna'. The one hundred and ten suttas that proceed in the manner beginning with 'Thus was this spoken by the Blessed One' are to be known as 'Itivuttaka'. The five hundred and fifty Jātakas, beginning with the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, are to be known as 'Jātaka'. All suttas connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, which proceed in the manner beginning with 'Monks, these four are the wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda', are to be known as 'Abbhutadhamma'. The Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Sammādiṭṭhi, Sakka Pañha, Saṅkhārabhājaniya, Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta, and others, and all suttas wherein questions are asked after having obtained both knowledge and satisfaction, are to be known as 'Vedalla'. The phrase 'not having understood the meaning and not having understood the Dhamma' means not having known the commentary and the Pāḷi. 'Not practicing in accordance with the Dhamma' means: one is not practicing the preliminary path together with virtue, which is the practice conforming to the nine supramundane states. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases. Here, in the first case, the one with little learning and bad virtue is spoken of; in the second, the one with little learning whose cankers are destroyed; in the third, the one with much learning and bad virtue; in the fourth, the one with much learning whose cankers are destroyed.

Sīlesu [P 3.0007] asamāhitoti sīlesu aparipūrakārī. Sīlato ca sutena cāti sīlabhāgena ca [V 2.0245] sutabhāgena ca “ayaṃ dussīlo appassuto”ti evaṃ taṃ garahantīti attho. Tassa sampajjate sutanti tassa puggalassa yasmā tena sutena sutakiccaṃ kataṃ, tasmā tassa sutaṃ sampajjati nāma. Nāssa sampajjateti sutakiccassa akatattā na sampajjati. Dhammadharanti sutadhammānaṃ ādhārabhūtaṃ. Sappaññanti supaññaṃ. Nekkhaṃ jambonadassevāti jambunadaṃ vuccati jātisuvaṇṇaṃ, tassa jambunadassa nekkhaṃ viya, pañcasuvaṇṇaparimāṇaṃ suvaṇṇaghaṭikaṃ viyāti attho.

'Unsettled in virtue' means not fulfilling virtue. 'By virtue and learning' means by the state of virtue and the state of learning—thus they criticize him as 'This one is immoral and unlearned'—this is the meaning. 'His learning succeeds' means that because that person has accomplished the task of learning with that learning, therefore his learning is said to succeed. 'It does not succeed for him' means it does not succeed because the task of learning has not been accomplished. 'Dhamma-bearer' means a support for the learned Dhamma. 'Wise' means having good wisdom. 'Like an ornament of Jambonada gold' means Jambunada is called natural gold; like an ornament of that Jambunada gold, that is, like a golden ingot of five suvaṇṇas in measure—this is the meaning.

7. Sobhanasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sobhana Sutta

7. Sattame viyattāti paññāveyyattiyena samannāgatā. Vinītāti vinayaṃ upetā suvinītā. Visāradāti vesārajjena somanassasahagatena ñāṇena samannāgatā. Dhammadharāti sutadhammānaṃ ādhārabhūtā. Bhikkhu ca sīlasampannoti gāthāya kiñcāpi ekekasseva ekeko guṇo kathito, sabbesaṃ pana sabbepi vaṭṭantīti.

7. In the seventh, 'accomplished' means endowed with the sharpness of wisdom. 'Trained' means having approached discipline, well-trained. 'Confident' means endowed with confidence, which is knowledge accompanied by joy. 'Dhamma-bearers' means being supports for the Dhamma that has been heard. Regarding the verse 'And the monk accomplished in virtue,' although a single quality is spoken of for each one, all qualities are applicable to all.

8. Vesārajjasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Vesārajja Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0253] vesārajjānīti ettha sārajjapaṭipakkho vesārajjaṃ, catūsu ṭhānesu sārajjābhāvaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasomanassamayañāṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ uttamaṭṭhānaṃ. Āsabhā vā pubbabuddhā, tesaṃ ṭhānanti attho. Apica gavasatajeṭṭhako usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho. Vajasatajeṭṭhako vā usabho, vajasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho[P 3.0008], sabbagavaseṭṭho sabbaparissayasaho seto pāsādiko mahābhāravaho asanisatasaddehipi asampakampiyo nisabho, so idha usabhoti adhippeto. Idampi hi tassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ. Ṭhānanti catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā vavatthānaṃ. Idaṃ pana āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yatheva hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi catūhi vesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisapathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci paccatthikena paccāmittena akampiyo acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānova taṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti upagacchati na paccakkhāti, attani āropeti. Tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti.

8. In the eighth, regarding 'assurances' (vesārajjāni): assurance is the opposite of timidity (sārajja); it is the name for the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises in one who reflects on the absence of timidity in the four instances. 'The bull's place' (āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ) means the foremost place, the supreme place. Or, the former Buddhas are 'bulls' (āsabhā); this means their place. Furthermore, the leader of a hundred cattle is an usabha (bull), and the leader of a thousand cattle is a vasabha (great bull). Or, the leader of a hundred pens is an usabha, and the leader of a thousand pens is a vasabha. The best of all cattle, enduring all dangers, white, inspiring, bearing great burdens, and unshakable even by the sounds of a hundred thunderbolts, is a nisabha (chief bull); it is this one that is intended here by usabha. Indeed, this (usabha) is also a synonym for that (nisabha). Āsabhaṃ means 'belonging to the usabha'. 'Place' (ṭhānaṃ) means a firm standing, having pressed upon the earth with four feet. But this is āsabhaṃ because it is like a bull (āsabhaṃ viya). For just as the bull known as nisabha stands with an unmoving stance, having pressed upon the earth with its four feet, so too the Tathāgata, with the four feet of the assurances, having pressed upon the earth of the eight assemblies, stands with an unmoving stance, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world with its devas. Standing thus, he claims that bull's place, attains it, does not reject it, and establishes it in himself. Therefore it is said, 'He claims the bull's place.'

Parisāsūti [V 2.0246] aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadati, sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadati. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena dassetabbo. Yathā vā sīho sahanato ca hananato ca sīhoti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgato lokadhammānaṃ sahanato parappavādānañca hananato sīhoti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttassa sīhassa nādaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Tattha yathā sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso “iti rūpa”ntiādinā nayena nānāvidhadesanāvilāsasampannaṃ [P 3.0009] sīhanādaṃ nadati. Tena vuttaṃ “parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadatī”ti.

'In assemblies' means in the eight assemblies. 'He roars the lion's roar' means he utters the supreme roar, the fearless roar; or, he utters a roar similar to that of a lion. This meaning should be shown by the Sīhanāda Sutta. Or, just as a lion is called a lion because of enduring and destroying, so the Tathāgata is called a lion because he endures the worldly conditions and destroys the doctrines of others. The roar of such a lion is the lion's roar. Therein, just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, confident in all matters and free from horripilation, roars the lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the Tathāgata's powers, confident in the eight assemblies and free from horripilation, utters the lion's roar, endowed with the grace of diverse discourses, by the method beginning with, "Such is form." Therefore, it is said, "He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies."

Brahmacakkaṃ [M 2.0254] pavattetīti ettha brahmanti seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ visuddhaṃ. Cakkasaddo panāyaṃ –

'He sets rolling the Brahma-wheel' – here, 'brahma' means excellent, supreme, pure. The word 'wheel,' however, is seen in the following senses:

“Sampattiyaṃ lakkhaṇe ca, rathaṅge iriyāpathe;

Dāne ratanadhammūra-cakkādīsu ca dissati;

Dhammacakke idha mato, tañca dvedhā vibhāvaye”.

It is seen in accomplishment, characteristic mark, chariot-part, and deportment; in giving, in a jewel-wheel, a Dhamma-wheel, a razor-wheel, and so on. Here, it is understood as the Dhamma-wheel, and one should discern it as twofold.

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.31) hi ayaṃ sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Pādatalesu cakkāni jātānī”ti (dī. ni. 2.35) ettha lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti (dha. pa. 1) ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) ettha iriyāpathe. “Dadaṃ bhuñja mā ca pamādo, cakkaṃ vattaya sabbapāṇina”nti (jā. 1.7.149) ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti (dī. ni. 2.243; ma. ni. 3.256) ettha ratanacakke. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562) ettha dhammacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti (jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103) ettha uracakke. “Khurapariyantena cepi cakkenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166) ettha paharaṇacakke. “Asanivicakka”nti (dī. ni. 3.61; saṃ. ni. 2.162) ettha asanimaṇḍale. Idha [P 3.0010] panāyaṃ dhammacakke mato.

In passages such as, 'These four wheels, monks, by which gods and humans are endowed...' (AN 4.31), this word 'cakka' is seen in the sense of accomplishment. In 'Wheels were born on the soles of his feet' (DN 14), it is in the sense of a characteristic mark. In 'As the wheel [follows] the foot of the one pulling...' (Dhp 1), it is in the sense of a chariot-part. In 'Four-wheeled, with nine doors' (SN 1.29), it is in the sense of deportment. In 'Give and enjoy, and do not be heedless; set the wheel rolling for all beings' (Ja 40), it is in the sense of giving. In 'A divine wheel-jewel appeared' (DN 17), it is in the sense of the jewel-wheel. In 'The wheel set in motion by me' (Snp 3.11), it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In 'For a person overcome by craving, the wheel spins on his head' (Ja 78), it is in the sense of the razor-wheel. In 'Even with a wheel having a razor-sharp rim' (DN 2), it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In 'Like a thunderbolt-wheel' (DN 28), it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel.

Taṃ panetaṃ dhammacakkaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti paṭivedhañāṇañca desanāñāṇañca. Tattha paññāpabhāvitaṃ attano ariyaphalāvahaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ, karuṇāpabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyaphalāvahaṃ desanāñāṇaṃ. Tattha [V 2.0247] paṭivedhañāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi abhinikkhamanato yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato vā yāva mahābodhipallaṅke arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Dīpaṅkarato paṭṭhāya vā yāva bodhipallaṅke arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Desanāñāṇampi pavattamānaṃ pavattanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi yāva aññāsikoṇḍaññassa sotāpattimaggā pavattamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāma. Tesu paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ. Ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ, buddhānaṃyeva orasañāṇaṃ.

Furthermore, this Wheel of Dhamma is of two kinds: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Among these, the knowledge of penetration, imbued with wisdom, brings the noble fruit to oneself, while the knowledge of teaching, imbued with compassion, brings the noble fruit to the disciples. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: 'arising' (uppajjamānaṃ) and 'arisen' (uppannaṃ). For it is 'arising' from the Great Renunciation up to the path of Arahantship, and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' Or, from the Tusita realm up to the path of Arahantship at the great Bodhi-seat, it is 'arising,' and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' Or, beginning from the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the path of Arahantship at the Bodhi-seat, it is 'arising,' and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: 'occurring' (pavattamānaṃ) and 'occurred' (pavattaṃ). For it is 'occurring' up to the path of stream-entry of Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'occurred.' Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of teaching is mundane. Furthermore, both of these are not shared with others; they are the innate knowledge of the Buddhas alone.

Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sabbe dhammā mayā abhisambuddhā”ti evaṃ paṭijānato tava. Anabhisambuddhāti ime nāma [M 2.0255] dhammā tayā anabhisambuddhā. Tatra vatāti tesu “anabhisambuddhā”ti evaṃ dassitadhammesu. Sahadhammenāti sahetunā sakāraṇena vacanena. Nimittametanti ettha puggalopi dhammopi nimittanti adhippeto[P 3.0011]. Taṃ puggalaṃ na passāmi, yo maṃ paṭicodessati. Taṃ dhammaṃ na passāmi, yaṃ dassetvā “ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddho”ti maṃ paṭicodessatīti ayamettha attho. Khemappattoti khemaṃ patto. Sesapadadvayaṃ imasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbampetaṃ vesārajjañāṇameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dasabalassa hi “ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddho”ti codakaṃ puggalaṃ vā codanākāraṇaṃ anabhisambuddhadhammaṃ vā apassato “sabhāvabuddhoyeva vata samāno ahaṃ buddhosmīti vadāmī”ti paccavekkhantassa balavataraṃ somanassaṃ uppajjati, tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ vesārajjaṃ nāma. Taṃ sandhāya “khemappatto”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo.

‘Of you who claims to be a Perfectly Enlightened One’ (sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato) means of you who declares, ‘I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully awakened to by me.’ ‘Not fully awakened to’ (anabhisambuddhā) means ‘these phenomena have not been fully awakened to by you.’ ‘In that case’ (tatra vata) means among those phenomena thus indicated as ‘not fully awakened to.’ ‘With reason’ (sahadhammena) means with a statement that has a cause and a reason. ‘This is a sign’ (nimittametaṃ) – here, both a person and a phenomenon are intended as a ‘sign.’ ‘I do not see that person who would challenge me. I do not see that phenomenon which, having been shown, someone would challenge me, saying, “This phenomenon has not been fully awakened to by you”’—this is the meaning here. ‘Attained to safety’ (khemappatto) means ‘has reached safety.’ The remaining two phrases are synonyms of this. All this is said with reference to the knowledge of confidence (vesārajjañāṇa). For the one endowed with the ten powers, when not seeing a person to challenge him or a cause for challenge—an unawakened-to phenomenon—about which it could be said, ‘This phenomenon has not been fully awakened to by you,’ and reflecting, ‘Being indeed a Buddha by nature, I declare, “I am a Buddha,”’ a very strong gladness arises. The knowledge associated with that is called confidence. With reference to that, he said, ‘attained to safety,’ and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Antarāyikā dhammāti ettha pana antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā. Te atthato sañcicca vītikkantā satta āpattikkhandhā. Sañcicca vītikkantaṃ hi antamaso dukkaṭadubbhāsitampi maggaphalānaṃ antarāyaṃ karoti. Idha pana methunadhammo adhippeto. Methunaṃ sevato hi yassa kassaci nissaṃsayameva maggaphalānaṃ antarāyo hoti.

‘Obstructive phenomena’ (antarāyikā dhammā): here, because they create an obstruction, they are called ‘obstructive.’ In essence, these are the seven classes of offenses intentionally transgressed. For an intentional transgression, even down to an offense of wrong-doing or wrong speech, creates an obstruction to the path and its fruits. Here, however, the practice of sexual intercourse is intended. For anyone who engages in sexual intercourse, there is undoubtedly an obstruction to the path and its fruits.

Yassa kho pana te atthāyāti rāgakkhayādīsu yassa atthāya. Dhammo desitoti asubhabhāvanādidhammo kathito. Tatra vata manti tasmiṃ aniyyānikadhamme maṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

‘For whose sake’ (yassa kho pana te atthāya) means for the sake of which goal among the destruction of lust, and so on. ‘The teaching has been taught’ (dhammo desito) means the teaching on such as the development of the perception of foulness has been spoken. ‘In that case, me’ (tatra vata maṃ) refers to ‘me’ in that teaching which does not lead out of saṃsāra. The rest should be understood in the same way as has been stated.

Vādapathāti [V 2.0248] vādāyeva. Puthūti bahū. Sitāti [P 3.0012] upanibaddhā abhisaṅkhatā. Atha vā puthussitāti puthubhāvaṃ sitā upagatā, puthūhi vā sitātipi puthussitā. Yaṃ nissitāti etarahipi yaṃ vādapathaṃ nissitā. Na te bhavantīti te vādapathā na bhavanti bhijjanti vinassanti. Dhammacakkanti desanāñāṇassapi paṭivedhañāṇassapi etaṃ nāmaṃ. Tesu desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ, paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ. Kevalīti sakalaguṇasamannāgato. Tādisanti tathāvidhaṃ.

“Paths of views” means simply views. “Numerous” means many. “Bound” means tied up, constructed. Or alternatively, “diversely bound” means they have reached a state of diversity, or they are bound by many, and are therefore called “diversely bound”. “Relying on which” means even now, whichever path of views they rely upon. “They do not exist” means those paths of views do not exist; they are broken, they perish. “The Wheel of the Dhamma” is a name for both the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration. Of these, the knowledge of teaching is worldly, and the knowledge of penetration is supramundane. “The Accomplished One” means endowed with all qualities. “Such” means of that kind.

9. Taṇhuppādasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Arising of Craving

9. Navame [M 2.0256] uppajjati etesūti uppādā. Kā uppajjati? Taṇhā. Taṇhāya uppādā taṇhuppādā, taṇhāvatthūni taṇhākāraṇānīti attho. Cīvarahetūti “kattha manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti cīvarakāraṇā uppajjati. Itibhavābhavahetūti ettha itīti nidassanatthe nipāto. Yathā cīvarādihetu, evaṃ bhavābhavahetupīti attho. Bhavābhavoti cettha paṇītatarāni sappinavanītādīni adhippetāni. Sampattibhavesu paṇītatarapaṇītatamabhavotipi vadantiyeva.

9. In the ninth sutta: because it arises in these, they are called ‘arisings.’ What arises? Craving. The arising of craving is ‘taṇhuppādā’; the meaning is the bases of craving, the causes of craving. “On account of robes” means craving arises for the reason of a robe, as in: “Where shall I obtain a pleasing robe?” In the phrase “thus on account of lesser and greater existence,” the word ‘iti’ here is a particle in the sense of an example. The meaning is: just as craving arises on account of robes and so on, so too it arises on account of lesser and greater existence. And here, by ‘lesser and greater existence,’ more excellent things such as ghee, fresh butter, and so on are intended. In prosperous existences, they also speak of a more excellent and a most excellent existence.

Taṇhādutiyoti ayañhi satto anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe saṃsaranto na ekakova saṃsarati, taṇhaṃ pana dutiyikaṃ labhantova saṃsarati. Tena vuttaṃ “taṇhādutiyo”ti. Itthabhāvaññathābhāvanti [P 3.0013] ettha itthabhāvo nāma ayaṃ attabhāvo, aññathābhāvo nāma anāgatattabhāvo. Evarūpo vā aññopi attabhāvo itthabhāvo nāma, na evarūpo aññathābhāvo nāma. Taṃ itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ. Saṃsāranti khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ paṭipāṭiṃ. Nātivattatīti nātikkamati. Evamādīnavaṃ ñatvāti evaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannesu khandhesu ādīnavaṃ jānitvā. Taṇhaṃ dukkhassa sambhavanti taṇhaṃ ca “ayaṃ vaṭṭadukkhasambhūto sabhāvo kāraṇa”nti evaṃ jānitvā. Ettāvatā imassa bhikkhuno vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattabhāvo dassito. Idāni taṃ khīṇāsavaṃ thomento vītataṇhotiādimāha. Tattha anādānoti niggahaṇo. Sato bhikkhu paribbajeti satisampajaññe vepullappatto khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sato sampajāno careyya vihareyyāti attho. Iti suttante vaṭṭaṃ kathetvā gāthāsu vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti.

‘Craving as a companion’: For this being, wandering through the beginningless round of saṃsāra, does not wander alone; he wanders only having obtained craving as a companion. Therefore, it is said, ‘craving as a companion.’ ‘Existence in this state and in another state’: Here, ‘existence in this state’ is this present personal existence; ‘existence in another state’ is a future personal existence. Or, another personal existence of such a nature is called ‘existence in this state’; one not of such a nature is called ‘existence in another state.’ That is ‘existence in this state and in another state.’ ‘Wanders on in saṃsāra’ refers to the sequence of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. ‘Does not go beyond’ means does not transcend. ‘Knowing the danger thus’ means having thus known the danger in the past, future, and present aggregates. ‘Craving, the origin of suffering’ means and knowing craving thus: ‘This is the nature, the cause, that arises from the suffering of the round.’ Thus far, the attainment of arahantship by this monk through the development of insight has been shown. Now, praising that one whose taints are destroyed, the text says, beginning with ‘free from craving,’ etc. Therein, ‘not grasping’ means without grasping. ‘A mindful monk should wander’: a monk whose taints are destroyed, having attained abundance in mindfulness and clear comprehension, should fare, should dwell, mindful and clearly comprehending—this is the meaning. Thus, having spoken of the round in the sutta discourse, the round and that which is free from the round are spoken of in the verses.

10. Yogasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sutta on Yokes

10. Dasame [V 2.0249] vaṭṭasmiṃ yojentīti yogā. Kāmayogotiādīsu pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo kāmayogo. Rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo bhavayogo, tathā jhānanikanti. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagato ca rāgo dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo ca diṭṭhiyogo. Catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ avijjāyogo. Kāmesu vā yojetīti kāmayogo. Bhavesu yojetīti [M 2.0257] bhavayogo. Diṭṭhīsu yojetīti diṭṭhiyogo. Avijjāya yojetīti avijjāyogoti heṭṭhā vuttadhammānaṃyevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

10. In the tenth sutta: because they yoke one to the round of existence, they are called ‘yokes.’ In the passage beginning with ‘the yoke of sensuality’: lust related to the five cords of sensual pleasure is the yoke of sensuality. Desire and lust for form and formless existences, as well as delight in meditative attainments, is the yoke of existence. Lust accompanied by the view of eternalism and the sixty-two views is the yoke of views. Ignorance regarding the four truths is the yoke of ignorance. Alternatively: because it yokes to sensual pleasures, it is the yoke of sensuality. Because it yokes to existences, it is the yoke of existence. Because it yokes to views, it is the yoke of views. Because it yokes through ignorance, it is the yoke of ignorance. This is simply a designation for the states mentioned above.

Idāni [P 3.0014] te vitthāretvā dassento katamo ca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha samudayanti uppattiṃ. Atthaṅgamanti bhedaṃ. Assādanti madhurabhāvaṃ. Ādīnavanti amadhurabhāvaṃ dosaṃ. Nissaraṇanti nissaṭabhāvaṃ. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Kāmarāgoti kāme ārabbha uppannarāgo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Anusetīti nibbattati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kāmayogoti, bhikkhave, idaṃ kāmesu yojanakāraṇaṃ bandhanakāraṇaṃ vuccatīti evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo.

Now, wishing to show them by explaining in detail, He said, 'And what, O monks?' and so on. Therein, 'arising' means origination. 'Passing away' means disintegration. 'Gratification' means the state of being pleasant. 'Danger' means the state of being unpleasant, the fault. 'Escape' means the state of having escaped. 'In sensual pleasures' means in objective sensual pleasures. 'Lust for sensuality' is the lust that has arisen with sensual pleasures as its object. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. 'Lies latent' means it arises. As for 'This, O monks, is called the yoke of sensuality': O monks, this cause of yoking and binding in regard to sensual pleasures is called the yoke of sensuality. Thus the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Phassāyatanānanti cakkhādīnaṃ cakkhusamphassādikāraṇānaṃ. Avijjā aññāṇanti ñāṇapaṭipakkhabhāvena aññāṇasaṅkhātā avijjā. Iti kāmayogoti ettha iti saddo catūhipi yogehi saddhiṃ yojetabbo “evaṃ kāmayogo, evaṃ bhavayogo”ti. Saṃyuttoti parivārito. Pāpakehīti lāmakehi. Akusalehīti akosallasambhūtehi. Saṃkilesikehīti saṃkilesanakehi, pasannassa cittassa pasannabhāvadūsakehīti attho. Ponobbhavikehīti punabbhavanibbattakehi. Sadarehīti sadarathehi. Dukkhavipākehīti vipākakāle dukkhuppādakehi. Āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇikehīti anāgate punappunaṃ jātijarāmaraṇanibbattakehi. Tasmā [P 3.0015] ayogakkhemīti vuccatīti yasmā appahīnayogo puggalo etehi dhammehi sampayutto hoti, tasmā catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbānaṃ anadhigatattā na yogakkhemīti vuccati.

‘Of the bases of contact’ means: of the eye and so on, which are the causes of eye-contact and so on. ‘Ignorance is non-knowledge’ means: ignorance, so designated because it is the opposite of knowledge. Regarding ‘Thus, the yoke of sensuality’: here the word ‘thus’ should be connected with all four yokes, as in ‘Thus the yoke of sensuality, thus the yoke of existence.’ ‘Connected’ means encompassed. ‘By evil things’ means by base things. ‘By unwholesome things’ means arisen from unskillfulness. ‘By defiling things’ means by things that defile, that corrupt the clear state of a clear mind; this is the meaning. ‘Leading to renewed existence’ means producing renewed existence. ‘With vexation’ means with vexation. ‘Painful in result’ means producing suffering at the time of result. ‘Leading to future birth, aging, and death’ means repeatedly producing birth, aging, and death in the future. As for ‘Therefore, one is called not secure from the yokes’: because a person whose yokes are not abandoned is associated with these states, therefore, due to not having attained Nibbāna, the security from the four yokes, one is called ‘not secure from the yokes’.

Visaṃyogoti visaṃyojanakāraṇāni. Kāmayogavisaṃyogoti kāmayogato visaṃyojanakāraṇaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha asubhajjhānaṃ kāmayogavisaṃyogo, taṃ pādakaṃ katvā adhigato anāgāmimaggo ekanteneva kāmayogavisaṃyogo nāma. Arahattamaggo bhavayogavisaṃyogo nāma, sotāpattimaggo diṭṭhiyogavisaṃyogo [M 2.0258] nāma, arahattamaggo avijjāyogavisaṃyogo [V 2.0250] nāma. Idāni te vitthāravasena dassento katamo ca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tassattho vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

‘Disunion’ means the causes of disuniting. ‘Disunion from the yoke of sensuality’ means the cause of disuniting from the yoke of sensuality. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, meditation on the unattractive is disunion from the yoke of sensuality; the path of non-return attained by making that its basis is absolutely called disunion from the yoke of sensuality. The path of arahantship is called disunion from the yoke of existence. The path of stream-entry is called disunion from the yoke of views. The path of arahantship is called disunion from the yoke of ignorance. Now, wishing to explain them in detail, He says, beginning with, “And which, monks?” Its meaning should be understood in the manner already stated.

Bhavayogena cūbhayanti bhavayogena ca saṃyuttā, kiñci bhiyyo ubhayenāpi sampayuttā, yena kenaci yogena samannāgatāti attho. Purakkhatāti purato katā, parivāritā vā. Kāme pariññāyāti duvidhepi kāme parijānitvā. Bhavayogañca sabbasoti bhavayogañca sabbameva parijānitvā. Samūhaccāti samūhanitvā. Virājayanti virājento, virājetvā vā. “Virājento”ti hi vutte maggo kathito hoti, “virājetvā”ti vutte phalaṃ. Munīti khīṇāsavamuni. Iti imasmiṃ suttepi gāthāsupi vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitanti.

‘And both by the yoke of existence’ means associated with the yoke of existence; and further, associated with both yokes, meaning endowed with any yoke whatsoever. ‘Placed foremost’ means made foremost, or surrounded. ‘Having fully understood sensual pleasures’ means having fully known both kinds of sensual pleasures. ‘And the yoke of existence completely’ means having fully known all of the yoke of existence. ‘Having eradicated’ means having uprooted. ‘Making dispassionate’ means making dispassionate, or having made dispassionate. For when ‘making dispassionate’ is said, the path is spoken of; when ‘having made dispassionate’ is said, the fruit is spoken of. ‘A sage’ means a sage whose taints are destroyed. Thus, in this sutta and in the verses, only the cycle and that which is not the cycle are taught.

Bhaṇḍagāmavaggo paṭhamo.

The Bhaṇḍagāma Chapter, the First.

2. Caravaggo

2. The Chapter on Wandering

1. Carasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Cara Sutta

11. Dutiyassa [V 2.0251][P 3.0016] paṭhame adhivāsetīti cittaṃ adhiropetvā vāseti. Nappajahatīti na pariccajati. Na vinodetīti na nīharati. Na byantīkarotīti na vigatantaṃ paricchinnaparivaṭumaṃ karoti. Na anabhāvaṃ gametīti na anuabhāvaṃ avaḍḍhiṃ vināsaṃ gameti. Carampīti carantopi. Anātāpīti nibbīriyo. Anottāpīti upavādabhayarahito. Satatanti niccaṃ. Samitanti nirantaraṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha atthaṃ ñatvā sukkapakkhe vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo.

2.
