In the first sutta of the second chapter, ‘endures’ means one causes it to dwell by placing it upon the mind. ‘Does not abandon’ means does not give up. ‘Does not dispel’ means does not remove. ‘Does not bring to an end’ means does not make it ended, limited, or circumscribed. ‘Does not cause to cease’ means does not lead it to repeated non-existence, to non-growth, or to destruction. ‘Even while walking’ means even while moving about. ‘Without ardor’ means without energy. ‘Without dread’ means free from the fear of blame. ‘Constantly’ means unceasingly. ‘Persistently’ means without interruption. Having understood the meaning in this way throughout, the meaning for the wholesome aspect should be understood in the opposite way to what has been stated.

Gāthāsu gehanissitanti kilesanissitaṃ. Mohaneyyesūti mohajanakesu ārammaṇesu. Abhabboti abhājanabhūto. Phuṭṭhuṃ sambodhimuttamanti arahattamaggasaṅkhātaṃ uttamañāṇaṃ phusituṃ.

1. In the verses, ‘dependent on home’ means dependent on defilements. ‘In what deludes’ means in objects that generate delusion. ‘Incapable’ means one who is unfit. ‘To reach the supreme enlightenment’ means to touch the highest knowledge, which is called the path of arahantship.

2. Sīlasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta

12. Dutiye [M 2.0259] sampannasīlāti paripuṇṇasīlā. Sampannapātimokkhāti paripuṇṇapātimokkhā. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutāti [P 3.0017] pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena saṃvutā pihitā upetā hutvā viharatha. Ācāragocarasampannāti ācārena ca gocarena ca sampannā samupāgatā bhavatha. Aṇumattesu vajjesūti aṇuppamāṇesu dosesu. Bhayadassāvinoti tāni aṇumattāni vajjāni bhayato dassanasīlā. Samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesūti sabbasikkhākoṭṭhāsesu samādātabbaṃ samādāya gahetvā sikkhatha. “Sampannasīlānaṃ…pe… sikkhāpadesū”ti ettakena dhammakkhānena sikkhattaye samādāpetvā ceva paṭiladdhaguṇesu ca vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni uttari kātabbaṃ dassento kimassātiādimāha. Tattha kimassāti kiṃ bhaveyya.

11. In the second, ‘endowed with virtue’ means complete in virtue. ‘Endowed with the Pātimokkha’ means complete in the Pātimokkha. ‘Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha’ means you should dwell, having become restrained, protected, and endowed with the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. ‘Perfect in conduct and resort’ means you should be accomplished and endowed with conduct and resort. ‘In the slightest faults’ means in faults of minute measure. ‘Seeing danger’ means having the nature of seeing those faults of minute measure as a danger. ‘Having undertaken, you should train in the training rules’ means: you should train, having undertaken and grasped what is to be undertaken among all the divisions of the training. With this exposition of the Dhamma from ‘Endowed with virtue…’ to ‘…in the training rules,’ having both encouraged them to undertake the threefold training and praised the qualities they had attained, He now shows what further should be done by saying the words beginning with ‘What more is there?’. Therein, ‘What more is there?’ means ‘What would be?’.

Yataṃ careti yathā caranto yato hoti saṃyato, evaṃ careyya. Esa nayo sabbattha. Accheti [V 2.0252] nisīdeyya. Yatamenaṃ pasārayeti yaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ pasāreyya, taṃ yataṃ saṃyatameva katvā pasāreyya. Uddhanti upari. Tiriyanti majjhaṃ. Apācīnanti adho. Ettāvatā atītā paccuppannā anāgatā ca pañcakkhandhā kathitā. Yāvatāti paricchedavacanaṃ. Jagato [P 3.0018] gatīti lokassa nipphatti. Samavekkhitā ca dhammānaṃ, khandhānaṃ udayabbayanti etesaṃ sabbaloke atītādibhedānaṃ pañcakkhandhadhammānaṃ udayañca vayañca samavekkhitā. “Pañcakkhandhānaṃ udayaṃ passanto pañcavīsati lakkhaṇāni passati, vayaṃ passanto pañcavīsati lakkhaṇāni passatī”ti vuttehi samapaññāsāya lakkhaṇehi sammā avekkhitā hoti. Cetosamathasāmīcinti cittasamathassa anucchavikaṃ paṭipadaṃ. Sikkhamānanti paṭipajjamānaṃ, pūrayamānanti attho. Pahitattoti pesitatto. Āhūti kathayanti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Imasmiṃ pana sutte sīlaṃ missakaṃ kathetvā gāthāsu khīṇāsavo kathito.

Regarding `yataṃ care` (one should act with restraint): one should act in such a way that, while acting, one is restrained and controlled. This is the method in all cases. `Accheti` means one should sit. Regarding `yatamenaṃ pasāraye` (whatever one extends): whatever limb one extends, one should extend it having made it restrained and controlled. `Uddhaṃ` (upward) means above. `Tiriyaṃ` (across) means the middle. `Apācīnaṃ` (downward) means below. By this much, the past, present, and future five aggregates have been discussed. `Yāvatā` (as much as) is a term denoting limitation. `Jagato gati` (the course of the world) means the world's production. Regarding 'and one who has thoroughly observed the phenomena, the arising and passing away of the aggregates': this means one who has thoroughly observed the arising and passing away of these five aggregate-phenomena in the entire world, with their distinctions of past, present, and future. 'One who sees the arising of the five aggregates sees twenty-five characteristics; one who sees their passing away sees twenty-five characteristics'—by means of these fifty characteristics that have been mentioned, it is rightly observed. `Cetosamathasāmīciṃ` (that which is suitable for the calming of the mind) means the practice suitable for the calming of the mind, that is, the path of arahatship. `Sikkhamānaṃ` (one who trains) means one who is practicing, that is, one who is fulfilling. `Pahitatto` (one with a resolute mind) means one whose mind is sent forth to Nibbāna. `Āhu` (they say) means they declare. The rest here is clear. In this discourse, however, after discussing virtue as a mixed category, the one whose cankers are destroyed is described in the verses.

3. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta

13. Tatiye [M 2.0260] sammappadhānānīti sundarapadhānāni uttamavīriyāni. Sammappadhānāti paripuṇṇavīriyā. Māradheyyābhibhūtāti tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhātaṃ māradheyyaṃ abhibhavitvā samatikkamitvā ṭhitā. Te asitāti te khīṇāsavā anissitā nāma. Jātimaraṇabhayassāti jātiñca maraṇañca paṭicca uppajjanakabhayassa, jātimaraṇasaṅkhātasseva vā bhayassa. Pāragūti pāraṅgatā. Te tusitāti te khīṇāsavā tuṭṭhā nāma. Jetvā māraṃ savāhininti sasenakaṃ māraṃ jinitvā ṭhitā. Te [P 3.0019] anejāti te khīṇāsavā taṇhāsaṅkhātāya ejāya anejā niccalā nāma. Namucibalanti mārabalaṃ. Upātivattāti atikkantā. Te sukhitāti te khīṇāsavā lokuttarasukhena sukhitā nāma. Tenevāha –

13. In the third [sutta], `sammappadhānāni` means excellent strivings, supreme efforts. `Sammappadhāna` means complete effort. `Māradheyyābhibhūtā` means having subdued and transcended the domain of Māra, which is reckoned as the cycle of the three planes, they are established. `Te asitā` means those whose cankers are destroyed are called 'unattached'. `Jātimaraṇabhayassa` means of the fear that arises in dependence on birth and death, or of the fear that is reckoned as birth and death itself. `Pāragū` means they have reached the far shore. `Te tusitā` means those whose cankers are destroyed are called 'content'. `Jetvā māraṃ savāhiniṃ` means having conquered Māra together with his army, they are established. `Te anejā` means those whose cankers are destroyed are called 'unagitated' by the agitation called craving, indeed 'unmoving'. `Namucibalaṃ` means Māra's army. `Upātivattā` means they have transcended. `Te sukhitā` means those whose cankers are destroyed are called 'happy' with supramundane happiness. Therefore, he said:

“Sukhitā vata arahanto, taṇhā nesaṃ na vijjati;

Asmimāno samucchinno, mohajālaṃ padālita”nti. (saṃ. ni. 3.76);

“Indeed, the Arahants are happy! For them, craving is not found. The conceit ‘I am’ is uprooted; the net of delusion is shattered.”

4. Saṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta

14. Catutthe padhānānīti vīriyāni. Saṃvarappadhānanti cakkhādīni saṃvarantassa uppannavīriyaṃ[V 2.0253]. Pahānappadhānanti kāmavitakkādayo pajahantassa uppannavīriyaṃ. Bhāvanāppadhānanti sambojjhaṅge bhāventassa uppannavīriyaṃ. Anurakkhaṇāppadhānanti samādhinimittaṃ anurakkhantassa uppannavīriyaṃ.

14. In the fourth [sutta], `padhānāni` means efforts. `Saṃvarappadhānaṃ` is the effort that arises in one who restrains the eye and other faculties. `Pahānappadhānaṃ` is the effort that arises in one who abandons sensual thoughts and so on. `Bhāvanāppadhānaṃ` is the effort that arises in one who develops the factors of enlightenment. `Anurakkhaṇāppadhānaṃ` is the effort that arises in one who guards the sign of concentration.

Vivekanissitantiādīsu viveko, virāgo, nirodhoti tīṇipi nibbānassa nāmāni. Nibbānaṃ hi upadhivivekattā viveko, taṃ āgamma rāgādayo virajjantīti virāgo, nirujjhantīti nirodho. Tasmā vivekanissitantiādīsu ārammaṇavasena vā adhigantabbavasena vā nibbānanissitanti attho.

In the phrases 'dependent on seclusion' etc., seclusion, dispassion, and cessation are three names for Nibbāna. Indeed, Nibbāna is called 'seclusion' because it is seclusion from the substrates; it is called 'dispassion' because in dependence on it, lust and other defilements fade away; and it is called 'cessation' because they cease. Therefore, in the phrases 'dependent on seclusion' etc., the meaning is 'dependent on Nibbāna' either by way of object or by way of what is to be attained.

Vossaggapariṇāminti ettha dve vossaggā – pariccāgavossaggo ca pakkhandanavossaggo ca. Tattha vipassanā tadaṅgavasena kilese ca khandhe ca rāgaṃ pariccajatīti pariccāgavossaggo. Maggo ārammaṇavasena nibbānaṃ pakkhandatīti pakkhandanavossaggo. Tasmā vossaggapariṇāminti yathā bhāviyamāno [M 2.0261] satisambojjhaṅgo vossaggatthāya pariṇamati, vipassanābhāvañca maggabhāvañca pāpuṇāti, evaṃ taṃ bhāvetīti ayamettha attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Bhaddakanti [P 3.0020] laddhakaṃ. Samādhinimittaṃ vuccati aṭṭhikasaññādivasena adhigato samādhiyeva. Anurakkhatīti samādhipāripanthikadhamme rāgadosamohe sodhento rakkhati. Ettha ca aṭṭhikasaññādikā pañceva saññā vuttā, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne dasapi asubhāni vitthāretvā kathetabbāni. Tesaṃ vitthāro visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.102 ādayo) vuttoyeva. Gāthāya saṃvarādinipphādakaṃ vīriyameva vuttaṃ. Khayaṃ dukkhassa pāpuṇeti dukkhakkhayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyyāti.

In the phrase 'converging upon relinquishment' (`vossaggapariṇāmiṃ`), there are two kinds of relinquishment: the relinquishment of abandonment (`pariccāgavossagga`) and the relinquishment of plunging (`pakkhandanavossagga`). Among these, insight (`vipassanā`), by means of abandonment by substitution of opposites (`tadaṅgavasena`), abandons both the defilements (`kilese`) and the aggregates (`khandhe`); this is the relinquishment of abandonment. The path (`magga`), by means of its object (`ārammaṇavasena`), plunges into Nibbāna; this is the relinquishment of plunging. Thus, 'converging upon relinquishment' (`vossaggapariṇāmiṃ`) has this meaning here: one develops that mindfulness enlightenment factor (`satisambojjhaṅga`) in such a way that, when being developed, it inclines for the sake of relinquishment (`vossaggatthāya`), and attains both the state of insight (`vipassanābhāva`) and the state of the path (`maggabhāva`). This same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Excellent' (`bhaddakaṃ`) means 'obtained' (`laddhakaṃ`). The 'sign of concentration' (`samādhinimittaṃ`) is said to be the concentration itself, attained by means of perceptions such as that of the skeleton (`aṭṭhikasaññā`). 'Preserves' (`anurakkhati`) means one guards it by purifying lust (`rāga`), hatred (`dosa`), and delusion (`moha`), which are obstructive phenomena to concentration (`samādhipāripanthikadhamme`). And here, only five perceptions (`saññā`) are mentioned, such as the perception of a skeleton (`aṭṭhikasaññā`); however, in this place, the ten kinds of foulness (`asubhāni`) should also be explained by way of expansion. Their detailed explanation has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. In the verse, only the energy (`vīriya`) that accomplishes restraint (`saṃvara`) and so on is spoken of. 'Reaches the destruction of suffering' (`khayaṃ dukkhassa pāpuṇeti`) means one should attain Arahantship, which is designated as the destruction of suffering (`dukkhakkhaya`).

5. Paññattisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Paññatti Sutta

15. Pañcame aggapaññattiyoti uttamapaññattiyo. Attabhāvīnanti attabhāvavantānaṃ. Yadidaṃ rāhu asurindoti yo esa rāhu asurindo ayaṃ aggoti. Ettha rāhu kira asurindo cattāri yojanasahassāni aṭṭha ca yojanasatāni ucco, bāhantaramassa dvādasayojanasatāni, hatthatalapādatalānaṃ puthulatā tīṇi yojanasatāni. Aṅgulipabbāni paṇṇāsa yojanāni, bhamukantaraṃ paṇṇāsayojanaṃ, nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasataṃ, sīsaṃ navayojanasataṃ. Kāmabhogīnaṃ yadidaṃ rājā mandhātāti yo esa rājā mandhātā nāma, ayaṃ dibbepi mānusakepi kāme paribhuñjanakānaṃ [V 2.0254] sattānaṃ aggo nāma. Esa hi asaṅkheyyāyukesu manussesu nibbattitvā icchiticchitakkhaṇe hiraññavassaṃ vassāpento mānusake kāme dīgharattaṃ paribhuñji. Devaloke [P 3.0021] pana yāva chattiṃsāya indānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, tāva paṇīte kāme paribhuñjīti kāmabhogīnaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Ādhipateyyānanti adhipatiṭṭhānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṭṭhānaṃ karontānaṃ. Tathāgato aggamakkhāyatīti lokiyalokuttarehi guṇehi tathāgato aggo seṭṭho uttamo akkhāyati.

15. In the fifth sutta, 'the highest designations' means the supreme designations. 'Among embodied beings' means among those who possess great bodies. 'Namely, Rāhu, the lord of asuras' means that this Rāhu, the lord of asuras, is the highest. Here, Rāhu, the lord of asuras, is said to be four thousand and eight hundred yojanas tall; the span between his arms is twelve hundred yojanas; the breadth of his palms and soles is three hundred yojanas; his finger joints are fifty yojanas; the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas; his forehead is three hundred yojanas; and his head is nine hundred yojanas. 'Among enjoyers of sensual pleasures, namely, King Mandhātā' means that this King Mandhātā is the highest among beings who enjoy divine and human sensual pleasures. For he was reborn among humans with incalculable lifespans and, at any moment he wished, caused a rain of gold to fall, enjoying human sensual pleasures for a long time. In the deva world, he enjoyed refined sensual pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indras. Thus, he became known as the highest among enjoyers of sensual pleasures. 'Among those who exercise sovereignty' means among those who hold the position of a sovereign, the position of a chief. 'The Tathāgata is declared the highest' means the Tathāgata is declared the highest, the best, the supreme, on account of worldly and transcendental qualities.

Iddhiyā yasasā jalanti dibbasampattisamiddhiyā ca parivārasaṅkhātena yasasā ca jalantānaṃ. Uddhaṃ tiriyaṃ apācīnanti upari ca majjhe ca heṭṭhā ca. Yāvatā jagato gatīti yattakā lokanipphatti.

'They shine with power and fame' means among those who shine with the prosperity of divine attainments and with fame reckoned as a retinue. 'Above, across, and downwards' means above, in the middle, and below. 'As far as the world's extent' means as far as the world's manifestation.

6. Sokhummasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Subtlety

16. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0262] sokhummānīti sukhumalakkhaṇapaṭivijjhanakāni ñāṇāni. Rūpasokhummena samannāgato hotīti rūpe saṇhasukhumalakkhaṇapariggāhakena ñāṇena samannāgato hoti. Paramenāti uttamena. Tena ca rūpasokhummenāti tena yāva anulomabhāvaṃ pattena sukhumalakkhaṇapariggāhakañāṇena. Na samanupassatīti natthibhāveneva na passati. Na patthetīti natthibhāveneva na pattheti. Vedanāsokhummādīsupi eseva nayo.

16. In the sixth sutta, 'subtleties' means the knowledges that penetrate the subtle characteristics. 'Endowed with subtlety of form' means endowed with the knowledge that grasps the gentle and subtle characteristics in form. 'Supreme' means the highest. 'And with that subtlety of form' means with that knowledge that grasps the subtle characteristics, which has reached as far as the state of adaptation. 'Does not perceive' means one does not see, simply due to its non-existence. 'Does not long for' means one does not long for it, simply due to its non-existence. This same method applies also to the subtlety of feeling and so on.

Rūpasokhummataṃ ñatvāti rūpakkhandhassa saṇhasukhumalakkhaṇapariggāhakena ñāṇena sukhumataṃ jānitvā. Vedanānañca sambhavanti vedanākkhandhassa ca pabhavaṃ jānitvā. Saññā yato samudetīti yasmā kāraṇā saññākkhandho samudeti nibbattati, tañca jānitvā. Atthaṃ [P 3.0022] gacchati yattha cāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne nirujjhati, tañca jānitvā. Saṅkhāre parato ñatvāti saṅkhārakkhandhaṃ aniccatāya lujjanabhāvena parato jānitvā. Iminā hi padena aniccānupassanā kathitā. Dukkhato no ca attatoti iminā dukkhānattānupassanā. Santoti kilesasantatāya santo. Santipade ratoti nibbāne rato. Iti suttante catūsu ṭhānesu vipassanāva kathitā, gāthāsu lokuttaradhammopīti.

'Having known the subtlety of form' means having known the subtlety of the form aggregate with the knowledge that grasps its gentle and subtle characteristics. 'And the origin of feelings' means having known the origin of the feeling aggregate. 'From where perception arises' means having known the cause from which the perception aggregate arises and is produced. 'And where it ceases' means having known the place where it ceases. 'Having known formations as other' means having known the formations aggregate as other on account of its impermanence and its nature of perishing. Indeed, by this phrase, the contemplation of impermanence is spoken of. By the phrase 'as suffering, and not as self', the contemplations of suffering and not-self are spoken of. 'Peaceful' means peaceful on account of the pacification of defilements. 'Delighting in the state of peace' means delighting in Nibbāna. Thus, in the prose of the sutta, insight alone is spoken of in four places, and in the verses, the supramundane Dhamma is also spoken of.

7. Paṭhamaagatisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the First Discourse on Wrong Courses

17-19. Sattame [V 2.0255] agatigamanānīti nagatigamanāni. Chandāgatiṃ gacchatīti chandena agatiṃ gacchati, akattabbaṃ karoti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Chandā dosā bhayā mohāti chandena, dosena, bhayena, mohena. Ativattatīti atikkamati. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānameva. Navame tathābujjhanakānaṃ vasena dvīhipi nayehi kathitaṃ.

In the seventh sutta, 'wrong courses' means goings that should not be gone. 'Goes the wrong course through desire' means one goes the wrong course through desire, doing what should not be done. This same method applies to the remaining cases. 'Through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion' means by desire, by hatred, by fear, or by delusion. 'Transgresses' means one exceeds. The eighth is self-evident. In the ninth, it is explained in two ways for the sake of those who are to understand it so.

10. Bhattuddesakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Appointer of Meals

20. Dasame bhattuddesakoti salākabhattādīnaṃ uddesako. Kāmesu asaṃyatāti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmehi asaṃyatā. Parisākasaṭo [M 2.0263] ca panesa vuccatīti ayañca pana so evarūpā parisākacavaro nāma vuccatīti attho. Samaṇenāti buddhasamaṇena. Parisāya maṇḍo ca panesa vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpā parisā vippasannena parisāmaṇḍoti vuccatīti.

20. In the tenth sutta, 'an appointer of meals' is one who designates meals, such as those distributed by ticket. 'Unrestrained in sensual pleasures' means unrestrained by the defilements of sensual desire with regard to the objects of sensual pleasure. 'And this one is called the refuse of the assembly' means: and this person of such a nature is also called the refuse of the assembly; this is the meaning. 'By the ascetic' means by the ascetic who is the Buddha. 'And this one is called an ornament of the assembly' means: this person of such a nature is called an ornament of the assembly on account of being serene in the assembly.

Caravaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Wandering is the second.

3. Uruvelavaggo

3. The Chapter on Uruvelā

1. Paṭhamauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse at Uruvelā

21. Tatiyassa [V 2.0256][P 3.0023] paṭhame uruvelāyanti ettha uruvelāti mahāvelā, mahāvālikarāsīti attho. Atha vā urūti vālukā vuccati, velāti mariyādā. Velātikkamanahetu āhaṭā uru uruvelāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Atīte kira anuppanne buddhe dasasahassā kulaputtā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tasmiṃ padese viharantā ekadivasaṃ sannipatitvā katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “kāyakammavacīkammāni nāma paresampi pākaṭāni honti, manokammaṃ pana apākaṭaṃ. Tasmā yo kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā vitakketi, tassa añño codako nāma natthi. So attanāva attānaṃ codetvā pattapuṭena vālukaṃ āharitvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ākiratu, idamassa daṇḍakamma”nti. Tato paṭṭhāya yo tādisaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi, so tattha pattapuṭena vālukaṃ ākirati, evaṃ tattha anukkamena mahāvālukarāsi jāto. Tato naṃ pacchimā janatā parikkhipitvā cetiyaṭṭhānamakāsi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “uruvelāti mahāvelā, mahāvālikarāsīti attho”ti. Tameva sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha vā urūti vālukā vuccati, velāti mariyādā, velātikkamanahetu āhaṭā uru uruvelāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo”ti.

21. In the first sutta of the third chapter, herein, regarding 'at Uruvelā', 'Uruvelā' means a great sandbank, that is, a great heap of sand; this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'uru' is said to mean sand, and 'velā' means boundary. The sand ('uru') brought on account of transgressing the boundary ('velā') is 'Uruvelā'; thus the meaning should be understood here. It is said that in the past, before a Buddha had arisen, ten thousand sons of good family, having gone forth into the ascetic life, were dwelling in that region. One day, they gathered and made an agreement: ‘Bodily and verbal actions are indeed evident to others, but mental action is not evident. Therefore, whoever thinks a thought of sensual desire, or a thought of ill will, or a thought of harm, has no one else to accuse him. He himself should accuse himself, bring sand in a leaf-cup, and scatter it in this place; this shall be his penalty.’ From then on, whoever entertained such a thought would scatter sand there in a leaf-cup. Thus, gradually, a great heap of sand formed there. Later, the people enclosed it and made it a cetiya-site. It is with reference to this that it was said: ‘'Uruvelā' means a great sandbank, that is, a great heap of sand; this is the meaning.’ It is with reference to this same reason that it was said: ‘Alternatively, 'uru' is said to mean sand, and 'velā' means boundary; the sand ('uru') brought on account of transgressing the boundary ('velā') is 'Uruvelā'; thus the meaning should be understood here.’

Najjā nerañjarāya tīreti uruvelagāmaṃ nissāya nerañjarānadītīre viharāmīti dasseti. Ajapālanigrodheti [P 3.0024] ajapālakā tassa nigrodhassa [M 2.0264] chāyāya nisīdantipi tiṭṭhantipi, tasmā so ajapālanigrodhotveva saṅkhaṃ gato, tassa heṭṭhāti attho. Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti sambuddho hutvā paṭhamameva. Udapādīti ayaṃ vitakko pañcame sattāhe udapādi. Kasmā udapādīti? Sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇattā ceva pubbāsevanatāya ca. Tattha pubbāsevanāya pakāsanatthaṃ tittirajātakaṃ āharitabbaṃ. Hatthivānaratittirā kira ekasmiṃ padese viharantā “yo amhākaṃ mahallako, tasmiṃ sagāravā viharissāmā”ti nigrodhaṃ dassetvā “ko nu kho amhākaṃ mahallako”ti vīmaṃsantā tittirassa mahallakabhāvaṃ ñatvā tassa jeṭṭhāpacāyanakammaṃ katvā aññamaññaṃ [V 2.0257] samaggā sammodamānā viharitvā saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā rukkhe adhivatthā devatā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Regarding “on the bank of the Nerañjarā River”: it shows that he dwells near the village of Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River. Regarding the Ajapāla banyan tree: goatherds used to sit and stand in the shade of that banyan tree, hence it became known as the Ajapāla banyan tree; the meaning is “beneath it.” Regarding “first enlightened”: it means immediately after becoming enlightened. Regarding “arose”: this thought arose in the fifth week. Why did it arise? Due to its being the habitual practice of all Buddhas and also due to previous cultivation. To illustrate previous cultivation in this regard, the Tittira Jātaka should be related. It is said that an elephant, a monkey, and a partridge, dwelling together in a certain place, decided: “We will live respectfully towards whoever is the eldest among us.” Pointing to a banyan tree, they asked, “Who among us is the eldest?” After investigating, they recognized the partridge as the eldest. They performed the duty of honoring their elder and lived together in harmony and mutual joy, destined for heaven. Understanding this reason, the deity dwelling in the tree spoke this verse:

“Ye vuḍḍhamapacāyanti, narā dhammassa kovidā;

Diṭṭheva dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca suggatī”ti. (jā. 1.1.37);

“Those people skilled in the principle of honoring elders, who respect the aged, are praiseworthy in this very life, and in the next, they have a good destiny.”

Evaṃ ahetukatiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi tathāgato sagāravavāsaṃ rocesi, idāni kasmā na rocessatīti. Agāravoti aññasmiṃ gāravarahito, kañci garuṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvāti attho. Appatissoti patissayarahito, kañci jeṭṭhakaṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvāti attho. Samaṇaṃ [P 3.0025] vā brāhmaṇaṃ vāti ettha samitapāpabāhitapāpāyeva samaṇabrāhmaṇā adhippetā. Sakkatvā garuṃ katvāti sakkārañceva katvā garukārañca upaṭṭhapetvā.

Thus, even when reborn in a rootless animal realm, the Tathāgata approved of living respectfully; why would he not approve of it now? Regarding “disrespectful”: it means lacking respect toward others, that is, not placing anyone in a position of reverence. Regarding “unyielding”: it means lacking deference, that is, not placing anyone in a position of seniority. Regarding “a contemplative or a brahmin”: here, only those contemplatives and brahmins who have stilled and driven away evil are intended. Regarding “having honored and having revered”: it means having performed an act of honoring and having established reverence.

Sadevake loketiādīsu saddhiṃ devehi sadevake. Devaggahaṇena cettha mārabrahmesu gahitesupi māro nāma vasavattī sabbesaṃ upari vasaṃ vatteti, brahmā nāma mahānubhāvo, ekaṅguliyā ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷasahasse ālokaṃ pharati, dvīhi dvīsu, dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu ālokaṃ pharati. So iminā sīlasampannataroti vattuṃ mā labhantūti samārake sabrahmaketi visuṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā samaṇā nāma ekanikāyādivasena bahussutā sīlavanto paṇḍitā, brāhmaṇāpi vatthuvijjādivasena bahussutā paṇḍitā. Te iminā sampannatarāti vattuṃ [M 2.0265] mā labhantūti sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāyāti vuttaṃ. Sadevamanussāyāti idaṃ pana nippadesato dassanatthaṃ gahitameva gahetvā vuttaṃ. Apicettha purimāni tīṇi padāni lokavasena vuttāni, pacchimāni dve pajāvasena. Sīlasampannataranti sīlena sampannataraṃ, adhikataranti attho. Ettha ca sīlādayo cattāro dhammā lokiyalokuttarā kathitā, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ lokiyameva. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇameva hetaṃ. Pāturahosīti “ayaṃ satthā avīcito yāva bhavaggā sīlādīhi attanā adhikataraṃ apassanto ‘mayā paṭividdhanavalokuttaradhammameva sakkatvā upanissāya viharissāmī’ti cinteti, kāraṇaṃ bhagavā cinteti, atthaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ visesaṃ [P 3.0026] cinteti, gacchāmissa ussāhaṃ janessāmī”ti cintetvā purato pākaṭo ahosi, abhimukhe aṭṭhāsīti attho.

Regarding 'in the world with its devas,' etc.: 'with its devas' means together with the devas. By the mention of 'devas' here, even though Māra and Brahmā are included, Māra is called Vasavattī, who wields power over all, and Brahmā is called the Greatly Powerful, who with one finger can illuminate a thousand world-systems, with two fingers two thousand, and with ten fingers ten thousand world-systems. Lest they should be able to say that he is more accomplished in virtue than this one, 'with its Māra and with its Brahmā' is stated separately. Similarly, contemplatives are learned, virtuous, and wise by way of the various Nikāyas, and brahmins are learned and wise by way of knowledge of sites and so forth. Lest they should be able to say that they are more accomplished than this one, 'with its generation of contemplatives and brahmins' is stated. As for 'with its devas and humans,' this is stated by taking again what has already been taken, for the purpose of showing it without remainder. Moreover, here the first three terms are spoken by way of the world-as-location, and the last two by way of the world-of-beings. 'More accomplished in virtue' means more accomplished through virtue, that is, more excellent. And here, the four qualities beginning with virtue are said to be both mundane and supramundane, while the knowledge and vision of liberation is only mundane. For this is the reviewing knowledge. Regarding 'he appeared': This is the meaning: having reflected, “This Teacher, not seeing anyone from Avīci up to the highest state of existence more excellent than himself in virtue and other qualities, thinks: ‘I will dwell honoring and depending only on the nine supramundane Dhammas realized by me.’ The Blessed One reflects on the cause, the meaning, the growth, and the distinction. I shall go and arouse his enthusiasm,” he became manifest before him and stood facing him.

Vihaṃsu [V 2.0258] viharanti cāti ettha yo vadeyya – “viharantīti vacanato paccuppannepi bahū buddhā”ti, so “bhagavāpi bhante etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti iminā vacanena paṭibāhitabbo.

Regarding 'they dwelt' and 'they dwell': Here, if someone should say, “Because of the plural form 'viharantī' (they dwell), there are many Buddhas even in the present,” he should be refuted by this statement: “But, venerable sir, even now the Blessed One is the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

“Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo”ti. (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 2.341) –

“I have no teacher; one equal to me is not found. In the world with its devas, there is no counterpart to me.”

Ādīhi cassa suttehi aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ abhāvo dīpetabbo. Tasmāti yasmā sabbepi buddhā saddhammagaruno, tasmā. Mahattamabhikaṅkhatāti mahantabhāvaṃ patthayamānena. Saraṃ buddhāna sāsananti buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ sarantena.

By these and other suttas, the non-existence of other Buddhas should be shown. Regarding 'therefore': because all Buddhas hold the True Dhamma in reverence, therefore. Regarding 'desiring greatness': by one desiring a great state. Regarding 'remembering the dispensation of the Buddhas': by one remembering the dispensation of the Buddhas.

Yatoti yasmiṃ kāle. Mahattena samannāgatoti rattaññumahattaṃ vepullamahattaṃ brahmacariyamahattaṃ lābhaggamahattanti iminā catubbidhena mahattena samannāgato. Atha me saṅghepi gāravoti atha mayhaṃ saṅghepi gāravo jāto. Kismiṃ pana kāle bhagavatā saṅghe gāravo katoti? Mahāpajāpatiyā dussayugadānakāle. Tadā hi bhagavā attano upanītaṃ dussayugaṃ “saṅghe, gotami, dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi saṅgho cā”ti vadanto saṅghe gāravaṃ akāsi nāma.

Regarding 'at which time': it means at which time. Regarding 'endowed with greatness': endowed with this fourfold greatness: the greatness of seniority, the greatness of abundance, the greatness of the holy life, and the greatness of the foremost gain. Regarding 'Then I also had reverence for the Saṅgha': this means, then reverence arose in me even for the Saṅgha. But at what time was reverence for the Saṅgha made by the Blessed One? At the time of Mahāpajāpatī’s offering of the pair of cloths. For at that time, the Blessed One, saying of the pair of cloths offered to him, “Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha; when it is given by you to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored,” indeed made reverence for the Saṅgha.

2. Dutiyauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Second Uruvelā Sutta.

22. Dutiye [M 2.0266] sambahulāti bahukā. Brāhmaṇāti huhukkajātikena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ āgatā brāhmaṇā. Jiṇṇāti [P 3.0027] jarājiṇṇā. Vuḍḍhāti vayovuddhā. Mahallakāti jātimahallakā. Addhagatāti tayo vaye addhe atikkantā. Sutametanti amhehi sutaṃ etaṃ. Tayidaṃ bho, gotama, tathevāti bho, gotama, etaṃ amhehi sutakāraṇaṃ tathā eva. Tayidaṃ bho, gotama, na sampannamevāti taṃ etaṃ abhivādanādiakaraṇaṃ ananucchavikameva.

22. In the second sutta, 'many' (sambahulā) means numerous. 'Brahmins' (brāhmaṇā) refers to the brahmins who came with the brahmin of a haughty and impetuous nature. 'Aged' (jiṇṇā) means worn out by old age. 'Elderly' (vuḍḍhā) means advanced in age. 'Venerable' (mahallakā) means senior by birth. 'Far gone in years' (addhagatā) means having passed beyond the three stages of life. 'We have heard this' (sutametaṃ) means 'this has been heard by us'. 'Indeed, Master Gotama, it is just so' (tayidaṃ bho, gotama, tatheva) means 'Master Gotama, this matter we have heard is exactly so'. 'But, Master Gotama, this is not proper' (tayidaṃ bho, gotama, na sampannameva) means that this non-performance of salutation and other respects is indeed unsuitable.

Akālavādītiādīsu akāle vadatīti akālavādī. Asabhāvaṃ vadatīti abhūtavādī. Anatthaṃ vadati, no atthanti anatthavādī. Adhammaṃ vadati, no dhammanti adhammavādī. Avinayaṃ vadati[V 2.0259], no vinayanti avinayavādī. Anidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti na hadaye nidhetabbayuttakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā. Akālenāti kathetuṃ ayuttakālena. Anapadesanti apadesarahitaṃ, sāpadesaṃ sakāraṇaṃ katvā na katheti. Apariyantavatinti pariyantarahitaṃ, na paricchedaṃ dassetvā katheti. Anatthasaṃhitanti na lokiyalokuttaraatthanissitaṃ katvā katheti. Bālo therotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti andhabālo theroti saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

In the terms beginning with 'one who speaks at the wrong time,' the meaning should be understood as follows. He speaks at the wrong time; therefore, he is one who speaks at the wrong time (akālavādī). He speaks of what is non-existent; therefore, he is one who speaks falsely (abhūtavādī). He speaks of what is unbeneficial, not of what is beneficial; therefore, he is one who speaks of the unbeneficial (anatthavādī). He speaks of what is not the Dhamma, not of the Dhamma; therefore, he is one who speaks of what is not the Dhamma (adhammavādī). He speaks of what is not the Vinaya, not of the Vinaya; therefore, he is one who speaks of what is not the Vinaya (avinayavādī). 'He speaks speech that is not worth treasuring' means he does not speak words that are fit to be stored in the heart. 'At the wrong time' means at a time unsuitable for speaking. 'Without reference' means devoid of justification; he does not speak by providing a reference with a reason. 'Without a limit' means devoid of a boundary; he does not speak by showing a limit. 'Not connected with the goal' means he does not speak by basing it on worldly and supramundane benefit. 'He is reckoned only as a foolish elder' means he is reckoned as an utterly foolish elder.

Kālavādītiādīni vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbāni. Paṇḍito therotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti paṇḍiccena samannāgatattā [P 3.0028] paṇḍito, thirabhāvappattiyā theroti saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

The terms beginning with 'one who speaks at the right time' (kālavādī) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been said. As for 'he is reckoned only as a wise elder': because he is endowed with wisdom, he is reckoned as 'wise'; because he has attained a state of steadfastness, he is reckoned as 'elder'.

Bahussuto hotīti bahuṃ assa sutaṃ hoti, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ pāḷianusandhipubbāparavasena uggahitaṃ hotīti attho. Sutadharoti sutassa ādhārabhūto. Yassa hi ito gahitaṃ ito palāyati, chiddaghaṭe udakaṃ viya na tiṭṭhati, parisamajjhe ekasuttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā kathetuṃ vā vācetuṃ vā na sakkoti, ayaṃ na sutadharo nāma. Yassa pana uggahitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahitakālasadisameva hoti, dasapi vīsatipi vassāni sajjhāyaṃ akarontassa neva nassati, ayaṃ sutadharo nāma. Sutasannicayoti sutassa sannicayabhūto. Yassa hi sutaṃ hadayamañjūsāya sannicitaṃ silāya lekhā viya suvaṇṇapatte pakkhittasīhavasā viya [M 2.0267] ca tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ sutasannicayo nāma. Dhātāti dhātā paguṇā. Ekaccassa hi uggahitabuddhavacanaṃ dhātaṃ paguṇaṃ niccalikaṃ na hoti, “asukaṃ suttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā kathehī”ti vutte “sajjhāyitvā saṃsanditvā samanuggāhitvā jānissāmī”ti vadati. Ekaccassa dhātaṃ paguṇaṃ bhavaṅgasotasadisaṃ hoti, “asukaṃ suttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā kathehī”ti vutte uddharitvā tameva katheti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “dhātā”ti. Vacasā [P 3.0029] paricitāti suttadasaka-vaggadasakapaṇṇāsadasakavasena vācāya sajjhāyitā. Manasānupekkhitāti cittena anupekkhitā. Yassa vācāya sajjhāyitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ manasā cintentassa tattha tattha pākaṭaṃ hoti, mahādīpaṃ jāletvā ṭhitassa rūpagataṃ viya paññāyati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti atthato ca kāraṇato ca paññāya suppaṭividdhā.

‘He is learned’ (bahussuto hoti) means he has heard much; the nine-limbed teaching of the Teacher has been mastered by way of the sequential connection of the preceding and subsequent Pāḷi text—this is the meaning. ‘A bearer of what has been heard’ (sutadharo) means one who is a repository for what has been heard. For one from whom what is grasped here flees from here, not remaining like water in a broken pot, who in the midst of an assembly is unable to speak or teach even a single discourse or Jātaka—such a one is not called a bearer of what has been heard. But for one for whom the learned word of the Buddha remains just as it was at the time it was learned, not being lost even after ten or twenty years without recitation—such a one is called a bearer of what has been heard. ‘An accumulator of what has been heard’ (sutasannicayo) means one who is a storehouse for what has been heard. For one in whom what has been heard is accumulated in the casket of the heart, remaining like an inscription on stone or like lion's fat placed in a golden bowl—such a one is called an accumulator of what has been heard. ‘Borne’ (dhātā) means the teachings are borne and proficient. For a certain person, the learned word of the Buddha is unpracticed and unsteady. When told, ‘Recite such-and-such a discourse or Jātaka,’ he says, ‘I will know it after reciting, connecting, and investigating.’ For another person, it is borne, proficient, and like the stream of subconsciousness. When told, ‘Recite such-and-such a discourse or Jātaka,’ he draws it out and recites that very thing. It is with reference to him that it is said, ‘borne’ (dhātā). ‘Familiarized by speech’ (vacasā paricitā) means they have been recited by speech in sets of ten discourses, sets of ten sections, or sets of fifty. ‘Repeatedly contemplated by mind’ (manasānupekkhitā) means they are repeatedly contemplated by the mind. For one who thinks with the mind upon the word of the Buddha that has been recited by speech, it becomes manifest here and there, appearing like an object in the hand for one standing with a great lamp lit—it is with reference to this that it was said. ‘Well-penetrated by view’ (diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā) means they are well-penetrated by wisdom with regard to meaning and cause.

Ābhicetasikānanti abhicetoti abhikkantaṃ visuddhaṃ cittaṃ vuccati, adhicittaṃ vā, abhicetasi jātāni ābhicetasikāni, abhicetosannissitānīti vā ābhicetasikāni. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti [V 2.0260] diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihārānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkho attabhāvo vuccati, tattha sukhavihārabhūtānanti attho. Rūpāvacarajjhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāni hi appetvā nisinnā jhāyino imasmiṃyeva attabhāve asaṃkiliṭṭhanekkhammasukhaṃ vindanti, tasmā “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānī”ti vuccati. Nikāmalābhīti nikāmena lābhī, attano icchāvasena lābhī, icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akicchalābhīti sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvā samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akasiralābhīti akasirānaṃ lābhī vipulānaṃ, yathāparicchedena vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi lābhīyeva hoti, na pana icchiticchitakkhaṇe sakkoti samāpajjituṃ. Ekacco sakkoti tathāsamāpajjituṃ, pāripanthike [P 3.0030] ca pana kicchena vikkhambheti. Ekacco tathā ca samāpajjati, pāripanthike ca akiccheneva vikkhambheti, na sakkoti nāḷikayantaṃ viya yathāparicchedeyeva vuṭṭhātuṃ. Yassa pana ayaṃ tividhāpi sampadā atthi, so “akicchalābhī akasiralābhī”ti vuccati. Āsavānaṃ khayātiādīni vuttatthāneva. Evamidha sīlampi bāhusaccampi khīṇāsavasseva sīlaṃ bāhusaccañca, jhānānipi khīṇāsavasseva vaḷañjanakajjhānāni kathitāni. “Āsavānaṃ khayā”tiādīhi [M 2.0268] pana arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Phalena cettha maggakiccaṃ pakāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'pertaining to the higher mind' (ābhicetasikānaṃ): by 'higher mind' (abhiceto) is meant the mind that is surpassing and purified, which is said to be the access concentration mind; or, it is said to be the superior mind. Those that have arisen in the superior mind are 'pertaining to the higher mind' (ābhicetasikāni); or, those that are dependent on the superior mind are 'pertaining to the higher mind' (ābhicetasikāni). 'Of blissful abidings in the present life' (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ): these are blissful abidings in the present life (diṭṭhadhamma). 'Present life' (diṭṭhadhamma) is said to be the directly experienced individual existence, and the meaning is that they are states of blissful abiding therein. This is a designation for the jhānas of the form realm. For meditators, seated after attaining these, experience the undefiled bliss of renunciation in this very individual existence. Therefore, they are called 'blissful abidings in the present life'. 'One who gains at will' (nikāmalābhī): one who gains according to desire, who gains as one wishes. It is said that one is capable of entering absorption at any desired moment. 'One who gains without difficulty' (akicchalābhī): it is said that one is capable of entering absorption after suppressing opposing states with ease. 'One who gains without trouble' (akasiralābhī): one who gains the abundant jhānas without trouble. It is said that one is capable of emerging precisely as predetermined. For some are indeed gainers but cannot enter absorption at any desired moment. Some can enter absorption in that way but suppress obstacles with difficulty. Some can enter absorption in that way and suppress obstacles with ease, but cannot emerge precisely as predetermined, like a water-clock mechanism. But one who possesses this threefold accomplishment is called 'one who gains without difficulty and without trouble'. 'The destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khayā), etc., have the meaning already stated. Thus, here, virtue and great learning are spoken of as the virtue and great learning of one whose taints are destroyed only. The jhānas, too, are spoken of as the jhānas for the use of one whose taints are destroyed only. But by 'the destruction of the taints,' etc., Arahantship is spoken of. And here it should be understood that the function of the path is revealed by the fruit.

Uddhatenāti uddhaccasahagatena. Samphanti palāpakathaṃ. Asamāhitasaṅkappoti aṭṭhapitasaṅkappo. Magoti magasadiso. Ārāti dūre. Thāvareyyamhāti thāvarabhāvato. Pāpadiṭṭhīti lāmakadiṭṭhi. Anādaroti ādararahito. Sutavāti sutena upagato. Paṭibhānavāti duvidhena paṭibhānena samannāgato. Paññāyatthaṃ vipassatīti sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya catunnaṃ saccānaṃ atthaṃ vinivijjhitvā passati. Pāragū sabbadhammānanti sabbesaṃ khandhādidhammānaṃ [P 3.0031] pāraṃ gato, abhiññāpāragū, pariññāpāragū, pahānapāragū, bhāvanāpāragū, sacchikiriyāpāragū, samāpattipāragūti evaṃ chabbidhena pāragamanena sabbadhammānaṃ pāraṃ pariyosānaṃ gato. Akhiloti rāgakhilādivirahito. Paṭibhānavāti duvidheneva paṭibhānena samannāgato. Brahmacariyassa kevalīti sakalabrahmacariyo. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

'Accompanied by restlessness' (uddhatena) means accompanied by agitation. 'Frivolous talk' (sampha) means idle talk. 'Unsettled thoughts' (asamāhitasaṅkappo) means unestablished thoughts. 'A deer' (mago) means like a deer. 'Far' (ārā) means distant. 'From a state of steadiness' (thāvareyyamhā) means from a state of stability. 'Evil view' (pāpadiṭṭhi) means bad view. 'Without respect' (anādaro) means devoid of respect for persons and the Dhamma. 'Endowed with learning' (sutavā) means endowed with what has been heard. 'Endowed with ready wit' (paṭibhānavā) means endowed with two kinds of ready wit. 'One sees the meaning by wisdom' (paññāyatthaṃ vipassati) means one sees the meaning of the four truths by penetrating with the wisdom of the path together with insight. 'One who has gone beyond all phenomena' (pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ) means one who has gone to the further shore, the end, of all phenomena, such as the aggregates, through six kinds of going beyond: going beyond by direct knowledge, going beyond by full understanding, going beyond by abandonment, going beyond by development, going beyond by realization, and going beyond by attainment. 'Free from mental barrenness' (akhilo) means free from the mental barrenness of lust and the like. 'Endowed with ready wit' (paṭibhānavā) means endowed with just two kinds of ready wit. 'One who is whole in the holy life' (brahmacariyassa kevalī) means one who is complete in the holy life. The rest here is self-explanatory.

3. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Lokasutta.

23. Tatiye lokoti dukkhasaccaṃ. Abhisambuddhoti ñāto paccakkho kato. Lokasmāti [V 2.0261] dukkhasaccato. Pahīnoti mahābodhimaṇḍe arahattamaggañāṇena pahīno. Tathāgatassa bhāvitāti tathāgatena bhāvitā.

23. In the third sutta, 'the world' (loka) means the truth of suffering. 'Fully awakened' (abhisambuddha) means known and directly realized. 'From the world' (lokasmā) means from the truth of suffering. 'Abandoned' (pahīna) means abandoned at the great seat of enlightenment by the knowledge of the path of arahantship. 'Developed by the Tathāgata' (Tathāgatassa bhāvitā) means developed by the Tathāgata.

Evaṃ ettakena ṭhānena catūhi saccehi attano buddhabhāvaṃ kathetvā idāni tathāgatabhāvaṃ kathetuṃ yaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha diṭṭhanti rūpāyatanaṃ. Sutanti saddāyatanaṃ. Mutanti patvā gahetabbato gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ. Viññātanti sukhadukkhādi dhammārammaṇaṃ. Pattanti pariyesitvā vā apariyesitvā vā pattaṃ. Pariyesitanti pattaṃ vā appattaṃ vā pariyesitaṃ. Anuvicaritaṃ manasāti cittena anusañcaritaṃ.

Thus, having declared his own Buddhahood on this basis with the four truths, he now declares his Tathāgatahood, beginning with 'Bhikkhus, whatever…' Herein, 'seen' (diṭṭha) means the visual base. 'Heard' (suta) means the sound base. 'Sensed' (muta) means the smell base, taste base, and tangible base, because they are to be grasped by way of contact. 'Cognized' (viññāta) means the mental object, such as pleasure and pain. 'Attained' (patta) means attained, whether sought or unsought. 'Sought' (pariyesita) means sought, whether attained or unattained. 'Pondered over by the mind' (anuvicaritaṃ manasā) means traversed by the mind.

Tathāgatena [M 2.0269] abhisambuddhanti iminā etaṃ dasseti – yaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu imassa sadevakassa lokassa nīlaṃ pītakantiādi rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhudvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchati, “ayaṃ satto imasmiṃ khaṇe imaṃ nāma rūpārammaṇaṃ [P 3.0032] disvā sumano vā dummano vā majjhatto vā jāto”ti sabbaṃ tathāgatassa evaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ. Tathā yaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu imassa sadevakassa lokassa bherisaddo mudiṅgasaddotiādi saddārammaṇaṃ sotadvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchati, mūlagandho tacagandhotiādi gandhārammaṇaṃ ghānadvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchati, mūlaraso khandharasotiādi rasārammaṇaṃ jivhādvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchati, kakkhaḷaṃ mudukantiādi pathavīdhātutejodhātuvāyodhātubhedaṃ phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ kāyadvāre āpāthaṃ āgacchati, “ayaṃ satto imasmiṃ khaṇe imaṃ nāma phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ phusitvā sumano vā dummano vā majjhatto vā jāto”ti sabbaṃ tathāgatassa evaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ. Tathā yaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu imassa sadevakassa lokassa sukhadukkhādibhedaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ manodvārassa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, “ayaṃ satto imasmiṃ khaṇe imaṃ nāma dhammārammaṇaṃ vijānitvā sumano vā dummano vā majjhatto vā jāto”ti sabbaṃ tathāgatassa evaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ. Yañhi, bhikkhave, imesaṃ sabbasattānaṃ diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ, tattha tathāgatena adiṭṭhaṃ vā asutaṃ vā amutaṃ vā aviññātaṃ vā natthi, imassa pana mahājanassa pariyesitvā appattampi atthi, apariyesitvā appattampi atthi, pariyesitvā pattampi atthi, apariyesitvā pattampi atthi, sabbampi tathāgatassa appattaṃ nāma natthi ñāṇena asacchikataṃ.

By the phrase 'fully awakened by the Tathāgata,' this is shown: In immeasurable world-systems, whatever visual object of this world with its devas, such as blue or yellow, comes into the range of the eye-door, and a being at that moment, having seen that particular visual object, becomes joyful, sorrowful, or neutral—all this is thus fully understood by the Tathāgata. Similarly, in immeasurable world-systems, whatever sound object of this world with its devas, such as the sound of a large drum or a small drum, comes into the range of the ear-door; whatever smell object, such as root scents or bark scents, comes into the range of the nose-door; whatever taste object, such as root tastes or stem tastes, comes into the range of the tongue-door; whatever tangible object, differentiated as the earth, fire, and wind elements, such as hard or soft, comes into the range of the body-door, and a being at that moment, having contacted that particular tangible object, becomes joyful, sorrowful, or neutral—all this is thus fully understood by the Tathāgata. Likewise, in immeasurable world-systems, whatever mental object of this world with its devas, differentiated as pleasure, pain, and so forth, comes into the range of the mind-door, and a being at that moment, having cognized that particular mental object, becomes joyful, sorrowful, or neutral—all this is thus fully understood by the Tathāgata. For, Bhikkhus, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by all these beings, there is nothing among them that is unseen, unheard, unsensed, or uncognized by the Tathāgata. For this great multitude of people, however, some things are unattained even after seeking, some are unattained without seeking, some are attained after seeking, and some are attained without seeking. But for the Tathāgata, there is nothing at all that is unattained, nothing that is not realized by his knowledge.

Tasmā tathāgatoti vuccatīti yaṃ yathā lokena gataṃ, tassa tatheva [P 3.0033] gatattā tathāgatoti vuccati[V 2.0262]. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “abhisambuddha”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ gatasaddena ekatthaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu tathāgatoti nigamassa attho veditabbo. Tassa yutti ekapuggalavaṇṇanāyaṃ tathāgatasaddavitthāre vuttāyeva. Apicettha aññadatthūti ekaṃsatthe nipāto. Dakkhatīti daso. Vasaṃ vattetīti vasavattī.

Regarding the phrase 'Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata': he is called the Tathāgata because what is known by the world in a certain way has been understood by him in that very same way. However, in the Pāḷi, 'fully awakened' (abhisambuddha) is stated; this has the same meaning as the word 'gata'. In this way, the meaning of the conclusion 'Tathāgata' should be understood in all instances. The justification for this has already been stated in the commentary on the Ekapuggala, in the detailed explanation of the word 'Tathāgata'. Furthermore, herein, 'aññadatthu' is a particle in the sense of 'certainly'. Because he sees (dakkhati), he is 'dasa'. Because he wields power (vasaṃ vatteti), he is 'vasavattī'.

Sabbaṃ lokaṃ abhiññāti tedhātukaṃ lokasannivāsaṃ jānitvā. Sabbaṃ loke yathātathanti tasmiṃ tedhātukalokasannivāse yaṃkiñci neyyaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ yathātathaṃ aviparītaṃ jānitvā. Visaṃyuttoti catunnaṃ [M 2.0270] yogānaṃ pahānena visaṃyutto. Anūpayoti taṇhādiṭṭhiupayehi virahito. Sabbābhibhūti rūpādīni sabbārammaṇāni abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Dhīroti dhitisampanno. Sabbaganthappamocanoti sabbe cattāropi ganthe mocetvā ṭhito. Phuṭṭhassāti phuṭṭhā assa. Idañca karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Paramā santīti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi tena ñāṇaphusanena phuṭṭhaṃ. Tenevāha – nibbānaṃ akutobhayanti. Atha [P 3.0034] vā paramāsantīti uttamā santi. Katarā sāti? Nibbānaṃ. Yasmā pana nibbāne kutoci bhayaṃ natthi, tasmā taṃ akutobhayanti vuccati. Vimutto upadhisaṅkhayeti upadhisaṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne tadārammaṇāya phalavimuttiyā vimutto. Sīho anuttaroti parissayānaṃ sahanaṭṭhena kilesānañca hiṃsanaṭṭhena tathāgato anuttaro sīho nāma. Brahmanti seṭṭhaṃ. Itīti evaṃ tathāgatassa guṇe jānitvā. Saṅgammāti samāgantvā. Taṃ namassantīti taṃ tathāgataṃ te saraṇaṃ gatā namassanti. Idāni yaṃ vadantā te namassanti, taṃ dassetuṃ dantotiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ uttānatthamevāti.

‘He comprehends the entire world’ (sabbaṃ lokaṃ abhiññāti) means having known the world-abode consisting of the three elements. ‘Everything in the world as it really is’ (sabbaṃ loke yathātathaṃ) means having known as it really is, without distortion, whatever is to be known in that world-abode consisting of the three elements. ‘Detached’ (visaṃyutta) means detached by the abandonment of the four yokes (yoga). ‘Without acquisitions’ (anūpaya) means devoid of the acquisitions of craving and views. ‘All-vanquishing’ (sabbābhibhū) means one who stands having overcome all objects such as form, and so forth. ‘Steadfast’ (dhīra) means endowed with fortitude. ‘Released from all ties’ (sabbaganthappamocana) means one who stands having been released from all four ties (gantha). ‘Of one who has touched’ (phuṭṭhassa) means ‘it has been touched by him.’ And this is the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental. ‘Supreme peace’ (paramā santi) is Nibbāna. For that has been touched by him with the contact of knowledge. Therefore he said: ‘Nibbāna, the fearless.’ Or alternatively, ‘supreme peace’ (paramā santi) means the highest peace. What is that? Nibbāna. And since in Nibbāna there is no fear from any quarter, therefore it is called ‘the fearless.’ ‘Liberated at the destruction of the substrates’ (vimutto upadhisaṅkhaye) means liberated by the liberation of fruition which has as its object Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of the substrates. ‘The unsurpassed lion’ (sīho anuttara) means the Tathāgata is named the unsurpassed lion because of his endurance of dangers and his destruction of defilements. ‘Brahmā’ (brahma) means the supreme. ‘Thus’ (iti) means: having thus known the qualities of the Tathāgata. ‘Having assembled’ (saṅgamma) means having come together. ‘They pay homage to him’ (taṃ namassanti) means: those who have gone for refuge pay homage to that Tathāgata. Now, to show what they say while paying homage, “the tamed one” (danta), etc., was said. That has a plain meaning.

4. Kāḷakārāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta

24. Catutthaṃ atthuppattiyaṃ nikkhittaṃ. Katarāya atthuppattiyanti? Dasabalaguṇakathāya. Anāthapiṇḍikassa kira dhītā cūḷasubhaddā “sāketanagare kāḷakaseṭṭhiputtassa gehaṃ gacchissāmī”ti satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, ahaṃ micchādiṭṭhikakulaṃ gacchāmi. Sace tattha sakkāraṃ labhissāmi, ekasmiṃ purise pesiyamāne papañco bhavissati, maṃ āvajjeyyātha bhagavā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā agamāsi. Seṭṭhi “suṇisā me āgatā”ti maṅgalaṃ karontova bahuṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādetvā pañca acelakasatāni nimantesi. So tesu nisinnesu “dhītā [P 3.0035] me āgantvā arahante vandatū”ti cūḷasubhaddāya pesesi. Āgataphalā ariyasāvikā arahanteti [V 2.0263] vuttamatteyeva “lābhā vata me”ti uṭṭhahitvā gatā te nissirikadassane acelake disvāva “samaṇā nāma na evarūpā honti, tāta, yesaṃ neva ajjhattaṃ hirī, na bahiddhā ottappaṃ atthī”ti vatvā “na ime samaṇā, dhīdhī”ti kheḷaṃ pātetvā nivattitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gatā.

24. The fourth sutta is set forth in connection with its occasion. What occasion? The discussion of the qualities of the Ten-Powered One. It is said that Anāthapiṇḍika’s daughter, Cūḷasubhaddā, thinking, “I will go to the house of the merchant Kāḷaka’s son in the city of Sāketa,” approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, I am going to a family holding wrong views. If I receive honor there, when a messenger is sent, there will be delay. May the Blessed One pay attention to me.” Having received his assent, she went. The merchant, thinking, “My daughter-in-law has arrived,” preparing much food and drink for a celebration, invited five hundred naked ascetics. When they were seated, he sent word to Cūḷasubhaddā, saying, “Let my daughter come and pay respects to the arahants.” The noble female disciple, who had attained the fruit, upon merely hearing the word “arahants,” rose up, thinking, “What a gain for me!” and went. But as soon as she saw those naked ascetics of ungraceful appearance, she said, “Father, ascetics are not like this, those who have no inner shame nor outer moral dread.” Saying, “These are not ascetics, shame! Shame!” she spat and turned back, going only to her own dwelling.

Tato [M 2.0271] acelakā “mahāseṭṭhi kuto te evarūpā kālakaṇṇī laddhā, kiṃ sakalajambudīpe aññā dārikā natthī”ti seṭṭhiṃ paribhāsiṃsu. So “ācariyā jānitvā vā kataṃ hotu ajānitvā vā, ahamettha jānissāmī”ti acelake uyyojetvā subhaddāya santikaṃ gantvā “amma, kasmā evarūpaṃ akāsi, kasmā arahante lajjāpesī”ti āha. Tāta, arahantā nāma evarūpā na hontīti. Atha naṃ so āha –

Then the naked ascetics reviled the merchant, saying, “Great merchant, from where did you get such a wretched person? Are there no other young women in all of Jambudīpa?” He replied, “Teachers, whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly, let it be. I will find out about this.” Having dismissed the naked ascetics, he went to Subhaddā and said, “Dear daughter, why did you do such a thing? Why did you embarrass the arahants?” She replied, “Father, those called arahants are not like that.” Then he said to her:

“Kīdisā samaṇā tuyhaṃ, bāḷhaṃ kho ne pasaṃsasi;

Kiṃsīlā kiṃsamācārā, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchitā”ti.

“What sort of ascetics are yours, whom you so highly praise? What is their virtue, what their way of life? Tell me this, as you are asked.”

Sā āha –

She said:

“Santindriyā santamanā, santatejā guṇamaggasaṇṭhitā;

Okkhittacakkhū mitabhāṇī, tādisā samaṇā mama.

“Calm in senses, calm in mind, of peaceful power, established in the path of virtue; with downcast eyes, speaking moderately—such are my ascetics.

“Vasanti vanamogayha, nāgo chetvāva bandhanaṃ;

Ekakiyā adutiyā, tādisā samaṇā mamā”ti.

“They dwell in the forest, having entered it, like an elephant that has broken its bonds; solitary, without a companion—such are my ascetics.”

Evañca [P 3.0036] pana vatvā seṭṭhissa pure ṭhatvā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ kathesi. Seṭṭhi tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “yadi evaṃ, tava samaṇe ānetvā maṅgalaṃ karomā”ti. Sā pucchi “kadā karissatha, tātā”ti. Seṭṭhi cintesi – “katipāhaccayenāti vutte pesetvā pakkosāpeyyā”ti. Atha naṃ “sve ammā”ti āha. Sā sāyanhasamaye uparipāsādaṃ āruyha mahantaṃ pupphasamuggaṃ gahetvā satthu guṇe anussaritvā aṭṭha pupphamuṭṭhiyo dasabalassa vissajjetvā añjaliṃ paggayha namassamānā aṭṭhāsi. Evañca avaca – “bhagavā sve pañcahi [V 2.0264] bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Tāni pupphāni gantvā dasabalassa matthake vitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Satthā āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ addasa. Dhammadesanāpariyosāne anāthapiṇḍikamahāseṭṭhi dasabalaṃ vanditvā “sve, bhante, pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mama gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Cūḷasubhaddāya nimantitamha seṭṭhīti. Na, bhante, kañci āgataṃ passāmāti. Āma, seṭṭhi, saddhā pana upāsikā dūre yojanasatamatthakepi yojanasahassamatthakepi ṭhitā himavanto viya paññāyatīti vatvā –

And having said this, standing before the merchant, she spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels. The merchant, having heard her words, said, 'If that is so, let us bring your ascetics and perform the auspicious ceremony.' She asked, 'When will you do it, father?' The merchant thought, 'If I say, "After a few days," she will send for them and have them summoned.' Then he said to her, 'Tomorrow, dear daughter.' In the evening, she ascended to the upper palace, took a large flower basket, recollected the virtues of the Teacher, and released eight handfuls of flowers for the One with Ten Powers. Raising her joined palms, she stood paying homage. And she spoke thus: 'O Blessed One, tomorrow, together with five hundred monks, may you accept my alms-food.' Those flowers went and became a canopy above the head of the One with Ten Powers and remained there. The Teacher, reflecting, saw that reason. At the conclusion of the Dhamma discourse, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having paid homage to the One with Ten Powers, said, 'Venerable Sir, tomorrow, together with five hundred monks, please accept alms-food in my house.' The Teacher said, 'O merchant, we have been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā.' 'Venerable Sir, I do not see anyone who has come,' he replied. 'Yes, merchant. However, a faithful female lay disciple, standing far away, even a hundred yojanas away or a thousand yojanas away, appears like the Himālaya mountain,' he said, and then spoke this verse:

“Dūre [M 2.0272] santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā”ti. (dha. pa. 304) –

“The good shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountain; the wicked, though near, are not seen, like arrows shot in the night.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Anāthapiṇḍiko “bhante, mama, dhītu saṅgahaṃ karothā”ti vanditvā pakkāmi.

He spoke this verse. Anāthapiṇḍika, saying, “Venerable sir, please give assistance to my daughter,” paid homage and then departed.

Satthā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi – “ahaṃ, ānanda, sāketaṃ gamissāmi, pañcannaṃ [P 3.0037] bhikkhusatānaṃ salākaṃ dehi. Dadanto ca chaḷabhiññānaṃyeva dadeyyāsī”ti. Thero tathā akāsi. Cūḷasubhaddā rattibhāgasamanantare cintesi – “buddhā nāma bahukiccā bahukaraṇīyā, maṃ sallakkheyya vā na vā, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe vessavaṇo mahārājā cūḷasubhaddāya kathesi – “bhadde, mā kho tvaṃ vimanā ahosi, mā dummanā. Adhivutthaṃ te bhagavatā svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti. Sā tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā dānameva saṃvidahi. Sakkopi kho devarājā vissakammaṃ āmantesi – “tāta, dasabalo cūḷasubhaddāya santikaṃ sāketanagaraṃ gacchissati, pañca kūṭāgārasatāni māpehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Satthā pañcahi chaḷabhiññasatehi parivuto kūṭāgārayānena maṇivaṇṇaṃ ākāsaṃ vilikhanto viya sāketanagaraṃ agamāsi.

The Teacher addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, I will go to Sāketa. Give a token to five hundred monks. And when giving, you should give only to those with the six superknowledges.” The Venerable did so. Just before dawn, Cūḷasubhaddā thought: “Buddhas indeed have many duties and much to do; whether he might notice me or not, what should I do?” At that moment, the great king Vessavaṇa said to Cūḷasubhaddā: “Good lady, do not be disheartened or sad. The Blessed One has accepted your meal for tomorrow, together with the community of monks.” Delighted and overjoyed, she prepared the offering. Sakka, the king of the gods, also addressed Vissakamma: “Dear one, the Ten-Powered One will go to the city of Sāketa to the presence of Cūḷasubhaddā. Construct five hundred peaked pavilions.” He did so. Surrounded by five hundred monks possessing the six superknowledges, the Teacher traveled to the city of Sāketa in a vehicle of peaked pavilions, as if inscribing a jeweled line across the sky.

Subhaddā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ datvā satthāraṃ vanditvā āha – “bhante, mayhaṃ sasurapakkho micchādiṭṭhiko, sādhu tesaṃ anucchavikadhammaṃ kathethā”ti. Satthā dhammaṃ desesi. Kāḷakaseṭṭhi sotāpanno hutvā attano uyyānaṃ dasabalassa adāsi. Acelakā “amhākaṃ paṭhamaṃ dinna”nti nikkhamituṃ na icchanti. “Gacchatha nīharitabbaniyāmena te nīharathā”ti sabbe nīharāpetvā tattheva satthu vihāraṃ kāretvā brahmadeyyaṃ katvā [P 3.0038] udakaṃ pātesi[V 2.0265]. So kāḷakena kāritatāya kāḷakārāmo nāma jāto. Bhagavā tasmiṃ samaye tattha viharati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sākete viharati kāḷakārāme”ti.

Having offered alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, Subhaddā paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, my father-in-law's family holds wrong views. Please teach them the Dhamma appropriate to them.” The Teacher taught the Dhamma. The merchant Kāḷaka became a stream-enterer and gave his park to the Ten-Powered One. The naked ascetics, claiming, “It was given to us first,” refused to leave. He had them all removed, saying, “Go! Remove them by the rule for expulsion.” Right there he had a monastery built for the Teacher, made it a sublime gift, and poured the water of dedication. Because it was established by Kāḷaka, it became known as Kāḷakārāma. The Blessed One dwelt there at that time. Hence it is said, “He dwelt at Sāketa in Kāḷakārāma.”

Bhikkhū āmantesīti pañcasate bhikkhū āmantesi. Te kira sāketanagaravāsino kulaputtā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā satthu santike pabbajitvā upaṭṭhānasālāya nisinnā “aho buddhaguṇā nāma mahantā, evarūpaṃ nāma micchādiṭṭhikaṃ kāḷakaseṭṭhiṃ diṭṭhito mocetvā sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpetvā [M 2.0273] sakalanagaraṃ satthārā devalokasadisaṃ kata”nti dasabalassa guṇaṃ kathenti. Satthā tesaṃ guṇaṃ kathentānaṃ cittaṃ upaparikkhitvā – “mayi gate mahatī desanā samuṭṭhissati, desanāpariyosāne ca ime pañcasatā bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahissanti, mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā kampissatī”ti dhammasabhaṃ gantvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno te bhikkhū ādiṃ katvā yaṃ, bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassāti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Evamidaṃ suttaṃ guṇakathāya nikkhittanti veditabbaṃ.

He addressed the monks: this means he addressed five hundred monks. It is said that these were clansmen residing in the city of Sāketa who, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, went forth in the Teacher’s presence. Seated in the attendance hall, they were speaking of the qualities of the Ten-Powered One: ‘Oh, how great indeed are the qualities of the Buddha! Having liberated such a holder of wrong views as the merchant Kāḷaka from his view and caused him to attain the fruit of stream-entry, the entire city was made by the Teacher to be like a world of the devas!’ The Teacher, examining the minds of those who were speaking of his qualities, thought: ‘When I go there, a great discourse will arise. At the end of the discourse, these five hundred monks will be established in arahantship, and the great earth will shake down to its water-boundary.’ Having gone to the Dhamma hall and seated himself on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat, he began this discourse, starting with those monks: ‘That which, O monks, for the world with its devas…’ Thus, it should be understood that this discourse was set down on account of the discussion of qualities.

Tattha “tamahaṃ jānāmī”ti padapariyosāne mahāpathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā akampittha. Abbhaññāsinti abhiaññāsiṃ, jāninti attho. Viditanti pākaṭaṃ katvā ñātaṃ. Iminā etaṃ dasseti – aññe jānantiyeva, mayā pana pākaṭaṃ katvā viditanti. Imehi tīhi padehi sabbaññutabhūmi nāma kathitā. Taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsīti taṃ chadvārikaṃ ārammaṇaṃ tathāgato taṇhāya vā diṭṭhiyā vā na upaṭṭhāsi na upagañchi. Ayañhi passati bhagavā cakkhunā rūpaṃ, chandarāgo [P 3.0039] bhagavato natthi, suvimuttacitto so bhagavā. Suṇāti bhagavā sotena saddaṃ. Ghāyati bhagavā ghānena gandhaṃ. Sāyati bhagavā jivhāya rasaṃ. Phusati bhagavā kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Vijānāti bhagavā manasā dhammaṃ, chandarāgo bhagavato natthi, suvimuttacitto so bhagavā. Tena vuttaṃ – “taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsī”ti. Iminā padena khīṇāsavabhūmi kathitāti veditabbā.

There, at the end of the phrase, “That I know,” the great earth shook down to its water-boundary. ‘Abbhaññāsiṃ’ means ‘I directly knew’; this is the meaning. ‘Viditaṃ’ means known, having been made manifest. By this, it is shown: others indeed know, but by me it has been made manifest and is known. “The Tathāgata did not attend to that” means the Tathāgata did not attend to or approach that six-doored sense object with craving or wrong view. For the Blessed One sees a form with the eye, but there is no desire and passion in the Blessed One; that Blessed One’s mind is well liberated. The Blessed One hears a sound with the ear. The Blessed One smells an odor with the nose. The Blessed One tastes a flavor with the tongue. The Blessed One feels a tangible object with the body. The Blessed One cognizes a mental object with the mind, but there is no desire and passion in the Blessed One; that Blessed One’s mind is well liberated. Therefore it is said, “The Tathāgata did not attend to that.” It should be understood that by this phrase the domain of one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of.

Taṃ mamassa musāti taṃ me vacanaṃ musāvādo nāma bhaveyya. Taṃ passa tādisamevāti tampi musāvādo bhaveyya. Taṃ mamassa kalīti taṃ vacanaṃ mayhaṃ doso bhaveyyāti attho. Ettāvatā saccabhūmi nāma kathitāti veditabbā.

‘That would be a lie for me’ means that statement of mine would be a falsehood. ‘That would be just the same for me’ means that too would be a falsehood. ‘That would be a blemish for me’ means that statement would be a fault for me; this is the meaning. It should be understood that by this much, the domain of truth is spoken of.

Daṭṭhā [V 2.0266] daṭṭhabbanti disvā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Diṭṭhaṃ na maññatīti taṃ diṭṭhaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ “ahaṃ mahājanena diṭṭhameva passāmī”ti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi na maññati. Adiṭṭhaṃ na maññatīti “ahaṃ mahājanena adiṭṭhameva etaṃ passāmī”ti evampi taṇhādīhi maññanāhi na maññati. Daṭṭhabbaṃ na maññatīti “mahājanena diṭṭhaṃ passāmī”ti evampi tāhi maññanāhi na maññati. Daṭṭhabbañhi adiṭṭhampi hotiyeva. Evarūpāni hi vacanāni tīsupi kālesu labbhanti, tenassa attho vutto. Daṭṭhāraṃ [P 3.0040] na maññatīti passitāraṃ [M 2.0274] ekasattaṃ nāma tāhi maññanāhi na maññatīti attho. Sesaṭṭhānesupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Iminā ettakena ṭhānena suññatābhūmi nāma kathitā.

‘Having seen what is to be seen.’ ‘One does not conceive the seen’ means: one does not conceive that seen form-base with craving, conceit, and views, thinking, “I see that very thing which has been seen by the great multitude.” ‘One does not conceive the unseen’ means: one also does not conceive with conceivings such as craving, thinking, “I see this very thing which is unseen by the great multitude.” ‘One does not conceive what is to be seen’ means: one also does not conceive with those conceivings, thinking, “I see what is seen by the great multitude.” For what is to be seen may indeed also be unseen. Such statements are found in all three times; therefore, this meaning is stated. ‘One does not conceive of those who have seen’ means: one does not conceive of the beings who have seen with those conceivings; this is the meaning. The meaning in the remaining instances should be understood in this same way. By this much, the domain of emptiness is spoken of.

Iti kho, bhikkhaveti evaṃ kho, bhikkhave. Tādīyeva tādīti tāditā nāma ekasadisatā. Tathāgato ca yādiso lābhādīsu, tādisova alābhādīsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “lābhepi tādī, alābhepi tādī. Yasepi tādī, ayasepi tādī. Nindāyapi tādī, pasaṃsāyapi tādī. Sukhepi tādī, dukkhepi tādī”ti (mahāni. 38, 192). Imāya tāditāya tādī. Tamhā ca pana tādimhāti tato tathāgatatādito añño uttaritaro vā paṇītataro vā tādī natthīti ettāvatā tādibhūmi nāma kathitā. Imāhi pañcabhūmīhi desanaṃ niṭṭhāpentassa pañcasupi ṭhānesu mahāpathavī sakkhibhāvena akampittha. Desanāpariyosāne te pañcasate adhunāpabbajite kulaputte ādiṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ pattānaṃ devamanussānaṃ caturāsīti pāṇasahassāni amatapānaṃ piviṃsu.

Thus indeed, bhikkhus. 'Such' is indeed 'such'; 'suchness' means uniformity. And as the Tathāgata is in gain and so on, so is he in loss and so on. Therefore it was said: “The same in gain, the same in loss; the same in fame, the same in disgrace; the same in blame, the same in praise; the same in pleasure, the same in pain.” By this suchness, he is 'such.' And from that suchness of the Tathāgata, there is no other 'such' that is higher or more excellent. To this extent, the ground of suchness has been spoken of. As he was concluding the teaching with these five grounds, the great earth shook on all five occasions by way of being a witness. At the conclusion of the teaching, beginning with those five hundred clansmen who had recently gone forth, eighty-four thousand living beings among the gods and humans who had arrived at that place drank the deathless nectar.

Bhagavāpi suttaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā gāthāhi kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto yaṃkiñcītiādimāha. Tattha [P 3.0041] ajjhositaṃ saccamutaṃ paresanti paresaṃ saddhāya parapattiyāyanāya saccamutanti maññitvā ajjhositaṃ gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā gahitaṃ. Sayasaṃvutesūti sayameva saṃvaritvā piyāyitvā gahitagahaṇesu, diṭṭhigatikesūti attho. Diṭṭhigatikā hi sayaṃ saṃvutāti vuccanti. Saccaṃ musā vāpi paraṃ daheyyāti tesu sayaṃ saṃvutasaṅkhātesu diṭṭhigatikesu tathāgato tādī tesaṃ ekampi vacanaṃ “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti evaṃ saccaṃ musā vāpi paraṃ uttamaṃ katvā na odaheyya, na saddaheyya, na pattiyāyeyya. Etañca sallanti etaṃ diṭṭhisallaṃ. Paṭikacca disvāti puretaraṃ bodhimūleyeva disvā. Visattāti laggā lagitā palibuddhā. Jānāmi passāmi tatheva etanti yathāyaṃ pajā ajjhositā gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā visattā laggā lagitā, evaṃ ahampi [V 2.0267] jānāmi passāmi. Tathā evaṃ yathā etāya pajāya gahitanti evaṃ ajjhositaṃ natthi tathāgatānanti attho.

The Blessed One, having concluded the sutta and wishing to crown it with verses, spoke the words beginning with 'Whatever...'. Therein, 'settled upon as true or false regarding others' means: that which is settled upon, swallowed, brought to a conclusion, and grasped, having thought 'This is true' or 'This is false' through faith connected with trust in others. 'In those self-restrained' means: in those holding to their own graspings, that is, in those with wrong views who have reflected for themselves and come to a conclusion. Indeed, those with wrong views are called 'self-restrained'. 'Whether true or false, one should not place it as supreme' means: regarding those with wrong views, who are known as 'self-restrained', the Tathāgata is 'such' (unshaken); he would not place, believe, or trust even a single statement of theirs—whether true or false—such as 'This alone is true, the other is vain,' making it supreme. 'And this dart' means: this dart of views. 'Having seen beforehand' means: having seen it earlier, right at the root of the Bodhi tree. 'Attached' means: clinging, stuck, entangled. 'I know, I see, it is just so' means: Just as this populace is settled upon, has swallowed, has brought to a conclusion, and is attached, stuck, and entangled, so do I know and see. The meaning is: For the Tathāgatas, there is no such settling upon in the way that it is grasped by this populace.

5. Brahmacariyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Holy Life

25. Pañcame [M 2.0275] janakuhanatthanti tīhi kuhanavatthūhi janassa kuhanatthāya. Na janalapanatthanti na janassa upalāpanatthaṃ. Na lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsatthanti na cīvarādithutivacanatthaṃ. Na itivādappamokkhānisaṃsatthanti na tena tena kāraṇena [P 3.0042] katavādānisaṃsatthaṃ, na vādassa pamokkhānisaṃsatthaṃ. Na iti maṃ jano jānātūti na “evaṃ kira esa bhikkhu, evaṃ kira esa bhikkhū”ti janassa jānanatthāya. Saṃvaratthanti pañcahi saṃvarehi saṃvaraṇatthāya. Pahānatthanti tīhi pahānehi pajahanatthāya. Virāgatthanti rāgādīnaṃ virajjanatthāya. Nirodhatthanti tesaṃyeva nirujjhanatthāya. Anītihanti itihaparivajjitaṃ, aparapattiyanti attho. Nibbānogadhagāminanti nibbānassa antogāminaṃ. Maggabrahmacariyañhi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā nibbānassa antoyeva vattati pavattati. Paṭipajjantīti duvidhampi paṭipajjanti. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathetvā gāthāsu vivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

25. In the fifth sutta, 'for deceiving people' means with the three grounds for deception, for the purpose of deceiving people. 'Not for coaxing people' means not for the purpose of coaxing people. 'Not for the sake of being released from disputation' means not for the sake of a view made for this or that reason, nor for the sake of release from disputation. 'Not so that people may know me' means not for the purpose of people knowing, 'This monk is like this, this monk is like that.' 'For restraint' means for the purpose of restraint through the five kinds of restraint. 'For abandoning' means for the purpose of giving up through the three kinds of abandonment. 'For dispassion' means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate toward lust and so on. 'For cessation' means for the purpose of the cessation of those very things. 'Without hearsay' means free from hearsay; the meaning is 'not based on trust in another.' 'Leading to Nibbāna' means leading inward to Nibbāna. For the holy life of the path, taking Nibbāna as its object, proceeds and continues only within Nibbāna. 'They practice' means they practice in both ways. In this sutta, having spoken of the round of existence, in the verses only the escape from the round is spoken of.

6. Kuhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Kuhasutta

26. Chaṭṭhe kuhāti kuhakā. Thaddhāti kodhena ca mānena ca thaddhā. Lapāti upalāpakā. Siṅgīti “tattha katamaṃ siṅgaṃ, yaṃ siṅgaṃ siṅgāratā cāturatā cāturiyaṃ parikkhattatā pārikkhattiya”nti (vibha. 852) evaṃ vuttehi siṅgasadisehi pākaṭakilesehi samannāgatā. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitā. Asamāhitāti cittekaggamattassāpi alābhino. Na [P 3.0043] me te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū māmakāti te mayhaṃ bhikkhū mama santakā na honti. “Te mayha”nti idaṃ pana satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajitattā vuttaṃ. Te kho me, bhikkhave, bhikkhū māmakāti idhāpi meti attānaṃ uddissa pabbajitattā vadati, sammāpaṭipannattā pana “māmakā”ti āha. Vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjantīti sīlādīhi guṇehi vaḍḍhanato vuddhiṃ, niccalabhāvena virūḷhiṃ, sabbattha patthaṭatāya vepullaṃ pāpuṇanti. Te panete yāva [V 2.0268] arahattamaggā viruhanti, arahattaphalaṃ patte virūḷhā nāma honti. Iti imasmiṃ suttepi gāthāsupi vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

26. In the sixth sutta, 'deceitful' means those who are deceitful. 'Obstinate' means stiff with anger and conceit. 'Coaxers' means flatterers. 'Horned' means endowed with evident defilements similar to horns, as described: 'What is the horn? The horn is ornamentation, cleverness, adroitness, cunning, and craftiness' (Vibhanga 852). 'Puffed up' means those who stand, having raised up empty conceit. 'Unconcentrated' means lacking even the slightest one-pointedness of mind. 'These monks, bhikkhus, are not mine' means these monks are not my property. As for 'They are mine,' this is said because they have gone forth with the Teacher in mind. Also in this passage, 'Indeed, bhikkhus, those monks are mine,' he says 'me' because they have gone forth with him in mind, but he says 'mine' because they practice rightly. 'They attain growth, increase, and abundance' means they attain growth through the increase of virtues such as morality, increase because of having the unfailing fruit, and abundance by spreading everywhere. Furthermore, these are growing up to the path of Arahantship; when they reach the fruit of Arahantship, they are called 'fully grown.' Thus, in this sutta and in the verses too, both the round of existence and the escape from it are discussed.

7. Santuṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse on Contentment

27. Sattame [M 2.0276] appānīti parittāni. Sulabhānīti sukhena laddhabbāni, yattha katthaci sakkā honti labhituṃ. Anavajjānīti niddosāni. Piṇḍiyālopabhojananti jaṅghāpiṇḍiyabalena caritvā ālopamattaṃ laddhaṃ bhojanaṃ. Pūtimuttanti yaṃkiñci muttaṃ. Yathā hi suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo pūtikāyoti vuccati, evaṃ abhinavampi muttaṃ pūtimuttameva.

27. In the seventh sutta, 'few' means limited. 'Easily obtained' means obtainable with ease; they can be obtained anywhere. 'Blameless' means faultless. 'Eating almsfood' means food obtained by wandering for alms, a mere mouthful. 'Putrid urine' means any urine. Just as even a golden-colored body is called a putrid body, so even fresh urine is putrid.

Vighātoti vigataghāto, cittassa dukkhaṃ na hotīti attho. Disā [P 3.0044] nappaṭihaññatīti yassa hi “asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gato cīvarādīni labhissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa disā paṭihaññati nāma. Yassa evaṃ na uppajjati, tassa nappaṭihaññati nāma. Dhammāti paṭipattidhammā. Sāmaññassānulomikāti samaṇadhammassa anulomā. Adhiggahitāti sabbete tuṭṭhacittassa bhikkhuno adhiggahitā honti antogatā na paribāhirāti.
