“Vighāta” means the absence of weariness; the meaning is that suffering does not arise for the mind. “The directions are not struck” means: for whichever monk the thought arises, “Having gone to such and such a place, I will not obtain robes and so forth,” for him the directions are said to be struck. For one in whom such a thought does not arise, for him they are said to be not struck. “Dhammā” means the dhammas of practice. “Sāmaññassānulomikā” means conforming to the practice of a recluse. “Adhiggahitā” means all these dhammas are mastered by a monk with a contented mind; they are internalized, not external.

8. Ariyavaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on the Lineage of the Noble Ones

28. Aṭṭhamassa ajjhāsayiko nikkhepo. Imaṃ kira mahāariyavaṃsasuttantaṃ bhagavā jetavanamahāvihāre dhammasabhāyaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno attanopi parapuggalānampi ajjhāsayavasena parivāretvā nisinnāni cattālīsa bhikkhusahassāni, “bhikkhave”ti āmantetvā cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsāti ārabhi. Tattha ariyavaṃsāti ariyānaṃ vaṃsā. Yathā hi khattiyavaṃso brāhmaṇavaṃso vessavaṃso suddavaṃso samaṇavaṃso kulavaṃso rājavaṃso, evaṃ ayampi aṭṭhamo ariyavaṃso ariyatanti ariyapaveṇī nāma hoti. So kho panāyaṃ ariyavaṃso imesaṃ vaṃsānaṃ mūlagandhādīnaṃ kāḷānusārigandhādayo viya aggamakkhāyati.

28. For the eighth, there is an exposition based on disposition. It is said that the Blessed One, seated on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall in the great monastery of Jetavana, by the power of the disposition of both himself and other persons, addressed the forty thousand monks seated surrounding him, saying, “Bhikkhus,” and began with, “Bhikkhus, these four are the noble lineages.” Therein, “noble lineages” means the lineages of the noble ones. For just as there is the lineage of warriors, the lineage of brahmins, the lineage of merchants, the lineage of workers, and the lineage of recluses, so too this eighth is called the noble lineage, the noble tradition, and the noble succession. Indeed, this noble lineage is declared the foremost among these lineages, just as fragrances such as black aloeswood are declared foremost among root fragrances and others.

Ke pana te ariyā, yesaṃ ete vaṃsāti? Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca tathāgatasāvakā ca, etesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Ito pubbe hi satasahassakappādhikānaṃ [V 2.0269] catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake taṇhaṅkaro, medhaṅkaro[P 3.0045], saraṇaṅkaro, dīpaṅkaroti cattāro [M 2.0277] buddhā uppannā, te ariyā, tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Tesaṃ buddhānaṃ parinibbānato aparabhāge asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā koṇḍañño nāma buddho uppanno…pe… imasmiṃ kappe kakusandho, koṇāgamano, kassapo, amhākaṃ bhagavā gotamoti cattāro buddhā uppannā, tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Apica atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ sabbabuddha-paccekabuddha-buddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā.

But who are those noble ones, whose lineages are these? The noble ones are called Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata. The lineages of these noble ones are the noble lineages. For before this, at the culmination of four incalculable eons exceeding a hundred thousand eons, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—arose. They were noble, and the lineages of those noble ones are the noble lineages. After the Parinibbāna of those Buddhas, after an incalculable eon had passed, the Buddha Koṇḍañña arose… and so on… in this aeon, the four Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One Gotama arose. The lineages of those noble ones are the noble lineages. Furthermore, the lineages of all past, future, and present Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Buddha-disciples, who are noble, are the noble lineages.

Te kho panete aggaññā aggāti jānitabbā, rattaññā dīgharattaṃ pavattāti jānitabbā, vaṃsaññā vaṃsāti jānitabbā. Porāṇā na adhunuppattikā. Asaṃkiṇṇā avikiṇṇā anapanītā. Asaṃkiṇṇapubbā atītabuddhehipi na saṃkiṇṇapubbā, “ki imehī”ti na apanītapubbā. Na saṃkīyantīti idānipi na apanīyanti. Na saṃkīyissantīti anāgatabuddhehipi na apanīyissanti. Ye loke viññū samaṇabrāhmaṇā, tehi appaṭikuṭṭhā, samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhi aninditā agarahitā.

Indeed, these should be known as foremost, as supreme; as long-standing, as having long endured; and as lineages, as traditions. They are ancient, not newly arisen. They are unadulterated, not discarded, not removed. They were not previously adulterated, not even by past Buddhas, nor were they previously removed with the thought, “What is the use of these?” They are not adulterated, meaning that even now they are not removed. They will not be adulterated, meaning that they will not be removed even by future Buddhas. The wise ascetics and brahmins in the world do not reject them; they are not blamed or censured by wise ascetics and brahmins.

Santuṭṭho hotīti paccayasantosavasena santuṭṭho hoti. Itarītarenāti na thūlasukhumalūkhapaṇītathirajiṇṇānaṃ yena kenaci, atha kho yathāladdhādīnaṃ itarītarena yena kenaci santuṭṭho hotīti attho. Cīvarasmiñhi tayo santosā [P 3.0046] yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantosoti. Piṇḍapātādīsupi eseva nayo. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā “santuṭṭhassa, bhikkhave, anuppannā ceva kusalā dhammā uppajjantī”ti imasmiṃ sutte vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Iti ime tayo santose sandhāya “santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena, yathāladdhādīsu yena kenaci cīvarena santuṭṭho hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

“He is content” means he is content by way of contentment with the requisites. “With this or that” means he is not content with just any coarse, fine, rough, exquisite, durable, or worn-out robe, but rather, he is content with this or that, with any whatsoever among what is obtained, and so on; this is the meaning. Indeed, regarding the robe, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment according to one's capacity, and contentment with what is suitable. This same method applies to alms-food and so on. The detailed explanation of these should be understood in the very way stated in the sutta: “For one who is content, O bhikkhus, unarisen wholesome states arise.” Thus, with reference to these three kinds of contentment, it was said: “He is content with this or that robe,” meaning, “he is content with any robe whatsoever among those that are obtained, and so on.”

Ettha ca cīvaraṃ jānitabbaṃ, cīvarakkhettaṃ jānitabbaṃ, paṃsukūlaṃ jānitabbaṃ, cīvarasantoso jānitabbo, cīvarappaṭisaṃyuttāni dhutaṅgāni jānitabbāni. Tattha cīvaraṃ jānitabbanti khomādīni cha cīvarāni dukūlādīni cha anulomacīvarāni jānitabbāni. Imāni dvādasa kappiyacīvarāni. Kusacīraṃ, vākacīraṃ, phalakacīraṃ, kesakambalaṃ, vāḷakambalaṃ, potthako, cammaṃ, ulūkapakkhaṃ, rukkhadussaṃ, latādussaṃ, erakadussaṃ, kadalidussaṃ, veḷudussanti evamādīni pana akappiyacīvarāni.

And here, the robe should be known, the field of robes should be known, the refuse-rag robe should be known, contentment with the robe should be known, and the ascetic practices connected with the robe should be known. Therein, that the robe should be known means that the six robes beginning with linen and the six conforming robes beginning with fine cloth should be known. These twelve are allowable robes. However, robes such as a robe of kusa grass, a robe of bark-fibre, a robe of wood-strips, a blanket of human hair, a blanket of yak-tail hair, a robe of hemp-fibre, leather, a robe of owl's wings, a robe of tree-bark, a robe of creepers, a robe of eraka grass, a robe of banana-fibre, and a robe of bamboo-fibre are unallowable robes.

Cīvarakkhettanti [V 2.0270][M 2.0278] “saṅghato vā gaṇato vā ñātito vā mittato vā attano vā dhanena, paṃsukūlaṃ vā”ti evaṃ uppajjanato cha khettāni, aṭṭhannañca mātikānaṃ vasena aṭṭha khettāni jānitabbāni.

“The field of robes” means: “from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives, or from friends, or from one’s own wealth, or from refuse-rags.” Thus, from the way they arise, there are six fields; and by way of the eight headings, eight fields should be known.

Paṃsukūlanti sosānikaṃ, pāpaṇikaṃ, rathiyaṃ, saṅkārakūṭakaṃ, sotthiyaṃ, sinānaṃ, titthaṃ, gatapaccāgataṃ, aggidaḍḍhaṃ, gokhāyitaṃ, upacikakhāyitaṃ, undūrakhāyitaṃ[P 3.0047], antacchinnaṃ, dasacchinnaṃ, dhajāhaṭaṃ, thūpaṃ, samaṇacīvaraṃ, sāmuddiyaṃ, ābhisekiyaṃ, panthikaṃ, vātāhaṭaṃ, iddhimayaṃ, devadattiyanti tevīsati paṃsukūlāni veditabbāni. Ettha ca sotthiyanti gabbhamalaharaṇaṃ. Gatapaccāgatanti matakasarīraṃ pārupitvā susānaṃ netvā ānītacīvaraṃ. Dhajāhaṭanti dhajaṃ ussāpetvā tato ānītaṃ. Thūpanti vammike pūjitacīvaraṃ. Sāmuddiyanti samuddavīcīhi thalaṃ pāpitaṃ. Panthikanti panthaṃ gacchantehi corabhayena pāsāṇehi koṭṭetvā pārutacīvaraṃ. Iddhimayanti ehibhikkhucīvaraṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

Regarding rag-robes: twenty-three kinds of rag-robes are to be known: a robe from a charnel ground, a robe from a market stall, a robe from a road, a robe from a rubbish heap, a childbirth-cleansing robe, a bather's robe, a robe from a bathing place, a robe taken to a cemetery and brought back, a fire-scorched robe, a cow-chewed robe, a termite-chewed robe, a rat-chewed robe, a robe with a torn edge, a robe with a torn fringe, a banner-robe, a robe offered at an anthill, a recluse's robe, a robe cast ashore by the sea, a consecration robe, a traveler's robe, a wind-carried robe, a robe created by psychic power, and a robe given by a deva. Herein, 'a childbirth-cleansing robe' refers to a cloth for removing the impurities of childbirth. 'A robe taken to a cemetery and brought back' means a robe used to shroud a corpse, taken to the cemetery, and then brought back. 'A banner-robe' is a robe brought by the wind from a place where a banner has been raised. 'A robe offered at an anthill' is a robe offered at an anthill. 'A robe cast ashore by the sea' is a robe brought to shore by ocean waves. 'A traveler's robe' is a robe worn by travelers who, out of fear of thieves, have beaten it with stones. 'A robe created by psychic power' is an 'ehi bhikkhu' robe. The rest is self-evident.

Cīvarasantosoti vīsati cīvarasantosā – cīvare vitakkasantoso, gamanasantoso, pariyesanasantoso, paṭilābhasantoso, mattapaṭiggahaṇasantoso, loluppavivajjanasantoso, yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantoso, udakasantoso, dhovanasantoso, karaṇasantoso, parimāṇasantoso, suttasantoso, sibbanasantoso, rajanasantoso, kappasantoso, paribhogasantoso, sannidhiparivajjanasantoso, vissajjanasantosoti.

There are twenty kinds of contentment with robes: contentment with reflection, contentment with going, contentment with seeking, contentment with receiving, contentment with accepting a measured amount, contentment with avoiding greed, contentment with whatever is received, contentment according to one's strength, contentment according to suitability, contentment with dye-water, contentment with washing, contentment with making, contentment with the measure, contentment with thread, contentment with sewing, contentment with dyeing, contentment with making the determination mark, contentment with using, contentment with avoiding storing, and contentment with giving up.

Tattha sādakabhikkhunā temāsaṃ nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitvā ekamāsamattaṃ vitakketuṃ vaṭṭati. So hi pavāretvā cīvaramāse cīvaraṃ karoti, paṃsukūliko aḍḍhamāseneva karoti. Idaṃ māsaḍḍhamāsamattaṃ vitakkanaṃ vitakkasantoso nāma. Vitakkasantosena pana santuṭṭhena bhikkhunā pācīnakhaṇḍarājivāsikapaṃsukūlikattherasadisena [P 3.0048] bhavitabbaṃ.

Therein, a monk who accepts offered robes, having dwelt in continuous residence for three months, is allowed to reflect for about a month. For having performed Pavāraṇā, he makes a robe during the robe-making month; but a rag-robe wearer makes it in only half a month. This reflection for about a month or half a month is called 'contentment with reflection.' Furthermore, a monk who is content with contentment with reflection should be like the rag-robe-wearing elder of Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji.

Thero kira “cetiyapabbatavihāre cetiyaṃ vandissāmī”ti āgato cetiyaṃ vanditvā cintesi – “mayhaṃ cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ, bahūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne labhissāmī”ti. So mahāvihāraṃ gantvā saṅghattheraṃ disvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā tattha vuttho punadivase cīvaraṃ ādāya āgantvā theraṃ vandi. Thero “kiṃ[M 2.0279], āvuso”ti āha. Gāmadvāraṃ, bhante, gamissāmīti. Ahampāvuso, gamissāmīti[V 2.0271]. Sādhu, bhanteti gacchanto mahābodhidvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā “puññavantānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne manāpaṃ labhissāmī”ti cintetvā “aparisuddho me vitakko”ti tatova paṭinivatti. Punadivase ambaṅgaṇasamīpato, punadivase mahācetiyassa uttaradvārato tattheva paṭinivattitvā catutthadivase therassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Thero “imassa bhikkhuno vitakko na parisuddho bhavissatī”ti cīvaraṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃyeva pañhaṃ pucchamāno gāmaṃ pāvisi. Tañca rattiṃ eko manusso uccārapalibuddho sāṭakeyeva vaccaṃ katvā taṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesi. Paṃsukūlikatthero taṃ nīlamakkhikāhi samparikiṇṇaṃ disvā añjaliṃ paggahesi. Mahāthero “kiṃ, āvuso, saṅkāraṭṭhānassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhāsī”ti. Nāhaṃ, bhante, saṅkāraṭṭhānassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhāmi, mayhaṃ pitu dasabalassa paggaṇhāmi, puṇṇadāsiyā sarīraṃ pārupitvā chaḍḍitaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ tumbamatte pāṇake vidhunitvā susānato gaṇhantena dukkarataraṃ kataṃ[P 3.0049], bhanteti. Mahāthero “parisuddho vitakko paṃsukūlikassā”ti cintesi. Paṃsukūlikattheropi tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhito vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tīṇi phalāni patto taṃ sāṭakaṃ gahetvā cīvaraṃ katvā pārupitvā pācīnakhaṇḍarājiṃ gantvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

It is said that the elder, thinking, 'I will pay homage to the shrine at Cetiyapabbata Monastery,' went there, paid respects, and then reflected: 'My robe is worn out; I shall obtain one in a place where many dwell.' He went to the Great Monastery, saw the senior monk, asked for a place to stay, and having stayed there, on the next day he took his robe, came, and paid homage to the elder. The elder asked, 'What is it, friend?' 'I am going to the village gate, venerable sir.' 'I too will go, friend.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' he said, and as he walked, he stopped at the gatehouse of the Great Bodhi Tree and thought, 'In the dwelling place of the meritorious, I shall obtain something pleasing.' Then he reflected, 'My thought is impure,' and turned back from there. The next day, he turned back from near the mango grove; the following day, he turned back from the northern gate of the Great Shrine. On the fourth day, he approached the elder. The elder thought, 'This monk’s thought must be impure,' and taking the robe, he entered the village with him, questioning him along the way. That night, a certain man, afflicted by the urge to defecate, relieved himself on a cloth and discarded it in a refuse heap. The rag-robed elder, seeing it covered with blue flies, raised his folded hands in reverence. The great elder asked, 'Why, friend, do you pay respects to a refuse heap?' 'Venerable sir, I do not pay homage to the refuse heap; I pay homage to my father, the Ten-Powered One. A far more difficult deed was done by him, venerable sir, when he took from a charnel ground a rag-robe that had been discarded after wrapping the body of the slave woman Puṇṇā, having shaken off creatures the size of a gourd.' The great elder thought, 'The rag-robed monk’s thought is purified.' The rag-robed elder, standing right there, deepened his insight, attained the three fruits, took that cloth, made it into a robe, wore it, went to Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji, and reached the supreme fruit of arahantship.

Cīvaratthāya gacchantassa pana “kattha labhissāmī”ti acintetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva gamanaṃ gamanasantoso nāma. Pariyesantassa pana yena vā tena vā saddhiṃ apariyesitvā lajjiṃ pesalaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā pariyesanaṃ pariyesanasantoso nāma. Evaṃ pariyesantassa āhariyamānaṃ cīvaraṃ dūrato disvā “etaṃ manāpaṃ bhavissati, etaṃ amanāpa”nti evaṃ avitakketvā thūlasukhumādīsu yathāladdheneva santussanaṃ paṭilābhasantoso nāma. Evaṃ laddhaṃ gaṇhantassāpi “ettakaṃ dupaṭṭassa bhavissati, ettakaṃ ekapaṭṭassā”ti attano pahonakamatteneva santussanaṃ mattapaṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma. Cīvaraṃ pariyesantassa pana “asukassa gharadvāre manāpaṃ labhissāmī”ti acintetvā dvārapaṭipāṭiyā caraṇaṃ loluppavivajjanasantoso nāma.

Furthermore, for one going for the sake of a robe, going without thinking, “Where shall I obtain it?” but simply with the meditation subject foremost, is called contentment with going. Again, for one searching, not searching haphazardly with this one or that one, but taking a modest and well-behaved monk and searching, is called contentment with searching. For one searching in this way, seeing a robe being brought from afar, not thinking, “This will be pleasing, this will not be pleasing,” but being content with whatever is obtained, whether coarse or fine, is called contentment with receiving. Even when taking what has been obtained in this way, being content with just what is adequate for oneself, without thinking, “So much will be for the double-layered robe, so much for the single-layered robe,” is called contentment with accepting a measured amount. Again, for one searching for a robe, walking in order from door to door without thinking, “I will obtain something pleasing at the door of so-and-so,” is called contentment with avoiding greed.

Lūkhapaṇītesu yena kenaci yāpetuṃ sakkontassa yathāladdheneva yāpanaṃ yathālābhasantoso nāma. Attano thāmaṃ jānitvā yena yāpetuṃ sakkoti, tena yāpanaṃ yathābalasantoso nāma. Manāpaṃ aññassa [M 2.0280] datvā attanā yena kenaci yāpanaṃ yathāsāruppasantoso nāma.

For one who is able to sustain oneself with anything whatsoever, whether coarse or fine, sustaining oneself with whatever is received is called contentment with whatever is received. Knowing one's own strength and sustaining oneself with what one is able to is called contentment according to one's strength. Giving what is pleasing to another and sustaining oneself with anything whatsoever is called contentment according to suitability.

“Kattha udakaṃ manāpaṃ, kattha amanāpa”nti avicāretvā yena kenaci dhovanūpagena udakena [V 2.0272] dhovanaṃ udakasantoso nāma. Paṇḍumattikagerukapūtipaṇṇarasakiliṭṭhāni pana udakāni vajjetuṃ vaṭṭati. Dhovantassa pana muggarādīhi apaharitvā [P 3.0050] hatthehi madditvā dhovanaṃ dhovanasantoso nāma. Tathā asujjhantaṃ paṇṇāni pakkhipitvā tāpitaudakenāpi dhovituṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ dhovitvā karontassa “idaṃ thūlaṃ, idaṃ sukhuma”nti akopetvā pahonakanīhāreneva karaṇaṃ karaṇasantoso nāma. Timaṇḍalapaticchādanamattasseva karaṇaṃ parimāṇasantoso nāma. Cīvarakaraṇatthāya pana manāpaṃ suttaṃ pariyesissāmīti avicāretvā rathikādīsu vā devaṭṭhāne vā āharitvā pādamūle vā ṭhapitaṃ yaṃkiñcideva suttaṃ gahetvā karaṇaṃ suttasantoso nāma.

‘Where is the water agreeable, where is it disagreeable?’ Without considering this, washing with any kind of water suitable for washing is called contentment with water. However, it is proper to avoid water stained by pale clay, red ochre, and the juice of putrid leaves. For one who is washing, washing by rubbing with the hands without beating with mallets and the like, is called contentment with washing. Similarly, if it is not becoming clean, it is proper to wash it even with heated water after putting in leaves. Having washed it thus, for one who is making it, not destroying one's contentment by thinking, ‘This is coarse, this is fine,’ but making it only in a manner that is sufficient, is called contentment with making. Making it only to the extent of covering the three circles is called contentment with measure. For the purpose of making a robe, without considering, ‘I will search for agreeable thread,’ but taking whatever thread is brought from streets and so forth or from a shrine, or is placed at one's feet, and making it, is called contentment with thread.

Kusibandhanakāle pana aṅgulamatte satta vāre na vijjhitabbaṃ. Evaṃ karontassa hi yo bhikkhu sahāyo na hoti, tassa vattabhedopi natthi. Tivaṅgulamatte pana satta vāre vijjhitabbaṃ. Evaṃ karontassa maggappaṭipannenāpi sahāyena bhavitabbaṃ. Yo na hoti, tassa vattabhedo. Ayaṃ sibbanasantoso nāma. Rajantena pana kāḷakacchakādīni pariyesantena na caritabbaṃ, somavakkalādīsu yaṃ labhati, tena rajitabbaṃ. Alabhantena pana manussehi araññe vākaṃ gahetvā chaḍḍitarajanaṃ vā bhikkhūhi pacitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ vā gahetvā rajitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ rajanasantoso nāma. Nīlakaddamakāḷasāmesu yaṃkiñci gahetvā hatthipiṭṭhe nisinnassa paññāyamānakappakaraṇaṃ kappasantoso nāma.

At the time of sewing the border, one should not pierce seven times in the space of a finger's breadth. Indeed, for one who does so, if he is a monk who has no companion, for him there is no breach of duty. But in the space of three finger's breadths, one should pierce seven times. For one who does so, he should have a companion, even one who has entered upon the path. For one who does not, there is a breach of duty. This is called contentment with sewing. When dyeing, one should not wander about searching for black kacchaka and so forth; one should dye with whatever one obtains from somavakkala bark and so forth. If not obtaining any, one should dye by taking either dye discarded in the forest by people after they have taken bark, or dregs discarded by monks after boiling. This is called contentment with dyeing. Taking any one of the colors blue, mud-colored, black, or dark brown, and making the `kappa` mark so that it is visible even to one sitting on an elephant's back, is called contentment with the marking.

Hirikopīnappaṭicchādanamattavasena paribhuñjanaṃ paribhogasantoso nāma. Dussaṃ pana labhitvā suttaṃ vā sūciṃ vā kārakaṃ vā alabhantena ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, labhantena na vaṭṭati. Katampi sace antevāsikādīnaṃ [P 3.0051] dātukāmo hoti, te ca asannihitā, yāva āgamanā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Āgatamattesu dātabbaṃ. Dātuṃ asakkontena adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Aññasmiṃ cīvare sati paccattharaṇampi adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati. Anadhiṭṭhitameva hi sannidhi [M 2.0281] hoti, adhiṭṭhitaṃ na hotīti mahāsīvatthero āha. Ayaṃ sannidhiparivajjanasantoso nāma. Vissajjentena pana na mukhaṃ oloketvā dātabbaṃ, sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhatvā vissajjetabbanti ayaṃ vissajjanasantoso nāma.

Using it only for the purpose of covering one's private parts out of shame is called contentment with use. Furthermore, having obtained cloth for a robe, for one who does not obtain thread, a needle, or a maker, it is permissible to set it aside; for one who does obtain them, it is not permissible to set it aside. Even if it is made, if one wishes to give it to pupils and so forth, and they are not present, it is permissible to set it aside until their arrival. As soon as they arrive, it must be given. If unable to give, it must be formally designated. If there is another robe, it is permissible to designate it even as a ground-sheet. For indeed, only what is undesignated is accumulation; what is designated is not, so said the Great Elder Sīva. This is called contentment by avoiding accumulation. Furthermore, when giving away, one should not give by looking at the face, but should give away while abiding in the amiable qualities. This is called contentment in giving away.

Cīvarappaṭisaṃyuttāni dhutaṅgāni nāma paṃsukūlikaṅgañceva tecīvarikaṅgañca. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.24-25) veditabbā. Iti cīvarasantosamahāariyavaṃsaṃ pūrayamāno [V 2.0273] bhikkhu imāni dve dhutaṅgāni gopeti. Imāni gopento cīvarasantosamahāariyavaṃsavasena santuṭṭho hotīti.

The ascetic practices connected with robes are the practice of wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūlikaṅga) and the practice of using only three robes (tecīvarikaṅga). Their detailed explanation should be understood from the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk fulfilling the great noble lineage of contentment with robes maintains these two ascetic practices. It should be understood that by maintaining these practices, he is content by means of the great noble lineage of contentment with robes.

Vaṇṇavādīti eko santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ na katheti. Eko na santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Eko neva santuṭṭho hoti, na santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Eko santuṭṭho ceva hoti, santosassa ca vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Taṃ dassetuṃ “itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'a praiser of virtue' (vaṇṇavādī): one person is content but does not speak of the virtue of contentment. Another is not content but speaks of the virtue of contentment. Another is neither content nor speaks of the virtue of contentment. Another is both content and speaks of the virtue of contentment. To indicate that latter person, it was said, '...and a praiser of contentment with any kind of robe.'

Anesananti dūteyyapahinagamanānuyogapabhedaṃ nānappakāraṃ anesanaṃ. Appatirūpanti ayuttaṃ. Aladdhā [P 3.0052] cāti alabhitvā. Yathā ekacco “kathaṃ nu kho cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti puññavantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā kohaññaṃ karonto uttasati paritassati, santuṭṭho bhikkhu evaṃ aladdhā cīvaraṃ na paritassati. Laddhā cāti dhammena samena labhitvā. Agadhitoti vigatalobhagiddho. Amucchitoti adhimattataṇhāya mucchaṃ anāpanno. Anajjhopannoti taṇhāya anotthato apariyonaddho. Ādīnavadassāvīti anesanāpattiyañca gedhitaparibhoge ca ādīnavaṃ passamāno. Nissaraṇapaññoti “yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāyā”ti vuttaṃ nissaraṇameva pajānanto.

“Improper seeking” (anesana) means the various kinds of improper livelihood, distinguished by the practice of acting as a messenger and going on errands. “Improper” (appatirūpa) means unsuitable. “And not having gained” (aladdhā ca) means not having obtained. For example, a certain monk thinks, “How shall I obtain robes?” and, associating with virtuous monks, becomes agitated and anxious while engaging in hypocrisy. But a contented monk does not fret even when he has not gained robes. “Having gained” (laddhā ca) means having obtained them righteously and justly. “Not greedy” (agadhitoti) means free from greed and avarice. “Not infatuated” (amucchito) means not fallen into infatuation through excessive craving. “Not overcome” (anajjhopanno) means not overwhelmed or completely enveloped by craving. “Seeing the danger” (ādīnavadassāvī) means seeing the peril both in the offense of improper seeking and in the use with greed. “Understanding the escape” (nissaraṇapañño) means knowing only the escape that has been taught, as in: “just for warding off the cold.”

Itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyāti yena kenaci cīvarena santuṭṭhiyā. Nevattānukkaṃsetīti “ahaṃ paṃsukūliko, mayā upasampadamāḷeyeva paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ gahitaṃ, ko mayā sadiso atthī”ti attukkaṃsanaṃ na karoti. No paraṃ vambhetīti “ime panaññe bhikkhū na paṃsukūlikā”ti vā, “paṃsukūlikaṅgamattampi etesaṃ natthī”ti vā evaṃ paraṃ na vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkhoti yo tasmiṃ cīvarasantose vaṇṇavādādīsu vā dakkho cheko [M 2.0282] byatto. Analasoti sātaccakiriyāya ālasiyavirahito. Sampajāno paṭissatoti sampajānapaññāya ceva satiyā ca yutto. Ariyavaṃse ṭhitoti ariyavaṃse patiṭṭhito.

“Contentment with any kind of robe” (itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā) means being satisfied with whatever robe one has. “He does not exalt himself” (nevattānukkaṃseti) means he does not boast, saying, “I am a rag-robe wearer; I undertook the rag-robe practice right at my ordination—who is like me?” “Nor does he disparage others” (no paraṃ vambheti) means he does not belittle others by saying, “These other monks are not rag-robe wearers,” or “They do not even have the rag-robe practice.” “One who is skilled in this” (yo hi tattha dakkho) means one who is skilled (dakkho), clever (cheko), and expert (byatto) in that contentment with robes or in praising its virtues, etc. “Not lazy” (analaso) means free from laziness in continuous practice. “Mindful with clear comprehension” (sampajāno paṭissato) means endowed with the wisdom of clear comprehension and with mindfulness. “Established in the noble lineage” (ariyavaṃse ṭhito) means established in the noble lineage.

Itarītarena [P 3.0053] piṇḍapātenāti yena kenaci piṇḍapātena. Etthāpi piṇḍapāto jānitabbo, piṇḍapātakkhettaṃ jānitabbaṃ, piṇḍapātasantoso jānitabbo, piṇḍapātappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ jānitabbaṃ[V 2.0274]. Tattha piṇḍapātoti odano kummāso sattu maccho maṃsaṃ khīraṃ dadhi sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitaṃ yāgu khādanīyaṃ sāyanīyaṃ lehanīyanti soḷasa piṇḍapātā.

By 'with any kind of almsfood' is meant with whatever almsfood. Herein also, almsfood should be known, the field of almsfood should be known, contentment with almsfood should be known, and the ascetic practice connected with almsfood should be known. Therein, by 'almsfood' is meant: cooked rice, barley-meal, roasted grain flour, fish, meat, milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, gruel, hard food, food to be savored, and food to be licked. These sixteen kinds of almsfood should be known.

Piṇḍapātakkhettanti saṅghabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ uposathikaṃ pāṭipadikabhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ gamikabhattaṃ gilānabhattaṃ gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ kuṭibhattaṃ vārabhattaṃ vihārabhattanti pannarasa piṇḍapātakkhettāni.

By 'the field of almsfood' is meant: food offered to the Sangha, food offered by designation, food offered by invitation, food offered by ticket, food offered fortnightly, food offered on the Uposatha day, food offered on the first day of the fortnight, food for visiting monks, food for traveling monks, food for sick monks, food for attendants of the sick, food offered at the first house, food offered for a hut, food offered by turn, and food offered for a monastery. These are the fifteen fields of almsfood.

Piṇḍapātasantosoti piṇḍapāte vitakkasantoso gamanasantoso pariyesanasantoso paṭilābhasantoso paṭiggahaṇasantoso mattapaṭiggahaṇasantoso loluppavivajjanasantoso yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantoso upakārasantoso parimāṇasantoso paribhogasantoso sannidhiparivajjanasantoso vissajjanasantosoti pannarasa santosā.

By 'contentment with almsfood' is meant, in regard to almsfood: contentment in thinking, contentment in going, contentment in seeking, contentment in obtaining, contentment in receiving, contentment in receiving a measured amount, contentment in avoiding greed, contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, contentment according to what is suitable, contentment with the support, contentment with the measure, contentment in consuming, contentment in avoiding storing, and contentment in relinquishing. These are the fifteen kinds of contentment.

Tattha sādako bhikkhu mukhaṃ dhovitvā vitakketi. Piṇḍapātikena pana gaṇena saddhiṃ caratā sāyaṃ therūpaṭṭhānakāle “sve kattha piṇḍāya carissāmāti? Asukagāme, bhante”ti ettakaṃ cintetvā tato paṭṭhāya na vitakketabbaṃ. Ekacārikena vitakkamāḷake ṭhatvā vitakketabbaṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya vitakkento ariyavaṃsā cuto hoti paribāhiro. Ayaṃ [P 3.0054] vitakkasantoso nāma.

Therein, a monk who takes pleasure in almsfood washes his mouth and reflects. But for an alms-goer wandering together with a group, in the evening at the time of attending on an elder, when asked by the elder, 'Tomorrow, where shall we wander for alms?' he should think only this much: 'Venerable sir, in such-and-such village,' and from then on, he should not reflect. A monk who wanders alone should stand on a terrace for reflection and reflect. A monk who reflects from that point on falls away from the noble lineage and becomes an outsider. This is called contentment in thinking.

Piṇḍāya pavisantena “kuhiṃ labhissāmī”ti acintetvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena gantabbaṃ. Ayaṃ gamanasantoso nāma. Pariyesantena yaṃ vā taṃ vā aggahetvā lajjiṃ pesalameva gahetvā pariyesitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pariyesanasantoso nāma. Dūratova āhariyamānaṃ disvā “etaṃ manāpaṃ[M 2.0283], etaṃ amanāpa”nti cittaṃ na uppādetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paṭilābhasantoso nāma. “Imaṃ manāpaṃ gaṇhissāmi, imaṃ amanāpaṃ na gaṇhissāmī”ti acintetvā yaṃkiñci yāpanamattaṃ gahetabbameva. Ayaṃ paṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma.

When entering for almsfood, one should go with the meditation subject as foremost, without thinking, “Where shall I obtain it?” This is called contentment in going. When seeking, one should not take just any monk, but should seek taking only a monk who is conscientious and virtuous. This is called contentment in seeking. Seeing almsfood being brought from afar, one should not give rise to the thought, “This is agreeable, this is disagreeable.” This is called contentment in obtaining. Without thinking, “I will take this agreeable one; I will not take this disagreeable one,” one should take whatever is just enough for sustenance. This is called contentment in receiving.

Ettha pana deyyadhammo bahu, dāyako appaṃ dātukāmo, appaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammopi bahu, dāyakopi bahuṃ dātukāmo, pamāṇeneva gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammo na bahu, dāyakopi appaṃ dātukāmo, appaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammo na bahu, dāyako pana bahuṃ dātukāmo, pamāṇena gahetabbaṃ[V 2.0275]. Paṭiggahaṇasmiñhi mattaṃ ajānanto manussānaṃ pasādaṃ makkheti, saddhādeyyaṃ vinipāteti, sāsanaṃ na karoti, vijātamātuyāpi cittaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti. Iti mattaṃ jānitvāva paṭiggahetabbanti ayaṃ mattapaṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma. Aḍḍhakulāniyeva agantvā dvārapaṭipāṭiyā gantabbaṃ. Ayaṃ loluppavivajjanasantoso nāma. Yathālābhasantosādayo cīvare vuttanayā eva.

Furthermore, in this matter: if the item to be given is abundant, but the donor wishes to give little, a little should be taken. If the item to be given is also abundant, and the donor also wishes to give much, it should be taken only according to measure. If the item to be given is not abundant, and the donor also wishes to give little, a little should be taken. If the item to be given is not abundant, but the donor wishes to give much, it should be taken according to measure. For one who does not know the measure in receiving defiles the confidence of people, ruins the gift of faith, does not practice the teaching, and is unable to capture the heart even of his own mother. Thus, having known the measure, one should receive. This is called contentment with receiving in measure. Without going only to wealthy families, one should go in the order of doors. This is called contentment in avoiding greed. Contentment with whatever is obtained and the others are just as was explained in the section on robes.

Piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā “samaṇadhammaṃ anupālessāmī”ti evaṃ upakāraṃ ñatvā paribhuñjanaṃ upakārasantoso nāma. Pattaṃ pūretvā ānītaṃ na paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Anupasampanne sati tena gāhāpetabbaṃ, asati harāpetvā paṭiggahaṇamattaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ parimāṇasantoso [P 3.0055] nāma. “Jighacchāya paṭivinodanaṃ idamettha nissaraṇa”nti evaṃ paribhuñjanaṃ paribhogasantoso nāma. Nidahitvā na paribhuñjitabbanti ayaṃ sannidhiparivajjanasantoso nāma. Mukhaṃ anoloketvā sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhitena vissajjetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vissajjanasantoso nāma.

Having consumed the almsfood, reflecting, “I will maintain the practice of a recluse,” thus, consuming with the knowledge of its support is called contentment with support. Almsfood brought having filled the bowl should not be accepted. If an unordained person is present, one should have him take it; if not, having had it carried, one should accept only the amount sufficient for a formal acceptance. This is called contentment with measure. Reflecting, 'The dispelling of hunger is the escape herein,' thus consuming is called contentment with use. One should not consume after having stored it. This is called contentment with avoiding accumulation. Without looking at the face, one should relinquish it while established in the amiable qualities. This is called contentment with relinquishing.

Piṇḍapātappaṭisaṃyuttāni pana pañca dhutaṅgāni piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ ekāsanikaṅgaṃ pattapiṇḍikaṅgaṃ khalupacchābhattikaṅganti. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.26-30) vuttā. Iti piṇḍapātasantosamahāariyavaṃsaṃ pūrayamāno bhikkhu imāni pañca dhutaṅgāni gopeti, imāni gopento piṇḍapātasantosamahāariyavaṃsena santuṭṭho hoti. Vaṇṇavādītiādīni vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices connected with almsfood: the alms-gatherer's practice, the practice of going for alms from house to house without omission, the one-sessioner's practice, the bowl-eater's practice, and the practice of not eating after the meal has been refused. Their detailed explanation has been given in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk fulfilling the great noble lineage of contentment with almsfood guards these five ascetic practices. Guarding these, he is content by means of the great noble lineage of contentment with almsfood. The phrases beginning with 'a speaker of praise' should be understood in the way already stated.

Senāsanenāti idha senāsanaṃ jānitabbaṃ, senāsanakkhettaṃ jānitabbaṃ, senāsanasantoso jānitabbo, senāsanappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ [M 2.0284] jānitabbaṃ. Tattha senāsananti mañco pīṭhaṃ bhisi bimbohanaṃ vihāro aḍḍhayogo pāsādo hammiyaṃ guhā leṇaṃ aṭṭo māḷo veḷugumbo rukkhamūlaṃ yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamantīti imāni pannarasa senāsanāni.

Regarding 'with lodging' (senāsanena): here, lodging should be understood, the field of lodging should be understood, contentment with lodging should be understood, and the ascetic practice connected with lodging should be understood. Therein, 'lodging' refers to these fifteen types: a bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery, a half-gabled building, a storied building, a flat-roofed building, a cave, a rock-shelter, a watch-tower, a pavilion, a bamboo grove, the foot of a tree, or wherever monks may retreat.

Senāsanakkhettanti saṅghato vā gaṇato vā ñātito vā mittato vā attano vā dhanena paṃsukūlaṃ vāti cha khettāni.

'The field of lodging' means these six fields: from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, with one's own wealth, or from discarded materials.

Senāsanasantosoti senāsane vitakkasantosādayo pannarasa santosā. Te piṇḍapāte vuttanayeneva [V 2.0276] veditabbā. Senāsanappaṭisaṃyuttāni pana pañca dhutaṅgāni āraññikaṅgaṃ rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ sosānikaṅgaṃ yathāsanthatikaṅganti. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.31-35) vuttā. Iti [P 3.0056] senāsanasantosamahāariyavaṃsaṃ pūrayamāno bhikkhu imāni pañca dhutaṅgāni gopeti. Imāni gopento senāsanasantosamahāariyavaṃsena santuṭṭho hoti.

Regarding contentment with lodging: there are fifteen types of contentment, such as contentment with thoughts concerning lodging. These should be understood in the same way as explained for almsfood. Now, the five ascetic practices connected with lodging are: the forest-dweller's practice, the tree-root-dweller's practice, the open-air-dweller's practice, the charnel-ground-dweller's practice, and the practice of accepting whatever lodging is assigned. Their detailed explanation has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, a monk fulfilling the great tradition of the noble ones regarding contentment with lodging guards these five ascetic practices. By guarding these, he is content through the great tradition of the noble ones regarding contentment with lodging.

Gilānapaccayo pana piṇḍapāteyeva paviṭṭho. Tattha yathālābhayathābalayathāsāruppasantoseneva santussitabbaṃ. Nesajjikaṅgaṃ bhāvanārāmaariyavaṃsaṃ bhajati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Now, the requisite for the sick is included under almsfood itself. In that regard, one should be content only with what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to suitability. The sitter's practice pertains to the great tradition of the noble ones regarding delight in development. And this has been said:

“Pañca senāsane vuttā, pañca āhāranissitā;

Eko vīriyasaṃyutto, dve ca cīvaranissitā”ti.

Five are stated in regard to lodging, five are dependent on food; one is connected with energy, and two are dependent on robes.

Iti bhagavā pathaviṃ pattharamāno viya sāgarakucchiṃ pūrayamāno viya ākāsaṃ vitthārayamāno viya ca paṭhamaṃ cīvarasantosaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ kathetvā candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya sūriyaṃ ullaṅghento viya ca dutiyaṃ piṇḍapātasantosaṃ kathetvā sineruṃ ukkhipanto viya tatiyaṃ senāsanasantosaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ kathetvā idāni sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ catutthaṃ bhāvanārāmaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ kathetuṃ puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhāvanārāmo hotīti desanaṃ ārabhi.

Thus, the Blessed One, as if spreading out the earth, filling the belly of the ocean, or expanding the sky, first taught the great tradition of the noble ones regarding contentment with robes. Then, as if causing the moon to rise or the sun to ascend, he taught the second great tradition of the noble ones, contentment with almsfood. Next, as if lifting up Mount Sineru, he taught the third great tradition of the noble ones, contentment with lodging. Now, to teach the fourth great tradition of the noble ones, delight in development, adorned with a thousand methods, he began the discourse, saying: 'Furthermore, monks, a monk delights in development...'

Tattha āramaṇaṃ ārāmo, abhiratīti attho. Bhāvanāya ārāmo assāti bhāvanārāmo. Bhāvanāya ratoti bhāvanārato. Pañcavidhe pahāne ārāmo assāti pahānārāmo. Apica bhāvento [M 2.0285] ramatīti bhāvanārāmo. Pajahanto ramatīti pahānārāmoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ayañhi cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvento ramati, ratiṃ vindatīti attho. Tathā cattāro sammappadhāne. Cattāro iddhipāde, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅge, satta anupassanā, aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā, sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhamme, aṭṭhatiṃsa [P 3.0057] ārammaṇavibhattiyo bhāvento ramati, ratiṃ vindati. Kāmacchandādayo pana kilese pajahanto ramati, ratiṃ vindati.

Herein, the meaning is: delighting (āramaṇaṃ) is delight (ārāmo), which means finding pleasure (abhirati). 'Bhāvanārāma' is one for whom there is delight (ārāmo) in development (bhāvanā). 'Bhāvanārato' is one who delights (rato) in development (bhāvanā). 'Pahānārāma' is one for whom there is delight (ārāmo) in the fivefold abandonment (pahāna). Furthermore, 'bhāvanārāma' means one who delights (ramati) while developing (bhāvento), and 'pahānārāma' means one who delights (ramati) while abandoning (pajahanto); thus the meaning should be understood herein. Indeed, this monk delights while developing the four foundations of mindfulness; he finds delight—this is the meaning. Similarly, while developing the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven contemplations, the eighteen great insights, the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment, and the thirty-eight classifications of objects, he delights and finds delight. However, while abandoning defilements such as sensual desire, he delights and finds delight.

Imesu pana catūsu ariyavaṃsesu purimehi tīhi terasannaṃ dhutaṅgānaṃ catupaccayasantosassa ca vasena sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kathitaṃ hoti, bhāvanārāmena avasesaṃ piṭakadvayaṃ. Imaṃ pana bhāvanārāmaṃ [V 2.0277] ariyavaṃsaṃ kathentena bhikkhunā paṭisambhidāmagge nekkhammapāḷiyā kathetabbo, dīghanikāye dasuttarasuttantapariyāyena kathetabbo, majjhimanikāye satipaṭṭhānasuttantapariyāyena kathetabbo, abhidhamme niddesapariyāyena kathetabbo.

Furthermore, among these four great traditions of the noble ones, by the first three, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is spoken of by way of the thirteen ascetic practices and contentment with the four requisites. By the great tradition of the noble ones regarding delight in development, the remaining two Piṭakas are spoken of. Furthermore, a monk explaining this great tradition of the noble ones regarding delight in development should explain it in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by the Pāḷi on renunciation; in the Dīghanikāya by way of the Dasuttara Sutta discourse; in the Majjhimanikāya by way of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta discourse; and in the Abhidhamma by way of the Niddesa discourse.

Tattha paṭisambhidāmagge nekkhammapāḷiyāti –

Therein, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, by the Pāḷi on renunciation:

“Nekkhammaṃ bhāvento ramati, kāmacchandaṃ pajahanto ramati. Abyāpādaṃ, byāpādaṃ… ālokasaññaṃ… thinamiddhaṃ… avikkhepaṃ, uddhaccaṃ… dhammavavatthānaṃ… vicikicchaṃ… ñāṇaṃ… avijjaṃ… pāmojjaṃ… aratiṃ… paṭhamajjhānaṃ, pañca nīvaraṇe… dutiyajjhānaṃ… vitakkavicāre… tatiyajjhānaṃ… pītiṃ… catutthajjhānaṃ… sukhadukkhe… ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiṃ bhāvento ramati, rūpasaññaṃ paṭighasaññaṃ nānattasaññaṃ pajahanto ramati. Viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattiṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ bhāvento ramati, ākiñcaññāyatanasaññaṃ pajahanto ramati.

“Developing renunciation, one delights; abandoning sensual desire, one delights. Developing non-ill will, one delights; abandoning ill will… developing the perception of light… abandoning sloth and torpor… developing non-distraction, one delights; abandoning restlessness… developing the discrimination of phenomena… abandoning doubt… developing knowledge… abandoning ignorance… developing gladness… abandoning discontent… developing the first jhāna, one delights; abandoning the five hindrances… developing the second jhāna… abandoning thought and examination… developing the third jhāna… abandoning rapture… developing the fourth jhāna… abandoning pleasure and pain… developing the attainment of the base of infinite space, one delights; abandoning the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity, one delights. Developing the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness… and so on… developing the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one delights; abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness, one delights.

“Aniccānupassanaṃ bhāvento ramati, niccasaññaṃ pajahanto ramati. Dukkhānupassanaṃ… sukhasaññaṃ… anattānupassanaṃ… attasaññaṃ… nibbidānupassanaṃ… nandiṃ… virāgānupassanaṃ… rāgaṃ… nirodhānupassanaṃ… samudayaṃ… paṭinissaggānupassanaṃ… ādānaṃ… khayānupassanaṃ [P 3.0058]… ghanasaññaṃ… vayānupassanaṃ… āyūhanaṃ… vipariṇāmānupassanaṃ… dhuvasaññaṃ… animittānupassanaṃ [M 2.0286]… nimittaṃ… appaṇihitānupassanaṃ… paṇidhiṃ… suññatānupassanaṃ… abhinivesaṃ… adhipaññādhammavipassanaṃ… sārādānābhinivesaṃ… yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ… sammohābhinivesaṃ… ādīnavānupassanaṃ… ālayābhinivesaṃ… paṭisaṅkhānupassanaṃ… appaṭisaṅkhaṃ… vivaṭṭānupassanaṃ… saṃyogābhinivesaṃ… sotāpattimaggaṃ… diṭṭhekaṭṭhe kilese… sakadāgāmimaggaṃ… oḷārike kilese… anāgāmimaggaṃ… anusahagate kilese… arahattamaggaṃ bhāvento ramati, sabbakilese pajahanto ramatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.41,95).

“Developing the contemplation of impermanence, one delights; abandoning the perception of permanence, one delights. Developing the contemplation of suffering… abandoning the perception of pleasure… developing the contemplation of non-self… abandoning the perception of self… developing the contemplation of disenchantment… abandoning delight… developing the contemplation of dispassion… abandoning lust… developing the contemplation of cessation… abandoning arising… developing the contemplation of relinquishment… abandoning grasping… developing the contemplation of destruction… abandoning the perception of compactness… developing the contemplation of vanishing… abandoning accumulation… developing the contemplation of change… abandoning the perception of stability… developing the contemplation of the signless… abandoning the sign… developing the contemplation of the desireless… abandoning desire… developing the contemplation of emptiness… abandoning adherence… developing the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena… abandoning adherence to the appropriation of essence… developing the knowledge and vision of things as they are… abandoning adherence to delusion… developing the contemplation of danger… abandoning adherence to attachment… developing the contemplation of reflection… abandoning non-reflection… developing the contemplation of turning away… abandoning adherence to entanglement… developing the path of stream-entry… abandoning the defilements that have a basis in wrong view… developing the path of once-returning… abandoning the coarse defilements… developing the path of non-returning… abandoning the subtle defilements… developing the path of Arahantship, one delights; abandoning all defilements, one delights.”

Evaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge nekkhammapāḷiyā kathetabbo.

Thus it should be explained in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by the Pāḷi on renunciation.

Dīghanikāye [V 2.0278] dasuttarasuttantapariyāyenāti –

In the Dīgha Nikāya, by way of the Dasuttara Suttanta:

“Ekaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento ramati, ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahanto ramati…pe… dasa dhamme bhāvento ramati, dasa dhamme pajahanto ramati. Katamaṃ ekaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento ramati? Kāyagatāsatiṃ sātasahagataṃ, imaṃ ekaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento ramati. Katamaṃ ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahanto ramati? Asmimānaṃ, imaṃ ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahanto ramati. Katame dve dhamme…pe… katame dasa dhamme bhāvento ramati? Dasa kasiṇāyatanāni, ime dasa dhamme bhāvento ramati. Katame dasa dhamme pajahanto ramati? Dasa micchatte, ime dasa dhamme pajahanto ramati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhāvanārāmo hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.351-360).

A bhikkhu delights in developing one dhamma; he delights in abandoning one dhamma... he delights in developing ten dhammas; he delights in abandoning ten dhammas. In developing what one dhamma does he delight? Mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasant feeling; in developing this one dhamma, he delights. In abandoning what one dhamma does he delight? The conceit ‘I am’; in abandoning this one dhamma, he delights. What two dhammas... in developing what ten dhammas does he delight? The ten kasiṇa bases; in developing these ten dhammas, he delights. In abandoning what ten dhammas does he delight? The ten wrongnesses; in abandoning these ten dhammas, he delights. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who delights in development.

Evaṃ dīghanikāye dasuttarasuttantapariyāyena kathetabbo.

Thus it should be explained in the Dīgha Nikāya by way of the Dasuttara Sutta discourse.

Majjhimanikāye satipaṭṭhānasuttantapariyāyenāti –

In the Majjhima Nikāya, by way of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta discourse:

“Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo…pe… yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya. Anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci [P 3.0059] loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhāvanārāmo hoti bhāvanārato. Pahānārāmo hoti pahānarato. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gacchanto vā gacchāmīti pajānāti…pe… puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ…pe… pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni. So imameva kāyaṃ [M 2.0287] upasaṃharati ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhāvanārāmo hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.106 ādayo).

“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path... for the sake of mere knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells unattached, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way, too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who delights in development, is devoted to development. He is one who delights in abandoning, is devoted to abandoning. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when walking, knows: ‘I am walking.’... Furthermore, bhikkhus, just as one might see a body discarded in a charnel ground... putrid and reduced to powder, he applies that to this very body thus: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it has not gone beyond that state.’ Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... In this way, too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who delights in development.”

Evaṃ majjhimanikāye satipaṭṭhānasuttantapariyāyena kathetabbo.

Thus it should be explained in the Majjhima Nikāya by way of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta discourse.

Abhidhamme niddesapariyāyenāti sabbepi saṅkhate “aniccato dukkhato rogato gaṇḍato [V 2.0279] …pe… saṃkilesikadhammato passanto ramati, evaṃ kho bhikkhu bhāvanārāmo hotī”ti (mahāni. 13; cūḷani. upasīvamāṇavapucchāniddeso 39, nandamāṇavapucchāniddeso 51). Evaṃ niddesapariyāyena kathetabbo.

In the Abhidhamma, by way of exposition, it is said: 'One delights while seeing all conditioned things as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil... as subject to defilement. In this way, a bhikkhu is one who delights in development.' Thus, it should be explained by way of exposition.

Nevattānukkaṃsetīti “ajja me saṭṭhi vā sattati vā vassāni aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti vipassanāya kammaṃ karontassa ko mayā sadiso atthī”ti evaṃ attukkaṃsanaṃ na karoti. No paraṃ vambhetīti “aniccaṃ dukkhanti vipassanāmattakampi natthi, kiṃ ime vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānā carantī”ti evaṃ paravambhanaṃ na karoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

He does not praise himself: 'Today, sixty or seventy years have passed for me practicing the work of insight into impermanence, suffering, and non-self—who is there equal to me?' Thus, he does not engage in self-praise. Nor does he disparage others: 'For these bhikkhus, there is not even a mere measure of insight into impermanence and suffering; why do they wander about, having abandoned their meditation subject?' Thus, he does not engage in disparaging others. The rest is as has been explained.

Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro ariyavaṃsāti, bhikkhave, ime cattāro ariyavaṃsā ariyatantiyo ariyapaveṇiyo ariyañjasā ariyavaṭumānīti suttantaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā idāni mahāariyavaṃsaparipūrakassa [P 3.0060] bhikkhuno vasanadisā dassento imehi ca pana, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sveva aratiṃ sahatīti soyeva aratiṃ anabhiratiṃ ukkaṇṭhitaṃ sahati abhibhavati. Na taṃ arati sahatīti taṃ pana bhikkhuṃ yā esā pantesu senāsanesu adhikusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya arati nāma hoti, sā sahituṃ adhibhavituṃ na sakkoti. Aratiratisahoti aratiñca pañcakāmaguṇaratiñca sahati, adhibhavituṃ sakkoti.

‘These, O bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages.’ O bhikkhus, these four are the noble lineages, the noble traditions, the noble heritages, the noble highways, the noble paths. Having concluded the discourse, now, showing the direction of life for a bhikkhu who fulfills the great noble lineage, he spoke beginning with ‘And furthermore, O bhikkhus.’ Therein, ‘he himself endures discontent’ means that he himself endures and overcomes discontent, dissatisfaction, and weariness. ‘Discontent does not overcome him’ means that the discontent which arises in remote lodgings concerning the development of exceedingly skillful qualities is not able to endure or overcome that bhikkhu. ‘He endures discontent and delight’ means he is able to endure and overcome both discontent and the delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Idāni gāthāhi kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto nāratītiādimāha. Tattha dhīranti vīriyavantaṃ. Nārati dhīraṃ sahatīti idaṃ purimasseva kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā sā dhīraṃ na sahati nappahoti dhīraṃ sahituṃ adhibhavituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā nārati [M 2.0288] sahati dhīraṃ. Dhīro hi aratissahoti aratisahattā hi so dhīro nāma, tasmā aratiṃ sahatīti attho. Sabbakammavihāyīnanti sabbaṃ tebhūmakakammaṃ cajitvā paricchinnaṃ parivaṭumaṃ katvā ṭhitaṃ. Panuṇṇaṃ ko nivārayeti kilese panuditvā ṭhitaṃ ko nāma rāgo vā doso vā nivāreyya. Nekkhaṃ [P 3.0061] jambonadasseva, ko taṃ ninditumarahatīti jambonadasaṅkhātassa jātirattasuvaṇṇassa nikkhasadisaṃ garahitabbadosavimuttaṃ ko taṃ puggalaṃ nindituṃ arahati. Brahmunāpi pasaṃsitoti mahābrahmunāpi esa puggalo pasaṃsitoyevāti. Desanāpariyosāne cattālīsa bhikkhusahassāni arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

Now, taking up the main point with verses, he says, ‘Discontent does not overcome the resolute,’ etc. Herein, ‘the resolute’ means one endowed with energy. ‘Discontent does not overcome the resolute’ is a statement of reason for the preceding phrase. Because discontent cannot overcome or overpower the resolute, therefore, ‘discontent does not overcome the resolute.’ For the resolute overcomes discontent—because he overcomes discontent, he is called resolute. Thus, the meaning is ‘he overcomes discontent.’ ‘Having abandoned all kamma’ means having relinquished all kamma pertaining to the three realms, remaining established after clearly defining and limiting them. ‘Who can restrain one who has dispelled defilements?’ means: what lust or hatred could restrain one who stands having dispelled the defilements? ‘Like a coin of refined gold, who is fit to blame him?’ means: who is worthy to blame that person, who is free from blameworthy faults and like a ‘nikkha’ of jambonada gold? ‘Praised even by Brahmā’ means this person is praised even by the great Brahmā. At the conclusion of the teaching, forty thousand bhikkhus were established in arahantship.

9. Dhammapadasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Exposition of the Dhammapada Sutta

29. Navame [V 2.0280] dhammapadānīti dhammakoṭṭhāsā. Anabhijjhātiādīsu abhijjhāpaṭikkhepena anabhijjhā, byāpādapaṭikkhepena abyāpādo, micchāsatipaṭikkhepena sammāsati, micchāsamādhipaṭikkhepena sammāsamādhi veditabbo.

29. In the ninth sutta, ‘dhammapadāni’ means ‘constituents of Dhamma’. In the phrases beginning with ‘non-covetousness’, it should be understood thus: through the rejection of covetousness, ‘non-covetousness’ is to be understood; through the rejection of ill-will, ‘non-ill-will’ is to be understood; through the rejection of wrong mindfulness, ‘right mindfulness’ is to be understood; and through the rejection of wrong concentration, ‘right concentration’ is to be understood.

Anabhijjhālūti nittaṇho hutvā. Abyāpannena cetasāti sabbakālaṃ pakatibhāvaṃ avijahantena cittena. Sato ekaggacittassāti satiyā samannāgato ārammaṇe ekaggacitto assa. Ajjhattaṃ susamāhitoti niyakajjhatte suṭṭhu ṭhapitacitto imasmiṃ suttepi gāthāyapi vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

‘Free from covetousness’ means having become without craving. ‘With a mind free from ill will’ means with a mind not abandoning its natural state at any time. ‘Mindful and with unified mind’ means one endowed with mindfulness and having a mind one-pointed on the object. ‘Internally well-composed’ means having the mind well-established in one's own internal continuum. In this sutta and also in the verse, the round of existence and that which is free from the round are taught.

10. Paribbājakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Discourse on Wanderers

30. Dasame abhiññātāti ñātā pākaṭā. Annabhārotiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhito. Sā hi idha paṭisallānanti adhippetā. Paccakkhāyāti paṭikkhipitvā. Abhijjhālunti sataṇhaṃ. Kāmesu [P 3.0062] tibbasārāganti vatthukāmesu bahalarāgaṃ. Tamahaṃ tattha evaṃ vadeyyanti taṃ ahaṃ tasmiṃ kāraṇe evaṃ vadeyyaṃ. Paṭikkositabbaṃ maññeyyāti paṭikkositabbāni paṭibāhitabbani vā maññeyya. Sahadhammikāti sakāraṇā. Vādānupātāti dhammikavāde ghaṭṭayamānā adhammikavādānupātā, vādappavattiyoti attho. Gārayhā ṭhānāti garahitabbayuttakā paccayā. Āgacchantīti upagacchanti.

30. In the tenth sutta. 'Well-known' means known and evident. 'Annabhāra' and so on are their names. 'Having emerged from seclusion' means having emerged from the attainment of fruition. For that indeed is intended here by 'seclusion'. 'Having rejected' means having refused. 'Greedy' means with craving. 'Intensely lustful for sensual pleasures' means strong lust for sensual objects. 'I would say thus to him there' means I would say thus to him in that matter. 'One might think it is to be rebuked' means one might think they are to be rebuked or rejected. 'With good reason' means with a valid reason. 'The arising of disputes' means: when clashing in a righteous dispute, unrighteous disputes arise; the meaning is the occurrence of disputes. 'Blameworthy grounds' means conditions fit to be blamed. 'They come' means they approach.

Ukkalāti [M 2.0289] ukkalajanapadavāsino. Vassabhaññāti vasso ca bhañño cāti dve janā. Ahetukavādāti “natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tievamādivādino. Akiriyavādāti “karoto na karīyati pāpa”nti evaṃ kiriyapaṭikkhepavādino. Natthikavādāti “natthi dinna”ntiādivādino. Te imesu tīsupi dassanesu okkantaniyāmā ahesuṃ. Kathaṃ pana tesu niyāmo hotīti? Yo hi evarūpaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu nisinno sajjhāyati vīmaṃsati, tassa “natthi hetu natthi paccayo karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ…pe… natthi dinnaṃ…pe… kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”ti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe [V 2.0281] micchāsati santiṭṭhati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, javanāni javanti. Paṭhamajavane satekiccho hoti, tathā dutiyādīsu, sattame buddhānampi atekiccho anivatti ariṭṭhakaṇṭakasadiso hoti[P 3.0063]. Tattha koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamati, koci dve, koci tīṇipi. Niyatamicchādiṭṭhikova hoti, patto saggamaggāvaraṇañceva mokkhamaggāvaraṇañca, abhabbo tassa attabhāvassa anantaraṃ saggampi gantuṃ, pageva mokkhaṃ. Vaṭṭakhāṇuko nāmesa satto pathavigopako, yebhuyyena evarūpassa bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ natthi. Vassabhaññāpi edisā ahesuṃ. Nindābyārosanaupārambhabhayāti attano nindabhayena ghaṭṭanabhayena upavādabhayena cāti attho. Abhijjhāvinaye sikkhanti abhijjhāvinayo vuccati arahattaṃ, arahatte sikkhamāno appamatto nāma vuccatīti suttante vaṭṭaviṭṭaṃ kathetvā gāthāya phalasamāpatti kathitāti.

'Ukkalā' means inhabitants of the Ukkala country. 'Vassabhiññā' refers to two people: Vassa and Bhiñña. 'Ahetukavādā' means those who hold views such as, 'There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings.' 'Akiriyavādā' means those who reject action, saying, 'For one who acts, no evil is done.' 'Natthikavādā' means those who hold views such as, 'There is no [result of what is] given.' They were fixed in these three views. But how does one become fixed in them? For one who, having grasped such a belief, sits reflecting and examining it day and night, wrong mindfulness becomes established on such an object as, 'There is no cause, no condition; for one who acts, no evil is done... there is no [result of what is] given... upon the breakup of the body, one is annihilated.' The mind becomes one-pointed, and the impulsions proceed. In the first impulsion, one is remediable, and likewise in the second and so on; but in the seventh, one becomes irremediable even by the Buddhas, irreversible, like a fatal thorn. Here, some enter into one view, some into two, some into all three. One becomes fixed in wrong view, having reached an obstruction to the path to heaven and an obstruction to the path to liberation. One is incapable of going even to heaven immediately after that existence, let alone to liberation. Such a being is called a 'stump in the round of existence' (vaṭṭakhāṇuko), a guardian of the earth. For the most part, for such a one, there is no rising up from the state of existence. Vassa and Bhiñña were also of such a nature [i.e., irremediable]. 'Out of fear of blame, conflict, and reproach' means: through fear of blame for oneself, through fear of conflict, and through fear of reproach. Regarding 'they train in the discipline of non-covetousness': the discipline of non-covetousness is called Arahantship. One training in Arahantship is called 'diligent'. Thus, in the sutta, having taught about the round of existence and that which is free from the round, the attainment of fruition is taught in the verse.

Uruvelavaggo tatiyo.

The Uruvela Chapter is the third.

4. Cakkavaggo

4. The Wheel Chapter

1. Cakkasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Wheel Discourse

31. Catutthassa [V 2.0282] paṭhame cakkānīti sampattiyo. Catucakkaṃ vattatīti cattāri sampatticakkāni vattanti ghaṭiyantiyevāti attho. Patirūpadesavāsoti yattha catasso parisā sandissanti, evarūpe anucchavike dese vāso. Sappurisāvassayoti buddhādīnaṃ sappurisānaṃ avassayanaṃ sevanaṃ [M 2.0290] bhajanaṃ, na rājānaṃ. Attasammāpaṇidhīti attano sammā ṭhapanaṃ, sace pubbe assaddhādīhi [P 3.0064] samannāgato hoti, tāni pahāya saddhādīsu patiṭṭhāpanaṃ. Pubbe ca katapuññatāti pubbe upacitakusalatā. Idameva cettha pamāṇaṃ. Yena hi ñāṇasampayuttacittena kusalakammaṃ kataṃ hoti, tadeva kusalaṃ taṃ purisaṃ patirūpadese upaneti, sappurise bhajāpeti, so eva ca puggalo attānaṃ sammā ṭhapeti. Puññakatoti katapuñño. Sukhañcetaṃdhivattatīti sukhañca etaṃ puggalaṃ adhivattati, avattharatīti attho.

31. In the first of the fourth, 'wheels' means accomplishments. 'The four wheels turn' means: the four wheels of accomplishment are established and indeed connected; this is the meaning. 'Living in a suitable region' means dwelling in a suitable and appropriate place where the four assemblies are present. 'Relying on the virtuous' means relying upon, frequenting, and associating with the virtuous, beginning with the Buddha, not with kings. 'Right self-direction' means rightly establishing oneself; if one was previously endowed with lack of faith and so on, abandoning those qualities and establishing oneself in faith and so on. 'And merit done in the past' means the state of having accumulated wholesome actions in the past. This very accomplishment is the standard in this matter. Indeed, this is true. For by whatever mind associated with knowledge a wholesome action is done, that very wholesome action leads that person to a suitable region, causes them to attend upon the virtuous, and that very person establishes themselves rightly. 'One who has done merit' means one who has done merit. 'And happiness overcomes this one' means: and happiness overcomes that person, it overwhelms them; this is the meaning.

2. Saṅgahasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary to the Discourse on Integration

32. Dutiye saṅgahavatthūnīti saṅgaṇhanakāraṇāni. Dānañcātiādīsu ekacco hi dāneneva saṅgaṇhitabbo hoti, tassa dānameva dātabbaṃ. Peyyavajjanti piyavacanaṃ. Ekacco hi “ayaṃ dātabbaṃ nāma deti, ekekena pana vacanena sabbaṃ makkhetvā nāseti, kiṃ tassa dāna”nti vattā hoti. Ekacco “ayaṃ kiñcāpi dānaṃ na deti, kathento pana telena viya makkheti. Esa detu vā mā vā, vacanamevassa sahassaṃ agghatī”ti vattā hoti. Evarūpo puggalo dānaṃ na paccāsīsati, piyavacanameva paccāsīsati. Tassa piyavacanameva vattabbaṃ. Atthacariyāti atthavaḍḍhanakathā. Ekacco hi neva dānaṃ, na piyavacanaṃ paccāsīsati, attano hitakathaṃ vaḍḍhikathameva paccāsīsati. Evarūpassa puggalassa “idaṃ te kātabbaṃ, idaṃ na kātabbaṃ, evarūpo puggalo sevitabbo, evarūpo na sevitabbo”ti evaṃ atthacariyakathāva kathetabbā. Samānattatāti [P 3.0065] samānasukhadukkhabhāvo. Ekacco hi dānādīsu ekampi na paccāsīsati[V 2.0283], ekāsane nisajjaṃ, ekapallaṅke sayanaṃ, ekato bhojananti evaṃ samānasukhadukkhataṃ paccāsīsati. So sace gahaṭṭhassa jātiyā pabbajitassa sīlena sadiso hoti, tassāyaṃ samānattatā kātabbā. Tattha tattha yathārahanti tesu tesu dhammesu yathānucchavikaṃ samānattatāti attho. Rathassāṇīva yāyatoti yathā rathassa gacchato āṇi saṅgaho nāma hoti, sā rathaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, evamime saṅgahā lokaṃ saṅgaṇhanti. Na mātā puttakāraṇāti yadi mātā ete saṅgahe puttassa na kareyya, puttakāraṇā mānaṃ vā pūjaṃ vā na labheyya. Saṅgahā [M 2.0291] eteti upayogavacane paccattaṃ. Saṅgahe eteti vā pāṭho. Samavekkhantīti sammā pekkhanti. Pāsaṃsā ca bhavantīti pasaṃsanīyā ca bhavanti.

32. In the second sutta, `saṅgahavatthūni` means the bases of sympathy. Regarding 'giving and so on,' some individuals should be won over solely through generosity—for them, only gifts should be given. 'Pleasant speech' (`peyyavajja`) refers to pleasant speech. For some people say, 'This person may give gifts, but with every word, they spoil and destroy everything—what use is their generosity?' Others say, 'Even if this person does not give gifts, when speaking, they soothe as if with oil. Whether they give or not, their words alone are worth a thousand.' Such a person does not expect gifts but expects pleasant words—so only pleasant words should be spoken to them. 'Helpful conduct' means talk that promotes welfare. Some neither expect gifts nor pleasant words but only talk of their own benefit, talk that increases benefit. For such a person, one should offer helpful advice, saying, 'This should be done, this should not be done; associate with such people, avoid such people.' 'Impartiality' means a state of shared joy and sorrow. Some do not expect even a single thing among gifts and so on, but expect a state of shared happiness and suffering, such as sitting on the same seat, sleeping on the same couch, and eating together. If that person is similar to a householder by birth, or to a monastic by virtue, this impartiality should be practiced towards them. The phrase `Tattha tattha yathārahaṃ` means impartiality that is suitable in each of those respective matters; this is the meaning. 'Like the linchpin of a moving chariot': just as the linchpin is a means of cohesion for a moving chariot, holding the chariot together, so these bases of sympathy hold the world together. Regarding `Na mātā puttakāraṇā`: If a mother were not to practice these acts of sympathy for her son, she would not receive honor or respect on account of her son. In the phrase `Saṅgahā ete`, the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative; or, the reading is `Saṅgahe ete`. `Samavekkhanti` means they see rightly. `Pāsaṃsā ca bhavanti` means they also become worthy of praise.

3. Sīhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Lion Discourse

33. Tatiye sīhoti cattāro sīhā – tiṇasīho, kāḷasīho, paṇḍusīho, kesarasīhoti. Tesu tiṇasīho kapotavaṇṇagāvisadiso tiṇabhakkho ca hoti. Kāḷasīho kāḷagāvisadiso tiṇabhakkhoyeva. Paṇḍusīho paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇagāvisadiso maṃsabhakkho. Kesarasīho lākhāparikammakateneva mukhena agganaṅguṭṭhena catūhi ca pādapariyantehi samannāgato, matthakatopissa paṭṭhāya lākhātūlikāya katā viya tisso rājiyo piṭṭhimajjhena gantvā antarasatthimhi dakkhiṇāvattā hutvā ṭhitā. Khandhe panassa satasahassagghanikakambalaparikkhepo viya kesarabhāro hoti, avasesaṭṭhānaṃ parisuddhasālipiṇḍasaṅkhacuṇṇapiṇḍavaṇṇaṃ hoti. Imesu catūsu sīhesu ayaṃ kesarasīho idha adhippeto.

33. In the Third Sutta, regarding the word 'lion': there are four lions—the grass-lion, the black-lion, the paṇḍu-lion, and the kesara-lion. Among them, the grass-lion is similar to a cow the color of a dove and is a grass-eater. The black-lion is similar to a black cow and is solely a grass-eater. The paṇḍu-lion is similar to a cow the color of a pale, withered leaf and is a flesh-eater. The kesara-lion is endowed with a mouth as if perfected with lac, with the tip of its tail, and with the extremities of its four feet, which are also as if perfected with lac. Starting from the top of its head, three stripes, as if drawn with a brush dipped in lac, run along the middle of its back and, having turned clockwise in its groin, are established there. On its shoulders is a mass of mane like a covering of red blanket worth one hundred thousand. The remaining area has the color of a lump of pure rice flour and a lump of conch powder. Among these four lions, it is this kesara-lion that is intended here.

Migarājāti [P 3.0066] sabbamigagaṇassa rājā. Āsayāti vasanaṭṭhānato, suvaṇṇaguhato vā rajatamaṇiphalikamanosilāguhato vā nikkhamatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nikkhamamāno panesa catūhi kāraṇehi nikkhamati andhakārapīḷito vā ālokatthāya, uccārapassāvapīḷito vā tesaṃ vissajjanatthāya, jighacchāpīḷito vā gocaratthāya, sambhavapīḷito vā assaddhammapaṭisevanatthāya. Idha pana gocaratthāya nikkhamanto adhippeto.

'King of beasts' means the king of the entire host of beasts. 'From his abode' means he emerges from his dwelling place, whether from a golden cave, or from a cave of silver, gems, crystal, or realgar; thus it is meant. When emerging, he emerges for four reasons: either being oppressed by darkness, he emerges for the sake of light; or being oppressed by feces and urine, he emerges for the sake of discharging them; or being oppressed by hunger, he emerges for the sake of food; or being overcome by lust, he emerges for the sake of practicing unrighteous conduct. Here, however, the one emerging for the sake of food is intended.

Vijambhatīti suvaṇṇatale vā rajatamaṇiphalikamanosilātalānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ dve pacchimapāde samaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā purimapāde purato pasāretvā sarīrassa pacchābhāgaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā purimabhāgaṃ [V 2.0284] abhiharitvā piṭṭhiṃ nāmetvā gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā asanisaddaṃ karonto viya nāsapuṭāni pothetvā sarīralaggaṃ rajaṃ vidhunanto vijambhati. Vijambhanabhūmiyañca pana taruṇavacchako viya aparāparaṃ javati, javato panassa sarīraṃ andhakāre paribbhamantaṃ alātaṃ viya khāyati.

'He stretches' means: on a golden surface, or on one of the surfaces of silver, gems, crystal, or realgar, having established his two hind feet evenly, having extended his forefeet forward, having drawn back the rear part of his body and brought the front part forward, having bent his back and lifted up his neck, as if making the sound of thunder, shaking off the dust clinging to his body, he stretches. Furthermore, in the place of stretching, he moves quickly to and fro like a young calf. And as he moves quickly, his body appears in the darkness like a firebrand whirling about.

Anuviloketīti [M 2.0292] kasmā anuviloketi? Parānuddayatāya. Tasmiṃ kira sīhanādaṃ nadante papātāvāṭādīsu visamaṭṭhānesu carantā hatthigokaṇṇamahiṃsādayo pāṇā papātepi āvāṭepi patanti, tesaṃ anuddayāya anuviloketi. Kiṃ panassa luddassa paramaṃsakhādino anuddayā nāma atthīti? Āma atthi. Tathā hi “kiṃ me bahūhi ghātitehī”ti attano [P 3.0067] gocaratthāyāpi khuddake pāṇe na gaṇhāti. Evaṃ anuddayaṃ karoti, vuttampi cetaṃ – “māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesi”nti (a. ni. 10.21).

He surveys—why does he survey? Out of compassion for others. It is said that when he roars his lion's roar, creatures such as elephants, cattle, and buffaloes, wandering in uneven places like cliffs and pits, fall into cliffs and pits; he surveys out of compassion for them. But does this cruel one, who eats the flesh of others, really have compassion? Yes, he does. For he thinks, 'What use to me are many slain beings?' and does not take even small creatures for his own food. In this way, he shows compassion, and this was also spoken by the Blessed One: 'May I not bring to destruction small beings who have gone to uneven places' (A.N. 10.21).

Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti tikkhattuṃ tāva abhītanādaṃ nadati. Evañca panassa vijambhanabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā nadantassa saddo samantā tiyojanapadesaṃ ekaninnādaṃ karoti, tamassa ninnādaṃ sutvā tiyojanabbhantaragatā dvipadacatuppadagaṇā yathāṭhāne ṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Gocarāya pakkamatīti āhāratthāya gacchati. Kathaṃ? So hi vijambhanabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā dakkhiṇato vā vāmato vā uppatanto usabhamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaṇhāti, uddhaṃ uppatanto cattāripi aṭṭhapi usabhaṭṭhānāni uppatati, same ṭhāne ujukaṃ pakkhandanto soḷasausabhamattampi vīsatiusabhamattampi ṭhānaṃ pakkhandati, thalā vā pabbatā vā pakkhandanto saṭṭhiusabhamattampi asītiusabhamattampi ṭhānaṃ pakkhandati, antarāmagge rukkhaṃ vā pabbataṃ vā disvā taṃ pariharanto vāmato vā dakkhiṇato vā uddhaṃ vā usabhamattaṃ apakkamati. Tatiyaṃ pana sīhanādaṃ naditvā teneva saddhiṃ tiyojane ṭhāne paññāyati, tiyojanaṃ gantvā nivattitvā ṭhito attanova nādassa anunādaṃ suṇāti. Evaṃ sīghena javena pakkamati.

He roars a lion's roar—he lets out a fearless roar three times. And when, standing on his stretching ground, he roars, the sound makes the surrounding three-yojana region have a single resonance. Hearing this resonance, all two-footed and four-footed beings within three yojanas are unable to remain in their places. He sets out for his feeding ground—he goes for the purpose of food. How? Standing on his stretching ground, if he leaps to the right or left, he covers the distance of an usabha. If he leaps upward, he leaps four or even eight usabha-distances. If he charges straight ahead on level ground, he charges sixteen or even twenty usabha-lengths. Charging from high ground or from a mountain, he charges sixty or even eighty usabha-lengths. If he sees a tree or mountain along the way, avoiding it, he deviates an usabha-length to the left, right, or upward. After roaring the third lion's roar, he is perceived in a place three yojanas away along with that very sound; and having traveled three yojanas, he turns back and, standing still, listens to the echo of his own roar. Thus, he departs with swift speed.

Yebhuyyenāti pāyena. Bhayaṃ santāsaṃ saṃveganti sabbaṃ cittutrāsasseva nāmaṃ. Sīhassa hi saddaṃ sutvā bahū bhāyanti, appakā na [P 3.0068] bhāyanti. Ke pana teti? Samasīho hatthājānīyo assājānīyo usabhājānīyo purisājānīyo khīṇāsavoti. Kasmā panete na bhāyantīti? Samasīho tāva “jātigottakulasūrabhāvehi samānosmī”ti na bhāyati, hatthājānīyādayo attano [V 2.0285] sakkāyadiṭṭhibalavatāya na bhāyanti, khīṇāsavo sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pahīnattā na bhāyati.

Yebhuyyena means for the most part. Fear, terror, and agitation are all names for mental trembling. For upon hearing the lion's roar, many are afraid, but few are not. Who then are they? A lion of equal prowess, a noble elephant, a noble horse, a noble bull, a noble man, and one whose taints are destroyed. But why are these not afraid? The lion of equal prowess, for one, does not fear, thinking, “I am equal in birth, lineage, family, and bravery.” The noble elephant and others do not fear due to the strength of their personality view. The one whose taints are destroyed does not fear because personality view has been abandoned.

Bilāsayāti [M 2.0293] bile sayantā bilavāsino ahinakulagodhādayo. Udakāsayāti udakavāsino macchakacchapādayo. Vanāsayāti vanavāsino hatthiassagokaṇṇamigādayo. Pavisantīti “idāni āgantvā gaṇhissatī”ti maggaṃ oloketvā pavisanti. Daḷhehīti thirehi. Varattehīti cammarajjūhi. Mahiddhikotiādīsu vijambhanabhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā dakkhiṇapassādīhi usabhamattaṃ, ujuṃ vīsatiusabhamattādilaṅghanavasena mahiddhikatā, sesamigānaṃ adhipatibhāvena mahesakkhatā, samantā tiyojanaṭṭhāne saddaṃ sutvā palāyantānaṃ vasena mahānubhāvatā veditabbā.

“Those who dwell in holes” means creatures who live in holes, such as snakes, mongooses, monitor lizards, and others. “Those who dwell in water” means creatures who live in water, such as fish, turtles, and others. “Those who dwell in the forest” means creatures who live in the forest, such as elephants, horses, gokaṇṇa-deer, other deer, and others. “They enter” means, looking at the path and thinking, “Now he will come and seize us,” they enter. “Strong” means firm. “With ropes” means with leather ropes. Regarding “of great power,” etc., its great power is to be understood by its leaping—while standing on its stretching ground—an usabha-length with its right side, etc., and straight ahead twenty or more usabha-lengths; its great influence is to be understood by its being the overlord of the remaining animals; and its great majesty is to be understood by the fact that creatures flee upon hearing its sound from a place three yojanas all around.

Evameva khoti bhagavā tesu tesu suttantesu tathā tathā attānaṃ kathesi. “Sīhoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti (a. ni. 5.99; 10.21) imasmiṃ tāva sutte sīhasadisaṃ attānaṃ kathesi. “Bhisakko sallakattoti kho, sunakkhatta, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (ma. ni. 3.65) imasmiṃ [P 3.0069] vejjasadisaṃ, “brāhmaṇoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (a. ni. 8.85) imasmiṃ brāhmaṇasadisaṃ, “puriso maggakusaloti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.84) imasmiṃ maggadesakapurisasadisaṃ, “rājāhamasmi, selā”ti (su. ni. 559; ma. ni. 2.399) imasmiṃ rājasadisaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte sīhasadisameva katvā attānaṃ kathento evamāha.

Indeed, in just this way, the Blessed One spoke of himself in various ways in those diverse suttas. First, in this sutta, he spoke of himself as being like a lion: ‘Monks, “lion” is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.’ In this sutta, he spoke of himself as being like a physician: ‘Sunakkhatta, “physician, surgeon” is a designation for the Tathāgata.’ In this sutta, he spoke of himself as being like a brahmin: ‘Monks, “brahmin” is a designation for the Tathāgata.’ In this sutta, he spoke of himself as being like a man who points out the path: ‘Tissa, “a man skilled in the path” is a designation for the Tathāgata.’ In this sutta, he spoke of himself as being like a king: ‘I am a king, Sela.’ But in this sutta, having presented himself as being just like a lion and wishing to speak, he spoke thus.

Tatrāyaṃ sadisatā – sīhassa kañcanaguhādīsu vasanakālo viya hi tathāgatassa dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhārassa aparimitakālaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā pacchimabhave paṭisandhiggahaṇena ceva mātukucchito nikkhamanena ca dasasahassilokadhātuṃ kampetvā vuddhimanvāya dibbasampattisadisaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavamānassa tīsu pāsādesu nivāsakālo daṭṭhabbo.
