Sīhassa kañcanaguhādito nikkhantakālo viya tathāgatassa ekūnatiṃsasaṃvacchare vivaṭena dvārena kaṇḍakaṃ āruyha channasahāyassa nikkhamitvā tīṇi rajjāni atikkamitvā anomānadītīre brahmunā dinnāni kāsāyāni paridahitvā pabbajitassa sattame divase rājagahaṃ gantvā [V 2.0286] tattha [M 2.0294] piṇḍāya caritvā paṇḍavagiripabbhāre katabhattakiccassa sammāsambodhiṃ patvā paṭhamameva magadharaṭṭhaṃ āgamanatthāya yāva rañño paṭiññādānakālo.

Herein is the similarity. The time of a lion's dwelling in golden caves and so forth is like the time of the Tathāgata's dwelling in the three palaces. This was the Tathāgata who, having made his aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and fulfilled the perfections for an immeasurable time, in his final existence caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to quake by taking rebirth and by emerging from his mother's womb, and who, having attained growth, experienced a fortune like divine fortune. The time of a lion's emerging from a golden cave and so forth is like the time concerning the Tathāgata up to the giving of the promise to the king. This was the Tathāgata who, in his twenty-ninth year, mounted Kaṇṭaka through the opened gate with Channa as his companion, went forth, crossed three kingdoms, and on the bank of the river Anomā, donned the ochre robes given by Brahmā and went forth into homelessness. On the seventh day, he went to Rājagaha, wandered there for alms, and after finishing his meal in the valley of Paṇḍava mountain, attained perfect enlightenment, in order to come to the country of Magadha for the very first time.

Sīhassa vijambhanakālo viya tathāgatassa dinnapaṭiññassa āḷārakālāmaupasaṅkamanaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva sujātāya [P 3.0070] dinnapāyāsassa ekūnapaṇṇāsāya piṇḍehi paribhuttakālo veditabbo. Sīhassa sarīravidhunanaṃ viya sāyanhasamaye sottiyena dinnā aṭṭha tiṇamuṭṭhiyo gahetvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi thomiyamānassa gandhādīhi pūjiyamānassa tikkhattuṃ bodhiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha cuddasahatthubbedhe ṭhāne tiṇasantharaṃ attharitvā caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nisinnassa taṃkhaṇaññeva mārabalaṃ vidhametvā tīsu yāmesu tisso vijjā visodhetvā anulomappaṭilomaṃ paṭiccasamuppādamahāsamuddaṃ yamakañāṇamanthanena manthentassa sabbaññutaññāṇe paṭividdhe tadanubhāvena dasasahassilokadhātukampanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Like the time of a lion's stretching, the period from the Tathāgata's approach to Āḷāra Kālāma, after he had given his promise, up to the time he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā in forty-nine mouthfuls, should be understood. Like the shaking of a lion's body, the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world-system should be understood, which occurred by the power of his omniscient knowledge when it was penetrated by the Tathāgata, who, in the evening, having taken the eight handfuls of grass offered by Sotthiya, being praised by the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system and honored with perfumes and other offerings, having circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times, ascended the Bodhi-maṇḍala, spread a grass mat in a place fourteen cubits high, and sat down with a firm resolve for the four-factored effort; at that very moment, having dispelled the army of Māra and purified the three kinds of knowledge in the three watches, he churned the great ocean of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order with the churning-stick of paired knowledge.

Sīhassa catudisāvilokanaṃ viya paṭividdhasabbaññutaññāṇassa sattasattāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe viharitvā paribhuttamadhupiṇḍikāhārassa ajapālanigrodhamūle mahābrahmuno dhammadesanāyācanaṃ paṭiggahetvā tattha viharantassa ekādasame divase “sve āsāḷhipuṇṇamā bhavissatī”ti paccūsasamaye “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti āḷārudakānaṃ kālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā dhammadesanatthāya pañcavaggiyānaṃ olokanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīhassa gocaratthāya tiyojanaṃ gamanakālo viya attano pattacīvaraṃ ādāya “pañcavaggiyānaṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattessāmī”ti [P 3.0071] pacchābhatte ajapālanigrodhato vuṭṭhitassa aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ gamanakālo.

Like a lion surveying the four directions, the Tathāgata, having penetrated omniscient knowledge, dwelt at the Bodhi-maṇḍala for seven weeks, having consumed a lump of honey-cake as food. While dwelling at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he accepted the request of Mahā Brahmā to teach the Dhamma. On the eleventh day after the seven weeks, realizing at dawn that 'tomorrow will be the full moon of Āsāḷha,' he considered, 'To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?' Knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, his looking towards the group of five ascetics for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma should be understood. Like the time of a lion's going three yojanas for pasture, so should be understood the time of the Tathāgata's journey along the eighteen-yojana path, when, after his meal, having risen from the Ajapāla banyan tree and taken his bowl and robe, he resolved, 'I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma for the group of five.'

Sīhassa sīhanādakālo viya tathāgatassa aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ gantvā pañcavaggiye saññāpetvā acalapallaṅke nisinnassa dasahi cakkavāḷasahassehi sannipatitena devagaṇena parivutassa “dveme, bhikkhave, antā pabbajitena na sevitabbā”tiādinā nayena dhammacakkappavattanakālo veditabbo. Imasmiṃ ca pana pade desiyamāne tathāgatasīhassa dhammaghoso heṭṭhā avīciṃ upari bhavaggaṃ gahetvā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ paṭicchādesi. Sīhassa saddena khuddakapāṇānaṃ santāsāpajjanakālo [M 2.0295] viya tathāgatassa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni dīpetvā cattāri saccāni soḷasahākārehi saṭṭhiyā ca nayasahassehi vibhajitvā dhammaṃ kathentassa dīghāyukānaṃ devānaṃ ñāṇasantāsassa uppattikālo veditabbo.

Like the time of the lion's roar, so should be known the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by the Tathāgata—who, having traveled the eighteen-yojana path, made the group of five aware of his state of Buddhahood, sat on the unshakeable seat, and was surrounded by a host of devas assembled from ten thousand world-systems—by the method beginning with, 'Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.' Furthermore, while this discourse was being taught, the Dhamma-sound of the Tathāgata-lion, taking hold of Avīci below and the summit of existence above, pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system. Just as there is a time when small creatures are struck with terror by the lion's sound, so should be known the time of the arising of the terror that is knowledge for the long-lived devas, when the Tathāgata was teaching the Dhamma, having shown the three characteristics and analyzed the four truths with sixteen aspects and by sixty thousand methods.

Aparo [V 2.0287] nayo – sīho viya sabbaññutaṃ patto tathāgato, āsayabhūtāya kanakaguhāya nikkhamanaṃ viya gandhakuṭito nikkhamanakālo, vijambhanaṃ viya dhammasabhaṃ upasaṅkamanakālo, disāvilokanaṃ viya parisāvilokanaṃ, sīhanādanadanaṃ viya dhammadesanākālo, gocarāya pakkamanaṃ viya paravādanimmaddanatthāya gamanaṃ.

Another method: The Tathāgata, who has attained omniscience, is to be known as being like a lion. The time of emerging from the Fragrant Chamber is like emerging from a golden cave that is his dwelling; the time of approaching the Dhamma Hall is like stretching; surveying the assembly is like surveying the directions; the time of teaching the Dhamma is like a lion's roar; and going for the purpose of crushing the views of others is like setting out for the feeding ground.

Aparo nayo – sīho viya tathāgato, himavantanissitāya kañcanaguhāya nikkhamanaṃ viya ārammaṇavasena nibbānanissitāya [P 3.0072] phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ, vijambhanaṃ viya paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ, disāvilokanaṃ viya veneyyasattavilokanaṃ, sīhanādo viya sampattaparisāya dhammadesanā, gocarāya pakkamanaṃ viya asampattānaṃ veneyyasattānaṃ santikūpasaṅkamanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Another method: The Tathāgata is to be known as being like a lion. Arising from the fruition attainment, which is based on Nibbāna by way of its object, is like emerging from a golden cave situated in the Himālaya. The knowledge of reviewing is like stretching. Surveying beings to be trained is like surveying the directions. Teaching the Dhamma to the assembly that has arrived is like a lion's roar. Approaching the presence of beings to be trained who have not yet arrived is like setting out for the feeding ground. This should be known.

Yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Tathāgatoti heṭṭhā vuttehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi tathāgato. Loketi sattaloke. Uppajjatīti abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva bodhipallaṅkā vā arahattamaggañāṇā vā uppajjati nāma, arahattaphale pana patte uppanno nāma. Arahaṃ sammāsambuddhotiādīni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.124 ādayo) buddhānussatiniddese vitthāritāni.

Yadā: at what time. Tathāgato: the Tathāgata by the eight reasons stated below. Loke: in the world of beings. Uppajjati: from the aspiration onwards, up to the Bodhi seat or up to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, it is called 'arising'; but when the fruit of Arahantship is attained, it is called 'arisen.' Arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, etc.: these are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the recollection of the Buddha (Visuddhi. 1.124 onwards).

Iti sakkāyoti ayaṃ sakkāyo, ettako sakkāyo, na ito bhiyyo sakkāyo atthīti. Ettāvatā sabhāvato sarasato pariyantato paricchedato parivaṭumato sabbepi pañcupādānakkhandhā dassitā honti. Iti sakkāyasamudayoti ayaṃ sakkāyassa samudayo nāma. Ettāvatā “āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādi sabbaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Iti sakkāyassa atthaṅgamoti ayaṃ sakkāyassa atthaṅgamo. Imināpi “āhāranirodhā rūpanirodho”tiādi sabbaṃ dassitaṃ hoti.

Iti sakkāyo: 'This is sakkāya, this much is sakkāya, there is no more sakkāya than this.' By this much, all the five aggregates subject to clinging are shown with respect to their intrinsic nature, function, limit, definition, and consummation. Iti sakkāyasamudayo: 'This is called the origin of sakkāya.' By this much, everything is shown, such as 'with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form,' and so forth. Iti sakkāyassa atthaṅgamo: 'This is the cessation of sakkāya.' By this too, everything is shown, such as 'with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form,' and so forth.

Vaṇṇavantoti [M 2.0296] sarīravaṇṇena vaṇṇavanto. Dhammadesanaṃ sutvāti pañcasu khandhesu paṇṇāsalakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā. Yebhuyyenāti [P 3.0073] idha ke ṭhapeti? Ariyasāvake deve. Tesaṃ hi khīṇāsavattā cittutrāsabhayampi na uppajjati, saṃviggassa yoniso padhānena pattabbaṃ pattatāya ñāṇasaṃvegopi. Itarāsaṃ pana devatānaṃ “tāso heso, bhikkhave, anicca”nti manasikarontānaṃ cittutrāsabhayampi, balavavipassanākāle ñāṇabhayampi uppajjati. Bhoti dhammālapanamattametaṃ. Sakkāyapariyāpannāti pañcakkhandhapariyāpannā. Iti tesaṃ sammāsambuddhe [V 2.0288] vaṭṭadosaṃ dassetvā tilakkhaṇāhataṃ katvā dhammaṃ desente ñāṇabhayaṃ nāma okkamati.

Vaṇṇavanto: endowed with beauty of complexion. Dhammadesanaṃ sutvā: having heard the Tathāgata’s Dhamma teaching, adorned with the fifteen characteristics concerning the five aggregates. Yebhuyyena: Who are set aside here? The noble disciple devas. For them, since their taints are destroyed, mental trembling, which is fear, does not arise; and because they have attained what is to be attained through proper effort by one who is agitated, the spiritual urgency of knowledge also does not arise. But for other deities, while considering, 'This trembling, monks, is impermanent,' both mental trembling, which is fear, and, at the time of strong insight, fear born of knowledge arise. Bho: this is merely a term for addressing. Sakkāyapariyāpannā: included in the five aggregates. Thus, when the Sammāsambuddha teaches the Dhamma to them, having shown the fault of the round of existence and having made it struck by the three characteristics, what is called fear born of knowledge descends.

Abhiññāyāti jānitvā. Dhammacakkanti paṭivedhañāṇampi desanāñāṇampi. Paṭivedhañāṇaṃ nāma yena ñāṇena bodhipallaṅke nisinno cattāri saccāni soḷasahākārehi saṭṭhiyā ca nayasahassehi paṭivijjhi. Desanāñāṇaṃ nāma yena ñāṇena tiparivaṭṭaṃ dvādasākāraṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattesi. Ubhayampetaṃ dasabalassa ure jātañāṇameva. Tesu dhammadesanāñāṇaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Taṃ panesa yāva aṭṭhārasabrahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ aññākoṇḍaññattherassa sotāpattiphalaṃ na uppajjati, tāva pavatteti nāma. Tasmiṃ uppanne pavattitaṃ nāma hotīti veditabbaṃ. Appaṭipuggaloti sadisapuggalarahito. Yasassinoti parivārasampannā. Tādinoti [P 3.0074] lābhālābhādīhi ekasadisassa.

Abhiññāya: having known. Dhammacakka: both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. The knowledge of penetration is that knowledge by which, seated on the Bodhi-seat, he penetrated the four truths with their sixteen aspects and sixty thousand modes. The knowledge of teaching is that knowledge by which he set in motion the Dhamma wheel with its three rounds and twelve aspects. Both of these are indeed knowledges born in the breast of the One with Ten Powers. Among these, the knowledge of teaching the Dhamma should be taken. Furthermore, he is said to set it in motion for as long as the fruit of stream-entry does not arise in the Venerable Aññākoṇḍañña together with eighteen koṭis of brahmās. When that has arisen, it should be understood as 'having been set in motion'. Appaṭipuggalo: one devoid of a similar person. Yasassino: those endowed with a retinue. Tādino: one who is equanimous amidst gain, loss, and so on.

4. Pasādasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Pasāda Sutta.

34. Catutthe aggesu pasādā, aggā vā pasādāti aggappasādā. Yāvatāti yattakā. Apadāti nippadā ahimacchādayo. Dvipadāti manussapakkhiādayo. Catuppadāti hatthiassādayo. Bahuppadāti satapadiādayo. Nevasaññināsaññinoti bhavagge nibbattasattā. Aggamakkhāyatīti guṇehi aggo uttamo seṭṭhoti akkhāyati. Asaṅkhatāti nibbānameva gahetvā vuttaṃ. Virāgotiādīni nibbānasseva nāmāni. Tañhi āgamma sabbakilesā virajjanti, sabbe rāgamadādayo madā nimmadā honti, abhāvaṃ gacchanti, sabbā pipāsā vinayaṃ upenti, sabbe ālayā [M 2.0297] samugghātaṃ gacchanti, vaṭṭāni upacchijjanti, taṇhā khīyanti, vaṭṭadukkhā nirujjhanti, sabbe pariḷāhā nibbāyanti. Tasmā etāni nāmāni labhati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

34. In the fourth [sutta], aggappasādā means 'confidence in the supreme things' or 'the supreme confidence'. Yāvatā: however many. Apadā: footless creatures, such as snakes and fish. Dvipadā: two-footed beings, such as humans and birds. Catuppadā: four-footed beings, such as elephants and horses. Bahuppadā: many-footed beings, such as centipedes. Nevasaññināsaññino: beings reborn at the peak of existence. Aggamakkhāyati: it is called 'supreme, highest, and best' on account of its qualities. Asaṅkhata is stated, referring to Nibbāna itself. Virāga and so on are names for Nibbāna itself. For, having reached it, all defilements fade away; all intoxications, such as that of lust, are dispelled and cease to exist; all thirsts are removed; all attachments are uprooted; the cycles are cut off; craving is exhausted; the suffering of the cycle ceases; and all fevers are extinguished. Therefore, it obtains these names. The rest here has a plain meaning.

5. Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta.

35. Pañcame anussaritāti anugantvā saritā, aparāparaṃ sarituṃ samatthoti attho. Dakkhoti cheko. Tatrupāyāyāti “imasmiṃ kāle imaṃ nāma kattabba”nti evaṃ tattha tattha upāyabhūtāya [V 2.0289] paññāya samannāgato. Anumoditabbanti abhinanditabbaṃ. Paṭikkositabbanti paṭikkhipitabbaṃ. Neva kho tyāhanti neva kho te ahaṃ. Kasmā panetaṃ bhagavā nābhinandati, nappaṭikkhipatīti? Lokiyattā nābhinandati[P 3.0075], lokiyaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā ṭhitattā nappaṭikkosati. Bahussa janatāti bahu assa janatā. Idañca karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ariye ñāyeti sahavipassanake magge. Kalyāṇadhammatā kusaladhammatātipi tasseva nāmāni. Yaṃ vitakkanti nekkhammavitakkādīsu aññataraṃ. Na taṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketīti kāmavitakkādīsu ekampi na vitakketi. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Vitakkapatheti ettha vitakkoyeva vitakkapatho. Ahañhi brāhmaṇātiādīsu paṭhamanayena khīṇāsavassa sīlañceva bāhusaccañca kathitaṃ, dutiyatatiyehi khīṇāsavassa kiriyavitakkāni ceva kiriyajjhānāni ca, catutthena khīṇāsavabhāvo kathitoti veditabbo.

35. In the fifth [sutta], anussaritā means 'having followed and remembered'; the meaning is 'capable of repeatedly recalling.' Dakkho: skilled. Tatrupāyāya: endowed with wisdom that is a means in various situations, as in, 'At this time, this should be done.' Anumoditabbaṃ: it should be rejoiced in. Paṭikkositabbaṃ: it should be rejected. The phrase Neva kho tyāhaṃ is to be parsed as neva kho te ahaṃ. Why, then, does the Blessed One neither approve nor reject this? He does not approve because it is worldly; he does not reject it because it stands on the basis of a worldly meaning. The phrase Bahussajanatā is to be parsed as bahu assa janatā. And this genitive case should be understood in the sense of the instrumental. Ariye ñāye: in the noble path together with insight. Kalyāṇadhammatā and kusaladhammatā are also names for that very thing. Yaṃ vitakkaṃ: any one of the thoughts of renunciation and so forth. Na taṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi: he does not think even a single thought of sensual desire and so forth. The other is a synonym for that very one. In the phrase vitakkapathe, thought itself is the 'path of thought.' In 'Ahañhi brāhmaṇa', and so forth, it should be understood that by the first method, the virtue and great learning of one whose cankers are destroyed are stated; by the second and third methods, the functional thoughts and functional jhānas of one whose cankers are destroyed; and by the fourth, the state of one whose cankers are destroyed is stated.

Maccupāsappamocananti maccupāsā pamocanakaṃ maggaṃ. Ñāyaṃ dhammanti sahavipassanakaṃ maggaṃ. Disvā ca sutvā cāti ñāṇeneva passitvā ca suṇitvā ca. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Maccupāsappamocanaṃ: the path that liberates from the snare of death. Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ: the path together with insight. Disvā ca sutvā ca: having seen and heard with knowledge alone. The rest here is clear in meaning.

6. Doṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta.

36. Chaṭṭhe antarā ca ukkaṭṭhaṃ antarā ca setabyanti ettha ukkaṭṭhāti ukkāhi dhārīyamānāhi māpitattā evaṃladdhavohāraṃ nagaraṃ. Setabyanti atīte kassapasammāsambuddhassa jātanagaraṃ. Antarāsaddo pana kāraṇakhaṇacittavemajjhavivarādīsu vattati. “Tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya aññatra tathāgatā”ti [M 2.0298] (a. ni. 6.44; 10.75) ca, “janā [P 3.0076] saṅgamma mantenti, mañca tañca kimantara”nti ca ādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.228) kāraṇe. “Addasā maṃ, bhante, aññatarā itthī vijjantarikāya bhājanaṃ dhovantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) khaṇe. “Yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) citte. “Antarāvosānamāpādī”tiādīsu vemajjhe. “Apicāyaṃ tapodā dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 231) vivare. Svāyamidha vivare vattati. Tasmā ukkaṭṭhāya ca setabyassa ca vivareti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Antarāsaddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Īdisesu ca ṭhānesu akkharacintakā “antarā gāmañca nadiñca yātī”ti [V 2.0290] evaṃ ekameva antarāsaddaṃ payuñjanti, so dutiyapadenapi yojetabbo hoti, ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Idha pana yojetvā eva vutto.

36. In the sixth sutta, regarding 'between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabyā,' here Ukkaṭṭhā refers to a city that gained such a designation because it was established by means of torches being held. Setabyā refers to the birth city of the past Sammāsambuddha Kassapa. The word `antara`, however, occurs in the sense of cause, moment, mind, middle, interval, and so forth. For example, in 'Who could know that cause, other than the Tathāgata?' and 'People gather and deliberate; for what reason concerning me and you?' and so forth, it refers to cause. In 'Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me while washing a vessel during a flash of lightning' and so forth, it refers to a moment. In 'For whom there are no angers within' and so forth, it refers to the mind. In 'He came to a halt in the middle' and so forth, it refers to the middle. In 'And this Tapodā River flows through the interval of two great hells' and so forth, it refers to an interval. Here, it occurs in the sense of interval. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'the interval between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabyā.' However, because it is connected with the word `antara`, the accusative case is used. And in such places, grammarians use the word `antara` only once, as in 'He goes between the village and the river,' and it must also be connected with the second term. If it is not connected, the accusative case is not obtained. Here, however, it is stated having been connected.

Addhānamaggappaṭipanno hotīti addhānasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno hoti, dīghamagganti attho. Kasmā paṭipannoti? Taṃ divasaṃ kira bhagavā idaṃ addasa “mayi taṃ maggaṃ paṭipanne doṇo brāhmaṇo mama padacetiyāni passitvā padānupadiko hutvā mama nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā pañhaṃ pucchissati. Athassāhaṃ ekaṃ saccadhammaṃ desessāmi[P 3.0077]. Brāhmaṇo tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni paṭivijjhitvā dvādasapadasahassaparimāṇaṃ doṇagajjitaṃ nāma vaṇṇaṃ vatvā mayi parinibbute sakalajambudīpe uppannaṃ mahākalahaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo bhājessatī”ti. Iminā kāraṇena paṭipanno. Doṇopi sudaṃ brāhmaṇoti doṇo brāhmaṇopi tayo vede paguṇe katvā pañcasate māṇavake sippaṃ vācento taṃdivasaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā satagghanakaṃ nivāsetvā pañcasatagghanakaṃ ekaṃsavaragataṃ katvā āmuttayaññasutto rattavaṭṭikā upāhanā ārohitvā pañcasatamāṇavakaparivāro tameva maggaṃ paṭipajji. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘He has entered upon a long journey’s path’ means he has entered upon the path called a long journey; he has entered upon a long path—this is the meaning. Why did he enter upon it? It is said that on that day the Blessed One saw this: ‘When I have entered upon that path, the brahmin Doṇa, having seen my footprint-shrines, will follow step by step, and having come to my sitting place, will ask a question. Then I shall teach him one truth of the Dhamma. The brahmin, having penetrated the three fruits of recluseship, will speak a praise named “Doṇa’s Roar,” having the measure of twelve thousand words. When I have attained Parinibbāna, he will quell the great conflict that has arisen in all of Jambudīpa and will distribute the relics.’ For this reason, he entered upon the path. As for ‘And the brahmin Doṇa, too’: the brahmin Doṇa, having become proficient in the three Vedas and teaching the craft to five hundred young men, rose very early on that day. Having attended to his body, having worn a lower garment worth one hundred, having placed an upper garment worth five hundred over one shoulder, having put on the sacrificial thread, and having put on sandals with red straps, he, surrounded by five hundred young men, entered upon that very path. Referring to that, this was said.

Pādesūti pādehi akkantaṭṭhānesu. Cakkānīti lakkhaṇacakkāni. Kiṃ pana bhagavato gacchantassa akkantaṭṭhāne padaṃ paññāyatīti? Na paññāyati[M 2.0299]. Kasmā? Sukhumattā mahābalattā mahājanānuggahena ca. Buddhānañhi sukhumacchavitāya akkantaṭṭhānaṃ tūlapicuno patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti, padavaḷañjo na paññāyati. Yathā ca balavato vātajavasindhavassa paduminipattepi akkantamattameva hoti, evaṃ mahābalatāya tathāgatena akkantaṭṭhānaṃ akkantamattameva hoti, na tattha padavaḷañjo paññāyati. Buddhānañca anupadaṃ mahājanakāyo [P 3.0078] gacchati, tassa satthu padavaḷañjaṃ disvā maddituṃ avisahantassa gamanavicchedo bhaveyya. Tasmā akkantaakkantaṭṭhāne yopi padavaḷañjo bhaveyya, so antaradhāyateva. Doṇo pana brāhmaṇo tathāgatassa adhiṭṭhānavasena passi. Bhagavā hi yassa padacetiyaṃ dassetukāmo hoti, taṃ ārabbha “asuko nāma passatū”ti adhiṭṭhāti. Tasmā māgaṇḍiyabrāhmaṇo viya ayampi brāhmaṇo tathāgatassa adhiṭṭhānavasena addasa.

Pādesu means 'in the places trodden by the feet.' Cakkāni means 'the wheel marks of auspicious signs.' But does a footprint appear in the place where the Blessed One has walked? It does not appear. Why? Because of his subtlety, great strength, and his compassion for the great multitude. For the Buddhas, due to their subtle skin, the place where they tread is like the place where a tuft of cotton-wool is laid down; no footprint is visible. Just as when a strong, swift Sindh horse with its wind-like speed touches a lotus leaf, it only makes the slightest contact, so too, due to the Tathāgata's great strength, only the slightest contact is made where he treads, and no footprint is visible there. Moreover, a great multitude follows the Buddha step by step; if they were to see the Teacher's footprints, not daring to trample them, their progress would be interrupted. Therefore, in each place he treads, even if a footprint were to appear, it would disappear. But the brahmin Doṇa saw it through the Tathāgata's power of determination. For the Blessed One, when he wishes to show a footprint-shrine to someone, focusing on that person, he determines, 'Let so-and-so see it.' Thus, like the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, this brahmin also saw it through the Tathāgata's power of determination.

Pāsādikanti pasādajanakaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Uttamadamathasamathamanuppattanti ettha uttamadamatho nāma arahattamaggo, uttamasamatho nāma arahattamaggasamādhi, tadubhayaṃ pattanti attho[V 2.0291]. Dantanti nibbisevanaṃ. Guttanti gopitaṃ. Saṃyatindriyanti rakkhitindriyaṃ. Nāganti chandādīhi agacchanato, pahīnakilese puna anāgacchanato, āguṃ akaraṇato, balavantaṭṭhenāti catūhi kāraṇehi nāgaṃ.

Pāsādika means 'inspiring confidence.' The other word is a synonym for that very one. Uttamadamathasamathamanuppattaṃ means 'one who has attained the highest taming and tranquility.' Here, 'the highest taming' is the path of Arahantship, and 'the highest tranquility' is the concentration of the path of Arahantship; the meaning is that he has attained both. Danta means 'having eradicated opposition.' Gutta means 'guarded.' Saṃyatindriya means 'with guarded senses.' He is called a Nāga for four reasons: because he does not go by way of desire and so forth; because he does not return to abandoned defilements; because he does not do evil; and because of his great strength.

Devo no bhavaṃ bhavissatīti ettha “devo no bhava”nti ettāvatāpi pucchā niṭṭhitā bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana brāhmaṇo “anāgate mahesakkho eko devarājā bhavissatī”ti anāgatavasena pucchāsabhāgeneva kathento evamāha. Bhagavāpissa pucchāsabhāgeneva kathento na kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, devo bhavissāmīti āha. Esa nayo sabbattha. Āsavānanti [P 3.0079] kāmāsavādīnaṃ catunnaṃ. Pahīnāti bodhipallaṅke sabbaññutaññāṇādhigameneva pahīnā. Anupalitto lokenāti taṇhādiṭṭhilepānaṃ pahīnattā saṅkhāralokena anupalitto. Buddhoti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ buddhattā buddho iti maṃ dhārehi.

Regarding the text, 'Will the venerable one become a god?': Here, although the question could have been concluded with just 'Is the venerable one a god?', this brahmin, thinking, 'In the future, he will become a king of gods of great power,' spoke in the manner of a question with a future sense, and said thus. The Blessed One also, replying in a manner that matched the question, said, 'Indeed, brahmin, I will not become a god.' This method should be understood in all instances. 'Of the taints' means of the four beginning with the taint of sensual desire. 'Abandoned' means they were abandoned through the very attainment of omniscient knowledge at the seat of awakening. 'Unstained by the world' means that because the stains of craving and views have been abandoned, he is unstained by the world of formations. 'Buddha' means that because of having understood the four truths, he is 'Buddha'; thus should you understand me.

Yenāti yena āsavena. Devūpapatyassāti devūpapatti assa mayhaṃ bhaveyya. Vihaṅgamoti ākāsacaro gandhabbakāyikadevo. Viddhastāti [M 2.0300] vidhamitā. Vinaḷīkatāti vigatanaḷā vigatabandhanā katā. Vaggūti sundaraṃ. Toyena nupalippatīti udakato ratanamattaṃ accuggamma ṭhitaṃ saraṃ sobhayamānaṃ bhamaragaṇaṃ hāsayamānaṃ toyena na lippati. Tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇāti desanāpariyosāne tīṇi maggaphalāni pāpuṇitvā dvādasahi padasahassehi doṇagajjitaṃ nāma vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, tathāgate ca parinibbute jambudīpatale uppannaṃ mahākalahaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo bhājesīti.

'By which' means by which taint. 'Rebirth as a god would be' means rebirth as a god might be for me. 'Sky-faring' means a sky-faring deva belonging to the host of gandhabbas. 'Destroyed' means destroyed. 'Made without reeds' means made to be without reeds, made to be without bonds. 'Beautiful' means lovely. 'Is not smeared by water' means: like a white lotus that, having risen a cubit's length from the water, stands beautifying the lake and delighting the swarm of bees, is not smeared by the water. 'Therefore, brahmin, I am a Buddha': at the conclusion of the discourse, having attained the three paths and fruits, he composed a praise in twelve thousand verses, named 'Doṇa's Roar'. And when the Tathāgata had attained Parinibbāna, having quelled the great dispute that had arisen in Jambudīpa, he distributed the relics.

7. Aparihāniyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sutta on Non-decline

37. Sattame nibbānasseva santiketi nibbānasantikeyeva carati. Sīle patiṭṭhitoti pātimokkhasīle patiṭṭhito. Evaṃ [P 3.0080] vihārīti evaṃ viharanto. Ātāpīti ātāpena vīriyena samannāgato. Yogakkhemassāti catūhi yogehi khemassa nibbānassa. Pamāde bhayadassivāti pamādaṃ bhayato passanto.

37. In the seventh sutta, 'in the vicinity of Nibbāna itself' means he practices only in the vicinity of the Nibbāna of defilements and the Nibbāna without residue of aggregates. 'Established in virtue' means established in the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint. 'Dwelling thus' means dwelling in this way. 'Ardent' means endowed with the energy that torments the defilements. 'For security from the yokes' means for Nibbāna, which is safe from the four yokes. 'Seeing danger in heedlessness' means seeing heedlessness as a danger, such as being born in hell.

8. Patilīnasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sutta on Seclusion

38. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0292] panuṇṇapaccekasaccoti “idameva dassanaṃ saccaṃ, idameva sacca”nti evaṃ pāṭiekkaṃ gahitattā paccekasaṅkhātāni diṭṭhisaccāni panuṇṇāni nīhaṭāni pahīnāni assāti panuṇṇapaccekasacco. Samavayasaṭṭhesanoti ettha avayāti anūnā, saṭṭhāti vissaṭṭhā, sammā avayā saṭṭhā esanā assāti samavayasaṭṭhesano, sammā vissaṭṭhasabbaesanoti attho. Patilīnoti nilīno ekībhāvaṃ upagato. Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānanti bahūnaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ. Ettha ca samaṇāti pabbajjūpagatā, brāhmaṇāti bhovādino. Puthupaccekasaccānīti bahūni pāṭekkasaccāni. Nuṇṇānīti nīhaṭāni. Panuṇṇānīti suṭṭhu nīhaṭāni. Cattānīti vissaṭṭhāni. Vantānīti vamitāni. Muttānīti chinnabandhanāni katāni. Pahīnānīti pajahitāni. Paṭinissaṭṭhānīti yathā na puna cittaṃ ārohanti, evaṃ paṭinissajjitāni. Sabbānevetāni [P 3.0081] gahitagahaṇassa vissaṭṭhabhāvavevacanāni.

38. In the eighth, 'one who has dispelled individual truths' (panuṇṇapaccekasacco) is so called because for him the truths of views—known as 'individual truths' because they are grasped individually with the thought, 'This view alone is true, this alone is true'—are dispelled, removed, and abandoned. As for 'one with quests rightly abandoned' (samavayasaṭṭhesano): here, `avayā` means 'without deficiency,' `saṭṭhā` means 'abandoned'; thus, `samavayasaṭṭhesano` is one for whom quests are rightly, without deficiency, abandoned. The meaning is 'one who has rightly abandoned all quests.' 'Withdrawn' (patilīno) means secluded, having attained a state of being alone. 'Of the many ascetics and brahmins' (puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ) means of many ascetics and brahmins. And here, 'ascetics' (samaṇā) are those who have gone forth; 'brahmins' (brāhmaṇā) are those who use the address 'bho.' 'Many individual truths' (puthupaccekasaccāni) means many individual truths. 'Dispelled' (nuṇṇāni) means removed. 'Well-dispelled' (panuṇṇāni) means well removed. 'Abandoned' (cattāni) means released. 'Vomited out' (vantāni) means vomited out. 'Freed' (muttāni) means with bonds severed. 'Abandoned' (pahīnāni) means relinquished. 'Relinquished' (paṭinissaṭṭhāni) means released in such a way that they do not arise in the mind again. All these are synonyms for the state of having abandoned the grasping of what has been grasped.

Kāmesanā pahīnā hotīti anāgāmimaggena pahīnā. Bhavesanā pana arahattamaggena pahīyati. “Brahmacariyaṃ esissāmi gavesissāmī”ti evaṃ [M 2.0301] pavattajjhāsayasaṅkhātā brahmacariyesanāpi arahattamaggeneva paṭippassaddhiṃ vūpasamaṃ gacchati. Diṭṭhibrahmacariyesanā pana sotāpattimaggeneva paṭippasambhatīti veditabbā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhaveti evaṃ catutthajjhānena passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro vūpasantaassāsapassāso nāma hoti. Asmimānoti asmīti uppajjanako navavidhamāno.

'The quest for sensual pleasures is abandoned' means it is abandoned by the path of the non-returner. But the quest for existence is abandoned by the path of arahantship. The quest for the holy life, defined as the intention that arises as, 'I will seek the holy life, I will search for it,' also reaches tranquilization and cessation only by the path of arahantship. But the quest for the holy life that is a view should be understood as being pacified only by the path of stream-entry. As for 'Thus indeed, O monks': thus, by means of the fourth jhāna, one whose bodily formation is tranquilized is called one whose in-and-out breathing has ceased. 'The conceit "I am"' is the ninefold conceit that arises as 'I am'.

Gāthāsu kāmesanā bhavesanāti etā dve esanā, brahmacariyesanā sahāti tāhiyeva saha brahmacariyesanāti tissopi etā. Idha ṭhatvā esanā paṭinissaṭṭhāti iminā padena saddhiṃ yojanā kātabbā. Iti saccaparāmāso, diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samussayāti “iti saccaṃ iti sacca”nti gahaṇaparāmāso ca diṭṭhisaṅkhātāyeva diṭṭhiṭṭhānā ca ye samussitattā uggantvā ṭhitattā samussayāti vuccanti, te sabbepi. Idha ṭhatvā diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samūhatāti iminā padena saddhiṃ yojanā kātabbā. Kassa pana etā esanā paṭinissaṭṭhā, ete ca diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samūhatāti? Sabbarāgavirattassa taṇhākkhayavimuttino. Yo hi sabbarāgehipi viratto, taṇhākkhaye ca nibbāne pavattāya [P 3.0082] arahattaphalavimuttiyā samannāgato, etassa esanā paṭinissaṭṭhā, diṭṭhiṭṭhānā ca samūhatā[V 2.0293]. Sa ve santoti so evarūpo kilesasantatāya santo. Passaddhoti dvīhi kāyacittapassaddhīhi passaddho. Aparājitoti sabbakilese jinitvā ṭhitattā kenaci aparājito. Mānābhisamayāti mānassa pahānābhisamayena. Buddhoti cattāri saccāni bujjhitvā ṭhito. Iti imasmiṃ suttepi gāthāsupi khīṇāsavova kathitoti.

In the verses, 'the quest for sensual pleasures' and 'the quest for existence'—these are the two quests. The phrase 'with the quest for the holy life' means that together with those very quests is the quest for the holy life; thus, there are these three. Having stated these here, a connection should be made with the phrase 'the quests are abandoned.' As for 'Thus, the misapprehension of truth, the foundations of views, are accumulations,' this refers to the misapprehension of grasping, thinking, 'This is true, this is true,' and the foundations of views, which are simply views. All of these are called 'accumulations' because they are well-raised, have arisen, and are established. Standing here, a connection should be made with the phrase 'the foundations of views are uprooted.' But for whom are these quests abandoned, and these foundations of views uprooted? For one who is dispassionate towards all passion, liberated through the destruction of craving. Indeed, for one who is dispassionate towards all passion and is endowed with the liberation that is the fruit of Arahantship, which occurs in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving—for such a one, the quests are abandoned, and the foundations of views are uprooted. As for 'He is truly peaceful,' such a person is called 'peaceful' due to being stilled of the defilements. As for 'tranquil,' he is tranquil with the twofold tranquility of body and mind. As for 'unconquered,' because of standing having conquered all defilements, he is unconquered by any defilement. As for 'through the penetration of conceit,' it means by the penetration that is the abandoning of conceit. As for 'awakened,' he stands having understood the four truths. Thus, in this sutta and also in the verses, only the one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of.

9. Ujjayasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ujjaya Sutta

39. Navame saṅghātaṃ āpajjantīti vadhaṃ maraṇaṃ āpajjanti. Niccadānanti salākabhattaṃ. Anukulayaññanti amhākaṃ pitūhi pitāmahehi dinnattā evaṃ kulānukulavasena yajitabbaṃ, dātabbanti attho. Assamedhantiādīsu assamettha medhantīti assamedho, dvīhi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa ekavīsatiyūpassa ṭhapetvā bhūmiñca purise ca avasesasabbavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Purisamettha medhantīti purisamedho, catūhi [M 2.0302] pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sammamettha pāsantīti sammāpāso, divase divase sammaṃ khipitvā tassa patitokāse vediṃ katvā saṃhārimehi yūpādīhi sarassatinadiyā nimuggokāsato pabhuti paṭilomaṃ gacchantena yajitabbassa sabbayāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vājamettha pivantīti vājapeyyaṃ, ekena pariyaññena sattarasahi pasūhi yajitabbassa beluvayūpassa sattarasakadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi [P 3.0083] ettha aggaḷāti niraggaḷo. Navahi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā purisehi ca assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa sabbamedhapariyāyanāmassa assamedhavikappassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Mahārambhāti mahākiccā mahākaraṇīyā. Apica pāṇātipātasamārambhassa mahantatāyapi mahārambhāyeva. Na te honti mahapphalāti ettha niravasesatthe sāvasesarūpanaṃ kataṃ. Tasmā iṭṭhaphalena nipphalāva hontīti attho. Idañca pāṇātipātasamārambhameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana tattha antarantarā dānaṃ diyyati, taṃ iminā samārambhena upahatattā mahapphalaṃ na hoti, mandaphalaṃ hotīti attho. Haññareti haññanti. Yajanti anukulaṃ sadāti ye aññe anukulaṃ yajanti, pubbapurisehi yiṭṭhattā pacchimapurisāpi yajantīti attho. Seyyo hotīti visesova hoti. Na pāpiyoti pāpaṃ kiñci na hoti.

39. In the ninth sutta, 'they meet with slaughter' (saṅghātaṃ āpajjanti) means they meet with killing and death (vadhaṃ maraṇaṃ āpajjanti). 'Constant giving' (niccadānaṃ) refers to the ticket-food (salākabhattaṃ). 'A sacrifice in keeping with the family' (anukulayaññaṃ) means that because it was given by our fathers and grandfathers, it should be sacrificed and given in accordance with family tradition—this is the meaning. Regarding 'horse sacrifice' (assamedha), etc.: 'They kill a horse here' (assamettha medhanti), hence it is called 'horse sacrifice' (assamedho). This is a designation for a sacrifice to be performed with two peripheral offerings and twenty-one sacrificial posts, where, setting aside the land and the men, the remainder of all wealth is given as the offering. 'They kill a man here' (purisamettha medhanti), hence it is called 'human sacrifice' (purisamedho). This is a designation for a sacrifice to be performed with four peripheral offerings, together with the land, with the offering of wealth as stated in the horse sacrifice. 'They cast the yoke-pin here' (sammamettha pāsanti), hence it is called 'sammāpāsa'. This is a designation for a sacrifice of all kinds, to be performed by one who, day by day, casts a yoke-pin, makes an altar at the place where it has fallen, and, using movable sacrificial posts and so on, proceeds upstream from the point of immersion in the Sarasvatī river. 'They drink the invigorating draught here' (vājamettha pivanti), hence it is called 'vājapeyya'. This is a designation for a sacrifice to be performed with one peripheral offering and seventeen animals, with a beluva wood sacrificial post and an offering of seventeen kinds of items. 'There is no bolt here' (natthi ettha aggaḷā), hence it is called 'unbolted' (niraggaḷo). This is a designation for a variation of the horse sacrifice, having the synonymous name 'all-sacrifice', to be performed with nine peripheral offerings, together with the land and the men, with the offering of wealth as stated in the horse sacrifice. 'Great undertakings' (mahārambhā) means great tasks, great duties. Moreover, because of the greatness of the undertaking of killing living beings, they are indeed great undertakings. 'They are not of great fruit' (na te honti mahapphalā): here, a statement that implies a remainder is made in the sense of there being no remainder. Therefore, it means they are fruitless with respect to the desired result. And this was said with reference to the undertaking of killing living beings. But whatever giving is done there in between, because it is afflicted by this undertaking, is not of great fruit; it is of little fruit. This is the meaning. 'They are killed' (haññare) means they are slain (haññanti). 'They always sacrifice in keeping with the family' (yajanti anukulaṃ sadā): this means that because the forefathers sacrificed, the later generations also sacrifice. This is the meaning. 'It is better' (seyyo hoti) means it is indeed superior. 'Not worse' (na pāpiyo) means there is no evil whatsoever.

10. Udāyisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Udāyi Sutta

40. Dasame [V 2.0294] abhisaṅkhatanti rāsikataṃ. Nirārambhanti pāṇasamārambharahitaṃ. Yaññanti deyyadhammaṃ. Tañhi yajitabbattā yaññanti vuccati. Kālenāti yuttappattakālena. Upasaṃyantīti upagacchanti. Kulaṃ gatinti vaṭṭakulañceva vaṭṭagatiñca atikkantā. Yaññassa [P 3.0084] kovidāti catubhūmakayaññe kusalā. Yaññeti pakatidāne. Saddheti matakadāne. Habyaṃ katvāti hunitabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ upakappetvā. Sukhette brahmacārisūti brahmacārisaṅkhāte sukhettamhīti attho. Suppattanti suṭṭhu pattaṃ. Dakkhiṇeyyesu yaṃ katanti yaṃ dakkhiṇāya [M 2.0303] anucchavikesu upakappitaṃ, taṃ suhutaṃ suyiṭṭhaṃ suppattanti attho. Saddhoti buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānaṃ saddahanatāya saddho. Muttena cetasāti vissaṭṭhena cittena. Imināssa muttacāgaṃ dīpetīti.

40. In the tenth sutta, 'prepared' (abhisaṅkhataṃ) means accumulated (rāsikataṃ). 'Without undertaking violence' (nirārambhaṃ) means devoid of undertakings that involve living beings (pāṇasamārambharahitaṃ). 'Sacrifice' (yaññaṃ) means a gift to be given (deyyadhammaṃ). Indeed, because it is to be offered, it is called a 'sacrifice'. 'In time' (kālena) means at a suitable and proper time (yuttappattakālena). 'They approach' (upasaṃyanti) means they go near (upagacchanti). 'Transcending the family and destiny' (kulaṃ gatiṃ) means they have transcended the family of the round of existence and the destiny within the round of existence. 'Skilled in sacrifice' (yaññassa kovidā) means skilled in the sacrifice of the four planes. 'In sacrifice' (yaññe) refers to ordinary giving (pakatidāne). 'In faith' (saddhe) refers to giving on behalf of the dead (matakadāne). 'Having made an oblation' (habyaṃ katvā) means having prepared the gift-object to be offered (hunitabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ upakappetvā). 'In the good field, among those leading the holy life' (sukhette brahmacārisūti) means in the good field designated as 'those leading the holy life'; this is the meaning. 'Well attained' (suppattaṃ) means well reached (suṭṭhu pattaṃ). 'What is done among the worthy of offerings' (dakkhiṇeyyesu yaṃ kataṃ) means: that which is prepared for those suitable for an offering, that is well offered (suhutaṃ), greatly offered (suyiṭṭhaṃ), and well attained (suppattaṃ); this is the meaning. 'Faithful' (saddho) means one is called 'faithful' because of belief in the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. 'With a liberated mind' (muttena cetasā) means with a released mind (vissaṭṭhena cittena). By this, it shows his liberated generosity.

Cakkavaggo catuttho.

The Chapter of the Wheel is the Fourth.

5. Rohitassavaggo

5. The Rohitassa Chapter

1. Samādhibhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Development of Concentration

41. Pañcamassa [V 2.0295] paṭhame ñāṇadassanappaṭilābhāyāti dibbacakkhuñāṇadassanassa paṭilābhāya. Divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhātīti divāti evaṃ saññaṃ adhiṭṭhāti. Yathā divā tathā rattinti yathā divā ālokasaññā manasi katā, tatheva taṃ rattimpi manasi karoti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Sappabhāsanti dibbacakkhuñāṇobhāsena sahobhāsaṃ. Kiñcāpi [P 3.0085] ālokasadisaṃ kataṃ, attho panettha na evaṃ sallakkhetabbo. Dibbacakkhuñāṇāloko hi idhādhippeto.

41. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, 'for the attainment of knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassanappaṭilābhāya) means for the attainment of the knowledge and vision of the divine eye. 'He resolves upon the perception of day' (divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhāti) means he establishes the perception, 'it is day'. 'As by day, so by night' (yathā divā tathā rattiṃ) means: just as the perception of light is attended to in the mind during the day, so too does he attend to it at night. The same method applies to the second phrase. 'Luminous' (sappabhāsaṃ) means together with the radiance, with the radiance of the divine eye-knowledge. Although it is made similar to light, the meaning here should not be understood in that way. For here, the light of the divine eye-knowledge is what is intended.

Viditāti pākaṭā hutvā. Kathaṃ pana vedanā viditā uppajjanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchantīti? Idha bhikkhu vatthuṃ pariggaṇhāti, ārammaṇaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Tassa pariggahitavatthārammaṇatāya tā vedanā “evaṃ uppajjitvā evaṃ ṭhatvā evaṃ nirujjhantī”ti viditā uppajjanti, viditā tiṭṭhanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti nāma. Saññāvitakkesupi eseva nayo.

'Known' (viditā) means having become manifest. How, then, do feelings arise as known and go to cessation as known? Here, a bhikkhu comprehends the base, comprehends the object. For him, because of having comprehended the base and the object, those feelings—'having arisen thus, having persisted thus, they cease thus'—are said to arise as known, persist as known, and go to cessation as known. In the case of perceptions and thoughts also, this is the same method.

Udayabbayānupassīti udayañca vayañca passanto. Iti rūpanti evaṃ rūpaṃ ettakaṃ rūpaṃ na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthīti. Iti rūpassa samudayoti evaṃ rūpassa uppādo. Atthaṅgamoti pana bhedo adhippeto. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Idañca pana metaṃ, bhikkhave, sandhāya bhāsitanti, bhikkhave, yaṃ mayā etaṃ puṇṇakapañhe “saṅkhāya lokasmi”ntiādi bhāsitaṃ, taṃ idaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ sandhāya bhāsitanti attho.

'One who observes arising and passing away' (udayabbayānupassī) means one observing both arising and passing away. 'Thus is form' (iti rūpaṃ) means: 'Form is thus; form is this much; beyond this, there is no form.' 'Thus is the origin of form' (iti rūpassa samudayo) means thus is the arising of form. By 'passing away' (atthaṅgamo), however, dissolution is intended. In the case of feelings and so on, this is the same method. 'And this, bhikkhus, was spoken by me with reference to that' (idañca pana metaṃ, bhikkhave, sandhāya bhāsitaṃ) means: 'Bhikkhus, that which was spoken by me in Puṇṇaka's Question, beginning with “having comprehended in the world” (saṅkhāya lokasmiṃ), that was spoken with reference to this attainment of fruition.' This is the meaning.

Tattha saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena jānitvā. Lokasminti sattaloke. Paroparānīti uccāvacāni uttamādhamāni. Iñjitanti calitaṃ. Natthi kuhiñci loketi [M 2.0304] lokasmiṃ katthaci ekakkhandhepi ekāyatanepi ekadhātuyāpi ekārammaṇepi natthi. Santoti paccanīkakilesavūpasamena santo. Vidhūmoti [V 2.0296][P 3.0086] kodhadhūmena vigatadhūmo. Evamettha suttante maggekaggatampi kathetvā gāthāya phalasamāpattiyeva kathitāti.

Therein, 'having comprehended' (saṅkhāya) means having known with knowledge. 'In the world' (lokasmiṃ) means in the world of beings. 'The high and the low' (paroparāni) means the lofty and the lowly, the superior and the inferior. 'Agitation' (iñjitaṃ) means trembling. 'There is nothing anywhere in the world' (natthi kuhiñci loke) means it does not exist anywhere in the world—not in a single aggregate, not in a single sense-base, not in a single element, not in a single object. 'Peaceful' (santo) means peaceful through the subsiding of opposing defilements. 'Smokeless' (vidhūmo) means free from the smoke of anger. Thus, here in the sutta text, having taught even the one-pointedness of the path, in the verse, only the attainment of fruition is taught.

2. Pañhabyākaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on Answering Questions

42. Dutiye yo ca tesaṃ tattha tattha, jānāti anudhammatanti yo etesaṃ pañhānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne byākaraṇaṃ jānāti. Catupañhassa kusalo, āhu bhikkhuṃ tathāvidhanti tathāvidhaṃ bhikkhuṃ tesu catūsu pañhesu kusaloti evaṃ vadanti. Durāsado duppasahoti parehi ghaṭṭetuṃ vā abhibhavituṃ vā na sakkā. Gambhīroti sattasīdantaramahāsamuddo viya gambhīro. Duppadhaṃsiyoti dummocāpayo, gahitaggahaṇaṃ vissajjāpetuṃ na sakkāti attho. Atthe anatthe cāti vaḍḍhiyañca avaḍḍhiyañca. Atthābhisamayāti atthasamāgamena. Dhīro paṇḍitoti pavuccatīti dhitisampanno puggalo “paṇḍito aya”nti evaṃ pavuccati.

42. In the second sutta, 'one who knows the associated dhamma in each case' means: a person who knows the explanation of those questions in each and every instance. 'Skilled in the four questions, they call such a monk' means: they say of such a monk, 'He is skilled in those four questions.' 'Hard to approach, hard to overcome' means: he cannot be attacked or overpowered by others. 'Deep' means: deep like the great ocean that lies between the seven mountain ranges. 'Hard to overthrow' means: hard to make release; the meaning is that it is not possible to make him relinquish what he has grasped. 'In meaning and non-meaning' means: in prosperity and adversity. 'Through the comprehension of meaning' means: through the union with the knowledge of the meaning. 'A steadfast one, a wise one, is called' means: a person endowed with steadfastness is called 'a wise one.'

3-4. Kodhagarusuttadvayavaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Two Discourses on One Who Values Anger

43-44. Tatiye kodhagaru na saddhammagarūti kodhaṃ gāravena garuṃ katvā gaṇhāti, na saddhammaṃ, saddhammaṃ pana agāravena lāmakaṃ katvā gaṇhāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

In the third sutta, 'one who values anger, not the true Dhamma' means: one who takes anger with reverence, having made it weighty, but not the true Dhamma; as for the true Dhamma, he takes it without reverence, having made it inferior. This same method applies also to the remaining phrases.

Virūhantīti vaḍḍhanti, sañjātamūlāya vā saddhāya patiṭṭhahanti acalā bhavanti. Catutthe kodhagarutāti kodhamhi sagāravatā. Esa [P 3.0087] nayo sabbattha.

'They grow' means: they increase. Or, they are established by means of faith that has arisen as a root, and they become unshakable. In the fourth sutta, 'valuing anger' means: the state of having reverence for anger. This method applies in all instances.

5. Rohitassasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta

45. Pañcame yatthāti cakkavāḷalokassa ekokāse bhummaṃ. Na cavati na upapajjatīti idaṃ aparāparaṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena gahitaṃ. Gamanenāti padagamanena. Lokassa antanti satthā saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ sandhāya vadati. Ñāteyyantiādīsu ñātabbaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ pattabbanti attho. Iti devaputtena cakkavāḷalokassa anto pucchito, satthārā saṅkhāralokassa kathito[M 2.0305]. So pana “attano [V 2.0297] pañhena saddhiṃ satthu byākaraṇaṃ sametī”ti saññāya sampahaṃsanto acchariyantiādimāha.

45. In the fifth sutta, the word 'where' is a locative, referring to a single location in the spatial world-sphere. The phrase 'does not pass away nor arise' is understood by way of successive death and rebirth. 'By going' means: by going on foot. Regarding 'the end of the world,' the Teacher speaks with reference to the end of the world of formations. In the words beginning with 'should be known,' the meaning is: what should be known, seen, and attained. Thus, the devaputta asked about the end of the spatial world-sphere, and the Teacher explained the end of the world of formations. However, that devaputta, perceiving, 'The Teacher's explanation agrees with my question,' rejoiced and said, 'Wonderful,' and so on.

Daḷhadhammāti daḷhadhanu uttamappamāṇena dhanunā samannāgato. Dhanuggahoti dhanuācariyo. Sikkhitoti dvādasa vassāni dhanusippaṃ sikkhito. Katahatthoti usabhappamāṇepi vālaggaṃ vijjhituṃ samatthabhāvena katahattho. Katūpāsanoti katasarakkhepo dassitasippo. Asanenāti kaṇḍena. Atipāteyyāti atikkameyya. Yāvatā so tālacchādiṃ atikkameyya, tāvatā kālena ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ atikkamāmīti attano javasampattiṃ dasseti.

'Daḷhadhamma' means one endowed with a strong bow, a bow of excellent measure. 'Dhanuggaha' means a teacher of archery. 'Sikkhita' means trained in the art of archery for twelve years. 'Katahattha' means having a practiced hand, in that one is capable of piercing the tip of a hair even at a distance of one usabha. 'Katūpāsana' means one who has shot arrows and demonstrated his skill. 'Asanena' means with an arrow. 'Atipāteyya' means one could surpass. 'In the time it would take for an arrow to surpass the shadow of a palm tree, I can traverse one world-system'—thus he demonstrates his own accomplishment of speed.

Puratthimā samuddā pacchimoti yathā puratthimā samuddā [P 3.0088] pacchimasamuddo dūre, evaṃ me dūre padavītihāro ahosīti vadati. So kira pācīnacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhito pādaṃ pasāretvā pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ atikkamati, puna dutiyapādaṃ pasāretvā paracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ atikkamati. Icchāgatanti icchā eva. Aññatrevāti nippapañcataṃ dasseti. Bhikkhācārakāle kiresa nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotatte mukhaṃ dhovitvā kāle sampatte uttarakurumhi piṇḍāya caritvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ nisinno bhattakiccaṃ karoti, tattha muhuttaṃ vissamitvā puna javati. Vassasatāyukoti tadā dīghāyukakālo hoti, ayaṃ pana vassasatāvasiṭṭhe āyumhi gamanaṃ ārabhi. Vassasatajīvīti taṃ vassasataṃ anantarāyena jīvanto. Antarāyeva kālaṅkatoti cakkavāḷalokassa antaṃ appatvā antarāva mato. So pana tattha kālaṃ katvāpi āgantvā imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe nibbatti.

As the eastern ocean is to the western ocean—that is, as far apart as the eastern ocean is from the western ocean—so vast was the range of my stride; thus he speaks. It is said that standing on the rim of the eastern world-sphere, he would stretch out his foot and cross over the rim of the western world-sphere, then stretch out his second foot and cross beyond the rim of another world-sphere. 'Icchāgata' means by wish alone. 'Aññatreva' indicates the absence of delay. It is said that at the time for the alms-round, he would chew a tooth-stick of nāgalatā creeper, rinse his mouth in Lake Anotatta, and when the time came, he would go to Uttarakuru for alms. Having finished his meal while sitting on the rim of the world-sphere, he would rest there for a moment before swiftly moving on again. 'Vassasatāyuka' means that at that time it was an era of long life; however, this one began his journey when one hundred years of his life remained. 'Vassasatajīvī' means living for that century without obstruction. 'Antarāyeva kālaṅkata' means he died midway, without reaching the end of the world-sphere. However, even after dying there, he was reborn in this very world-sphere.

Appatvāti saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ appatvā. Dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Antakiriyanti pariyantakaraṇaṃ. Kaḷevareti attabhāve. Sasaññimhi samanaketi sasaññe sacittake. Lokanti dukkhasaccaṃ. Lokasamudayanti [P 3.0089] samudayasaccaṃ. Lokanirodhanti nirodhasaccaṃ. Paṭipadanti maggasaccaṃ. Iti “nāhaṃ, āvuso, imāni cattāri saccāni tiṇakaṭṭhādīsu paññapemi, imasmiṃ pana catumahābhūtike kāyasmiṃyeva paññapemī”ti dasseti. Samitāvīti samitapāpo. Nāsīsatīti na pattheti. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

'Not having reached' means not having reached the end of the world of formations. 'Of suffering' means of the suffering of the cycle of existence. 'Making an end' means making an end. 'In the body' means in the existence. 'In one with perception and with mind' means in one with perception and with consciousness. 'The world' means the truth of suffering. 'The cessation of the world' means the truth of cessation. 'The path' means the truth of the path. Thus, it is shown: 'Friend, I do not declare these four truths in things like grass and wood; rather, it is in this very body, which is dependent on the four great elements, that I declare them.' 'One who is pacified' means one whose evil is calmed. 'Does not long for' means does not desire. The sixth has a clear meaning.

7. Suvidūrasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Suvidūra Sutta

47. Sattame [V 2.0298][M 2.0306] suvidūravidūrānīti kenaci pariyāyena anāsannāni hutvā suvidūrāneva vidūrāni. Nabhañca, bhikkhave, pathavī cāti ākāsañca mahāpathavī ca. Tattha kiñcāpi pathavito ākāsaṃ nāma na dūre, dvaṅgulamattepi hoti. Aññamaññaṃ alagganaṭṭhena pana “suvidūravidūre”ti vuttaṃ. Verocanoti sūriyo. Satañca, bhikkhave, dhammoti catusatipaṭṭhānādibhedo sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammo. Asatañca dhammoti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatabhedo assaddhammo.

47. In the seventh, 'very far, far' means that, not being near in any way, they are indeed very far, far. 'The sky, monks, and the earth' means space and the great earth. In this context, although what is called the sky is not far from the earth, and can be even two finger-breadths away, it is nevertheless said to be 'very far, far' because of their nature of not adhering to each other. 'Verocana' means the sun. 'And the Dhamma of the good, monks,' means the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, with distinctions beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness. 'And the Dhamma of the bad' means the false Dhamma, with its sixty-two kinds of wrong views.

Pabhaṅkaroti ālokakaro. Abyāyiko hotīti avigacchanasabhāvo hoti. Sataṃ samāgamoti paṇḍitānaṃ mittasanthavavasena samāgamo. Yāvāpi [P 3.0090] tiṭṭheyyāti yattakaṃ addhānaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Tatheva hotīti tādisova hoti, pakatiṃ na jahati. Khippaṃ hi vetīti sīghaṃ vigacchati.

'Light-maker' means the maker of light. 'Is not transient' means it has a nature of not passing away. 'The company of the good' means association with the wise by way of friendship. 'For however long it might stand' means for whatever duration it might remain. 'It is just so' means it is of such a nature; it does not abandon its intrinsic nature. 'For it quickly passes' means it quickly vanishes.

8. Visākhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Visākha Sutta

48. Aṭṭhame pañcālaputtoti pañcālabrāhmaṇiyā putto. Poriyā vācāyāti paripuṇṇavācāya. Vissaṭṭhāyāti apalibuddhāya. Anelagalāyāti niddosāya ceva agaḷitāya ca apatitapadabyañjanāya. Pariyāpannāyāti vivaṭṭapariyāpannāya. Anissitāyāti vaṭṭaṃ anissitāya. Vivaṭṭanissitameva katvā katheti, vaṭṭanissitaṃ katvā na kathetīti ayamettha adhippāyo.

48. In the eighth, 'Pañcālaputta' means the son of the brahmin woman Pañcāla. 'With urbane speech' means with complete speech. 'Clear' means unhindered. 'Without impediment' means both faultless and not faltering, with words and consonants not being dropped. 'Included' means included in that which is free from the round of rebirth. 'Unattached' means not dependent on the round of rebirth. He speaks having made it dependent only on that which is free from the round; he does not speak having made it dependent on the round—this is the intention here.

Nābhāsamānanti na akathentaṃ. Amataṃ padanti nibbānapadaṃ. Bhāsayeti obhāseyya. Jotayeti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paggaṇhe isinaṃ dhajanti abbhuggataṭṭhena navalokuttaradhammo isīnaṃ dhajo nāma vuccati, tameva paggaṇheyya ukkhipeyya, uccaṃ katvā katheyyāti attho. Navalokuttaradhammadīpakaṃ subhāsitaṃ dhajo etesanti subhāsitadhajā. Isayoti buddhādayo ariyā. Dhammo hi isinaṃ dhajoti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva lokuttaradhammo isīnaṃ dhajo nāmāti.

'Not speaking' means one who is not speaking. 'The deathless state' means the state of Nibbāna. 'One should make it shine' means one should illuminate. 'One should light it up' is a synonym for that very word. 'One should raise the banner of the seers' means: because of its meaning of having risen up, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is called the banner of the seers; one should extol just that, raise it up, and speak highly of it—this is the meaning. 'Those with the banner of the well-spoken' means those for whom the well-spoken word which illuminates the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is their banner. 'Seers' means the noble ones, beginning with the Buddha. 'For the Dhamma is the banner of the seers' means: in the same way as stated before, the supramundane Dhamma is called the banner of the seers.

9. Vipallāsasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Distortions Discourse

49. Navame [V 2.0299][M 2.0307] saññāvipallāsāti saññāya vipallatthabhāvā, catasso viparītasaññāyoti attho. Sesapadadvayepi [P 3.0091] eseva nayo. Anicce, bhikkhave, niccanti saññāvipallāsoti anicce vatthusmiṃ “niccaṃ ida”nti evaṃ gahetvā uppajjanakasaññā, saññāvipallāsoti attho. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

49. In the ninth, 'perversion of perception' means the state of perception being perverted; the meaning is the four inverted perceptions. The same method applies to the remaining two terms as well. 'The perversion of perception, monks, of perceiving the impermanent as permanent' means the perception that arises from grasping an impermanent object thus, 'This is permanent'; this is the meaning of 'perversion of perception'. The meaning in all instances should be understood by this method.

Anattani ca attāti anattani “attā”ti evaṃsaññinoti attho. Micchādiṭṭhihatāti na kevalaṃ saññinova, saññāya viya uppajjamānāya micchādiṭṭhiyāpi hatā. Khittacittāti te saññādiṭṭhiyo viya uppajjamānena khittena cittena samannāgatā. Visaññinoti desanāmattametaṃ, viparītasaññācittadiṭṭhinoti attho. Te yogayuttā mārassāti te mārassa yoge yuttā nāma honti. Ayogakkheminoti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbānaṃ appattā. Sattāti puggalā. Buddhāti catusaccabuddhā. Imaṃ dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ. Sacittaṃ paccaladdhāti sakaṃ cittaṃ paṭilabhitvā. Aniccato dakkhunti aniccabhāvena addasaṃsu. Asubhataddasunti asubhaṃ asubhatoyeva addasaṃsu. Sammādiṭṭhisamādānāti gahitasammādassanā. Sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ upaccagunti sakalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samatikkantā.

'And 'self in what is not-self'' means those who perceive thus: 'self' in what is not-self. 'Destroyed by wrong view' means they are destroyed not only by perception, but also by wrong view which arises in a similar way. 'With distracted minds' means they are possessed of a mind that is distracted and agitated, just as perception and wrong view arise. 'Without perception' is merely a term of the teaching; the meaning is having perverted perception, mind, and view. 'They are yoked to Māra' means they are indeed yoked to Māra's yoke. 'Not secure from the yokes' means not having attained Nibbāna, which is safe from the four yokes. 'Beings' means individuals. 'Buddhas' means those awakened to the four truths. 'This Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the four truths. 'Having recovered their own mind' means having regained their own mind. 'They saw as impermanent' means they saw it as impermanent. 'They saw the unattractive as unattractive' means they saw the unattractive as purely unattractive. 'Having undertaken right view' means having adopted right view. 'They overcame all suffering' means they completely transcended all suffering of the round.

10. Upakkilesasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Defilements

50. Dasame [P 3.0092] upakkilesāti virocituṃ adatvā upakkiliṭṭhabhāvakaraṇena upakkilesā. Mahikāti himaṃ. Dhūmo rajoti dhūmo ca rajo ca. Rāhūti purimā tayo asampattaupakkilesā, rāhu pana sampattaupakkilesavasena kathitoti veditabbo. Samaṇabrāhmaṇā na tapanti na bhāsanti na virocantīti guṇappatāpena na tapanti, guṇobhāsena na bhāsanti, guṇavirocanena na virocanti. Surāmerayapānā appaṭiviratāti pañcavidhāya surāya catubbidhassa merayassa ca pānato aviratā.

50. In the tenth, 'defilements' means they are defilements because, by causing a state of being defiled, they do not allow things to shine. 'Mist' means frost. 'Smoke and dust' means smoke and dust. 'Rāhu': the former three are defilements that do not reach their object, whereas Rāhu, it should be understood, is spoken of as a defilement that does reach it. 'Ascetics and brahmins do not glow, do not shine, do not radiate' means they do not glow with the power of virtue, do not shine with the brightness of virtue, do not radiate with the radiance of virtue. 'Not abstaining from drinking fermented and distilled drinks' means not abstaining from drinking the five kinds of fermented drinks and the four kinds of distilled drinks.

Avijjānivutāti [V 2.0300][M 2.0308] avijjāya nivāritā pihitā. Piyarūpābhinandinoti piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ abhinandamānā tussamānā. Sādiyantīti gaṇhanti. Aviddasūti andhabālā. Sanettikāti taṇhāyotteneva sayottā. Kaṭasinti attabhāvaṃ. Ghoranti kakkhaḷaṃ. Imasmiṃ suttepi gāthāsupi vaṭṭameva kathitanti.

'Enveloped by ignorance' means hindered and covered by ignorance. 'Delighting in pleasing forms' means rejoicing and taking pleasure in forms that are pleasing and agreeable. 'They consent' means they grasp. 'The ignorant' means blind fools. 'With a leash' means they are leashed by the leash of craving itself. 'The charnel ground' means personal existence. 'Terrible' means harsh. In this discourse, and in the verses, only the round of existence is discussed.

Rohitassavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Rohitassa, the Fifth.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is finished.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Puññābhisandavaggo

(6) 1. The Chapter on Streams of Merit

1. Paṭhamapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Streams of Merit

51. Dutiyassa [V 2.0301][M 2.0309] paṭhame puññābhisandāti puññassa abhisandā, puññappattiyoti attho. Kusalābhisandāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Te [P 3.0093] panete sukhaṃ āharantīti sukhassāhārā. Suṭṭhu aggānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ dāyakāti sovaggikā. Sukho nesaṃ vipākoti sukhavipākā. Sagge upapatti saggo, saggāya saṃvattantīti saggasaṃvattanikā. Cīvaraṃ paribhuñjamānoti cīvaratthāya vatthaṃ labhitvā sūcisuttādīnaṃ abhāvena taṃ nikkhipantopi karontopi pārupantopi jiṇṇakāle paccattharaṇaṃ karontopi paccattharitumpi asakkuṇeyyaṃ bhūmattharaṇaṃ karontopi bhūmattharaṇassa ananucchavikaṃ phāletvā pādapuñchanaṃ karontopi “paribhuñjamāno”tveva vuccati. Yadā pana “pādapuñchanampi na sakkā ida”nti sammajjitvā chaḍḍitaṃ hoti, tadā paribhuñjamāno nāma na hoti. Appamāṇaṃ cetosamādhinti arahattaphalasamādhiṃ. Appamāṇo tassa puññābhisandoti iminā dāyakassa puññacetanāya appamāṇataṃ katheti. Tassa hi “khīṇāsavo me cīvaraṃ paribhuñjatī”ti punappunaṃ anussaraṇavasena pavattā puññacetanā appamāṇā hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Piṇḍapātādīsu pana yo piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā sattāhampi teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na paribhuñjati, so sattāhampi taṃyeva piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjamāno nāma hoti. Ekasmiṃ pana senāsane rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīsu caṅkamantopi yāva taṃ senāsanaṃ pahāya aññaṃ na gaṇhāti, tāva paribhuñjamāno nāma hoti. Ekena pana bhesajjena byādhimhi vūpasante yāva aññaṃ bhesajjaṃ na paribhuñjati, tāvadeva paribhuñjamāno nāma hoti.

51. In the first sutta of the second fifty, 'accumulations of merit' (`puññābhisandā`) means accumulations of merit, occurrences of merit. `Kusalābhisandā` (accumulations of the wholesome) is a synonym for that very term. Furthermore, those bring happiness, therefore they are bringers of happiness (`sukhassāhārā`). They are givers of excellent, supreme things such as forms, therefore they are conducive to heaven (`sovaggikā`). Their result is happiness, therefore they have happy results (`sukhavipākā`). Rebirth in a heavenly realm is `sagga`; they lead to a heavenly realm, therefore they are conducive to a heavenly realm (`saggasaṃvattanikā`). As for 'one who is using a robe' (`cīvaraṃ paribhuñjamāno`): having received cloth for the sake of a robe, but due to the absence of a needle, thread, and so on, one who sets it aside; one who makes it; one who wears it; when it is old, one who makes it a bed cover; a worn-out robe that one is unable to use as a bed cover, one who makes it a ground covering; a worn-out robe that is unsuitable for a ground covering, having torn it, one who makes it a foot-wiper—such a one is indeed called 'one who is using'. However, when, thinking, 'It is not possible to make even a foot-wiper with this,' it is swept up and discarded, then one is not called 'one who is using'. 'Immeasurable concentration of mind' (`appamāṇaṃ cetosamādhi`) means the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship. By 'Immeasurable is his accumulation of merit' (`appamāṇo tassa puññābhisando`), it states the immeasurability of the donor's meritorious volition. For that donor, the meritorious volition that arises by way of repeatedly recollecting, 'One whose cankers are destroyed is using my robe,' becomes immeasurable. This was said in reference to that. Furthermore, in the case of almsfood and so on: one who, having consumed almsfood, sustains himself for seven days with just that and does not consume any other, he is called 'one who is using that very almsfood' for seven days. Furthermore, in a single lodging, even while doing walking meditation in places for the night, places for the day, and so on, for as long as one does not abandon that lodging and take another, for that long one is called 'one who is using' it. Furthermore, with a single medicine, when the illness has subsided, for as long as one does not use another medicine, for just that long is one called 'one who is using' it.

Bahubheravanti [P 3.0094] bahūhi bheravārammaṇehi samannāgataṃ. Ratanavarānanti sattannampi vararatanānaṃ. Ālayanti nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Puthū savantīti bahukā hutvā sandamānā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

'Bahubheravaṃ' means endowed with many terrifying objects. 'Ratanavarānaṃ' means of the seven excellent jewels. 'Ālayaṃ' means a dwelling place. 'Puthū savanti' means being many, they flow. The rest here is clear.

2. Dutiyapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Accumulations of Merit

52. Dutiye [V 2.0302][M 2.0310] ariyakantehīti maggaphalasampayuttehi. Tāni hi ariyānaṃ kantāni honti piyāni manāpāni. Sesaṃ suttante tāva yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.124 ādayo) vuttameva.

52. In the second [discourse], 'ariyakantehi' means by [virtues] associated with the path and its fruit. For those are indeed cherished, dear, and agreeable to the noble ones. As for the rest, whatever should be said in the Sutta, that has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.124 ff.).

Gāthāsu pana saddhāti sotāpannassa saddhā adhippetā. Sīlampi sotāpannassa sīlameva. Ujubhūtañca dassananti kāyavaṅkādīnaṃ abhāvena khīṇāsavassa dassanaṃ ujubhūtadassanaṃ nāma. Āhūti kathayanti. Pasādanti buddhadhammasaṅghesu pasādaṃ. Dhammadassananti catusaccadhammadassanaṃ.

But in the verses, by 'saddhā' is meant the faith of a stream-enterer. 'Sīla' also is the virtue of a stream-enterer. Regarding 'Ujubhūtañca dassanaṃ': the vision of one whose taints are destroyed is called 'straightened vision' (ujubhūtadassana) due to the absence of bodily crookedness and so on. 'Āhu' means they say. 'Pasādaṃ' means confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. 'Dhammadassanaṃ' means the vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

3. Paṭhamasaṃvāsasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the First Discourse on Living Together

53. Tatiye sambahulāpi kho gahapatī ca gahapatāniyo cāti bahukā gahapatayo ca gahapatāniyo ca āvāhavivāhakaraṇatthāya gacchantā tameva maggaṃ paṭipannā honti. Saṃvāsāti sahavāsā ekatovāsā. Chavo chavāyāti guṇamaraṇena matattā chavo guṇamaraṇeneva matāya chavāya saddhiṃ. Deviyā saddhinti guṇehi devibhūtāya saddhiṃ. Dussīloti nissīlo. Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo. Akkosakaparibhāsakoti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosako, bhayaṃ dassetvā santajjanena paribhāsako. Evaṃ [P 3.0095] sabbattha attho veditabbo.

53. In the third [discourse], 'sambahulāpi kho gahapatī ca gahapatāniyo cā' means: many householders and female householders, traveling for the purpose of arranging marriages, proceed along that very path. 'Saṃvāsā' means living together, residing in one place. 'Chavo chavāya' means a male corpse with a female corpse; that is, a man dead through the death of virtue with a woman dead through the death of virtue. 'Deviyā saddhiṃ' means together with one who has become like a goddess through virtues. 'Dussīlo' means without virtue. 'Pāpadhammo' means of an evil nature. 'Akkosakaparibhāsako' means one who abuses with the ten grounds for abuse and reviles by showing danger and with intimidation. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Kadariyāti thaddhamaccharino. Jānipatayoti jayampatikā. Vadaññūti yācakānaṃ vacanassa atthaṃ jānanti. Saññatāti sīlasaṃyamena samannāgatā. Dhammajīvinoti dhamme ṭhatvā jīvikaṃ kappentīti dhammajīvino. Atthāsaṃ pacurā hontīti vaḍḍhisaṅkhātā atthā etesaṃ bahū honti. Phāsukaṃ upajāyatīti aññamaññaṃ phāsuvihāro jāyati. Kāmakāminoti kāme kāmayamānā.

'Kadariya' means obstinately miserly. 'Jānipatayo' means husband and wife. 'Vadaññū' means they understand the meaning of the speech of beggars. 'Saññatā' means endowed with restraint through morality. 'Dhammajīvino' means those who maintain their livelihood by abiding in the Dhamma. 'Atthāsaṃ pacurā honti' means for them, benefits, known as increase, are many. 'Phāsukaṃ upajāyati' means a comfortable abiding arises for one another. 'Kāmakāmino' means those who desire sensual pleasures.

4. Dutiyasaṃvāsasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Living Together

54. Catutthe kammapathavasena desanā pavattitā. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Imesu pana dvīsupi suttesu agārikapaṭipadā kathitā. Sotāpannasakadāgāmīnampi vaṭṭati.

54. In the fourth [discourse], the teaching was delivered by way of the course of action. The rest is just the same. Furthermore, in these two discourses, the householder's practice is taught. It is also suitable for stream-enterers and once-returners.

5-6. Samajīvīsuttadvayavaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Harmonious Living

55-56. Pañcame [V 2.0303][M 2.0311] tenupasaṅkamīti kimatthaṃ upasaṅkami? Anuggaṇhanatthaṃ. Tathāgato hi taṃ raṭṭhaṃ pāpuṇanto imesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthāya pāpuṇāti. Nakulapitā kira pañca jātisatāni tathāgatassa pitā ahosi, pañca jātisatāni mahāpitā, pañca jātisatāni cūḷapitā. Nakulamātāpi pañca jātisatāni tathāgatassa mātā ahosi, pañca jātisatāni mahāmātā, pañca jātisatāni cūḷamātā. Te satthu diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya puttasinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā “hantāta, hantātā”ti vacchakaṃ disvā vacchagiddhinī gāvī viya viravamānā upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpannā jātā. Nivesane [P 3.0096] pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āsanāni sadā paññattāneva honti. Iti bhagavā tesaṃ anuggaṇhanatthāya upasaṅkami. Aticaritāti atikkamitā. Abhisamparāyañcāti paraloke ca. Samasaddhāti saddhāya samā ekasadisā. Sīlādīsupi eseva nayo. Chaṭṭhaṃ kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ desitaṃ. Sesamettha tādisameva.

In the fifth [discourse], regarding 'tena upasaṅkami' (he approached): for what purpose did he approach? For the purpose of favoring them. Indeed, the Tathāgata, arriving in that country, arrives for the purpose of favoring only these two. It is said that Nakula’s father had been the Tathāgata's father for five hundred lifetimes, his elder paternal uncle for five hundred lifetimes, and his younger paternal uncle for five hundred lifetimes. Nakula’s mother had likewise been the Tathāgata's mother for five hundred lifetimes, his elder maternal aunt for five hundred lifetimes, and his younger maternal aunt for five hundred lifetimes. From the time they saw the Teacher, they regained affection for a son and, calling out, 'Dear son, dear son!' like a cow crying out for her calf upon seeing it, they approached and became stream-enterers at the very first sight. In their home, seats for five hundred monks are always prepared. Thus, the Blessed One approached for the purpose of favoring them. 'Aticaritā' means transgressed. 'Abhisamparāyañca' means and in the next world. 'Samasaddhā' means equal and exactly the same in faith. The same method applies to morality and so forth. The sixth was taught solely to monks. The remainder here is just the same.

7. Suppavāsāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Suppavāsā Sutta

57. Sattame pajjanikanti tassa nigamassa nāmaṃ. Koliyānanti kolarājakulānaṃ. Āyuṃ kho pana datvāti āyudānaṃ datvā. Āyussa bhāginī hotīti āyubhāgapaṭilābhinī hoti, āyuṃ vā bhajanikā hoti, āyuppaṭilābhinīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

57. In the seventh discourse, 'Pajjanika' is the name of that market town. 'Of the Koliyans' means of the Koliya royal families. 'Having given life' means having given the gift of life. 'She becomes a partaker of life' means she becomes one who obtains a share of life, or she is one who causes life to arise; the meaning is she is one who obtains life. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Rasasā upetanti rasena upetaṃ rasasampannaṃ. Ujjugatesūti kāyavaṅkādirahitattā ujukameva gatesu khīṇāsavesu. Caraṇūpapannesūti pañcadasahi caraṇadhammehi samannāgatesu. Mahaggatesūti mahattaṃ gatesu. Khīṇāsavānaññevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Puññena puññaṃ saṃsandamānāti puññena saddhiṃ puññaṃ ghaṭayamānā. Mahapphalā lokavidūna vaṇṇitāti evarūpā dānasaṅkhātā dakkhiṇā tividhalokaṃ viditaṃ katvā ṭhitattā lokavidūnaṃ buddhānaṃ vaṇṇitā, buddhehi pasatthāti attho. Yaññamanussarantāti [P 3.0097] yaññaṃ dānaṃ anussarantā. Vedajātāti tuṭṭhijātā.

'Endowed with flavor' means endowed with flavor, rich in flavor. 'To the straight-going' means to the taint-destroyed ones who have gone straight, because they are free from bodily crookedness and the like. 'To those endowed with conduct' means to those endowed with the fifteen kinds of conduct. 'To the greatly gone' means to those who have reached greatness. This is a name for the taint-destroyed ones only. 'Merit merging with merit' means later merit connecting with prior merit. 'Of great fruit, praised by the knowers of the world' means such a gift, called an offering, is praised by the Buddhas, who are knowers of the world because they abide having made the threefold world known; it is extolled by the Buddhas. This is the meaning. 'Remembering the sacrifice' means remembering the gift. 'With joy arisen' means having become joyful.

8. Sudattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Sudatta Sutta

58. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0304][M 2.0312] saññatānanti kāyavācāhi saṃyatānaṃ. Paradattabhojinanti parehi dinnameva bhuñjitvā yāpentānaṃ. Kālenāti yuttappattakālena. Sakkacca dadātīti sahatthā sakkāraṃ katvā dadāti. Cattāri ṭhānāni anuppavecchatīti cattāri kāraṇāni anuppaveseti dadāti. Yasavā hotīti mahāparivāro hoti. Navamaṃ kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kathitaṃ. Sesamettha tādisameva.

58. In the eighth discourse, 'of the self-controlled' means of those restrained in body and speech. 'Of those who live on what is given by others' means of those who sustain themselves by consuming only what is given by others. 'In due time' means at a suitable and proper time. 'Gives respectfully' means one gives with one's own hand, having shown respect. 'Furnishes the four grounds' means one gives the four causes. 'Becomes famous' means one has a large retinue. The ninth discourse was taught solely to the monks. The remainder here is the same as that.

10. Gihisāmīcisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Gihisāmīci Sutta

60. Dasame gihisāmīcipaṭipadanti gihīnaṃ anucchavikaṃ paṭipattiṃ. Paccupaṭṭhito hotīti atiharitvā dātukāmatāya patiupaṭṭhito hoti upagato, bhikkhusaṅghassa cīvaraṃ detīti attho.

60. In the tenth discourse, 'the proper practice of a householder' means the practice suitable for householders. 'Is present' means having brought it forward, mindfulness is established with the desire to give; having approached, one gives a robe to the Saṅgha of monks. This is the meaning.

Upaṭṭhitāti upaṭṭhāyako. Tesaṃ divā ca ratto cāti ye evaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahanti, tesaṃ divā ca rattiñca pariccāgavasena ca anussaraṇavasena ca sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati. Saggañca kamatiṭṭhānanti tādiso ca bhaddakaṃ kammaṃ katvā saggaṭṭhānaṃ upagacchati. Imesu catūsupi suttesu āgāriyapaṭipadā kathitā. Sotāpannasakadāgāmīnampi vaṭṭati.

'One who has attended' means a supporter.
