Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo paṭhamaṃ vutto kappo, so dve vāre gaṇetvā ekena guṇena dve kappā honti, dutiyena cattāro, puna te cattāro kappāti imehi catūhi guṇehi guṇitā ekena guṇena aṭṭha honti, dutiyena soḷasa, tatiyena dvattiṃsa, catutthena catusaṭṭhīti. Evamidha paṇītajjhānavasena catusaṭṭhi kappā gahitāti veditabbā. Pañca kappasatānīti idaṃ paṇītasseva upapattijjhānassa vasena vuttaṃ. Vehapphalesu vā paṭhamajjhānabhūmiādīsu viya tiṇṇaṃ brahmalokānaṃ abhāvato ettakameva āyuppamāṇaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Two eons”—here too, the second jhāna is threefold in the manner already stated. Among them, for those born through the superior state, the lifespan is eight eons; for those of the middling state, four; and for the inferior, two. This was said in reference to that. “Four eons”—here, the meaning should be understood by also bringing in what was stated earlier as “an eon, two eons.” The term ‘kappa’ is also a name for a multiple. Therefore, “an eon, two eons, four eons”—this is the meaning to be understood here. This is what is meant: the first-mentioned eon, when taken twice, becomes two eons by one multiple, and four by a second. Then again, those four eons, when multiplied by these four multiples, become eight by the first multiple, sixteen by the second, thirty-two by the third, and sixty-four by the fourth. Thus, it should be understood that here sixty-four eons are taken on account of the superior jhāna. “Five hundred eons”—this is stated on account of the superior rebirth-producing jhāna itself. In the Vehapphala realm, since there are not three Brahmā worlds as there are in the planes of the first jhāna and so on, the lifespan is just this much. Therefore, it is stated thus.

4. Dutiyanānākaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Second Discourse on Diversity

124. Catutthe [M 2.0333] rūpameva rūpagataṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Aniccatotiādīsu hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccato, ābādhaṭṭhena rogato, anto padussanaṭṭhena gaṇḍato, anupaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sallato, sadukkhaṭṭhena aghato, sampīḷanaṭṭhena ābādhato, avidheyyaṭṭhena parato, palujjanaṭṭhena palokato, nissattaṭṭhena suññato, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattato. Ettha ca “aniccato palokato”ti [V 2.0329] dvīhi padehi aniccalakkhaṇaṃ kathitaṃ, “suññato anattato”ti dvīhi anattalakkhaṇaṃ, sesehi dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Samanupassatīti ñāṇena passati. Evaṃ pañcakkhandhe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā passanto tayo magge tīṇi phalāni sacchikaroti. Suddhāvāsānaṃ [P 3.0126] devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjatīti tattha ṭhito catutthajjhānaṃ bhāvetvā upapajjati.

124. In the fourth sutta, only form is what has gone to form. The same method applies to the remaining sections as well. Regarding 'impermanent' and so on: through the meaning of non-existence after having been, it is 'impermanent'; through the meaning of sickness, it is 'disease'; through the meaning of internal corruption, it is 'a boil'; through the meaning of being pierced, it is 'a dart'; through the meaning of being full of suffering, it is 'misery'; through the meaning of oppression, it is 'affliction'; through the meaning of uncontrollability, it is 'other'; through the meaning of disintegration, it is 'perishable'; through the meaning of insubstantiality, it is 'empty'; through the meaning of ungovernability, it is 'not-self.' And here, it should be understood that the characteristic of impermanence is stated by the two terms 'impermanent' and 'perishable,' the characteristic of not-self is stated by the two terms 'empty' and 'not-self,' and the characteristic of suffering is stated by the remaining terms. 'He contemplates' means he sees with knowledge. Thus, by contemplating the three characteristics applied to the five aggregates, one realizes three paths and three fruits. 'He is reborn in the company of the Pure Abode devas' means that, established therein, he develops the fourth jhāna and is reborn there.

5-6. Mettāsuttadvayavaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Loving-Kindness

125-126. Pañcame paṭhamajjhānavasena mettā, dutiyādivasena karuṇādayo dassitā. Chaṭṭhaṃ catutthe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

125-126. In the fifth, loving-kindness is shown by way of the first jhāna, and compassion and the others by way of the second jhāna and so on. The sixth should be understood in the same way as explained in the fourth.

7. Paṭhamatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Tathāgata's Marvelous Qualities

127. Sattame pātubhāvāti pātubhāvena. Kucchiṃ okkamatīti ettha kucchiṃ okkanto hotīti attho. Okkante hi tasmiṃ evaṃ hoti, na okkamamāne. Appamāṇoti vuḍḍhippamāṇo, vipuloti attho. Uḷāroti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Devānaṃ devānubhāvanti ettha devānaṃ ayamānubhāvo – nivatthavatthassa pabhā dvādasa yojanāni pharati, tathā sarīrassa, tathā vimānassa, taṃ atikkamitvāti attho. Lokantarikāti tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ antarā ekeko lokantariko hoti, tiṇṇaṃ sakaṭacakkānaṃ pattānaṃ vā aññamaññaṃ āhacca ṭhapitānaṃ majjhe okāso viya. So pana lokantarikanirayo parimāṇato aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇo hoti. Aghāti [M 2.0334] niccavivaṭā. Asaṃvutāti heṭṭhāpi appatiṭṭhā. Andhakārāti tamabhūtā. Andhakāratimisāti cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇato andhabhāvakaraṇatimisāya samannāgatā. Tattha kira cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na jāyati. Evaṃmahiddhikānanti candimasūriyā kira ekappahāreneva tīsu dīpesu paññāyanti, evaṃmahiddhikā. Ekekāya disāya [P 3.0127] nava nava yojanasatasahassāni andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokaṃ dassenti, evaṃmahānubhāvā. Ābhā nānubhontīti pabhā nappahonti. Te kira cakkavāḷapabbatassa vemajjhena caranti cakkavāḷapabbatañca atikkamitvā lokantaranirayā. Tasmā tesaṃ tattha ābhā nappahonti.

127. In the seventh, 'from manifestation' means by manifestation. 'Descends into the womb' here means that he has descended into the womb. For when he has descended, it is so, not while descending. 'Immeasurable' means great in measure; vast is the meaning. 'Splendid' is a synonym for that. Here, 'the divine majesty of the devas' means this is the majesty of the devas—the radiance of a worn garment spreads for twelve yojanas, likewise that of the body, and likewise that of the celestial mansion; the meaning is 'surpassing that'. 'The inter-world spaces' means: between every three world-systems there is one inter-world space, like the space in the middle of the felloes of three cart-wheels placed touching one another. That inter-world hell, moreover, is eight thousand yojanas in extent. 'Agha' means always open. 'Unenclosed' means without foundation below. 'Darkness' means utterly dark. 'Blinding darkness' means endowed with a darkness that causes blindness by preventing the arising of eye-consciousness. There, it is said, eye-consciousness does not arise. 'Of such great power' means: the moon and sun, it is said, appear in the three continents simultaneously; of such great power are they. In each direction, they dispel darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas and show light; of such great might are they. 'Their radiance does not reach' means their light is not sufficient. They, it is said, travel through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and the inter-world hells are beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Therefore, their radiance does not reach there.

Yepi tattha sattāti yepi tasmiṃ lokantaramahāniraye sattā upapannā. Kiṃ pana kammaṃ katvā [V 2.0330] tattha uppajjantīti? Bhāriyaṃ dāruṇaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānañca upari aparādhaṃ, aññañca divase divase pāṇavadhādisāhasikakammaṃ katvā uppajjanti tambapaṇṇidīpe abhayacoranāgacorādayo viya. Tesaṃ attabhāvo tigāvutiko hoti, vaggulīnaṃ viya dīghanakhā honti. Te rukkhe vagguliyo viya nakhehi cakkavāḷapabbatapāde lagganti. Yadā saṃsappantā aññamaññassa hatthapāsagatā honti, atha “bhakkho no laddho”ti maññamānā tattha byāvaṭā viparivattitvā lokasandhārakaudake patanti, vāte paharantepi madhukaphalāni viya chijjitvā udake patanti, patitamattāva accantakhāre udake piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya vilīyanti. Aññepi kira bho santi sattāti bho yathā mayaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavāma, evaṃ aññepi kira sattā idaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanatthāya idhūpapannāti taṃdivasaṃ passanti. Ayaṃ pana obhāso ekayāgupānamattampi na tiṭṭhati. Yāvatā niddāyitvā pabuddho ārammaṇaṃ vibhāveti[P 3.0128], tattakaṃ kālaṃ hoti. Dīghabhāṇakā pana “accharāsaṅghātamattameva vijjuobhāso viya niccharitvā kiṃ idanti bhaṇantānaṃyeva antaradhāyatī”ti vadanti.

“Those beings there” refers to those who have been reborn in that great inter-world hell. But what deeds have they done to be reborn there? By committing grave and cruel offenses against parents, righteous ascetics, and brahmins, and other daily violent acts like killing living beings, they are reborn there, like the robbers Abhaya and Nāga and others on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their bodies are three gāvutas in size, with long nails like bats. They cling to the feet of the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their nails like bats on trees. When they crawl and come within each other's reach, thinking, “We have found prey,” they struggle and roll about, then fall into the world-supporting waters. Even when struck by the wind, they break off like madhuka fruits and fall into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve like lumps of flour in the extremely caustic water. “And there are other beings, sirs”: on that day they see them, thinking, “Sirs, just as we experience great suffering, so too, it seems, other beings have been reborn here to experience this suffering.” But this radiance does not last even as long as it takes to drink one serving of rice gruel. It lasts only as long as it takes for one who has woken from sleep to discern an object. The Dīgha reciters, however, say, “For just the duration of a finger-snap, it flashes forth like a bolt of lightning and vanishes even as they are saying, ‘What is this?’”

8. Dutiyatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Tathāgata’s Marvelous Qualities

128. Aṭṭhame taṇhādiṭṭhīhi allīyitabbaṭṭhena ālayoti pañca kāmaguṇā, sakalameva vā vaṭṭaṃ. Āramanti etthāti ārāmo, ālayo ārāmo etissāti ālayārāmā. Ālaye ratāti ālayaratā[M 2.0335]. Ālaye sammuditāti ālayasammuditā. Anālaye dhammeti ālayapaṭipakkhe vivaṭṭūpanissite ariyadhamme. Sussūsatīti sotukāmo hoti. Sotaṃ odahatīti sotaṃ ṭhapeti. Aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapetīti ājānanatthāya cittaṃ paccupaṭṭhapeti. Mānoti maññanā, maññitabbaṭṭhena vā sakalaṃ vaṭṭameva. Mānavinaye dhammeti mānavinayadhamme. Upasamapaṭipakkho anupasamo, anupasantaṭṭhena vā vaṭṭameva anupasamo nāma. Opasamiketi upasamakare vivaṭṭūpanissite. Avijjāya gatā samannāgatāti avijjāgatā. Avijjaṇḍakosena pariyonaddhattā aṇḍaṃ viya bhūtāti aṇḍabhūtā. Samantato onaddhāti pariyonaddhā. Avijjāvinayeti avijjāvinayo vuccati arahattaṃ, taṃnissite dhamme desiyamāneti attho. Iti [P 3.0129] imasmiṃ sutte catūsu ṭhānesu vaṭṭaṃ, catūsu vivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

128. In the eighth, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called 'ālaya' (attachment) in the sense that they are to be clung to by craving and wrong views; or, it is the entire cycle of existence. They delight in this, thus it is a delight (ārāma). One for whom attachment is a delight is 'ālayārāmā'. One who delights in attachment is 'ālayaratā'. One who rejoices in attachment is 'ālayasammuditā'. 'The Dhamma that is without attachment' means the noble Dhamma which is the opposite of attachment, supportive of the unbinding. 'Sussūsati' means one is desirous of hearing. 'Sotaṃ odahati' means one applies the ear. 'Aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhapeti' means one establishes the mind for the purpose of final knowledge. 'Māna' is conceiving; or, in the sense of that which is to be conceived, it is the entire cycle of existence. 'The Dhamma for the removal of conceit' means the Dhamma that removes conceit. The opposite of peace is non-peace (anupasamo); or, in the sense of being unpeaceful, the cycle of existence itself is called 'anupasamo'. 'Opasamike' means that which brings peace, supportive of the unbinding. 'Avijjāgatā' means gone to and possessed by ignorance. Because of being enveloped by the shell of ignorance, they are like an egg, thus 'aṇḍabhūtā'. Bound all around, thus 'pariyonaddhā'. 'The removal of ignorance': the removal of ignorance is said to be Arahantship; the meaning is when the Dhamma based on that is being taught. Thus, in this sutta, the cycle of existence is spoken of in four places, and the unbinding in four.

9. Ānandaacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Marvelous Qualities of Ānanda

129. Navame [V 2.0331] bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāyāti ye bhagavantaṃ passitukāmā theraṃ upasaṅkamanti, ye vā “āyasmā kirānando samantapāsādiko abhirūpo dassanīyo bahussuto saṅghasobhano”ti therassa guṇe sutvā āgacchanti, te sandhāya “bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamatī”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Attamanāti “savanena no dassanaṃ sametī”ti sakamanā tuṭṭhacittā. Dhammanti “kacci, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci yonisomanasikārakammaṃ karotha, ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ pūrethā”ti evarūpaṃ paṭisanthāradhammaṃ. Tattha bhikkhunīsu “kacci, bhaginiyo, aṭṭha garudhamme samādāya vattathā”ti idampi nānākaraṇaṃ hoti. Upāsakesu “svāgataṃ, upāsaka, na te kiñci sīsaṃ vā aṅgaṃ vā rujjati, arogā te puttabhātaro”ti na evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti, evaṃ pana karoti – “kathaṃ, upāsakā, tīṇi saraṇāni pañca sīlāni rakkhatha, māsassa aṭṭha uposathe karotha, mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhānavattaṃ pūretha, dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇe paṭijaggathā”ti. Upāsikāsupi eseva nayo.

129. In the ninth sutta, the phrase 'the assembly of monks approaches Ānanda to see him' refers to those who, wishing to see the Blessed One, approach the elder, or those who, having heard of the elder’s qualities—'Venerable Ānanda is universally pleasing, handsome, inspiring, learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha'—come because of that. This is the method throughout. 'Attamanā' means being delighted in mind, thinking, 'Our hearing is met by seeing.' 'Dhamma' refers to the Dhamma of friendly inquiry, such as asking: 'Friend, are you keeping well? Are you managing? Are you practicing appropriate attention? Are you fulfilling your duties toward teachers and preceptors?' Therein, with regard to nuns, this distinction is also made: 'Sisters, are you observing the eight weighty rules?' With regard to male lay devotees, one does not make a friendly inquiry in this way: 'Welcome, lay follower! Is your head or any limb in pain? Are your sons and brothers healthy?' Instead, one does it in this way: 'Lay followers, how is it? Do you observe the three refuges and the five precepts? Do you observe the eight Uposatha days of the month? Do you fulfill your duties toward your parents? Do you attend to righteous ascetics and brahmins?' This same method applies to female lay followers.

10. Cakkavattiacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Marvelous Qualities of a Wheel-Turning Monarch

130. Dasame khattiyaparisāti abhisittā anabhisittā ca khattiyā[P 3.0130]. Te hi kira “rājā cakkavattī nāma abhirūpo pāsādiko hoti, ākāsena [M 2.0336] vicaranto rajjaṃ anusāsati, dhammiko dhammarājā”ti tassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā savanena dassanamhi samente attamanā honti. Bhāsatīti “kathaṃ, tātā, rājadhammaṃ pūretha, paveṇiṃ rakkhathā”ti paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Brāhmaṇesu pana “kathañca, ācariyā, mante vācetha, antevāsikā mante gaṇhanti, dakkhiṇaṃ vā vatthāni vā sīlaṃ vā labhathā”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Gahapatīsu “kathaṃ, tātā, na vo rājakulato daṇḍena vā bandhanena vā pīḷā atthi, sammā devo dhāraṃ anuppavecchati, sassāni sampajjantī”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Samaṇesu “kathaṃ, bhante, kacci pabbajitaparikkhārā sulabhā, samaṇadhamme nappamajjathā”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karotīti.

130. In the tenth sutta, 'the assembly of Khattiyas' refers to Khattiyas, both anointed and unanointed. For they, having heard the account of his virtues—'A king, a Wheel-Turner, is handsome and pleasing; traveling through the sky, he governs the kingdom; he is a righteous king of Dhamma'—are pleased in mind when what they see agrees with what they have heard. He speaks, making friendly conversation thus: 'How, sirs, do you fulfill the royal duties? Do you protect the tradition?' As for the brahmins, he makes friendly conversation thus: 'And how, teachers, do you recite the mantras? Do your pupils learn the mantras? Do you obtain gifts, or garments, or a tawny cow?' To householders, he makes friendly conversation thus: 'How, sirs, is there no oppression for you from the royal family by way of punishment or imprisonment? Does the deva send down rain in proper streams? Do the crops prosper?' To ascetics, he makes friendly conversation thus: 'How, venerable sirs, are the requisites for one gone forth easily obtained? Are you not heedless in the ascetic's duties?'

Bhayavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Fear is the third.

(14) 4. Puggalavaggo

(14) 4. The Chapter on Individuals

1. Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta

131. Catutthassa [V 2.0332] paṭhame upapattipaṭilābhiyānīti yehi anantarā upapattiṃ paṭilabhati. Bhavapaṭilābhiyānīti upapattibhavassa paṭilābhāya paccayāni. Sakadāgāmissāti idaṃ appahīnasaṃyojanesu ariyesu uttamakoṭiyā gahitaṃ. Yasmā pana antarāparinibbāyissa antarā upapatti natthi, yaṃ pana so tattha jhānaṃ samāpajjati, taṃ [P 3.0131] kusalattā “upapattibhavassa paccayo” teva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tasmāssa “upapattipaṭilābhiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni, bhavapaṭilābhiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnānī”ti vuttaṃ. Orambhāgiyesu ca appahīnaṃ upādāya sakadāgāmissa avisesena “orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnānī”ti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

131. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'upapattipaṭilābhiyāni' refers to those fetters by which one obtains immediate rebirth. 'Bhavapaṭilābhiyāni' refers to the conditions for obtaining rebirth-existence. The term 'once-returner' here is taken as the highest instance among noble ones who have unabandoned fetters. Because for one who attains parinibbāna in the interval there is no intermediate rebirth, but whatever jhāna that person attains there, being wholesome, is reckoned only as a 'condition for rebirth-existence.' Therefore, it is said of them: 'The fetters that are causes for obtaining rebirth are abandoned, but the fetters that are causes for obtaining existence are unabandoned.' And with regard to the lower fetters, with reference to what is unabandoned for a once-returner, it is said in a general sense: 'The lower fetters are unabandoned.' The rest here is clear indeed.

2. Paṭibhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Paṭibhāna Sutta

132. Dutiye yuttappaṭibhāno no muttappaṭibhānoti pañhaṃ kathento yuttameva katheti, sīghaṃ pana na katheti, saṇikameva kathetīti attho. Iminā nayena sabbapadāni veditabbāni.

132. In the second sutta, as for 'one of suitable inspiration, not of loose inspiration': when answering a question, he speaks only what is suitable; he does not speak quickly, but speaks only slowly. This is the meaning. In this way, all terms should be understood.

3. Ugghaṭitaññūsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Ugghaṭitaññū Sutta

133. Tatiye [M 2.0337] catunnampi puggalānaṃ iminā suttena viseso veditabbo –

133. In the third sutta, the distinction of the four individuals should be understood by this sutta.

“Katamo ca puggalo ugghaṭitaññū, yassa puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū. Katamo ca puggalo vipañcitaññū, yassa puggalassa vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Katamo ca puggalo neyyo, yassa puggalassa uddesato [V 2.0333] paripucchato yonisomanasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Katamo ca puggalo padaparamo, yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi dhārayato bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo”ti (pu. pa. 148-151).

And what is the ugghaṭitaññū person? The person for whom there is realization of the Dhamma at the same time as a brief statement is made. This person is called an ugghaṭitaññū. And what is the vipañcitaññū person? The person for whom there is realization of the Dhamma when the meaning is analyzed in detail. This person is called a vipañcitaññū. And what is the neyyo person? The person for whom there is realization of the Dhamma gradually through learning the Pali text, through learning the commentary, through wise attention, and through associating with, attending on, and serving good friends. This person is called a neyyo. And what is the padaparamo person? The person for whom, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, there is no realization of the Dhamma in that life. This person is called a padaparamo.

4. Uṭṭhānaphalasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Uṭṭhānaphala Sutta

134. Catutthe uṭṭhānavīriyeneva divasaṃ vītināmetvā tassa nissandaphalamattaṃ kiñcideva labhitvā jīvikaṃ kappeti, taṃ pana uṭṭhānaṃ āgamma kiñci puññaphalaṃ nappaṭilabhati[P 3.0132], ayaṃ uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvī na kammaphalūpajīvī nāma. Cātumahārājike pana deve ādiṃ katvā sabbepi devā uṭṭhānavīriyena vinā puññaphalasseva upajīvanato kammaphalūpajīvino na uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino nāma. Rājarājamahāmattādayo uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino ca kammaphalūpajīvino ca. Nerayikasattā neva uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino na kammaphalūpajīvino. Imasmiṃ sutte puññaphalameva kammaphalanti adhippetaṃ, tañca tesaṃ natthi.

134. In the fourth sutta, one passes the day only with the effort of exertion and, having obtained merely some consequential fruit of that, sustains one's life. However, relying on that exertion, one does not obtain any fruit of merit. This person is called one who lives sustained by the fruit of exertion, not one who lives sustained by the fruit of kamma. Furthermore, all devas, beginning with those in the realm of the Four Great Kings, live sustained only by the fruit of merit, without the effort of exertion. Therefore, they are called those who live sustained by the fruit of kamma, not those who live sustained by the fruit of exertion. Kings, great ministers, and the like are those who live sustained by the fruit of exertion and also by the fruit of kamma. Beings in hell are neither those who live sustained by the fruit of exertion nor those who live sustained by the fruit of kamma. In this sutta, the fruit of merit is intended as the fruit of kamma, and that does not exist for them.

5. Sāvajjasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Sāvajja Sutta

135. Pañcame paṭhamo andhabālaputhujjano, dutiyo antarantarā kusalakārako lokiyaputhujjano, tatiyo sotāpanno, sakadāgāmianāgāminopi [M 2.0338] eteneva saṅgahitā. Catuttho khīṇāsavo. So hi ekanteneva anavajjo.

135. In the fifth sutta, the first is the blind, foolish worldling; the second is the worldly worldling who intermittently performs wholesome deeds; the third is a stream-enterer, and the once-returner and non-returner are also included with this one. The fourth is an arahant. Indeed, that one is entirely faultless.

6-7. Sīlasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta, etc.

136-137. Chaṭṭhe paṭhamo lokiyamahājano, dutiyo sukkhavipassako sotāpanno ca sakadāgāmī ca, tatiyo anāgāmī. So hi yasmā taṅkhaṇikampi upapattinimittakaṃ jhānaṃ paṭilabhatiyeva, tasmā sukkhavipassakopi samādhismiṃ paripūrakārīyeva. Catuttho khīṇāsavoyeva[V 2.0334]. So hi sabbesaṃ sīlādipaccanīkānaṃ pahīnattā sabbattha paripūrakārī nāma. Sattamepi chaṭṭhe vuttanayeneva puggalaparicchedo veditabbo.

In the sixth sutta, the first is the worldly populace; the second is a dry-insight meditator who is a stream-enterer or a once-returner; the third is a non-returner. Indeed, since that one certainly obtains, even at the moment of death, the jhāna that is a sign and condition for rebirth, therefore even a non-returner who is a dry-insight meditator is indeed one who fulfills concentration. The fourth is only an arahant. Indeed, since for that one all defilements which are opponents of virtue and so on have been abandoned, that one is called one who fulfills in all respects. In the seventh sutta as well, the distinction of persons should be understood by the very method stated for the sixth.

8. Nikaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Expelled Sutta

138. Aṭṭhame nikaṭṭhakāyoti niggatakāyo. Anikaṭṭhacittoti anupaviṭṭhacitto. Kāyeneva gāmato nikkhanto, cittena araññe vasantopi gāmameva paviṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

In the eighth sutta, 'remote in body' means the body has gone out. 'Not remote in mind' means the mind has entered. It is meant that although one has gone out from the village with the body and dwells in the forest, the mind has entered the village itself. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

9. Dhammakathikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Dhamma-Preachers

139. Navame asahitanti atthena asaṃyuttaṃ. Na kusalā hotīti na chekā hoti. Sahitāsahitassāti [P 3.0133] atthanissitassa vā anissitassa vā. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo.

8. In the ninth sutta, `asahitaṃ` means 'unconnected with the beneficial meaning.' `Na kusalo hoti` means 'one is not skilled.' `Sahitāsahitassa` means 'of that which is connected to the beneficial meaning or of that which is not connected.' In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

10. Vādīsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Disputant Sutta

140. Dasame atthato pariyādānaṃ gacchatīti aṭṭhakathaṃ pucchito pariyādānaṃ parikkhayaṃ gacchati, kathetuṃ na sakkoti. No byañjanatoti byañjanaṃ panassa pavattati na pariyādiyati. Eseva nayo sabbatthāti.

138. In the tenth sutta, `atthato pariyādānaṃ gacchati` means that when asked about the commentary, one reaches exhaustion and depletion, and is unable to speak. `No byañjanato` means that for this person, the letter, however, continues and is not depleted. This is the method in all instances.

Puggalavaggo catuttho.

9. The Chapter on Persons is the fourth.

(15) 5. Ābhāvaggo

(15) 5. The Radiance Chapter

1. Ābhāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Radiance Sutta

141. Pañcamassa [V 2.0335][M 2.0339] paṭhame ābhāsanavasena candova candābhā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

139. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, `candābhā` is the moon itself by way of its excellent shining. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

2-5. Pabhāsuttādivaṇṇanā

2-5. Commentary on the Splendor Sutta, etc.

142-145. Dutiyādīsupi pabhāsanavasena candova candappabhā. Ālokanavasena candova candāloko. Obhāsanavasena candova candobhāso. Pajjotanavasena candova candapajjototi. Evaṃ sabbapadesupi attho veditabbo.

10. In the second sutta and so on, `candappabhā` is the moon itself by way of its intense shining. `Candāloko` is the moon itself by way of its light. `Candobhāso` is the moon itself by way of its radiance. `Candapajjoto` is the moon itself by way of its shining. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

6. Paṭhamakālasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Occasion Sutta

146. Chaṭṭhe kālāti yuttappayuttakālā. Kālena dhammassavananti yuttappayuttakāle dhammassavanaṃ. Dhammasākacchāti pañhapucchanavissajjanavasena pavattā saṃsandanakathā.

140. In the sixth sutta, `kālā` means 'suitable and proper times.' `Kālena dhammassavanaṃ` means 'listening to the Dhamma at a suitable and proper time.' `Dhammasākacchā` is a discussion that proceeds by way of asking and answering questions.

7. Dutiyakālasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Occasion Sutta

147. Sattame kālāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle dhammassavanādivasena pavattānaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te bhāviyanti ceva anuparivattiyanti ca. Āsavānaṃ [P 3.0134] khayanti arahattaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva.

In the seventh sutta, `kālā` is a designation for the wholesome states that arise on each occasion through listening to the Dhamma and so on. They are both developed and practiced. `Āsavānaṃ khayaṃ` is Arahantship. The eighth has a clear meaning.

9-10. Sucaritasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Good Conduct Sutta, etc.

149-150. Navame [V 2.0336] saṇhā vācāti mudukavācā. Mantabhāsāti mantasaṅkhātāya paññāya paricchinditvā kathitakathā. Dasame sīlasāroti sārasampāpakaṃ sīlaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

In the ninth sutta, `saṇhā vācā` means 'soft speech.' `Mantabhāsā` is speech spoken after having determined it with the wisdom called `manta`. In the tenth, `sīlasāro` is virtue that leads to the attainment of the essence, which is Nibbāna. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Ābhāvaggo pañcamo.

1. The Radiance Chapter is the fifth.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

141. The Third Fifty is finished.

4. Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ

4. The Fourth Fifty

(16) 1. Indriyavaggo

(16) 1. The Chapter on the Faculties

1. Indriyasuttādivaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Faculty Sutta, etc.

151. Catutthassa [V 2.0337][M 2.0340] paṭhame saddhādhurena indaṭṭhaṃ karotīti saddhindriyaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Dutiye assaddhiye akampanaṭṭhena saddhābalaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tatiye anavajjabalanti niddosabalaṃ. Saṅgahabalanti saṅgaṇhitabbayuttakānaṃ saṅgaṇhanabalaṃ. Catutthapañcamāni uttānāneva.

In the first sutta of the fourth, faith performs the function of a ruler by the burden of clarifying associated states; therefore, it is called the faculty of faith. This same method applies to the remaining terms. In the second, because of its unshakable nature in the face of faithlessness, it is the strength of faith. This same method applies to the remaining terms. In the third, 'the strength of being blameless' means the strength that is faultless. 'The strength of gathering' means the strength of gathering those who are fit to be gathered. The fourth and fifth suttas are self-evident.

6. Kappasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Kappa Sutta

156. Chaṭṭhe saṃvaṭṭatīti ettha tayo saṃvaṭṭā āposaṃvaṭṭo, tejosaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti. Tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā ābhassarā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalāti. Yadā kappo tejena saṃvaṭṭati, ābhassarato heṭṭhā agginā ḍayhati. Yadā āpena saṃvaṭṭati, subhakiṇhato heṭṭhā udakena vilīyati. Yadā vātena [P 3.0135] saṃvaṭṭati, vehapphalato heṭṭhā vātena viddhaṃsati. Vitthārato pana sadāpi ekaṃ buddhakkhettaṃ vinassati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārakathā pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.403-404 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

In the sixth sutta, regarding the text 'it dissolves' (saṃvaṭṭati), there are three dissolutions: dissolution by water, dissolution by fire, and dissolution by wind. There are three limits of dissolution: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm. When the eon dissolves by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is burned by fire. When it dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is destroyed by wind. But in detail, at all times a single Buddha-field is destroyed. This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be understood just by the method stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. XIII, 27-30).

7. Rogasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Roga Sutta

157. Sattame vighātavāti mahicchāpaccayena vighātena dukkhena samannāgato. Asantuṭṭhoti catūsu paccayesu tīhi santosehi asantuṭṭho. Anavaññappaṭilābhāyāti parehi anavajānanassa paṭilābhatthāya. Lābhasakkārasilokappaṭilābhāyāti susaṅkhatacatupaccayasaṅkhātassa lābhasakkārassa [V 2.0338] ceva vaṇṇabhaṇanasaṅkhātassa silokassa ca paṭilābhatthāya. Saṅkhāya kulāni upasaṅkamatīti “iti maṃ ete jānissantī”ti jānanatthāya kulāni upasaṅkamati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

6. In the seventh sutta, 'one with vexation' (vighātavā) means one endowed with suffering, which is vexation, due to great desire. 'One who is not content' (asantuṭṭho) means one not content with the four requisites through the three kinds of contentment. 'For the purpose of obtaining non-contempt' (anavaññappaṭilābhāya) means for the purpose of obtaining non-despisal from others. 'For the purpose of obtaining gain, honor, and fame' (lābhasakkārasilokappaṭilābhāya) means for the purpose of obtaining gain and honor, reckoned as the well-prepared four requisites, and fame, reckoned as the speaking of praise. 'He deliberately approaches families' (saṅkhāya kulāni upasaṅkamati) means he approaches families for the purpose of being known, thinking, 'Thus they will know me.' This same method applies to the remaining terms.

8. Parihānisuttavaṇṇanā

146. Commentary on the Parihāni Sutta

158. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0341] gambhīresūti atthagambhīresu. Ṭhānāṭhānesūti kāraṇākāraṇesu. Na kamatīti nāvagāhati nappavattati. Paññācakkhūti ettha uggahaparipucchāpaññāpi vaṭṭati, sammasanappaṭivedhapaññāpi vaṭṭatiyeva.

7. In the eighth sutta, 'in profound things' (gambhīresu) means in things profound in meaning. 'In the possible and the impossible' (ṭhānāṭhānesu) means in what is a cause and what is not a cause. 'Does not proceed' (na kamati) means does not penetrate, does not proceed. Regarding 'the eye of wisdom' (paññācakkhu), here the wisdom of learning and questioning is appropriate, and the wisdom of reflection and penetration is also appropriate.

9. Bhikkhunīsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Sutta

159. Navame ehi tvanti there paṭibaddhacittā taṃ pahiṇituṃ evamāha. Sasīsaṃ pārupitvāti saha sīsena kāyaṃ pārupitvā. Mañcake nipajjīti vegena mañcakaṃ paññāpetvā tattha nipajji. Etadavocāti [P 3.0136] tassākāraṃ sallakkhetvā lobhappahānatthāya saṇheneva asubhakathaṃ kathetuṃ etaṃ avoca. Āhārasambhūtoti āhārena sambhūto āhāraṃ nissāya vaḍḍhito. Āhāraṃ nissāya āhāraṃ pajahatīti paccuppannaṃ kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ nissāya taṃ evaṃ yoniso sevamāno pubbakammasaṅkhātaṃ āhāraṃ pajahati. Paccuppannepi pana kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantitaṇhā pajahitabbā.

159. In the ninth sutta: 'Come, you'—she, with a mind bound by passion for the Elder, spoke thus in order to send a certain man. 'Sasīsaṃ pārupitvā' means having covered the body together with the head. 'Mañcake nipajji' means having quickly prepared the bed, she lay down there. 'Etadavoca' means having observed her demeanor, for the purpose of abandoning greed, he spoke this gently in order to give a talk on foulness. 'Āhārasambhūto' means arisen from nutriment, grown dependent on nutriment. 'Āhāraṃ nissāya āhāraṃ pajahati' means that by depending on present edible nutriment and partaking of it thus with wise attention, one abandons the nutriment reckoned as past kamma. Moreover, even in regard to present edible nutriment, the craving that is delight should be abandoned.

Taṇhaṃ pajahatīti idāni evaṃ pavattaṃ paccuppannataṇhaṃ nissāya vaṭṭamūlikaṃ pubbataṇhaṃ pajahati. Ayaṃ pana paccuppannataṇhā kusalā akusalāti? Akusalā. Sevitabbā na sevitabbāti? Sevitabbā. Paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati nākaḍḍhatīti? Nākaḍḍhati. Etissāpi pana paccuppannāya sevitabbataṇhāya nikanti pajahitabbāyeva. So hi nāma āyasmā āsavānaṃ khayā upasampajja viharissati, kimaṅgaṃ panāhanti ettha kimaṅgaṃ panāti kāraṇaparivitakkanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – so āyasmā arahattaphalaṃ sacchikatvā viharissati, ahaṃ kena kāraṇena na sacchikatvā viharissāmi. Sopi hi āyasmā sammāsambuddhasseva putto, ahampi sammāsambuddhasseva putto, mayhampetaṃ uppajjissatīti. Mānaṃ nissāyāti idaṃ evaṃ uppannasevitabbamānaṃ [V 2.0339] nissāya. Mānaṃ [P 3.0137] pajahatīti vaṭṭamūlakaṃ pubbamānaṃ pajahati. Yaṃ nissāya panesa taṃ pajahati, sopi taṇhā viya akusalo ceva sevitabbo ca, no ca paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati. Nikanti pana tasmimpi pajahitabbāva.

'Taṇhaṃ pajahati' means that by depending on the presently occurring craving, one abandons the past craving that is the root of the cycle. Now, is this present craving wholesome or unwholesome? Unwholesome. Should it be cultivated or not cultivated? It should be cultivated. Does it draw one into rebirth or not? It does not. However, even in regard to this present craving that should be cultivated, delight must certainly be abandoned. In the passage 'Indeed, that venerable one will dwell having attained the destruction of the taints—what more is there for me?', the phrase 'kimaṅgaṃ pana' is for reflecting on a reason. This is what is meant: That venerable one will dwell having realized the fruit of Arahantship; for what reason should I not dwell having realized it? Indeed, that venerable one too is a son of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and I too am a son of the Perfectly Enlightened One. This will arise for me too. 'Mānaṃ nissāya' means depending on this conceit that has arisen and should be cultivated. 'Mānaṃ pajahati' means one abandons the past conceit that is the root of the cycle. And that conceit depending on which one abandons the other, it too, like the craving, is both unwholesome and to be cultivated, and it does not draw one into rebirth. However, delight in that conceit too must certainly be abandoned.

Setughāto [M 2.0342] vutto bhagavatāti padaghāto paccayaghāto buddhena bhagavatā kathito. Iti imehi catūhi aṅgehi there desanaṃ vinivaṭṭente tassā bhikkhuniyā theraṃ ārabbha uppanno chandarāgo apagañchi. Sāpi theraṃ khamāpetuṃ accayaṃ desesi, theropissā paṭiggaṇhi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho sā bhikkhunītiādi vuttaṃ.

'Setughāto vutto bhagavatā' means the destruction of the cause, the destruction of the condition, spoken by the Blessed One, the Buddha. Thus, as the elder was turning back the discourse with these four factors, the passionate desire that had arisen in that bhikkhunī with respect to the elder departed. She also confessed her transgression to ask for forgiveness from the elder, and the elder accepted it from her. To show this, the passage beginning with 'Then, that bhikkhunī...' was spoken.

10. Sugatavinayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sugatavinaya Sutta

160. Dasame duggahitanti uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitaṃ. Pariyāpuṇantīti vaḷañjenti kathenti. Padabyañjanehīti ettha padameva atthassa byañjanato byañjananti vuttaṃ. Dunnikkhittassāti duṭṭhu nikkhittassa uppaṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitassa. Atthopi dunnayo hotīti aṭṭhakathā nīharitvā kathetuṃ na sakkā hoti. Chinnamūlakoti mūlabhūtānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upacchinnattā chinnamūlako. Appaṭisaraṇoti appatiṭṭho. Bāhulikāti paccayabāhullāya paṭipannā. Sāthalikāti tisso sikkhā sithilaggahaṇena gaṇhanakā. Okkamane [P 3.0138] pubbaṅgamāti pañca nīvaraṇāni avagamanato okkamananti vuccanti, tattha pubbaṅgamāti attho. Paviveketi tividhe viveke. Nikkhittadhurāti nibbīriyā. Iminā nayena pana sabbattha attho veditabbo.

160. In the tenth sutta, 'duggahitaṃ' means grasped out of order. 'Pariyāpuṇanti' means they use and teach. Here, in the phrase 'padabyañjanehi', the word itself, because it makes the meaning manifest, is called 'byañjana'. 'Dunnikkhittassa' means badly placed, placed out of order. 'Atthopi dunnayo hoti' means it is not possible to speak by extracting from the commentary. 'Chinnamūlako' means having the root cut off because the root-bhikkhus are cut off. 'Appaṭisaraṇo' means without foundation. 'Bāhulikā' means those who have undertaken an abundance of requisites. 'Sāthalikā' means those who grasp the three trainings with a loose grasp. 'Okkamane pubbaṅgama' means: the five hindrances are called 'okkamana' from 'avagamana' (going down); herein, it has the meaning of 'forerunner'. 'Paviveke' means in the three kinds of seclusion. 'Nikkhittadhurā' means without effort. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Indriyavaggo paṭhamo.

The Chapter on the Faculties, the First.

(17) 2. Paṭipadāvaggo

(17) 2. The Chapter on the Path

1. Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Concise Sutta

161. Dutiyassa [V 2.0340] paṭhame sukhapaṭikkhepena dukkhā paṭipajjitabbato paṭipadā etissāti dukkhāpaṭipadā. Asīghappavattitāya garubhāvena dandhā abhiññā etissāti dandhābhiññā. Imināva nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

161. In the first discourse of the second section: The path is called 'painful practice' because one must practice with suffering by rejecting pleasure. The direct knowledge is slow, thus it is called 'slow direct knowledge,' due to its not-swift proceeding and its heaviness. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all passages.

2. Vitthārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Extensive Sutta

162. Dutiye [M 2.0343] abhikkhaṇanti abhiṇhaṃ. Ānantariyanti anantaravipākadāyakaṃ maggasamādhiṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayāyāti arahattaphalatthāya. Pañcindriyānīti vipassanāpañcamakāni pañcindriyāni. Paññindriyanti hi ettha vipassanāpaññāva paññindriyanti adhippetaṃ. Sesamettha pāḷivasena uttānameva.

162. In the second discourse, 'abhikkhaṇaṃ' means frequently. 'Ānantariyaṃ' refers to the path's concentration that yields immediate results. 'Āsavānaṃ khayāya' means for the purpose of the fruit of Arahantship. 'Pañcindriyāni' refers to the five faculties which have insight as the fifth. Indeed, here by 'the faculty of wisdom', only insight-wisdom is intended. The rest here is clear by way of the Pāḷi itself.

Imāsaṃ pana paṭipadānaṃ ayaṃ āvibhāvakathā – idha bhikkhu pubbe akatābhiniveso pubbabhāge rūpapariggahe kilamati, arūpapariggahe kilamati, paccayapariggahe kilamati, tīsu addhāsu kilamati, maggāmagge kilamati. Evaṃ pañcasu [P 3.0139] ṭhānesu kilamanto vipassanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanaṃ patvāpi udayabbayānupassane, bhaṅgānupassane, bhayatupaṭṭhāne, ādīnavānupassane, nibbidānupassane, muccitukamyatāñāṇe, saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇe, anulomañāṇe, gotrabhuñāṇeti imesu navasu vipassanāñāṇesupi kilamitvāva lokuttaramaggaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tassa so lokuttaramaggo evaṃ dukkhena garubhāvena sacchikatattā dukkhapaṭipado dandhābhiñño nāma jāto. Yo pana pubbabhāge pañcasu ñāṇesu kilamanto aparabhāge navasu vipassanāñāṇesu akilamitvāva maggaṃ sacchikaroti, tassa so maggo evaṃ dukkhena agarubhāvena sacchikatattā dukkhapaṭipado khippābhiñño nāma jāto. Iminā upāyena itarāpi dve veditabbā.

Furthermore, this is the discourse that explains the manifestation of these paths: Here, a bhikkhu who in a previous existence has not made a firm resolve struggles in the preliminary stage in the comprehension of material form, struggles in the comprehension of immaterial form, struggles in the comprehension of conditions, struggles in the three periods of time, and struggles in discerning what is the path and what is not the path. Thus, struggling in these five instances, he attains insight. Even after attaining insight, only after struggling also in these nine insight knowledges—contemplation of arising and passing away, contemplation of dissolution, appearance of terror, contemplation of drawbacks, contemplation of aversion, knowledge of the desire for deliverance, knowledge of equanimity towards formations, knowledge of adaptation, and knowledge of change-of-lineage—does he attain the supramundane path. For him, that supramundane path, because it is realized with such difficulty and gravity, becomes named 'painful practice with slow direct-knowledge'. But as for the one who, while struggling in the five knowledges in the preliminary stage, realizes the path in the later stage without struggling in the nine insight knowledges, for him, that path, because it is realized with difficulty and without gravity, becomes named 'painful practice with quick direct-knowledge'. By this method, the other two should also be understood.

Goṇapariyesakaupamāhi [V 2.0341] cetā vibhāvetabbā – ekassa hi purisassa cattāro goṇā palāyitvā aṭaviṃ paviṭṭhā. So sakaṇṭake sagahane vane te pariyesanto gahanamaggeneva kicchena kasirena gantvā gahanaṭṭhāneyeva nilīne goṇepi kicchena kasirena addasa. Eko kicchena gantvā abbhokāse ṭhite khippameva addasa. Aparo abbhokāsamaggena sukhena gantvā gahanaṭṭhāne nilīne kicchena kasirena addasa. Aparo abbhokāsamaggeneva sukhena gantvā abbhokāse ṭhiteyeva khippaṃ addasa. Tattha cattāro goṇā viya cattāro ariyamaggā daṭṭhabbā, goṇapariyesako puriso viya yogāvacaro, gahanamaggena kicchena kasirena [P 3.0140] gamanaṃ viya pubbabhāge pañcasu ñāṇesu kilamato dukkhāpaṭipadā. Gahanaṭṭhāne nilīnānaṃ kiccheneva dassanaṃ viya aparabhāge navasu ñāṇesu kilamantassa [M 2.0344] ariyamaggānaṃ dassanaṃ. Iminā upāyena sesaupamāpi yojetabbā.

Furthermore, these practices should be made clear by the similes of the ox-seeker. Indeed, a certain man had four oxen that fled and entered a forest. Searching for them in the thorny, dense woods, he traveled by a dense path with difficulty and hardship, and with difficulty and hardship, he saw the oxen hidden in a very dense place. Another man, traveling with difficulty, saw them very quickly standing in an open space. Another, traveling with ease by an open path, saw with difficulty and hardship the oxen hidden in a dense place. Yet another, traveling with ease by that very open path, saw them quickly standing in an open space. Therein, the four oxen should be seen as the four noble paths, and the man searching for the oxen as the yogī. Traveling with difficulty and hardship by a dense path is like the painful practice of one who becomes weary in the five knowledges in the preliminary stage. Seeing with difficulty the oxen hidden in a dense place is like the seeing of the noble paths of one who becomes weary in the nine knowledges in the later stage. By this method, the remaining similes should also be applied.

3. Asubhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Unattractiveness

163. Tatiye asubhānupassī kāye viharatīti attano karajakāye “yathā etaṃ, tathā ida”nti iminā nayena bahiddhā diṭṭhānaṃ dasannaṃ asubhānaṃ upasaṃharaṇavasena asubhānupassī viharati, attano kāyaṃ asubhato paṭikūlato ñāṇena passatīti attho. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññīti navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasena kabaḷīkārāhāre paṭikūlasaññī. Sabbaloke anabhiratisaññīti sabbasmimpi tedhātuke lokasannivāse anabhiratāya ukkaṇṭhitasaññāya samannāgato. Sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccānupassīti sabbepi tebhūmakasaṅkhāre aniccato anupassanto. Maraṇasaññāti maraṇaṃ ārabbha uppannasaññā. Ajjhattaṃ sūpaṭṭhitā hotīti niyakajjhatte suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitā hoti. Ettāvatā balavavipassanā kathitā. Sekhabalānīti sikkhanakānaṃ balāni. Sesamettha pāḷivasena uttānameva. “Asubhānupassī”tiādīni pana dukkhāya paṭipadāya dassanatthaṃ vuttāni, paṭhamajjhānādīni sukhāya. Asubhādīni hi paṭikūlārammaṇāni, tesu pana pakatiyāva sampiyāyamānaṃ cittaṃ allīyati. Tasmā tāni bhāvento dukkhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno nāma hoti. Paṭhamajjhānādīni paṇītasukhāni[P 3.0141], tasmā tāni paṭipanno sukhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno nāma hoti.

163. In the third discourse, 'one dwells contemplating the unattractive in the body' means: by way of applying the ten externally seen unattractive objects to one's own karaja-body according to the method 'As that is, so is this,' one dwells contemplating the unattractive. The meaning is that one sees one's own body with wisdom as unattractive and repulsive. 'Perceiving the repulsiveness in food' means one has the perception of repulsiveness towards physical food by means of the nine kinds of repulsiveness. 'Perceiving non-delight in the whole world' means one is endowed with a perception of non-delight and weariness towards the entire world-abode of the three realms. 'Contemplating impermanence in all formations' means repeatedly contemplating all formations of the three planes as impermanent. 'The perception of death' is the perception that has arisen taking death as its object. 'Is well-established internally' means it is well-established within oneself. By this much, strong insight is taught. 'The powers of a trainee' are the powers of those who are training. The remainder here is indeed clear by means of the Pāli itself. However, the words beginning with 'contemplating the unattractive' are spoken for the purpose of showing the painful practice, while the first jhāna and so on are for the pleasant practice. For the unattractive and so on are repulsive objects; the mind, which is naturally desirous, does not cling to them. Therefore, one who develops them is said to be one who has undertaken the painful practice. The first jhāna and so on are refined pleasures; therefore, one who undertakes them is said to be one who has undertaken the pleasant practice.

Ayaṃ panettha sabbasādhāraṇā upamā – saṅgāmāvacarapuriso hi phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ katvā pañcāvudhāni [V 2.0342] sannayhitvā saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, so antarā vissamitukāmo phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā vissamati ceva pānabhojanādīni ca paṭisevati. Tato puna saṅgāmaṃ pavisitvā kammaṃ karoti. Tattha saṅgāmo viya kilesasaṅgāmo daṭṭhabbo, phalakakoṭṭhako viya pañcanissayabalāni, saṅgāmapavisanapuriso viya yogāvacaro, pañcāvudhasannāho viya vipassanāpañcamāni indriyāni, saṅgāmaṃ pavisanakālo viya vipassanāya kammakaraṇakālo, vissamitukāmassa phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā vissamanapānabhojanāni paṭisevanakālo viya [M 2.0345] vipassanāya kammaṃ karontassa cittuppādassa nirassādakkhaṇe pañca balāni nissāya cittaṃ sampahaṃsanakālo, vissamitvā khāditvā pivitvā ca puna saṅgāmassa pavisanakālo viya pañcahi balehi cittaṃ sampahaṃsetvā puna vipassanāya kammaṃ karontassa vivaṭṭetvā arahattaggahaṇakālo veditabbo. Imasmiṃ pana sutte balāni ceva indriyāni ca missakāneva kathitānīti.

Here is a universal simile: A warrior enters battle having prepared a shield-fortress and equipped himself with five weapons. If he wishes to rest in the interim, he enters the shield-fortress, rests, and partakes of food and drink. Then he re-enters the battle to fight. In this simile, the battle should be seen as the battle against defilements; the shield-fortress as the five powers of support; the warrior entering battle as the yogī; the arming with five weapons as these five faculties; the time of entering battle as the time of engaging in the work of insight; the time of wishing to rest, entering the shield-fortress to rest and partake of food and drink as the time of gladdening the mind by relying on the five powers when a mental state finds the work of insight distasteful; and the time of re-entering the battle after resting, eating, and drinking as the time of grasping the fruit of Arahantship, having turned away from the round of existence, for one who does the work of insight again after gladdening the mind with the five powers. In this sutta, both the powers and the faculties are spoken of as mixed.

4. Paṭhamakhamasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Sutta on Forbearance

164. Catutthe akkhamāti anadhivāsikapaṭipadā. Khamāti adhivāsikapaṭipadā. Damāti indriyadamanapaṭipadā. Samāti akusalavitakkānaṃ vūpasamanapaṭipadā. Rosantaṃ paṭirosatīti ghaṭṭentaṃ paṭighaṭṭeti. Bhaṇḍantaṃ [P 3.0142] paṭibhaṇḍatīti paharantaṃ paṭipaharati. Pañcamachaṭṭhāni uttānatthāneva.

164. In the fourth sutta, ‘non-forbearance’ (akkhamā) is the practice of non-endurance. ‘Forbearance’ (khamā) is the practice of endurance. ‘Taming’ (dama) is the practice of taming the faculties. ‘Tranquillity’ (sama) is the practice of pacifying unwholesome thoughts. ‘He retaliates against one who is angry’ means he harasses in return one who harasses him. ‘He quarrels with one who quarrels’ means he strikes back against one who strikes. The fifth and sixth suttas are clear in meaning.

7. Mahāmoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta

167. Sattame mahāmoggallānattherassa heṭṭhimā tayo maggā sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā ahesuṃ, arahattamaggo dukkhapaṭipado khippābhiñño. Tasmā evamāha – “yāyaṃ paṭipadā dukkhā khippābhiññā, imaṃ me paṭipadaṃ āgamma anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti.

167. In the seventh sutta, for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the three lower paths were of pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge; the path to Arahantship was of painful practice with quick direct knowledge. Therefore, he said: ‘Relying on this practice that is painful with quick direct knowledge, my mind was liberated from the taints without grasping.’

8. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

168. Aṭṭhame dhammasenāpatittherassa heṭṭhimā tayo maggā sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā, arahattamaggo [V 2.0343] sukhapaṭipado khippābhiñño. Tasmā “yāyaṃ paṭipadā sukhā khippābhiññā”ti āha. Imesu pana dvīsupi suttesu missikāva paṭipadā kathitāti veditabbā.

168. In the eighth sutta, for the Elder, the General of the Dhamma, the three lower paths were of pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge; the path to Arahantship is of pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Therefore, he said: ‘This practice is pleasant with quick direct knowledge.’ It should be known that in both these suttas, a mixed practice is taught.

9. Sasaṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sasaṅkhāra Sutta

169. Navame paṭhamadutiyapuggalā sukkhavipassakā sasaṅkhārena sappayogena saṅkhāranimittaṃ upaṭṭhapenti. Tesu eko vipassanindriyānaṃ balavattā idheva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati, eko indriyānaṃ dubbalatāya [M 2.0346] idha asakkonto anantare attabhāve tadeva mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ paṭilabhitvā sasaṅkhārena sappayogena saṅkhāranimittaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati, tatiyacatutthā samathayānikā. Tesaṃ eko asaṅkhārena appayogena indriyānaṃ balavattā idheva kilese khepeti, eko indriyānaṃ dubbalattā idha asakkonto anantare attabhāve tadeva mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ paṭilabhitvā asaṅkhārena appayogena kilese khepetīti veditabbo.

169. In the ninth sutta, the first and second individuals are dry-insight practitioners; with exertion and with effort, they establish the sign of formations. Among them, one, due to the strength of the insight faculties, attains final Nibbāna through the extinguishing of the defilements right in this present existence. Another, due to the weakness of the faculties, being unable to do so in this life, obtains that same root meditation subject in the immediately following existence and, having established the sign of formations with exertion and with effort, attains final Nibbāna through the extinguishing of the defilements. The third and fourth individuals are practitioners of the serenity vehicle. Among them, one, without exertion and without effort, due to the strength of the faculties, eradicates the defilements right in this present existence. Another, due to the weakness of the faculties, being unable to do so in this life, obtains that same root meditation subject in the immediately following existence and, without exertion and without effort, eradicates the defilements. Thus it should be understood.

10. Yuganaddhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Yuganaddha Sutta

170. Dasame samathapubbaṅgamanti samathaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā. Maggo sañjāyatīti paṭhamo lokuttaramaggo nibbattati. So [P 3.0143] taṃ magganti ekacittakkhaṇikamaggassa āsevanādīni nāma natthi, dutiyamaggādayo pana uppādento tameva āsevati bhāveti bahulīkarotīti vuccati. Vipassanāpubbaṅgamanti vipassanaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā samathaṃ bhāveti, pakatiyā vipassanālābhī vipassanāya ṭhatvā samādhiṃ uppādetīti attho.

170. In the tenth sutta, ‘With tranquillity as the forerunner’ means having made tranquillity the forerunner and precursor. ‘The path arises’ means the first supramundane path is produced. As for ‘that path’: for the path of a single mind-moment, there are no such things as repetition, etc., but one who produces the second path and so on is said to repeat, develop, and cultivate that very path. ‘With insight as the forerunner’ means having made insight the forerunner and precursor, one develops tranquillity. The meaning is: a person who has naturally gained insight, having established themself in insight, produces concentration.

Yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetīti yuganaddhaṃ katvā bhāveti. Tattha teneva cittena samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā teneva saṅkhāre sammasituṃ na sakkā. Ayaṃ pana yāvatā samāpattiyo samāpajjati, tāvatā saṅkhāre sammasati. Yāvatā saṅkhāre sammasati, tāvatā samāpattiyo samāpajjati. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjati, tato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasati, saṅkhāre sammasitvā dutiyajjhānaṃ samāpajjati. Tato vuṭṭhāya puna saṅkhāre sammasati. Saṅkhāre sammasitvā [V 2.0344] tatiyajjhānaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, tato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasati. Evamayaṃ samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāveti nāma.

‘Develops in tandem’ means one develops by yoking them together. Here, it is not possible to enter an attainment with that very mind and then contemplate formations with that same mind. But this one enters attainments to whatever extent, and to that extent contemplates formations. To whatever extent one contemplates formations, to that extent one enters attainments. How? One enters the first jhāna, emerges from it, and contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, one enters the second jhāna. Emerging from it, one again contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, one enters the third jhāna… up to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; one enters it, emerges from it, and contemplates formations. Thus, this person is said to develop tranquillity and insight in tandem.

Dhammuddhaccaviggahitanti samathavipassanādhammesu dasavipassanupakkilesasaṅkhātena uddhaccena viggahitaṃ, suggahitanti attho. So, āvuso, samayoti iminā sattannaṃ sappāyānaṃ paṭilābhakālo kathito. Yaṃ taṃ cittanti yasmiṃ samaye taṃ vipassanāvīthiṃ okkamitvā pavattaṃ cittaṃ. Ajjhattameva [M 2.0347] santiṭṭhatīti vipassanāvīthiṃ paccottharitvā [P 3.0144] tasmiṃyeva gocarajjhattasaṅkhāte ārammaṇe santiṭṭhati. Sannisīdatīti ārammaṇavasena sammā nisīdati. Ekodi hotīti ekaggaṃ hoti. Samādhiyatīti sammā ādhiyati suṭṭhapitaṃ hoti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

‘Seized by agitation concerning phenomena’ means seized by agitation—which is reckoned as one of the ten imperfections of insight—concerning the phenomena of serenity and insight; it is wrongly grasped. This is the meaning. ‘That, friend, is the time’—by this, the time for obtaining the seven suitable conditions is spoken of. ‘Whatever that mind’ means that mind which has arisen, having entered upon the course of insight. ‘It settles inwardly’ means, having descended again into the course of insight, it settles well on that very object called the internal range. ‘It becomes composed’ means it settles well by way of the object. ‘It becomes unified’ means it becomes one-pointed. ‘It becomes concentrated’ means it is well placed, it becomes well established. The rest here has a clear meaning.

Paṭipadāvaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Practice, the Second.

(18) 3. Sañcetaniyavaggo

(18) 3. The Section on Volition

1. Cetanāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Volition

171. Tatiyassa [V 2.0345] paṭhame kāyeti kāyadvāre, kāyaviññattiyā satīti attho. Kāyasañcetanāhetūtiādīsu kāyasañcetanā nāma kāyadvāre cetanā pakappanā. Sā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalavasena aṭṭhavidhā, akusalavasena dvādasavidhāti vīsatividhā. Tathā vacīsañcetanā, tathā manosañcetanā. Apicettha nava mahaggatacetanāpi labbhanti. Kāyasañcetanāhetūti kāyasañcetanāpaccayā. Uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhanti aṭṭhakusalakammapaccayā niyakajjhatte sukhaṃ uppajjati, dvādasaakusalakammapaccayā dukkhaṃ. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Avijjāpaccayāvāti avijjākāraṇeneva. Sace hi avijjā chādayamānā paccayo hoti, evaṃ sante tīsu dvāresu sukhadukkhānaṃ paccayabhūtā cetanā uppajjati. Iti mūlabhūtāya avijjāya vasenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

171. In the first discourse of the third section, by ‘body’ is meant the body-door; when there is bodily intimation is the meaning. In phrases such as ‘due to bodily volition,’ bodily volition means volition, planning, at the body-door. It is twentyfold: eightfold by way of wholesome volition of the sense-sphere and twelvefold by way of unwholesome. Similarly with verbal volition, and similarly with mental volition. Moreover, here the nine sublime volitions are also obtained. ‘Due to bodily volition’ means conditioned by bodily volition. ‘Internally, pleasure and pain arise’—pleasure arises internally in oneself due to the eight wholesome kammas, and pain due to the twelve unwholesome kammas. This is the method in the remaining doors as well. ‘Conditioned by ignorance’ means precisely because of ignorance as the cause. For if ignorance, while concealing, is a condition, this being so, volition which is the condition for pleasure and pain arises in the three doors. Thus, this was said by way of ignorance which has become the root.

Sāmaṃ vātiādīsu parehi anāṇatto sayameva abhisaṅkharonto [P 3.0145] sāmaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti nāma. Yaṃ pana pare samādapetvā āṇāpetvā kārenti, tassa taṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ pare abhisaṅkharonti nāma. Yo pana kusalaṃ kusalanti akusalaṃ akusalanti kusalavipākaṃ kusalavipākoti akusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākoti jānanto kāyadvāre vīsatividhaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, ayaṃ sampajāno abhisaṅkharoti nāma. Yo evaṃ ajānanto abhisaṅkharoti, ayaṃ asampajāno abhisaṅkharoti nāma. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo.

In such phrases as ‘by oneself,’ one who, uncommanded by others, generates a bodily formation of one's own accord, is said to generate a bodily formation by oneself. Furthermore, whatever bodily formation one causes to be done by encouraging and commanding others, that bodily formation of that person is said to be generated by others. Furthermore, one who, knowing the wholesome as wholesome, the unwholesome as unwholesome, the result of the wholesome as the result of the wholesome, and the result of the unwholesome as the result of the unwholesome, generates the twenty kinds of bodily formation at the body-door—this person is said to generate with clear comprehension. One who generates without knowing thus is said to generate without clear comprehension. This same method applies to the remaining doors as well.

Tattha [M 2.0348] asampajānakammaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – daharadārakā “mātāpitūhi kataṃ karomā”ti cetiyaṃ vandanti, pupphapūjaṃ karonti, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vandanti, tesaṃ kusalanti ajānantānampi taṃ kusalameva hoti. Tathā migapakkhiādayo tiracchānā dhammaṃ suṇanti, saṅghaṃ vandanti, cetiyaṃ vandanti, tesaṃ jānantānampi ajānantānampi taṃ kusalameva hoti. Daharadārakā pana mātāpitaro hatthapādehi paharanti, bhikkhūnaṃ talasattikaṃ uggiranti, daṇḍaṃ khipanti, akkosanti[V 2.0346]. Gāviyo bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anubandhanti, sunakhā anubandhanti, ḍaṃsanti, sīhabyagghādayo anubandhanti, jīvitā voropenti. Tesaṃ jānantānampi ajānantānampi akusalakammaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, action without clear comprehension should be understood thus: Young children, thinking, “Let us do what our parents do,” venerate a shrine, offer flowers, and venerate the community of monks; for them, even though they do not know it as wholesome, it is indeed wholesome. Similarly, animals such as deer and birds listen to the Dhamma, venerate the Sangha, and venerate a shrine; for them, whether they know it or not, it is indeed wholesome. Furthermore, young children strike their parents with their hands and feet, raise a palm-leaf fan at monks, throw sticks, and revile them. Cows chase after the community of monks; dogs chase and bite; lions, tigers, and the like chase and deprive beings of life. For them, whether they know it or not, it is unwholesome kamma—thus it should be understood.

Idāni tīsupi dvāresu āyūhanacetanā samodhānetabbā. Seyyathidaṃ – kāyadvāre sayaṃkatamūlikā vīsati cetanā, āṇattimūlikā vīsati, sampajānamūlikā vīsati, asampajānamūlikā vīsatīti asīti cetanā honti, tathā vacīdvāre. Manodvāre [P 3.0146] pana ekekasmimpi vikappe ekūnatiṃsa katvā satañca soḷasa ca honti. Iti sabbāpi tīsu dvāresu dve satāni chasattati ca cetanā. Tā sabbāpi saṅkhārakkhandhoteva saṅkhaṃ gacchanti, taṃsampayutto vedayitākāro vedanākkhandho, sañjānanākāro saññākkhandho, cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, kāyo upādārūpaṃ, tassa paccayā catasso dhātuyo cattāri bhūtānīti ime pañcakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ nāma.

Now, the volition of exertion should be brought together in the three doors. That is to say: in the body-door, there are twenty volitions rooted in self-initiated action, twenty rooted in command, twenty rooted in clear comprehension, and twenty rooted in lack of clear comprehension, thus there are eighty volitions. Similarly, in the speech-door. However, in the mind-door, by making twenty-nine in each instance, there come to be one hundred and sixteen volitions. Thus, in all three doors, there are two hundred and seventy-six volitions. All these are reckoned as the aggregate of volitional formations. The associated aspect of feeling is the aggregate of feeling, the aspect of perceiving is the aggregate of perception, the mind is the aggregate of consciousness, the body is derived matter, and its conditions, the four elements, are the four primary elements—these five aggregates are called the truth of suffering.

Imesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu avijjā anupatitāti imesu vuttappabhedesu cetanādhammesu avijjā sahajātavasena ca upanissayavasena ca anupatitā. Evaṃ vaṭṭañceva vaṭṭamūlikā ca avijjā dassitā hoti.

The meaning of 'In these dhammas, bhikkhus, ignorance is pervasive' is this: in these aforementioned volitional phenomena, ignorance is pervasive both by way of co-nascence and by way of strong dependence. Thus, both the round of kamma and ignorance which is the root of the round are shown.

Ettāvatā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattassa khīṇāsavassa idāni thutiṃ karonto avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhātiādimāha. Tattha asesavirāganirodhāti asesavirāgena ceva asesanirodhena ca. So kāyo na hotīti khīṇāsavassa kāyena karaṇakammaṃ paññāyati, cetiyaṅgaṇasammajjanaṃ bodhiyaṅgaṇasammajjanaṃ abhikkamanaṃ paṭikkamanaṃ vattānuvattakaraṇanti evamādi. Kāyadvāre panassa vīsati cetanā avipākadhammataṃ [M 2.0349] āpajjanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “so kāyo na hoti, yaṃ paccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkha”nti. Kāyadvārappavattā hi cetanā idha kāyoti adhippetā. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Khettantiādīnipi [P 3.0147] kusalākusalakammasseva nāmāni. Tañhi vipākassa viruhanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena khettaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthu, kāraṇaṭṭhena āyatanaṃ, adhikaraṇaṭṭhena adhikaraṇanti vuccati.

Having thus developed insight and attained Arahantship, now, praising the one whose taints are destroyed, he spoke the words beginning with 'With the utter fading away and cessation of ignorance itself...'. Herein, 'utter fading away and cessation' means by utter fading away and by utter cessation. As for 'That body does not exist': for the one whose taints are destroyed, the performance of action by the body is apparent, such as sweeping the stupa courtyard, going forward, going back, and performing one's duties. However, for him, the twenty volitions at the body-door become non-resultant. Therefore, it is said: 'That body does not exist, conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain would arise for him.' For here, the volitions that arise at the body-door are meant by 'body.' The same method applies to the other two doors as well. Terms such as 'field' are indeed names for wholesome and unwholesome kamma. For that kamma is called a 'field' because it is the place where results sprout, a 'foundation' because it is the support, a 'base' because it is the cause, and a 'ground' because it is the basis.

Iti satthā ettakena ṭhānena tīhi dvārehi āyūhitakammaṃ dassetvā idāni tassa kammassa [V 2.0347] vipaccanaṭṭhānaṃ dassetuṃ cattārome bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha attabhāvappaṭilābhāti paṭiladdhaattabhāvā. Attasañcetanā kamatīti attanā pakappitacetanā vahati pavattati.

Thus, the Teacher, having shown with this much detail the action undertaken through the three doors, now, to show the place where that kamma ripens, spoke the words beginning with 'These four, O bhikkhus...'. Herein, 'acquisitions of individual existences' means acquired individual existences. As for 'One's own volition proceeds': the volition planned by oneself carries on and occurs.

Attasañcetanāhetu tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā kāyā cuti hotītiādīsu khiḍḍāpadosikā devā attasañcetanāhetu cavanti. Tesañhi nandanavanacittalatāvanaphārusakavanādīsu dibbaratisamappitānaṃ kīḷantānaṃ pānabhojane sati sammussati, te āhārupacchedena ātape khittamālā viya milāyanti. Manopadosikā devā parasañcetanāhetu cavanti, ete cātumahārājikā devā. Tesu kira eko devaputto “nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti saparivāro rathena vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Athañño nikkhamanto taṃ purato gacchantaṃ disvā “kiṃ, bho, ayaṃ kapaṇo adiṭṭhapubbaṃ viya etaṃ disvā pītiyā uddhumāto viya gajjamāno viya ca gacchatī”ti kujjhati. Purato gacchantopi nivattitvā taṃ kuddhaṃ disvā kuddhā nāma suvijānā hontīti kuddhabhāvamassa ñatvā “tvaṃ kuddho [P 3.0148] mayhaṃ kiṃ karissasi, ayaṃ sampatti mayā dānasīlādīnaṃ vasena laddhā, na tuyhaṃ vasenā”ti paṭikujjhati. Ekasmiñhi kuddhe itaro akuddho rakkhati, ubhosu pana kuddhesu ekassa kodho itarassa paccayo hoti, tassapi kodho itarassa paccayo hotīti ubho kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ cavanti. Manussā attasañcetanā ca parasañcetanā ca hetu cavanti, attasañcetanāya ca parasañcetanāya ca hetubhūtāya cavantīti attho. Manussā hi kujjhitvā attanāva attānaṃ hatthehipi daṇḍehipi paharanti, rajjubandhanādīhipi bandhanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti, visampi khādanti, papātepi patanti, udakampi pavisanti, aggimpi pavisanti, parepi daṇḍena vā satthane vā paharitvā mārenti. Evaṃ tesu attasañcetanāpi parasañcetanāpi kamati.

In such phrases as, 'Due to the cause of their own volition, those beings pass away from that body,' the sporting deities pass away due to the cause of their own volition. For them, while indulging in divine pleasures in Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so on, and amusing themselves, mindfulness regarding drink and food is forgotten. Due to the cutting off of nourishment, they wither like garlands tossed in the sun's heat. The deities prone to anger pass away due to the cause of another's volition; these are the devas of the Cātumahārājika realm. It is said that among them, one devaputta, thinking, 'I will play at the festival,' sets out on the main road by chariot with his retinue. Then another, coming out and seeing him going in front, becomes angry, thinking, 'What, sirs, is this wretched one? As if never seen before, he goes along as if puffed up with joy and as if roaring.' The one going in front, having turned back and seen that angry one—for angry ones are indeed easy to recognize—and thus knowing his state of anger, becomes angry in return, saying, 'You are angry with me; what can you do? This prosperity was obtained by me through the power of giving, virtue, and so on, not by yours.' For when one is angry and the other is not angry, the latter offers protection. But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other, and the other's anger also becomes a condition for the first. Therefore, both pass away even while their consorts are wailing. Humans pass away due to the cause of their own volition and the cause of another's volition; the meaning is that they pass away due to a cause that is their own volition and a cause that is another's volition. Indeed, humans, having become angry, strike themselves with their own hands and with sticks; they bind themselves with ropes and so on; they cut off their own heads with a sword; they also eat poison; they fall from a precipice; they enter water; and they enter fire. Others, too, having struck them with a stick or with a weapon, kill them. Thus, in their case, both their own volition and the volition of others are operative.

Katame [M 2.0350] tena devā daṭṭhabbāti katame nāma te devā daṭṭhabbāti attho. Tena vā attabhāvena katame devā daṭṭhabbātipi attho. Kasmā pana thero imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati, kiṃ attanā kathetuṃ nappahotīti? Pahoti, idaṃ pana padaṃ attano sabhāvena buddhavisayaṃ pañhanti thero na kathesi. Tena daṭṭhabbāti tena attabhāvena daṭṭhabbā. Ayaṃ pana pañho heṭṭhā kāmāvacarepi rūpāvacarepi labbhati, bhavaggena pana paricchinditvā kathito nippadesena kathito hotīti bhagavatā evaṃ kathito.

As for 'By that, what devas are to be regarded?,' the meaning is: 'By what name are those devas to be regarded?' Or, this is also the meaning: 'By that existence, what devas are to be regarded?' Why, then, does the Elder ask this question? Is it that he is unable to answer it himself? He is able. However, the Elder did not speak on this matter, thinking, 'This question is, by its own nature, within the domain of a Buddha.' As for 'to be regarded by that,' it means to be regarded by that existence. Now, this question is found below in the sense-sphere and in the form-sphere, but when it is explained as delimited by the peak of existence, it becomes an explanation without remainder; for this reason, it was thus spoken by the Blessed One.

Āgantāro [V 2.0348] itthattanti itthabhāvaṃ kāmāvacarapañcakkhandhabhāvameva [P 3.0149] āgantāro, neva tatrūpapattikā na uparūpapattikā honti. Anāgantāro itthattanti imaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ anāgantāro, heṭṭhūpapattikā na honti, tatrūpapattikā vā uparūpapattikā vā tattheva vā parinibbāyino hontīti attho. Ettha ca heṭṭhimabhave nibbattānaṃ vasena uparūpapattikā veditabbā. Bhavagge panetaṃ natthi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

As for 'comers to this state,' they are comers to the human state, that is, only to the state of the five aggregates of the sense-sphere; they are neither reborn there nor reborn in a higher realm. As for 'non-comers to this state,' they are non-comers to these five aggregates; they are not reborn in a lower realm, but they are reborn there, or are reborn in a higher realm, or attain final Nibbāna right there—this is the meaning. And here, rebirth in a higher realm should be understood with reference to those reborn in a lower existence. But at the peak of existence, this does not exist. The remainder is clear in every respect.

2. Vibhattisuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Vibhatti Sutta

172. Dutiye atthapaṭisambhidāti pañcasu atthesu pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ. Odhisoti kāraṇaso. Byañjanasoti akkharaso. Anekapariyāyenāti anekehi kāraṇehi. Ācikkhāmīti kathemi. Desemīti pākaṭaṃ katvā kathemi. Paññāpemīti jānāpemi. Paṭṭhapemīti paṭṭhapetvā pavattetvā kathemi. Vivarāmīti vivaṭaṃ katvā kathemi. Vibhajāmīti vibhajitvā kathemi. Uttānīkaromīti gambhīraṃ uttānakaṃ katvā kathemi. So maṃ pañhenāti so maṃ pañhena upagacchatu. Ahaṃ veyyākaraṇenāti ahamassa pañhakathanena cittaṃ ārādhessāmi. Yo no dhammānaṃ sukusaloti yo amhākaṃ adhigatadhammānaṃ [P 3.0150] sukusalo satthā, so esa sammukhībhūto. Yadi mayā atthapaṭisambhidā na sacchikatā, “sacchikarohi tāva sāriputtā”ti vatvā maṃ paṭibāhissatīti satthu purato nisinnakova sīhanādaṃ nadati. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Imāsu ca pana paṭisambhidāsu tisso paṭisambhidā lokiyā, atthapaṭisambhidā lokiyalokuttarāti.

172. In the second sutta, 'discrimination of meaning' is the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in the five kinds of meaning. 'Odhisoti' means by way of cause. 'Byañjanasoti' means by way of syllables. 'Anekapariyāyena' means by various causes. 'Ācikkhāmi' means I will speak. 'Desemi' means I will speak, having made it manifest. 'Paññāpemi' means I will cause to know. 'Paṭṭhapemi' means I will speak, having established and set it forth. 'Vivarāmi' means I will speak, having made it open. 'Vibhajāmi' means I will speak, having analyzed it. 'Uttānīkaromi' means I will speak, having made the profound plain. 'So maṃ pañhena' means let him approach me with a question. 'Ahaṃ veyyākaraṇena' means I will please his mind by answering the question. 'Yo no dhammānaṃ sukusalo' means: The Teacher who is very skilled in the teachings to be attained by us, that very one is present. Thinking, 'If the discrimination of meaning had not been realized by me, he would have forbidden me, saying, “Sāriputta, first realize it,”' he utters a lion’s roar while sitting right before the Teacher. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere. Furthermore, among these discriminations, three are worldly, while the discrimination of meaning is worldly and supramundane.

3. Mahākoṭṭhikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika Sutta

173. Tatiye [M 2.0351] phassāyatanānanti phassākarānaṃ, phassassa uppattiṭṭhānānanti attho. Atthaññaṃ kiñcīti etesu asesato niruddhesu tato paraṃ koci appamattakopi kileso atthīti pucchati. Natthaññaṃ kiñcīti idhāpi “appamattakopi kileso natthī”ti pucchati. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Ime pana cattāropi pañhe sassatucchedaekaccasassataamarāvikkhepavasena pucchati. Tenassa thero pucchitapucchitaṃ paṭibāhanto mā hevanti āha. Ettha hiiti nipātamattaṃ, evaṃ mā bhaṇīti attho. Attūpaladdhivaseneva “atthaññaṃ kiñci añño [V 2.0349] koci attā nāma atthī”ti sassatādiākārena pucchati. Kiṃ panesa attūpaladdhikoti? Na attūpaladdhiko. Evaṃladdhiko pana tattheko bhikkhu nisinno, so pucchituṃ na sakkoti. Tassa laddhiṃ vissajjāpanatthaṃ evaṃ pucchati. Yepi ca anāgate evaṃladdhikā bhavissanti, tesaṃ “buddhakālepeso pañho mahāsāvakehi vissajjito”ti vacanokāsupacchedanatthaṃ pucchatiyeva.

173. In the third sutta, 'the bases for contact' means the grounds for contact, the places of arising for contact; this is the meaning. 'Is there anything else?' asks whether, after these have ceased without remainder, there is any defilement, even a slight one, remaining thereafter. 'There is nothing else' here also asks, 'Is there not even a slight defilement?' This same method applies to the remaining two pairs. He asks these four questions, however, by way of the views of eternalism, annihilationism, partial eternalism, and evasive equivocation. Therefore, the Elder, refuting each question as it was asked, said, 'Do not say so.' Herein, 'hi' is merely a particle; the meaning is, 'Do not speak thus.' By way of the assumption of a self, he asks in the manner of eternalism and so forth, 'Is there anything else, is there some other so-called self?' But is this one a person who holds the view of a self? He is not a person who holds the view of a self. However, a certain monk with such a view was seated there, but he was not able to ask. He asks thus for the purpose of having that monk's view dispelled. And also for those in the future who will hold such a view, he asks for the very purpose of cutting off their opportunity to speak, by establishing that 'this question was answered by the great disciples even in the time of the Buddha.'

Appapañcaṃ [P 3.0151] papañcetīti na papañcetabbaṭṭhāne papañcaṃ karoti, anācaritabbaṃ maggaṃ carati. Tāvatā papañcassa gatīti yattakā channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ gati, tattakāva taṇhādiṭṭhimānappabhedassa papañcassa gati. Channaṃ, āvuso, phassāyatanānaṃ asesavirāganirodhā papañcanirodho papañcavūpasamoti etesu chasu āyatanesu sabbaso niruddhesu papañcāpi niruddhāva honti, vūpasantāva hontīti attho. Āruppe pana puthujjanadevatānaṃ kiñcāpi pañca phassāyatanāni niruddhāni, chaṭṭhassa pana aniruddhattā tayopi papañcā appahīnāva. Apica pañcavokārabhavavaseneva pañho kathitoti. Catutthe imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

'He proliferates what is non-proliferation' means he makes proliferation in a place where one should not proliferate; he follows a path that should not be followed. 'So far as the range of proliferation extends' means that to whatever extent the range of the six bases for contact extends, to that same extent extends the range of proliferation, which is divided into craving, views, and conceit. 'Friend, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six bases for contact, there is the cessation of proliferation, the pacification of proliferation' means that when these six bases are entirely ceased, the proliferations too are indeed ceased, are indeed pacified; this is the meaning. In the formless realm, however, although for ordinary devas the five bases for contact are ceased, because the sixth is not ceased, the three proliferations are indeed unabandoned. Moreover, the question is spoken of only in terms of the five-constituent existence. In the fourth sutta, the meaning should be understood by this same method.

5. Upavāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta

175-176. Pañcame vijjāyantakaro hotīti vijjāya vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaro hoti, sakalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ paricchinnaṃ parivaṭumaṃ katvā tiṭṭhatīti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Saupādānoti sagahaṇova hutvā. Antakaro abhavissāti vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ katvā ṭhito abhavissa. Caraṇasampannoti pannarasadhammabhedena caraṇena samannāgato. Yathābhūtaṃ jānaṃ [M 2.0352] passaṃ antakaro hotīti yathāsabhāvaṃ maggapaññāya jānitvā passitvā vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ katvā ṭhito nāma hotīti arahattanikūṭena pañhaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Chaṭṭhaṃ heṭṭhā ekakanipātavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.
