In the fifth, “one who makes an end through knowledge” means one who makes an end to the suffering of the round through knowledge, having completely delimited and brought to a conclusion all the suffering of the round, he stands. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. “With clinging” means being with grasping. “Would have made an end” means he would have stood having made an end to the suffering of the round. “Perfect in conduct” means endowed with conduct in its fifteen aspects. “Knowing and seeing things as they really are, one makes an end” means having known and seen with the wisdom of the path according to their true nature, one is called one who stands having made an end to the suffering of the round—thus he concluded the question with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The sixth should be understood in the way explained previously in the commentary on the Ekakanipāta.

7. Rāhulasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta

177. Sattame [P 3.0152] ajjhattikāti kesādīsu vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu thaddhākāralakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu. Bāhirāti bahiddhā anindriyabaddhesu pāsāṇapabbatādīsu thaddhākāralakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu[V 2.0350]. Imināva nayena sesāpi dhātuyo veditabbā. Netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attāti idaṃ tayaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhiggāhapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ. Sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbanti hetunā kāraṇena maggapaññāya passitabbaṃ. Disvāti sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya passitvā. Acchecchi taṇhanti maggavajjhataṇhaṃ samūlakaṃ chindi. Vivattayi saṃyojananti dasavidhampi saṃyojanaṃ vivattayi ubbattetvā pajahi. Sammā mānābhisamayāti hetunā kāraṇena navavidhassa mānassa pahānābhisamayā. Antamakāsi dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ paricchinnaṃ parivaṭumaṃ akāsi, katvā ṭhitoti attho. Iti satthārā saṃyuttamahānikāye rāhulovāde (saṃ. ni. 3.91 ādayo) vipassanā kathitā, cūḷarāhulovādepi (ma. ni. 3.416 ādayo) vipassanā kathitā, ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāde (ma. ni. 2.107 ādayo) daharasseva sato musāvādā veramaṇī kathitā, mahārāhulovāde (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) vipassanā kathitā. Imasmiṃ aṅguttaramahānikāye ayaṃ catukoṭikasuññatā nāma kathitāti.

177. In the seventh, ‘internal’ refers to the earth element characterized by hardness in the twenty bodily parts such as hair. ‘External’ refers to the earth element characterized by hardness in external things not connected with the sense faculties, such as rocks and mountains. By this very method, the remaining elements should also be known. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this triad is spoken by way of rejecting the grasping of craving, conceit, and views. ‘Should be seen with right wisdom’ means it should be seen with the wisdom of the path, by reason and cause. ‘Having seen’ means having seen with the wisdom of the path which is together with insight. ‘He cut off craving’ means he severed the craving that is to be destroyed by the path, together with its root. ‘He turned away from the fetters’ means having uprooted, he abandoned all ten fetters. ‘Through the full understanding of conceit’ means because of the abandoning and full understanding of the ninefold conceit, by reason and cause. ‘He made an end to suffering’ means he made the suffering of the round of rebirth limited and circumscribed; having done so, he is established—this is the meaning. Thus, by the Teacher, in the Saṃyutta Mahānikāya, in the Rāhulovāda, insight was taught. In the Cūḷarāhulovāda, insight was also taught. In the Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda, abstinence from false speech was taught to him when he was still young. In the Mahārāhulovāda, insight was taught. In this Aṅguttara Mahānikāya, this insight called the four-ended emptiness is taught.

8. Jambālīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Jambālī Sutta

178. Aṭṭhame [P 3.0153] santaṃ cetovimuttinti aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ aññataraṃ samāpattiṃ. Sakkāyanirodhanti tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhātassa sakkāyassa nirodhaṃ, nibbānanti attho. Na pakkhandatīti ārammaṇavasena na pakkhandati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Na pāṭikaṅkhoti na pāṭikaṅkhitabbo. Lepagatenāti lepamakkhitena.

178. In the eighth, ‘peaceful liberation of mind’ means any one of the eight attainments. ‘Cessation of identity’ means the cessation of identity, which is designated as the round of existence in the three realms; the meaning is Nibbāna. ‘Does not rush in’ means it does not rush in by way of the object. The same principle applies to the remaining phrases. ‘Should not be longed for’ means it should not be longed for. ‘Smeared with resin’ means smeared with resin.

Imasmiñca [M 2.0353] panatthe nadīpāraṃ gantukāmapurisopammaṃ āharitabbaṃ – eko kira puriso caṇḍasotāya vāḷamacchākulāya nadiyā pāraṃ gantukāmo “orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ, kiṃ nu kho katvā pāraṃ gamissāmī”ti paṭipāṭiyā ṭhite aṭṭha kakudharukkhe disvā “sakkā imāya rukkhapaṭipāṭiyā gantu”nti manasikatvā “kakudharukkhā nāma maṭṭhasākhā honti, sākhāya hatthā na saṇṭhaheyyu”nti nigrodhapilakkharukkhādīnaṃ aññatarassa lākhāya hatthapāde makkhetvā dakkhiṇahatthena ekaṃ sākhaṃ gaṇhi. Hattho tattheva lagi. Puna vāmahatthena dakkhiṇapādena vāmapādenāti cattāropi hatthapādā tattheva lagiṃsu. So adhosiro lambamāno uparinadiyaṃ deve vuṭṭhe puṇṇāya nadiyā sote nimuggo kumbhīlādīnaṃ bhakkho ahosi.

And in this context, the simile of a man wishing to cross a river should be brought forward—it is said that a certain man, wishing to cross a river with a violent current and infested with fierce fish, thought: 'This near shore is risky and perilous, the far shore is safe and free from peril. What should I do to reach the far shore?' Seeing eight kakudha trees standing in a row, he considered, 'It is possible to go by means of this row of trees.' But he reflected, 'Kakudha trees have smooth branches; hands would not get a firm grip on the branches.' So he smeared his hands and feet with resin from a banyan, pilakkha, or similar tree, and with his right hand grasped one branch. His hand stuck right there. Then his left hand, right foot, and left foot—all four limbs stuck right there. Hanging head downward, when it rained from above and the river swelled, he was submerged by the current and became food for crocodiles and other creatures.

Tattha [V 2.0351] nadīsotaṃ viya saṃsārasotaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, sotassa pāraṃ gantukāmapuriso viya yogāvacaro, orimatīraṃ viya sakkāyo, pārimatīraṃ viya nibbānaṃ, paṭipāṭiyā ṭhitā aṭṭha kakudharukkhā viya aṭṭha samāpattiyo, lepamakkhitena [P 3.0154] hatthena sākhāgahaṇaṃ viya jhānavipassanānaṃ pāripanthike asodhetvā samāpattisamāpajjanaṃ, catūhi hatthapādehi sākhāya baddhassa olambanaṃ viya paṭhamajjhāne nikantiyā laggakālo, uparisote vuṭṭhi viya chasu dvāresu kilesānaṃ uppannakālo, nadiyā puṇṇāya sote nimuggassa kumbhīlādīnaṃ bhakkhabhūtakālo viya saṃsārasote nimuggassa catūsu apāyesu dukkhānubhavanakālo veditabbo.

Here, the river current should be seen as the current of saṃsāra. The man wishing to cross the current is like the yogi. The near shore is like identity (sakkāya), the far shore like Nibbāna. The eight kakudha trees standing in a row are like the eight attainments. Grasping a branch with a resin-smeared hand is like entering attainments without purifying the obstacles to jhāna and insight. Being suspended by four limbs clinging to the branch is like the time of clinging with delight to the first jhāna. The rain falling from above is like the time of the arising of defilements at the six sense doors. The time of being submerged in the current of the swollen river and becoming food for crocodiles and other creatures is to be understood as like the time of experiencing suffering in the four woeful realms for one submerged in the current of saṃsāra.

Suddhena hatthenāti sudhotena parisuddhahatthena. Imasmimpi atthe tādisameva opammaṃ kātabbaṃ – tatheva hi pāraṃ gantukāmo puriso “kakudharukkhā nāma maṭṭhasākhā, kiliṭṭhahatthena gaṇhantassa hattho parigaleyyā”ti hatthapāde sudhote katvā ekaṃ sākhaṃ gaṇhitvā paṭhamaṃ rukkhaṃ āruḷho. Tato otaritvā dutiyaṃ…pe… tato otaritvā aṭṭhamaṃ, aṭṭhamarukkhato otaritvā pārimatīre khemantabhūmiṃ gato.

‘With a clean hand’ means with a well-washed, purified hand. In this case too, a similar analogy should be drawn: Just so, a man wishing to go to the other shore, thinking, 'Kakudha trees have smooth branches; if one grasps them with a dirty hand, the hand will slip,' having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, grasped one branch and climbed the first tree. Then descending, he climbed the second...and so on... then descending from the eighth tree, he reached the secure ground of the opposite shore.

Tattha “imehi rukkhehi pārimatīraṃ gamissāmī”ti tassa purisassa cintitakālo viya yogino “aṭṭha samāpattiyo samāpajjitvā samāpattito [M 2.0354] vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ gamissāmī”ti cintitakālo, suddhena hatthena sākhāgahaṇaṃ viya jhānavipassanānaṃ pāripanthikadhamme sodhetvā samāpattisamāpajjanaṃ. Tattha paṭhamarukkhārohaṇakālo viya paṭhamajjhānasamāpattikālo, paṭhamarukkhato oruyha dutiyaṃ [P 3.0155] āruḷhakālo viya paṭhamajjhāne nikantiyā abaddhassa tato vuṭṭhāya dutiyajjhānasamāpannakālo…pe… sattamarukkhato oruyha aṭṭhamaṃ āruḷhakālo viya ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ nikantiyā abaddhassa tato vuṭṭhāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpannakālo. Aṭṭhamarukkhato oruyha pārimatīraṃ khemantabhūmiṃ gatakālo viya nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nikantiyā abaddhassa samāpattito vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattappattakālo veditabbo.

Therein, the time when the man thinks, 'I will go to the far shore with these trees,' is like the time when a yogi thinks, 'Having attained the eight attainments and emerged from them, I will reach arahantship.' Grasping a branch with a clean hand is like the attainment of meditative states after purifying the obstructive factors of jhāna and insight. Therein, the time of climbing the first tree is like the time of attaining the first jhāna. The time of descending from the first tree and climbing the second is like the time when one, not being bound by delight in the first jhāna, emerges from it and attains the second jhāna… The time of descending from the seventh tree and climbing the eighth is like the time when one, not being bound by delight in the base of nothingness, emerges from it and attains the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The time of descending from the eighth tree and reaching the far shore, the safe ground, is to be understood as like the time when one, not being bound by delight in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, emerges from that attainment, contemplates the formations, and attains arahantship.

Avijjāppabhedaṃ manasi karotīti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu aññāṇabhūtāya gaṇabahalamahāavijjāya pabhedasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ manasi karoti. Na pakkhandatīti ārammaṇavaseneva na pakkhandati. Jambālīti gāmato nikkhantassa mahāudakassa patiṭṭhānabhūto mahāāvāṭo. Anekavassagaṇikāti [V 2.0352] gāmassa vā nagarassa vā uppannakāleyeva uppannattā anekāni vassagaṇāni uppannāya etissāti anekavassagaṇikā. Āyamukhānīti catasso pavisanakandarā. Apāyamukhānīti apavāhanacchiddāni. Na āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkhoti na pāḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkhitabbo. Na hi tato udakaṃ uṭṭhāya pāḷiṃ bhinditvā kacavaraṃ gahetvā mahāsamuddaṃ pāpuṇāti.

'He considers the breaking of ignorance' (avijjāppabhedaṃ manasi karoti) means he contemplates Arahantship, which is designated as the breaking of the great, dense mass of ignorance that is unknowing concerning the eight places. 'He does not plunge in' (na pakkhandati) means he does not plunge in by way of the object. 'Jambālī' (quagmire) is a great pit that serves as a receptacle for the great waters that have flowed out from a village. 'Having many years' (anekavassagaṇikā) means it has existed for many years, having arisen at the same time as the village or city. 'Inlets' (āyamukhāni) are the four entrance channels. 'Outlets' (apāyamukhānīti) are the drainage holes. 'No breaking of the bank is to be expected' (na āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkho) means no breaking of the bank should be expected, for the water does not rise from there, break the bank, take the rubbish, and reach the great ocean.

Imassa panatthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ uyyānagavesakaopammaṃ āharitabbaṃ. Eko [P 3.0156] kira nagaravāsiko kulaputto uyyānaṃ gavesanto nagarato nātidūre naccāsanne mahantaṃ jambāliṃ addasa. So “imasmiṃ ṭhāne ramaṇīyaṃ uyyānaṃ bhavissatī”ti sallakkhetvā kuddālaṃ ādāya cattāripi kandarāni pidhāya apavāhanacchiddāni vivaritvā aṭṭhāsi. Devo na sammā vassi, avasesaudakaṃ apavāhanacchiddena parissavitvā gataṃ. Cammakhaṇḍapilotikādīni tattheva pūtikāni jātāni, pāṇakā saṇṭhitā, samantā anupagamanīyā jātā. Upagatānampi nāsāpuṭe pidhāya pakkamitabbaṃ hoti[M 2.0355]. So katipāhena āgantvā paṭikkamma ṭhito oloketvā “na sakkā upagantu”nti pakkāmi.

To illustrate this point, the simile of the garden seeker should be brought forward. It is said that a certain clansman living in the city, while searching for a garden not too far from the city, yet not too near, saw a large quagmire (jambālī). Thinking, 'In this place, there will be a delightful garden,' he took a spade, covered all four inlets, opened the drainage holes, and stood by. The rain did not fall properly, and the remaining water flowed away through the drainage holes. Pieces of hide, rags, and so on became rotten right there, living beings settled in, and the area became completely unapproachable. Even those who approached had to cover their nostrils and leave. After a few days, he came back, stood at a distance, looked around, and thinking, 'It is impossible to approach,' he left.

Tattha nagaravāsī kulaputto viya yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo, uyyānaṃ gavesantena gāmadvāre jambāliyā diṭṭhakālo viya cātumahābhūtikakāyo, āyamukhānaṃ pihitakālo viya dhammassavanodakassa aladdhakālo, apāyamukhānaṃ vivaṭakālo viya chadvārikasaṃvarassa vissaṭṭhakālo, devassa sammā avuṭṭhakālo viya sappāyakammaṭṭhānassa aladdhakālo, avasesaudakassa apāyamukhehi parissavitvā gatakālo viya abbhantare guṇānaṃ parihīnakālo, udakassa uṭṭhāya pāḷiṃ bhinditvā kacavaraṃ ādāya mahāsamuddaṃ pāpuṇituṃ asamatthakālo viya arahattamaggena avijjāpāḷiṃ bhinditvā kilesarāsiṃ vidhamitvā nibbānaṃ sacchikātuṃ asamatthakālo, cammakhaṇḍapilotikādīnaṃ tattheva pūtibhāvo viya abbhantare rāgādikilesehi paripūritakālo, tassa āgantvā disvā [P 3.0157] vippaṭisārino gatakālo viya vaṭṭasamaṅgipuggalassa vaṭṭe abhiratakālo veditabbo.

Therein, the yogi should be seen as being like the city-dwelling clansman. The body composed of the four great elements is like the quagmire at the village gate when it is seen by one searching for a park. The time of not having obtained the water of hearing the Dhamma is like the time when the inlets are closed. The time of having relinquished restraint at the six sense doors is like the time when the outlets are open. The time of not having obtained a suitable meditation subject is like the time when the rain-god does not rain properly. The time of being deficient in internal virtues is like the time when the remaining water has flowed away through the outlets. The time of being unable to realize Nibbāna by breaking the embankment of ignorance with the path to arahantship and destroying the mass of defilements is like the time when the water is unable to rise, break the bank, carry away the rubbish, and reach the great ocean. The time of being filled internally with defilements such as lust is like the putrefaction of pieces of hide, rags, and so on right there. The time when a person endowed with the round of existence delights in that round should be understood as being like the time when that clansman, having come and seen it, departs with regret.

Āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkhoti pāḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkhitabbo. Tato hi udakaṃ uṭṭhāya pāḷiṃ bhinditvā kacavaraṃ ādāya mahāsamuddaṃ pāpuṇituṃ sakkhissatīti attho.

‘The breaking of the bank is to be expected’ (āḷippabhedo pāṭikaṅkho) means the breaking of the bank should be expected. For then the water will be able to rise, break the bank, carry away the rubbish, and reach the great ocean—this is the meaning.

Idhāpi [V 2.0353] tadeva opammaṃ āharitabbaṃ. Tattha āyamukhānaṃ vivaṭakālo viya sappāyadhammassavanassa laddhakālo, apāyamukhānaṃ pihitakālo viya chasu dvāresu saṃvarassa paccupaṭṭhitakālo, devassa sammā vuṭṭhakālo viya sappāyakammaṭṭhānassa laddhakālo, udakassa uṭṭhāya pāḷiṃ bhinditvā kacavaraṃ ādāya mahāsamuddaṃ pattakālo viya arahattamaggena avijjaṃ bhinditvā akusalarāsiṃ vidhamitvā arahattaṃ sacchikatakālo, āyamukhehi paviṭṭhena udakena sarassa paripuṇṇakālo viya abbhantare lokuttaradhammehi paripuṇṇakālo, samantato vatiṃ katvā rukkhe ropetvā uyyānamajjhe pāsādaṃ māpetvā nāṭakāni paccupaṭṭhapetvā subhojanaṃ bhuñjantassa nisinnakālo viya dhammapāsādaṃ āruyha [M 2.0356] nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā nisinnakālo veditabbo. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Desanā pana lokiyalokuttaramissikā kathitāti.

Here too, the same simile should be brought forward. There, the time when the inlets are open is like having obtained the opportunity to hear the conducive Dhamma. The time when the outlets are closed is like having established restraint at the six sense doors. The time when the rain falls properly is like having obtained a conducive meditation subject. The time when the water rises, breaks the bank, carries away the rubbish, and reaches the great ocean is like having broken ignorance with the path to arahantship, destroyed the mass of unwholesome states, and realized arahantship. The time when the lake is filled with water that has entered through the inlets is like being filled internally with supramundane qualities. The time when one sits enjoying fine food after building a fence all around, planting trees, constructing a mansion in the middle of the park, and setting up entertainments is like having ascended the palace of Dhamma, entered into the fruition attainment with Nibbāna as its object, and sitting—this should be understood. The rest here is clear in meaning. The teaching, however, is said to be a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

9. Nibbānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse on Nibbāna

179. Navame hānabhāgiyā saññātiādīsu “paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhiṃ kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti, hānabhāginī paññā”ti (vibha. 799) abhidhamme vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Yathābhūtaṃ [P 3.0158] nappajānantīti yathāsabhāvato maggañāṇena na jānanti.

179. In the ninth, regarding 'perceptions pertaining to decline' and so on, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Abhidhamma: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and attention associated with sensual desire arise; this is wisdom pertaining to decline' (Vibh. 799). 'They do not understand as it really is' means they do not know it with path-knowledge according to its true nature.

10. Mahāpadesasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Great Authorities

180. Dasame bhoganagare viharatīti parinibbānasamaye cārikaṃ caranto taṃ nagaraṃ patvā tattha viharati. Ānandacetiyeti ānandayakkhassa bhavanaṭṭhāne patiṭṭhitavihāre. Mahāpadeseti mahāokāse mahāapadese vā, buddhādayo mahante mahante apadisitvā vuttāni mahākāraṇānīti attho. Neva abhinanditabbanti haṭṭhatuṭṭhehi sādhukāraṃ datvā pubbeva na sotabbaṃ. Evaṃ kate hi pacchā “idaṃ na sametī”ti vuccamānopi “kiṃ pubbeva ayaṃ dhammo, idāni na dhammo”ti vatvā laddhiṃ na vissajjeti. Nappaṭikkositabbanti “kiṃ esa bālo vadatī”ti evaṃ pubbeva na vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ vutte hi vattuṃ yuttampi na vakkhati. Tenāha – anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvāti. Padabyañjanānīti padasaṅkhātāni byañjanāni. Sādhukaṃ uggahetvāti “imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāḷi vuttā, imasmiṃ ṭhāne attho vutto, imasmiṃ ṭhāne anusandhi kathitā[V 2.0354], imasmiṃ ṭhāne pubbāparaṃ kathita”nti suṭṭhu gahetvā. Sutte otāretabbānīti sutte otaritabbāni. Vinaye sandassetabbānīti vinaye saṃsandetabbāni.

180. “He dwells in the tenth, at Bhoganagara” (Dasame bhoganagare viharatīti) means that at the time of his final passing, while wandering, he arrived at that city and stayed there. “Ānandacetīya” (Ānandacetiyeti) refers to the monastery established at the dwelling place of the yakkha Ānanda. “Great authority” (Mahāpadeseti) means in a great opportunity or with great reference; it refers to the great reasons stated by citing the great ones such as the Buddha. “One should neither approve” (Neva abhinanditabbanti) means one should not listen to it beforehand with joy and delight, giving praise. For if this is done, even when later told, “This does not fit,” one might say, “Was this not the Dhamma before? Is it not the Dhamma now?” and refuse to relinquish one's view. “Nor should one reject” (Nappaṭikkositabbanti) means one should not beforehand say, “What is this fool saying?” For if this is said, even what is proper to say will not be spoken. Therefore, He said: “without approving or rejecting” (anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvāti). “Words and syllables” (Padabyañjanānīti) means the syllables enumerated as words. “Having thoroughly learned” (Sādhukaṃ uggahetvāti) means having well grasped: “In this place the Pāḷi is stated, in this place the meaning is explained, in this place the connection is discussed, in this place the sequence is explained.” “They should be examined in the Sutta” (Sutte otāretabbānīti) means they should be compared with the Sutta. “They should be verified in the Vinaya” (Vinaye sandassetabbānīti) means they should be compared with the Vinaya.

Ettha ca suttanti vinayo vutto. Yathāha – “kattha paṭikkhittaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ suttavibhaṅge”ti (cūḷava. 457) vinayoti khandhako. Yathāha – “vinayātisāre”ti. Evaṃ vinayapiṭakampi na pariyādiyati. Ubhatovibhaṅgā pana [P 3.0159] suttaṃ, khandhakaparivārā [M 2.0357] vinayoti evaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ pariyādiyati. Atha vā suttantapiṭakaṃ suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayoti evaṃ dveyeva piṭakāni pariyādiyanti. Suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni vā suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayoti evampi tīṇi piṭakāni na tāva pariyādiyanti. Asuttanāmakañhi buddhavacanaṃ nāma atthi. Seyyathidaṃ – jātakaṃ paṭisambhidā niddeso suttanipāto dhammapadaṃ udānaṃ itivuttakaṃ vimānavatthu petavatthu theragāthā therīgāthā apadānanti.

And here, 'Sutta' (suttaṃ) is said to be the Vinaya. As it is said: 'Where was it prohibited? In the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī' (Cūḷavagga 457). 'Vinaya' (vinayo) is the Khandhakas. As it is said: 'In transgressing the Vinaya.' Thus, the Vinaya Piṭaka is not encompassed. However, the two Vibhaṅgas are the Sutta, and the Khandhakas and Parivāra are the Vinaya—thus the Vinaya Piṭaka is encompassed. Alternatively, the Suttanta Piṭaka is the Sutta, and the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya—thus only the two Piṭakas are encompassed. Or, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the Sutta, and the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya—thus even the three Piṭakas are not encompassed. For there is indeed the word of the Buddha that is not named 'Sutta,' namely: the Jātaka, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Niddesa, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Apadāna.

Sudinnatthero pana “asuttanāmakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ natthī”ti taṃ sabbaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “tīṇi piṭakāni suttaṃ, vinayo pana kāraṇa”nti āha. Tato taṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento idaṃ suttamāhari –

However, the Elder Sudinna, rejecting all that, said: 'There is no word of the Buddha that is not named "Sutta."' And he stated: 'The three Piṭakas are the Sutta; the Vinaya, however, is the cause.' Then, showing that cause, he adduced this Sutta:

“Ye kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi, ime dhammā sarāgāya saṃvattanti no virāgāya, saṃyogāya saṃvattanti no visaṃyogāya, saupādānāya saṃvattanti no anupādānāya, mahicchatāya saṃvattanti no appicchatāya, asantuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no santuṭṭhiyā, kosajjāya saṃvattanti no vīriyārambhāya, saṅgaṇikāya saṃvattanti no pavivekāya, ācayāya saṃvattanti no apacayāya. Ekaṃsena, gotami, jāneyyāsi ‘neso dhammo neso vinayo netaṃ satthu sāsana’nti.

'Gotami, regarding those things of which you might know that they lead to passion, not to dispassion; to entanglement, not to disentanglement; to grasping, not to non-grasping; to great desire, not to little desire; to discontent, not to contentment; to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; to gregariousness, not to seclusion; to accumulation, not to diminution—you may know for certain, Gotami: "This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction."

“Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi, ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti no sarāgāya, visaṃyogāya saṃvattanti no saṃyogāya. Anupādānāya saṃvattanti no saupādānāya, appicchatāya saṃvattanti no mahicchatāya, santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no asantuṭṭhiyā, vīriyārambhāya saṃvattanti no kosajjāya, pavivekāya saṃvattanti no saṅgaṇikāya, apacayāya saṃvattanti no ācayāya. Ekaṃsena, gotami[P 3.0160], jāneyyāsi ‘eso [V 2.0355] dhammo eso vinayo etaṃ satthu sāsana’”nti (cūḷava. 406; a. ni. 8.53).

'Gotami, regarding those things of which you might know that they lead to dispassion, not to passion; to disentanglement, not to entanglement; to non-grasping, not to grasping; to fewness of wishes, not to great desire; to contentment, not to discontent; to the arousing of energy, not to laziness; to seclusion, not to gregariousness; to diminution, not to accumulation—you may know for certain, Gotami: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction."' (Cūḷavagga 406; Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.53).

Tasmā sutteti tepiṭakabuddhavacane otāretabbāni. Vinayeti etasmiṃ rāgādivinayakāraṇe saṃsandetabbānīti ayamettha attho. Na ceva sutte otarantīti suttapaṭipāṭiyā katthaci anāgantvā challiṃ uṭṭhapetvā [M 2.0358] guḷhavessantara-guḷhaummagga-guḷhavinayavedallapiṭakānaṃ aññatarato āgatāni paññāyantīti attho. Evaṃ āgatāni hi rāgādivinaye ca apaññāyamānāni chaḍḍetabbāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ – “iti hidaṃ, bhikkhave, chaḍḍeyyāthā”ti. Etenupāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, catutthaṃ mahāpadesaṃ dhāreyyāthāti imaṃ, bhikkhave, catutthaṃ dhammassa patiṭṭhānokāsaṃ dhāreyyāthāti.

Therefore, 'in the Suttas' (sutte) means they should be compared with the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s words. 'In the Vinaya' (vinaye) means they should be checked against this cause for the removal of passion and the like—this is the meaning here. 'If they do not accord with the Suttas' (na ceva sutte otaranti) means it is understood that they have come from one of the hidden Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhaummagga, or Guḷhavinayavedalla Piṭakas, not appearing anywhere in the sequence of the Suttas but presenting a counterfeit. Indeed, teachings that have come in this way and are not seen in the removal of passion and the like should be discarded. Therefore it was said: 'Monks, you should discard this.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases. 'Monks, you should remember this fourth great authority' (Idaṃ, bhikkhave, catutthaṃ mahāpadesaṃ dhāreyyāthāti) means: 'Monks, you should remember this fourth basis for the Dhamma.'

Sañcetaniyavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on Intention.

(19) 4. Brāhmaṇavaggo

(19) 4. The Brahmin Chapter

1. Yodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta

181. Catutthassa [V 2.0356] paṭhame ṭhānakusaloti yena ṭhānena ṭhito avirādhetvā vijjhituṃ sakkoti, tasmiṃ ṭhāne kusalo. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

181. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'skilled in positioning' means being skilled in a position from which, while standing, one is able to strike without missing. The rest should be understood in the manner explained previously.

2. Pāṭibhogasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Pāṭibhoga Sutta

182. Dutiye natthi koci pāṭibhogoti ahaṃ te pāṭibhogoti evaṃ pāṭibhogo bhavituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Jarādhammanti jarāsabhāvaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

182. In the second sutta, 'there is no surety' means there is no one capable of becoming a surety by saying, 'I will be your surety.' 'Subject to old age' means having the nature of aging. This is the principle in all cases.

3. Sutasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Suta Sutta

183. Tatiye [P 3.0161] natthi tato dosoti tasmiṃ doso nāma natthīti attho.

183. In the third sutta, 'there is no fault in that' means there is indeed no fault in it.

4. Abhayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta

184. Catutthe kicchājīvitakāraṇaṭṭhena rogova rogātaṅko nāma. Phuṭṭhassāti tena rogātaṅkena samannāgatassa. Urattāḷiṃ kandatīti uraṃ tāḷetvā rodati. Akatakalyāṇotiādīsu kalyāṇaṃ vuccati puññakammaṃ[M 2.0359], taṃ akataṃ etenāti akatakalyāṇo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Puññakammameva hi kosallasambhūtattā kusalaṃ, bhītassa parittāyakattā bhīruttāṇanti vuccati. Katapāpotiādīsu pāpaṃ vuccati lāmakaṃ akusalakammaṃ. Luddanti kakkhaḷakammaṃ. Kibbisanti samalaṃ aparisuddhakammaṃ. Kaṅkhī hotīti buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇesu ceva sikkhāya ca pubbante ca aparante ca pubbantāparante ca paṭiccasamuppāde cāti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kaṅkhāya samannāgato [V 2.0357] hoti. Vicikicchīti vicikicchāya samannāgato sāsanasaddhamme na niṭṭhaṃ gato, uggahaparipucchāvasena niṭṭhaṃ gantuṃ na sakkoti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

184. In the fourth sutta, 'affliction of disease' (rogātaṅko) is simply disease, in the sense of being a cause of difficult living. 'Phuṭṭhassa' means one who is endowed with that affliction of illness. 'Urattāḷiṃ kandati' means striking one's chest and crying. In 'not having done good' and so forth, 'good' (kalyāṇaṃ) is said to be meritorious action; 'one by whom that has not been done' is 'one who has not done good.' The same method applies to the remaining terms. Indeed, meritorious action itself, being born of skill, is called 'skillful,' and being a protector for the frightened, it is called 'refuge for the fearful.' In 'having done evil' and so forth, 'evil' (pāpaṃ) is said to be inferior, unwholesome action. 'Cruel' (luddaṃ) means harsh action. 'Corrupt' (kibbisaṃ) means defiled, impure action. 'Is doubtful' (kaṅkhī hoti) means one is endowed with doubt concerning the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and also concerning the training, the past, the future, both past and future, and dependent origination—thus, being endowed with doubt in these eight instances. 'Is perplexed' (vicikicchī) means one is endowed with perplexity, not having reached a conclusion regarding the true Dhamma of the teaching, being unable to arrive at a conclusion through learning and questioning. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances.

5. Brāhmaṇasaccasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Brāhmaṇasacca Sutta

185. Pañcame brāhmaṇasaccānīti brāhmaṇānaṃ saccāni tathāni. So tena na samaṇoti maññatīti so khīṇāsavo tena saccena “ahaṃ samaṇo”ti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi na maññati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Yadeva tattha saccaṃ, tadabhiññāyāti yaṃ tattha “sabbe pāṇā [P 3.0162] avajjhā”ti paṭipattiyā saccaṃ tathaṃ aviparītaṃ. Iminā vacīsaccaṃ abbhantaraṃ katvā paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānaṃ dasseti. Tadabhiññāyāti taṃ ubhayampi abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya jānitvā. Anuddayāya anukampāya paṭipanno hotīti anuddayatthāya ca anukampatthāya ca yā paṭipadā, taṃ paṭipanno hoti, pūretvā ṭhitoti attho. Sesapaṭipadāsupi eseva nayo.

185. In the fifth sutta, 'the truths of the brahmins' means the truths of the brahmins are actual. 'By that, he does not consider himself a recluse' means that the one whose taints are destroyed does not, through craving, conceit, or views, consider 'I am a recluse' by that truth. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Having directly known what is true therein' means: the truth therein, which is actual and not contrary, is the practice that 'all beings are not to be killed.' By this, having included verbal truth, he shows the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. 'Having directly known that' means having known both with distinguished wisdom. 'He is one who has undertaken the practice out of compassion and kindness' means that he has undertaken the practice that is for the sake of compassion and kindness; the meaning is that he has fulfilled it and is established in it. The same method applies to the remaining practices.

Sabbe kāmāti sabbe vatthukāmakilesakāmā. Iti vadaṃ brāhmaṇo saccamāhāti evampi vadanto khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo saccameva āha. Sabbe bhavāti kāmabhavādayo tayopi. Nāhaṃ kvacanīti ettha pana catukkoṭikasuññatā kathitā. Ayañhi “nāhaṃ kvacanī”ti kvaci attānaṃ na passati, kassaci kiñcanatasminti attano attānaṃ kassaci parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ na passati, bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ, parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāraṃ maññitvā upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mamasaddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā “na ca kvacani parassa ca attānaṃ kvaci na passatī”ti ayamattho. Idāni “mamasaddaṃ āharitvā [M 2.0360] mama kismiñci kiñcanaṃ natthī”ti so parassa attā mama kismiñci kiñcanabhāve atthīti na passati, attano bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne [P 3.0163] sahāyaṃ, parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāranti kismiñci ṭhāne parassa attānaṃ iminā kiñcanabhāvena upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Evamayaṃ yasmā neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passatīti. Iti vadaṃ brāhmaṇoti evaṃ catukkoṭikaṃ suññataṃ vadantopi khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo tassā paṭipadāya sammā paṭividdhattā saccameva āha, na musāti sabbesupi vāresu maññanānaṃ pahīnattāyeva na maññatīti ca attho veditabbo. Ākiñcaññaṃyeva [V 2.0358] paṭipadanti kiñcanabhāvavirahitaṃ nippalibodhaṃ niggahaṇameva paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti pūretvā ṭhito.

'All sensual pleasures' means all sensual pleasures related to objects and defilements. 'Speaking thus, the brahmin speaks truth' means that even when speaking thus, the brahmin whose taints are destroyed speaks only the truth. 'All states of existence' means all three, such as the sensual state of existence. 'I am not of anyone'—here, the fourfold emptiness is spoken of. For this one, by the phrase 'I am not of anyone,' does not see a self anywhere, nor does he see his own self as something to be brought into the state of being a possession for any other person; the meaning is that he does not see it as something to be brought into such a relation by conceiving of a brother in the role of a brother, a friend in the role of a friend, or a requisite in the role of a requisite. 'Nor is anything of anyone mine'—here, first setting aside the word 'mine,' the meaning is this: 'and he does not see another's self anywhere.' Now, bringing in the word 'mine,' the meaning is 'for me there is no possession in anything.' He does not see another's self as existing in the state of being a possession for him in any way; the meaning is that he does not see another's self as something to be brought into this state of being a possession in any place, for instance, as a brother in the role of his brother, a friend in the role of his friend, or a requisite in the role of his requisite. Thus, because he neither sees a self anywhere, nor sees that self as something to be brought into the state of being another's possession, nor sees another's self, nor sees another's self as something to be brought into the state of being his own possession—'speaking thus, the brahmin'—even speaking thus of the fourfold emptiness, the brahmin whose taints are destroyed, because of his correct penetration of that practice, speaks only the truth, not falsehood. And in all cases, the meaning should be understood that he does not conceive precisely because conceiving is abandoned. 'The very path of nothingness' means he has undertaken the path that is free from the state of being a possession, unobstructed, and is restraint itself; he has fulfilled it and is established in it.

Imāni kho paribbājakā cattāri brāhmaṇasaccāni mayā sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā paveditānīti yāni tumhe bhovādibrāhmaṇānaṃ saccāni vadetha, tehi aññāni mayā imāni bāhitapāpabrāhmaṇassa cattāri saccāni catūhi maggehi soḷasavidhena kiccena jānitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā paveditāni desitāni jotitānīti attho. Iti imasmiṃ sutte catūsupi ṭhānesu khīṇāsavassa vacīsaccameva kathitanti.

'These, wanderers, are the four truths of the brahmins, declared by me after having directly known and realized them myself.' This means: different from the truths that you brahmins who use the address 'bho' speak of, these four truths of the brahmin who has expelled evil have been declared, taught, and illuminated by me after having known them through the four paths with their sixteen aspects and having made them directly present. Thus, in this sutta, in all four instances, it is the verbal truth of the one whose taints are destroyed that is spoken of.

6. Ummaggasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Ummagga Sutta

186. Chaṭṭhe parikassatīti ākaḍḍhiyati. Ummaggoti ummujjanaṃ, paññāgamananti attho. Paññā eva vā ummujjanaṭṭhena ummaggoti vuccati. Sāva paṭibhānaṭṭhena paṭibhānaṃ. Cittassa [P 3.0164] uppannassa vasaṃ gacchatīti ye cittassa vasaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃyevettha gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atthamaññāya dhammamaññāyāti atthañca pāḷiñca jānitvā. Dhammānudhammappaṭipanno hotīti lokuttaradhammassa anucchavikadhammaṃ saha sīlena pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti. Nibbedhikapaññoti nibbijjhanakapañño. Idaṃ dukkhanti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ sesaṃ tebhūmakakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhanti sutaṃ hoti. Paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti vaṭṭamūlakataṇhā tassa dukkhassa samudayoti sutaṃ [M 2.0361] hoti. Iminā upāyena sesadvayepi attho veditabbo. Catutthapañhavissajjanena arahattaphalaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

186. In the sixth, 'is dragged along' means 'is pulled along.' 'Ummagga' means 'emergence'; the meaning is the attainment of wisdom. Or, wisdom itself is called 'ummagga' in the sense of 'emerging.' That same wisdom is called 'paṭibhāna' in the sense of ready wit. 'Comes under the sway of an arisen thought'—it should be understood that what is meant here are those who come under the sway of the mind. 'Understanding the meaning and the Dhamma' means knowing both the meaning and the Pāli text. 'Is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma' means one has undertaken the preliminary path, together with virtue, which is a practice suitable for the supramundane Dhamma. 'Penetrative wisdom' means wisdom that penetrates. 'This is suffering'—it is heard that, excluding craving, the remaining five aggregates pertaining to the three realms are suffering. 'By wisdom' means by the wisdom of the path. 'This is the origin of suffering'—it is heard that craving, the root of the cycle of existence, is the origin of that suffering. The meaning of the remaining two should be understood in the same way. It should be understood that by the answer to the fourth question, the fruit of arahantship is explained.

7. Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta

187. Sattame todeyyassāti tudigāmavāsikassa. Parisatīti sannipatitāya parisāya. Parūpārambhaṃ vattentīti paragarahaṃ pavattenti kathenti. Bālo ayaṃ rājātiādi yaṃ te upārambhaṃ vattenti, tassa dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Samaṇe rāmaputteti udake rāmaputte. Abhippasannoti atikkamma pasanno. Paramanipaccakāranti uttamanipātakiriyaṃ nīcavuttiṃ. Parihārakāti paricārakā. Yamakotiādīni [P 3.0165] tesaṃ nāmāni. Tesu hi eko yamako nāma, eko moggallo nāma, eko uggo [V 2.0359] nāma, eko nāvindakī nāma, eko gandhabbo nāma, eko aggivesso nāma. Tyāssudanti ettha assudanti nipātamattaṃ, te attano parisati nisinneti attho. Iminā nayena netīti iminā kāraṇena anuneti jānāpeti. Karaṇīyādhikaraṇīyesūti paṇḍitehi kattabbakiccesu ca atirekakattabbakiccesu ca. Vacanīyādhivacanīyesūti vattabbesu ca atirekavattabbesu ca. Alamatthadasatarehīti ettha atthe passituṃ samatthā alamatthadasā, te atisitvā ṭhitā alamatthadasatarā, tehi alamatthadasatarehi. Alamatthadasataroti alamatthadasatāya uttaritaro, chekehi chekataro paṇḍitehi paṇḍitataroti pucchanto evamāha. Athassa te paṭipucchantā evaṃ bhotiādimāhaṃsu. Iti brāhmaṇo attano sappurisatāya taṃ eḷeyyarājānampi tassa parivārikepi udakampi rāmaputtaṃ pasaṃsi. Andho viya hi asappuriso, cakkhumā viya sappuriso. Yathā andho neva anandhaṃ na andhaṃ passati, evaṃ asappuriso neva sappurisaṃ na asappurisaṃ jānāti. Yathā cakkhumā andhampi anandhampi passati, evaṃ sappuriso sappurisampi asappurisampi jānāti. Todeyyopi sappurisatāya [P 3.0166] asappurise aññāsīti imamatthavasaṃ paṭicca tuṭṭhamānaso brāhmaṇo acchariyaṃ bho, gotamātiādīni vatvā tathāgatassa bhāsitaṃ anumoditvā pakkāmi.

187. In the seventh, 'of Todeyya' means 'of the resident of Tudigāma'. 'In the assembly' means 'in the assembled gathering'. 'Engaging in blame of others' means 'they initiate and speak disparagingly of others'. The phrase 'This king is foolish,' and so on, is said to illustrate the blame they utter. 'The ascetic Rāmaputta' refers to Udaka Rāmaputta. 'Greatly pleased' means 'exceedingly pleased'. 'Utterly servile conduct' means 'the highest act of prostration, a lowly practice'. 'Attendants' means 'servants'. 'Yamaka and so on' are their names. Among them, one was named Yamaka, one Moggalla, one Ugga, one Nāvindakī, one Gandhabba, and one Aggivessa. In 'Tyāssudanti', 'assudanti' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'they were seated in his own assembly'. 'Leads in this way' means 'he persuades or informs by this reason'. 'In duties and additional duties' refers to 'in duties to be done by the wise and in extra duties to be done'. 'In speech and additional speech' refers to 'in things to be said and in extra things to be said'. Regarding 'by those who see the meaning even more sufficiently': Herein, those capable of seeing the meaning are 'those who see sufficiently'; those who stand surpassing them are 'those who see more sufficiently'; the phrase means 'by these latter ones'. 'One who sees the meaning even more sufficiently' means 'more superior than one who sees the meaning sufficiently, more skilled than the skilled, wiser than the wise'—thus he asks. Then, those he questioned replied, 'Venerable sir,' and so on. Thus, the brahmin, by his own worthiness, praised King Eḷeyya, his retinue, and even Udaka Rāmaputta. For an unworthy person is like a blind man, while a worthy one is like a sighted man. Just as a blind man sees neither the sighted nor the blind, so an unworthy person recognizes neither the worthy nor the unworthy. And just as a sighted man sees both the blind and the sighted, so a worthy person recognizes both the worthy and the unworthy. Todeyya, too, recognized the unworthy through his own worthiness—delighted by this meaning, the brahmin exclaimed, 'It is wonderful, Master Gotama!' and so on, rejoiced in the Tathāgata’s words, and departed.

8. Upakasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Upaka Sutta

188. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0362] upakoti tassa nāmaṃ. Maṇḍikāputtoti maṇḍikāya putto. Upasaṅkamīti so kira devadattassa upaṭṭhāko, “kiṃ nu kho satthā mayi attano santikaṃ upagate vaṇṇaṃ kathessati, udāhu avaṇṇa”nti pariggaṇhanatthaṃ upasaṅkami. “Nerayiko devadatto kappaṭṭho atekiccho”ti (cūḷava. 348) vacanaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ ghaṭṭetukāmo upasaṅkamītipi vadanti. Parūpārambhaṃ vattetīti paragarahaṃ katheti. Sabbo so na upapādetīti sabbopi so kusaladhammaṃ na uppādeti, attano vā vacanaṃ upapādetuṃ anucchavikaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Anupapādento gārayho hotīti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ uppādetuṃ asakkonto attano ca vacanaṃ upapannaṃ anucchavikaṃ kātuṃ asakkonto gārayho hoti. Upavajjoti upavaditabbo ca hoti, vajjena vā upeto hoti, sadoso hotīti attho.

188. In the eighth, 'Upaka' is his name. 'Maṇḍikāputta' means 'the son of Maṇḍikā'. 'He approached'—it is said that he was Devadatta’s attendant, and he approached in order to ascertain, 'Will the Teacher speak praise or blame of me now that I have come near him?' Some also say he approached intending to provoke the Teacher after hearing the words, 'Devadatta is destined for hell, confined to an aeon, incurable.' 'He engages in blaming others' means 'he speaks criticism of others'. 'He does not bring about any of it' means he does not generate any wholesome qualities, nor is he able to make his own statement established and fitting. 'Failing to bring it about, he is blameworthy' means that, being unable to generate wholesome qualities and to make his own statement established and fitting, he is blameworthy. 'Reproachable' means he is to be censured, or he is endowed with faults, meaning he is flawed.

Atha bhagavā tassa vādaṃ gahetvā tasseva gīvāya paṭimuñcanto parūpārambhantiādimāha. Ummujjamānakaṃyevāti [V 2.0360] udakato sīsaṃ ukkhipantaṃyeva. Tattha aparimāṇā padātiādīsu tasmiṃ akusalanti paññāpane padānipi akkharānipi dhammadesanāpi aparimāṇāyeva. Itipidaṃ [P 3.0167] akusalanti idampi akusalaṃ idampi akusalaṃ imināpi kāraṇena imināpi kāraṇena akusalanti evaṃ akusalapaññattiyaṃ āgatānipi aparimāṇāni. Athāpi aññenākārena tathāgato taṃ dhammaṃ deseyya, evampissa desanā aparimāṇā bhaveyya. Yathāha – “apariyādinnāvassa tathāgatassa dhammadesanā, apariyādinnaṃ dhammapadabyañjana”nti (ma. ni. 1.161). Iminā upāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Yāva dhaṃsī vatāyanti yāva guṇadhaṃsī vata ayaṃ. Loṇakāradārakoti loṇakāragāmadārako. Yatra hi nāmāti yo hi nāma. Āsādetabbaṃ maññissatīti ghaṭṭetabbaṃ maññissati. Apehīti apagaccha, mā me purato aṭṭhāsi. Evañca pana vatvā gīvāya gaṇhāpetvā nikkaḍḍhāpesiyevāti.

Then the Blessed One, taking up his argument and placing it back on his own neck, spoke the verse beginning with 'Blaming others'. 'Just as it emerges' means 'just as it lifts its head from the water'. Here, in the phrase 'countless are the words,' and so on, regarding the designation of that as unwholesome, both the words and letters and the teaching of the Dhamma are indeed countless. Thus, 'this is unwholesome'—this too is unwholesome, that too is unwholesome, for this reason and that reason it is unwholesome—in this way, the designations of the unwholesome that have arisen are also countless. Moreover, even if the Tathāgata were to teach that Dhamma in another way, even then his teaching would also be limitless. As it is said: 'The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is inexhaustible, the phrases and syllables of the Dhamma are inexhaustible.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases. 'Alas, what a destroyer this one is!' means 'Alas, this one is a destroyer of virtue'. 'The salt-maker’s son' means 'the son from the salt-maker’s village'. 'For indeed' means 'who indeed'. 'He thinks he should be provoked' means 'he thinks he should be assaulted'. 'Away with you' means 'go away, do not stand before me'. And having said this, he had him seized by the neck and thrown out.

9. Sacchikaraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sacchikaraṇīya Sutta

189. Navame [M 2.0363] kāyenāti nāmakāyena. Sacchikaraṇīyāti paccakkhaṃ kātabbā. Satiyāti pubbenivāsānussatiyā. Cakkhunāti dibbacakkhunā. Paññāyāti jhānapaññāya vipassanāpaññā sacchikātabbā, vipassanāpaññāya maggapaññā, maggapaññāya phalapaññā, phalapaññāya paccavekkhaṇapaññā sacchikātabbā, pattabbāti attho. Āsavānaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ pana arahattaṃ [P 3.0168] paccavekkhaṇavasena paccavekkhaṇapaññāya sacchikaraṇīyaṃ nāmāti.

189. In the ninth, 'by body' means by the mental body. 'To be realized' means to be made directly known. 'By mindfulness' means by the recollection of past lives. 'By vision' means by the divine eye. 'By wisdom' means that insight-wisdom is to be realized by the wisdom of jhāna; path-wisdom by insight-wisdom; fruition-wisdom by path-wisdom; and reviewing-wisdom by fruition-wisdom. This is the meaning of 'to be attained'. However, arahantship, designated as the destruction of the taints, is to be realized by reviewing-wisdom through the mode of reviewing.

10. Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

190. Dasame tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yato yato anuviloketi, tato tato tuṇhībhūtameva. Bhikkhū āmantesīti paṭipattisampanne bhikkhū pasannehi cakkhūhi anuviloketvā uppannadhammapāmojjo thometukāmatāya āmantesi. Apalāpāti palāparahitā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Suddhāti nimmalā. Sāre patiṭṭhitāti sīlādisāre patiṭṭhitā. Alanti yuttaṃ. Yojanagaṇanānīti ekaṃ yojanaṃ yojanameva, dasapi yojanāni yojanāneva. Tato uddhaṃ “yojanagaṇanānī”ti vuccati. Idha pana yojanasatampi yojanasahassampi adhippetaṃ. Puṭosenāpīti puṭosaṃ vuccati pātheyyaṃ, pātheyyaṃ gahetvāpi upasaṅkamituṃ yuttamevāti attho. Puṭaṃsenātipi [V 2.0361] pāṭho. Tassattho – puṭo aṃse assāti puṭaṃso, tena puṭaṃsena, aṃsena pātheyyapuṭaṃ vahantenāpīti vuttaṃ hoti.

190. In the tenth, 'silent, being silent' means that wherever he looks, it is simply silent. 'He addressed the bhikkhus' means that having observed bhikkhus accomplished in the practice with serene eyes, with joy in the Dhamma having arisen, and desiring to praise them, he addressed them. 'Without chatter' means devoid of chatter. The other word is a synonym for that. 'Pure' means stainless. 'Established in the essence' means established in the essence of virtue and so on. 'Fitting' means appropriate. 'Numbers of yojanas' means that one yojana is just a yojana, and ten yojanas are just yojanas; beyond that, it is called 'numbers of yojanas.' Here, however, a hundred or even a thousand yojanas are intended. 'Even with provisions' means that 'puṭosa' is called provisions; the meaning is that it is fitting to approach even while carrying provisions. There is also the reading 'puṭaṃsena'. Its meaning is as follows: 'puṭaṃso' is one who has a bundle on their shoulder; therefore, 'by that puṭaṃsena' means 'even by one carrying a provision-bundle on the shoulder'.

Idāni evarūpehi evarūpehi ca guṇehi samannāgatā ettha bhikkhū atthīti dassetuṃ santi bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha devappattāti upapattidevanibbattakaṃ dibbavihāraṃ dibbavihārena ca arahattaṃ pattā. Brahmappattāti [P 3.0169] niddosaṭṭhena brahmabhāvasādhakaṃ brahmavihāraṃ brahmavihārena ca arahattaṃ pattā. Āneñjappattāti aniñjanabhāvasādhakaṃ āneñjaṃ āneñjena ca arahattaṃ pattā. Ariyappattāti puthujjanabhāvaṃ atikkamma ariyabhāvaṃ pattā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu devappatto hotītiādīsu evaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhāne ṭhatvā cittaṃ vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ patto devappatto nāma hoti[M 2.0364], catūsu brahmavihāresu ṭhatvā cittaṃ vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ patto brahmappatto nāma, catūsu arūpajjhānesu ṭhatvā cittaṃ vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ patto āneñjappatto nāma. Idaṃ dukkhantiādīhi catūhi saccehi cattāro maggā tīṇi ca phalāni kathitāni. Tasmā imaṃ ariyadhammaṃ patto bhikkhu ariyappatto nāma hotīti.

Now, to show that bhikkhus endowed with such and such qualities exist here, he says, 'There are, bhikkhus...' and so forth. Herein, 'attained to the devas' means having attained the divine abiding that produces rebirth among devas, and having attained arahantship through that divine abiding. 'Attained to Brahmā' means having attained the Brahmā-abiding, which accomplishes the state of Brahmā by being free from defects, and having attained arahantship through that Brahmā-abiding. 'Attained to the imperturbable' means having attained the imperturbable, which accomplishes the state of non-agitation, and having attained arahantship through that imperturbable. 'Attained to the noble' means having transcended the state of ordinary beings and attained the noble state. Thus, bhikkhus, in phrases like 'a bhikkhu is attained to the devas,' when a bhikkhu, having established himself in the fourth jhāna of the form realm, directs his mind to insight and attains arahantship, he is called 'attained to the devas.' When he, having established himself in the four Brahmā-abidings, directs his mind to insight and attains arahantship, he is called 'attained to Brahmā.' When he, having established himself in the four formless jhānas, directs his mind to insight and attains arahantship, he is called 'attained to the imperturbable.' By means of the four truths—'This is suffering,' etc.—the four paths and the three fruits are taught. Therefore, a bhikkhu who attains this noble Dhamma is called 'attained to the noble'.

Brāhmaṇavaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Chapter: The Brahmin.

(20) 5. Mahāvaggo

(20) 5. The Great Chapter

1. Sotānugatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sotānugata Sutta

191. Pañcamassa [V 2.0362] paṭhame sotānugatānanti pasādasotaṃ odahitvā ñāṇasotena vavatthapitānaṃ. Cattāro ānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhāti cattāro guṇānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā. Idaṃ pana bhagavatā atthuppattivasena āraddhaṃ. Kataraatthuppattivasenāti? Bhikkhūnaṃ dhammassavanāya anupasaṅkamanaatthuppattivasena. Pañcasatā kira brāhmaṇapabbajitā “sammāsambuddho liṅgavacanavibhattipadabyañjanādīhi kathento amhehi ñātameva kathessati, aññātaṃ kiṃ kathessatī”ti dhammassavanatthaṃ na gacchanti. Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā te pakkosāpetvā [P 3.0170] “kasmā evaṃ karotha, sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ suṇātha, sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ suṇantānañca sajjhāyantānañca ime ettakā ānisaṃsā”ti dassento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

191. In the first [discourse] of the fifth [chapter], 'for those who follow the stream' means for those who, having established the stream of faith, have determined with the stream of wisdom. 'Four benefits are to be expected' means four qualities and benefits should be expected. This, however, was begun by the Blessed One on account of the arising of a matter. On account of the arising of what matter? On account of the arising of the matter of bhikkhus not approaching to hear the Dhamma. It is said that five hundred Brahmin ascetics did not go to hear the Dhamma, thinking, 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, speaking with gender, number, case-endings, words, syllables, and so on, will teach us only what we already know; what unknown thing will he teach?' The Teacher, having heard of that occurrence, had them summoned and began this discourse, pointing out: 'Why do you act thus? Listen respectfully to the Dhamma. For those who listen respectfully to the Dhamma and recite it, these many benefits arise.'

Tattha dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇātīti suttaṃ geyyantiādikaṃ navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanabhūtaṃ tantidhammaṃ vaḷañjeti. Sotānugatā hontīti sotaṃ anuppattā anupaviṭṭhā honti. Manasānupekkhitāti cittena olokitā. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti atthato ca kāraṇato ca paññāya suṭṭhu paṭividdhā paccakkhaṃ katā. Muṭṭhassati kālaṃ kurumānoti nayidaṃ buddhavacanaṃ anussaraṇasatiyā abhāvena vuttaṃ, puthujjanakālakiriyaṃ pana sandhāya vuttaṃ. Puthujjano hi muṭṭhassati kālaṃ karoti nāma. Upapajjatīti suddhasīle patiṭṭhito devaloke nibbattati. Dhammapadā plavantīti antarābhave nibbattamuṭṭhassatino, yepi pubbe sajjhāyamūlikā vācāparicitabuddhavacanadhammā, te sabbe pasanne [M 2.0365] ādāse chāyā viya plavanti, pākaṭā hutvā paññāyanti. Dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādoti buddhavacanānussaraṇasatiyā uppādo dandho garu. Atha so satto khippaṃyeva visesagāmī hoti, nibbānagāmī hotīti attho.

There, 'learns the Dhamma' means one cultivates the textual Dhamma, the ninefold Teacher's instruction, such as discourses, verses, and so forth. ‘They follow with the ear’ means they have reached and entered into it through the ear. ‘Examined with the mind’ means inspected with the mind. ‘Penetrated well by view’ means thoroughly comprehended in meaning and reasoning by wisdom, directly realized. ‘One who is of lapsed mindfulness at the time of death’—this is not said due to the absence of mindfulness in recollecting the Buddha’s words, but rather it is said in reference to the death of an ordinary person. For an ordinary person, indeed, is one who dies with lapsed mindfulness. ‘He is reborn’ means, being established in pure virtue, he is reborn in a heavenly world. ‘Phrases of the Dhamma float up’ means that for one of lapsed mindfulness who has arisen in the intermediate state, even those teachings of the Buddha’s word which were previously rooted in recitation and familiar to the speech, all of them float up like a reflection in a clear mirror; they become manifest and are discerned. ‘Slow, bhikkhus, is the arising of mindfulness’ means that the arising of mindfulness in recollecting the Buddha’s words is slow and weighty. Then that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction; he becomes one who goes to Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

Iddhimā cetovasippattoti iddhisampanno cittassa vasibhāvapatto khīṇāsavo. Ayaṃ [P 3.0171] vā so dhammavinayoti ettha vibhāvanattho vā-saddo. Yatthāti yasmiṃ dhammavinaye. Brahmacariyaṃ acarinti [V 2.0363] brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasiṃ. Idampi buddhavacanaṃ mayā pubbe vaḷañjitanti buddhavacanānussaraṇavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Devaputtoti pañcālacaṇḍo viya hatthakamahābrahmā viya sanaṅkumārabrahmā viya ca eko dhammakathikadevaputto. Opapātiko opapātikaṃ sāretīti paṭhamaṃ uppanno devaputto pacchā uppannaṃ sāreti. Sahapaṃsukīḷikāti etena nesaṃ dīgharattaṃ kataparicayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Samāgaccheyyunti sālāya vā rukkhamūle vā sammukhībhāvaṃ gaccheyyuṃ. Evaṃ vadeyyāti sālāya vā rukkhamūle vā paṭhamataraṃ nisinno pacchā āgataṃ evaṃ vadeyya. Sesamettha pāḷinayeneva veditabbaṃ.

'Possessing psychic power, attained to mastery of mind' means one accomplished in psychic powers, attained to mastery over the mind, a taintless one. 'Or that Dhamma and Discipline'—here, the word 'or' serves to indicate specification. 'Wherein' means in which Dhamma and Discipline. 'I led the spiritual life' means I lived the spiritual life. 'This too is the Buddha's word, previously mastered by me'—this is said with reference to the recollection of the Buddha's words. 'A young deva' means a certain deva who preaches the Dhamma, like Pañcālacaṇḍa, or the great Brahmā Hatthaka, or the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra. 'One spontaneously born reminds another spontaneously born' means a deva born earlier reminds one born later. 'Companions in play'—this shows their long-standing acquaintance. 'They would meet' means they would come together face to face in a hall or at the foot of a tree. 'One would speak thus' means one seated earlier in a hall or at the foot of a tree would speak thus to one arriving later. The rest here should be understood according to the method of the Pāli text.

2. Ṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ṭhāna Sutta

192. Dutiye ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Ṭhānehīti kāraṇehi. Soceyyanti sucibhāvo. Saṃvasamānoti ekato vasamāno. Na santatakārīti na satatakārī. Na santatavutti sīlesūti satataṃ sabbakālaṃ sīlajīvitaṃ na jīvatīti attho. Saṃvohāramānoti [P 3.0172] kathento. Ekena eko voharatīti ekena saddhiṃ eko hutvā katheti. Vokkamatīti okkamati. Purimavohārā pacchimavohāranti purimakathāya pacchimakathaṃ, purimakathāya ca pacchimakathā, pacchimakathāya ca purimakathā na sametīti attho.

192. In the second sutta, ‘reasons’ means causes. ‘By reasons’ means by causes. ‘Purity’ means a state of purity. ‘Living together’ means living together. ‘Not one who acts continuously’ means not one who acts constantly. ‘Not one who lives continuously by virtue’ means not living a life of virtue at all times; this is the meaning. ‘Engaging in conversation’ means speaking. ‘One speaks with another’ means one speaks together with another. ‘Deviates’ means diverges. ‘Earlier conversation and later conversation’ means the later talk does not agree with the earlier talk, and the earlier talk does not agree with the later talk; this is the meaning.

Ñātibyasanenātiādīsu ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ ñātibyasanaṃ, ñātivināsoti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Rogabyasane pana rogoyeva ārogyavināsanato byasanaṃ rogabyasanaṃ. Anuparivattantīti anubandhanti. Lābho cātiādīsu ekaṃ attabhāvaṃ lābho anuparivattati, ekaṃ alābhoti evaṃ nayo netabbo. Sākacchāyamānoti pañhapucchanavissajjanavasena sākacchaṃ karonto. Yathāti yenākārena[M 2.0366]. Ummaggoti pañhummaggo. Abhinīhāroti pañhābhisaṅkharaṇavasena cittassa abhinīhāro. Samudāhāroti pañhapucchanaṃ. Santanti paccanīkasantatāya santaṃ katvā na kathetīti attho. Paṇītanti atappakaṃ. Atakkāvacaranti [P 3.0173] yathā takkena nayaggāhena gahetuṃ sakkā hoti, evaṃ na kathetīti attho. Nipuṇanti saṇhaṃ. Paṇḍitavedanīyanti paṇḍitehi jānitabbakaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase beginning with ‘by the misfortune of relatives,’ the misfortune of relatives is ‘ñātibyasana,’ meaning the ruin of relatives; this is the meaning. This same method applies to the second term. In ‘misfortune of disease,’ however, disease itself is ‘byasana’ because it destroys health. ‘They follow’ means they pursue. In the phrase beginning with ‘gain,’ the method should be understood thus: gain follows one existence, and loss follows one existence. ‘Engaging in discussion’ means one engaging in discussion by way of asking and answering questions. ‘As’ means in whatever manner. ‘Investigation’ means the investigation of a question. ‘Application’ means the application of mind by way of formulating the question. ‘Utterance’ means the asking of the question. ‘Calm’ means that one does not speak having made it calm by the calming of opposing states; this is the meaning. ‘Excellent’ means that which one does not tire of. ‘Beyond the sphere of reasoning’ means that one does not speak in such a way that it can be grasped by reasoning or by adopting a method; this is the meaning. ‘Subtle’ means fine. ‘To be known by the wise’ means that which is to be known by the wise. The rest should be understood everywhere in accordance with what has been stated.

3. Bhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Bhaddiya Sutta.

193. Tatiye [V 2.0364] upasaṅkamīti bhuttapātarāso hutvā mālāgandhavilepanaṃ gahetvā bhagavantaṃ vandissāmīti upasaṅkami. Mā anussavenātiādīsu anussavavacanena mama kathaṃ mā gaṇhathāti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Sārambhoti karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho. Alobhādayo lobhādipaṭipakkhavasena veditabbā. Kusaladhammūpasampadāyāti kusaladhammānaṃ sampādanatthāya, paṭilābhatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ime cepi, bhaddiya, mahāsālāti purato ṭhite sālarukkhe dassento evamāha. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca suviññeyyameva. Satthari pana desanaṃ vinivaṭṭente bhaddiyo sotāpanno jātoti.

193. In the third sutta, ‘he approached’ means: having eaten his morning meal and taken flowers, perfumes, and ointments, he approached with the thought, ‘I will pay homage to the Blessed One.’ In the phrase beginning with ‘not by hearsay,’ the meaning should be understood in this way: ‘Do not accept my word by way of hearsay.’ ‘Contention’ is that which has the characteristic of outdoing in action. Non-greed and so on should be known as the opposites of greed and the like. ‘For the accomplishment of wholesome qualities’ means for the sake of fulfilling and for the sake of attaining wholesome qualities. Regarding the words ‘These great sāl trees, Bhaddiya,’ pointing to the sāl trees standing in front, he spoke thus. The rest here is easy to understand both because of the method already stated below and because of its clear meaning. Furthermore, when the Teacher concluded the discourse, Bhaddiya became a stream-enterer.

4. Sāmugiyāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Sāmugiya Sutta.

194. Catutthe sāmugiyāti sāmuganigamavāsino. Byagghapajjāti te ālapanto evamāha. Kolanagarassa hi kolarukkhe hāretvā katattā kolanagaranti ca byagghapathe māpitattā byagghapajjanti ca dve nāmāni. Etesañca pubbapurisā tattha vasiṃsūti byagghapajjavāsitāya byagghapajjavāsino byagghapajjāti vuccanti. Te ālapanto evamāha. Pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgānīti [P 3.0174] pārisuddhiatthāya padhāniyaṅgāni padahitabbavīriyassa aṅgāni, koṭṭhāsāti attho. Sīlapārisuddhipadhāniyaṅganti sīlaparisodhanavīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tañhi sīlapārisuddhiparipūraṇatthāya padhāniyaṅganti sīlapārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tattha tattha paññāya anuggahessāmīti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne vipassanāpaññāya anuggahessāmi[M 2.0367]. Yo tattha chandotiādīsu yo tasmiṃ anuggaṇhane kattukāmatāchandoti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Satisampajaññaṃ panettha satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā vīriyapaggahanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Rajanīyesu dhammesu cittaṃ virājetīti rāgapaccayesu iṭṭhārammaṇesu yathā cittaṃ virajjati, evaṃ karoti. Vimocanīyesu dhammesu cittaṃ vimocetīti yehi ārammaṇehi cittaṃ vimocetabbaṃ, tesu yathā vimuccati, evaṃ karoti. Virājetvāti ettha maggakkhaṇe virājeti nāma, phalakkhaṇe virattaṃ nāma hoti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Sammāvimuttiṃ phusatīti hetunā nayena arahattaphalavimuttiṃ ñāṇaphassena phusatīti.

194. In the fourth sutta, ‘of Sāmuga’ means the inhabitants of the market town of Sāmuga. Addressing them as ‘Byagghapajjans,’ he spoke thus. For, because it was made by clearing away kola trees, it had the name Kolanagara, and because it was established on a tiger’s path, it had the name Byagghapajja; thus, it had two names. And since their ancestors lived there, due to living on the tiger’s path, the inhabitants of Byagghapajja are called ‘Byagghapajjans.’ Addressing them, he spoke thus. ‘The constituents of the striving for purity’ means the constituents of striving for the sake of purity; they are the components, the portions of the effort to be exerted—this is the meaning. ‘The constituent of striving for the purity of virtue’ is the name for the effort of purifying virtue. For that is a constituent of striving for the sake of the fulfillment of the purity of virtue; therefore, it is called ‘the constituent of striving for the purity of virtue.’ In the remaining cases, this is the method. ‘I will support with wisdom in each and every case’ means: in each and every instance, I will support with insight-wisdom. In phrases such as ‘Whatever desire is there,’ the meaning should be understood by this method: whatever desire to act is in that supporting. Here, ‘mindfulness and clear comprehension’ is mentioned for the purpose of arousing energy, having established mindfulness and having discerned with knowledge. ‘He dispassionates the mind towards things that incite passion’ means: he acts in such a way that the mind becomes dispassionate towards desirable objects that are conditions for lust. ‘He liberates the mind from phenomena from which it should be liberated’ means: he acts in such a way that the mind is liberated from those objects from which it should be liberated. Here, in the phrase ‘having dispassioned,’ at the moment of the path, it is called ‘dispassionating’; at the moment of fruition, it becomes what is called ‘dispassioned.’ In the second phrase also, this is the method. ‘He touches right liberation’ means: by the appropriate method, he touches the liberation that is the fruit of Arahantship with the contact of knowledge.

5. Vappasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Vappa Sutta.

195. Pañcame [V 2.0365] vappoti dasabalassa cūḷapitā sakyarājā. Nigaṇṭhasāvakoti vesāliyaṃ sīhasenāpati viya nāḷandāyaṃ upāligahapati viya ca nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa upaṭṭhāko. Kāyena saṃvutoti kāyadvārassa saṃvutattā pihitattā kāyena saṃvuto nāma. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Avijjāvirāgāti [P 3.0175] avijjāya khayavirāgena. Vijjuppādāti maggavijjāya uppādena. Taṃ ṭhānanti taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Avipakkavipākanti aladdhavipākavāraṃ. Tatonidānanti taṃhetu tappaccayā. Dukkhavedaniyā āsavā assaveyyunti dukkhavedanāya paccayabhūtā kilesā assaveyyuṃ, tassa purisassa uppajjeyyunti attho. Abhisamparāyanti dutiye attabhāve. Kāyasamārambhapaccayāti kāyakammapaccayena. Āsavāti kilesā. Vighātapariḷāhāti ettha vighātoti dukkhaṃ. Pariḷāhoti kāyikacetasiko pariḷāho. Phussa phussa byantīkarotīti ñāṇavajjhaṃ kammaṃ ñāṇaphassena phusitvā phusitvā khayaṃ gameti, vipākavajjhaṃ kammaṃ vipākaphassena phusitvā phusitvā khayaṃ gameti. Nijjarāti kilesajīraṇakapaṭipadā. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Idha ṭhatvā ayaṃ bhikkhu khīṇāsavo kātabbo, cattāri mahābhūtāni nīharitvā catusaccavavatthānaṃ dassetvā yāva arahattaphalaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetabbaṃ.

195. In the fifth, 'Vappa' refers to the Sakyan king, the younger paternal uncle of the Ten-Powered One. 'A disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas' refers to a supporter of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, like General Sīha in Vesālī or the householder Upāli in Nāḷandā. 'Restrained in body' means he is called 'restrained in body' because the body-door is restrained and closed. The same principle applies to the other two. 'Through the fading of ignorance'—through the destruction and fading away of ignorance. 'Through the arising of knowledge'—through the arising of path-knowledge. 'That reason'—that cause. 'Not yet ripened as result'—a turn for result not yet obtained. 'Because of that'—because of that cause and that condition. 'The taints that are to be felt as suffering would flow'—the defilements that are the condition for painful feeling would arise in that person. 'In the future life'—in the second existence. 'Because of bodily action'—because of the condition of bodily kamma. 'Taints'—defilements. 'Distress and fever'—here, 'distress' means suffering, and 'fever' means bodily and mental burning. 'Touching again and again, he eliminates'—kamma to be destroyed by knowledge, having touched it again and again with the contact of knowledge, he brings to destruction; kamma to be destroyed by its result, having touched it again and again with the contact of the result, he brings to destruction. 'Wearing away'—the practice that causes the wearing away of defilements. The same principle applies in the remaining instances. At this point, this monk should be made one with destroyed taints; having extracted the four great elements and shown the determination of the four truths, the meditation subject should be taught up to the fruit of Arahantship.

Idāni pana tassa khīṇāsavassa satatavihāre dassetuṃ evaṃ sammā vimuttacittassātiādimāha. Tattha sammā vimuttacittassāti hetunā kāraṇena [M 2.0368] sammā vimuttassa. Satatavihārāti [P 3.0176] niccavihārā nibaddhavihārā. Neva sumano hotīti iṭṭhārammaṇe rāgavasena na somanassajāto hoti. Na dummanoti aniṭṭhārammaṇe paṭighavasena na domanassajāto hoti. Upekkhako viharati sato sampajānoti satisampajaññapariggahitāya majjhattākāralakkhaṇāya upekkhāya tesu ārammaṇesu upekkhako majjhatto hutvā viharati.

Now, however, to show the constant dwellings of that one whose taints are destroyed, he spoke the words beginning with 'for one with a mind well-liberated.' Therein, 'for one with a mind well-liberated' means: for one who is well-liberated from the defilements by a suitable cause, by a reason. 'Constant dwellings' means perpetual dwellings, uninterrupted dwellings. 'He is not glad-minded' means: he does not become one in whom joy has arisen through the power of lust with regard to a desirable object. 'Nor is he sad-minded' means: he does not become one in whom displeasure has arisen through the power of aversion with regard to an undesirable object. 'He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending' means: he dwells, having become equanimous and neutral towards those objects, with an equanimity that is embraced by mindfulness and clear comprehension and has the characteristic of a neutral state.

Kāyapariyantikanti kāyantikaṃ kāyaparicchinnaṃ, yāva pañcadvārakāyo pavattati, tāva pavattaṃ pañcadvārikavedananti attho. Jīvitapariyantikanti jīvitantikaṃ jīvitaparicchinnaṃ, yāva jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva pavattaṃ manodvārikavedananti attho. Tattha pañcadvārikavedanā pacchā uppajjitvā paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati, manodvārikavedanā paṭhamaṃ uppajjitvā pacchā nirujjhati. Sā hi paṭisandhikkhaṇe vatthurūpasmiṃyeva patiṭṭhāti. Pañcadvārikā pavatte pañcadvāravasena pavattamānā paṭhamavaye [V 2.0366] vīsativassakāle rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena adhimattā balavatī hoti, paṇṇāsavassakāle ṭhitā hoti, saṭṭhivassakālato paṭṭhāya parihāyamānā, asītinavutivassakāle mandā hoti. Tadā hi sattā “cirarattaṃ ekato nisīdimhā nipajjimhā”ti vadantepi na [P 3.0177] jānāmāti vadanti. Adhimattānipi rūpādiārammaṇāni na passāma, sugandhaduggandhaṃ vā sāduasāduṃ vā thaddhamudukaṃ vāti na jānāmātipi vadanti. Iti nesaṃ pañcadvārikavedanā bhaggā hoti, manodvārikā pavattati. Sāpi anupubbena parihāyamānā maraṇasamaye hadayakoṭiṃyeva nissāya pavattati. Yāva panesā pavattati, tāva satto jīvatīti vuccati. Yadā nappavattati, tadā “mato niruddho”ti vuccati.

Limited by the body means having the five doors as its limit, demarcated by the five doors. As long as the five-door body functions, so long does the feeling at the five doors function—this is the meaning. Limited by life means having the life faculty as its limit, demarcated by the life faculty. As long as the life faculty functions, so long does the feeling at the mind door function—this is the meaning. Among these two, feeling at the five doors arises later and ceases first, while feeling at the mind door arises first and ceases later. For it is established precisely on the heart-base materiality at the moment of rebirth-linking. In the course of existence, the five-door feeling, occurring by way of the five doors, is exceedingly great and strong in the first age, around twenty years of age, due to lust, aversion, and delusion. At fifty years of age, it is stable. Starting from sixty years of age, it declines, and by eighty or ninety years of age, it becomes weak. For at that time, even while saying, 'We have sat together, we have lain down together for a long time,' beings say, 'We do not know.' They also say, 'We do not see even exceedingly great visible objects and other sense objects,' and, 'We do not know a pleasant or unpleasant smell, a tasty or untasty flavor, or a hard or soft touch.' Thus, their feeling at the five doors is broken, while the mind-door feeling continues to function. That too, gradually declining, functions at the time of death dependent solely on the heart-base. Furthermore, as long as this functions, a being is said to be alive. When it no longer functions, he is said to be 'dead, ceased.'

Svāyamattho vāpiyā dīpetabbo – yathā hi puriso pañcaudakamaggasampannaṃ vāpiṃ kareyya. Paṭhamaṃ deve vuṭṭhe pañcahi udakamaggehi udakaṃ pavisitvā antovāpiyaṃ āvāṭe pūreyya. Punappunaṃ deve vassante udakamagge pūretvā gāvutaḍḍhayojanamattaṃ ottharitvā udakaṃ tiṭṭheyya tato tato vissandamānaṃ. Atha niddhamanatumbe vivaritvā khettesu kamme kayiramāne udakaṃ nikkhamantaṃ, sassapākakāle udakaṃ nikkhantaṃ udakaṃ parihīnaṃ, “macche gaṇhāmā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjeyya. Tato katipāhena āvāṭesuyeva [M 2.0369] udakaṃ saṇṭhaheya. Yāva pana taṃ āvāṭesu hoti, tāva mahāvāpiyaṃ udakaṃ atthīti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Yadā pana tattha chijjati, tadā “vāpiyaṃ udakaṃ natthī”ti vuccati. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

This meaning should be illustrated by means of a reservoir. It is as if a man were to construct a reservoir endowed with five water channels. First, when it has rained, water would enter through the five water channels and fill the hollows within the reservoir. Again and again, when it rains, the water would fill the channels, spread over an area of a gāvuta and a half-yojana, and remain, flowing out from here and there. Then, when the outlet pipes are opened and work is being done in the fields, the water is flowing out. At the time the crops ripen, the water has flowed out and diminished, and it would come to be said, 'Let us catch the fish.' After a few days, the water would remain only in the hollows. For as long as there is water in those hollows, it is reckoned that the great reservoir has water. But when the water there is cut off, then it is said, 'There is no water in the reservoir.' Thus should this analogy be understood.

Paṭhamaṃ [P 3.0178] deve vassante pañcahi maggehi udake pavisante āvāṭānaṃ pūraṇakālo viya hi paṭhamameva paṭisandhikkhaṇe manodvārikavedanāya vatthurūpe patiṭṭhitakālo, punappunaṃ deve vassante pañcamaggānaṃ pūraṇakālo viya pavatte pañcadvārikavedanāya pavatti, gāvutaḍḍhayojanamattaṃ ajjhottharaṇaṃ viya paṭhamavaye vīsativassakāle rajjanādivasena tassa adhimattabalavabhāvo, yāva vāpito udakaṃ na niggacchati, tāva pūrāya vāpiyā ṭhitakālo viya paññāsavassakāle tassa ṭhitakālo, niddhamanatumbesu vivaṭesu kamme kayiramāne udakassa nikkhamanakālo viya saṭṭhivassakālato paṭṭhāya tassa parihāni, udake bhaṭṭhe udakamaggesu parittaudakassa ṭhitakālo viya asītinavutikāle pañcadvārikavedanāya mandakālo, āvāṭesuyeva udakassa patiṭṭhitakālo viya hadayavatthukoṭiṃ nissāya manodvāre vedanāya pavattikālo, āvāṭesu parittepi udake sati “vāpiyaṃ udakaṃ atthī”ti vattabbakālo viya yāva [V 2.0367] sā pavattati, tāva “satto jīvatī”ti vuccati. Yathā pana āvāṭesu udake chinne “natthi vāpiyaṃ udaka”nti vuccati, evaṃ manodvārikavedanāya appavattamānāya satto matoti vuccati. Imaṃ vedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno”ti.

Indeed, just as when the rain first falls and water enters through five channels, it is like the time the small pits are filled; so too, at the very first moment of rebirth-linking, it is the time the mind-door feeling is established in the heart-base material form. Just as when the rain falls again and again, it is like the time the five channels are filled; so too, is the arising of the five-door feeling during the course of life. Just as there is the overwhelming of an area of one gāvuta and half a yojana; so too, in the first age, during the period of twenty years, by the power of lust and so on, that feeling is exceedingly intense and powerful. Just as, for as long as water does not exit from the great reservoir, it remains in the full reservoir; so too, during the period of fifty years, that feeling is stable. Just as, when the outlet pipes are opened and cultivation is being done, it is the time for the water to exit; so too, starting from the period of sixty years, that feeling declines. Just as, when the water has receded, a little water remains in the water channels; so too, during the period of eighty or ninety years, the five-door feeling is weak. Just as water becomes established only in the small pits; so too, feeling arises at the mind-door, depending on the heart-base as its final resort. Just as, when there is even a little water in the small pits, it is said, 'There is water in the great reservoir'; so too, for as long as that feeling occurs, it is said, 'The being is alive.' And just as, when the water in the small pits is cut off, it is said, 'There is no water in the great reservoir'; so too, when the mind-door feeling does not occur, it is said, 'The being is dead.' Referring to this feeling, it was said: 'feeling a feeling that is life-terminating.'

Kāyassa bhedāti kāyassa bhedena. Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitakkhayato uddhaṃ. Idhevāti paṭisandhivasena parato agantvā idheva. Sītī [P 3.0179] bhavissantīti pavattivipphandanadaratharahitāni sītāni appavattanadhammāni bhavissanti.

'With the breakup of the body' means: on account of the breakup of the appropriated body of aggregates. 'Upwards from the termination of life' means: upwards from the exhaustion of life. 'Right here' means: without going to the next world by way of rebirth-linking, right here in this present world. 'They will become cool' means: they will become cool, devoid of the trembling of continued existence, things whose nature is not to arise again.

Thūṇaṃ paṭiccāti rukkhaṃ paṭicca. Kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāyāti kuddālañca khaṇittiñca pacchiñca gahetvāti attho. Desanā pana kuddālavaseneva katā. Mūle chindeyyāti mūlamhi kuddālena chindeyya. Palikhaṇeyyāti khaṇittiyā samantā khaṇeyya.

“Depending on the post” means depending on the tree. “Taking a hoe and basket” means taking a hoe, a digging tool, and a basket—this is the meaning. The teaching, however, was given by means of the hoe alone. “One should cut at the root” means one should cut at the root with the hoe. “One should dig around” means one should dig all around with the digging tool.

Evameva [M 2.0370] khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – rukkho viya hi attabhāvo daṭṭhabbo, rukkhaṃ paṭicca chāyā viya kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ, chāyaṃ appavattaṃ kātukāmo puriso viya yogāvacaro, kuddālo viya paññā, piṭakaṃ viya samādhi, khaṇitti viya vipassanā, khaṇittiyā mūlānaṃ palikhaṇanakālo viya arahattamaggena avijjāya chedanakālo, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karaṇakālo viya khandhavasena diṭṭhakālo, phālanakālo viya āyatanavasena diṭṭhakālo, sakalīkaraṇakālo viya dhātuvasena diṭṭhakālo, vātātapena visosanakālo viya kāyikacetasikassa vīriyassa karaṇakālo, agginā ḍahanakālo viya ñāṇena kilesānaṃ ḍahanakālo, masikaraṇakālo viya vattamānaka-pañcakkhandhakālo, mahāvāte ophunanakālo viya nadīsote pavāhanakālo viya ca chinnamūlakānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ appaṭisandhikanirodho, ophunanappavāhanehi [P 3.0180] apaññattikabhāvūpagamo viya punabbhave vipākakkhandhānaṃ anuppādena apaṇṇattikabhāvo veditabbo.
