Just so, here is the connection of the simile: the individual existence should be regarded like a tree; wholesome and unwholesome kamma like the shade dependent on the tree; the meditator like a man wishing to make the shade not occur; wisdom like a hoe; concentration like a basket; insight like a digging tool; the time of digging around the roots with the digging tool like the time of cutting off ignorance with the path of Arahantship; the time of making into pieces like the time of seeing in terms of aggregates; the time of splitting like the time of seeing in terms of sense bases; the time of making into fragments like the time of seeing in terms of elements; the time of drying by wind and sun like the time of making bodily and verbal effort; the time of burning with fire like the time of burning the defilements with knowledge; the time of making into charcoal like the time of the present five aggregates; the time of winnowing in a great wind and the time of sweeping away in a river current like the cessation without relinking of the five aggregates whose roots are cut off; just as through winnowing and sweeping away it reaches a state beyond designation, so the state of being beyond designation should be understood as being due to the non-arising of resultant aggregates in a future existence.

Bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti satthari desanaṃ vinivaṭṭente sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā etaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha udayatthikoti vaḍḍhiatthiko. Assapaṇiyaṃ poseyyāti pañca assapotasatāni kiṇitvā pacchā vikkiṇissāmīti poseyya. Sahassagghanakassa assassa pañcasatamattaṃ upakaraṇaṃ gandhamālādivasena posāvanikaṃyeva agamāsi. Athassa te assā ekadivaseneva [V 2.0368] rogaṃ phusitvā sabbe jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇeyyunti iminā adhippāyena evamāha. Udayañceva nādhigaccheyyāti vaḍḍhiñca gehato nīharitvā dinnamūlañca kiñci na labheyya. Payirupāsinti catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahiṃ. Svāhaṃ udayañceva nādhigacchinti so ahaṃ neva udayaṃ na gehato dinnadhanaṃ adhigacchiṃ, paṇiyaassajagganako nāma jātosmīti dasseti. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

When the Teacher concluded the teaching, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, he spoke this utterance to the Blessed One, beginning with, “Just as, venerable sir.” Therein, ‘one who desires increase’ means one who desires growth. ‘One might rear a trade-horse’ means: having bought five hundred young horses, thinking, “I will sell them later,” one would rear them. For a horse worth a thousand, about five hundred was spent on accessories such as perfumes and garlands, which went just for its upkeep. Then, if those horses of his were afflicted by disease in a single day and all met their end—with this intention, he spoke thus. ‘He would not get the increase’ means: he would get neither the growth nor any of the capital given after taking it from home. ‘I attended’ means: I served with the four requisites. ‘And I did not get the increase’ shows this: “So I gained neither the increase nor the wealth given from home; I have become one who tends to trade-horses.” The rest here is of clear meaning.

6. Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta

196. Chaṭṭhe dvayenāti dvīhi koṭṭhāsehi. Oghassa [P 3.0181] nittharaṇanti caturoghanittharaṇaṃ. Tapojigucchāhetūti dukkarakārikasaṅkhātena tapena pāpajigucchanahetu[M 2.0371]. Aññataraṃ sāmaññaṅganti ekaṃ samaṇadhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Aparisuddhakāyasamācārātiādīsu purimehi tīhi padehi kāyikavācasikacetasikasīlānaṃ aparisuddhataṃ dassetvā pacchimena padena aparisuddhājīvataṃ dasseti. Ñāṇadassanāyāti maggañāṇasaṅkhātāya dassanāya. Anuttarāya sambodhāyāti arahattāya, arahattañāṇaphassena phusituṃ abhabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sālalaṭṭhinti sālarukkhaṃ. Navanti taruṇaṃ. Akukkuccakajātanti “bhaveyya nu kho, na bhaveyyā”ti ajanetabbakukkuccaṃ. Lekhaṇiyā likheyyāti avalekhanamattakena avalikheyya. Dhoveyyāti ghaṃseyya. Anto avisuddhāti abbhantare asuddhā apanītasārā.

196. In the sixth, ‘by a pair’ means with two sections. ‘Crossing the flood’ refers to overcoming the four floods. ‘Due to austerity and disgust’ means due to disgust toward evil through the austerity known as difficult practice. ‘One of the qualities of a recluse’ refers to one section of a recluse's practice. In the phrases ‘impure bodily conduct,’ etc., the first three phrases show the impurity of bodily, verbal, and mental virtue, while the last phrase shows impure livelihood. ‘For knowledge and vision’ refers to the vision known as path knowledge. ‘For unsurpassed enlightenment’ refers to arahantship; it is said that one is incapable of touching it through the contact of the knowledge of arahantship. ‘Sālalaṭṭhi’ means a sāl tree. ‘New’ means young. ‘Of a nature free of remorse’ means the remorse that should not be generated, thinking, “Would it be? Would it not be?” ‘Would scrape with a stylus’ means would scrape with just a line. ‘Would wash’ means would rub. ‘Impure inside’ means internally impure, with unremoved heartwood.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – sālalaṭṭhi viya hi attabhāvo daṭṭhabbo, nadīsotaṃ viya saṃsārasotaṃ, pāraṃ gantukāmapuriso viya dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo gahetvā ṭhitapuriso, sālalaṭṭhiyā bahiddhā suparikammakatakālo viya bahiddhā tapacaraṇaṃ gāḷhaṃ katvā gahitakālo, anto asuddhakālo [P 3.0182] viya abbhantare sīlānaṃ aparisuddhakālo, sālalaṭṭhiyā saṃsīditvā adhogamanaṃ viya diṭṭhigatikassa saṃsārasote saṃsīdanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Just so, herein this is the connection of the simile: individual existence should be seen as like a sāl log; the stream of saṃsāra, as like a river current; a person standing while grasping the sixty-two wrong views, as like a person who wishes to go to the other shore; the time when external ascetic practices are firmly undertaken, as like the time when the outside of the sāl log is well-finished; the time when moral conduct within is impure, as like the time when the inside is impure. The sinking in the stream of saṃsāra of one who holds wrong views should be known as like the sinking and downward movement of the sāl log.

Phiyārittaṃ bandheyyāti phiyañca arittañca yojeyya. Evamevāti etthāpi idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – sālalaṭṭhi viya attabhāvo, nadīsotaṃ viya saṃsārasotaṃ, pāraṃ gantukāmapuriso viya yogāvacaro, bahiddhā suparikammakatakālo viya chasu dvāresu saṃvarassa paccupaṭṭhitakālo, anto suvisodhitabhāvo viya abbhantare parisuddhasīlabhāvo, phiyārittabandhanaṃ viya [V 2.0369] kāyikacetasikavīriyakaraṇaṃ, sotthinā pārimatīragamanaṃ viya anupubbena sīlaṃ pūretvā samādhiṃ pūretvā paññaṃ pūretvā nibbānagamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'He should bind the oar and rudder' means he should join the oar and the rudder. Just so, herein also, this is the connection of the simile: individual existence is like a sāl log; the stream of saṃsāra is like a river current; a yogī is like a person who wishes to go to the other shore; the time when restraint is established at the six sense doors is like the time when the outside is well-prepared; the state of having pure moral conduct internally is like the state of being well-purified inside; the making of bodily and mental effort is like the binding of the oar and rudder. The going to Nibbāna by gradually fulfilling moral conduct, fulfilling concentration, and fulfilling wisdom should be seen as like the going to the far shore in safety.

Kaṇḍacitrakānīti saralaṭṭhisararajjusarapāsādasarasāṇisarapokkharaṇisarapadumānīti anekāni kaṇḍehi kattabbacitrāni. Atha kho so tīhi ṭhānehīti so evaṃ bahūni kaṇḍacitrakāni jānantopi na rājāraho hoti, tīhiyeva pana ṭhānehi hotīti attho. Sammāsamādhi [M 2.0372] hotīti maggasamādhinā ca phalasamādhinā ca samāhito hotīti ayamettha attho. Sammādiṭṭhīti maggasammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Idaṃ dukkhantiādīhi catūhi saccehi cattāro maggā tīṇi ca phalāni kathitāni. Ayaṃ pana maggeneva avirādhitaṃ vijjhati nāmāti veditabbo. Sammāvimuttīti arahattaphalavimuttiyā samannāgato. Avijjākkhandhaṃ padāletīti arahattamaggena padāleti nāmāti vuccati. Iminā hi heṭṭhā arahattamaggena avijjākkhandho padālito[P 3.0183], idha pana padālitaṃ upādāya padāletīti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

Arrow-designs means the many intricate things to be made with arrows, such as arrow-vines, arrow-ropes, arrow-palaces, arrow-curtains, arrow-ponds, and arrow-lotuses. 'But then by three qualities' means: even though he knows many such arrow-designs, he is not worthy of a king; it is, however, only through three qualities that he becomes worthy of a king—this is the meaning. 'He has right concentration' means he is concentrated with the concentration of the path and the concentration of the fruit—this is the meaning here. 'Right view' means he is endowed with the right view of the path. By means of the four truths, beginning with 'This is suffering,' the four paths and the three fruits are taught. However, it should be understood that this person is said to pierce without fail only by means of the path. 'Right liberation' means he is endowed with the liberation which is the fruit of arahantship. 'He shatters the aggregate of ignorance' means it is said that he shatters it with the path of arahantship. Indeed, by this person the aggregate of ignorance was previously shattered by the path of arahantship; here, however, with reference to what has been shattered, it is fitting to say, 'he shatters'.

7. Mallikādevīsuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Mallikādevī Sutta

197. Sattame mallikā devīti pasenadirañño devī. Yena midhekacco mātugāmoti yena idhekaccā itthī. Dubbaṇṇāti bībhacchavaṇṇā. Durūpāti dussaṇṭhitā. Supāpikāti suṭṭhu pāpikā suṭṭhu lāmikā. Dassanāyāti passituṃ. Daliddāti dhanadaliddā. Appassakāti sakena dhanena rahitā. Appabhogāti upabhogaparibhogabhaṇḍakarahitā. Appesakkhāti appaparivārā. Aḍḍhāti issarā. Mahaddhanāti vaḷañjanakadhanena mahaddhanā. Mahābhogāti upabhogaparibhogabhaṇḍabhogena mahābhogā. Mahesakkhāti mahāparivārā. Abhirūpāti uttamarūpā. Dassanīyāti dassanayuttā. Pāsādikāti dassanena pāsādikā. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānena ca.

197. In the seventh [sutta], ‘Queen Mallikā’ means the queen of King Pasenadi. ‘By which some woman here’ means ‘by which a certain woman here’. ‘Ugly’ means of disgusting complexion. ‘Ill-formed’ means badly shaped. ‘Very wicked’ means thoroughly wicked, thoroughly base. ‘To see’ means for seeing. ‘Poor’ means poor in wealth. ‘Having little’ means lacking her own wealth. ‘Having few possessions’ means lacking goods for consumption and use. ‘Of little influence’ means with a small retinue. ‘Wealthy’ means powerful. ‘Very rich’ means very wealthy with wealth for daily use. ‘Of great possessions’ means very wealthy with goods for consumption and use. ‘Of great influence’ means with a large retinue. ‘Beautiful’ means of outstanding appearance. ‘Lovely’ means worthy to be seen. ‘Charming’ means pleasing to see. ‘Beauty of complexion’ means by complexion and by bodily form.

Abhisajjatīti laggati. Byāpajjatīti pakatiṃ pajahati. Patitthīyatīti kodhavasena thinabhāvaṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ āpajjati. Na [P 3.0184] dātā hotīti na dāyikā hoti. Seyyāvasathapadīpeyyanti ettha seyyāti mañcapallaṅkādisayanaṃ. Āvasathoti āvasathāgāraṃ. Padīpeyyaṃ vuccati vaṭṭitelādipadīpūpakaraṇaṃ. Issāmanikāti issāya sampayuttacittā. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo[V 2.0370]. Kodhanā ahosinti kodhamanā ahosiṃ. Anissāmanikā ahosinti issāvirahitacittā ahosiṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

‘He is hostile’ means he clings. ‘He is malicious’ means he abandons his natural disposition. ‘He is obstinate’ means he falls into a state of rigidity and stiffness due to anger. ‘She is not a giver’ means she is not disposed to giving. ‘Beds, dwellings, and lamps’—here, ‘beds’ means couches, divans, and the like for sleeping. ‘Dwelling’ means a dwelling place. ‘Lamps’ means the equipment for lamps, such as wicks and oil. ‘Jealous’ means having a mind connected with jealousy. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere. ‘I was angry’ means I was of an angry mind. ‘I was not jealous’ means I was of a mind devoid of jealousy. The rest here is clear in meaning.

8. Attantapasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Self-Tormentor

198. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0373] attantapādīsu attānaṃ tapati dukkhāpetīti attantapo. Attano paritāpanānuyogaṃ attaparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Paraṃ tapatīti parantapo. Paresaṃ paritāpanānuyogaṃ paraparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Nicchātoti chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā, sā assa natthīti nicchāto. Sabbakilesānaṃ nibbutattā nibbuto. Anto tāpanakilesānaṃ abhāvā sītalo jātoti sītībhūto. Jhānamaggaphalanibbānasukhāni paṭisaṃvedetīti sukhappaṭisaṃvedī. Brahmabhūtena attanāti seṭṭhabhūtena attanā.

198. In the eighth, regarding the self-tormentor and others: ‘He torments and afflicts himself’; therefore, he is a self-tormentor. The practice of tormenting oneself is the practice of self-torment. ‘He torments another’; therefore, he is a tormentor of others. The practice of tormenting others is the practice of tormenting others. ‘In this very life’ means in this very existence. ‘Unfamished’: craving is called ‘famine’; he for whom that is not, is ‘unfamished’. ‘Extinguished’ because all defilements are extinguished. ‘He has become cool’ because of the absence of defilements that burn within; thus, he is ‘cooled’. ‘An experiencer of happiness’ means he experiences the happiness of jhāna, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. ‘With a self that has become sublime’ means with a self that has become supreme.

Acelakotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Orabbhikādīsu urabbhā vuccanti eḷakā, urabbhe hanatīti orabbhiko. Sūkarikādīsupi eseva nayo. Luddoti dāruṇo kakkhaḷo. Macchaghātakoti macchabandho kevaṭṭo. Bandhanāgārikoti bandhanāgāragopako. Kurūrakammantāti dāruṇakammantā.

The terms beginning with ‘a naked ascetic’ have meanings that have already been stated. Among the terms beginning with ‘a butcher of rams’: sheep are called ‘urabbha’; ‘he kills sheep (urabbhe)’; therefore, he is an ‘orabbhika’ (a butcher of rams). This same method applies to the terms beginning with ‘a butcher of pigs’. ‘A hunter’ means one who is cruel and harsh. ‘A fish-killer’ means a fisherman who traps fish. ‘A jailer’ means a prison guard. ‘Those of cruel occupations’ means those who perform cruel deeds.

Muddhāvasittoti [P 3.0185] khattiyābhisekena muddhani abhisitto. Puratthimena nagarassāti nagarato puratthimāya disāya. Santhāgāranti yaññasālaṃ. Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvāti sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ nivāsetvā. Sappitelenāti sappinā ceva telena ca. Ṭhapetvā hi sappiṃ avaseso yo koci sneho telanti vuccati. Kaṇḍuvamānoti nakhānaṃ chinnattā kaṇḍuvitabbakāle tena kaṇḍuvamāno. Anantarahitāyāti asanthatāya. Sarūpavacchāyāti sadisavacchāya. Sace gāvī setā hoti, vacchopi setakova. Sace kapilā vā rattā vā, vacchakopi tādisovāti evaṃ sarūpavacchāya. So evamāhāti so rājā evaṃ vadeti. Vacchatarāti taruṇavacchakabhāvaṃ atikkantā balavavacchā. Vacchatarīsupi eseva nayo. Barihisatthāyāti parikkhepakaraṇatthāya ceva yaññabhūmiyaṃ attharaṇatthāya ca.

‘Muddhāvasitto’ refers to one anointed on the head with the consecration of a khattiya. ‘Puratthimena nagarassa’ means to the east of the city. ‘Santhāgāra’ refers to a sacrificial hall. ‘Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā’ means having worn a black antelope hide complete with its hoofs. ‘Sappitelena’ refers to ghee and oil. Indeed, having set aside ghee, any remaining oily substance is called ‘oil’. ‘Kaṇḍuvamāno’ means scratching with that horn at a time when one needs to scratch, because one's nails have been cut. ‘Anantarahitāya’ means without a covering. ‘Sarūpavacchāya’ means having a calf of similar appearance. If the cow is white, the calf is also white; if the cow is tawny or red, the calf is likewise. Thus, ‘having a calf of similar appearance’. ‘So evamāha’ means that king speaks thus. ‘Vacchatarā’ refers to strong calves that have passed the stage of being young calves. The same principle applies to ‘vacchatarī’ (heifers). ‘Barihisatthāya’ means for the purpose of making an enclosure and for spreading on the sacrificial ground.

Catutthapuggalaṃ buddhuppādato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ idha, bhikkhave, tathāgatotiādimāha. Tattha tathāgatotiādīni [V 2.0371] vuttatthāneva. Taṃ dhammanti taṃ vuttappakārasampadaṃ dhammaṃ. Suṇāti, gahapati, vāti kasmā paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ [M 2.0374] niddisati? Nihatamānattā ussannattā ca. Yebhuyyena hi khattiyakulato pabbajitā jātiṃ nissāya mānaṃ karonti. Brāhmaṇakulā [P 3.0186] pabbajitā mante nissāya mānaṃ karonti, hīnajaccakulā pabbajitā attano vijātitāya patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Gahapatidārakā pana kacchehi sedaṃ muñcantehi piṭṭhiyā loṇaṃ pupphamānāya bhūmiṃ kasitvā tādisassa mānassa abhāvato nihatamānadappā honti. Te pabbajitvā mānaṃ vā dappaṃ vā akatvā yathābalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karontā sakkonti arahatte patiṭṭhātuṃ. Itarehi ca kulehi nikkhamitvā pabbajitā na bahukā, gahapatikāva bahukā. Iti nihatamānattā ussannattā ca paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ niddisatīti.

To show the fourth person, starting from the arising of a Buddha, He spoke the words beginning with, 'Here, a Tathāgata...'. Therein, the words beginning with 'Tathāgata' have the meaning already stated. 'That Dhamma' means that Dhamma endowed with the qualities already mentioned. In the passage 'he hears, or a householder,' why does the Blessed One indicate the householder first? Because of having subdued pride and because of being numerous. For the most part, those gone forth from the warrior clan produce pride relying on their birth. Those gone forth from the brahmin clan produce pride relying on the sacred texts; those gone forth from low-born families are not able to establish themselves in the Dispensation because of their own inferior birth. But the sons of householders, with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt efflorescing on their backs from tilling the ground, are, due to the absence of such pride, those with subdued pride and arrogance. Having gone forth, not producing pride or arrogance, they learn the word of the Buddha according to their ability and, while doing the work of insight meditation, are able to establish themselves in Arahantship. And those who have gone forth from other families are not many; it is the householders who are many. Thus, because of having subdued pride and because of being numerous, He indicates the householder first.

Aññatarasmiṃ vāti itaresaṃ vā kulānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ. Paccājātoti patijāto. Tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti parisuddhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā dhammasāmimhi tathāgate “sammāsambuddho vata bhagavā”ti saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti evaṃ paccavekkhati. Sambādho gharāvāsoti sacepi saṭṭhihatthe ghare yojanasatantarepi vā dve jāyampatikā vasanti, tathāpi nesaṃ sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhova. Rajāpathoti rāgarajādīnaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Āgamanapathotipi vaṭṭati. Alagganaṭṭhena [P 3.0187] abbhokāso viyāti abbhokāso. Pabbajito hi kūṭāgāraratanapāsādadevavimānādīsu pihitadvāravātapānesu paṭicchannesu vasantopi neva laggati na sajjati na bajjhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “abbhokāso pabbajjā”ti. Apica sambādho gharāvāso kusalakiriyāya yathāsukhaṃ okāsābhāvato, rajāpatho asaṃvutasaṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ viya rajānaṃ, kilesarajānaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānato. Abbhokāso pabbajjā kusalakiriyāya yathāsukhaṃ okāsasabbhāvato.

‘Or in some or another’ means: in some or another of the other families. ‘Is reborn’ means is born into. ‘He gains faith in the Tathāgata’ means that after hearing the pure Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata, the master of the Dhamma, thinking, “Indeed, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.” ‘Thus he reflects’ means he considers in this way. ‘The household life is confinement’ means that even if a couple lives in a house sixty cubits wide or even one a hundred yojanas apart, still, because of its nature of having hindrances and anxieties, the household life is indeed confinement. ‘A path of dust’ means the place of arising for the dust of passion and so on; so it is said in the Great Commentary. It is also suitable to say it is a path of arising. In the sense of non-clinging, it is like an open space; therefore, it is called ‘open space’. For one who has gone forth, even while living in roofed places such as gabled halls, jeweled palaces, and celestial mansions with closed doors and windows, does not cling, is not attached, and is not bound. Therefore, it is said: “Going forth is an open space.” Furthermore, the household life is confinement because of the lack of opportunity to perform wholesome actions at ease; it is a path of dust because it is a gathering place for the dust of defilements, like an uncovered rubbish heap is for dust. Going forth is an open space because of the existence of an opportunity to perform wholesome actions at ease.

Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ…pe… pabbajeyyanti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepakathā – yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ, ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalinaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ [M 2.0375] pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ, saṅkhalikhitaṃ likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ kese ca massuñca ohāretvā kasāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā paridahitvā [V 2.0372] agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyanti. Ettha ca yasmā agārassa hitaṃ kasivaṇijjādikammaṃ agāriyanti vuccati, tañca pabbajjāya natthi, tasmā pabbajjā anagāriyāti ñātabbā, taṃ anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajeyyanti [P 3.0188] paṭipajjeyyaṃ.

In the passage 'This is not easy... I would go forth,' this is the brief discourse: That which is the holy life of the three trainings must be practiced, for even a single day, having made it unbroken, it is wholly complete because it must be brought to the final consciousness; and for even a single day, having made it unstained by the stain of defilements, it is wholly pure because it must be brought to the final consciousness. It must be practiced like a polished conch shell, resembling a washed conch shell. This is not easy for one who rules over a house, dwelling in the midst of a house, to practice... wholly completely. What if I, having shaved off my hair and beard, having covered myself and put on the saffron robes—so-called because they are dyed with an astringent solution, garments suitable for those who practice the holy life—were to go forth from the household life into the homeless life? And here, because work beneficial to the house, such as farming and trade, is called 'of the house' (agāriya), and that does not exist in the state of one who has gone forth, therefore the state of one who has gone forth should be known as 'not of the house' (anagāriya). That is the homeless state. 'I would go forth' means 'I would undertake'.

Appaṃ vāti sahassato heṭṭhā bhogakkhandho appo nāma hoti, sahassato paṭṭhāya mahā. Ābandhanaṭṭhena ñātiyeva ñātiparivaṭṭo. So vīsatiyā heṭṭhā appo nāma hoti, vīsatiyā paṭṭhāya mahā. Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannoti yā bhikkhūnaṃ adhisīlasaṅkhātā sikkhā, tañca, yattha cete saha jīvanti, ekajīvikā sabhāgavuttino honti, taṃ bhagavatā paññattasikkhāpadasaṅkhātaṃ sājīvañca tattha sikkhanabhāvena samāpannoti bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Samāpannoti sikkhaṃ paripūrento sājīvañca avītikkamanto hutvā tadubhayaṃ upagatoti attho.

As for 'small': an aggregate of wealth below a thousand is called 'small'; from a thousand onwards, it is 'great'. In the sense of binding, relatives themselves are the circle of relatives. That, below twenty, is called 'small'; from twenty onwards, it is 'great'. As for 'one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood of the bhikkhus': he has undertaken, by way of training, that training of the bhikkhus called higher virtue, and also that common livelihood—called the training rule laid down by the Blessed One—wherein they live together, have a common livelihood, and are of a similar nature; therefore, he is called 'one who has undertaken the training and common livelihood of the bhikkhus'. 'Undertaken' means: having approached both, by fulfilling the training and not transgressing the common livelihood. This is the meaning.

Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyātiādīni vuttatthāneva. Imesaṃ bhedāyāti yesaṃ itoti vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ, tesaṃ bhedāya. Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta”ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā. Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā, dve jane samagge disvā “tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ anucchavikameta”ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho. Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo. Yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na icchatīti attho. Samaggarāmotipi pāḷi, ayameva attho. Samaggaratoti [P 3.0189] samaggesu rato, te pahāya aññattha gantuṃ na icchatīti attho. Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī. Samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā [M 2.0376] vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti, taṃ sāmaggiguṇaparidīpikameva vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti.

‘Having abandoned the destruction of life’ and so forth: the meaning is as stated previously. ‘For their division’ means: for the division of those who were spoken of as ‘from here,’ in whose presence it was heard. ‘Or a reconciler of the divided’: one who, when two friends, or those with the same preceptor, and so on, have become divided for some reason, approaches each one and says, ‘For you, who are born in such a family and are so learned, this is not suitable,’ and so on, thus acting to reconcile them. ‘One who promotes concord’: one who, seeing two people in harmony, acts to strengthen it by saying, ‘For you, who are born in such a family and are endowed with such virtues, this is suitable,’ and so on; this is the meaning. ‘One whose delight is concord’ (samaggārāmo) is so called because concord is his delight (samaggo ārāmo assā). The meaning is: he does not wish even to dwell where there are no harmonious people. Samaggarāmo is also a Pali reading; the meaning is the very same. ‘Delighting in concord’: one who delights in the harmonious; the meaning is that, abandoning them, he does not wish to go elsewhere. ‘Rejoicing in concord’: one who rejoices upon seeing or hearing of the harmonious. ‘Speaking words that create concord’: one who speaks speech that makes beings harmonious, that is, speech that illuminates the virtue of harmony; he does not speak otherwise.

Nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssā elanti nelā, niddosāti attho “nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti (udā. 65) ettha vuttanelaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā, sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati appaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā[V 2.0373]. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī. Pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī, nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi yuttakathā honti, pitimattaṃ pitāti, bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Kantabhāveneva bahujanassa manāpā cittavuḍḍhikarāti bahujanamanāpā.

‘Nela’: ela is said to mean fault; nāssa elaṃ means ‘it has no fault,’ thus nelā means faultless, as in the word nela mentioned in ‘nelaṅgo setapacchādo’ (Ud 5.5). ‘Pleasing to the ears’ (kaṇṇasukhā): it is pleasing to the ears due to the sweetness of expression; it does not produce ear pain like the piercing of a needle. Because of the sweetness of its meaning, it generates affection instead of provoking anger in the whole body—thus, it is ‘lovable’ (pemanīyā). It goes to the heart; not being obstructed, it enters the mind with ease—hence, ‘heart-reaching’ (hadayaṅgamā). Because it is complete in virtues (guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavā), it is porī (urbane). Like a woman raised in a city (pure), it is exceedingly refined, hence also porī. It is of the city (purassa esā), hence also porī; the meaning is, it is the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers speak appropriately; they call one who is like a father, ‘father,’ and one who is like a brother, ‘brother.’ Speech of such a kind is dear to many people, thus it is ‘dear to many people’ (bahujanakantā). Precisely because it is dear, it is pleasing to many people and causes the mind to grow, thus it is ‘pleasing to many people’ (bahujanamanāpā).

Kāle [P 3.0190] vadatīti kālavādī, vattabbayuttakālaṃ sallakkhetvā vadatīti attho. Bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ sabhāvameva vadatīti bhūtavādī. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaatthasannissitameva katvā vadatīti atthavādī. Navalokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti dhammavādī. Saṃvaravinayapahānavinayasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti vinayavādī. Nidhānaṃ vuccati ṭhapanokāso, nidhānamassā atthīti nidhānavatī. Hadaye nidhetabbayuttakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti attho. Kālenāti evarūpiṃ bhāsamānopi ca “ahaṃ nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsissāmī”ti na akālena bhāsati, yuttakālaṃ pana avekkhitvāva bhāsatīti attho. Sāpadesanti saupamaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Pariyantavatinti paricchedaṃ dassetvā, yathāssā paricchedo paññāyati, evaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Atthasaṃhitanti anekehipi nayehi vibhajantena pariyādātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya atthasampannaṃ bhāsati. Yaṃ vā so atthavādī atthaṃ vadati, tena atthena saṃhitattā atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, na aññaṃ nikkhipitvā aññaṃ bhāsatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘He speaks at the proper time’ (kālavādī): he speaks after considering the appropriate time to speak—this is the meaning. ‘He speaks what is real’ (bhūtavādī): he speaks what is true, factual, and in accordance with reality. ‘He speaks what is beneficial’ (atthavādī): he speaks in connection with benefits in this life and the next. ‘He speaks connected with the Dhamma’ (dhammavādī): he speaks in connection with the ninefold transcendent Dhamma. ‘He speaks connected with discipline’ (vinayavādī): he speaks in connection with the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment. ‘A repository’ (nidhāna) refers to a place of storing; ‘it has a repository’ (nidhānavatī) means he speaks words worthy of being stored in the heart—this is the meaning. ‘At the proper time’ (kālena): even while speaking in such a manner, he does not speak out of season, thinking, ‘I will speak words that are worth storing,’ but speaks only after examining the appropriate time—this is the meaning. ‘With a reason’ (sāpadesaṃ): with an illustration, with a cause—this is the meaning. ‘With a limit’ (pariyantavatiṃ): showing a boundary; he speaks in such a way that its limit is evident—this is the meaning. ‘Connected with benefit’ (atthasaṃhitaṃ): he speaks words endowed with benefit, which cannot be exhausted by analyzing them through many methods. Or, because that speaker of benefits speaks of benefits, his speech is connected with benefit—he does not set aside one thing to speak of another—this is what is meant.

Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhāti [M 2.0377] mūlabījaṃ khandhabījaṃ phaḷubījaṃ aggabījaṃ bījabījanti pañcavidhassa bījagāmassa [P 3.0191] ceva yassa kassaci nīlatiṇarukkhādikassa bhūtagāmassa ca samārambhā, chedanabhedanapacanādibhāvena vikopanā paṭiviratoti attho.

‘From the destruction of seed-growth and plant-growth’: this means refraining from destroying the five kinds of seed-growth—root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, sprout-seeds, and seed-seeds—and any kind of plant-growth such as green grass, trees, etc., by means of cutting, splitting, burning, or the like; this is the meaning.

Ekabhattikoti pātarāsabhattaṃ sāyamāsabhattanti dve bhattāni. Tesu pātarāsabhattaṃ antomajjhanhikena paricchinnaṃ, itaraṃ majjhanhikato uddhaṃ antoaruṇena. Tasmā antomajjhanhike dasakkhattuṃ bhuñjamānopi ekabhattikova hoti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ekabhattiko”ti. Rattiyā bhojanaṃ ratti, tato uparatoti rattūparato. Atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāma, tato viratattā virato vikālabhojanā.

‘One who eats one meal’: there are two meals, the morning meal and the evening meal. Of these, the morning meal is defined by the period before midday, and the other is defined by the period from after midday until the following dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within the period before midday, one is still a one-meal eater. It is with reference to this that ‘one who eats one meal’ was stated. ‘Refraining from eating at night’ (rattūparato): eating at night is ‘night-eating’ (ratti); one who has ceased from that is ‘one who refrains from eating at night’. Eating after midday has passed until sunset is called ‘eating at an improper time’ (vikālabhojanaṃ); because of having abstained from that, one is ‘one who abstains from eating at an improper time’ (virato vikālabhojanā).

Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo lohamāsako jatumāsako dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ [V 2.0374] gacchanti. Tassa ubhayassāpi paṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato, neva taṃ uggaṇhāti, na uggaṇhāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatīti attho.

‘Gold’ (jātarūpaṃ) is gold. ‘Silver’ (rajataṃ) refers to whatever is used in commerce, such as a kahāpaṇa, a copper māsaka, a lac māsaka, or a wooden māsaka. He is one who abstains from accepting both of these. He neither accepts it himself, nor does he have it accepted by another, nor does he consent to it being placed near him; this is the meaning.

Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇāti sālivīhiyavagodhūmakaṅguvarakakudrūsakasaṅkhātassa sattavidhassapi āmakadhaññassa paṭiggahaṇā. Na kevalañca etesaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva, āmasanampi bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha aññatra odissa anuññātā āmakamaṃsamacchānaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati, no āmasananti.

‘From accepting raw grain’: from the acceptance of raw grain of the seven kinds, namely: sāli-rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panic-seed, and kodo millet. And it is not only the acceptance of these that is not allowable for bhikkhus; even touching them is not proper. Regarding ‘accepting raw meat’: here, apart from that which is specifically permitted, it is only the acceptance of raw meat and fish that is not allowable for bhikkhus, not the touching of them.

Itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha itthīti purisantaragatā, itarā kumārikā nāma, tāsaṃ paṭiggahaṇampi āmasanampi akappiyameva. Dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇāti [P 3.0192] ettha dāsidāsavaseneva tesaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati, “kappiyakārakaṃ dammi, ārāmikaṃ dammī”ti evaṃ vutte pana vaṭṭati. Ajeḷakādīsupi khettavatthupariyosānesu kappiyākappiyanayo vinayavasena upaparikkhitabbo. Tattha khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayampi ruhati, taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya akatabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpi-taḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāneva.

Herein, regarding 'the acceptance of women and young girls': a 'woman' is one who has been with a man; the other is called a 'young girl.' Accepting or even touching them is indeed improper. Regarding 'the acceptance of female and male slaves': accepting them simply by virtue of being female and male slaves is not allowable. However, when it is said, 'I give a suitable worker,' or 'I give a monastery attendant,' then it is allowable. Regarding goats, sheep, and so on, up to fields and lands, the method concerning what is allowable and unallowable should be investigated by means of the Vinaya. Therein, a 'field' is that in which grain grows. 'Land' is that in which pulses grow. Alternatively, where both grow, that is a 'field.' An uncultivated portion of land for that purpose is 'land.' And here, under the heading of 'field' and 'land,' reservoirs, ponds, and so on are also included.

Dūteyyaṃ [M 2.0378] vuccati dūtakammaṃ gihīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Pahiṇagamanaṃ vuccati gharā gharaṃ pesitassa khuddakagamanaṃ. Anuyogo nāma tadubhayakaraṇaṃ. Tasmā duteyyapahiṇagamanānaṃ anuyogoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Kayavikkayāti kayā ca vikkayā ca. Tulākūṭādīsu kūṭanti vañcanaṃ. Tattha tulākūṭaṃ tāva rūpakūṭaṃ, aṅgakūṭaṃ, gahaṇakūṭaṃ, paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā samarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti[P 3.0193], dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

‘Messenger work’ (dūteyya) is called the task of a messenger: taking a letter or a message from householders and going to various places. ‘Going on an errand’ (pahiṇagamana) is called the minor going of one who is sent from house to house. ‘Application’ (anuyoga) is the doing of both of these. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as ‘application to messenger work and going on errands.’ ‘Buying and selling’ (kayavikkaya) is from buying and from selling. In ‘deception with scales and so on,’ ‘deception’ (kūṭa) means cheating. Therein, ‘deception with scales’ is of four kinds: deception by appearance (rūpakūṭa), deception by a part (aṅgakūṭa), deception by holding (gahaṇakūṭa), and deception by concealment (paṭicchannakūṭa). Therein, deception by appearance is when, having made two scales of identical appearance, one takes with the large one when receiving and gives with the small one when giving. Deception by a part is when one presses down on the back part of the scale with one’s hand when receiving, and on the front part when giving. Deception by holding is when one holds the cord at the base when receiving, and at the tip when giving. Deception by concealment is when, having made the scale hollow and put iron powder inside, one causes it to be in the back part when receiving, and in the front part when giving.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti, tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇā karoti. Tato janapadaṃ gantvā kiñcideva aḍḍhakulaṃ [V 2.0375] pavisitvā “suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇathā”ti vatvā agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti. Tato tehi “kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo”ti vutte “vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā”ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbapātiyo datvā gacchati.

A golden bowl is called kaṃsa, and deception with it is kaṃsakūṭa. How so? Having made one golden bowl, one makes two or three other bronze bowls the color of gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering some wealthy household, one says, 'Buy golden bowls!' When the price is asked, they are willing to give a very fair price. Then, when they ask, 'How is the golden nature of these bowls to be known?', one replies, 'Examine them and then take them.' Having rubbed the golden bowl on a touchstone, one gives all the bowls and departs.

Mānakūṭaṃ nāma hadayabheda-sikhābheda-rajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha hadayabhedo sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhāchiddena mānena “saṇikaṃ āsiñcā”ti vatvā attano bhājane bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā deti. Sikhābhedo tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto vegena pūretvā sikhaṃ chindanto deti. Rajjubhedo khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Lañjaṃ alabhantā hi khettaṃ amahantampi mahantaṃ katvā minanti.

Deception with measures (mānakūṭa) is of three kinds: breaking the interior (hadayabheda), breaking the peak (sikhābheda), and breaking the rope (rajjubheda). Among these, 'breaking the interior' is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so forth. For when taking, having said, 'Pour slowly,' one takes by causing much to flow into one's own container through a measure with a hole at the bottom. When giving, having blocked the hole, one fills it quickly and gives. 'Breaking the peak' is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so forth. For when taking, one slowly raises up the peak and takes. When giving, one fills it quickly and gives, while cutting off the peak. 'Breaking the rope' is found when measuring fields and grounds. For those who do not receive a bribe measure a field, making it large even if it is not.

Ukkoṭanādīsu ukkoṭananti sāmike assāmike kātuṃ lañjaggahaṇaṃ. Vañcananti tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃ vatthu [M 2.0379] – eko [P 3.0194] kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā āgacchati. Tameko dhutto “kiṃ bho migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti ca vutte ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivatto “na me bho migapotakenattho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Tena hi dve kahāpaṇe dehīti. So āha – “nanu te bho mayā paṭhamaṃ eko kahāpaṇo dinno”ti? Āma dinnoti. Imampi migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo ayañca kahāpaṇagghanako migapotako”ti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantīti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti. Nikatīti yogavasena vā māyāvasena vā apāmaṅgaṃ pāmaṅganti, amaṇiṃ maṇinti, asuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇanti katvā patirūpakena vañcanaṃ. Sāciyogoti kuṭilayogo. Etesaṃyeva ukkoṭanādīnametaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā ukkoṭanasāciyogo vañcanasāciyogo nikatisāciyogoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Keci aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ sāciyogoti vadanti, taṃ pana vañcaneneva saṅgahitaṃ.

Regarding bribery and so forth (ukkoṭanādīsu): 'bribery' (ukkoṭana) is the taking of a bribe to make an owner into a non-owner. 'Deception' (vañcana) is the deceiving of others by various means. Herein is one story: A certain hunter, having caught a deer and a fawn, was coming along. A rogue asked him, 'Sir, what is the deer worth, and what is the fawn worth?' When it was said, 'The deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, and the fawn one,' the rogue gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after going a short distance, returned and said, 'Sir, I have no use for the fawn; give me the deer.' The hunter replied, 'In that case, give two kahāpaṇas.' The rogue said, 'Sir, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa at first?' 'Yes, you did,' said the hunter. The rogue then said, 'Take this fawn as well. Thus, that kahāpaṇa and this fawn, which is worth one kahāpaṇa, will become two kahāpaṇas.' The hunter, perceiving, 'He speaks reason,' took the fawn and gave him the deer. 'Fraud' (nikati) is deceiving with a counterfeit by means of effort or illusion, making what is not coral into 'coral,' what is not a gem into 'a gem,' or what is not gold into 'gold.' 'Crooked practice' (sāciyoga) is a crooked application. This is just a name for these same things: bribery and so forth. Therefore, the meaning here should be regarded as: the crooked practice of bribery, the crooked practice of deception, and the crooked practice of fraud. Some say that 'crooked practice' is exchanging one thing for another after having shown a different one, but that is already included under 'deception'.

Chedanādīsu chedananti hatthacchedanādi. Vadhoti māraṇaṃ. Bandhoti rajjubandhanādīhi bandhanaṃ. Viparāmosoti himaviparāmoso, gumbaviparāmosoti duvidho. Yaṃ himapātasamaye himena paṭicchannā hutvā maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ musanti, ayaṃ himaviparāmoso. Yaṃ gumbādīhi paṭicchannā [V 2.0376] musanti, ayaṃ gumbaviparāmoso. Ālopo vuccati gāmanigamādīnaṃ vilopakaraṇaṃ. Sahasākāroti [P 3.0195] sāhasikakiriyā, gehaṃ pavisitvā manussānaṃ ure satthaṃ ṭhapetvā icchitabhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ. Evametasmā chedana…pe… sahasākārā paṭivirato hoti.

Regarding cutting and so forth (chedanādīsu): 'cutting' (chedana) means cutting off hands and the like. 'Killing' (vadha) means putting to death (māraṇa). 'Binding' (bandha) means binding with ropes and so forth. 'Waylaying' (viparāmosa) is of two kinds: waylaying by snow and waylaying by thicket. When, during snowfall, being covered by snow, they waylay people on the path, this is waylaying by snow. When, being covered by thickets and so forth, they waylay, this is waylaying by thicket. 'Plundering' (ālopa) is said to be the act of plundering villages, towns, and so forth. 'A violent act' (sahasākāra) means a coercive action: entering a house, placing a weapon on people's chests, and taking desired goods. Thus, one is abstained from this cutting... up to... this violent act.

So santuṭṭho hotīti svāyaṃ bhikkhu heṭṭhā vuttena catūsu paccayesu dvādasavidhena itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgato hoti. Iminā pana dvādasavidhena itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgatassa bhikkhuno aṭṭha parikkhārā vaṭṭanti – tīṇi cīvarāni, patto, dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsi, ekā sūci, kāyabandhanaṃ parissāvananti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

“He is content” (so santuṭṭho hoti) means that this bhikkhu is endowed with the twelvefold contentment with whatever requisites are obtained regarding the four requisites, as previously described. For a bhikkhu endowed with this twelvefold contentment with whatever requisites are obtained, eight requisites are allowable: three robes, a bowl, an adze for cutting tooth-sticks, one needle, a waistband, and a water strainer. And this has also been said:

“Ticīvarañca [M 2.0380] patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti.

“Three robes and a bowl, an adze, a needle, and a waistband; with a water strainer, these are the eight for a bhikkhu devoted to striving.”

Te sabbe kāyaparihārikāpi honti, kucchiparihārikāpi. Kathaṃ? Ticīvaraṃ tāva nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca vicaraṇakāle kāyaṃ pariharati posetīti kāyaparihārikaṃ hoti. Cīvarakaṇṇena udakaṃ parissāvetvā pivanakāle, khāditabbaphalāphalaṃ gahaṇakāle ca kucchiṃ pariharati posetīti kucchiparihārikaṃ hoti. Pattopi tena udakaṃ uddharitvā nhānakāle kuṭiparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihāriko hoti, āhāraṃ gahetvā bhuñjanakāle kucchiparihāriko. Vāsipi tāya dantakaṭṭhacchedanakāle mañcapīṭhānaṃ aṅgapādacīvarakuṭidaṇḍakasajjanakāle ca kāyaparihārikā hoti, ucchucchedananāḷikerāditacchanakāle [P 3.0196] kucchiparihārikā. Sūcipi cīvarasibbanakāle kāyaparihārikā hoti, pūvaṃ vā phalaṃ vā vijjhitvā khādanakāle kucchiparihārikā. Kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā vicaraṇakāle kāyaparihārikaṃ, ucchuādīni bandhitvā gahaṇakāle kucchiparihārikaṃ. Parissāvanaṃ tena udakaṃ parissāvetvā nhānakāle senāsanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇakāle ca kāyaparihārikaṃ, pānīyapānakaparissāvanakāle teneva tilataṇḍulaputhukādīni gahetvā khādanakāle ca kucchiparihārikaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva aṭṭhaparikkhārikassa parikkhāramattā.

All of them serve for the maintenance of the body and also for the maintenance of the stomach. How so? Firstly, when wearing and draping the three robes while wandering, one maintains and nourishes the body; thus, they serve for the maintenance of the body. When straining water with the corner of a robe for drinking, or when taking edible fruits, one maintains and nourishes the stomach; thus, they serve for the maintenance of the stomach. The bowl, too, when used to draw water for bathing or to prepare the hut’s furnishings, serves for the maintenance of the body; when taking food to eat, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach. The adze, too, when used to cut tooth-sticks or to prepare the legs and feet of beds and chairs and poles for drying robes, serves for the maintenance of the body; when cutting sugarcane or scraping coconuts and so forth, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach. The needle, too, when sewing robes, serves for the maintenance of the body; when piercing cakes or fruits to eat, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach. The waistband, when tied while wandering, serves for the maintenance of the body; when bundling sugarcane and so forth to carry, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach. The water strainer, when used to strain water for bathing or to prepare the lodging’s furnishings, serves for the maintenance of the body; when straining drinking water and beverages, or when taking sesame, rice, parched grain, and so forth with it to eat, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach. This, for now, is the extent of the requisites for one possessing the eight requisites.

Navaparikkhārikassa pana seyyaṃ pavisantassa tatraṭṭhakapaccattharaṇaṃ vā kuñcikā vā vaṭṭati. Dasaparikkhārikassa nisīdanaṃ vā cammakhaṇḍaṃ vā vaṭṭati. Ekādasaparikkhārikassa kattarayaṭṭhi [V 2.0377] vā telanāḷikā vā vaṭṭati. Dvādasaparikkhārikassa chattaṃ vā upāhanaṃ vā vaṭṭati. Etesu ca aṭṭhaparikkhārikova santuṭṭho, itare asantuṭṭhā mahicchā mahābhārāti na vattabbā. Etepi appicchāva santuṭṭhāva subharāva sallahukavuttinova. Bhagavā pana na imaṃ suttaṃ tesaṃ vasena kathesi, aṭṭhaparikkhārikassa vasena kathesi. So hi khuddakavāsiñca sūciñca parissāvane pakkhipitvā pattassa anto ṭhapetvā pattaṃ aṃsakūṭe laggetvā ticīvaraṃ kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ katvā yenicchakaṃ sukhaṃ pakkamati, paṭinivattitvā gahetabbaṃ nāmassa [P 3.0197] na hoti. Iti imassa bhikkhuno [M 2.0381] sallahukavuttitaṃ dassento bhagavā santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarenātiādimāha.

For one possessing nine requisites, when entering his lodging, a bed-covering placed there or a key is allowable. For one possessing ten requisites, a sitting-cloth or a piece of hide is allowable. For one possessing eleven requisites, a staff or an oil-tube is allowable. For one possessing twelve requisites, a parasol or footwear is allowable. And among these, it should not be said: 'Only the one with eight requisites is content; the others are discontented, of great desire, and heavily burdened.' These others, too, are of few desires, content, easy to support, and of light livelihood. However, the Blessed One did not teach this discourse with reference to them, but with reference to the one with eight requisites. For he, having put a small adze and a needle into the water-strainer, having placed them inside the bowl, having hung the bowl on his shoulder-tip, and having made the three robes bound to his body, departs happily wherever he wishes; for him, there is nothing that needs to be taken upon returning. Thus, showing the light livelihood of this monk, the Blessed One said, 'He is content with the robe that protects his body,' and so forth.

Tattha kāyaparihārikenāti kāyapariharaṇamattakena. Kucchiparihārikenāti kucchipariharaṇamattakena. Samādāyeva pakkamatīti taṃ aṭṭhaparikkhāramattakaṃ sabbaṃ gahetvāva kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ katvāva gacchati, “mama vihāro pariveṇaṃ upaṭṭhāko”tissa saṅgo vā bandho vā na hoti. So jiyā mutto saro viya, yūthā apakkanto mattahatthī viya icchiticchitaṃ senāsanaṃ, vanasaṇḍaṃ, rukkhamūlaṃ, navaṃ pabbhāraṃ paribhuñjanto eko tiṭṭhati, eko nisīdati, sabbiriyāpathesu eko adutiyo.

Therein, 'with body-maintenance' (kāyaparihārikena) means with mere maintenance of the body. 'With stomach-maintenance' (kucchiparihārikena) means with mere maintenance of the stomach. 'He departs having taken them up' (samādāyeva pakkamati) means he goes having taken all of those mere eight requisites, having made them bound to his body; for him there is no clinging or bond thinking, 'This is my monastery, my monastic compound, my attendant.' Like an arrow released from the bowstring, like a musth elephant that has departed from the herd, he makes use of whatever lodging he wishes—a forest grove, the root of a tree, a new mountain-slope—he stands alone, he sits alone; in all postures he is alone, without a second.

“Cātuddiso appaṭigho ca hoti,

Santussamāno itarītarena;

Parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhī,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. (su. ni. 42; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddeso 128) –

Open to all quarters and unresisting, Contented with whatever comes; Enduring dangers, undaunted, Let him wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Evaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ khaggavisāṇakappataṃ āpajjati.

Thus, he reaches the praised state of being like a rhinoceros horn.

Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha pakkhī sakuṇoti pakkhayutto sakuṇo. Ḍetīti uppatati. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – sakuṇā nāma “asukasmiṃ padese rukkho paripakkaphalo”ti ñatvā nānādisāhi āgantvā nakhapakkhatuṇḍādīhi [P 3.0198] tassa phalāni vijjhantā vidhunantā khādanti, “idaṃ ajjatanāya, idaṃ svātanāya bhavissatī”ti nesaṃ [V 2.0378] na hoti. Phale pana khīṇe neva rukkhassa ārakkhaṃ ṭhapenti, na tattha pakkhaṃ vā pattaṃ vā nakhaṃ vā tuṇḍaṃ vā ṭhapenti, atha kho tasmiṃ rukkhe anapekkhā hutvā yo yaṃ disābhāgaṃ icchati, so tena sapattabhārova uppatitvā gacchati. Evameva ayaṃ bhikkhu nissaṅgo nirapekkhoyeva pakkamati, samādāyeva pakkamati. Ariyenāti niddosena. Ajjhattanti sake attabhāve. Anavajjasukhanti niddosasukhaṃ.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, he spoke the words beginning with 'seyyathāpi'. Therein, 'pakkhī sakuṇo' means a bird endowed with wings. 'Ḍeti' means it flies up. This, however, is the concise meaning here: Birds, by name, knowing, 'In such-and-such a place there is a tree with ripe fruit,' come from various directions and, with their claws, wings, beaks, and so on, piercing and shaking them, eat the fruits of that tree. It does not occur to them, 'This will be for today, this will be for tomorrow.' But when the fruit is exhausted, they do not place a guard for the tree, nor do they leave a mature feather, a young feather, a claw, or a beak there. Rather, having become unconcerned with that tree, whichever direction a bird wishes to go, it flies up and goes in that direction, having only the burden of its own wings. Just so, this bhikkhu, being unattached and unconcerned, departs to whatever direction he wishes. 'Ariyena' means faultless. 'Ajjhattaṃ' means in one's own being. 'Anavajjasukhaṃ' means blameless happiness.

So cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti so iminā ariyena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato bhikkhu cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ passitvāti attho. Sesapadesupi [M 2.0382] yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.15) vuttaṃ. Abyāsekasukhanti kilesehi anāsittasukhaṃ, avikiṇṇasukhantipi vuttaṃ. Indriyasaṃvarasukhaṃ hi diṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhamattādivasena pavattatāya avikiṇṇaṃ hoti.

'So cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā' (He, having seen a form with the eye) means: that bhikkhu, who is endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with eye-consciousness. This is the meaning. As for the remaining phrases, whatever should be said has all been said by me in the Visuddhimagga. 'Abyāsekasukhaṃ' (happiness of non-interfusion) means happiness not sprinkled by defilements; it is also called 'avikiṇṇasukhaṃ' (unmixed happiness). For the happiness of sense-restraint is unmixed because it occurs in regard to the seen and so forth by way of the mere seen, etc.

So abhikkante paṭikkanteti so manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ saṃvarena samannāgato bhikkhu imesu abhikkantapaṭikkantādīsu sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññavasena sampajānakārī hoti. Tattha abhikkantanti purato gamanaṃ. Paṭikkantanti pacchāgamanaṃ.

'So abhikkante paṭikkante' (He, in going forward and in going backward) means: that bhikkhu, endowed with restraint of the sense faculties with the mind as the sixth, is one who acts with clear comprehension by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances, such as going forward and going backward. Therein, 'abhikkantaṃ' means going forward. 'Paṭikkantaṃ' means going backward.

Sampajānakārī [P 3.0199] hotīti sātthakasampajaññaṃ, sappāyasampajaññaṃ, gocarasampajaññaṃ, asammohasampajaññanti imesaṃ catunnaṃ satisampayuttānaṃ sampajaññānaṃ vasena satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ñāṇena paricchinditvāyeva tāni abhikkantapaṭikkantāni karoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana icchantena dīghanikāye sāmaññaphalavaṇṇanāto vā majjhimanikāye satipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanāto vā gahetabbo.

He acts with clear comprehension: that is, with clear comprehension of purpose, of suitability, of the domain, and of non-delusion. By means of these four kinds of clear comprehension conjoined with mindfulness, having established mindfulness, it is only after having discerned them with knowledge that he performs those actions of going forward and going backward. This same method applies to the remaining passages. This is the summary here; but one who wishes for a detailed explanation should take it from the commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya or from the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya.

So iminā cātiādinā kiṃ dasseti? Araññavāsassa paccayasampattiṃ dasseti. Yassa hi ime cattāro paccayā natthi, tassa araññavāso na ijjhati, tiracchānagatehi vā vanacarakehi vā saddhiṃ vatthabbataṃ āpajjati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā “kiṃ evarūpassa pāpabhikkhuno araññavāsenā”ti bheravasaddaṃ sāventi, hatthehi sīsaṃ paharitvā palāyanākāraṃ karonti. “Asuko bhikkhu araññaṃ pavisitvā idañcidañca pāpakammamakāsī”ti ayaso pattharati. Yassa panete cattāro paccayā atthi, tassa araññavāso ijjhati. So hi attano sīlaṃ [V 2.0379] paccavekkhanto kiñci kāḷakaṃ vā tilakaṃ vā apassanto pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ khayato vayato sammasanto ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā attamanā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Itissa udake pakkhittatelabindu viya yaso vitthāriko hoti.

What does it show by the phrase beginning with 'So iminā ca...'? It shows the accomplishment of the conditions for forest dwelling. For a monk who lacks these four conditions, forest dwelling does not succeed; he comes to the state of having to live together with animals or with forest wanderers. The deities dwelling in the forest, thinking, 'What is the use of forest dwelling for such an evil monk?', make terrifying sounds; they strike their heads with their hands and make a show of fleeing. Ill repute spreads: 'The monk so-and-so, having entered the forest, committed this and that evil deed.' But for a monk who possesses these four conditions, forest dwelling succeeds. For he, reflecting on his own virtue and seeing no fault like a black spot or a subtle transgression like a sesame seed, generates rapture. Contemplating it by way of its destruction and vanishing, he enters the noble plane. The deities dwelling in the forest are delighted and speak his praise. Thus, his fame becomes widespread like a drop of oil cast upon water.

Tattha vivittanti suññaṃ, appasaddaṃ, appanigghosanti attho. Etadeva hi sandhāya vibhaṅge “vivittanti santike cepi [P 3.0200] senāsanaṃ hoti, tañca anākiṇṇaṃ gahaṭṭhehi pabbajitehi, tena taṃ vivitta”nti (vibha. 526) vuttaṃ. Seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanaṃ. Mañcapīṭhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenāha – “senāsananti [M 2.0383] mañcopi senāsanaṃ, pīṭhampi, bhisipi, bimbohanampi, vihāropi, aḍḍhayogopi, pāsādopi, hammiyampi, guhāpi, aṭṭopi, māḷopi, leṇampi, veḷugumbopi, rukkhamūlampi, maṇḍapopi senāsanaṃ, yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamanti, sabbametaṃ senāsana”nti (vibha. 527). Apica vihāro, aḍḍhayogo, pāsādo, hammiyaṃ, guhāti idaṃ vihārasenāsanaṃ nāma. Mañco, pīṭhaṃ, bhisi, bimbohananti idaṃ mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ nāma. Cimilikā, cammakhaṇḍo, tiṇasanthāro, paṇṇasanthāroti idaṃ santhatasenāsanaṃ nāma. Yattha vā pana bhikkhū paṭikkamantīti etaṃ okāsasenāsanaṃ nāmāti evaṃ catubbidhaṃ senāsanaṃ hoti. Taṃ sabbampi senāsanaggahaṇena gahitameva.

Herein, 'secluded' means devoid of human sounds, without sound, and without clamor. This is precisely what is referred to in the Vibhaṅga: 'Even if a lodging is nearby, if it is not crowded with householders and monastics, it is considered secluded.' 'Lodging' (senāsana) is so called because one lies down (seti) and sits (āsati) there. This term is a designation for beds and chairs. Hence it is said: 'A lodging includes a bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery, a half-gabled building, a long mansion, a storied building, a cave, a watchtower, a hall, a rock-shelter, a bamboo grove, the foot of a tree, a pavilion; or any place where monks retreat—all this is a lodging.' Furthermore, a monastery, a half-gabled building, a long mansion, a storied building, or a cave is called a 'dwelling-lodging.' A bed, a chair, a mattress, or a pillow is called a 'bed-and-chair lodging.' A covering, a piece of hide, a grass spread, or a leaf spread is called a 'spread-lodging.' 'Any place where monks retreat' is called a 'space-lodging.' Thus, there are four types of lodgings. All of these are included under the term 'lodging.'

Imassa pana sakuṇasadisassa cātuddisassa bhikkhuno anucchavikaṃ dassento araññaṃ rukkhamūlantiādimāha. Tattha araññanti “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) “idaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgataṃ araññaṃ. “Āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) idaṃ pana imassa bhikkhuno anurūpaṃ. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge dhutaṅganiddese vuttaṃ. Rukkhamūlanti [P 3.0201] yaṃkiñci sītacchāyaṃ vivittaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ. Pabbatanti selaṃ. Tattha hi udakasoṇḍīsu udakakiccaṃ katvā sītāya rukkhacchāyāya nisinnassa nānādisāsu khāyamānāsu sītena vātena bījiyamānassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Kandaranti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena dāritaṃ udakabhinnaṃ pabbatapadesaṃ, yaṃ nitambantipi nadīnikuñjantipi vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisā vālikā hoti, matthake maṇivitānaṃ viya vanagahanaṃ, maṇikkhandhasadisaṃ udakaṃ sandati. Evarūpaṃ kandaraṃ oruyha pānīyaṃ pivitvā gattāni sītāni katvā vālikaṃ ussāpetvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ paññāpetvā nisinnassa samaṇadhammaṃ karoto cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Giriguhanti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ, ekasmiṃyeva [V 2.0380] vā umaṅgasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ. Susānalakkhaṇaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.34) vuttaṃ. Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasanti na vapanti. Tenevāha – “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādi. Abbhokāsanti acchannaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasati. Palālapuñjanti [P 3.0202] palālarāsiṃ[M 2.0384]. Mahāpalālapuñjato hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbādīnampi upari palālaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisinnā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, to show a suitable dwelling for this monk, who is like a bird of the four quarters, He said, 'the forest, the root of a tree,' and so on. Therein, 'forest' refers to 'having gone out, everything outside the threshold (indakhīla) is forest' (Vibh 529). This definition of 'forest' was given in the context of bhikkhunīs. 'A forest dwelling is one at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths' (cf. Pārā. 654); this, however, is what is appropriate for this monk. Its characteristics are described in the Visuddhimagga’s exposition of the ascetic practices. 'The root of a tree' refers to any cool, shaded, and secluded root of a tree. 'A mountain' means a rocky mountain. For there, when a monk has performed his water duties at water pools and sits in the cool shade of a tree, with various directions appearing and being fanned by a cool wind, his mind becomes one-pointed. 'A ravine' (kandara): 'kaṃ' is said to be water; it is a mountain area split or cleft by water, which they also call a mountain slope (nitamba) or a river glen (nadīkuñja). For there, the sand is like a silver sheet, the forest thicket overhead is like a jeweled canopy, and the water flows like a mass of jewels. When a monk descends into such a ravine, drinks water, cools his limbs, heaps up the sand, spreads his rag-robe, and sits practicing the ascetic’s duties, his mind becomes one-pointed. 'A mountain cave' is the space between two mountains, or a large opening in a single one resembling a tunnel. The characteristics of a charnel ground are described in the Visuddhimagga (Vism I, 118). 'A remote jungle tract' is a place beyond the village outskirts, a place not frequented by humans, where they do not plow or sow. Hence He said: 'A remote jungle tract is a designation for distant dwellings,' and so on. 'An open space' means an uncovered place. If he wishes, a monk may build a robe-hut there and dwell. 'A heap of straw' refers to a pile of straw. For from a large heap of straw, they pull out straw to make shelters resembling overhanging caves; or they place straw over trees, bushes, and so on, and, sitting beneath, practice the ascetic’s duties. This was said in reference to that.

Pacchābhattanti bhattassa pacchato. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭikkanto. Pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimasarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā na uppajjanti. Tāsu na uppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati, vuddhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā, mukhasamīpe vā katvāti attho. Teneva vibhaṅge vuttaṃ – “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti sūpaṭṭhitā nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā. Tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (vibha. 537). Atha vā “parīti pariggahaṭṭho. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho. Satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati – ‘parimukhaṃ sati’”nti evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vuttanayena panettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo “pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvā”ti.

'After the meal' means after the meal. 'Having returned from the alms round' means having returned from the quest for alms-food. 'Cross-legged' means a seat with the thighs bound all around. 'Having folded' (ābhujitvā) means having bound. 'Setting the body upright' means keeping the upper body straight, making the eighteen vertebrae meet end to end. For one seated thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, those feelings that might arise moment by moment because of their bending do not arise. When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it grows and flourishes. 'Establishing mindfulness before him' means establishing mindfulness facing the meditation subject, or it means having placed it near the mouth. For this reason it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'This mindfulness is established, well-established, at the tip of the nose or at the mouth-sign. Therefore it is said: “establishing mindfulness before him.”' Alternatively, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: '“Pari” has the sense of encompassing. “Mukha” has the sense of outlet. “Sati” has the sense of establishment. Therefore it is called “parimukhaṃ sati.”' The summary of this is: 'having made mindfulness the encompassed outlet.'

Abhijjhaṃ loketi ettha lujjana-palujjanaṭṭhena pañcupādānakkhandhā [P 3.0203] loko. Tasmā pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu rāgaṃ pahāya kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambhetvāti ayamettha attho. Vigatābhijjhenāti vikkhambhanavasena pahīnattā vigatābhijjhena, na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenāti attho. Abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodhetīti abhijjhāto cittaṃ parimoceti, yathā naṃ sā muñcati ceva muñcitvā ca na puna gaṇhāti, evaṃ karotīti attho. Byāpādapadosaṃ pahāyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Byāpajjati iminā cittaṃ pūtikummāsādayo viya purimapakatiṃ pajahatīti byāpādo. Vikārappattiyā padussati, paraṃ vā padūseti vināsetīti padoso. Ubhayampetaṃ kodhasseva adhivacanaṃ[V 2.0381]. Thinaṃ cittagelaññaṃ, middhaṃ cetasikagelaññaṃ. Thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Ālokasaññīti rattimpi divāpi diṭṭhaālokasañjānanasamatthāya vigatanīvaraṇāya parisuddhāya saññāya samannāgato[M 2.0385]. Sato sampajānoti satiyā ca ñāṇena ca samannāgato. Idaṃ ubhayaṃ ālokasaññāya upakārakattā vuttaṃ. Uddhaccañca kukkuccañca uddhaccakukkuccaṃ. Tiṇṇavicikicchoti vicikicchaṃ taritvā atikkamitvā ṭhito. “Kathamidaṃ kathamida”nti evaṃ nappavattatīti akathaṃkathī. Kusalesu dhammesūti anavajjesu dhammesu. “Ime nu kho kusalā, kathamime kusalā”ti evaṃ na vicikicchati na kaṅkhatīti attho. Ayamettha [P 3.0204] saṅkhepo. Imesu pana nīvaraṇesu vacanatthalakkhaṇādibhedato yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.71-72) vuttaṃ. Paññāya dubbalīkaraṇeti yasmā ime pañca nīvaraṇā uppajjamānā anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na denti, uppannāpi aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca vā abhiññā ucchinditvā pātenti. Tasmā paññāya dubbalīkaraṇāti vuccanti. Vivicceva kāmehītiādīni visuddhimagge vitthāritāni.

In the phrase 'abhijjhaṃ loke,' 'the world' (loko) refers to the five aggregates subject to clinging, in the sense of perishing and dissolving. Therefore, the meaning here is that having abandoned passion for the five aggregates subject to clinging, one has suppressed sensual desire. As for 'with covetousness departed' (vigatābhijjhena): because it has been abandoned by means of suppression, one is with a mind free from covetousness, not with a mind similar to eye-consciousness; this is the meaning. As for 'he cleanses the mind of covetousness' (abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti): he liberates the mind from covetousness in such a way that it (covetousness) both releases the mind and, having released it, does not grasp it again; this is the meaning. The same method applies to 'having abandoned ill will and malice,' and so on. The mind is corrupted by this, like spoiled sour-milk cakes, and abandons its former nature; therefore, it is called 'ill will' (byāpāda). It is defiled by reaching a state of distortion, or it defiles and destroys another; therefore, it is called 'malice' (padoso). Both of these are designations for anger itself. Sickness of the mind is 'sloth' (thina); sickness of the mental factors is 'torpor' (middha). Sloth and torpor are 'sloth-and-torpor' (thinamiddha). As for 'perceiving light' (ālokasaññī): one is endowed with a perception, by night and by day, that is free from hindrances, purified, and capable of recognizing the light that has been seen. As for 'mindful and clearly comprehending' (sato sampajāno): one is endowed with mindfulness and with knowledge. This pair is mentioned because it is helpful to the perception of light. Restlessness and remorse are 'restlessness-and-remorse' (uddhaccakukkucca). As for 'one who has crossed over doubt' (tiṇṇavicikiccho): one stands having crossed over and overcome doubt. Because one does not proceed thus, "How is this? How is this?", one is called 'one free from uncertainty' (akathaṃkathī). As for 'in wholesome states' (kusalesu dhammesu): in blameless states. The meaning is that one does not doubt or hesitate thus: "Are these states wholesome? How are these states wholesome?" This is the summary here. Furthermore, regarding these hindrances, whatever should be said with respect to the distinctions of definition, characteristic, and so on, has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. As for 'the weakening of wisdom' (paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe): because when these five hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise, and even when it has arisen, they cut it off and cause the eight attainments or the five higher knowledges to fall. Therefore, they are called 'the weakening of wisdom.' Such phrases as 'secluded from sensual pleasures' (vivicceva kāmehi) have been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga.

Ime āsavātiādi aparenāpi pariyāyena catusaccappakāsanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātīti ettāvatā heṭṭhā tīhi aṅgehi bāhirasamayassa nipphalabhāvaṃ dassetvā catutthena aṅgena attano sāsanassa gambhīrabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā desanāya arahattena kūṭaṃ gaṇhi. Idāni desanaṃ appento evaṃ kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha.

The words 'These are the taints,' etc., were also stated in another way for the purpose of explaining the Four Truths. By this much—'He understands: there is nothing further for this state of being'—having shown the fruitlessness of external doctrines with the three factors below and having revealed the profundity of his own teaching with the fourth factor, he took the discourse to its peak with Arahantship. Now, wishing to conclude the discourse, he said, 'Thus, O monks,' and so forth.

9. Taṇhāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Craving Sutta

199. Navame jālininti jālasadisaṃ. Yathā hi jālaṃ samantato saṃsibbitaṃ ākulabyākulaṃ, evaṃ taṇhāpīti jālasadisattā jālinīti vuttā. Tayo vā bhave ajjhottharitvā ṭhitāya etissā tattha tattha attano koṭṭhāsabhūtaṃ jālaṃ atthītipi jālinī. Saritanti tattha tattha saritvā saṃsaritvā ṭhitaṃ. Visaṭanti patthaṭaṃ vikkhittaṃ. Visattikanti tattha tattha visattaṃ laggaṃ lagitaṃ. Apica [P 3.0205] “visamūlāti visattikā. Visaphalāti visattikā”tiādināpi (mahāni. 3; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddeso 22) nayenettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Uddhastoti upari dhaṃsito. Pariyonaddhoti samantā veṭhito. Tantākulakajātoti tantaṃ viya ākulajāto. Yathā nāma dunnikkhittaṃ mūsikacchinnaṃ pesakārānaṃ tantaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ ākulaṃ [V 2.0382] hoti, “idaṃ aggaṃ idaṃ mūla”nti aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaraṃ hoti, evaṃ sattā imāya taṇhāya [M 2.0386] pariyonaddhā ākulabyākulā na sakkonti attano nissaraṇamaggaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ. Gulāguṇṭhikajātoti gulāguṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ. Gulā nāma sakuṇikā, tassā kulāvakotipi eke. Yathā tadubhayampi ākulaṃ aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaranti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Muñjapabbajabhūtoti muñjatiṇaṃ viya pabbajatiṇaṃ viya ca bhūto, tādiso jāto. Yathā tāni tiṇāni koṭṭetvā katarajjuṃ jiṇṇakāle katthaci patitaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ tiṇānaṃ “idaṃ aggaṃ idaṃ mūla”nti aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaraṃ. Tampi ca paccattapurisakāre ṭhatvā sakkā bhaveyya ujuṃ kātuṃ, ṭhapetvā pana bodhisatte añño satto attano dhammatāya taṇhājālaṃ padāletvā attano nissaraṇamaggaṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Evamayaṃ loko taṇhājālena pariyonaddho apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati. Tattha [P 3.0206] apāyoti niraya-tiracchānayoni-pettivisaya-asurakāyā. Sabbepi hi te vaḍḍhisaṅkhātassa āyassa abhāvato apāyāti vuccanti. Tathā dukkhassa gatibhāvato duggati. Sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipāto. Itaro pana –

199. In the ninth, ‘Jālinī’ means like a net. Just as a net is interwoven all around, tangled and confused, so too is craving—thus it is called ‘jālinī’ because it resembles a net. Alternatively, because it stands having overspread the three realms of existence, it is called ‘jālinī,’ as it has its own net-like portion everywhere. ‘Saritaṃ’ means flowing here and there, wandering and remaining. ‘Visaṭaṃ’ means spread out, scattered. ‘Visattikaṃ’ means that which, being spread here and there, is clinging, attached, and stuck. Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood through the method explained in such texts as: “Because it has a root of poison, it is ‘visattikā’; because it has a fruit of poison, it is ‘visattikā’.” ‘Uddhasto’ means overthrown. ‘Pariyonaddho’ means enveloped all around. ‘Tantākulakajāto’ means tangled like threads. Just as poorly laid threads, gnawed by mice, become tangled here and there for weavers, making it difficult to align end with end or root with root, saying, “This is the end, this is the root,” so too are beings, enveloped and confused by this craving, unable to straighten their path of escape. ‘Gulāguṇṭhikajāto’ means like a ‘gulāguṇṭhika,’ which is called a weaver’s tangled skein. ‘Gulā’ is a small bird, and some say its nest is also called this. Just as both are tangled, making it difficult to align end with end or root with root, it should be interpreted in the same way as before. ‘Muñjapabbajabhūto’ means having become like muñja grass or pabbaja grass. Just as with a rope made from those grasses by pounding them, if one picks it up where it has fallen when old and decayed, it is difficult to align the end with the end or the root with the root of those grasses, saying, 'This is the end, this is the root'. And yet, it might be possible for an individual to straighten them through personal effort; but, setting aside the Bodhisattas, no other being is capable of breaking through the net of craving by their own nature and making their path of escape straight. Thus this world, enveloped by the net of craving, does not escape from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the downfall, and saṃsāra. Therein, ‘apāya’ refers to hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, and the realm of asuras. Indeed, all of them are called ‘apāya’ because of the absence of that increase which is designated as growth. Similarly, ‘duggati’ (bad destination) is so called because it is a destination of suffering. ‘Vinipāta’ (downfall) is so called because it is a fall from the accumulation of happiness. As for the other—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccati.

The sequence of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, ongoing and unbroken, is called saṃsāra.

Taṃ sabbaṃ nātivattati nātikkamati, atha kho cutito paṭisandhiṃ paṭisandhito cutinti evaṃ punappunaṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo gaṇhamāno tīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu navasu sattāvāsesu mahāsamudde vātakkhittanāvā viya yante yuttagoṇo viya ca paribbhamatiyeva.

One does not pass beyond, does not transcend all that. Rather, from death to rebirth-linking, from rebirth-linking to death, thus again and again taking up death and rebirth-linking, one wanders on in the three existences, the four modes of generation, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, just like a ship tossed by the wind on the great ocean and like an ox yoked to a machine.

Ajjhattikassa upādāyāti ajjhattikaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Idañhi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Bāhirassa upādāyāti bāhiraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya, idampi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Asmīti, bhikkhave, satīti, bhikkhave, yadetaṃ ajjhattaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena samūhaggāhato asmīti hoti, tasmiṃ satīti attho. Itthasmīti hotītiādīsu pana evaṃ samūhato ahanti gahaṇe sati tato anupanidhāya [M 2.0387] ca upanidhāya cāti [V 2.0383] dvidhā gahaṇaṃ hoti. Tattha anupanidhāyāti aññaṃ ākāraṃ anupagamma [P 3.0207] sakabhāvameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā itthasmīti hoti, khattiyādīsu idaṃpakāro ahanti evaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena hotīti attho. Idaṃ tāva anupanidhāya gahaṇaṃ. Upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti samato ca asamato ca. Taṃ dassetuṃ evaṃsmīti aññathāsmīti ca vuttaṃ. Tattha evaṃsmīti idaṃ samato upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ, yathāyaṃ khattiyo yathāyaṃ brāhmaṇo, evamahampīti attho. Aññathāsmīti idaṃ pana asamato gahaṇaṃ, yathāyaṃ khattiyo yathāyaṃ brāhmaṇo, tato aññathā ahaṃ, hīno vā adhiko vāti attho. Imāni tāva paccuppannavasena cattāri taṇhāvicaritāni.

As for 'with reference to the internal': it means with reference to the internal five aggregates. Indeed, this is a genitive case in the sense of the object. As for 'with reference to the external': it means with reference to the external five aggregates; this too is a genitive case in the sense of the object. As for 'Monks, when there is..., "I am"': O monks, the meaning is: when there is that collective grasping with reference to the internal five aggregates by way of craving, conceit, and views, [the thought] 'I am' occurs. 'When that exists' is the meaning. Furthermore, in such cases as 'I am thus', when there is such a collective grasping of 'I am', this grasping is twofold: without comparison and with comparison. Therein, 'without comparison' means that without resorting to another mode, taking only one's own nature as the object, [the thought] 'I am thus' occurs. The meaning is: among khattiyas and so on, [the thought] 'I am of this kind' occurs by way of craving, conceit, and views. This, in the first place, is grasping without comparison. Grasping with comparison, however, is twofold: as equal and as unequal. To show this, 'I am thus' and 'I am otherwise' are stated. Therein, 'I am thus' is grasping by comparing as equal; the meaning is: 'Just as this one is a khattiya, just as this one is a brahmin, so too am I.' 'I am otherwise', however, is grasping by comparing as unequal; the meaning is: 'Just as this one is a khattiya, just as this one is a brahmin, I am otherwise than that—inferior or superior.' These, in the first place, are the four roamings of craving with respect to the present.

Asasmīti satasmīti imāni pana dve yasmā atthīti asaṃ, niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sīdatīti sataṃ, aniccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā sassatucchedavasena vuttānīti veditabbāni. Ito parāni santi evamādīni cattāri saṃsayaparivitakkavasena vuttāni. Santi hotīti evamādīsu ahaṃ siyanti hotīti evamattho veditabbo. Adhippāyo panettha purimacatukke vuttanayeneva gahetabbo. Apihaṃ santiādīni pana cattāri api nāma ahaṃ bhaveyyanti evaṃ patthanākappanavasena vuttāni. Tānipi purimacatukke vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Bhavissantiādīni [P 3.0208] pana cattāri anāgatavasena vuttāni. Tesampi purimacatukke vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Evamete –

As for 'I am permanent' and 'I am perishable'—these two terms: because it 'is' (atthi), it is called 'asa'; this is a designation for the permanent.
